# Qualitative Badminton Player Analysis

**Status:** Completed

In this group project carried out with Anannya Popat (@Anannyap7), the aim is to take a professional badminton match video as an input and predict the most probable space on the court where the shot will be hit by the player on the near side of the court. This is done by considering the positions of the players relative to each other and their body pose at the point-of-contact with the shuttle. Efficient use of Computer Vision ensures that this model is immune to subtle camera angle changes that are prominent across different tournaments with slight change of parameters in the setup stage. (More on this in the process explanation further!)

# Why this project?

The inspiration for the project stems from my deep interest in badminton. Unfortunately, not a lot of technological support can be seen in badminton to the extent seen in sports like tennis and cricket. With this project, we have two major goals:

Helping aspiring badminton players to use the model as a guide for their own matches to get a most-likely shot placement that would have been done by a professional badminton player at the point-of-contact with the shuttle in a particular position on the court.

Enhancing user viewing experience. Greater inclusion of AI tools in sports makes it more appealing for the audience watching which subsequently helps the sport to grow.

# Process Walkthrough

## 1. Court Line Detection

The task here is to detect the boundaries of the court to get the court corner coordinates. This is required so that all the processing and prediction going forward is with respect to relative positions of the players on the court, and not the frame. This is required because the differences in camera angles across different tournaments will change the players' position even if they are standing at the exact same position on the court, which is bound to give inaccurate results.

**Image Binarization**: The video frame is binarized using Binary Threshold to highlight the white lines of the court and remove as much of the surroundings as possible.

**Drawing Hough Lines**: Next, Hough Lines are drawn over all the edges. The vertical and horizontal ones are filtered and we craft a function to extract the lines we need using length of the lines as the constraint. This is the parameter that has to be tweaked for a new tournament match in order to extract the border lines for new tournament matches.

[![](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/53689018/202634282-2b7ee279-0fa7-4529-89c4-9ba711b8a1db.png)](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/53689018/202634282-2b7ee279-0fa7-4529-89c4-9ba711b8a1db.png)

![](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/53689018/202634282-2b7ee279-0fa7-4529-89c4-9ba711b8a1db.png)

[![](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/53689018/202634363-9f669a53-6b5e-4ff1-89d0-41c729bae77c.png)](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/53689018/202634363-9f669a53-6b5e-4ff1-89d0-41c729bae77c.png)

![](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/53689018/202634363-9f669a53-6b5e-4ff1-89d0-41c729bae77c.png)

[![](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/53689018/202634418-2c7a6db5-e75f-4800-9579-e43291753680.png)](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/53689018/202634418-2c7a6db5-e75f-4800-9579-e43291753680.png)

![](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/53689018/202634418-2c7a6db5-e75f-4800-9579-e43291753680.png)

## 2. Player Detection

It is crucial to detect the player positions on the court as it's one of the most important parameters for predicting shot direction (if we plan to implement it in the future) in most cases. For this purpose, we tried using three methods for object detection:

### 2.1 Automatic Color Detection

Particle Filter works by tracking RGB values of a target pixel. To ensure that the script picks up the target color for any particular match, we automated the color detection of the target by the following means:

[![](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/53689018/203215591-b1cdfbb7-8997-4f14-8b2a-c5072c8b6cb8.png)](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/53689018/203215591-b1cdfbb7-8997-4f14-8b2a-c5072c8b6cb8.png)

![](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/53689018/203215591-b1cdfbb7-8997-4f14-8b2a-c5072c8b6cb8.png)

### 2.2 Replay Detection using CNN

While making our particle filter script, we noticed the script completely crashing whenever a close-up replay frame was encountered. We're also only interested in the over-the-court camera angle rather than the close-ups. For this purpose, we developed a CNN model to classify a frame into a "play" or "non" play frame. The frame IDs for a non-play frame are stored in a textfile which is referenced by the algorithm in section 2.3. Figures below show "non-play" and "play" frames.

[![](https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/59221653/239442355-65ceb0b4-d37a-4bc0-8097-8457026f19d7.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9..l6wsvtwQqaIucjL-EEMZPSanYkIkajd_a6uAAlLuWak)](https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/59221653/239442355-65ceb0b4-d37a-4bc0-8097-8457026f19d7.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9..l6wsvtwQqaIucjL-EEMZPSanYkIkajd_a6uAAlLuWak)
[![](https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/59221653/239442519-83fd11e9-afee-49e2-8211-1b651a9f6fc7.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9..zPlHheS3O5wWX-2v_Etf7zNewyJ9ZQEYzYcdNHH_BV8)](https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/59221653/239442519-83fd11e9-afee-49e2-8211-1b651a9f6fc7.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9..zPlHheS3O5wWX-2v_Etf7zNewyJ9ZQEYzYcdNHH_BV8)

![](https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/59221653/239442519-83fd11e9-afee-49e2-8211-1b651a9f6fc7.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9..zPlHheS3O5wWX-2v_Etf7zNewyJ9ZQEYzYcdNHH_BV8)

### 2.3 Particle Filter

We won't be talking about how this algorithm works, but rather the configuration unique to our implementation used for particle filter:

Two sets of particles, one for each player

Particles for bottom player spread out in the trapezium-like shape (as seen in the image in the previous section), while particles for upper player spread out in a rectangular region extending slightly outside the court (because the actual body of the player appears outside the court coordinates)

For each frame in the video, draw pure black lines on the vertical court boundaries to avoid particles from converging on the court boundaries in case the player jersey color is similar to that of the court boundaries.

For each frame, check if that frame id has been identified as a replay frame (done in section 2.2). If yes, re-initialize particles and pause object tracking till a "play" frame is encountered again.

[![](https://github.com/ChaosAdmStudent/badminton-shot-prediction/raw/main/demos/ParticleFilterDemo.gif)](https://github.com/ChaosAdmStudent/badminton-shot-prediction/blob/main/demos/ParticleFilterDemo.gif)

![](https://github.com/ChaosAdmStudent/badminton-shot-prediction/raw/main/demos/ParticleFilterDemo.gif)

## 3. Player Stroke Detection

Another important component of this project is to predict the kind of stroke/shot played by the players. Here, we have considered 3 primary types of shots for demonstration purposes, namely, 'net-drop return', 'smash' and 'defense'. In order to predict these shots, we have manually collected the training data by extracting the frames where these shots occur and labeling them. After this, the training data is passed through a multi-class classifier and a stroke detection is made using an Artificial Neural Network model like CNN. The **accuracy** of this model is currently around **81%**, which can be improved upon by expanding the dataset manually.

Convolutional Neural Networks architecture of the proposed system is given below:

[![](https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/59221653/239447370-d86df4bb-b3c1-4ee7-b58b-147eb3f7af71.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9..qSJl5ORL9aEohJP2O_KkjsbO6ng8r2bYnmzrOejUYkI)](https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/59221653/239447370-d86df4bb-b3c1-4ee7-b58b-147eb3f7af71.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9..qSJl5ORL9aEohJP2O_KkjsbO6ng8r2bYnmzrOejUYkI)

![](https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/59221653/239447370-d86df4bb-b3c1-4ee7-b58b-147eb3f7af71.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9..qSJl5ORL9aEohJP2O_KkjsbO6ng8r2bYnmzrOejUYkI)

The types of strokes predicted (net-drop return, smash and defense) using the proposed CNN model are as follows:

[![](https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/59221653/239443479-a18bddd4-56fd-4712-97f1-35efbb7e0439.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9..fC9nG176PA1OK0U08Up7ryOhOWjAw_eIgXiwXEQPLtk)](https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/59221653/239443479-a18bddd4-56fd-4712-97f1-35efbb7e0439.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9..fC9nG176PA1OK0U08Up7ryOhOWjAw_eIgXiwXEQPLtk)

[![](https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/59221653/239444062-d6352f6a-07c8-4ef2-acc8-4b1d3f89fb07.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9..LoLlL3aZM1B7eUVJBbTcmZupZHT6YAEH8yR35Oa76vo)](https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/59221653/239444062-d6352f6a-07c8-4ef2-acc8-4b1d3f89fb07.png?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9..LoLlL3aZM1B7eUVJBbTcmZupZHT6YAEH8yR35Oa76vo)

args.summary:
This GitHub repository, "Qualitative Badminton Player Analysis" by @lgupta-mle (completed as a group project with Anannya Popat @Anannyap7), presents a Computer Vision system that takes a professional badminton match video as input and predicts the most probable court location where a shot will be hit by the near-side player. The prediction is based on players' relative positions and body pose at the point-of-contact with the shuttle. The approach uses Computer Vision to remain immune to subtle camera angle changes across different tournaments.

The project's motivation is two-fold: (1) helping aspiring badminton players use the model as a guide for shot placement at the point-of-contact, and (2) enhancing user viewing experience by integrating AI tools into badminton (a sport with less technological support compared to tennis and cricket).

The process consists of four main steps:
1. **Court Line Detection**: Detects court boundaries via image binarization using Binary Threshold to highlight white lines, then draws Hough Lines to extract border lines (using line length as a constraint parameter that must be tuned per tournament).
2. **Player Detection**: Uses three methods — automatic color detection (automating target pixel RGB color detection for particle filter), replay detection using a CNN (classifying frames as "play" vs "non-play" to handle close-up replay frames that crash the particle filter), and a Particle Filter with two sets of particles (one per player), with trapezium-shaped spread for the bottom player and rectangular spread extending outside the court for the upper player.
3. **Player Stroke Detection**: Predicts three shot types — 'net-drop return', 'smash', and 'defense' — using a CNN-based multi-class classifier trained on manually collected and labeled frame data. Current model accuracy is approximately 81%, improvable with a larger dataset.
4. **Pose Estimation using OpenPose**: Defines 19 individual body parts with paired connections, using a predefined TensorFlow model to generate a graph of lines and points indicating each joint connection.

The repository contains 64 commits and includes notebooks for court line detection, player detection using particle filter, replay frame detection using CNN, pose estimation using OpenPose, and player stroke detection, along with demos and manual folders.

Improving Tennis Court Line Detection with Machine Learning

Share this on:

Improving Tennis Court Line Detection with Machine Learning

12:24

![Tennis court with ball prints](https://www.ml6.eu/hs-fs/hubfs/Imported%20sitepage%20images/646c696569e82b23056f0eff_1*V2FLKas2Lmdyaa8z6jkBUg.png?width=700&height=427&name=646c696569e82b23056f0eff_1*V2FLKas2Lmdyaa8z6jkBUg.png)Detecting the lines of a tennis court

Tennis is a sport played all over the world and a lot of single camera video streams are broadly available. All these streams contain information that could be turned into structured stats about games and players. Watching a tennis game, you could enrich the view automatically with numbers of serves through the middle or in the corners, how deep the ball is being played, preferences for left or right, depending on where the player is positioned... The list of insights you can extract from converting these video streams into structured data is huge.

Before getting any stats, the analysis of these video streams needs to be broken down into several tasks:

* detection of the court (lines) and the net
* detection of the players and their pose
* detection and tracking of the ball
* player shot detection

This idea formed the base of my internship at ML6. Many thanks to the team for their help and especially to [Jules](https://medium.com/@jules.talloen) for being a great mentor. For my internship, we decided to start with the detection of the court lines

Every tennis fan knows that the Hawk-Eye system is capable of doing line (and ball) detection with very high precision using six or more high speed camera’s from different angles of the court.

![Ball print animation](https://www.ml6.eu/hs-fs/hubfs/Imported%20sitepage%20images/Ball%20print%20animation.gif?width=700&height=367&name=Ball%20print%20animation.gif)Hawk-Eye in action

We however want to perform the task with the standard video streams of one fixed camera and be able to make near real time predictions.

## Related Work and Inspiration

It is not the first time that somebody tries to detect a sports field. Before deciding on our approach we had a look at the following related work.

In the earlier days the task was mostly tackled with a symbolic AI approach following a similar pattern to detect the boundaries of the tennis court. At first, some technique is used to extract the lines from the frame. Hough line transformations are a great fit for purpose. A detailed explanation of Hough transformations and their use in OpenCV can be found [here](https://medium.com/@tomasz.kacmajor/hough-lines-transform-explained-645feda072ab). The next step is to find out which of these lines are the outer court lines. By taking the intersections of 4 of the found lines, you can determine the transformation matrix (also called the homography) that projects a reference tennis court onto the 4 line intersections in the frame. Using this matrix, you can project the reference court on the frame and then count the overlaps between the line pixels in the frame and the projected reference court lines. By repeating this process for all possible found line intersections, we can find the best overlap which theoretically should be the outer court lines.

One can also combine a lightweight CNN with a Hough layer, which is in detail described in [this paper](https://arxiv.org/ftp/arxiv/papers/2008/2008.08884.pdf). Similar work can be found in [LSDNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.04642) where a classical Line Segment Detector is combined with a lightweight CNN.

Other sports often have moving cameras, only showing part of the field. Defining a key point grid on the field has proven to give good results for this particular use case. This [paper](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/WACV2021/papers/Nie_A_Robust_and_Efficient_Framework_for_Sports-Field_Registration_WACV_2021_paper.pdf) details this approach.

Let’s first see how well the symbolic approach can reach the goals of doing near real time line detection on different courts. Secondly, let’s investigate if transfer learning on a trained model for classification can learn to predict the key points at the court line intersections. To conclude, we see if performance can be further improved by combining the two approaches.

## Symbolic AI Approach (Hough transform / Homography)

Before diving into transfer learning, we have a look at how far we could get with a symbolic AI approach.

As described above, the high level steps are:

* Preprocess the image for Hough line detection
* Detect the lines and categorize the lines into horizontal and vertical lines
* Try to find the lines which best fit the tennis court. That can be done by determining how well a projection of the lines of a reference court overlap with the a binary image of the frame (assuming white pixels for the court lines in the binary image). To determine how one plane can be projected onto another plane, you can calculate the projection matrix (also called the [homography](https://docs.opencv.org/4.x/d9/dab/tutorial_homography.html) matrix) based on 4 known points from the first plane and 4 known points on the projected plane. So by taking the 4 intersection points of the reference court lines and the 4 intersection points of 2 horizontal found lines and 2 vertical found lines, the homography matrix can be determined that projects the reference court on the frame. Next step is to perform the [warp perspective](https://docs.opencv.org/4.x/da/d54/group__imgproc__transform.html#gaf73673a7e8e18ec6963e3774e6a94b87) of the reference court lines using this homography matrix and count the hits (overlaps between a reference court line pixel and a white pixel of the binary image of the frame) and misses with the binary image of the frame. More hits and fewer losses are an indication of the likelihood that these found lines are the court lines. This is repeated for all the found combinations of horizontal and vertical line pairs to determine the best matching lines.

The preprocessing step is very important as this will determine how good the Hough transformation can extract the lines.

![Dark tennis court with fine lines](https://www.ml6.eu/hs-fs/hubfs/Imported%20sitepage%20images/Tennis%20court%20after%20preprocessing.png?width=700&height=455&name=Tennis%20court%20after%20preprocessing.png)Tennis court after preprocessing

Starting from a good preprocessed image, the results are very accurate:

![Hough lines (green) drawn over the original image](https://www.ml6.eu/hs-fs/hubfs/Imported%20sitepage%20images/Hough%20lines%20(green)%20drawn%20over%20the%20original%20image.png?width=700&height=476&name=Hough%20lines%20(green)%20drawn%20over%20the%20original%20image.png)Hough lines (green) drawn over the original image

While giving good results for some courts, it is difficult to generalize this approach for all types of courts. Another downside is that the iterative process of determining the homography, creating the warp perspective and calculating the hits and misses is slow and resource-intensive.

![Tennis court animation with red lines](https://www.ml6.eu/hs-fs/hubfs/Imported%20sitepage%20images/Tennis%20court%20animation%20with%20red%20lines.gif?width=700&height=394&name=Tennis%20court%20animation%20with%20red%20lines.gif)Detection of lines of a tennis court with Hough transform (good)

![Tennis court animation line detection bad example](https://www.ml6.eu/hs-fs/hubfs/Imported%20sitepage%20images/Tennis%20court%20animation%20red%20lines%20bad%20example.gif?width=700&height=393&name=Tennis%20court%20animation%20red%20lines%20bad%20example.gif)Detection of lines of a tennis court with Hough transform (bad)

## AI Approach: CNN Model for Keypoint Detection

The basic idea is to take a relatively simple existing Computer Vision backbone for classification and put a custom head on it to determine 16 key points at the line intersections of the tennis court.

![Example tennis court key points](https://www.ml6.eu/hs-fs/hubfs/Imported%20sitepage%20images/Example%20tennis%20court%20key%20points.png?width=400&height=787&name=Example%20tennis%20court%20key%20points.png)16 key points of a tennis court

We start with a ResNet50v2 backbone (Keras application) and experiment with a full CNN head and a Fully Connected Network head. The following parameters provide the best results with a ResNet50v2 backbone:

![ResNet50v2 backbone results example](https://www.ml6.eu/hs-fs/hubfs/Imported%20sitepage%20images/ResNet50v2%20backbone%20results%20example.png?width=700&height=365&name=ResNet50v2%20backbone%20results%20example.png)Result with best parameters for ResNet50v2 backbone

The predictions (blue dots) are still quite off but we learned that

* this approach is more robust than the symbolic approach
* Data augmentation is important for making the model more robust
* A full CNN head leads to better results than a fully connected head
* MAE loss provided better results than MSE
* Our backbone is not expressive enough (even when trying to overfit)
* Our dataset needs to be larger and more diverse

To increase our dataset, we use the [OpenCV Annotation Tool](https://www.cvat.ai/) which has a great interface to label data and export it to — among others — COCO key point format. A bonus is that it also support interpolation so you only have to label the key frames.

Continuing the learning and tuning with different backends keeping in mind near real time inference speed, the results improved considerably

![EfficientNetV2Small backend results](https://www.ml6.eu/hs-fs/hubfs/Imported%20sitepage%20images/EfficientNetV2Small%20backend%20results.png?width=700&height=247&name=EfficientNetV2Small%20backend%20results.png)EfficientNetV2Small backend performs best

We still see that the predictions (blue dots) are a bit off target. In order to look for patterns in the learned model, we project the reference court (black lines) with the homography of the outer predicted key points.

![Projected reference court](https://www.ml6.eu/hs-fs/hubfs/Imported%20sitepage%20images/Projected%20reference%20court.png?width=700&height=509&name=Projected%20reference%20court.png)Projected reference court (black lines) exactly on predicted key points (blue dots)

This shows that the trained model finds the relations between the line intersections with very high accuracy (predicted blue dots are exactly on the intersections of the black lines). Are we maybe putting to much emphasize on the relationship between the points in our model?

So we try to only predict the 4 outer key points of the court. Cutting a long story short, the trained models on the 4 key points produced very similar results as the 16 key points.

During training and experiments, a few other backbones were tried as well and especially MobileNetv3Small performed much better than the other backbones.

So switching back to the 16 key point output, similar improvements were to be expected with the new backbone, MobileNetv3Small, and indeed the Mean Pixel Error reduced by more than 50% compared to the previously best results with EfficientNetV2Small.

This is a pretty good result but we want to improve and decided to post process the model using a variation of the symbolic approach from the previous section.

## Post-processing

The idea is to take a rectangular area around every predicted key point of the original image and determine in every rectangle the lines and their intersection point.

![Small area around the predicted key points](https://www.ml6.eu/hs-fs/hubfs/Imported%20sitepage%20images/Small%20area%20around%20the%20predicted%20key%20points.png?width=400&height=673&name=Small%20area%20around%20the%20predicted%20key%20points.png)Small area around the predicted key points

If we crop a standard area around the predicted key points (red crosses), the zoomed in starting point for the post-processing looks like this:

![Small area around the predicted key points (red cross)](https://www.ml6.eu/hs-fs/hubfs/Imported%20sitepage%20images/Small%20area%20around%20the%20predicted%20key%20points%20(red%20cross).png?width=700&height=579&name=Small%20area%20around%20the%20predicted%20key%20points%20(red%20cross).png)Small area around the predicted key points (red cross)

You can see that determining the line intersection can be more complicated through players (15), unclear lines (5). It will also be hard to work with the key points at the net (8, 9).

The line intersection detection algorithm is as described in the symbolic AI section:

Prepare the image for Hough transformation

* Reduce the # of colors and remove the most dominant colors
* Thicken the lines of the images far away from the camera (1, 2, 3, 4)
* Thin the lines with the [Zhang Suen algorithm](https://rstudio-pubs-static.s3.amazonaws.com/302782_e337cfbc5ad24922bae96ca5977f4da8.html)

![Preprocessing of the image example](https://www.ml6.eu/hs-fs/hubfs/Imported%20sitepage%20images/Preprocessing%20of%20the%20image%20example.png?width=600&height=265&name=Preprocessing%20of%20the%20image%20example.png)Preprocessing of the image

* Performing the Hough transformation, selecting the most relevant lines and determine their intersection

![Intersecting lines after Hough transform and line selection](https://www.ml6.eu/hs-fs/hubfs/Imported%20sitepage%20images/Intersecting%20lines%20after%20Hough%20transform%20and%20line%20selection.png?width=300&height=266&name=Intersecting%20lines%20after%20Hough%20transform%20and%20line%20selection.png)Intersecting lines after Hough transform and line selection

This results in the following improvements:

![Clear improvement in top baseline key points example before after](https://www.ml6.eu/hs-fs/hubfs/Imported%20sitepage%20images/Clear%20improvement%20in%20top%20baseline%20key%20points%20example%20before%20after.png?width=700&height=386&name=Clear%20improvement%20in%20top%20baseline%20key%20points%20example%20before%20after.png)Clear improvement in top baseline key points

Or in the complete image:

![MobileNetV3Small with post-processing](https://www.ml6.eu/hs-fs/hubfs/Imported%20sitepage%20images/MobileNetV3Small%20with%20post-processing.png?width=700&height=375&name=MobileNetV3Small%20with%20post-processing.png)MobileNetV3Small with post-processing

Looking at the before and after post-processing image, the performance is clearly better. Sometimes however, post-processing can be a bit of because the lines are not accurately extracted. Comparing the mean absolute error now shows very similar results with or without post-processing. This can probably be improved by an additional verification step that only take post-processing into account when the calculated post-processing intersection is on a white pixel or matches a small filter specific for the key point (for example an L-shaped filter for the left lower baseline). This last verification step is not tested yet.

Performance was good, what about inference speed?

On a 8 core Intel i9 2.3 GHz processor with GPU NVIDIA T2000 4GB, the AI model roughly predicted 100 frames/sec. When including the post-processing, the inference speed dropped to 50 frames/sec. These figures are just indicative without any effort in speed optimalization.

## Conclusion

These are promising results in both performance and inference speed.

We can conclude that our ML model is more robust and faster than our symbolic model.

For the ML model, it is vital to find a backbone with a good balance between performance and inference speed, in our case MobileNetv3Small. For all our tested backbones, Full CNN variants were best as head and MAE as loss function produced better performance. Data augmentation was crucial but make sure that the majority of transformations still make sense for a tennis court. Post-processing can further increase the performance as seen in some samples but you need to make sure it generalizes well.

With a little extra investment in post-processing, adding some temporal smoothing (there will only be slight changes in camera movement between frames) and giving some love to inference speed optimalisation, this approach is a good candidate for doing near real time court line detection... A first step in automating the stats of a tennis game.

This article is written by Bart Timmermans as part of his internship at ML6 and supervised by Jules Talloen.

[>> Read the blog-post on Medium platform.](https://blog.ml6.eu/improving-tennis-court-line-detection-with-machine-learning-90f82dccdf1d)

###### The answers you've been looking for

## Frequently asked questions

1. Without specialized setups like Hawk-Eye, it's hard to apply high-precision line detection in real time using only standard video—requiring robust ML methods.
2. They used Hough transforms to detect lines, built a homography projection, and matched overlaps to identify court boundaries—but it struggled to generalize efficiently.
3. They used CNN-based keypoint detection (e.g. ResNet50v2 backbone) to find court line intersections, which proved more robust and scalable.
4. Data augmentation, a full CNN head, MAE loss, a bigger dataset, and using EfficientNetV2Small as the backbone delivered better accuracy and inference speed.
5. Yes—with post-processing (temporal smoothing) and efficient inference tuning, this approach becomes a promising solution for real-time court analytics.

Published March 13, 2023 (updated September 16, 2025), the article explores methods for detecting tennis court lines from standard single-camera video streams to enable automated tennis game statistics (serve locations, ball depth, player positioning, etc.), in contrast to the Hawk-Eye system which requires six or more high-speed cameras.

The article compares two approaches:
1. **Symbolic AI Approach** (Hough transform / Homography): Preprocesses the image, detects lines via Hough transformations, categorizes lines as horizontal/vertical, then finds the best court match by projecting a reference court via homography and counting pixel overlaps. This works well on some courts but struggles to generalize across court types and is slow/resource-intensive due to iterative processing.

2. **CNN Keypoint Detection Approach**: Uses a computer vision backbone with a custom head to predict 16 key points at tennis court line intersections. Key findings from experiments:

3. **Post-processing**: Combines the CNN model with the symbolic approach by cropping rectangular areas around each predicted key point, preprocessing (reducing colors, thickening/thinning lines via Zhang Suen algorithm), then using Hough transformations to find precise line intersections. **Performance**: On an 8-core Intel i9 2.3 GHz processor with NVIDIA T2000 4GB GPU, the AI model predicted roughly 100 frames/sec; with post-processing it dropped to 50 frames/sec.

**Conclusions**: The ML model is more robust and faster than the symbolic model. A good backbone balancing performance and speed (MobileNetv3Small) is vital. # Benchmarking Badminton Action Recognition with a New Fine-Grained Dataset

###### Abstract.

In the dynamic and evolving field of computer vision, action recognition has become a key focus, especially with the advent of sophisticated methodologies like Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Convolutional 3D, Transformer and spatial-temporal feature fusion. These technologies have shown promising results on well-established benchmarks but face unique challenges in real-world applications, particularly in sports analysis, where the precise decomposition of activities and the distinction of subtly different actions are crucial. Existing datasets like UCF101, HMDB51, and Kinetics have offered a diverse range of video data for various scenarios. However, there’s an increasing need for fine-grained video datasets that capture detailed categorizations and nuances within broader action categories. In this paper, we introduce the VideoBadminton dataset, which is derived from high-quality badminton footage. Through an exhaustive evaluation of leading methodologies on this dataset, this study aims to advance the field of action recognition, particularly in badminton sports. The introduction of VideoBadminton could not only serve for badminton action recognition but also provide a dataset for recognizing fine-grained actions. The insights gained from these evaluations are expected to catalyze further research in action comprehension, especially within sports contexts.

![Refer to caption](2403.12385v2/videobadminton_data_collection_workflow.png)

## 1. Introduction

Action recognition has become a key focus within the computer vision community, with methodologies leveraging Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) ([LeCun et al. 1989](#bib.bib26)), Long Short-Term Memory networks (LSTMs) ([Hochreiter and
Schmidhuber 1997](#bib.bib16)), and the integration of spatial-temporal features ([Karpathy et al. 2014a](#bib.bib21)) showing notable success on established benchmarks. Nonetheless, real-world applications, particularly in sports analysis, introduce challenges not present in controlled environments ([Poppe 2010](#bib.bib31)). These include decomposing activities into distinct phases and distinguishing between different actions ([Soomro
et al. 2012](#bib.bib39)).

The last decade has seen a surge in the development and use of video datasets that have been fundamental to the progression of the computer vision field. Landmark datasets such as UCF101 ([Soomro
et al. 2012](#bib.bib39)), HMDB51 ([Kuehne et al. 2011](#bib.bib25)) and Kinetics ([Kay
et al. 2017](#bib.bib23)) have provided a wealth of video data across a multitude of scenarios and actions. These datasets have been pivotal in advancing the state-of-the-art, inspiring new methodologies ([Simonyan and
Zisserman 2014](#bib.bib38)), and enhancing existing ones ([Szegedy et al. 2015](#bib.bib40)). The diverse and extensive content of these datasets has been crucial in training robust models capable of action recognition in various settings and conditions.

Moreover, there has been a shift towards fine-grained video datasets, which aim to capture detailed categorizations within broader action classes, significant in practical applications where the distinction between minor action variations is substantial ([Gkioxari and
Malik 2015](#bib.bib13)).

Alongside the evolution of video datasets, deep learning methodologies for action recognition have rapidly advanced. CNNs and RNNs, in particular, have taken the lead, utilizing extensive data to extract complex spatial and temporal features from videos ([Donahue et al. 2015](#bib.bib9)). Innovative approaches such as two-stream CNNs ([Simonyan and
Zisserman 2014](#bib.bib38)) and 3D CNNs ([Ji
et al. 2013](#bib.bib18)), along with the combination of CNNs with LSTMs ([Donahue et al. 2015](#bib.bib9)) or Transformers ([Vaswani et al. 2017](#bib.bib45)), have set new standards in interpreting video sequences.

To contribute to this field, we introduce VideoBadminton, an innovative dataset curated from high-quality badminton footage. This dataset provides diversity and a finer level of action categorization and requires algorithms that can decode temporal patterns and subtle action differences within continuous activity. This paper presents a comprehensive evaluation of prominent methodologies using the VideoBadminton dataset, offering insights that are expected to stimulate further research in action recognition, particularly in the sports domain.

Our primary contributions are:

We introduce VideoBadminton, a dataset specifically designed for badminton action recognition which is a comprehensive collection of player movements and stroke techniques.

We perform a detailed and systematic evaluation of contemporary state-of-the-art video recognition architectures. This evaluation is not merely an assessment of their performance metrics but also an exploration of their applicability and efficacy in the nuanced context of badminton action recognition.

## 2. Related works

### 2.1. Video dataset for action recognition

In the domain of action recognition, there has been a substantial enhancement in the richness, quality, and variety of datasets for video classification tasks. Seminal datasets such as HMDB51 ([Kuehne et al. 2011](#bib.bib25)) and UCF101 ([Soomro
et al. 2012](#bib.bib39)) were among the first to augment the variety of action categories and the volume of video content, laying the groundwork for training deep learning models. More recently, the advent of expansive datasets like THUMOS14 ([Jiang et al. 2014](#bib.bib19)), Sports-1M ([Karpathy et al. 2014b](#bib.bib22)), Kinetics ([Kay
et al. 2017](#bib.bib23)), and Moments in Time ([Monfort
et al. 2019](#bib.bib29)) have significantly contributed to the advancement of action recognition methodologies. Despite these developments, the primary focus of these datasets remains on coarse-grained recognition. The classification boundaries defined by these datasets are efficient in identifying clear-cut positive instances but deficient in distinguishing between closely related negative actions, which are prevalent in practical settings. Additionally, the entanglement of background context with the actions during the learning process remains a persistent challenge.

### 2.2. Fine-grained video dataset for action recognition

Efforts have been undertaken to construct datasets geared toward fine-grained action recognition. Notably, the Breakfast and MPII-Cooking 2 ([Rohrbach et al. 2012](#bib.bib34)) datasets offer annotations for individual stages of various cooking processes. In the context of the Breakfast dataset, coarse actions (e.g., Juice) are dissected into granular action units (e.g., cut orange), while in MPII-Cooking 2, the verbal segments are characterized as fine-grained categories (e.g., cut as an element of the action cutting onion). The Something-Something ([Goyal et al. 2017](#bib.bib14)) dataset incorporates 147 categories of everyday human-object interactions, encompassing actions such as lowering an object and retrieving something from a location. The Diving48 ([Kanojia
et al. 2019](#bib.bib20)) dataset is established on 48 intricate diving actions, wherein the labels are amalgamations of four attributes, such as back+15som+15twis+free.

While there have been prior efforts ([Davar et al. 2011](#bib.bib8)), ([Teng and
Paramesran 2011](#bib.bib41)), ([Careelmont 2013](#bib.bib3)), ([Ting
et al. 2014](#bib.bib42)), ([Ramasinghe et al. 2014](#bib.bib32)), ([Shan
et al. 2015](#bib.bib35)),
  
 ([Ting
et al. 2016](#bib.bib43)), ([Chu and Situmeang 2017](#bib.bib5)), ([Weeratunga et al. 2017](#bib.bib47)) in badminton dataset creation, most have predominantly focused on image-level data rather than video. Notably, two research projects have contributed to establishing badminton video datasets, each with unique features and applications.

The Badminton Olympic dataset, as detailed in ([Ghosh
et al. 2018](#bib.bib12)), comprises 10 videos sourced from YouTube, each showcasing individual badminton matches with an average duration of one hour. This dataset is enriched with diverse annotations, including: 1. Bounding boxes marking player positions in 1,500 frames. 2. Notations of 751 instances where players score points. 3. Comprehensive annotations delineating time boundaries and stroke labels across 12 stroke categories, such as serves and lobs. ShuttleNet ([Wang
et al. 2022](#bib.bib46)) represents a more recent contribution, encompassing 43,191 meticulously selected video clips. Each clip in this dataset focuses on a particular stroke from 10 distinct categories, including smashes, pushes, and lobs. ShuttleNet extends its utility beyond mere action recognition; it is tailored for stroke prediction, where the model is trained to anticipate the next stroke based on the sequence of preceding strokes during a rally.

Our work, VideoBadminton, however, surpasses these datasets in scope and depth. It incorporates 18 categories of badminton actions, with a total of 7,822 clips spanning 145 minutes of self-recorded footage. It is particularly valuable for research in fine-grained action recognition, offering a rich data source for training and evaluating state-of-the-art video recognition models focusing on the nuanced movements and strokes found in badminton. Additionally, VideoBadminton includes detailed annotations of player locations and the trajectory of the shuttle. Given these features, we posit that VideoBadminton currently stands as the most comprehensive dataset for badminton video analysis, setting a new benchmark in the field. ### 2.3. Action recognition models

The field of action recognition has witnessed substantial advancements in recent years, driven by the development of diverse models that leverage the increasing computational power and sophistication of machine learning techniques. Pioneering efforts in this domain have primarily focused on leveraging convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which have proven effective in extracting spatial features from individual frames. Seminal models like the two-stream CNN ([Simonyan and
Zisserman 2014](#bib.bib38)), as proposed by Simonyan and Zisserman, combine spatial and temporal network streams to capture both appearance and motion information, setting a foundation for subsequent innovations.

Building upon this, the integration of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks has been explored to better understand temporal dynamics in video sequences better. These models, such as the work by ([Donahue et al. 2015](#bib.bib9)), aim to capture the temporal evolution of actions, offering a more nuanced understanding compared to frame-based approaches.

More recent developments have seen the emergence of 3D Convolutional Neural Networks (3D CNNs), which directly process spatio-temporal information in video data. ([Carreira and
Zisserman 2017](#bib.bib4))’s introduction of the I3D model, which extends the concept of 2D CNNs to 3D, has been particularly influential in capturing more complex motion patterns.

Furthermore, attention mechanisms and transformer-based models, like the Vision Transformer (ViT) for action recognition, have gained traction. By focusing on salient features in both spatial and temporal dimensions, these models offer promising avenues for enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of action recognition systems.

The landscape of action recognition models is thus characterized by a continuous evolution from basic frame-level feature extraction to complex spatio-temporal and attention-based models, each contributing to the progress of this field towards more accurate and efficient recognition of human actions in videos.

## 3. The VideoBadminton dataset

In this section, we delve into the comprehensive process of constructing the VideoBadminton dataset. This detailed exposition encompasses the phases of data collection, meticulous data cleaning, preprocessing, and the annotation process. To provide a more granular understanding, we will illustrate the annotation tools and offer examples of video samples. In our commitment to fostering research and collaboration in this field, we will make the complete dataset and the associated codes available for research purposes. This initiative aims to facilitate further advancements and explorations in badminton action recognition and related areas.

### 3.1. Row data collection

In our pursuit of accuracy and comprehensiveness within the VideoBadminton dataset, we meticulously curated practice game videos featuring 19 adept players from National Central University’s badminton school team. This cohort included 15 male and 4 female players, each exhibiting a high level of skill closely paralleling professional standards. Their advanced proficiency and tactical prowess in badminton provided a rich reference point for our analytical endeavors. The selection of these players was strategic, enabling us to encapsulate a wide spectrum of badminton actions.

The selected action classes for the badminton dataset aligned with the Badminton World Federation (BWF) standards. These classes are integral for training video recognition models in badminton and include 18 distinct stroke types such as 𝖲𝗁𝗈𝗋𝗍​𝖲𝖾𝗋𝗏𝖾\mathsf{Short~Serve}, 𝖢𝗋𝗈𝗌𝗌−𝖢𝗈𝗎𝗋𝗍​𝖥𝗅𝗂𝗀𝗁𝗍\mathsf{Cross-Court~Flight}, 𝖫𝗂𝖿𝗍\mathsf{Lift}, 𝖳𝖺𝗉​𝖲𝗆𝖺𝗌𝗁\mathsf{Tap~Smash}, 𝖡𝗅𝗈𝖼𝗄\mathsf{Block}, 𝖣𝗋𝗈𝗉​𝖲𝗁𝗈𝗍\mathsf{Drop~Shot}, 𝖯𝗎𝗌𝗁​𝖲𝗁𝗈𝗍\mathsf{Push~Shot}, 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌𝗂𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇𝖺𝗅​𝖲𝗅𝗂𝖼𝖾\mathsf{Transitional~Slice}, 𝖢𝗎𝗍\mathsf{Cut}, 𝖱𝗎𝗌𝗁​𝖲𝗁𝗈𝗍\mathsf{Rush~Shot}, 𝖣𝖾𝖿𝖾𝗇𝗌𝗂𝗏𝖾​𝖢𝗅𝖾𝖺𝗋\mathsf{Defensive~Clear}, 𝖣𝖾𝖿𝖾𝗇𝗌𝗂𝗏𝖾​𝖣𝗋𝗂𝗏𝖾\mathsf{Defensive~Drive}, 𝖢𝗅𝖾𝖺𝗋\mathsf{Clear}, 𝖫𝗈𝗇𝗀​𝖲𝖾𝗋𝗏𝖾\mathsf{Long~Serve}, 𝖲𝗆𝖺𝗌𝗁\mathsf{Smash}, 𝖥𝗅𝖺𝗍​𝖲𝗁𝗈𝗍\mathsf{Flat~Shot}, 𝖱𝖾𝖺𝗋​𝖢𝗈𝗎𝗋𝗍​𝖥𝗅𝖺𝗍​𝖣𝗋𝗂𝗏𝖾\mathsf{Rear~Court~Flat~Drive}, and 𝖲𝗁𝗈𝗋𝗍​𝖥𝗅𝖺𝗍​𝖲𝗁𝗈𝗍\mathsf{Short~Flat~Shot}. ### 3.2. Camera settings

We used a high-quality camera from The Imaging Source during data collection, specifically the model DFK 37AUX273. This camera was equipped with specific parameters to capture detailed video footage of badminton actions. The camera’s resolution was set at 1280\*960 pixels to represent the badminton movements clearly. Operating at a frame rate of 60fps, the DFK 37AUX273 captured the fast-paced movements inherent in badminton, resulting in smooth and high-definition video recordings. The XRGB video format was selected to preserve essential color information during data collection.

Strategic camera placement was considered essential. The camera was positioned approximately 2 meters behind the baseline of the badminton court and elevated to a height of approximately 4.5 meters (see Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.2. Camera settings ‣ 3. The VideoBadminton dataset ‣ Benchmarking Badminton Action Recognition with a New Fine-Grained Dataset")). Tilted at a 30-degree angle, the DFK 37AUX273’s lens offered an optimal field of view, reducing distortions and facilitating precise documentation of the various badminton actions. Utilizing this specific model from The Imaging Source allowed for the accurate capture of the intricate movements and techniques of the players, contributing to the comprehensive and detailed dataset.

### 3.3. Data preprocessing

We used a wide-angle lens and positioned the camera high up to simulate the broadcast camera used in formal games. However, distortion caused by the wide-angle lens can affect the model’s training, resulting in inaccurate court coordinates and deviations in player and shuttlecock positions, leading to errors. This can reduce the availability and accuracy of the data, thereby interfering with the model training results. Therefore, it is necessary to correct the original video. We will use OpenCV to calculate the calibration parameters of the camera used to remove the distortion caused by the lens. The calculation method is to use OpenCV to obtain the 2D coordinates of the chessboard in the 3D world and integrate the information captured from multiple angles of the chessboard image into the calculation, as shown in Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.3. ### 3.4. Human/Expert labeling

Human labeling was a critical aspect of data processing. Five students participated in the labeling process, including a member of National Central University’s badminton team and two from different badminton clubs. Their expertise and experience in the sport ensured accurate identification and labeling of the diverse badminton actions captured in the video data.

The labeled data underwent meticulous review by the head coach of National Central University’s badminton team. The coach diligently examined the annotations, addressing any discrepancies or errors encountered during the labeling process. This rigorous review process ensured the reliability and validity of the labeled data, minimizing potential errors.

### 3.5. Labeling process

We use Shot-By-Shot (S2S^{2}) Labeling introduced in ([Huang
et al. 2022](#bib.bib17)) as our main labeling tool. This tool consists of three parts: recording basic game data, cropping the video for each round, recording the score, and labeling micro-level game data. The interface of S2S^{2} Labeling is shown in Figure [5](#S3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 3.6. Data post-processing ‣ 3. The VideoBadminton dataset ‣ Benchmarking Badminton Action Recognition with a New Fine-Grained Dataset").
The process of labeling a badminton match video involves four stages. The first stage involves obtaining the match video and recording fundamental details about the competition. In the second stage, the beginning, end, and score of each rally are marked. Stage three focuses on pre-processing the video, which includes detecting the shuttlecock’s trajectory, to aid in the microscopic labeling that follows in stage four, where each shot is analyzed in detail.

### 3.6. Data post-processing

Upon completing the data labeling, our research embarked on the task of segmenting the competition’s content, which consisted of two primary areas. First, we addressed video segmenting: the full-length match videos were strategically divided into individual clips corresponding to specific ball types. This segmentation was executed post-data annotation, enhancing its applicability in video categorization or action recognition tasks. The slicing was performed based on FFmpeg, following the use of the Shot-By-Shot (S2S^{2}) Labeling tool, with segmentation guided by the labeled CSV file generated by this tool. File naming followed a convention encapsulating essential details like date, time, ID, start and end timestamps, halves of the game, and types of balls. Second, our data augmentation process filled gaps where some actions were less commonly found in actual gameplay. We enriched the dataset by employing controlled ball-feeding techniques and utilized the previously described camera setup to capture the diversity and complexity of gameplay actions. These combined efforts serve to create a robust and nuanced dataset, vital for our analytical and recognition tasks within the context of the sport.

#### 3.7.1. Entropy of Video Frames

Higher entropy suggests more complex and information-rich frames, whereas lower entropy indicates uniform and less detailed content. Computing the entropy of frames in a video provides insights into the variation and richness of visual information, which is essential in tasks like anomaly detection, content summarization, and activity recognition.

## 4. Methods

The selection of methods for our benchmark is comprehensive and representative of the most popular approaches in current action recognition research. By incorporating a diverse set of methodologies, ranging from video-based deep learning architectures to skeleton-based models, our study covers a wide spectrum of techniques prevalent in the field. Our results provide a holistic and detailed understanding of badminton action recognition.

The inclusion of various types of methods, such as R(2+1)D([Tran et al. 2018](#bib.bib44)), SlowFast([Feichtenhofer et al. 2019](#bib.bib11)), TimeSformer([Bertasius
et al. 2021](#bib.bib2)), Swim([Liu
et al. 2022](#bib.bib28)), and MViT-V2([Li et al. 2022](#bib.bib27)) for their state-of-the-art performance in video-based action recognition, and two skeleton-based methods, ST-GCN([Yan
et al. 2018](#bib.bib48)) and PoseC3D([Duan
et al. 2022](#bib.bib10)), allows us to evaluate and compare different approaches to action recognition. This comparison is particularly valuable in understanding the strengths and weaknesses of each method when applied to the specific challenges presented by badminton action recognition.

### 4.1. "R(2+1)D" spatiotemporal convolutional block

The "R(2+1)D" spatiotemporal convolutional block is an approach that factorizes 3D convolutions into a combination of 2D spatial and 1D temporal convolutions. This method presents two primary advantages: increased model complexity without additional parameters and ease of optimization.
(2+1)D convolutions incorporate an extra nonlinear rectification between the spatial and temporal components. This effectively doubles the number of nonlinearities compared to traditional 3D convolutions, allowing the network to represent more complex functions without increasing the parameter count.
The decomposition of 3D convolutions into separate spatial and temporal operations results in lower training and testing losses. This indicates that the (2+1)D blocks are simpler to optimize than the intertwined spatiotemporal filters in full 3D convolutions.

### 4.2. Spatial Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (ST-GCN)

Spatial-Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (ST-GCN) is for skeleton-based action recognition. The ST-GCN model operates on a spatial-temporal graph of a skeleton sequence, where the body joints are represented as nodes and the natural connections between them are defined as edges. The model uses graph convolutional networks to learn the spatial patterns and temporal convolutional networks to learn the temporal patterns.

The TimeSformer model achieves state-of-the-art results on several action recognition benchmarks, has low training and inference cost, and can be applied to longer video clips.

### 4.4. PoseConv3D

The PoseConv3D proposes a new approach for skeleton-based action recognition. The method involves creating 2D heatmaps for each joint and limb in each video frame, and then stacking these heatmaps along the temporal dimension to create a 3D heatmap volume. The authors then apply 3D convolutional neural networks to this volume to classify the action.

The formula for creating a joint heatmap JJ is:

|  |  |  |  |

| (13) |  | Jk​i​j=e−D​((i,j),jk)22​σj2,J\_{kij}=e^{-\frac{D((i,j),j\_{k})^{2}}{2\sigma\_{j}^{2}}}, |  |

where jkj\_{k} is the k-th joint, DD is the distance from the point (i,j)(i,j) to the joint jkj\_{k}, and σj\sigma\_{j} is a parameter that controls the spread of the Gaussian.

The formula for creating a limb heatmap LL is:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (14) |  | Lk​i​j=e−D​((i,j),s​e​g​[a​k,b​k])22​σl2⋅min⁡(c​ak,c​bk),L\_{kij}=e^{-\frac{D((i,j),seg[ak,bk])^{2}}{2\sigma\_{l}^{2}\cdot\min(ca\_{k},cb\_{k})}}, |  |

where a​kak and b​kbk are the two joints connected by the k-th limb, s​e​g​[a​k,b​k]seg[ak,bk] is the line segment connecting these joints, DD is the distance from the point (i,j)(i,j) to this segment, c​akca\_{k} and c​bkcb\_{k} are the confidence scores of the two joints, and σl\sigma\_{l} is a parameter that controls the spread of the Gaussian.

### 4.5. SlowFast Network

The SlowFast network architecture for video recognition captures both spatial semantics and motion at fine temporal resolution. The Slow pathway operates at a low frame rate and captures spatial semantics, while the Fast pathway operates at a high frame rate and captures motion. The two pathways are fused together to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on major video recognition benchmarks.

Let TT be the number of frames in a video, CC be the number of input channels, and SS be the spatial resolution of the input frames. The SlowFast network takes as input a video tensor of size T×C×S×ST\times C\times S\times S and outputs a classification score for each action class. The Slow pathway operates on a downsampled version of the input tensor, obtained by applying a temporal stride of α\alpha. The Fast pathway operates on the original input tensor, with a temporal stride of β=αk\beta=\frac{\alpha}{k} where kk is an integer. The output of the two pathways is fused together using a lateral connection and a fusion operation, either summation or concatenation. The final output is obtained by applying a fully connected layer to the fused tensor.

### 4.6. Multiscale Vision Transformers (MViTv2)

The Multiscale Vision Transformers (MViTv2) are designed for visual recognition tasks including image classification, object detection, and video classification. The improvements include shift-invariant positional embeddings and a residual pooling connection to compensate for the effect of pooling strides in attention computation. These upgrades lead to significantly better results compared to prior work. The paper also introduces a generic MViT architecture for object detection and video recognition and provides five concrete instantiations of MViTv2 in increasing complexity.

The computation of the attention weights between the query tensor QQ and the key tensor KK, which are then used to weight the values in VV. The softmax function is applied to the dot product of QQ and KTK^{T} divided by the square root of dkd\_{k}. The resulting attention weights are then multiplied by VV to obtain the output of the attention mechanism.

## 5. Empirical Studies

We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of various action recognition methods for badminton videos. We also include a practical study on the most typical action recognition method using MMAction2 ([Contributors 2020](#bib.bib6)). Unless specified otherwise, all training protocols adhere to the original papers. Our primary objective is to gain a deeper understanding of fine-grained actions.

### 5.1. Evaluation metrics

We follow the standard practices ([Duan
et al. 2022](#bib.bib10)) in action recognition to evaluate the performance of models. Our evaluation framework primarily incorporates Top-1 Accuracy and Mean Class Accuracy. These metrics are widely recognized for their effectiveness in assessing model performance in action recognition tasks. Additionally, we include Top-5 Accuracy as an auxiliary metric to offer a more comprehensive comparison across models.

Top-1 Accuracy: This metric, essential in our evaluation, measures the proportion of instances where the model’s highest-confidence prediction aligns with the true label. It directly indicates the model’s precision in accurately identifying the most probable action.

Top-5 Accuracy: As an additional measure, Top-5 Accuracy evaluates whether the true label is among the top five predictions made by the model. This metric provides a broader perspective on the model’s predictive capacity, accommodating a wider array of potential correct predictions.

Mean Class Accuracy: Reflecting the ethos of balanced and equitable model assessment, Mean Class Accuracy calculates the average accuracy across various action categories. This metric is particularly vital for our study as it addresses potential class imbalances and ensures a uniform evaluation standard across all classes, thereby reflecting the model’s overall effectiveness in recognizing diverse badminton actions.

### 5.2. The experimental setup

Following a structured experimental setup, our VideoBadminton dataset was partitioned into training, validation, and test subsets, following an 8:1:1 distribution ratio. The training subset was the foundation for model training, while the validation subset was utilized for hyperparameter optimization. Performance evaluation and results are reported based on the test subset.

Furthermore, to enhance the generalizability of our models and mitigate the risk of overfitting, we incorporated a series of data augmentation techniques. These included random cropping, horizontal flipping, and color jittering - strategies that introduce a degree of variability and robustness into the training process.

## Benchmarking Badminton Action Recognition with a New Fine-Grained Dataset

This paper introduces **VideoBadminton**, a novel fine-grained video dataset for badminton action recognition, and presents a comprehensive benchmark evaluation of state-of-the-art action recognition methods on this dataset.

### Dataset Overview
- **VideoBadminton** contains **7,822 video clips** spanning **145 minutes** of self-recorded footage featuring **18 badminton action classes** aligned with Badminton World Federation (BWF) standards (e.g., Short Serve, Cross-Court Flight, Lift, Tap Smash, Block, Drop Shot, Push Shot, Transitional Slice, Cut, Rush Shot, Defensive Clear, Defensive Drive, Clear, Long Serve, Smash, Flat Shot, Rear Court Flat Drive, Short Flat Shot).
- Data was collected from **19 players** (15 male, 4 female) of National Central University's badminton school team.
- Camera setup: DFK 37AUX273 camera (The Imaging Source), 1280×960 resolution, 60fps, positioned ~2 meters behind the baseline and ~4.5 meters high at a 30-degree tilt, using XRGB video format.
- Data was processed with OpenCV for lens distortion correction, labeled by 5 students (including badminton team members) using the Shot-By-Shot (S²) Labeling tool, and reviewed by the team's head coach.
- The dataset includes annotations of player locations and shuttlecock trajectories.

### Dataset Comparison
VideoBadminton surpasses existing badminton datasets (Badminton Olympic dataset with 10 videos/12 stroke categories, ShuttleNet with 43,191 clips/10 categories) and general fine-grained datasets, positioning itself as the most comprehensive badminton video analysis dataset. It is compared against Kinetics400, Something-Something, MPII-Cooking2, Breakfast, THUMOS14, ActivityNet-1.3, Charades, FineGym-1.1, UCF-sports, Epic-kitchens-100, ADL, J-HMDB, and UCF101-24.

### Methods Evaluated
Seven state-of-the-art action recognition methods were benchmarked:
1. **R(2+1)D** - Factorizes 3D convolutions into 2D spatial + 1D temporal convolutions
2. **ST-GCN** - Spatial-Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (skeleton-based)
3. **TimeSformer** - Transformer-based, uses self-attention without convolutions
4. **PoseC3D** - Skeleton-based using 3D heatmap volumes + 3D CNNs
5. **SlowFast** - Dual-pathway (slow/low frame rate for spatial, fast/high frame rate for motion)
6. **MViT-V2** - Multiscale Vision Transformers with pooling attention and decomposed relative positional embeddings
7. **Swin** - Swin Transformer-based video recognition

### Key Results (VideoBadminton-50: 50 samples/class)
| Method | Top1 Acc | Top5 Acc | Mean Cls Acc |
|--------|----------|----------|--------------|
| ST-GCN | 60.70% | 89.25% | 54.86% |
| PoseC3D | 59.98% | 89.87% | 50.21% |
| Swim | 53.53% | 87.51% | 48.92% |
| TimeSformer | 45.45% | 85.16% | 42.68% |
| R(2+1)D | 40.84% | 77.18% | 35.35% |
| SlowFast | 12.28% | 49.44% | 21.16% |
| MViT-V2 | 12.69% | 21.49% | 5.56% |

**Skeleton-based methods (ST-GCN and PoseC3D) outperformed all video-based methods**, indicating their particular suitability for fine-grained badminton action recognition.

### Evaluation Setup
- Dataset split: 8:1:1 (train/validation/test)
- Metrics: Top-1 Accuracy, Top-5 Accuracy, Mean Class Accuracy
- Data augmentation: random cropping, horizontal flipping, color jittering
- Fine-tuning approach: transfer learning from Kinetics/ImageNet pre-trained weights, frozen early layers with training on later layers, lower learning rates, regularization (dropout, weight decay)

### Dataset Statistics Methods
The paper employs frame entropy (measuring spatial complexity) and mean difference of frame-level features (using a modified ResNet-50 for temporal dynamics) to characterize the dataset's richness.

### Contributions
1. Introduction of VideoBadminton dataset for badminton action recognition with detailed annotations
2. Systematic evaluation of contemporary video recognition architectures in the nuanced context of badminton action recognition
3. The dataset and associated code are made publicly available for research purposes

# [Literature Review] Benchmarking Badminton Action Recognition with a New Fine-Grained Dataset

The paper titled "Benchmarking Badminton Action Recognition with a New Fine-Grained Dataset" presents a comprehensive examination of action recognition in badminton, focusing particularly on the introduction of a new dataset called VideoBadminton. This dataset features high-quality footage of badminton match play, capturing 18 distinct action classes relevant to the sport. Here's an in-depth look at its core methodology and findings.

### Core Methodology

Dataset Creation

The VideoBadminton dataset was curated by recording badminton practice sessions featuring players from National Central University’s badminton team. This team included both male and female players of a high skill level. The aim was to encapsulate a rich variety of badminton actions and techniques, aligning with the classifications set out by the Badminton World Federation (BWF).

**Data Collection:**

* The dataset consists of 7,822 video clips covering 145 minutes of recorded footage.
* It includes actions such as "Short Serve," "Smash," "Drop Shot," and others, making it ideal for detailed analysis and modeling of badminton actions.

**Camera Settings:**

* A camera (from The Imaging Source, model DFK 37AUX273) was utilized, set to 1280x960 resolution at 60 frames per second.
* Camera placement was strategically chosen to capture a clear view of players from a height and angle that minimized distortion and ensured accurate documentation of actions.

**Data Preprocessing:**

* An essential preprocessing step involved correcting lens distortion using OpenCV, specifically adapting the images to align with the true positions of players and the court.
* Noisy frames and irrelevant data were filtered out, ensuring the dataset focused on significant interactions during play.

Annotation Process

Human annotation played a crucial role in shaping the VideoBadminton dataset. Experienced annotators, including members of the badminton team, labeled the videos, which were subsequently reviewed by a head coach to ensure accuracy and completeness. The labeling was performed using the Shot-By-Shot (S2) Labeling tool, allowing for granularity in categorizing each action shot.

**Labeling Steps:**

1. Basic match metadata was recorded.
2. The beginning and end of each rally were identified, along with scoring data.
3. Shuttlecock trajectories and individual strokes were meticulously labeled post-game recording.

Benchmarking and Model Evaluation

The paper further highlights the performance of various state-of-the-art video action recognition models applied to the VideoBadminton dataset, including R(2+1)D, SlowFast, TimeSformer, Swim, MViT-V2, ST-GCN, and PoseC3D. A series of metrics were used to measure the efficacy of these models:

* **Top-1 Accuracy:** Percentage of instances where the model's top prediction matches the true class.
* **Top-5 Accuracy:** Measures if the true class is among the top five predictions.
* **Mean Class Accuracy:** Average accuracy across all action categories, essential for assessing model performance on imbalanced datasets.

**Experimental Setup:**

* The dataset was split into training, validation, and testing sets (8:1:1 ratio).
* Data augmentation techniques were employed during training to enhance model robustness against overfitting.

Statistical Analysis

The authors performed a statistical analysis of frame entropy (a measure of randomness or complexity in a frame) and mean feature differences to capture the variance in action dynamics across videos. This dual analysis approach helped in understanding the characteristics of action sequences within the dataset.

### Experimental Results

The results indicated varying levels of success among the tested models. The SlowFast model, for instance, stood out with an impressive Top-1 accuracy score of 82.80% in some configurations, demonstrating robustness in recognizing detailed actions. Meanwhile, models like MViT-V2 struggled, failing to match the accuracy metrics achieved by others.

### Conclusion and Future Work

In summary, the VideoBadminton dataset represents a significant advancement in sports-related action recognition, particularly by providing a fine-grained categorization of badminton actions. args.summary:
This webpage summarizes the research paper "Benchmarking Badminton Action Recognition with a New Fine-Grained Dataset," which introduces a new dataset called VideoBadminton for fine-grained badminton action recognition.

**Dataset Creation:** The VideoBadminton dataset was curated by recording badminton practice sessions featuring high-skill male and female players from National Central University's badminton team, with action classifications aligned to Badminton World Federation (BWF) standards. It consists of 7,822 video clips covering 145 minutes of footage, capturing 18 distinct action classes including "Short Serve," "Smash," and "Drop Shot." Footage was captured using an Imaging Source DFK 37AUX273 camera at 1280x960 resolution and 60 frames per second, positioned to minimize distortion. Preprocessing involved correcting lens distortion using OpenCV and filtering out noisy or irrelevant frames.

**Annotation Process:** Experienced annotators (including badminton team members) labeled videos using the Shot-By-Shot (S2) Labeling tool, with a head coach reviewing for accuracy. Labeling steps included recording basic match metadata, identifying rally boundaries and scoring data, and meticulously labeling shuttlecock trajectories and individual strokes.

**Benchmarking:** The paper evaluated several state-of-the-art video action recognition models on VideoBadminton, including R(2+1)D, SlowFast, TimeSformer, Swin, MViT-V2, ST-GCN, and PoseC3D. Metrics used were Top-1 Accuracy, Top-5 Accuracy, and Mean Class Accuracy. The dataset was split into training, validation, and testing sets at an 8:1:1 ratio, with data augmentation applied during training.

**Results:** The SlowFast model performed best, achieving a Top-1 accuracy of 82.80% in some configurations, while MViT-V2 struggled to match other models' accuracy.

**Statistical Analysis:** The authors performed frame entropy analysis and mean feature difference analysis to capture variance in action dynamics across videos.

**Conclusion:** The VideoBadminton dataset represents a significant advancement in sports-related action recognition through fine-grained categorization of badminton actions. Future directions include exploring novel modeling techniques and refining the dataset to address emerging action recognition challenges in sports analytics.

Year: 2024, Pages: 1387-1392

#### Abstract

In the dynamic and evolving field of computer vision, action recognition has become a key focus, especially with the advent of sophisticated methodologies like Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Convolutional 3D, Transformer and spatial-temporal feature fusion. These technologies have shown promising results on well-established benchmarks but face unique challenges in real-world applications, particularly in sports analysis, where the precise decomposition of activities and the distinction of subtly different actions are crucial. Existing datasets like UCF101, HMDB51, and Kinetics have offered a diverse range of video data for various scenarios. However, there’s an increasing need for fine-grained video datasets that capture detailed categorizations and nuances within broader action categories. In this paper, we introduce the VideoBadminton dataset, which is derived from high-quality badminton footage. Through an exhaustive evaluation of leading methodologies on this dataset, this study aims to advance the field of action recognition, particularly in badminton sports. The introduction of VideoBadminton could not only serve for badminton action recognition but also provide a dataset for recognizing fine-grained actions. The insights gained from these evaluations are expected to catalyze further research in action comprehension, especially within sports contexts.

Incredible progress has been made in human action recognition (HAR), significantly impacting computer vision applications in sports analytics. However, identifying dynamic and complex movements in sports like badminton remains challenging due to the need for precise recognition accuracy and better management of complex motion patterns. Deep learning techniques like convolutional neural networks (CNNs), long short-term memory (LSTM), and graph convolutional networks (GCNs) improve recognition in large datasets, while the traditional machine learning methods like SVM (support vector machines), RF (random forest), and LR (logistic regression), combined with handcrafted features and ensemble approaches, perform well but struggle with the complexity of fast-paced sports like badminton. We proposed an ensemble learning model combining support vector machines (SVM), logistic regression (LR), random forest (RF), and adaptive boosting (AdaBoost) for badminton action recognition. The data in this study consist of video recordings of badminton stroke techniques, which have been extracted into spatiotemporal data. The three-dimensional distance between each skeleton point and the right hip represents the spatial features. The temporal features are the results of Fast Dynamic Time Warping (FDTW) calculations applied to 15 frames of each video sequence. The weighted ensemble model employs soft voting classifiers from SVM, LR, RF, and AdaBoost to enhance the accuracy of badminton action recognition. The E2 ensemble model, which combines SVM, LR, and AdaBoost, achieves the highest accuracy of 95.38%.

Skeleton-based motion data, as a compact and robust representation of human movement, plays a critical role in multimodal perception for interactive entertainment systems. To address these challenges, this study proposes a lightweight multimodal action perception framework based on an Improved Channel-wise Topology Refinement Graph Convolutional Network (ICTR-GCN). The proposed model enhances spatio-temporal perception by integrating channel-specific topology refinement, multi-branch temporal modeling, and depthwise separable convolutions, while incorporating dynamic channel attention and DropBlock regularization to improve robustness under noisy and interactive environments. This design enables efficient perception of fine-grained human actions while maintaining low computational overhead. Experimental evaluations on the Kinetics Skeleton 400 and NTU RGB+D 60 datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves recognition accuracies of 81.35% and 89.73%, respectively, with only 4.95 million parameters and 10.41 GFLOPs. On the edge device NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX, the model inference latency is 28.6 ms, processing 35.0 frames per second, and the single inference energy consumption is only 429.0 mJ, significantly better than the comparison model. Published on 17 December 2022 in the 2022 IEEE International Conference on Big Data (Big Data), pages 5542-5548, with DOI 10.1109/BigData55660.2022.10020984 (Corpus ID: 256318302).

The paper's TLDR states that results showed a large difference between the performance of individual and generalized models; however, generalized models could be improved by increasing the number of players in the training set, by data augmentation, and by transfer learning, highlighting the necessity of larger datasets in this field.

The paper has 10 citations and 22 references, and includes 11 figures and tables. Full text is available via IEEE and via biblio.ugent.be (PDF link).

Notable citing papers include: "Wearable sensing for badminton stroke recognition with one-dimensional convolutional neural network" (Scientific Reports, 2025) using two sensors with a lightweight 1D-CNN; "MultiSenseBadminton: Wearable Sensor–Based Biomechanical Dataset" (Scientific Data, 2024) covering forehand clear and backhand drive strokes; "Rallying Innovations: CNN-SVM Frameworks for Badminton Shot Recognition" (2024); "From IMU Streams to Real-Time Decisions" (Sensors, 2026); "BadminSense: Enabling Fine-Grained Badminton Strokes Evaluation on Single Smartwatch" (CHI, 2026); and "Strategy analysis of badminton players using deep learning from IMU and UWB wearables" (Internet of Things, 2024) by the same research group.

Key references include earlier work by the same group: "Badminton Activity Recognition Using Accelerometer Data" (Steels et al., Sensors, 2020) which achieved 86% precision distinguishing nine activities with a convolutional neural network at 50 Hz sampling; "Automatic Badminton Action Recognition Using CNN with Adaptive Feature Extraction on Sensor Data" (Wang et al., 2019) achieving 98.65% accuracy; and related works on badminton stroke recognition using HMM, vision-based CNN approaches, and sensor-based classification.
