## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110)Abstract

Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are a powerful class of dynamical models for representing complex systems that are partially observed through sensory data. Existing data collection methods for HMMs, typically based on active learning or heuristic approaches, face challenges in terms of efficiency in stochastic domains with costly data. This paper introduces a Bayesian lookahead data collection method for inferring HMMs with finite state and parameter spaces. The method optimizes data collection under uncertainty using a belief state that captures the joint distribution of system states and models. Unlike traditional approaches that prioritize short-term gains, this policy accounts for the long-term impact of data collection decisions to improve inference performance over time. We develop a deep reinforcement learning policy that approximates the optimal Bayesian solution by simulating system trajectories offline. This pre-trained policy can be executed in real-time, dynamically adapting to new conditions as data is collected. The proposed framework supports a wide range of inference objectives, including point-based, distribution-based, and causal inference. Experimental results across three distinct systems demonstrate significant improvements in inference accuracy and robustness, showcasing the effectiveness of the approach in uncertain and data-limited environments.

**Index Terms—:**Hidden Markov Models, Inference, Reinforcement Learning, Causality

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110)Introduction

I.
Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are widely recognized statistical models employed in numerous domains, including network security, ecology, transportation, image processing, sentiment analysis, autonomous driving, health monitoring, and disaster evaluation [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R1)]–[[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R8)]. Inference of HMMs is crucial for understanding and predicting sequential data patterns, offering insights into underlying processes masked by noisy or incomplete observations.

Several inference techniques have been developed for modeling and constructing HMMs. A stochastic variational inference algorithm for learning the parameters of HMMs is introduced in [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R9)], where its efficacy is demonstrated on synthetic experiments and a large genomics dataset. Wiuf et al. [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R10)] suggest a novel reaction network scheme, the Baum-Welch reaction network, which effectively learns parameters for HMMs and demonstrates that its expectation and maximization steps converge exponentially fast. An online expectation-maximization algorithm is proposed in [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R11)] for enabling realtime parameter estimation in HMMs. Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R12)], [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R13)] are also a popular class of methods used for Bayesian inference of HMMs. Moreover, combining approximate Bayesian computation with MCMC techniques is proposed in [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R14)] to improve computational efficiency, especially when dealing with intractable likelihoods and poor prior knowledge about model parameters. The existing inference methods can be categorized broadly into point-based, such as a maximum likelihood or maximum a posteriori inference, and distribution-based, such as Bayesian inference.

The accuracy of the inference methods is limited to the capacity in which the available data represent the underlying complex mechanism of systems. One of the main challenges in the inference of HMMs is the non-identifiability issue [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R15)], which refers to cases where different sets of model parameters can produce the observed data. This can lead to difficulties in model interpretation and inference. The non-identifiability issue often happens in systems under normal conditions or tightly controlled systems, where available data (though large) only represent a small portion of the state space. Therefore, collecting additional data to properly learn the underlying mechanism of systems is essential. Data collection can be achieved by influencing the system state transitions, such as through excitation or perturbation into the system states, intelligently selecting the sensors to monitor the system, or any other actions that may lead to obtaining different information from the systems.

Several data collection approaches have been developed to enhance the inference of HMMs and overcome the non-identifiability issue [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R16)], [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R17)]. For instance, a method for inferring human behaviors in human-robot collaboration tasks is proposed in [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R18)] by collecting and analyzing data such as gestures, eye movements, and head motions, utilizing a Bayesian learning approach within a Partially Observed Markov Decision Process (POMDP) framework. Also, a Bayesian method for learning POMDP observation parameters in robot interaction management systems is introduced in [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R19)], allowing gradual adjustment of the robot’s behavior based on user interactions and an oracle’s optimal policy. These approaches, however, are application-specific and are not applicable to general HMMs. Sensor selection or scheduling approaches are another class of data collection techniques for HMMs [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R20)]–[[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R24)]. However, these methods can only optimize the allocation of monitoring resources rather than changing the system transitions to collect informative data. Also, the majority of these methods are developed to enhance state estimation performance and rely on the availability of full knowledge of HMMs. Experimental design techniques are the most relevant approaches for data collection for inference of HMMs. This class of methods aims to sequentially and greedily collect data to reduce model uncertainty (e.g., entropy or related measures) [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R25)]–[[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R27)]. For instance in [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R28)], expected information gain is utilized to optimize data selection in neurobiological research, aiming to improve inference with fewer data and potentially enhance the design of clinical trials. Also, a framework for active learning in latent variable models is proposed in [[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R29)], leveraging entropy measures to reduce data requirements for fitting mixtures of linear regressions and HMMs with generalized linear model observations. Despite the relative success of these techniques, they become inefficient in domains with a huge amount of uncertainty in state, measurement, and system models, as well as domains with limited data collection resources. This comes from the incapability of these methods to account for the long-term impacts of decisions on system uncertainty and inference accuracy.

In recent years, Reinforcement Learning (RL) techniques have been extensively applied to the inference and control of complex dynamical systems [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R30)], [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R31)]. For example, a fuzzy-model-based approach has been proposed in [[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R32)] to optimize nonlinear Markov jump singularly perturbed systems using RL. In [[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R33)], an inference method is developed that incorporates expert knowledge into the inference process for HMMs. The expert is modeled as a sub-optimal RL agent, and the method aims to extract its knowledge for inference rather than collecting new data. Furthermore, an RL-based data collection method for offline meta-RL is presented in [[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R34)]. This method addresses the identifiability issue and sample-efficient interactions across domains modeled by a Markov Decision Process (MDP). However, this approach focuses on task adaptation in offline meta-RL and does not address the challenge of identifying unknown model parameters. Moreover, in some complex systems, such as cyber-physical and biological systems, non-Markovian behavior can emerge, where the future state depends not only on the current state but also on past states. Recent studies have proposed fractional-order derivatives and master equations to capture these long-range dependencies [[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R35)]–[[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R37)]. In such cases, data collection strategies may need to distinguish whether Markovian or non-Markovian dynamics are more appropriate for modeling these systems.

This paper proposes a deep reinforcement learning Bayesian data collection policy for inferring unknown HMMs. A Bayesian representation of unknown HMMs is provided through a belief state, which keeps track of the joint distribution of the possible system states and models. The optimal Bayesian data collection process is formulated in belief space, where the belief transition propagates the system and data uncertainty. The offline training is achieved through simulating belief trajectories for pre-training a deep reinforcement learning policy without the need for real data or prior knowledge of the system model. The offline-trained Bayesian policy is executable in real-time, according to the latest data collected from the real systems. Some of the key features of the proposed policy are as follows: Approximating the optimal Bayesian lookahead data collection policy, which accounts for uncertainty in the system and data and considers the long-term impact of decisions on the HMM’s inference performance.Learnable through offline trajectories synthetically generated from the uncertain model; the trained policy is executable in real-time during data collection from the real system and dynamically adapts to the system as new data is collected.Applicability to a wide range of inference criteria, including point-based criteria such as a maximum likelihood or maximum a posteriori, distribution-based criteria, and causal inference. Unlike existing data collection methods, such as active learning [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R28)] and maximum a posteriori approaches [[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R38)], which prioritize short-term or greedy objectives, our approach formulates data collection as a lookahead policy optimization problem. This allows us to consider the future impact of data collection actions, leading to more informed decisions that improve inference accuracy over time. Additionally, our method’s ability to operate offline, using synthetic belief trajectories during training, significantly reduces the amount of real-time data required, making the learning process more efficient and scalable across different domains.

The effectiveness of the proposed data collection approach is evaluated across three distinct systems. These include a general HMM with unknown state and measurement processes, a gene regulatory network characterized by an unknown state process, and a communication network featuring an unknown measurement process.

[Fig. 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#F1) illustrates a schematic diagram for the proposed data collection method. The blue arrows denote the already collected data, and the red dashed arrows indicate the future undecided decisions during data collection. The less visible network model in the early steps expresses the uncertainty about the network parameters. Given the already available data, the proposed data collection policy sequentially selects actions that can generate the most valuable data for quick and accurate inference.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: [Section II](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#S2) contains a background regarding finite-state HMMs and discusses the inference of unknown HMMs, followed by the formulation of data collection in HMMs. Further, [Section III](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#S7) presents the optimal Bayesian lookahead data collection policy for unknown HMMs. The proposed deep reinforcement learning Bayesian data collection policy is explained in detail in [Section IV](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#S11). [Section V](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#S14) includes the numerical results for three different HMM models, demonstrating the efficacy of the proposed method. Finally, [Section VI](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#S18) consists of the conclusion and a discussion of future work.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110)Background and Preliminaries

II.
### Finite-State Hidden Markov Models

A.
HMMs characterize the dynamical behavior of systems observed through noisy time-series data. The schematic diagram of HMMs with external inputs is shown in [Fig. 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#F2). The time-varying behavior of systems is represented through the state process, where $\mathbf{x}_{k}$ represents the system state at time step $k$. This paper assumes the state takes its value from a finite set $\mathcal{X} = \left{\mathbf{x}^{1} , \ldots , \mathbf{x}^{n}\right}$. The states are observed indirectly through observations, where $\mathbf{y}_{k}$ represents the measurement at time step $k$, taking in an arbitrary space. The following two processes represent the finite-state HMMs: (1) 

$$
\mathbf{x}_{k} \sim p \left(. \mid \mathbf{x}_{k - 1} , \mathbf{a}_{k - 1} , \theta\right) \left(\right. \text{state} \text{process} \left.\right) \\ \mathbf{y}_{k} \sim p \left(. \mid \mathbf{x}_{k} , \mathbf{a}_{k - 1} , \theta\right) \left(\right. \text{measurement} \text{process} \left.\right)
$$

 for $k = 1,2 , \ldots$; where $p \left(\right. \cdot \left.\right)$ denotes probability density or probability mass functions, $\mathbf{a}_{k - 1} \in \mathcal{A}$ is the external input to the system at time $k - 1$, and $\theta$ represents the unknown elements of the two processes. The state and measurement processes are stochastic; the state process represents the system dynamics, whereas the measurement process characterizes the data generated from sensors/technology. The parameter $\theta$ takes its value from a finite parameter space $\Theta = \left{\theta^{1} , \ldots , \theta^{r}\right}$, where each $\theta \in \Theta$ represents a possible HMM. Therefore, the terms parameter and model are used interchangeably throughout this paper.

### Formulation of Optimal Inference for HMMs

B.
#### Inference of Unknown HMMs:

1)
The inference in HMMs consists of estimating the unknown parameters of the model in ([1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD1)) represented by $\theta$ according to the available data. Let $\left{\left(\mathbf{a}_{0} , \mathbf{y}_{1}\right) , \left(\mathbf{a}_{1} , \mathbf{y}_{2}\right) , \ldots , \left(\mathbf{a}_{k - 1} , \mathbf{y}_{k}\right)\right}$ be the available timeseries data, where $\mathbf{a}_{i - 1}$ is the input or action at time step $i - 1$, which has led to the measurement $\mathbf{y}_{i}$ at time step $i$. Depending on the application, the inference objective can be expressed in terms of point-based or distribution-based criteria, as described below.

The _point-based inference_ aims to find a single best estimate of the unknown parameters. Two well-known point-based criteria are maximum likelihood (ML) and maximum a posteriori (MAP), which can be expressed as [[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R39)], [[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R40)]: (2) 

$$
\left(\hat{\theta}\right)_{k}^{\text{ML}} = \underset{\theta \in \Theta}{\text{argmax}} p \left(\right. y_{1 : k} \mid a_{0 : k - 1} , \theta \left.\right) , \\ \left(\hat{\theta}\right)_{k}^{\text{MAP}} = \underset{\theta \in \Theta}{\text{argmax}} p \left(\right. \theta \mid y_{1 : k} , a_{0 : k - 1} \left.\right) ,
$$

 where $\overset{\hat{}}{\theta}_{k}^{\text{ML}}$ and $\overset{\hat{}}{\theta}_{k}^{\text{MAP}}$ represent the parameters with the highest likelihood and posterior probability, respectively. Note that MAP and ML become the same under a uniform prior distribution of the unknown parameters.

The confidence of the MAP inference $\overset{\hat{}}{\theta}_{k}^{\text{MAP}}$ in ([2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD2)) can be assessed using the probability of the MAP model as: (3) 

$$
C_{k} = p \left(\overset{\hat{}}{\theta}_{k}^{\text{MAP}} \mid \mathbf{y}_{1 : k} , \mathbf{a}_{0 : k - 1}\right) = \underset{\theta \in \Theta}{\text{max}} p \left(\theta \mid \mathbf{y}_{1 : k} , \mathbf{a}_{0 : k - 1}\right) ,
$$

 where $1 / r \leq C_{k} \leq 1$ represents the highest posterior probability of the models. The closer $C_{k}$ to 1, the higher the confidence of the MAP inference is. The confidence rate of $1 / r$ corresponds to the poorest performance of the MAP inference. Note that $C_{k} = 1 / r$ is a special case where all the models have the same posterior probability given the available data; thus, the true model is not distinguishable from the others.

For _distribution-based inference_, the objective is to find the posterior distribution of the possible system models, as opposed to a model with the highest likelihood or posterior probability. Given the available data up to time step $k$, this can be expressed as [[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R39)]: (4) 

$$
p_{k} = p \left(\right. \Theta \mid y_{1 : k} , a_{0 : k - 1} \left.\right) \\ = \left(\left[\right. p \left(\right. \theta^{1} \mid y_{1 : k} , a_{0 : k - 1} \left.\right) , \ldots , p \left(\right. \theta^{r} \mid y_{1 : k} , a_{0 : k - 1} \left.\right) \left]\right.\right)^{T} .
$$

 Similar to the expected confidence in ([3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD3)) for point-based inference, the confidence of the distribution-based inference in ([4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD4)) can be assessed using the following entropy measure [[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R41)]: (5) 

$$
D_{k} = - \mathcal{H} \left[p \left(\Theta \mid \mathbf{y}_{1 : k} , \mathbf{a}_{0 : k - 1}\right)\right] = \sum_{i = 1}^{r} p_{k} \left(i\right) \text{log} p_{k} \left(i\right) ,
$$

 where $\mathcal{H} \left[\right. . \left]\right.$ represents the Shannon entropy and $\text{log} \left(\right. 1 / r \left.\right) \leq D_{k} \leq 0$. The values of $D_{k}$ close to zero represent cases with posterior distributions peaked over a single model and, consequently, the most confident inference. On the other hand, the values close to $D_{k} = \text{log} \left(\right. 1 / r \left.\right)$ indicate the poorest performance of distribution-based inference.

#### Formulation of Data Collection in HMMs:

2)
Data can be costly, in terms of time and/or money, in many practical domains, and it is often challenging or impossible to rely on only the available data for accurate inference of complex systems. This is due to the fact that the possible models in $\Theta$ often cannot be easily distinguished from each other through data collected from the system in normal conditions. Therefore, rather than collecting more data, targeted data should be collected to ensure the desired inference objective. Data collection in dynamic systems is challenging, as targeted actions should be made to intelligently change the system dynamics and generate data that reveal the true system model.

Depending on the inference criteria, the expected accuracy of the inference process can be assessed through the measures defined for the point-based and distribution-based inference in ([3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD3)) and ([5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD5)). Thus, given the huge cost of data collection, the goal is to select the best sequence of actions that leads to measurements under which the expected accuracy/confidence of inference is maximized. This can be expressed as: (6) 

$$
\mathbf{a}_{0 : k - 1}^{\star} = \underset{\mathbf{a}_{0 : k - 1} \in \mathcal{A}^{k}}{\text{argmax}} \mathbb{E} \left[C_{k} \text{or} D_{k} \mid \mathbf{a}_{0 : k - 1}\right] ,
$$

 where the expectation is with respect to stochasticity in the unobserved measurements. Finding the optimal sequence of actions in ([6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD6)) without full knowledge of the system model or access to large real data is impossible. Meanwhile, the batch selection of the action sequence makes it unsuitable for real-time and sequential data collection, as the latest data are not utilized to change the selections. Methods such as active learning [[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R42)] are developed to sequentially choose actions by accounting for possible changes in inference measures in a single step. While these methods make the computation of the expectation in ([6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD6)) tractable, they often provide non-optimal solutions for data collection due to their greedy nature and often require huge computations in real-time for their selection process. In the next paragraphs, our proposed sequential and lookahead data collection approach to overcome these challenges is described.

### Optimal Bayesian Lookahead Data Collection

III.
#### A. Bayesian Modeling of Decision-Making in Unknown HMMs

Let $\left(\mathbf{a}_{0 : k - 1} , \mathbf{y}_{1 : k}\right)$ be the available data collected up to time step $k$, where $\mathbf{a}_{1 : k - 1}$ and $\mathbf{y}_{1 : k}$ represent the sequence of selected actions and observed measurements, respectively. Let $p_{k} \left(\right. \theta \left.\right)$ also be the posterior probability of the model $\theta \in \Theta$, given the collected data up to time $k$. We represent the information carried by the sequence of data and the posterior probability of models into a single vector called belief state. The belief state captures the joint probability distribution of the possible system states and system models using an $n \times r$ vector. The belief state at time $k$ can be represented as: (7) 

$$
\mathbf{b}_{k} = p \left(\mathbf{x}_{k} = \mathcal{X} , \Theta \mid \mathbf{y}_{1 : k} , \mathbf{a}_{0 : k - 1}\right) = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{b}_{k}^{\theta^{1}} \\ \vdots \\ \mathbf{b}_{k}^{\theta^{r}} \end{bmatrix} ,
$$

 where (8) 

$$
\mathbf{b}_{k}^{\theta^{l}} = \begin{bmatrix} p \left(\mathbf{x}_{k} = \mathbf{x}^{1} , \theta^{l} \mid \mathbf{y}_{1 : k} , \mathbf{a}_{0 : k - 1}\right) \\ \vdots \\ p \left(\mathbf{x}_{k} = \mathbf{x}^{n} , \theta^{l} \mid \mathbf{y}_{1 : k} , \mathbf{a}_{0 : k - 1}\right) \end{bmatrix} .
$$

 The belief state is a sufficient statistic for representing the history of information as a compact form in unknown HMMs. The initial belief $\mathbf{b}_{0} = p \left(\mathbf{x}_{0} = \mathcal{X} , \Theta\right)$ demonstrates the initial joint probability of the system states and unknown parameters, which could be set as uniform if no prior information is available.

In this part, we describe that the belief transitions follow a Markov process and provide a recursive procedure to update the belief state as new action is taken and a new measurement is obtained. Let $\mathbf{b}_{0} , \mathbf{b}_{1} , \ldots , \mathbf{b}_{k}$ be the sequence of belief states, with $\mathbf{b}_{k} = p \left(\mathcal{X} , \Theta \mid \mathbf{a}_{0 : k - 1} , \mathbf{y}_{1 : k}\right)$ be the latest belief. The belief state after taking an action $\mathbf{a}_{k}$ and observing a new measurement $\mathbf{y}_{k + 1}$ can be updated as: (9) 

$$
b_{k + 1} = p \left(\right. x_{k + 1} = \mathcal{X} , \Theta \mid b_{0} , \ldots , b_{k} , a_{k} , y_{k + 1} \left.\right) \\ = \frac{p \left(\right. x_{k + 1} = \mathcal{X} , \Theta , y_{k + 1} \mid b_{0} , \ldots , b_{k} , a_{k} \left.\right)}{p \left(\right. y_{k + 1} \mid b_{0} , \ldots , b_{k} , a_{k} \left.\right)} \\ \propto p \left(\right. y_{k + 1} \mid x_{k + 1} = \mathcal{X} , a_{k} , \Theta \left.\right) \times p \left(\right. x_{k + 1} = \mathcal{X} , \Theta \mid b_{0} , \ldots , b_{k} , a_{k} \left.\right) ,
$$

 where the numerator of the second line is expanded in the last line. The first term of the last line of ([9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD9)) can be computed using the measurement process in ([1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD1)). The second term can be computed for any $\mathbf{x}^{i} \in \mathcal{X}$ and $\theta \in \Theta$ as: (10) 

$$
p \left(\right. x_{k + 1} = x^{i} , \theta \mid b_{0} , \ldots , b_{k} , a_{k} \left.\right) \\ = \sum_{j = 1}^{n} p \left(\right. x_{k + 1} = x^{i} , x_{k} = x^{j} , \theta \mid b_{0} , \ldots , b_{k} , a_{k} \left.\right) \\ = \sum_{j = 1}^{n} p \left(\right. x_{k + 1} = x^{i} \mid x_{k} = x^{j} , a_{k} , \theta \left.\right) p \left(\right. x_{k} = x^{j} , \theta \mid b_{0} , \ldots , b_{k} \left.\right) \\ = \sum_{j = 1}^{n} p \left(\right. x_{k + 1} = x^{i} \mid x_{k} = x^{j} , a_{k} , \theta \left.\right) b_{k}^{\theta} \left(\right. j \left.\right) ,
$$

 where $\mathbf{b}_{k}^{\theta} \left(\right. j \left.\right)$ denotes the $j \text{th}$ element of $\mathbf{b}_{k}^{\theta}$ and $p \left(\mathbf{x}_{k} = \mathbf{x}^{j} , \theta \mid\right) \mathbf{b}_{0} , \ldots , \mathbf{b}_{k} \left.\right)$ in the third line is equal to $\mathbf{b}_{k}^{\theta} \left(\right. j \left.\right)$ according to ([8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD8)). Replacing ([10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD10)) into ([9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD9)) leads to the following expression for the numerator of ([9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD9)): (11) 

$$
b_{k + 1}^{\theta} \left(\right. i \left.\right) \propto p \left(\right. y_{k + 1} \mid x_{k + 1} = x^{i} , a_{k} , \theta \left.\right) \times \sum_{j = 1}^{n} p \left(\right. x_{k + 1} = x^{i} \mid x_{k} = x^{j} , a_{k} , \theta \left.\right) b_{k}^{\theta} \left(\right. j \left.\right) ,
$$

 for $i = 1 , \ldots , n$ and $\theta \in \Theta$. [Equations (9)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD9) and [(11)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD11) enable a recursive update of the belief state and reflect the Markovian transition of the belief states.

### MDP Formulation of Data Collection

B.
This section provides the belief space and belief transition formulation within the context of the Markov Decision Process (MDP) for the data collection procedure. The belief state takes its value in a simplex of size $n \times r , \Delta_{n \times r}$, denoted by $\mathcal{B}$ and referred to as the belief space. If $\mathbf{b}$ is the current belief state, upon taking action $\mathbf{a}$, the next belief state before observing the next observation is stochastic, with the transition represented by: (12) 

$$
\mathbf{b}^{′} \sim p \left(\right. . \mid \mathbf{b} , \mathbf{a} \left.\right) .
$$

 The belief transition in ([12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD12)) represents the probability of the next belief state after taking action $\mathbf{a}$ from the current belief state $\mathbf{b}$. Therefore, the stochasticity in the next belief state corresponds to probable data that could be collected/observed in the next time step given all the available information reflected in the current belief state. Letting $\mathbf{b} = \left[\mathbf{b}^{\theta^{1}} , \hdots , \mathbf{b}^{\theta^{r}}\right]^{T}$ be the current belief state, the belief state after taking action $\mathbf{a}$ and observing a new measurement $\mathbf{y}$ can be written as $\mathbf{b}_{\mathbf{y} , \mathbf{a}} = \left[\mathbf{b}_{\mathbf{y} , \mathbf{a}}^{\theta^{1}} , \hdots , \mathbf{b}_{\mathbf{y} , \mathbf{a}}^{\theta^{r}}\right]^{T}$, where (13) 

$$
\mathbf{b}_{\mathbf{y} , \mathbf{a}}^{\theta} \left(i\right) = \frac{p \left(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x}^{i} , \mathbf{a} , \theta\right) \sum_{j = 1}^{n} p \left(\mathbf{x}^{i} \mid \mathbf{x}^{j} , \mathbf{a} , \theta\right) \mathbf{b}^{\theta} \left(j\right)}{\underset{\mathbf{x}^{′} \in \mathcal{X}}{\sum} \underset{\theta^{′} \in \Theta}{\sum} p \left(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x}^{′} , \mathbf{a} , \theta^{′}\right) \sum_{j = 1}^{n} p \left(\mathbf{x}^{′} \mid \mathbf{x}^{j} , \mathbf{a} , \theta^{′}\right) \mathbf{b}^{\theta^{′}} \left(j\right)} ,
$$

 for $i = 1 , \ldots , n$ and any $\theta \in \Theta$ according to ([9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD9)) and ([11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD11)). The belief transition probabilities in ([12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD12)) can be discrete or continuous distributions, depending on the size of the measurement space. Given that the measurement takes its value in a continuous space, the belief transition can be expressed as: (14) 

$$
p \left(\mathbf{b}^{′} \mid \mathbf{b} , \mathbf{a}\right) = \int_{\mathcal{Y}} p \left(\mathbf{y}∣\mathbf{b} , \mathbf{a}\right) I_{\mathbf{b}^{′} = \mathbf{b}_{\mathbf{y} , \mathbf{a}}} d \mathbf{y} ,
$$

 where $\mathcal{Y}$ represents the space of all potential measurements and $I_{\mathbf{b}^{′} = \mathbf{b}_{\mathbf{y} , \mathbf{a}}}$ is an indicator function which returns 1 if $\mathbf{b}^{′} = \mathbf{b}_{\mathbf{y} , \mathbf{a}}$ and 0 otherwise. Notice that for multi-variant measurements, a single integral can be replaced by multiple ones, and in scenarios with discrete/finite measurement outcomes, the integral in ([14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD14)) should be replaced with summations. ([14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD14)) shows that when an action is chosen for data collection at any particular belief state, multiple potential subsequent belief states exist before observing the next data. It is important to recognize that the potential subsequent belief states will differ depending on the chosen actions and collected data. This enables us to propagate uncertainty in the belief and evaluate which action choices could result in future beliefs that align better with our data collection goals.

We formulate the gain during the data collection as a reward function in the belief space. The reward function can be expressed as $R \left(\mathbf{b}_{k} , \mathbf{a}_{k} , \mathbf{b}_{k + 1}\right)$, which measures the immediate gain in the inference accuracy after taking action $\mathbf{a}_{k}$ in belief state $\mathbf{b}_{k}$ and moving to the next belief state $\mathbf{b}_{k + 1}$. Various reward functions can be defined given the inference and data collection objectives. If the goal is enhancing the confidence rate of point-based inference in ([2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD2)), the reward function can be formulated using ([3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD3)) as: (15) 

$$
R \left(\right. b_{k} , a_{k} , b_{k + 1} \left.\right) = C_{k + 1} - C_{k} \\ = \underset{\theta \in \Theta}{\text{max}} p_{k + 1} \left(\right. \theta \left.\right) - \underset{\theta \in \Theta}{\text{max}} p_{k} \left(\right. \theta \left.\right) \\ = \underset{\theta \in \Theta}{\text{max}} \left(\parallel b_{k + 1}^{\theta} \parallel\right)_{1} - \underset{\theta \in \Theta}{\text{max}} \left(\parallel b_{k}^{\theta} \parallel\right)_{1} ,
$$

 where $\parallel . \parallel_{1}$ is the L-1 norm, and $p_{k + 1}$ and $p_{k}$ express the model probabilities at time steps $k + 1$ and $k$, computable using belief states at time steps $k + 1$ and $k$, respectively. A positive reward characterizes a single-step increase in the maximum posterior probability of models, and a reward of zero represents that the maximum posterior probability is unchanged after observing the next observation as a result of the last taken action.

For the distribution-based inference in ([4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD4)), the reward function can be formulated using ([5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD5)) as: (16) 

$$
R \left(\right. b_{k} , a_{k} , b_{k + 1} \left.\right) = D_{k + 1} - D_{k} = - H \left[\right. p_{k + 1} \left]\right. + H \left[\right. p_{k} \left]\right. = \underset{\theta \in \Theta}{\sum} \left(\parallel b_{k + 1}^{\theta} \parallel\right)_{1} log \left(\parallel b_{k + 1}^{\theta} \parallel\right)_{1} - \underset{\theta \in \Theta}{\sum} \left(\parallel b_{k}^{\theta} \parallel\right)_{1} log \left(\parallel b_{k}^{\theta} \parallel\right)_{1} ,
$$

 where the positive values represent a reduction of uncertainty in the posterior distribution of models after the latest action. In the rest of the paper, ([15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD15)) and ([16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD16)) are referred to as the point-based reward and entropy reward respectively. Note that more complicated and time-dependent reward functions can be used instead of ([15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD15)) and ([16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD16)). For instance, the reward function could include the cost of actions in domains with different action costs and the causality of inference objectives in domains with specific data collection goals.

### Optimal Stationary Bayesian Data Collection

C.
The belief state provides the MDP representation of the unknown HMMs. The belief transition allows for the propagation of state, measurement, and model uncertainty, given all the available information. The belief state gets updated stochastically according to the belief transition upon taking any action, and a reward is observed according to the next belief state. We define a deterministic stationary data collection policy $\mu : \mathcal{B} \rightarrow \mathcal{A}$, which associates an action to any given belief state. The optimal Bayesian lookahead data collection policy $\mu^{\star}$ can be defined as: (17) 

$$
\mu^{\star} \left(\mathbf{b}\right) = \underset{\mu}{\text{argmax}} \mathbb{E} \left[\sum_{t = 0}^{\infty} \gamma^{t} R \left(\mathbf{b}_{t} , \mathbf{a}_{t} , \mathbf{b}_{t + 1}\right) \mid \mathbf{b}_{0} = \mathbf{b} , \mathbf{a}_{0 : \infty} \sim \mu\right] ,
$$

 for all $\mathbf{b} \in \mathcal{B}$; where $0 < \gamma < 1$ is a discount factor indicating the importance of early reward compared to the future ones. The optimal Bayesian lookahead policy $\mu^{\star} \left(\right. \mathbf{b} \left.\right)$ prescribes the best action that could be taken at the belief state $\mathbf{b}$ to maximize the long-term performance of inference (i.e., achieving the highest expected accumulated reward). The term “Bayesian” comes from the expectation in ([17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD17)), which is with respect to the future belief states generated from the belief transition. In other words, all probable next belief states propagating the uncertainty in state, measurement, and models from the current belief state $\mathbf{b}$ are taken into account for finding the optimal Bayesian data collection policy $\mu^{\star} \left(\right. \mathbf{b} \left.\right)$.

The exact computation of the optimal Bayesian policy in ([17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD17)) is not possible, primarily due to the continuity of the belief space $\mathcal{B}$. As previously noted, the belief space forms an $\left(\right. n \times r \left.\right) -\text{simplex} \left(\Delta_{n \times r}\right)$, preventing the use of dynamic programming approaches, such as value iteration or policy iteration [[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R43)], for computing the optimal policy. In the subsequent section, the proposed deep reinforcement learning approach is introduced to approximate the optimal data collection policy.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110)Deep Reinforcement Learning Bayesian Data Collection

IV.
The recent advances in deep reinforcement learning (RL) have enabled learning on much larger scales than before. In this paper, we develop a deep RL Bayesian data collection policy to approximate the solution to the optimization problem in ([17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD17)). To approximate the expectation in ([17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD17)), the proposed deep RL algorithm uses simulated samples from the belief transition, which propagates the system’s uncertainty without requiring data collection from real systems. The trained offline policy is executable for real-time and sequential data collection. In this section, the matrix-form implementation of the belief state is first described, followed by the proposed deep RL approach for learning the Bayesian data collection policy.

### Matrix-form Implementation of Belief State

A.
Let $\left{\mathbf{x}^{1} , \ldots , \mathbf{x}^{n}\right}$ and $\left{\theta^{1} , \ldots , \theta^{r}\right}$ be an arbitrary enumeration of the possible system states and models, respectively. We define the transition matrix of size $n \times n$ associated with the model $\theta \in \Theta$ under action $\mathbf{a}$ as: (18) 

$$
\left(M^{\theta} \left(\right. \mathbf{a} \left.\right)\right)_{i j} = p \left(\mathbf{x}_{k + 1} = \mathbf{x}^{i} \mid \mathbf{x}_{k} = \mathbf{x}^{j} , \mathbf{a}_{k} = \mathbf{a} , \theta\right) ,
$$

 for $i , j = 1 , \ldots , n$. The observation process can be expressed using the update vector $T^{\theta} \left(\right. \mathbf{y} , \mathbf{a} \left.\right)$ as: (19) 

$$
\left(T^{\theta} \left(\right. \mathbf{y} , \mathbf{a} \left.\right)\right)_{i} = p \left(\mathbf{y}_{k + 1} = \mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x}_{k + 1} = \mathbf{x}^{i} , \mathbf{a}_{k} = \mathbf{a} , \theta\right) ,
$$

 for $i = 1 , \ldots , n$. Letting $\mathbf{b} = \left[\mathbf{b}^{\theta^{1}} , \hdots , \mathbf{b}^{\theta^{r}}\right]^{T}$ be the current belief state, the next belief state $\mathbf{b}_{\mathbf{y} , \mathbf{a}}$ after taking action $\mathbf{a}$ and observing $\mathbf{y}$ can be computed according to ([13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD13)). This can be expressed in terms of the transition matrix and update vector in ([18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD18)) and ([19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD19)) as: (20) 

$$
\mathbf{b}_{\mathbf{y} , \mathbf{a}} = \frac{\begin{bmatrix} T^{\theta^{1}} \left(\right. \mathbf{y} , \mathbf{a} \left.\right) \circ \left(M^{\theta^{1}} \left(\right. \mathbf{a} \left.\right) \mathbf{b}^{\theta^{1}}\right) \\ \vdots \\ T^{\theta^{r}} \left(\right. \mathbf{y} , \mathbf{a} \left.\right) \circ \left(M^{\theta^{r}} \left(\right. \mathbf{a} \left.\right) \mathbf{b}^{\theta^{r}}\right) \end{bmatrix}}{\sum_{m = 1}^{r} \left‖T^{\theta^{m}} \left(\right. \mathbf{y} , \mathbf{a} \left.\right) \circ \left(M^{\theta^{m}} \left(\right. \mathbf{a} \left.\right) \mathbf{b}^{\theta^{m}}\right)\right‖_{1}} ,
$$

 where “$\circ$” denotes Hadamard product (i.e., the componentwise multiplication of two vectors), and $\parallel \cdot \parallel_{1}$ denotes the absolute sum of a vector’s elements. The belief transition probability in ([14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#FD14)) can also be expressed as: (21) 

$$
p \left(\mathbf{b}^{′} \mid \mathbf{b} , \mathbf{a}\right) = \int_{\mathcal{Y}} \left(\sum_{m = 1}^{r} \left‖T^{\theta^{m}} \left(\right. \mathbf{y} , \mathbf{a} \left.\right) \circ \left(M^{\theta^{m}} \left(\right. \mathbf{a} \left.\right) \mathbf{b}^{\theta^{m}}\right)\right‖_{1}\right) I_{\mathbf{b}^{′} = \mathbf{b}_{\mathbf{y} , \mathbf{a}}} d \mathbf{y} .
$$

### Deep Reinforcement Learning Bayesian Data Collection Policy

B.
For an arbitrary data collection policy $\mu : \mathcal{B} \rightarrow \mathcal{A}$ defined over the belief space, we define the Q-function or the expected discounted reward function at belief state $\mathbf{b} \in \mathcal{B}$ after taking action $\mathbf{a} \in \mathcal{A}$ and following policy $\mu$ afterward as: (22) 

$$
Q^{\mu} \left(\mathbf{b} , \mathbf{a}\right) = \mathbb{E} \left[\sum_{t = 0}^{\infty} \gamma^{t} R \left(\mathbf{b}_{t} , \mathbf{a}_{t} , \mathbf{b}_{t + 1}\right) \mid \mathbf{b}_{0} = \mathbf{b} , \mathbf{a}_{0} = \mathbf{a} , \mathbf{a}_{1 : \infty} \sim \mu\right] ,
$$

 where the expectation is with respect to the stochasticity of the belief transition. The optimal Q-function, denoted by $Q^{\star} := Q^{\mu^{\star}}$, provides the maximum expected return under the optimal policy $\mu^{\star}$, where $Q^{\mu^{\star}} \left(\mathbf{b} , \mathbf{a}\right) = \underset{\mu}{\text{max}} Q^{\mu} \left(\right. \mathbf{b} , \mathbf{a} \left.\right)$, for all $\mathbf{b} \in \mathcal{B}$ and $\mathbf{a} \in \mathcal{A}$.

Since the tabular representation of the Q-function is impossible over the continuous belief space, a deep reinforcement learning approach is employed for approximating the Q-function. This paper adopts the deep Q-network (DQN) approach [[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R44)] to learn the Bayesian data collection policy, aiming to approximate $Q^{\mu^{\star}} \left(\right. \mathbf{b} , \mathbf{a} \left.\right)$ according to neural networks. Note that other deep RL methods can also be used to derive the proposed data collection policy. The DQN method approximates this Q-function using two feed-forward deep neural networks with the same architecture: the Q-network, $Q_{\mathbf{w}}$, and the target network, $Q_{\mathbf{w}^{-}}$. The input for both networks is the belief state, and the outputs are $Q_{\mathbf{w}} \left(\mathbf{b} , \mathbf{a}^{1}\right) , \ldots , Q_{\mathbf{w}} \left(\mathbf{b} , \mathbf{a}^{\left|\right. \mathcal{A} \left|\right.}\right)$, each corresponding to an action. The initial weights for both the Q-network and the target-network are set randomly.

To train the neural networks, we utilize a fixed-size replay memory $\mathcal{D}$. This replay memory stores episodes containing belief states that are generated using actions selected by the epsilon-greedy policy [[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12045110#R43)]. When the replay memory reaches its capacity, the newest experience replaces the oldest. Each episode begins with an initial belief state, which, if unknown, can be randomly chosen from the belief space $\mathcal{B}$. At step $t$ of the episode, an action is chosen based on the epsilon-greedy policy defined using the Q-network $Q_{w}$: (23)

\mathbf{a}_{t} \sim \left{\begin{matrix} \text{argmax}_{\mathbf{a} \in \mathcal{A}} Q_{\mathbf{w}} \left(\mathbf{b}_{t} , \mathbf{a}\right) & \text{w}.\text{p}. 1 - \epsilon \\ \text{random} \left{\mathbf{a}^{1} , \ldots , \mathbf{a}^{\left|\right. \mathcal{A} \left|\right.}\right} & \text{w}.\text{p}. \epsilon , \end{matrix}\right
$$

$$

args.summary:
This is a scientific research paper published in IEEE Transactions on Artificial Intelligence (Dec 12, 2024; Vol 6, Issue 5, article 1217; DOI: 10.1109/tai.2024.3515939) by Mohammad Alali and Mahdi Imani from the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Northeastern University. The paper, titled "Deep Reinforcement Learning Data Collection for Bayesian Inference of Hidden Markov Models," addresses the challenge of efficiently collecting data to infer unknown Hidden Markov Models (HMMs).

KEY CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Proposes a Bayesian lookahead data collection method for inferring HMMs with finite state and parameter spaces.
- Uses a belief state capturing the joint distribution of system states and models to optimize data collection under uncertainty.
- Develops a deep reinforcement learning policy (using Deep Q-Network/DQN) that approximates the optimal Bayesian solution by simulating system trajectories offline.
- The pre-trained policy can be executed in real-time and dynamically adapts to new conditions as data is collected.
- Supports point-based inference (ML, MAP), distribution-based inference (Bayesian), and causal inference objectives.

BACKGROUND/PROBLEM:
- Existing data collection methods (active learning, experimental design, sensor selection) are often greedy, short-term oriented, inefficient in high-uncertainty domains, and cannot account for long-term impacts of decisions.
- The non-identifiability issue in HMMs arises when different parameter sets produce the same observed data, especially under normal or tightly controlled system conditions.
- Exact computation of the optimal Bayesian policy is intractable because the belief space is a continuous (n×r)-simplex, preventing dynamic programming approaches.

METHODOLOGY:
- Formulates data collection as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) in belief space.
- Defines belief state as an n×r vector representing the joint probability of system states and models.
- Provides recursive belief update equations (equations 9-11) and matrix-form implementation using transition matrices and update vectors.
- Defines point-based reward (based on MAP confidence) and entropy reward (based on Shannon entropy of model posterior) functions.
- Uses DQN with Q-network and target network, epsilon-greedy policy, and replay memory for offline training using synthetic belief trajectories.

EXPERIMENTS:
- Evaluated on three distinct systems: (1) a general HMM with unknown state and measurement processes, (2) a gene regulatory network with unknown state process, and (3) a communication network with unknown measurement process.
- Results demonstrate significant improvements in inference accuracy and robustness in uncertain and data-limited environments.

INDEX TERMS: Hidden Markov Models, Inference, Reinforcement Learning, Causality. PMCID: PMC12045110, PMID: 40313356.

# Badminton Feint: Mastering the Pros' Deceptive Shots

The badminton feint is the two-part shot that turns a point around. Feinted drop shot, feinted smash, net slice: break them down like the pros.

12 min

The badminton deceptive shot is the weapon that transforms a routine rally into a winning point. It's that two-part shot where your preparation makes your opponent believe they're going to receive a smash, and you finish with a short drop shot. The imbalance is immediate: they move in the wrong direction, your shot lands far from their racket. When mastered, deception can swing two or three points per set in your favor — and that's often enough to win a close match.

### Key Takeaways

* Badminton deception relies on a two-part motion: preparation identical to the expected shot, then a last-moment change.
* Three main families: deceptive drop shot (smash preparation), deceptive smash (drop shot preparation), and net deception (slice and reverse slice).
* The timing of the change is everything: too early, the opponent reads the shot; too late, you miss contact.
* Pros (Axelsen, Ginting, Kunlavut) execute 5 to 10 deceptive shots per set on the BWF circuit.
* Training involves 4 steps: identical motion, then static change, then with movement, then in free play.

## Why Badminton Deception Makes a Difference

Badminton is played in fractions of a second. A shuttlecock takes about 0.6 seconds to cross the court on a drive and 0.3 seconds on a full-power smash. The opponent decides their movement by reading your preparation: shoulder cock, elbow position, racket angle. If you produce the arm cock of a smash and then hit a drop shot, their brain has already initiated a backward movement of their feet. When the shuttlecock lands short, they are half a step late — enough to miss the defense.

Deception isn't just for winning the point you play it on. It forces the opponent to wait for your strike before reacting, which slows down their entire reading of subsequent points. You pose a question: "Can I trust your preparation?" When the answer becomes no, their reaction time increases by 0.1 to 0.2 seconds on your normal shots too. At a high level, that's huge. You make your standard smash more effective just by having placed a deceptive shot two points earlier.

Tactically, deception also works by contrast: you don't need to play it every rally. A well-placed deceptive shot per set creates permanent doubt. Too many deceptive shots and you become predictable in your "unpredictability" — the opponent stops falling for it. The golden rule is to use it when they've committed to a strong response, not when they're static.

## Anatomy of a Badminton Deceptive Shot: The Two-Part Motion

Deception relies on two clearly separated parts. Part 1, identical preparation: your arm cock, your leg bend, your shoulder orientation identically reproduce the motion of an expected shot (most often a powerful smash). The opponent identifies the pattern and commits to their response. Part 2, the change: at the last moment, your forearm or wrist changes direction and sends a different shot — a short drop, a high clear, a flat drive.

What ruins deception for amateurs is almost always Part 1. If you prepare weakly, the opponent reads the weak shot before the change and doesn't commit. The rule: the preparation for a deceptive shot must be as committed as that for a real shot — even more so, because you need to convince. If you tense up in anticipation of the change, your arm cock becomes soft, and the deception fails.

Part 2 requires grip and wrist mastery. You switch from a flexion strike (smash) to a placement strike (drop shot), which engages different muscles. Without repeated practice, the motion comes out choppy, and the deceptive effect disappears. To delve deeper into striking technique, the article [badminton striking technique](/en/blog/technique-frappe-badminton) covers the breakdown of the arm cock and acceleration that serves as the basis for all deceptive shots.

## Deceptive Drop Shot: The Most Accessible Badminton Deception

The deceptive drop shot is the first and most profitable deceptive shot to learn. You prepare for a full-power smash: high arm cock, elbow back, legs bent, eyes on the shuttlecock. The opponent retreats to the back to defend. At the moment of contact, you hold back the strike and guide the shuttlecock short, just behind the net.

Three technical keys to success:

* Keep the arm cock until the last moment. If you break your arm cock too early, the opponent sees the deceleration and moves to the net — the deception is ruined.
* Touch the shuttlecock with the racket face for placement. No sharp hit, just a soft contact that transfers 25 to 30% of the energy of a standard smash.
* Stay high on impact. A deceptive drop shot hit below shoulder level loses its deceptive effect — the downward trajectory becomes visible too early.

The deceptive drop shot is Viktor Axelsen's favorite weapon in close sets. Check out the analyses on his profile [Viktor Axelsen](/en/joueurs/viktor-axelsen) to see him in action: he often chains three to four deceptive drop shots per set when he feels his opponent retreating too early. The basic technique of the standard drop shot is covered in the [badminton drop shot guide](/en/blog/amorti-badminton), to be mastered before adding deception on top.

## Deceptive Smash: The Badminton Deception That Surprises in Attack

The deceptive smash is the opposite: you prepare a drop shot and finish with a smash. It's rarer in competition because it requires wrist explosiveness in Part 2, and the opponent must be sufficiently advanced to be surprised. But when it comes out, it hurts and often ends the rally.

A more common and profitable variation: drop shot preparation followed by a flat clear or a tight drive. You sell the short shot, the opponent moves their feet towards the net, you send a tight shuttlecock that passes over their head. The tactical advantage is immediate — they have to switch back urgently, and their return will be soft.

Anthony Sinisuka Ginting is a specialist in the jumping deceptive smash. His preparation is identical for the drop shot, the clear, and the full-power smash — he plays 100% on wrist angle and forearm speed at contact. His profile [Anthony Sinisuka Ginting](/en/joueurs/anthony-sinisuka-ginting) compiles his analyzed matches where this pattern regularly appears. For the acceleration technique and the grip of the standard smash, the [badminton smash technique complete guide](/en/blog/technique-smash-badminton-guide-complet) covers the fundamentals to master before adding deception.

## Badminton Net Deception: Slice and Reverse Slice

At the net, deception changes nature. You no longer hide power; you disguise the direction and speed of the shuttlecock. Two main variations dominate at a high level.

First, the cross-court slice. You prepare a short parallel placement (the expected shot on a service return), then at contact, you cut the racket diagonally to send the shuttlecock cross-court, to the opposite side. The opponent anticipated a straight trajectory to their side; they are poorly positioned for the diagonal. This is the classic successful short service return shot.

Then, the reverse slice. This is the gem of Asian players. You prepare an expected forehand on the diagonal, and at contact, you reverse the direction of the slice to send the shuttlecock to the opponent's backhand side. Technically difficult because you turn the racket against the natural movement of the wrist, but devastating when well executed — the opponent has already taken half a step in the wrong direction.

Kunlavut Vitidsarn is a master of the net slice. The match [Kunlavut Vitidsarn vs Anders Antonsen at the Thailand Open 2026](/en/pro/cmpcp41r400020umex9vujfhl) shows several of these on short service returns, especially at the beginning of the set when he calibrates his opponent's reading. His profile [Kunlavut Vitidsarn](/en/joueurs/kunlavut-vitidsarn) lists all his analyzed matches on the platform.

## Pro Masters of Badminton Deception

Three players stand out on the BWF World Tour for their use of deception in men's singles play. Each has their own style.

* Viktor Axelsen, the deceptive drop shot as a set-winning key, especially when the opponent is confident and playing aggressively. His arm cock is slow and ample, maximizing the deceptive effect on the change — the opponent has plenty of time to commit to their defense.
* Anthony Sinisuka Ginting, the deceptive smash and deceptive drive in fast play. His jumping motion remains identical for all three shots (smash, drop, drive) — he plays 100% on wrist angle and forearm speed.
* Kunlavut Vitidsarn, net deceptions (slice and reverse slice) on short service returns and short rallies. His touch is so precise that he can place the deceptive shot in a 30-centimeter zone on the opponent's court.

To go further on attack techniques used on the pro circuit, the [Badminton World Federation](https://bwfbadminton.com) regularly publishes shot-by-shot analyses of major finals. You can also refer to the [badminton](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badminton) entry on Wikipedia FR for the general context of rules and regulated shots.

## How to Practice Badminton Deception in Training

Training progression occurs in four stages. Skipping a stage results in a motion that never comes out in a match.

Stage 1, identical motion (weeks 1 to 2). You work solely on preparation. You chain 50 expected shots (smash, for example) with exactly the same arm cock. Objective: reproducibility of the preparation motion before adding the change. Film yourself from the front and side to visually verify that your 50 repetitions are identical.

Stage 2, motion plus change without movement (weeks 3 to 4). Multi-shuttles sent to the same spot, you alternate an expected shot and a deceptive shot. The partner or coach doesn't know which shot you're going to hit. You look for the right timing for the change — not too early, not too late. Allow five to six seconds of recovery between each shot to stay focused on quality.

Stage 3, motion plus change plus movement (weeks 5 to 6). You move before the shot. The deceptive shot comes at the end of a movement towards the back or towards the net. This is where it gets complicated — leg and shoulder coordination must remain clean. The hitting foot must land at the right moment for the arm cock to remain stable.

Stage 4, in directed play then free play (week 7 and beyond). You integrate a deceptive shot every five to six points in a themed rally, then in free play. You don't play the deceptive shot every time, otherwise the element of surprise disappears. To verify that your preparation truly remains identical between an expected shot and a deceptive shot, you can [upload a 30-second video to BadmintonPeak](/en/dashboard/new-analysis) — the AI analyzes your arm cock and tells you if the shot reading changes between the two versions.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### From what level can one start working on badminton deception?

You can start working on it as soon as your standard shot (smash, drop) is stable and reproducible. Without a clean drop shot, the deceptive drop shot won't come out. Allow one year of regular practice on the fundamentals before pushing deceptive shots in specific training. Before that, stick to simple shots — that's what pays off most in matches at an intermediate level.

### Is deception legal in competition?

Yes. The entire motion of the player up to contact with the shuttlecock is part of the allowed play, including last-moment angle changes. The only rule that applies is on the serve: no feinting forward or backward movement before contact (BWF rule 9.1.6). Outside of the serve, you can feint as much as your imagination allows.

### How many deceptive shots should be used per set in a match?

On the pro circuit, analyzed match statistics show between 5 and 10 deceptive shots per set in men's singles. For an amateur, aim for 2 to 3 well-placed deceptive shots per set — deception is effective by contrast with your normal shots, not by repetition. Too many deceptive shots and the opponent stops falling for the preparation.

### What most often ruins a deceptive shot in a match?

Three things repeatedly come up. A too-soft preparation (the opponent reads the weak shot before the change). A too-early change (the transition is visible before contact, the deceptive effect fails). And a bad choice of moment (the opponent is already well-placed or static, the deceptive shot has no effect). The golden rule: use deception when they've committed to a strong response, not when they're waiting.

### Can deceptive shots be practiced without a partner?

Partially. You can work on the motion with a wall or a shuttlecock basket — Stage 1 and the beginning of Stage 2 are accessible alone. But the timing of the change in real conditions can only be set with an opponent who reacts. A training partner remains indispensable for Stages 3 and 4, and even more so for free play.

Badminton deception is what separates the predictable player from the dangerous player. If you want to verify that your preparation is truly identical between an expected shot and a deceptive shot — the technical key to the entire mechanism — [upload a 30-second video to BadmintonPeak](/en/dashboard/new-analysis). The AI analyzes your arm cock, leg bend, and wrist angle, and tells you exactly when your intention becomes readable by the opponent.

This webpage from BadmintonPeak is a comprehensive guide to mastering deceptive shots ("feints") in badminton, aimed at helping players learn the techniques used by professional players to win points through deception.

**Key Concepts:**
- Badminton deception is a two-part motion: (1) preparation identical to the expected shot (e.g., a smash), and (2) a last-moment change that sends a different shot.
- A shuttlecock takes 0.6 seconds to cross the court on a drive and 0.3 seconds on a full-power smash, making deception effective because opponents commit to a movement based on reading the preparation.
- Deception also slows down the opponent's reading of subsequent points, increasing their reaction time by 0.1-0.2 seconds on normal shots.

**Three Main Deceptive Shot Families:**
1. **Deceptive drop shot** (smash preparation, finished with a short drop) — described as the most accessible and profitable; Viktor Axelsen's favorite weapon, using a slow, ample arm cock and often chaining 3-4 per set.
2. **Deceptive smash** (drop shot preparation, finished with a smash) and its variation (drop prep followed by flat clear/tight drive) — Anthony Sinisuka Ginting specializes in this, playing 100% on wrist angle and forearm speed with identical jumping motion for all shots.
3. **Net deception** (slice and reverse slice) — cross-court slice disguises direction; reverse slice is a technically difficult move favored by Asian players. Kunlavut Vitidsarn is a master, able to place deceptive shots in a 30-centimeter zone.

**Training Progression (4 Stages):**
- Stage 1 (weeks 1-2): Identical motion — chain 50 expected shots with identical arm cock.
- Stage 2 (weeks 3-4): Motion plus change without movement, alternating expected and deceptive shots.
- Stage 3 (weeks 5-6): Add movement before the shot, maintaining leg-shoulder coordination.
- Stage 4 (week 7+): Integrate deceptive shots every 5-6 points in directed then free play.

**FAQ Highlights:**
- Legal in competition except on serves (BWF rule 9.1.6 prohibits feinting before serve contact).
- Pros execute 5-10 deceptive shots per set in men's singles; amateurs should aim for 2-3 per set.
- Common failures: too-soft preparation, too-early change, and poor timing (using it when opponent is static).
- Can be practiced partially alone (Stages 1-2) but requires a partner for Stages 3-4.
- Recommended to start after one year of fundamentals practice.

The page also promotes BadmintonPeak's AI video analysis tool, which evaluates a player's arm cock, leg bend, and wrist angle by uploading a 30-second video.
