# ShuttleSet22: Benchmarking Stroke Forecasting with Stroke-Level Badminton Dataset

###### Abstract

In recent years, badminton analytics has drawn attention due to the advancement of artificial intelligence and the efficiency of data collection.
While there is a line of effective applications to improve and investigate player performance, there are only a few public badminton datasets that can be used for researchers outside the badminton domain.
Existing badminton singles datasets focus on specific matchups; however, they cannot provide comprehensive studies on different players and various matchups.
In this paper, we provide a badminton singles dataset, ShuttleSet22, which is collected from high-ranking matches in 2022.
ShuttleSet22 consists of 30,172 strokes in 2,888 rallies in the training set, 1,400 strokes in 450 rallies in the validation set, and 2,040 strokes in 654 rallies in the testing set with detailed stroke-level metadata within a rally.
To benchmark existing work with ShuttleSet22, we test the state-of-the-art stroke forecasting approach, ShuttleNet, with the corresponding stroke forecasting task, i.e., predict the future strokes based on the given strokes of each rally.
We also hold a challenge, Track 2: Forecasting Future Turn-Based Strokes in Badminton Rallies, at CoachAI Badminton Challenge 2023 to boost researchers to tackle this problem.
The baseline codes and the dataset will be made available at the GitHub repo11
1
https://github.com/wywyWang/CoachAI-Projects/tree/main/CoachAI-Challenge-IJCAI2023/Track%202%3A%20Stroke%20Forecasting.

## 1 Introduction

Sports analytics has captured increasing attention since the advancement of technology brings great convenience for data collection and increases data diversity.
In recent years, there is a line of studies applying advanced artificial intelligence techniques, e.g., computer vision on video frames [Kim et al. 2022](#bib.bib7), motion tracking with sensors [Ito and Gotoh 2018](#bib.bib6); [Pillitteri et al. 2021](#bib.bib9), and machine learning models for action valuing [Decroos et al. 2019](#bib.bib4); [Merhej et al. 2021](#bib.bib8).
Badminton serves as one of the major racket sports in the world in terms of participation, and it demands high physical and tactical conditions, which has attracted researchers on introducing novel applications [Wang et al. 2020](#bib.bib10); [Wang et al. 2021](#bib.bib11).
For instance, [Wang et al. 2022a](#bib.bib12) proposes long short-term extractors to quantify the win influence of each shot within a rally.
[Chang et al. 2022](#bib.bib3) designs the movement forecasting task to predict the players’ movements with graph-based approaches.

In this paper, we aim to release, ShuttleSet22, a stroke-level badminton singles dataset collected from high-ranking matches in 2022.
ShuttleSet22 is an extension from ShuttleSet [Wang et al. 2023](#bib.bib14) encompassing with 30,172 strokes (2,888 rallies), 1,400 strokes (450 rallies) in the validation set, and 2,040 strokes (654 rallies) in the testing set.
While ShuttleSet22 shares similar stroke-level data formats with ShuttleSet, ShuttleSet22 consists of matches in 2022 instead of between 2018 and 2021.
Therefore, ShuttleSet can be viewed as the latest iteration of the badminton singles dataset that can be used to examine the model’s effectiveness in recent matches.
ShuttleSet22 is obtained from the public videos22
2
http://bwf.tv/ and is labeled by domain experts with the shot-by-shot labeling tool [Huang et al. 2022](#bib.bib5).

To boost researchers’ engagements in badminton analytics, we, for the first time, create a challenge in CoachAI Badminton Challenge 202333
3
https://sites.google.com/view/coachai-challenge-2023/ in conjunction with IJCAI 2023.
Specifically, we hold the forecasting of future turn-based strokes in badminton rallies (Track 2) and provide the state-of-the-art stroke forecasting approach [Wang et al. 2022b](#bib.bib13) as the official baseline.
This track has attracted about 100 participants to join for improving the effectiveness of the stroke forecasting task.

The paper is organized as follows: Related work is described in Section 2, the details of the stroke forecasting task, the data exploration, and the official baseline are introduced in Section 3, methods of participants are summarized in Section 4, the results from participants are depicted in Section 5, and we conclude our findings in Section 6.
We select it as the official baseline due to not only the state-of-the-art performance but also the first work for turn-based sequence prediction.

## 2 Related Work: Public Badminton Datasets

|  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | # Players | # Match | # Rally | # Stroke | Year |
| ShuttleSet22 (Ours) | 35 | 58 | 3,992 | 33,612 | 2022 |
| BadmintonDB [Ban et al. 2022](#bib.bib1) | 2 | 9 | 811 | 9,671 | 2018-2020 |

Generally, there are only a few public badminton datasets due to the heavy cost of collecting and labeling fine-grained records by domain experts [Wang 2022](#bib.bib15).
Recently, researchers have released badminton datasets to foster the sports community.
For instance, the shuttlecock datasets [Cartron 2022](#bib.bib2) contains 8K images of shuttlecocks which are resized to 640\*640 pixels. This dataset includes the position of shuttlecocks which could train an object detection model.
The BadmintonDB [Ban et al. 2022](#bib.bib1) features rally, strokes, and outcome annotations between two players, which can be used in player-specific match analysis and prediction tasks, which is also the stroke-level dataset.
However, BadmintonDB only consists of the same matchup (i.e., Kento Momota and Anthony Sinisuka Ginting) instead of the various matchups.
Moreover, BadmintonDB collects matches from 2018 to 2020, while our ShuttleSet22 collects high-ranking matches in 2022 to reflect the state-of-the-art tactic records.
We summarize the discrepancies between our ShuttleSet and BadmintonDB in Table [1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 2 Related Work: Public Badminton Datasets ‣ ShuttleSet22: Benchmarking Stroke Forecasting with Stroke-Level Badminton Dataset").

## 3 Task Details

![Refer to caption](2306.15664v1/figure/flowchart.jpg)

The goal of this shared task is to forecasting future turn-based strokes in badminton rallies, which aims to design forecasting models that are able to predict future strokes including shot types and locations based on the past stroke sequences.
Figure [1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3 Task Details ‣ ShuttleSet22: Benchmarking Stroke Forecasting with Stroke-Level Badminton Dataset") shows the whole flowchart of our task. The task page is available on [Codalab](https://codalab.lisn.upsaclay.fr/competitions/12017?secret_key=ba1acc46-1279-4781-94f4-0510fdb017ca).

### 3.1 Problem Formulation

Following [Wang et al. 2022b](#bib.bib13), for each singles rally, given the observed τ\tau strokes with type-area pairs and two players, the goal is to predict the future strokes including shot types and area coordinates for the next nn steps.
To simplify the problem, τ\tau is set to be 4 in our challenge, and nn is various based on the length of the rally.

Let R={Sr,Pr}r=1|R|R=\{S\_{r},P\_{r}\}\_{r=1}^{|R|} denote historical rallies of badminton matches, where the rr-th rally is composed of a stroke sequence with type-area pairs Sr=(⟨s1,a1⟩,⋯,⟨s|Sr|,a|Sr|⟩)S\_{r}=(\langle s\_{1},a\_{1}\rangle,\cdots,\langle s\_{|S\_{r}|},a\_{|S\_{r}|}\rangle) and a player sequence Pr=(p1,⋯,p|Sr|)P\_{r}=(p\_{1},\cdots,p\_{|S\_{r}|}).
At the ii-th stroke, sis\_{i} represents the shot type, ai=⟨xi,yi⟩∈ℝ2a\_{i}=\langle x\_{i},y\_{i}\rangle\in\mathbb{R}^{2} are the coordinates of the shuttle destinations, and pip\_{i} is the player who hits the shuttle. We denote Player A as the served player and Player B as the other for each rally in this paper. For instance, given a singles rally between Player A and Player B, PrP\_{r} may become (A,B,⋯,A,B)(A,B,\cdots,A,B).
We formulate the problem of stroke forecasting as follows. For each rally, given the observed τ\tau strokes (⟨si,ai⟩)i=1τ(\langle s\_{i},a\_{i}\rangle)\_{i=1}^{\tau} with players (pi)i=1τ(p\_{i})\_{i=1}^{\tau}, the goal is to predict the future strokes including shot types and area coordinates for the next nn steps, i.e., (⟨si,ai⟩)i=τ+1τ+n(\langle s\_{i},a\_{i}\rangle)\_{i={\tau+1}}^{\tau+n}.
We note that nn is pre-defined as the actual length of the corresponding rally.

### 3.3 Evaluation Metrics

The evaluation scenarios will be evaluated by cross-entropy for shot type prediction and mean absolute error (MAE) for area coordinates prediction similar to the original work.
Since this task exists stochasticity, we will also ask each team to generate 6 predicted sequences of each rally and take the closest one to ground truth for evaluation.
We note that the original work of the stroke forecasting task is to generate 10 sequences, which we change to 6 for efficiency.

### 3.4 Official Baseline

Generally, ShuttleNet [Wang et al. 2022b](#bib.bib13) is a position-aware fusion of rally progress and player styles framework consisting of Transformer-based architectures.
ShuttleNet separates the contexts of both players to consider the overall playing habits for predicting the next strokes.

## 4 Participating Systems

There are about 95 participants joining the challenge system, and 16 teams submitted their testing results for the final phase in the CoachAI Badminton Challenge 2023 (Track 2).
Most teams modified the official baseline (i.e., ShuttleNet) to approach the task.
The brief descriptions of the submitted methods are summarized in Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 5 Results ‣ ShuttleSet22: Benchmarking Stroke Forecasting with Stroke-Level Badminton Dataset").

We can observe that Team Intro\_to\_AI\_team 8 outperforms the competition slightly than Team Badminseok, while Team YHY performs the best in terms of area predictions.
There are 11 teams that perform better than ShuttleNet; however, we notice that these methods are built on top of ShuttleNet, which demonstrates the flexibility of ShuttleNet and some designs (e.g., hyper-parameters and activation functions) can be improved.
In addition, the improvements of the participating teams mainly focus on the shot type prediction (2.1777 →\rightarrow 1.7892); however, the performance of area coordinates only slightly performs better than ShuttleNet (0.6997 →\rightarrow 0.6797), where most teams are inferior to the baseline.
This points out the challenge of effectively incorporating two predictions, which is a potential future direction to explore.

## 6 Conclusion

In this paper, we propose ShuttleSet22, an extended dataset from ShuttleSet with stroke-level badminton singles records.
ShuttleSet22 consists of fine-grained metadata for researchers to utilize various aspects for discovering thoughtful insights.
Exploratory data analysis is conducted to illustrate the fundamental compositions of the dataset to bridge the gap between researchers outside the badminton domain.
To foster researchers to incorporate advanced techniques with badminton analytics, we hold Track 2, a challenge in CoachAI Badminton Challenge 2023 that focuses on improving the effectiveness of stroke forecasting.
In addition, we replicate the state-of-the-art baseline for the task as the official baseline.
Methods and insights from participants are summarized and discussed to provide potential improvements for future research.

args.summary:
This paper introduces ShuttleSet22, a stroke-level badminton singles dataset collected from high-ranking matches in 2022, presented in conjunction with the CoachAI Badminton Challenge 2023 at IJCAI 2023 (Track 2: Forecasting Future Turn-Based Strokes in Badminton Rallies). The dataset contains 30,172 strokes in 2,888 rallies for training, 1,400 strokes in 450 rallies for validation, and 2,040 strokes in 654 rallies for testing, collected from 35 players across 58 matches (3,992 rallies, 33,612 strokes total) using publicly available videos from bwf.tv and labeled by domain experts. It extends the original ShuttleSet dataset (which covered 2018-2021 matches) and differs from the only other stroke-level public dataset, BadmintonDB, which covers only a single matchup (Kento Momota vs. Anthony Sinisuka Ginting) and matches from 2018-2020.

The stroke forecasting task is formulated as follows: given the observed τ=4 strokes (shot type-area pairs) with player sequences, predict the future strokes (shot types and landing coordinates) for the next n steps, where n equals the actual remaining rally length. Evaluation uses cross-entropy (CE) for shot type prediction and mean absolute error (MAE) for area coordinate prediction, with teams generating 6 predicted sequences per rally and taking the closest to ground truth. The official baseline is ShuttleNet, a Transformer-based position-aware fusion framework that separates both players' contexts.

About 95 participants joined the challenge, with 16 teams submitting final results. The winning team (Intro_to_AI_team8) achieved a total score of 2.5776 (CE: 1.7892, MAE: 0.7884) by simplifying the ShuttleNet architecture (removing unnecessary embeddings and activation functions), outperforming the ShuttleNet baseline (2.8774 total). Notably, 11 teams beat the baseline, with most improvements focused on shot type prediction (2.1777 → 1.7892) rather than area coordinates (0.6997 → 0.6797), highlighting the challenge of jointly optimizing both predictions. Key exploratory findings include that most players position themselves at court centers and four corners when attacking, and near center when defending; and that all shot types except Clear and Smash avoid around-head hits, with most short services hit below the net and most long services above it. The dataset and baseline codes are publicly available on GitHub.

## Abstract

The increasing demand for analyzing the insights in sports has stimulated a line of productive studies from a variety of perspectives, e.g., health state monitoring, outcome prediction. In this paper, we focus on objectively judging what and where to return strokes, which is still unexplored in turn-based sports. By formulating stroke forecasting as a sequence prediction task, existing works can tackle the problem but fail to model information based on the characteristics of badminton. To address these limitations, we propose a novel Position-aware Fusion of Rally Progress and Player Styles framework (ShuttleNet) that incorporates rally progress and information of the players by two modified encoder-decoder extractors. Moreover, we design a fusion network to integrate rally contexts and contexts of the players by conditioning on information dependency and different positions. Extensive experiments on the badminton dataset demonstrate that ShuttleNet significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art methods and also empirically validates the feasibility of each component in ShuttleNet. On top of that, we provide an analysis scenario for the stroke forecasting problem.

# Benchmarking Stroke Forecasting with Stroke-Level Badminton Dataset

###### Abstract

In recent years, badminton analytics has drawn attention due to the advancement of artificial intelligence and the efficiency of data collection.
While there is a line of effective applications to improve and investigate player performance, there are only a few public badminton datasets that can be used by researchers outside the badminton domain.
Existing badminton singles datasets focus on specific matchups; however, they cannot provide comprehensive studies on different players and various matchups.
In this paper, we provide a badminton singles dataset, ShuttleSet22, which is collected from high-ranking matches in 2022.
ShuttleSet22 consists of 30,172 strokes in 2,888 rallies in the training set, 1,400 strokes in 450 rallies in the validation set, and 2,040 strokes in 654 rallies in the testing set, with detailed stroke-level metadata within a rally.
To benchmark existing work with ShuttleSet22, we hold a challenge, Track 2: Forecasting Future Turn-Based Strokes in Badminton Rallies, at CoachAI Badminton Challenge @ IJCAI 2023, to encourage researchers to tackle this real-world problem through innovative approaches and to summarize insights between the state-of-the-art baseline and improved techniques, exchanging inspiring ideas.
The baseline codes and the dataset are made available at the GitHub repo11
1
https://github.com/wywyWang/CoachAI-Projects/tree/main/CoachAI-Challenge-IJCAI2023.

## 1 Introduction

Sports analytics has garnered increasing attention since the advancement of technology, which greatly facilitates data collection and increases data diversity.
In recent years, there has been a surge in studies applying advanced artificial intelligence techniques, e.g., computer vision on video frames [Kim et al. 2022](#bib.bib7), and machine learning models for action valuing [Decroos et al. 2019](#bib.bib5); [Merhej et al. 2021](#bib.bib8).
Badminton, as one of the major racket sports worldwide in terms of participation, demands high physical and tactical conditions, attracting researchers to introduce novel applications [Wang et al. 2020](#bib.bib9).
For instance, [Wang et al. 2022a](#bib.bib11) propose long short-term extractors to quantify the win influence of each shot within a rally, while [Chang et al. 2023](#bib.bib3) design the movement forecasting task to predict players’ movements using graph-based approaches.

In this paper, our aim is to introduce, ShuttleSet22, a stroke-level badminton singles dataset collected from real-world high-ranking matches in 2022.
ShuttleSet22 extends the original ShuttleSet [Wang et al. 2023](#bib.bib13), comprising 30,172 strokes (2,888 rallies), 1,400 strokes (450 rallies) in the validation set, and 2,040 strokes (654 rallies) in the testing set.
While ShuttleSet22 shares similar stroke-level data formats with ShuttleSet, it consists of matches in 2022 instead of the period between 2018 and 2021.
Therefore, ShuttleSet22 can be considered the most recent iteration of the badminton singles dataset, enabling the examination of model effectiveness in recent matches.
ShuttleSet22 is sourced from public videos22
2
http://bwf.tv/ and has been meticulously labeled by domain experts with the shot-by-shot labeling tool [Huang et al. 2022](#bib.bib6).

## 2 Related Work: Public Badminton Datasets

Generally, there are only a few public badminton datasets due to the heavy cost of collecting and labeling fine-grained records by domain experts [Wang 2022](#bib.bib14).
Recently, researchers have released badminton datasets to foster the sports community.
For instance, the shuttlecock datasets [Cartron 2022](#bib.bib2) contains 8K images of shuttlecocks which are resized to 640\*640 pixels. This dataset includes the position of shuttlecocks which could train an object detection model.
The BadmintonDB [Ban et al. 2022](#bib.bib1) features rally, strokes, and outcome annotations between two players, which can be used in player-specific match analysis and prediction tasks, which is also the stroke-level dataset.
However, BadmintonDB only consists of the same matchup (i.e., Kento Momota and Anthony Sinisuka Ginting) instead of the various matchups.
Moreover, BadmintonDB collects matches from 2018 to 2020, while our ShuttleSet22 collects high-ranking matches in 2022 to reflect the state-of-the-art tactic records.
We summarize the discrepancies between our ShuttleSet and BadmintonDB in Table [1](#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Benchmarking Stroke Forecasting with Stroke-Level Badminton Dataset").

## 3 The Challenge System

![Refer to caption](2306.15664v3/figure/flowchart.jpg)

Conventional applications in badminton mainly focus on quantifying stroke performance [Wang et al. 2021](#bib.bib10) or retrieving information from videos [Chu and Situmeang 2017](#bib.bib4), which motivates us to further investigate a more challenging yet critical real-world application.
The goal of this shared task is to forecasting future turn-based strokes in badminton rallies, which aims to design forecasting models capable of predicting future strokes, including shot types and locations, based on past stroke sequences.
Figure [1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3 The Challenge System ‣ Benchmarking Stroke Forecasting with Stroke-Level Badminton Dataset") illustrates the entire flowchart of our task.
As we have built the pipeline from data processing to evaluations, participants only need to modify the stroke forecasting model to swiftly iterate their approaches.
The task page is available on [Codalab](https://codalab.lisn.upsaclay.fr/competitions/12017?secret_key=ba1acc46-1279-4781-94f4-0510fdb017ca).

![Refer to caption](2306.15664v3/figure/player_opponent_location.jpg)

### 3.1 Problem Formulation

Following the definition outlined in [Wang et al. 2022b](#bib.bib12), for each singles rally, given the observed τ\tau strokes with type-area pairs and two players, the goal is to predict the future strokes, including shot types and area coordinates, for the next nn steps.
To simplify the problem, τ\tau is set to be 4 in our challenge, and nn is various based on the length of the rally, which is given to the participants.

Let R={Sr,Pr}r=1|R|R=\{S\_{r},P\_{r}\}\_{r=1}^{|R|} denote historical rallies of badminton matches, where the rr-th rally is composed of a stroke sequence with type-area pairs Sr=(⟨s1,a1⟩,⋯,⟨s|Sr|,a|Sr|⟩)S\_{r}=(\langle s\_{1},a\_{1}\rangle,\cdots,\langle s\_{|S\_{r}|},a\_{|S\_{r}|}\rangle) and a player sequence Pr=(p1,⋯,p|Sr|)P\_{r}=(p\_{1},\cdots,p\_{|S\_{r}|}).
At the ii-th stroke, sis\_{i} represents the shot type, ai=⟨xi,yi⟩∈ℝ2a\_{i}=\langle x\_{i},y\_{i}\rangle\in\mathbb{R}^{2} are the coordinates of the shuttle destinations, and pip\_{i} is the player who hits the shuttle. We denote Player A as the served player and Player B as the other for each rally in this paper. For instance, given a singles rally between Player A and Player B, PrP\_{r} may become (A,B,⋯,A,B)(A,B,\cdots,A,B).
We formulate the problem of stroke forecasting as follows. For each rally, given the observed τ\tau strokes (⟨si,ai⟩)i=1τ(\langle s\_{i},a\_{i}\rangle)\_{i=1}^{\tau} with players (pi)i=1τ(p\_{i})\_{i=1}^{\tau}, the goal is to predict the future strokes including shot types and area coordinates for the next nn steps, i.e., (⟨si,ai⟩)i=τ+1τ+n(\langle s\_{i},a\_{i}\rangle)\_{i={\tau+1}}^{\tau+n}.
We note that nn is pre-defined as the actual length of the corresponding rally.

### 3.2 Exploratory Data Analysis

We have released 58 matches, approximately 4,000 rallies with shot-level records following the BLSR format [Wang et al. 2022a](#bib.bib11) for this task, where parts of the matches from 2018 to 2021 are identical to those in [Wang et al. 2022b](#bib.bib12), while we have further included new matches collected from 2022.

Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 The Challenge System ‣ Benchmarking Stroke Forecasting with Stroke-Level Badminton Dataset") shows the heatmap of player location and opponent location, indicating that most players position themselves at both the center and the four corners of the courts when preparing to attack. On the contrary, when defending, players intend to stay predominantly in the center of the court to enable quick reactions to any type of shot.

Table [2](#S1.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Benchmarking Stroke Forecasting with Stroke-Level Badminton Dataset") presents the numbers of different strike orders by shot types.
It is evident that with the exception of the Clear and Smash shots, other shot types do not target around the head area.
Furthermore, more than half of the Push/Rush, Defensive Shot, and Short Service shots are executed with the backhand, while other shot types predominantly utilize the forehand.
Notably, there is a significant disparity in hitting position based on the service type, with almost all short services directed below the net and almost all long services aimed above the net.

### 3.3 Evaluation Metrics

The evaluation scenarios will be assessed by cross-entropy for shot type prediction and mean absolute error (MAE) for area coordinates prediction, similar to the original work.
Given the stochastic nature of this task, each team will be required to generate 6 predicted sequences for each rally, from which the closest one to the ground truth will be selected for evaluation.
It is worth noting that the original work on the stroke forecasting task involved generating 10 sequences, a number we have reduced to 6 for efficiency.

### 3.4 Official Baseline

Generally, ShuttleNet [Wang et al. 2022b](#bib.bib12) is a position-aware fusion of rally progress and player styles framework consisting of Transformer-based architectures.
ShuttleNet has demonstrated superior performance in predicting the next strokes compared to conventional sequential.
This is attributed to its turn-based architecture, which separates the styles of both players in a rally and integrates them with the current rally condition.

## 4 Participating System

Approximately 95 participants have joined the challenge system, with 16 teams submitting their testing results for the final phase of the CoachAI Badminton Challenge 2023 (Track 2).
Most teams modified the official baseline, ShuttleNet, to address the task.
The brief descriptions of the submitted methods are summarized in the video due to the page limit.

## 5 Results and Findings

Table [3](#S3.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 3.4 Official Baseline ‣ 3 The Challenge System ‣ Benchmarking Stroke Forecasting with Stroke-Level Badminton Dataset") reports the official leaderboard of the participants’ methods.
It is observed that Team Intro\_to\_AI\_team 8 slightly outperforms the competition Team Badminseok, while Team YHY demonstrates the best performance in terms of area predictions.
11 teams perform better than ShuttleNet; however, we notice that these methods are built on top of ShuttleNet, which highlights the flexibility of ShuttleNet and the potential for improvements in certain aspects, e.g., hyper-parameters and activation functions.
In addition, the improvements made by the participating teams primarily focus on the shot type prediction (2.1777 →\rightarrow 1.7892); however, the performance of area coordinates only marginally surpasses ShuttleNet (0.6997 →\rightarrow 0.6797), with most teams being inferior to the baseline.
This underscores the challenge of effectively integrating two predictions, which may be a potential future direction for exploration.

## 6 Conclusion

In this paper, we propose ShuttleSet22, an extended dataset from ShuttleSet with stroke-level badminton singles records.
ShuttleSet22 consists of fine-grained metadata to reinforce researchers to explore various aspects and derive insightful findings.
Exploratory data analysis is conducted to elucidate the fundamental compositions of the dataset, aiming to bridge the gap between researchers outside the badminton domain.
To foster researchers to incorporate advanced techniques into badminton analytics, we introduce Track 2, a challenge within CoachAI Badminton Challenge 2023, focused on enhancing the effectiveness of stroke forecasting.
In addition, we establish the state-of-the-art baseline for the task.
We summarize and discuss the methods and insights from participants to provide potential avenues for future research improvement.

args.summary:
This paper introduces ShuttleSet22, a stroke-level badminton singles dataset collected from high-ranking matches in 2022, and benchmarks stroke forecasting through the CoachAI Badminton Challenge @ IJCAI 2023 (Track 2: Forecasting Future Turn-Based Strokes in Badminton Rallies).

**Dataset Details:**
- ShuttleSet22 extends the original ShuttleSet (2018-2021) with 2022 matches, making it the most recent badminton singles dataset.
- Contains 35 players, 58 matches, 3,992 rallies, and 33,612 strokes total.
- Training set: 30,172 strokes in 2,888 rallies; Validation set: 1,400 strokes in 450 rallies; Testing set: 2,040 strokes in 654 rallies.
- Data sourced from public BWF videos and meticulously labeled by domain experts using a shot-by-shot labeling tool.

**Comparison to Existing Datasets:**
- BadmintonDB (the main prior stroke-level dataset) only covers 2 players, 9 matches, 811 rallies, and 9,671 strokes from 2018-2020, and focuses on a single matchup (Kento Momota vs. Anthony Sinisuka Ginting).
- ShuttleSet22 provides comprehensive coverage of various players and matchups, filling a critical gap in public badminton datasets.

**Problem Formulation:**
- Given observed τ=4 strokes with type-area pairs and two players, the goal is to predict future strokes (shot types and area coordinates) for the next n steps (n = actual rally length).
- Evaluation metrics: cross-entropy for shot type prediction and mean absolute error (MAE) for area coordinates.
- Teams generate 6 predicted sequences per rally, from which the closest to ground truth is selected (reduced from 10 in the original work).

**Exploratory Data Analysis Findings:**
- Players position themselves at both center and four corners of courts when attacking; defenders stay predominantly in the center for quick reactions.
- Except for Clear and Smash shots, most shot types do not target around the head area.
- More than half of Push/Rush, Defensive Shot, and Short Service shots are executed with backhand; other shot types predominantly use forehand.
- Almost all short services are directed below the net; almost all long services aim above the net.

**Challenge Results:**
- ~100 participants joined; 16 teams submitted final results.
- Winning team Intro_to_AI_team8 achieved CE 1.7892, MAE 0.7884, Total 2.5776.
- Team YHY demonstrated best MAE performance (0.6797).
- 11 teams outperformed the official ShuttleNet baseline (CE 2.1777, MAE 0.6997, Total 2.8774).
- Most improvements came from modifications to ShuttleNet (hyper-parameters, activation functions).
- Improvements primarily focused on shot type prediction (2.1777 → 1.7892), while area coordinate prediction only marginally improved (0.6997 → 0.6797), with most teams being inferior to baseline — highlighting the challenge of integrating the two predictions.

**Baseline Model:**
- ShuttleNet is a position-aware fusion of rally progress and player styles using Transformer-based architecture, with turn-based design that separates both players' styles and integrates them with current rally condition.

**Availability:**
- Baseline codes and dataset available at: https://github.com/wywyWang/CoachAI-Projects/tree/main/CoachAI-Challenge-IJCAI2023
- Challenge page on Codalab; presentation video at https://youtu.be/yhRouMpxb2M.
args.key_excerpts: "ShuttleSet22 consists of 30,172 strokes in 2,888 rallies in the training set, 1,400 strokes in 450 rallies in the validation set, and 2,040 strokes in 654 rallies in the testing set, with detailed stroke-level metadata within a rally."

# Computer Vision-Based Tracking and Tactical Analysis of Badminton Players

* Developed a real-time sports analysis system for badminton using a hybrid approach combining YOLOv8 for player detection and DeepSORT for multi-frame tracking.
* Built and annotated a custom dataset consisting of 200 clips from various real match footage to train the detection model, ensuring accurate performance across varied scenarios.
* Extracted key player movement metrics such as speed, acceleration, distance, and zone coverage for performance evaluation.
* Used LSTM for tactical zone prediction, achieving over 90% accuracy in anticipating player movement across court zones.

# Researchers develop a biomechanical dataset for badminton performance analysis

by [Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology](https://www.gist.ac.kr/en/)

![GIST-MIT CSAIL researchers develop a biomechanical dataset for badminton performance analysis](https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/800a/2024/gist-mit-csail-researc.jpg "The dataset proposed by the researchers captures badminton players' movements and responses, aiding AI-driven coaching assistants to improve stroke quality for all skill levels. Credit: SeungJun Kim at Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (GIST)")

In sports training, practice is the key, but being able to emulate the techniques of professional athletes can take a player's performance to the next level. AI-based personalized sports coaching assistants can make this a reality by utilizing published datasets. With cameras and sensors strategically placed on the athlete's body, these systems can track everything, including joint movement patterns, muscle activation levels, and gaze movements.

Using this data, personalized feedback is provided on player technique, along with improvement recommendations. Athletes can access this feedback anytime, and anywhere, making these systems versatile for athletes at all levels.

In a study published in the journal [*Scientific Data*](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-024-03144-z) on April 5, 2024, researchers led by Associate Professor SeungJun Kim from the Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (GIST), South Korea, in collaboration with researchers from Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), CSAIL, U.S., have developed a MultiSenseBadminton dataset for AI-driven badminton [training](https://techxplore.com/tags/training/).

"Badminton could benefit from these various sensors, but there is a scarcity of comprehensive badminton action datasets for analysis and training feedback," says Ph.D. candidate Minwoo Seong, the first author of the study.

The study took inspiration from MIT's ActionSense project, which used wearable sensors to track everyday kitchen tasks such as peeling, slicing vegetables, and opening jars. Seong collaborated with MIT's team, including MIT CSAIL postdoc researcher Joseph DelPreto and MIT CSAIL Director and MIT EECS Professor Daniela Rus and Wojciech Matusik. Together, they developed the MultiSenseBadminton dataset, capturing movements and physiological responses of badminton players.

This dataset, shaped with insights from professional badminton coaches, aims to enhance the quality of forehand clear and backhand drive strokes. For this, the researchers collected 23 hours of swing motion data from 25 players with varying levels of training experience.

During the study, players were tasked with repeatedly executing forehand clear and backhand drive shots while sensors recorded their movements and responses. These included inertial measurement units (IMU) sensors to track joint movements, electromyography (EMG) sensors to monitor muscle signals, insole sensors for foot pressure, and a camera to record both body movements and shuttlecock positions.

With a total of 7,763 data points collected, each swing was meticulously labeled based on stroke type, player's skill level, shuttlecock landing position, impact location relative to the player, and sound upon impact. The dataset was then validated using a machine learning model, ensuring its suitability for training AI models to evaluate stroke quality and offer feedback.

"The MultiSenseBadminton dataset can be used to build AI-based education and training systems for racket sports players. By analyzing the disparities in motion and [sensor data](https://techxplore.com/tags/sensor+data/) among different levels of players and creating AI-generated action trajectories, the dataset can be applied to personalized motion guides for each level of players," says Seong.

The gathered data can enhance training through haptic vibration or electrical muscle stimulation, promoting better motion and refining swing techniques. Additionally, player tracking data, like that in the MultiSenseBadminton dataset, could fuel virtual reality games or training simulations, making sports training more accessible and affordable, potentially transforming how people exercise.

Researchers at the Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (GIST) in South Korea, in collaboration with researchers from MIT CSAIL (including Joseph DelPreto, Daniela Rus, and Wojciech Matusik), have developed the MultiSenseBadminton dataset for AI-driven badminton training. The study was published in the journal Scientific Data on April 5, 2024, and led by Associate Professor SeungJun Kim of GIST, with Ph.D. candidate Minwoo Seong as first author.

The dataset captures biomechanical data from badminton players using multiple wearable sensors, including inertial measurement units (IMU) for joint movements, electromyography (EMG) sensors for muscle signals, insole sensors for foot pressure, and a camera for body movements and shuttlecock positions. The researchers collected 23 hours of swing motion data from 25 players with varying skill levels, resulting in 7,763 data points. Each swing was meticulously labeled based on stroke type, player skill level, shuttlecock landing position, impact location, and sound upon impact.

The dataset was inspired by MIT's ActionSense project and was shaped with insights from professional badminton coaches. It focuses on enhancing forehand clear and backhand drive strokes. The dataset was validated using a machine learning model to ensure its suitability for training AI models to evaluate stroke quality and offer feedback.

Potential applications include AI-based education and training systems for racket sports, personalized motion guides for different skill levels, haptic vibration or electrical muscle stimulation training, and virtual reality games or training simulations. The researchers note that badminton could benefit from these sensors, but there was previously a scarcity of comprehensive badminton action datasets for analysis and training feedback.

The study is published as: Minwoo Seong et al, MultiSenseBadminton: Wearable Sensor–Based Biomechanical Dataset for Evaluation of Badminton Performance, Scientific Data (2024), DOI: 10.1038/s41597-024-03144-z.

## Abstract

This paper introduces BadmintonDB, a new badminton dataset for training models for player-specific match analysis and prediction tasks, which are interesting challenges. The dataset features rally, strokes, and outcome annotations of 9 real-world badminton matches between two top players. We discussed our methodologies and processes behind selecting and annotating the matches. We also proposed player-independent and player-dependent Naive Bayes baselines for rally outcome prediction. The paper concludes with the analysis performed on the experiments to study the effects of player-dependent model on the prediction performances. We released our dataset at https://github.com/kwban/badminton-db.

## Kosolapov Sergey

# Tennis analysis using deep learning and machine learning.

![Kosolapov Sergey](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:64:64/0*Jd34YNro5bC4gYoA.jpg)

--

10

Listen

Share

Tennis is a sport played all over the world. Watching a tennis game, you could enrich the view automatically with numbers of serves through the middle or in the corners, how deep the ball is being played, preferences for left or right, depending on where the player is positioned. Such statistics can be provided by tools like Hawk-Eye, IBM Slamtracker and so on.

Hawk-Eye is a complex system comprising up to ten high-speed cameras, which are able to track the ball with high accuracy, obtain its real-world position and display a reconstruction of any bounces.

IBM Slamtracker, an application presenting real-time scores and statistics (between 15 and 25 parameters for each point) to augment the experience of fans. This system is extremely accurate but also highly sophisticated, comprising between 8 to 10 high-speed cameras (up to 1 000 fps) and an extremely powerful computer. The fact that this technology is equipment-intensive, costly and requires expertise to install it on a court restricts its availability to the high profile venues of major tournaments.

Our goal is to create a video analysis tool which includes ball tracking, court tracking, bounce detection and players tracking, based on only one single camera with 25–30 fps.

![]()

## **Court detection**

Detecting the court lines is a necessary step for our system in order to represent the position of the players and ball within a meaningful coordinate system

![]()

Existed approach, based on classical computer vision, consists of several steps:

We know that the lines of tennis courts are always white. For this reason, pixels with an intensity value higher than certain threshold in a monochrome image of the court are extracted from original image.

![]()

2. Detect lines (with Hough Transform) and classify them as horizontal and vertical ones

![]()

3. Compare resulting lines with reference court configuration

We know reference court configuration and how lines are located to each other. We want to compare binary map with vertical and horizontal lines with reference configuration. To determine how one image can be projected onto another one, we can calculate the projection matrix (also called the homography matrix) based on 4 known points from the first image and 4 known points on the projected one. By taking the 4 intersection points of the reference court lines and the 4 intersection points of 2 horizontal found lines and 2 vertical found lines, the homography matrix can be determined that projects the reference court on the frame. [2]

![]()

In this approach 12 configuration in reference court is used for finding homography matrix

![]()

The next step is to perform the warp perspective of the reference court lines using homography matrix and count the hits (overlaps between a reference court line pixel and a white pixel of the binary image of the frame). This is repeated for all the found combinations of horizontal and vertical line pairs to determine the best matching lines.

![]()
![]()

This approach has several drawbacks:

1. Extremely slow. In some cases, the speed of this algorithm comes to 15 seconds per one image. It depends on count of detected vertical and horizontal lines and comparison lines intersections with reference court.

2. Low quality. In many cases such detector did not find lines because of numerous hyperparameters of this algorithm.

3. Instability with different angles, colors, shadows and so on. While giving good results for some courts, it is difficult to generalize this approach for all court types.

### Deep learning approach

The basic idea is to use a neural network to detect 14 key points of tennis court. Using the resulting points, we can restore the whole court configuration in the image.

![]()

### Dataset collection

The dataset was created by semi-automated way. Video highlights from different tournaments with length from 2 to 3 minutes were downloaded from YouTube. Frames from video were extracted with 50 frames step and were run via classical computer vision algorithm. The quality of existing computer vision algorithm is not good therefore the resulting images were filtered manually. The resolution of images is 1280×720. This dataset consists of 8841 images and cover all court types (hard, clay, grass).

### **Model**

Proposed deep learning network is very similar to TrackNet architecture. [1]

![]()

The main difference is that input tensor consists of just 1 image (instead of 3 in TrackNet) and output tensor has 15 channels (14 points from dataset and one additional point which is center of tennis court). We used additional point for better convergence. The resolution of input and output image is 640x360.

### Training

The dataset was divided to train set (75%) and test set (25%). To speed up the training speed, all frames were resized from 1280x720 to 640x360. To optimize weights of the network, Adam optimizer was applied. Other parameters you can see in the table below.

![]()

### Postprocessing

It was implemented 2 types of postprocessing techniques:

The main idea is to get a rectangular area around predicted key point and determine white lines intersection inside crop image. Let’s apply our intermediate model (not the final one) to one image

![]()

If we crop a standard area around the predicted points we can see the following picture

![]()

Almost all of them are biased from the desired location. To overcome this issue, we will extract white pixels from crop, detect lines and get intersection of these lines by using classical computer vision techniques. Let’s apply this approach to the fifth point.

![]()

If we apply this approach to all key points we can see the following results:

![]()

For most of them postprocessing worked well. But in crop images with 8,9,12 points there is the net that may interfere results therefore we will skip technique for these points. In the first crop image we have 3 lines, that’s why our algorithm didn’t work.

2. Use homography matrix to reconstruct shifted key points.

The main thing is that we can compare predicted points with reference ones by using homography matrix. To detect homography matrix we use 4 predicted points and 4 points from reference court. Resulting matrix gives us one-to-one correspondence and we can move predicted point to the right position using reference points location. It can be helpful, for example, in case of occlusion.

![]()

### Evaluation

We will assume that key point is accurately detected if the Euclidean distance between the model prediction and the ground truth is less than 7 pixels. Based on this assumption we can calculate true positive and false positive rates. The overall performance in terms of precision, accuracy and median distance (in pixels) between predicted point and ground truth it can be seen in the table below. We will also show how postprocessing techniques affect the final metrics.

![]()

In this table Precision = TP/(TP+FP), Accuracy = (TP+TN)/(TP+TN+FP+FN)

### Example

Implementation of this method you can find here <https://github.com/yastrebksv/TennisCourtDetector>

## Ball detection

Other essential part of our work is to detect and track tennis ball during the game. For this purpose, we used TrackNet deep learning network. More details you can find in the original article [1]. I will briefly explain several important parts from this paper. If you want to take a look at the code, here is my implementation <https://github.com/yastrebksv/TrackNet>.

It is a challenging task to detect the tennis ball from broadcast videos in which the ball images are small, blurry, and sometimes even invisible. The proposed heatmap-based deep learning network is trained to not only recognize the ball image from a single frame but also learn flying patterns from consecutive frames. TrackNet takes images with the size of 640 × 360 to generate a detection heatmap from either a single frame or several consecutive frames to position the ball and can achieve high precision even on public domain videos.

### Dataset

Available dataset consists of video clips of 10 broadcast video. Each video contains several clips from ball serving to score. There are 19.835 labeled frames in the dataset. The resolution, frame rate are 1280×720, 30 fps respectively. In the label file, each frame may have the following attributes: “Frame Name”, “Visibility Class”, “X”, “Y”, and “Trajectory Pattern”. ”Visibility Class”, VC for short, indicates the visibility of the ball in each frame. The possible values are 0, 1, 2, and 3. VC = 0 implies the ball is not within the frame. VC = 1 implies the ball can be easily identified. VC = 2 implies the ball is in the frame but can not be easily identified. ”Trajectory Pattern” indicates the ball movement types and are classified into three categories: flying, hit, and bouncing.

### Training

The ground truth is the heatmap of an amplified 2D Gaussian distribution located at the center of the tennis ball. The variance of the Gaussian distribution refers to the diameter of tennis ball images, which the authors assumed to be about 10 pixels. It was used binary cross entropy loss to train the model. Other parameters you can find in the table below

![]()

### Evaluation

The diameter of tennis images in the video ranges from 2 to 12 pixels and the mean diameter is around 5 pixels. Since the prediction error within a unit size of the ball does not cause misleading in trajectory identification, authors define the positioning error (PE) specification as 5 pixels to indicate whether a ball is accurately detected. Detections with PE larger than 5 pixels belong to false predictions. PE is defined by the Euclidean distance between the model prediction and the ground truth. Authors proposed the following metrics to evaluate the model:

![]()

Where VC1, VC2, VC3 — number of frames in dataset with corresponding visibility classes. In the table below, you can see metrics comparison between authors and my implementation:

![]()

### Example

## Bounce detection

Bounce detection is an important part of our solution because we can determine in which frame the ball was touch to the ground. Based on the previous section we can track ball path during the game. One of the first proposal how to deal with it is to detect suddenly changes of ball direction. Thanks to the dataset used for tennis ball detection we have frames with annotation where ball was touched to the court. Let’s visualize ball trajectory in terms of x and y coordinates during the game.

![]()
![]()

In the graphics above we can see ball trajectory (x and y coordinates) during the game. Green dots indicate frames where ball touched the surface of the court, brown dots determine frames where players hit the ball.

It is not obvious how to predict bounce frame during the game, therefore we used machine learning to solve this problem. Specifically, CatBoostRegressor was used to determine bounce point. Features like difference between x and y coordinates of neighboring points, distance relations between previous and the following ball points and other features were applied. We used binary classification to tackle this task (class 1 — bounce, class 0 — others)

After processing dataset 18570 samples left in our data and 518 from them were labeled as bounce points. To overcome overfitting, we used 10 cross validation due to we have 10 labeled games (9 games were used as train data and remaining game used as test data). Also, greed search with essential parameters like iterations, learning rate and depth were applied during the training.

We will evaluate our method in term of precision and recall. In our demo it is not crucial to detect exact bounce frame, it is possible to make a mistake by 1 frame.

![]()

The second column means that there is not error if we predicted the neighboring point as bounce. If we mark bounce neighboring point with 0.5 weight before training, we will get the following metrics:

![]()

As expected, precision in exact matching dropped because we added false labels in ground truth but recall increased significantly.

### Pipeline

Let’s combine all techniques we discuss previously to one pipeline. We start with court detection, for which we use pretrained neural network. At this stage we get homography matrix for each frame, and now we can display everything that happens on the court to the reference court map. On the second stage we detect tennis ball during the game. We use 3 consecutive frames to find ball trajectory. On the third stage we define frames on which the bounce of the court surface occurs. Finally, we detect players based on pretrained Faster RCNN neural net and convey all movements to the reference court.

If you want to take a look at the code, here is my implementation: <https://github.com/yastrebksv/TennisProject>

## Possible improvements

It is possible to increase the speed of the algorithm. For example, if we replace backbone in neural network for court and ball detections with a lighter net we will speed up inference. Also, we can apply quantization and pruning to speed up inference.

2. Combine ball detection and court detection to one neural net.

In our solution we use almost the same architecture for court and ball detections. It is possible to combine both tasks to one neural network. To solve this problem, it is necessary to markup both datasets and combine them.

3. Improve quality of ball detection.

Sometimes our neural network works falsely in frames without ball. To handle this issue, we can add frames without ball to our training dataset and retrain the model

4. Use augmentation during training of court detection.

In frames with shadows, images with different angles and frames of incomplete court our neural network works not perfect. We can apply appropriate augmentations to handle with this problem.

## Conclusion

We proposed the tool for automatic analysis during tennis match based on deep learning and computer vision. Using such tool, you can detect and track court, ball trajectory, players movements and also you can automatically identify outs during the game.

Proposed neural network for court detection is much faster, more robust and more effective rather than previous solution based on classical computer vision techniques. Postprocessing techniques increased the performance of neural network.

This is a technical article by Kosolapov Sergey on Medium describing a tennis analysis system built using deep learning and machine learning, based on a single camera with 25-30 fps (as opposed to sophisticated commercial systems like Hawk-Eye and IBM Slamtracker that require 8-10 high-speed cameras at up to 1,000 fps and are restricted to major tournaments).

The system has four main components:

1. COURT DETECTION: The authors compared a classical computer vision approach (thresholding white pixels, Hough Transform line detection, homography matrix calculation, and reference court comparison) against a deep learning approach. The classical approach was found to be extremely slow (up to 15 seconds per image), low quality, and unstable with different angles/colors/shadows. The deep learning approach uses a neural network similar to TrackNet architecture to detect 14 key points of the tennis court plus one additional center point (15 output channels). The dataset consisted of 8,841 manually filtered images at 1280×720 resolution from YouTube video highlights covering hard, clay, and grass courts. Training used a 75/25 train/test split, Adam optimizer, and 640×360 input resolution. Two postprocessing techniques were applied: (1) cropping around predicted key points and detecting white line intersections using classical CV, and (2) using homography matrix to reconstruct shifted key points. Evaluation used a 7-pixel Euclidean distance threshold for accurate detection, with precision/accuracy/median distance metrics reported.

2. BALL DETECTION: Used TrackNet deep learning network trained on a dataset of 19,835 labeled frames from 10 broadcast videos (1280×720, 30 fps). The network generates a heatmap from a 2D Gaussian distribution centered on the ball (assumed ~10 pixel diameter variance). Training used binary cross entropy loss. Evaluation used a positioning error (PE) specification of 5 pixels (mean ball diameter in videos is ~5 pixels, ranging 2-12 pixels). Frames were labeled with Visibility Class (VC) values 0-3 indicating ball visibility.

3. BOUNCE DETECTION: Used CatBoostRegressor machine learning for binary classification to detect bounce frames from ball trajectory data (features included differences in x/y coordinates between neighboring points and distance relations). Dataset had 18,570 samples with 518 labeled as bounce points. Used 10-fold cross-validation (9 games train, 1 game test) with grid search for hyperparameters (iterations, learning rate, depth). Evaluated on precision and recall, with tolerance of ±1 frame error. Adding 0.5 weight to neighboring bounce points during training improved recall significantly.

4. PLAYER DETECTION: Used pretrained Faster RCNN neural network.

The complete pipeline: (1) court detection with pretrained neural network to get homography matrix per frame, (2) ball detection using 3 consecutive frames, (3) bounce detection, and (4) player detection and movement mapping to the reference court.

The article also lists possible improvements: replacing backbones with lighter nets, quantizing/pruning for speed, combining ball and court detection into one neural network, adding frames without balls to improve ball detection, and using augmentation for court detection training.

The conclusion states the tool can automatically detect and track court, ball trajectory, player movements, and identify outs during a match, with the neural network approach being faster, more robust, and more effective than classical CV methods.

Code implementations are available on GitHub: TennisCourtDetector (https://github.com/yastrebksv/TennisCourtDetector), TrackNet (https://github.com/yastrebksv/TrackNet), and TennisProject (https://github.com/yastrebksv/TennisProject).

Accurate Tennis Court Line Detection on Amateur Recorded Matches Sameer Agrawala, Ragoth Sundararajana, Vishak Sagara aNicheSolv India Private Limited, 129, 3rd floor, 8th Main Rd, 3rd Phase, J. P. Nagar, Bengaluru, Karnataka 560078, India ABSTRACT Typically, tennis court line detection is done by running Hough-Line-Detection to find straight lines in the image, and then computing a transformation matrix from the detected lines to create the final court structure. We propose numerous improvements and enhancements to this algorithm, including using pretrained State-of-the-Art shadow-removal and object-detection ML models to make our line-detection more robust. Compared to the original algorithm, our method can accurately detect lines on amateur, dirty courts. When combined with a robust ball-tracking system, our method will enable accurate, automatic refereeing for amateur and professional tennis matches alike. Keywords: Tennis court line detection, AI referee, Machine learning, Automatic sports analysis, AI based shadow removal, YOLO object detection, Image and video processing, Computer vision 1. INTRODUCTION Automatic tennis-court-line detection is an important step towards creating tennis-match analysis software. Although important in many sports, court-line detection is an especially salient problem in tennis due to the importance of in vs out-of-bounds balls. Tennis courts are also especially well-suited for this problem because they are relatively smaller in size compared to other courts, allowing most if not all of the court to be visible in a typical tennis match video. 1.1. Challenges to automatic court line detection However, there are numerous challenges to automatic court-line detection. The ideal court for this task would be recorded from a relatively high angle in which all important points on the court are clearly visible, as shown in Figure 1a. However, many courts, especially in amateur matches, are recorded from a lower angle (Figure 1b) in which the far side of the court is not visible, or the lines may be partially covered by another part of the video (Figure 1c), or the court may be scuffed so that the lines themselves are not clearly visible (Figure 1d). All of these present obstacles to any court-line detection model, especially when dealing with non-professional matches, and must therefore be dealt with. Figure 1. Examples of tennis courts. Top left: A “perfect” court. Top Right: Low camera angle. Bottom Left: court is obscured. Bottom Right: Scuffed court lines.
1.2. Our contributions • To allow our algorithm to handle extremely bright courts where the white lines are not clearly visible such as that in Figure 1d, a filtration algorithm based on detection of the court’s color is proposed, allowing pixels identified to be part of the court to be removed entirely from the image. • To handle instances in which a low camera angle makes the far side of the court practically impossible to see, such as in Figures 1b and 1d, the image is first cropped to include only the near side, using YOLO-detected net coordinates. This detected half-court is then extended to the full image. • To handle courts in which shadows obscure some of the field, such as in Figures 1c and 1d, advanced Shadow-Removal models are used to create an image which the algorithm can better parse through. 2. RELATED WORK 2.1. Homography estimation for sports-field registration The algorithm which we improve upon in this paper is a homography estimation algorithm. This algorithm first performs a filtration process on the court to make the court lines more visible. It then runs Hough Line Detection on this filtered image and calculates all the intersections between the detected lines. It then uses these intersection points to estimate a transformation matrix between a reference tennis court diagram and the tennis court in the frame1. 2.2. Introduction of AI models In the past, Deep Learning models have also been introduced to the problem2,3. Neural Networks can be used to optimize the initial homography matrix via the Gradient Descent algorithm2. In other methods, a homography matrix is not calculated, and instead a CNN is used to generate a mask highlighting important areas of the court3.
2.3. Key differences of our approach The method described in Section 2.1, although groundbreaking, is not optimized for non-professional recordings specifically, and is unable to handle amateur courts. Meanwhile, ML-based methods are limited by the data they were trained on, which favors professional, televised matches. By comparison, our method uses pre-trained models such as YOLO and ShadowFormer, which leads to a more robust algorithm capable of handling amateur courts. 3. OUR WORK Our work improves upon the homography-estimation algorithm by incorporating the following new approaches: First, we use a shadow-removal model to make court lines obscured by shadow more clear. Second, we use a tennis-net detection model to crop the frame to include only the near-side of a court. Third, we have modified the pixel-by-pixel filtering algorithm to use the court color. Fourth, we use a scoring algorithm to determine the best court-detection out on a set of detected courts. These improvements are described in more detail below. 3.1. Shadow removal We make use of two state-of-the-art shadow removal models: the MTMT model for shadow-detection4, and the ShadowFormer model for shadow-removal5. The MTMT model is used to generate a shadow-mask, and this shadow-mask, along with the original image, is passed into ShadowFormer for final shadow removal. An example of this in action on a real tennis-court frame can be seen in Figure 2. Figure 2. Our shadow-removal process. The original image is passed into a Multi-task Mean Teacher (MTMT) model, which generates a shadow-mask. Both images are then passed to Shadow-Former, which performs final shadow removal. 3.2. YOLO-v5 net detection After shadows are removed, a YOLO-v5 object detection model is used to detect the tennis net. The detected net coordinates are then used to crop the image to only include the near-side of the court, as shown in Figure 3. By only running court detection on the near side, and then simply extending the detected court to the far side, the algorithm is made more accurate and faster. Figure 3. Example of image cropping using YOLO net detection. Left: Original, shadow-removed image; Middle: Diagonal line representing YOLO-detected net coordinates; Right: Final cropped image. 3.3. Pixel-by-pixel filtering Previous methods for image filtering, such as that described in Section 2.1, use a simple pixel threshold to filter out any dark pixels in the image, thus theoretically only leaving the bright white lines behind. However, the ideal threshold value can change drastically from image to image, and is therefore not a robust method, as shown in Figure 4. By comparison, we propose a filtering algorithm based on finding the court color. The steps of the algorithm are: 1.
Place 1000 points randomly on the image. 2.
Find the color of each point, and then return the color shared by the most points. (Figure 5, middle column) 3.
Loop through the image pixel-by-pixel, and at a given pixel A, look in a 7x7 square around A. If at least 4 pixels within this square match the detected court color, AND pixel A itself does NOT match the detected court color, then pixel A is detected to be part of a court line and is white. (Figure 5, right column) Figure 5 shows this new filtration algorithm in action on the same two courts as in Figure 4. The new filtration algorithm is more capable of generalizing to a variety of courts compared to the original threshold-based filtration algorithm.
Figure 4. The old pixel filtration algorithm. A threshold value of 180 works well for the top image, but is too low for the bottom image, as it leaves behind residual white pixels throughout the court.
Figure 5. The new filtration algorithm. Left: Original Image; Middle: Detected court color; Right: Final filtered image 3.4. Scoring algorithm To ensure accurate court detections, the algorithm is run on a video, as opposed to individual images. The detection process is run on randomly selected frames from the video, and when a set of court-detections is obtained, a scoring algorithm is used to find the most accurate detection. The algorithm works as follows: 1.
The court detection is drawn onto the image. 2.
Given both this drawn image and the original image, the number of drawn pixels corresponding to bright white pixels in the original image are counted. This is the final score. Figure 6. Three court detections of varying scores. Left: Score of 356; Middle: 812; Right: 844. A higher score represents a more accurate detection.
4. RESULTS We compared our method with a version of the Homography-Estimation algorithm described in Section 2.1, which has been designated as the “Old Method” in the table. We used 180 as the threshold value. In order to draw a more accurate and fair comparison between the old method and our method, we do not run our algorithm on a video, and instead, only run it on individual frames. The results of our experiments are in Table 1. 4.1. Dataset There exist no compiled datasets of non-professional matches. So, we obtained our testing data by either recording our own tennis matches, or by taking videos from a website called AmateurTennis.tv, which features hundreds of amateur tennis match videos. In this paper, we present the results from 7 different videos, four of which are from amateur matches and three from professional matches. 4.2. Evaluation metrics To determine if a given court prediction is accurate, ground truth court lines were made for each video. If the score (described in Section 3.4) of a detected court was within 5% of the score of the ground truth court lines, then the given court detection was marked as correct. Table 1. Results of our experiments. 4.3. Analysis Matches 1-4 are non-professional, and our method uniformly performs better on these. The old method was limited because it frequently detected extraneous lines due to its filtering algorithm. Our method’s filtration algorithm was generally able to filter out non-court lines far better, leading to both more accurate and faster detections. Court 5 was a Wimbledon court with alternating bands of color, which led to confusion in the detected court-color. 5. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK We presented numerous enhancements and improvements to an existing court-detection framework, giving our method increased accuracy across the board, but especially on amateur and non-professional courts. We plan to further explore new filtration algorithms, including incorporating a CNN to extract and highlight features of a court. We also plan to investigate other net-detection and shadow-removal models for increased speed and accuracy. REFERENCES 1.
D. Farin, J. Han and P. H. N. de With, "Fast camera calibration for the analysis of sport sequences," 2005 IEEE International Conference on Multimedia and Expo, Amsterdam, Netherlands, 2005, pp. 4 pp.-, doi: 10.1109/ ICME.2005.1521465.
2.
Jiang, Wei & Higuera, Juan & Angles, Baptiste & Sun, Weiwei & Javan Roshtkhari, Mehrsan & Yi, Kwang. (2020). Optimizing Through Learned Errors for Accurate Sports Field Registration. 201-210. 10.1109/ WACV45572.2020.9093581. 3.
J. Arroyave López y R. A. Echavarría Echeverri, “Main areas detection on tennis court”, Trabajo de grado especialización, Especialización en Analítica y Ciencia de Datos, Universidad de Antioquia, Medellín, Antioquia, Colombia, 2021.
4.
Z. Chen, L. Zhu, L. Wan, S. Wang, W. Feng and P. -A. Heng, "A Multi-Task Mean Teacher for Semi-Supervised Shadow Detection," 2020 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), Seattle, WA, USA, 2020, pp. 5610-5619, doi: 10.1109/CVPR42600.2020.00565. 5.
Guo, Lanqing & Huang, Siyu & Liu, Ding & Cheng, Hao & Wen, Bihan. (2023). ShadowFormer: Global Context Helps Image Shadow Removal. 10.48550/arXiv.2302.01650. This is a research paper titled "Accurate Tennis Court Line Detection on Amateur Recorded Matches" by Sameer Agrawal, Ragoth Sundararajan, and Vishak Sagar from NicheSolv India Private Limited in Bengaluru, India. The paper proposes improvements to traditional homography-based tennis court line detection to handle amateur and non-professional matches.

**Problem:** Traditional Hough-Line-Detection with homography estimation fails on amateur courts due to low camera angles, obscured lines, scuffed courts, and shadows.

**Key Contributions (4 improvements):**
1. **Shadow removal:** Uses two state-of-the-art models — MTMT for shadow-detection (generating a shadow-mask) and ShadowFormer for shadow-removal.
2. **YOLO-v5 net detection:** Detects the tennis net and crops the image to the near-side of the court only, then extends the detected court to the full image — improving accuracy and speed.
3. **Pixel-by-pixel filtering based on court color:** Instead of a fixed pixel threshold (which fails to generalize), the algorithm places 1000 random points, finds the dominant court color, then scans each pixel with a 7x7 neighborhood — if at least 4 pixels match the court color and the central pixel doesn't, it's marked as a court line.
4. **Scoring algorithm:** Runs detection on randomly selected video frames and scores each detection by counting drawn pixels that correspond to bright white pixels in the original image, selecting the highest-scoring (most accurate) detection.

**Results:** Compared against the "Old Method" (threshold=180) on 7 videos (4 amateur, 3 professional). The new method performed better or significantly better on amateur courts (e.g., Court #4: 0.0% → 81.3%; Court #7: 50.8% → 100.0%; Court #1: 60.0% → 84.3%). The only failure was Court #5 (a Wimbledon court with alternating color bands, dropping from 96.0% to 86.0%). Data was collected from self-recorded matches and AmateurTennis.tv since no compiled non-professional datasets exist.

**Future Work:** Exploring CNN-based filtration algorithms, and investigating faster net-detection and shadow-removal models.

# TennisCourtDetector

Deep learning network for detecting tennis court

It was developed a deep learning network to detect tennis court keypoints from broadcast videos. The proposed heatmap-based deep learning network allows to detect 14 points of tennis court. Postprocessing techniques (based on classical computer vision methods) were implemented to enhance net predictions.

## Dataset

The dataset consists of 8841 images, which were separeted to train set (75%) and validation set (25%). Each image has 14 annotated points. The resolution of images is 1280×720. This dataset contains all court types (hard, clay, grass). Click the link <https://drive.google.com/file/d/1lhAaeQCmk2y440PmagA0KmIVBIysVMwu/view?usp=drive_link> to download the dataset

### Dataset collection

This dataset was created in semi-automated way. Video highlights from different tournaments with length from 2 to 3 minutes were downloaded from YouTube. Frames from video were extracted with step 50 frames to run them through classical computer vision algorithm. The quality of existing computer vision algorithm is not good therefore the resulting images were filtered manually.

## Model architecture

Proposed deep learning network is very similar to TrackNet architecture. [![](/yastrebksv/TennisCourtDetector/raw/main/imgs/tracknet_arch.png)](/yastrebksv/TennisCourtDetector/blob/main/imgs/tracknet_arch.png)   
 The difference is that input tensor consists of just 1 image (instead of 3 in TrackNet) and output tensor has 15 channels (14 from dataset and one additional point is center of tennis court). We used additional point for better convergence. The resolution of input and output image is 640x360.

## Postporcessing

It was implemented 2 types of postprocessing techniques:

### 1. Refine keypoints using classical computer vision

Lets apply our intermediate model to one image   
 [![](/yastrebksv/TennisCourtDetector/raw/main/imgs/net_prediction.png)](/yastrebksv/TennisCourtDetector/blob/main/imgs/net_prediction.png)   
 If we zoom, for example the fifth point, we can see that prediction is not perfect.   
 [![](/yastrebksv/TennisCourtDetector/raw/main/imgs/crop_example.png)](/yastrebksv/TennisCourtDetector/blob/main/imgs/crop_example.png)   
 To overcome this issue we will exctract white pixels from crop, detect lines and get intersection of these lines by using classical computer vision techniques. [![](/yastrebksv/TennisCourtDetector/raw/main/imgs/kps_refine.png)](/yastrebksv/TennisCourtDetector/blob/main/imgs/kps_refine.png)

### 2. Use homography to reconstruct shifted keypointes.

[![](/yastrebksv/TennisCourtDetector/raw/main/imgs/homography.png)](/yastrebksv/TennisCourtDetector/blob/main/imgs/homography.png)   
 The main thing is that we can compare predicted points with reference ones by using homography matrix. To detect homography matrix we use 4 predicted points and 4 points from reference court. Resulting matrix gives us one-to-one correspondense and we can move predicted point to the right position using reference points location. It can be helpful, for example, in case of occlusion. [![](/yastrebksv/TennisCourtDetector/raw/main/imgs/homography_example.png)](/yastrebksv/TennisCourtDetector/blob/main/imgs/homography_example.png)

## Evaluation (metrics)

We will assume that keypoint is accurately detected if the Euclidean distance between the model prediction and the ground truth is less than 7 pixels. Based on this assumption we can calculate true positive and false positive rates. The overall performance in terms of precision, accuracy and median distance between predicted point and ground truth you can see in the table below. We will also show how postprocessing techniques affect the final metrics.

| Precision | Accuracy | Median dist |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Base model (BM) | 0.936 | 0.933 | 2.83 |
| BM + refining kps | 0.939 | 0.936 | 2.23 |
| BM + homography | 0.961 | 0.959 | 2.27 |
| BM + refining kps + homography | 0.963 | 0.961 | 1.83 |

## Pretrained model

You can check these weights <https://drive.google.com/file/d/1f-Co64ehgq4uddcQm1aFBDtbnyZhQvgG/view?usp=drive_link> to try model

## How to train

1. Clone the repository `https://github.com/yastrebksv/TennisCourtDetector.git`
2. Run `pip install -r requirements.txt` to install packages required
3. Put dataset into `/data` folder
4. Run `python main.py` to start training
