## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598)Abstract

We built an Instant Review System (IRS) for badminton, also named a Challenge System. It allows players to verify linesmen in/out decisions and makes the game fairer. Elements such as lighting, the influence of air-conditioning on the flight trajectory, or the moving mats can significantly impact the final in/out decision. Due to the construction of the shuttlecock, it behaves differently during the flight than, for example, a tennis ball. This publication discusses the problems we encountered during our work with the proposed solution. We present the evolution of the system’s architecture: the first version with the cameras mounted above the court and placed around the court close to the lines, tracking the shuttlecock in 3D; and the second, improved version with cameras placed only around the court, without 3D reconstruction. We used our system during the BWF World Senior Badminton Championships in Katowice. We present the system’s results from this tournament and compare them with linesmen’s decisions. We describe the system’s verification process by the Badminton World Federation and Polish Badminton Federation and discuss evaluation methods for such systems. Our solution is comparable to the commercial product used in the biggest badminton tournaments in regard to processing time and accuracy. Still, our architecture and algorithms make installing it much easier and faster, making the system more adaptive, reliable, flexible, and universal in relation to the practical requirements of sports halls.

**Keywords:**image processing, sports, motion capture, instant review system, challenge, badminton

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598)1. Introduction

Badminton is the fastest sports game in the world. The shuttlecock can travel at a speed of over 400 km/h. The world record measured in a laboratory in 2013 is 493 km/h [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B1-sensors-22-08098)]. Because of such a high speed and human-eye perception, the line judges often cannot tell if the shuttlecock was in or out. Analyzing slow-motion video footage, a referee can judge if there was an out, but that process takes some time. The solution can be a computer vision system that automatically makes in/out decisions.

In this work, we present the results of theoretical, implementation, and experimental research on the location of the fall of a shuttlecock. The result of these studies is a working shuttlecock tracking system adapted to the conditions of the badminton game in a real-life scenario, in accordance with the applicable standards of the game and the time and quality requirements. We used our system at BWF World Senior Badminton Championships in Katowice, where over 1500 players competed on 12 courts. In this paper, we share our experience, the problems and challenges we encountered during building and operating our system, and how we solved them from a practical point of view.

Detection, segmentation, and tracking of objects are well-explored topics by researchers. Many algorithms have been developed, from simple shape and color segmentation methods to deep-learning algorithms. These algorithms are used in commercial systems such as Hawk-Eye [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B2-sensors-22-08098)], STATS SportVU [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B3-sensors-22-08098)], or ChyronHego TRACAB [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B4-sensors-22-08098)]. For example, TRACAB, which is mainly used during football games for tracking players, uses machine-learning algorithms and convolutional neural networks [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B5-sensors-22-08098)].

It should be noted that optical tracking data is prone to errors introduced by occlusions, which is why still, in existing systems, a human operator is required to correct these errors during measurement [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B6-sensors-22-08098)].

Still, offered systems are not 100% accurate—the Hawk-Eye’s claimed accuracy in tennis is 2.6 mm [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B7-sensors-22-08098)]. Despite the sometimes-erroneous decisions of the computer system, such systems are generally more accurate than humans [[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B8-sensors-22-08098)]. Thus since 2001, computer vision applications have been used in many sports [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B9-sensors-22-08098),[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B10-sensors-22-08098)].

Just before Hawk-Eye’s system was adapted and used in badminton for the first time in 2014, there were theoretical proposals from researchers to build such a system specifically for badminton [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B11-sensors-22-08098)].

The main challenge for scientists and developers for systems supporting linesmen’s decisions is improving ball detection speed and accuracy. Compared to detecting larger objects, detecting fast-moving small objects, such as shuttlecocks, is still challenging. The performance is relatively low and requires many hardware resources [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B12-sensors-22-08098)].

Our first attempt to build an instant review system was similar to the Hawk-Eye system architecture in the measurement part (cameras placement). It used six cameras above the court mounted just below the ceiling of the hall and 14 cameras located around the court 1 m above the ground.

After tests, we removed the cameras above the court to simplify and shorten installation. We had to introduce a new algorithm to detect the moment of contact of the shuttle with the ground. The current version of our system does not calculate shuttlecock trajectories in 3D. Still, it can inform the umpire and the players if there was an out or not with comparable accuracy. It can be ready to operate within two or three hours.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598)2. Materials and Methods

### 2.1. Requirements, Problems, and Proposed Solution

The system works as follows. The number of cameras and their location is selected, so they see at least all the lines and areas around them and a flying shuttlecock approaching the ground. Video streams from cameras go to computers, where our software processes them and, by analyzing the shuttle trajectory, calculates where the shuttle hits the ground by comparing this place with the court model or previously detected court lines.

A player who disagrees with the linesman’s decision raises his hand and asks the umpire for a challenge. The umpire sends the challenge request to the system operator. He then starts the procedure and receives information from the system about whether the line judge has made a good decision or not. The operator or a designated judge may verify the system’s result and manually correct it. After verification, the system generates an animation and presents it to the players, judges, spectators, and TV broadcasters.

When designing the system, we adopted the following assumptions. The system should be as accurate as possible. The whole verification procedure should not take longer than 25 s. The installation time should be as short as possible, no longer than 4 h per court. The installation should not require more than two people. All equipment should take up as little space and weigh as little as possible.

Problems we faced during our research can be divided into two major groups: operational, meaning connected with external conditions; and algorithmic. Each mentioned problem will be described further with the proposed solution methods. Operational problems: lighting conditions, lack of space between courts for cameras, hardware, wiring, and power-related issues, securing the cameras, bent court lines, court mats deforming during the game, drift caused by air-conditioning, and equipment transportation. Algorithmic issues: camera calibration, court recognition, object detection and tracking, object segmentation, motion blur, finding shuttlecock ground hit position with respect to the court, occlusion of the tracked object, speed of algorithms, and flickering light.

### 2.2. Hardware Limitations, Wiring, and Data-Transfer-Related Issues

The system’s accuracy is highly dependent on the camera’s resolution and frame rate. We use cameras with a resolution of 800 × 600, with a maximum speed of 200 frames per second. When we started our project in 2017, it was the best that the market had to offer in accordance with our budget. Such a resolution proved to be sufficient to achieve satisfactory localization accuracy of the falling shuttlecock with moderate requirements for computational complexity.

The velocity of a shuttlecock approaching the ground depends on the initial speed, and distance traveled [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B13-sensors-22-08098)]. For smashes, it can be over 33 m/s. For high clear shots, it is just a terminal velocity of 6.7 m/s [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B14-sensors-22-08098)]. Using cameras operating with 100 fps gives us the distance a shuttlecock is moving between two consecutive frames, from about 70 to 330 mm (roughly ten times the diameter of the cork of the shuttlecock: 26–28 mm). Lighting conditions (described in the next section) and the lens and matrices available on the market limit possibilities to increase the shutter speed. We set up cameras in our system to 150 fps and use interpolation in our software to increase accuracy when the shuttle hits the ground between recorded frames. Alternatively, one can use more cameras mounted close to each other with shutters triggered at different timestamps and merge streams from them.

There are four primary interfaces ([Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#sensors-22-08098-t001)): GigE, CoaXPress, USB, and CameraLink to transfer data from cameras. Any WiFi or other radio-based communication with cameras is not feasible in crowded and prone-to-interference areas, such as sports halls during tournaments, so cables are the only option.

Designing hardware infrastructure is challenging. One can keep computers outside the playing zone and use longer GigE or CoaXPress cables or place the computer close to the cameras and use USB or CameraLink cables. It is also possible to use concentrators close to cameras and transfer data between concentrators and computers with optical fiber.

The market offer changes rapidly. Today’s cameras offer 2832 px × 2840 px resolution at 190 fps with CoaXPress 2.0 interface (2× CXP-12). When we started working on our system a few years ago, cameras with similar speeds had much smaller resolutions and offered a GigE interface.

We decided then to use GigE cables. They are relatively cheap, robust, and easy to cut and assemble. They can be used to transfer data and power the cameras by using Power over Ethernet technology (PoE). We keep our servers away from the courts and do not use any devices close to the cameras. This approach simplifies the installation of cameras between courts when the space is tight, but the cabling is sometimes tricky and time-consuming.

The amount of data transferred from cameras and the efficiency of algorithms detecting and tracking shuttlecock imply the necessary computing power and count of servers.

The essential factor is the expected response time of the system. We were surprised that the audience did not expect an immediate result. If the system responds within 10 s, the audience waits tensely for the visualization of where the shuttle has fallen, and this additional break is beneficial for the show. However, the system’s response cannot take longer than 25 s because the audience becomes bored after that. The times cited are our observations from over a dozen tournaments where we tested our system. Knowing those limitations, we can select the appropriate hardware for our algorithms. We use 8 servers and 15 cameras: 14 around the court and 1 with a broader view of the whole court. Each server supports two cameras. The operator uses the extra camera and server to monitor the system.

During the tournament, players and the TV crew walk around the court. They may step on the wire or even disconnect it from the camera. Connection-monitoring tools must be available for the operator, who should be warned when too many communication errors arise.

### 2.3. Lighting Conditions

Different sports venues have different lighting. In order to record video with a speed of over 150 fps, the lights must be strong enough. That problem does not exist in tennis (excluding evening matches), where we usually have daylight.

To deal with that issue, we tested different lenses and chose the one with the lowest F-number.

If the light is not bright enough, more extended exposition and higher camera-gain values are necessary. Extending exposition makes the motion blur effect more visible, and deblurring algorithms must be applied to reduce it. Increasing the gain causes higher image noise.

Since, as mentioned in the previous section, we use cameras with limited resolution, it is possible to upgrade them to newer models with much higher resolutions to increase the system’s accuracy if required. However, most of our algorithms and other hardware should also be corrected and adapted to the new quality of the signals. According to our rough estimates, the benefits are not obvious.

Our experiments measured how increasing gain affects PSNR and SNR values. We tested two sensors ([Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#sensors-22-08098-t002)) with the same lenses, acquired 20 images of size 4096 × 2160 pixels of the same static scene, and calculated the average PSNR and SNR values ([Table 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#sensors-22-08098-t003)).

Increasing the gain increases the noise, but increasing the gain up to +12 dB does not affect our object segmentation and tracking algorithms described in later sections.

Even in a hall with the poorest light conditions, we were able to acquire images with a speed of 150 frames per second, but only one place had strong enough lights installed to record a video with a speed of over 200 fps.

### 2.4. Securing the Cameras

It is infrequent in badminton for players to jump over advertising boards, so the cameras behind them are safe. Despite this, we plan to equip our cameras with safety cases. Such cases are used in volleyball, where it is common to knock over cameras with the ball or by the jumping player.

After positioning the cameras with respect to the court, they should not be moved. Still, the line judges or players may unintentionally move our cameras while entering the court.

Cameras cannot be permanently attached to the floor; it is better to destroy the camera than break the leg of a player who jumps on it.

Our software warns the operator when the camera is moved. The displacement is detected by comparing the reference image with the current image from the camera. Our software recalculates the camera’s position when the movement is slight, and the camera still sees the line. The operator must react and fix the camera’s position if the line is not visible.

### 2.5. Bent Court Lines

Organizers of badminton tournaments place special rubber mats on each court. These mats consist of several pieces to facilitate their transport. The pieces are zipped together when put on the floor. Unfortunately, during installation, the parts of a mat may not be correctly assembled, and a slight shift may occur ([Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#sensors-22-08098-f001)).

Badminton is a high-speed game. Players rapidly change directions. Court mats are made from flex material to give additional amortization for the athletes. The drawback is that mats may deform during the game, and the court no longer fits the model ([Figure 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#sensors-22-08098-f002)). In fact, in a real-life situation, when the court deformation is significant enough to be spotted, the game is paused, and the court is fixed.

Our first version of the system used cameras above the court. The system had to recognize the court and transform it into a court model for further processing. We have learned from our experience that there are slight deviations in the actual court size from the dimensions prescribed by the regulations. It means that the court model defined with respect to the regulations cannot be used. Before each match, our system recognized the lines to create a precise model which matched the actual court.

The current version of our system uses only cameras located around the court, aimed at the court lines, and no court model is calculated. Instead, single lines are detected. They do not have to be perfectly straight for the system to work correctly.

### 2.6. Drift Caused by Air-Conditioning

A shuttlecock is a lightweight object (weighs 5 g), so it is easily affected by air drift. Equations that predict shuttlecock trajectory [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B15-sensors-22-08098),[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B16-sensors-22-08098)] do not consider that additional force. Moreover, the air currents’ temperature, direction, and strength change over time. For example, in the morning, when usually fewer spectators visit the venue, the air moves differently than when the hall is packed in the evening.

Instead of physical trajectory models, algorithms in the first system version have used adaptive methods such as the Kalman filter [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B17-sensors-22-08098)] as part of the tracking pipeline.

In the current system version, a camera only sees the shuttlecock in the last fragment of the trajectory when approaching the ground. We still use the Kalman filter for shuttlecock position interpolation.

### 2.7. Camera Calibration

The camera’s calibration is essential to achieve precise court model fitting when 3D tracking is involved.

We use zoom lenses to deal with different distances to the court lines. Zoom lenses have worse parameters than fixed-focal-length ones. Any change in lens settings requires camera recalibration. It is crucial that the calibration process is fast and easy to perform.

[Figure 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#sensors-22-08098-f003) shows an original image from the camera’s footage (upper) and the same image after applying distortion coefficients calculated during the calibration process.

Researchers widely investigated camera calibration and proposed many algorithms (see, for example, References [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B18-sensors-22-08098),[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B19-sensors-22-08098)]).

The calibration of cameras mounted high above the court is much more complex than calibration of cameras placed around the court, 1 m above the ground. Cameras from the first group are usually installed at least 15 m from the center of the court. Their depth of field starts from 5 m to infinity. A standard calibration board has dimensions of 1 m × 1 m or less, but for the best results, the markers should fill the whole image, which is impossible. Using more giant calibration boards is impractical because of transportation difficulties. Moreover, it is impossible to calibrate a camera that is already mounted because it is usually installed very high, and the light conditions are not good enough.

The cameras close to the court and the ground are much easier to calibrate. Their depth of field starts much closer to sensors. Thus, a standard 1 m × 1 m calibration board usually fills the whole image. The operator may calibrate cameras once installed in their final location. As mentioned earlier, for our algorithms working on streams from cameras close to the court, the accuracy of calibration is not essential. We can even use an automatic calibration process proposed by Daniel Santana-Cedrés et al. [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B20-sensors-22-08098)]. Our current system version uses only cameras close to the court, and we do not reconstruct 3D trajectories but instead detect the moment of and the place of the shuttlecock’s ground touch. For this algorithm, the court lines do not have to be ideally straight to produce correctly in/out decisions.

From our experiments, we learned that the following list of best practices could reduce reprojection error more than three times compared to the standard procedure [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B21-sensors-22-08098)]. We propose the following:Adjust the shutter and gain to the lighting conditions.Ensure that the lighting is even and that there are no overexposed or underexposed areas. Use a light diffuser if necessary.Place the camera and the calibration board in the distance that fits into the depth of field.Focus the camera. Use patches of regions around all detected markers. For each patch, calculate sharpness by using one of the methods proposed in Reference [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B22-sensors-22-08098)].Choose the right size calibration target. It should cover as much as possible of the total area when seen parallel to the camera. Ideally, the markers should fill the whole image area.Perform calibration at the working distance. The camera should be focused at this distance.The calibration board should have a high feature count. A board with circles is better than a chessboard.Collect images from 6 different areas and tilts: close parallel to the camera, far parallel to the camera, moved to the left and tilted 10–20 degrees, moved to the right and tilted 10–20 degrees, moved closer to the camera to the left and tilted 30–40 degrees, moved closer to the camera to the right, and tilted 30–40 degrees. The left and right positions must be symmetrical. Tilting more is not recommended as feature localization accuracy suffers.Use a good calibration board. Boards printed by specialized companies are better than inkjet- or laser-printed ones. If one must use an inkjet-printed pattern, glue it to a flat and rigid surface; glass might be a good option (ensure to paint its back with black color to avoid lighting from the back through the glass and paper).Mount the board vertically or flat on rigid support to minimize distortion and bow.Consider moving the camera instead of the board. Use a quality tripod, and do not touch lenses.Before starting the acquisition, make sure that the camera is warmed up.Inspect reprojection errors, both per-view and per-feature. If any of these appear as outliers, acquire a new set of images and recalibrate.Due to overfitting, obtaining a low reprojection error does not equal a good camera calibration but merely indicates that the provided data/evidence can be described with the used model. Parameter uncertainties are indications of how well the chosen camera model was constrained.Analyze the individual reprojection errors. Their direction and magnitude should not correlate with position; that is, they should point chaotically in all directions.

### 2.8. Court Recognition

Our current system version detects only single lines, but the earlier version with cameras mounted above the court detects the whole court before matches. The court’s dimensions are standardized, so it is pretty easy to recognize the court and fit it into the model. Hough transform can be applied to the Sobel filter output to find court lines. Then the intersections of the lines can be detected by using the Bentley—Ottmann algorithm [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B23-sensors-22-08098)]. Another method is to use the Harris corner detector to detect court corners [[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B24-sensors-22-08098)]. The implementation of a court recognition method proposed by Dirk Farin [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B25-sensors-22-08098)] can be found on GitHub [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B26-sensors-22-08098)].

We used a modified version [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B27-sensors-22-08098)] of the Mask R-CNN [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B28-sensors-22-08098)] to detect and segment the court from the image. The masks generated by the neural network are dilated before applying to the image to make sure that all court lines are visible. Then the Hough transform and pattern matching are applied to match the detected court with the model. We then analyzed the lines and corners fitting and adjust the model in case of inconsistencies caused by rubber court mat deformations described earlier in this paper.

We twice increased the number of deconvolution layers in the mask detection subnetwork to achieve a higher resolution of the mask before rescaling it to the original image size. An example of generated masks with original (a) and increased (b) layers is shown in [Figure 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#sensors-22-08098-f004) (notice the accuracy at the edges of the court). The model was trained partially on artificially generated images of the badminton courts. Original photos of the courts in our dataset were too similar, so they were filled with images generated from an artificial 3D court model. The accuracy of court detection is 97.7%.

### 2.9. Cameras Positions

Badminton regulations say that the distance from the court line to the closest object must be at least two meters clear space behind the baseline of the court (distance to any A-boards or similar advertising) and 1.5 m clear area from the sidelines of the court or between any two courts marked out side by side [[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B29-sensors-22-08098)]. This rule is not always strictly followed. Often, organizers place courts closer to each other during the first days of a tournament. On the other hand, only one court is set up during the finals, and the distance to the advertising boards is much more considerable (cameras are placed behind them).

We mounted cameras below the ceiling and around the court in the first version of the system. In the current version, we use only cameras around the court.

The optimal camera positions for the best 3D tracking can be calculated by using the algorithm from Reference [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B30-sensors-22-08098)]. Unfortunately, the number of places where cameras can be installed in sports halls is so limited that using such algorithms is usually not applicable. Instead, we mounted at least four, and at most six, cameras to the hall’s ceiling. The four cameras must see the court from the four corners, and the additional two were usually placed on the court’s shorter sides.

The extrinsic parameters must be calculated for the cameras mounted above the court to track flying shuttlecocks in 3D precisely. There are many methods to achieve this. A technician can walk around the court with a board with markers. A single perfect sphere can replace a board [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B31-sensors-22-08098)]. A stiff, precisely measured stick with two perfect spheres can replace a single sphere for more accurate scaling. Instead of walking around the court, a technician can place flat markers on the court floor.

To simplify and accelerate the setup, we decided to use the whole court and intersections of the lines as markers. We base our method on ideas from Reference [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B25-sensors-22-08098)]. This calibration step is not needed for our current system version, as we now do not track shuttlecocks in 3D.

For the 14 cameras located around the court on tripods approximately 1 m above the ground, the placement is dictated by our tracking and ground touch detection algorithms (see [Figure 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#sensors-22-08098-f005)). Each line must be seen by a camera from each end to minimize occlusion.

Switching to 2D space allowed us to skip building a 3D model of a court and simplify camera calibration. We pass an image with only a sideline or back line of a court to the model and algorithm described in the previous section and divide the image into two polygons—outside and inside the court—as shown in [Figure 6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#sensors-22-08098-f006). The in/out decision is made by checking inside which polygon (red or green) the shuttlecock hit the ground.

### 2.10. Speed of Algorithms

High-speed cameras must be used to detect the exact moment of a ground hit. Our experiments show that 150–200 fps is the best compromise. That means there are only 5 or 6 ms for processing one frame image for the system to work in real time. Any sophisticated algorithms of image analysis that require a long computation time cannot be used. When we started working on our system, the fastest tracker based on the neural network was GOTURN [[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B32-sensors-22-08098)]. We decided to develop a hybrid solution. It uses simple and fast detection and tracking methods and only sometimes uses a neural network on patches of single frames when the first method loses the tracked object.

### 2.11. Flickering Light

Algorithms based on differential frames are sensitive to flickering light. The newest and most modern sports halls are equipped with flicker-free lights, but most venues where national tournaments are played have old, flickering lights. We visited nine venues where badminton tournaments are organized, and only one had flicker-free lights installed.

Although many methods [[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B33-sensors-22-08098),[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B34-sensors-22-08098),[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B35-sensors-22-08098),[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B36-sensors-22-08098),[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B37-sensors-22-08098),[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B38-sensors-22-08098),[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B39-sensors-22-08098),[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B40-sensors-22-08098)] and commercial software [[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B41-sensors-22-08098),[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B42-sensors-22-08098)] remove flickering, they are not suitable for a fast video-stream processing. They are all designed for flicker removal’s effectiveness but not for execution speed. We concentrated on the speed with still reasonable and applicable results. We developed an adaptive pixel-wise method of generating masks that compensate for the flickering effect. Our method is 250–300 times faster than DeFlicker [[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B41-sensors-22-08098)] and FlickerFree [[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B42-sensors-22-08098)]. The method is described in detail in our paper [[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B43-sensors-22-08098)]. We use the fact that our cameras do not move, as this allows us to calculate the similarity level of each pixel to the same pixel from the previous frame. If a pixel has changed because of a local movement in a scene, then the similarity level would be low. If similarity levels are higher than the threshold, then we interpret it as the flickering effect, which is reduced by our algorithm.

### 2.12. Shuttlecock Detection and Tracking

To be able to track any object, firstly, it must be found within the image. Many methods can be used for finding a specific object, from the most straightforward, such as color and shape segmentation, to methods utilizing neural networks. In Reference [[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B44-sensors-22-08098)], the authors used the color segmentation method for detecting a tennis ball. In Reference [[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B45-sensors-22-08098)], the authors, for each frame, generated a set of connected components by frame difference operation. All of these components are treated as ball candidates. Then the final decision is made by using a set of filters (object size, color, transparency). Xinguo Yu and Hon Wai Leong proposed in Reference [[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B46-sensors-22-08098)] a two-phase trajectory-based algorithm that first generates a set of ball candidates for each frame and then uses them to compute the set of ball trajectories.

A similar approach, but instead using a shape-from-silhouette technique with multi-viewpoint images, was proposed by Shishido et al. [[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B47-sensors-22-08098)].

In 2021, Zhiguang Cao et al. proposed two novel networks named M-YOLOv2 and YOLOBR based on Tiny YOLOv2 [[48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B48-sensors-22-08098)]. The authors modified the loss function to adaptively improve the detection speed for small objects, such as shuttlecocks and the architecture of Tiny YOLOv2, to retain more semantic information about small objects. Unfortunately, the neural network approach is slower than traditional methods. The method proposed works at most at 30 fps.

The use of a generic, universal approach for detecting shuttlecock is problematic because of the following reasons:Depending on the camera’s view, badminton shuttlecock silhouette can be seen as a circle or a triangle, so finding it within the image is more complex than finding a ball.The size of the shuttlecock may significantly change when it approaches the camera.A shuttlecock moves at rapidly varying speeds, reaching very high values at times. The algorithm must work well with fast (400 km/h) and slow (24 km/h) shuttlecocks.The white color of the shuttlecock can be very similar to the scene (player socks, white court lines, and letters on advertisement boards).The shuttlecock often moves in complex contexts: moving players, fast rackets, and changing backgrounds.Because of the cone-like shape and center of gravity located next to the cork (not in the center), it is difficult to predict the trajectory following the physics laws described by simple formulas, especially after the hit, when the shuttlecock turns over and has an unstable trajectory.

In order to avoid as many problems as possible, in our current system version, we located cameras next to the court (behind advertisement boards), facing the lines. We do not use cameras over the court. This approach has one limit: we do not record the whole trajectory, but it is sufficient for in/out decisions.

By narrowing the field of view of the camera to the area of the field line, we limit the visibility of other moving objects (players, for example); thus, the shuttlecock is very often the only moving object. That also simplifies the problem with unstable trajectory: it is stable next to the ground. Moreover, the speed of a shuttlecock is almost constant.

We utilize the feature that a shuttlecock is a fast-moving object over a usually still background. Differential images generated from consecutive frames allow us to distinguish moving objects from static backgrounds.

On the other hand, when the shuttlecock hits the ground, it changes direction and may even stop moving for a moment and vanish from the differential image. Our solution generates an accumulative differential frame from 7 consecutive differential images. This allows us to keep sight of the shuttlecock when it hits the ground. The intensity of pixels in the accumulative frame corresponds to the order of images used to generate it. Pixels from later differential images obtain lower values than pixels from earlier images (from light to a dark shade of gray color). This way, we get additional information about the direction of the movement. [Figure 7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#sensors-22-08098-f007) shows an accumulative differential frame (a) and the direction of moving blobs marked by lines (b). The blob with the white outline in [Figure 7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#sensors-22-08098-f007)b is the one that was recognized as a shuttlecock. Other blobs in this figure were filtered out. The color of a blob represents the filter that filtered out the shuttlecock candidate.

Similar to Reference [[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B45-sensors-22-08098)], our solution generates a set of shuttlecock candidates (blobs) and, using a set of filters, selects the one most likely to be a shuttlecock. The filters are as follows:Remove big blobs (players)—marked with aqua color on [Figure 7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#sensors-22-08098-f007)b.Remove small blobs (noise)—gray color.Remove blobs whose shape is not pencil-like—magenta color.Remove blobs that move too slow or too fast—red color.Remove blobs that are moving in the wrong direction (pink color). In our scenario, we are interested in tracking the shuttlecock when it moves down to the ground.

Shape segmentation makes it easy to distinguish a shuttlecock from another moving object. The whole process takes less than 2 ms on an Intel Core i7 machine.

There are situations when, behind a shuttlecock, a player is moving. The blob of a player is usually much bigger than the blob of a shuttlecock, and both blobs overlap. The segmentation algorithm may mistakenly treat the shuttlecock as a fragment of a player. [Figure 8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#sensors-22-08098-f008) shows an example of this problem. To solve it, we follow the algorithm:With the use of a Kalman filter, predict where the shuttle should be, based on the trajectory from the previous frames ([Figure 9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#sensors-22-08098-f009)).Generate a patch (104 × 104 px) from the original frame with the center predicted by a Kalman filter.Pass a generated patch to a neural network detector as an input.

We perform this additional detection only if the first part of the detector fails.

Our neural network is a modified Tiny Yolo3 [[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B49-sensors-22-08098)] trained with a set of images collected during the tournaments. The original Tiny Yolo3 expects 3-channel photos, and we changed it to use only 1-channel ones. [Figure 10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#sensors-22-08098-f010) presents example patches passed to the neural network. With the CPU: 9th Gen. Intel® Core™ i7-processor and GPU: NVIDIA® GTX 1080, the detection of a shuttlecock with a neural network takes 12 ms and causes a delay, which is, however, acceptable. When the first method finds the shuttlecock again, it eliminates the delay caused by the neural network, and the entire algorithm works in almost-real time. The neural network with a single class (shuttlecock) achieves a mean average precision (mAP@0.50) of 94%, and for a threshold 0.25 precision, it achieves 0.96, a recall of 0.77, and an F1-score of 0.86. [Figure 11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#sensors-22-08098-f011) shows the algorithm’s structure. Two videos with the result of our algorithm are available at [https://drive.google.com/file/d/1rsvcY-5Q25iN5Hmcv4nW_DXIWq9ZAR7J/view?usp=sharing](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1rsvcY-5Q25iN5Hmcv4nW_DXIWq9ZAR7J/view?usp=sharing), [https://drive.google.com/file/d/1-Btu3YHeyYYm29MncjXMvjHcUePi2EI_/view?usp=sharing](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1-Btu3YHeyYYm29MncjXMvjHcUePi2EI_/view?usp=sharing) (accessed on 16 October 2022).

### 2.13. Tracker Performance

We collected data for the tests during the tournaments. Each time the player disagreed with the line judge’s decision and asked for verification, our system saved 30 s of camera footage at 150 fps. From recorded movies, we selected 52 sets of frames for annotation. Sets of images and the file with annotated shuttlecock positions are available to download from the location provided in the [Supplementary Materials Section](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#app1-sensors-22-08098). Each set consists of several consecutive frames before the shuttlecock hits the floor. We annotated a total of 20,788 frames. If the shuttlecock was visible, the operator marked its center position. More precisely, the operator marked positions of only a few frames where the shuttlecock was visible, and we interpolated the rest of the positions between those marked.

Our tracker detects if the shuttlecock is visible with an accuracy of 94%. We prefer false detections to missed, undetected shuttlecocks. These can be socks, shoes, and other white parts of clothing.

For the frames where the shuttlecock was visible, we measured if the detected position of a shuttlecock was correct. Due to the irregular shape of the shuttlecock, inaccuracies in interpolation, and blurriness, the shuttlecock’s annotated positions are not always accurate. The detection of a shuttlecock position was marked successful if the difference between annotated position and the position saved by the detector was less than 12 pixels. In all, 81% of the visible shuttlecocks were correctly detected and tracked.

### 2.14. Object Segmentation

While the shuttlecock moves at a high speed, it is blurred within the image. The motion blur effect causes segmentation difficulties due to ambiguous pixels between regions of the object and the background. Imprecise shuttlecock contour detection reduces the accuracy of localizing the cork when it comes into contact with the ground impairing the overall system’s accuracy.

Although there are many methods to remove or decrease blur (see, for example References [[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B50-sensors-22-08098),[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B51-sensors-22-08098),[52](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9655598#B52-sensors-22-08098)]), we do not use them. This is a peer-reviewed scientific paper published in Sensors (Basel) journal (2022 Oct 22;22(21):8098, doi: 10.3390/s22218098, PMC9655598, PMID 36365797) by Michał Kopania, Jarosław Nowisz, and Artur Przelaskowski from the Faculty of Mathematics and Information Science, Warsaw University of Technology, Poland. The paper describes the development of an Automatic Shuttlecock Fall Detection System (Instant Review System / Challenge System) for badminton that determines whether a shuttlecock landed in or out of court boundaries.

The authors built and tested their system at the BWF World Senior Badminton Championships in Katowice, where over 1500 players competed on 12 courts. The system evolved through two major architecture versions: (1) an initial version using 6 cameras mounted above the court (below the ceiling) plus 14 cameras around the court (1m above ground) with 3D trajectory reconstruction, and (2) an improved version using only 14 cameras around the court plus 1 wide-view camera, eliminating 3D reconstruction entirely. The current version detects single court lines rather than a full court model, simplifying calibration and installation.

Key technical details: The system uses cameras with 800×600 resolution at 150 fps (with interpolation for accuracy), GigE cables with Power over Ethernet, and 8 servers. The verification procedure must not exceed 25 seconds (audience tolerance), and installation must take no more than 4 hours per court with no more than 2 people. The authors identified operational problems (lighting, space constraints, wiring, bent court lines, mat deformation, air-conditioning drift, equipment transport) and algorithmic challenges (calibration, court recognition, detection/tracking, motion blur, occlusion, speed, flickering light).

Notable technical solutions include: an adaptive pixel-wise flicker compensation method 250-300 times faster than DeFlicker/FlickerFree; a hybrid detection approach combining fast differential-frame methods (generating accumulative differential frames from 7 consecutive frames) with a modified Tiny YOLO3 neural network (single-class, 1-channel input) used as fallback when the primary method fails; Kalman filter for trajectory prediction/interpolation; and a camera calibration best-practices list that reduces reprojection error by over 3x compared to standard procedures.

Performance results: Court detection accuracy of 97.7%; shuttlecock visibility detection accuracy of 94%; 81% of visible shuttlecocks correctly detected and tracked (success defined as <12 pixel error); neural network mAP@0.50 of 94% with precision 0.96, recall 0.77, and F1-score 0.86 at threshold 0.25; neural network detection takes 12 ms on Intel Core i7 with GTX 1080; the primary blob-filtering method takes less than 2 ms. The system was verified by the Badminton World Federation and Polish Badminton Federation and is comparable to commercial products (e.g., Hawk-Eye) in processing time and accuracy but is easier, faster to install, and more adaptive/flexible/universal for practical sports hall requirements.

# Fine reconstruction of badminton swing dynamic trajectory assisted by event camera

* [Yi Wang](#auth-Yi-Wang-Aff1)[1](#Aff1),
* [Bo Shi](#auth-Bo-Shi-Aff1)[1](#Aff1) &
* [Bin Lv](#auth-Bin-Lv-Aff1)[1](#Aff1)

[*Scientific Reports*](/srep)
**volume 16**, Article number: 15444 (2026) [Cite this article](#citeas)

[Save article](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8/save-research?_csrf=kGPP7YJ4FwtReqb40mh6ipGQGnygWaFD)

## Abstract

The instantaneous velocity of smash actions in badminton can exceed 100 m per second, with action durations of only tens of milliseconds. Traditional frame-based cameras, limited by fixed sampling frequencies and finite dynamic ranges, struggle to achieve fine reconstruction of high-speed swing trajectories. This study proposes a fine reconstruction method for badminton swing dynamic trajectories assisted by event cameras, utilizing the microsecond-level temporal resolution and 120-decibel high dynamic range sensing characteristics of event cameras to overcome motion blur problems. The system adopts a heterogeneous visual sensor collaborative acquisition scheme, converting asynchronous event streams into tensor representations processable by deep learning through voxel grid encoding, and designs an event optical flow estimation network based on the contrast maximization principle to extract high temporal resolution motion features. The human pose estimation module obtains skeletal keypoint coordinates, and an extended Kalman filter framework fuses event optical flow, visual keypoints, and inertial measurement data to generate continuous three-dimensional trajectories. The fusion framework explicitly models observation uncertainty from each sensor modality, enabling robust state estimation under heterogeneous noise conditions. Experiments on a dataset containing 960 swing samples from 12 athletes validated the method’s effectiveness, with trajectory reconstruction achieving a mean absolute error of 8.34 millimeters, a 42.3% reduction compared to traditional optical flow methods, and a processing frame rate of 82 FPS meeting real-time requirements. Ablation experiments show that the event optical flow module contributes 52.0% of the performance gain, and the multimodal fusion strategy further improves accuracy by 36.8%. Biomechanical analysis results reveal statistically significant differences between professional and amateur athletes in swing velocity curves, joint coordination, and other metrics, validating the system’s application value in sports training guidance. A systematic error decomposition analysis and discussion of generalization considerations across diverse venues, lighting conditions, player styles, and equipment types are further provided to guide future practical deployment.

## Introduction

As one of the racket sports with the highest global participation, the improvement of competitive level in badminton cannot be separated from the support of scientific training methods. Swing action is the core component of the badminton technical system, and parameters such as racket face angle, swing speed, and hitting point position at the moment of impact directly determine the quality and landing accuracy of the return shot[1](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR1 "Phomsoupha, M. & Laffaye, G. The science of badminton: Game characteristics, anthropometry, physiology, visual fitness and biomechanics. Sports Med. 45(4), 473–495 (2015)."). Traditional badminton training mainly relies on coaches’ visual observation and empirical judgment, which has limitations such as strong subjectivity and low quantification. In recent years, with the rapid development of computer vision technology and wearable sensors, fine reconstruction of motion trajectories has gradually become a hot research direction in sports science. However, badminton swing actions have significant characteristics such as high speed, large amplitude, and short duration. Professional athletes’ smash speeds can reach over 100 m per second, with the entire hitting process lasting only tens of milliseconds[2](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR2 "Towler, H., Mitchell, S. R. & King, M. A. Effects of racket moment of inertia on racket head speed, impact location and shuttlecock speed during the badminton smash. Sci. Rep. 13(1), 14060 (2023)."), which poses extremely high requirements for the temporal resolution of motion capture systems. Traditional frame-based cameras, limited by fixed frame rate acquisition modes, are prone to motion blur in high-speed motion scenarios and struggle to completely capture key detail information of swing trajectories.

Scholars at home and abroad have conducted extensive research on badminton motion analysis. Seong et al. constructed a multi-sensor badminton biomechanics dataset, fusing multimodal data such as eye tracking, skeleton tracking, electromyography signals, and plantar pressure, laying a data foundation for quantitative evaluation of swing actions[3](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR3 "Seong, M. et al. Multisensebadminton: Wearable sensor–based biomechanical dataset for evaluation of badminton performance. Sci. Data. 11 (1), 343 (2024)."). Van Herbruggen et al. combined inertial measurement units with ultra-wideband positioning technology to analyze tactical strategies of badminton players, achieving high classification accuracy[4](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR4 "Van Herbruggen, B. et al. Strategy analysis of badminton players using deep learning from IMU and UWB wearables. Internet of Things 27, 101260 (2024)."). Hsu et al. proposed a match analysis method integrating badminton trajectory tracking and hit detection, using the TrackNet deep network to extract shuttlecock flight trajectories and combining with the YOLOv7 model to recognize players’ swing actions[5](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR5 "Hsu, Y. H., Yu, C. C. & Cheng, H. Y. Enhancing badminton game analysis: An approach to shot refinement via a fusion of shuttlecock tracking and hit detection from monocular camera. Sensors 24(13), 4372 (2024)."). Towler et al. studied the influence mechanism of racket moment of inertia on smash performance through motion capture systems, revealing the intrinsic correlation between racket physical properties and hitting effects[2](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR2 "Towler, H., Mitchell, S. R. & King, M. A. Effects of racket moment of inertia on racket head speed, impact location and shuttlecock speed during the badminton smash. Sci. Rep. 13(1), 14060 (2023)."). Event cameras, as a new type of neuromorphic visual sensor, have shown tremendous potential in high-speed motion capture with advantages such as microsecond-level temporal resolution, high dynamic range, and low power consumption[6](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR6 "Gallego, G. et al. Event-based vision: A survey. IEEE Trans. Pattern Anal. Mach. Intell. 44 (1), 154–180 (2020)."). Shiba et al. achieved joint estimation of optical flow, depth, and ego-motion for event cameras based on a contrast maximization framework, providing a new technical path for dynamic scene understanding[7](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR7 "Shiba, S., Klose, Y., Aoki, Y. & Gallego, G. Secrets of event-based optical flow, depth and ego-motion estimation by contrast maximization. IEEE Trans. Pattern Anal. Mach. Intell. 46 (12), 7742–7759 (2024)."). Gehrig et al. proposed a dense continuous-time optical flow estimation method, parameterizing pixel motion trajectories using Bézier curves, breaking through the temporal discreteness limitation of traditional two-frame optical flow[8](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR8 "Gehrig, M., Muglikar, M. & Scaramuzza, D. Dense continuous-time optical flow from event cameras. IEEE Trans. Pattern Anal. Mach. Intell. 46 (7), 4736–4746 (2024)."). Zhang et al. modeled the event-driven image reconstruction problem as a linear inverse problem with depth regularization, effectively improving the quality and robustness of reconstructed images[9](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR9 "Zhang, Z., Yezzi, A. J. & Gallego, G. Formulating event-based image reconstruction as a linear inverse problem with deep regularization using optical flow. IEEE Trans. Pattern Anal. Mach. Intell. 45(7), 8372–8389 (2022)."). The above research indicates that event cameras have unique advantages in temporal modeling of high-speed motion scenarios, but their application in badminton swing trajectory reconstruction is still in the exploratory stage.

Although existing event camera-based methods have demonstrated promising results in general-purpose high-speed scene perception, they primarily focus on single-task objectives such as optical flow estimation or feature point tracking within open scenes, without addressing the specific demands of sports biomechanical analysis. In particular, challenges such as multi-source heterogeneous sensor fusion under extreme motion velocities, real-time human joint kinematics extraction, and integrated technical evaluation for training guidance remain insufficiently explored in the context of racket sports. Furthermore, when fusing observations from heterogeneous sensors with vastly different noise characteristics and sampling rates, quantifying and propagating observation uncertainty is a fundamental challenge that directly affects the reliability of the fused trajectory estimates. Recent advances in uncertainty-aware observation modeling for complex multi-source systems[10](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR10 "Li, X. & Dong, Y. A satellite cluster observation method for logistics status of industry chain with quantifiable uncertainty. Chin. J. Aeronaut. 38(6), 103305 (2025).") have highlighted the importance of incorporating quantifiable uncertainty into sensor fusion frameworks, which is also a key consideration in the multimodal fusion strategy adopted in this study. These gaps motivate the development of a dedicated event camera-assisted framework that combines high temporal resolution perception with a complete biomechanical analysis pipeline.

To formalize the research problem, the trajectory reconstruction task addressed in this study can be stated as follows. The system receives multimodal input consisting of an asynchronous event stream \(\mathcal{E}={e\_i}i={1^N}\) from the event camera, an RGB image sequence \({I\_k}k={1^K}\) from the frame-based camera, and IMU measurements \(({{\mathbf{a}}\_k},{{\mathbf{\omega }}\_k})\) comprising three-axis acceleration and angular velocity. The output is a continuous 3D swing trajectory \({\mathbf{T}}(t) \in {{\mathbb{R}}^3}\) representing the racket spatial position over time, along with associated biomechanical parameters including joint angles \({\theta \_j}(t)\) and swing velocity profiles \(v(t)\). The optimization objective is to minimize the spatial deviation between the reconstructed trajectory and the ground-truth trajectory \({{\mathbf{T}}^{gt}}(t)\) obtained from an optical motion capture system, subject to temporal continuity and physical plausibility constraints. Detailed formulations of the individual modules and the overall optimization strategy are presented in Sect. [3](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#Sec6).

The research framework of this study is shown in Fig. [1](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#Fig1). Targeting the insufficient temporal resolution problem of traditional frame-based cameras in high-speed swing capture, this study proposes a fine reconstruction method for badminton swing dynamic trajectories assisted by event cameras. The innovations of this research are mainly reflected in the following aspects: First, designing a heterogeneous visual acquisition system with coordinated event cameras and frame-based cameras, fully leveraging the high temporal resolution advantages of event streams and the rich texture information advantages of image frames, achieving complementary fusion of multi-source visual data; Second, proposing an event-driven swing trajectory extraction algorithm combining contrast maximization and deep learning, improving trajectory reconstruction accuracy and completeness while ensuring real-time performance; Third, constructing a multi-granularity spatiotemporal feature representation model for badminton swing actions, characterizing the dynamic evolution process of swing actions from multiple dimensions such as racket kinematic parameters, joint angle changes, and hitting timing features, providing quantitative basis for athletes’ personalized technical diagnosis and training optimization.

## Related work and theoretical foundation

### Event camera technology

Event cameras are a new type of neuromorphic sensor designed inspired by biological visual systems, with fundamental differences in working principles from traditional frame-based cameras. Traditional cameras synchronously capture brightness values of all pixels at a fixed frame rate, while each pixel in an event camera independently and asynchronously responds to local brightness changes, triggering an event when the brightness change exceeds a set threshold[6](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR6 "Gallego, G. et al. Event-based vision: A survey. IEEE Trans. Pattern Anal. Mach. Intell. 44 (1), 154–180 (2020)."). Each event contains quadruplet information: spatial coordinates (x, y), timestamp t, and polarity p, with polarity characterizing the direction of brightness increase or decrease. This asynchronous sampling mechanism endows event cameras with microsecond-level temporal resolution, improving by more than three orders of magnitude compared to traditional cameras. Event cameras also possess a high dynamic range of 140 decibels, far exceeding the 60-decibel level of traditional cameras, enabling stable operation under extreme lighting conditions[6](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR6 "Gallego, G. et al. Event-based vision: A survey. IEEE Trans. Pattern Anal. Mach. Intell. 44 (1), 154–180 (2020)."). Low power consumption is also a significant advantage of event cameras; since data is only output when brightness changes, their power consumption typically remains at the milliwatt level.

Guo and Gallego addressed the rotational motion estimation problem for event cameras, proposing the CMax-SLAM system[11](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR11 "Guo, S. & Gallego, G. CMax-SLAM: Event-based rotational-motion bundle adjustment and SLAM system using contrast maximization. IEEE Trans. Robot. 40, 2442–2461 (2024)."). This system adopts a contrast maximization framework for bundle adjustment of rotational motion, achieving high-precision pose estimation and panoramic map construction through global optimization of event alignment quality. Experimental results show that CMax-SLAM achieved positioning accuracy superior to existing methods on multiple public datasets. Dong and Fu’s MemFlow method introduces a memory mechanism into optical flow estimation networks[12](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR12 "Dong, Q. & Fu, Y. Memflow: Optical flow estimation and prediction with memory. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (pp. 19068–19078). (2024)."), achieving real-time multi-frame optical flow prediction by storing and aggregating historical motion information, surpassing baseline methods such as VideoFlow on Sintel and KITTI datasets with fewer parameters and faster inference speed. The sparsity and asynchronicity of event camera data pose challenges to traditional computer vision algorithms, and researchers have explored various event representation methods, including event frames, time surfaces, and voxel grids, to adapt to different downstream task requirements.

### Racket sport trajectory analysis

Trajectory analysis of racket sports covers multiple levels including athlete limb movement, racket swing, and ball flight. Wearable inertial sensors have been widely applied in sports data acquisition due to their portability and non-invasiveness. Ooi and Gouwanda developed a badminton stroke type recognition system using wireless inertial measurement units[13](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR13 "Ooi, J. H. & Gouwanda, D. Badminton stroke identification using wireless inertial measurement units and neural network. Sports Eng. 26, 15 (2023)."), classifying acceleration and angular velocity signals through neural networks to achieve automatic recognition of different stroke actions. Stoeve et al. applied inertial sensors to football motion analysis[14](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR14 "Stoeve, M., Schuldhaus, D., Gamp, A., Zwick, C. & Eskofier, B. M. From the laboratory to the field: IMU-based shot and pass detection in football training and game scenarios using deep learning. Sensors 21 (9), 3071 (2021)."), detecting shooting and passing actions based on deep learning methods, validating the effectiveness of IMU signals in sports event recognition tasks. Wang et al. constructed a badminton stroke recognition system based on one-dimensional convolutional neural networks[15](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR15 "Jin, G. & Li, X. Wearable sensing for badminton stroke recognition with one-dimensional convolutional neural network. Sci. Rep. 15(1), 41236 (2025)."), collecting swing motion data using dual-wrist inertial sensors and achieving high-precision classification of six stroke actions and fifteen motion trajectories.

Vision-based motion analysis methods have also made significant progress. Cao et al., targeting the shuttlecock detection problem for badminton robots, proposed an improved YOLO network architecture[16](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR16 "Cao, Z., Liao, T., Song, W., Chen, Z. & Li, C. Detecting the shuttlecock for a badminton robot: A YOLO based approach. Expert Syst. Appl. 164, 113833 (2021)."), enhancing small object detection speed and accuracy by modifying the loss function and network structure, laying a technical foundation for real-time shuttlecock tracking. Fang et al. developed the AlphaPose system for multi-person whole-body pose estimation[17](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR17 "Fang, H. S. et al. Alphapose: Whole-body regional multi-person pose estimation and tracking in real-time. IEEE Trans. Pattern Anal. Mach. Intell. 45 (6), 7157–7173 (2022)."), adopting a top-down detection-estimation framework and maintaining high keypoint localization accuracy under occlusion and complex background conditions. Deep learning-driven pose estimation technology provides strong support for extracting athlete limb trajectories, but monocular vision methods have inherent ambiguity in depth estimation, making multi-view or multimodal fusion an important approach to improving 3D reconstruction accuracy.

### Dynamic trajectory reconstruction methods

Fine reconstruction of motion trajectories requires addressing two core problems: spatiotemporal continuity modeling and multi-source data fusion. Sun et al. systematically reviewed the application status of motion capture technology in sports scenarios[18](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR18 "Suo, X., Tang, W. & Li, Z. Motion capture technology in sports scenarios: A survey. Sensors 24(9), 2947 (2024)."), analyzing the advantages and limitations of mainstream technical routes such as optical motion capture, inertial motion capture, and visual motion capture. Optical motion capture systems, represented by Vicon and OptiTrack, achieve sub-millimeter positioning accuracy through infrared marker points but have high equipment costs and strict requirements for marker placement. Inertial motion capture systems eliminate spatial limitations of external equipment and are suitable for outdoor and large-range motion scenarios but suffer from cumulative drift problems. Barzyk et al. explored markerless motion capture solutions based on smartphones[19](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR19 "Rojek, I., Mikołajewska, E., Małolepsza, O., Kozielski, M. & Mikołajewski, D. Comparative analysis of different AI approaches to Stroke Patients’ Gait Analysis. Appl. Sci. 15(20), 10896 (2025)."), combining artificial intelligence algorithms to extract human kinematic parameters from ordinary videos, reducing the technical threshold and economic cost of motion analysis. In addition to the selection of motion capture modalities, the measurement precision of multi-camera systems and the associated error propagation mechanisms are critical factors that affect the reliability of 3D trajectory reconstruction. Xing et al. addressed the calibration problem for multi-camera systems with limited overlapping fields of view and proposed a flexible calibration technique that improves the geometric consistency of multi-view measurements[20](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR20 "Xing, Z., Yu, J. & Ma, Y. A new calibration technique for multi-camera systems of limited overlapping field-of-views. In 2017 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS) (pp. 5892–5899). IEEE. (2017), September."). Chen et al. further developed a mathematical framework for modeling the measurement precision of multi-camera configurations, establishing the quantitative relationship between camera network geometry, calibration accuracy, and 3D reconstruction uncertainty[21](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR21 "Yin, Z. et al. Modeling the measurement precision of a multi-camera system. Opt. Lett. 50 (21), 6489–6492 (2025)."). These studies provide important theoretical foundations for understanding the precision limits of vision-based trajectory measurement systems and offer methodological guidance for the multi-sensor spatial calibration procedure adopted in the present study.

Rigozzi et al. conducted a systematic review of wearable technology in racket sports[22](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR22 "Rigozzi, C. J., Vio, G. A. & Poronnik, P. Application of wearable technologies for player motion analysis in racket sports: A systematic review. Int. J. Sports Sci. Coach. 18(6), 2321–2346. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/17479541221138015
                  
                 (2023)."), pointing out that sensor fusion and data synchronization are key bottlenecks constraining system performance. Chang et al. released the TTSwing table tennis dataset[23](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR23 "Chou, C. Y. et al. TtSwing: A Dataset for table tennis Swing and Racket Kinematics analysis. Sci. Data 12(1), 339 (2025)."), containing multi-view videos, inertial data, and 3D kinematic annotations, providing standardized benchmarks for training and evaluation of swing action analysis algorithms. Putra et al. established a mathematical model of badminton smashes[24](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR24 "Putra, V. G. V., Mohamad, J. N. & Irwan, & A novel mathematical model of the badminton smash: simulation and modeling in biomechanics. Comput. Methods Biomech. BioMed. Eng. 27 (4), 538–545 (2024)."), analyzing physical processes such as limb coordination, energy transfer, and racket-shuttlecock collision from a biomechanical perspective, revealing influencing factors and optimization space for smash speed. Li et al. proposed an event camera-based 3D feature tracking method[25](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR25 "Li, S. et al. 3d feature tracking via event camera. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (pp. 18974–18983). (2024)."), utilizing the high temporal resolution characteristics of event streams to achieve stable tracking of fast-moving targets, demonstrating clear advantages in high-speed scenarios where traditional cameras fail. The above research has advanced the development of motion trajectory analysis from different technical routes, providing theoretical reference and technical inspiration for the event camera-assisted swing trajectory reconstruction method in this study.

In summary, existing trajectory reconstruction approaches for racket sports can be broadly categorized into wearable sensor-based methods, frame camera-based visual methods, and emerging event camera-based methods. Wearable inertial sensors offer portability but suffer from cumulative drift and cannot directly capture racket spatial trajectories. Frame camera-based visual methods provide rich texture information but are fundamentally limited by fixed sampling frequencies, leading to motion blur and feature tracking failure during high-speed swing phases. Event camera-based methods such as the 3D feature tracking approach proposed by Li et al.[25](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR25 "Li, S. et al. 3d feature tracking via event camera. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (pp. 18974–18983). (2024).") have demonstrated the potential of neuromorphic sensors for high-speed perception, yet these methods typically address general-purpose tracking tasks and do not incorporate human pose estimation, multi-sensor fusion, or biomechanical parameter extraction. To the best of our knowledge, no existing work has systematically integrated event-driven perception with multimodal sensor fusion and biomechanical analysis to achieve fine trajectory reconstruction specifically tailored for high-speed racket sports. This gap constitutes the primary motivation of the present study, which aims to bridge event camera technology and sports science through a unified framework encompassing heterogeneous data acquisition, event-driven feature extraction, multi-source Kalman filter fusion, and automated technical evaluation.

## Method design

### Overall system framework

The event camera-assisted badminton swing dynamic trajectory fine reconstruction system proposed in this study consists of four core components: data acquisition module, preprocessing module, feature extraction module, and trajectory reconstruction module. The overall system architecture is shown in Fig. [2](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#Fig2). The data acquisition module is responsible for synchronously obtaining event streams, RGB image sequences, and inertial measurement data, constructing the hardware foundation for multimodal perception. The preprocessing module performs spatiotemporal alignment, noise filtering, and format conversion on raw data, ensuring data quality for subsequent processing. The feature extraction module separately extracts motion features such as event optical flow, human skeletal keypoints, and racket spatial position from multi-source data. The trajectory reconstruction module fuses the above feature information, generating high-precision 3D swing trajectories through temporal modeling and optimization algorithms. The entire system adopts a modular design philosophy, with standardized interfaces for data interaction between modules, facilitating independent optimization and expansion upgrades.

### Multimodal data acquisition system

Targeting the high-speed characteristics of badminton swing actions, this study designs a heterogeneous visual acquisition scheme with coordinated operation of event cameras and frame-based cameras. The event camera uses iniVation’s DAVIS346 model, which simultaneously outputs event streams and grayscale image frames, with event temporal resolution reaching the microsecond level and dynamic range exceeding 120 decibels[6](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR6 "Gallego, G. et al. Event-based vision: A survey. IEEE Trans. Pattern Anal. Mach. Intell. 44 (1), 154–180 (2020)."). The RGB camera uses an industrial-grade high-speed camera with a frame rate set to 240 frames per second, forming complementarity with the event camera. The inertial measurement unit uses a nine-axis IMU module with a sampling frequency configured at 500 Hz to capture acceleration and angular velocity information of athletes’ upper limbs. Kim et al.‘s research indicates that multi-sensor fusion schemes can effectively improve the accuracy and robustness of badminton action recognition[26](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR26 "Ji, M. et al. Machine learning – assisted triboelectric nanogenerator technology for intelligent sports. Sci. Adv. 11 (40), eadz3515 (2025).").

Multi-sensor temporal synchronization is a key link in ensuring data quality. This system adopts a synchronization strategy combining hardware triggering and software correction, sending synchronization pulses to all sensors through an external signal generator to achieve millisecond-level clock alignment. The software level further uses timestamp interpolation algorithms to eliminate residual temporal offsets. Luo et al.‘s proposed binocular vision positioning method provides technical reference for multi-camera calibration[27](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR27 "Luo, J. et al. Vision-based movement recognition reveals badminton player footwork using deep learning and binocular positioning. Heliyon 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.heliyon.2022.e10089
                  
                 (2022)."). Sensor spatial calibration uses a checkerboard calibration board, obtaining camera intrinsic parameters through Zhang’s calibration method and determining relative pose relationships between sensors using hand-eye calibration methods. The measurement precision of this multi-camera spatial calibration is influenced by factors such as the number of calibration images, checkerboard pattern density, and the geometric configuration of the camera network, as systematically analyzed by Xing et al.[20](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR20 "Xing, Z., Yu, J. & Ma, Y. A new calibration technique for multi-camera systems of limited overlapping field-of-views. In 2017 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS) (pp. 5892–5899). IEEE. (2017), September.") and Chen et al.[21](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR21 "Yin, Z. et al. Modeling the measurement precision of a multi-camera system. Opt. Lett. 50 (21), 6489–6492 (2025)."). The main technical parameters of the acquisition system are shown in Table [1](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#Tab1).
