To ensure the validity of trajectory reconstruction evaluation, the ground-truth reference is defined as follows. The OptiTrack optical motion capture system is employed as the reference standard, with four retroreflective markers attached to the badminton racket head forming a rigid body configuration. The geometric centroid of these four markers is computed at each time step and serves as the ground-truth reference point representing the racket spatial position. This centroid-based definition provides a stable and unambiguous physical reference that is robust to individual marker occlusion. The coordinate transformation from the OptiTrack world coordinate frame to the event camera coordinate frame is established through a rigid body registration procedure. Specifically, a set of corresponding 3D point pairs are obtained by simultaneously observing a calibration target with both the OptiTrack system and the camera system, and the transformation matrix comprising rotation R and translation t is computed by minimizing the point-to-point registration error using the singular value decomposition method. The IMU body frame is aligned to the camera frame through the hand-eye calibration procedure described above. To verify the temporal synchronization quality, the synchronization residual between the OptiTrack system and the event camera is measured by detecting a common sharp motion event, yielding an average temporal offset of less than 0.5 milliseconds, which is negligible relative to the swing durations of hundreds of milliseconds. It should be noted that although OptiTrack is widely regarded as a high-accuracy reference standard, it still has inherent measurement uncertainty. According to the manufacturer’s specifications and independent validation studies, the OptiTrack system provides sub-millimeter 3D positioning accuracy, typically in the range of 0.1 to 0.3 millimeters under controlled laboratory conditions with adequate marker visibility. This ground-truth uncertainty is approximately one to two orders of magnitude smaller than the trajectory reconstruction errors reported in this study, and therefore its influence on the evaluation of the proposed method is considered negligible. Nevertheless, the reported reconstruction errors should be interpreted as including a minor component attributable to ground-truth measurement noise, particularly during the impact phase when brief marker occlusion may occur.

### Event-driven feature extraction

Asynchronous event streams output by event cameras need to be converted into tensor representation forms suitable for deep learning processing. This study adopts the voxel grid encoding method, accumulating events within a time window into a fixed-size three-dimensional tensor. Let the event stream be \(\mathcal{E}={e\_i}\_{{i=1}}^{N}\), where each event \({e\_i}=({x\_i},{y\_i},{t\_i},{p\_i})\) contains spatial coordinates \(({x\_i},{y\_i})\), timestamp \({t\_i}\), and polarity \({p\_i} \in - 1,+1\). The construction formula for voxel grid \(t{V\in}{\text{R}}^{{B\times H\times W}}\) is:

$$V(b,x,y)=\sum\limits\_{{i=1}}^{N} {{p\_i}} \cdot \hbox{max} (0,1 - |b - t\_{i}^{\*}|)$$

(1)

where *B* represents the number of discretization bins in the temporal dimension, *H* and *W* are the spatial height and width respectively, and \(t\_{i}^{\*}=({t\_i} - {t\_1})/({t\_N} - {t\_1}) \cdot (B - 1)\) is the normalized temporal index. This encoding method preserves the temporal information and polarity features of events. In the experiments of this study, the number of temporal bins is set to \(B=5\), the spatial dimensions are configured as \(H=260\) and \(W=346\) matching the native resolution of the DAVIS346 sensor, and the time window length is set to \(\Delta t=10\) milliseconds, which is selected to balance temporal granularity and event density for the typical swing velocities encountered in badminton. Ponghiran et al.‘s research validated the effectiveness of voxel representation in optical flow estimation tasks[28](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR28 "Ponghiran, W., Liyanagedera, C. M. & Roy, K. Event-based temporally dense optical flow estimation with sequential learning. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF international conference on computer vision (pp. 9827–9836). (2023).").

The event optical flow estimation network is designed based on the contrast maximization principle, whose core idea is to find optimal pixel motion parameters that maximize image contrast after event alignment[7](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR7 "Shiba, S., Klose, Y., Aoki, Y. & Gallego, G. Secrets of event-based optical flow, depth and ego-motion estimation by contrast maximization. IEEE Trans. Pattern Anal. Mach. Intell. 46 (12), 7742–7759 (2024)."). Let the optical flow field be \({\mathbf{f}}=({f\_u},{f\_v})\), where \({f\_u}\) and \({f\_v}\) denote the horizontal and vertical components of pixel displacement respectively, and the event image \(I({\mathbf{f}})\) is generated by back-projecting events to the reference moment according to the optical flow. The optimization objective function is defined as:

$$\mathcal{L}({\mathbf{f}})= - {\text{Var}}(I({\mathbf{f}}))+\lambda |\nabla {\mathbf{f}}|\_{2}^{2}$$

(2)

where \({\text{Var}}( \cdot )\) represents image variance, i.e., contrast measurement, \(\nabla {\mathbf{f}}\) is the spatial gradient of optical flow measuring the local smoothness of the displacement field, and \(\lambda\) is the regularization coefficient used to constrain the smoothness of the optical flow field. The first term encourages temporal alignment of events by maximizing the sharpness of the warped event image, while the second term penalizes abrupt spatial variations in the flow field to ensure physical plausibility. Cuadrado et al. introduced spiking neural networks into event optical flow computation[29](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR29 "Cuadrado, J., Rançon, U., Cottereau, B. R., Barranco, F. & Masquelier, T. Optical flow estimation from event-based cameras and spiking neural networks. Front. Neurosci. 17, 1160034 (2023)."), and Zhang et al. further explored neuromorphic implementation schemes for event-driven optical flow[30](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#ref-CR30 "Zhang, Y. et al. Event-based optical flow estimation with spatio-temporal backpropagation trained spiking neural network. Micromachines 14(1), 203. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/MI14010203
                  
                 (2023)."), providing possibilities for low-power edge deployment.

The network architecture implements the contrast maximization objective through an encoder-decoder structure with skip connections, as shown in Fig. [3](/articles/s41598-026-46443-8#Fig3). The encoder consists of four convolutional blocks that progressively extract multi-scale motion features from the voxel grid input. The first block applies 3 × 3 convolutions with 64 output channels followed by batch normalization and ReLU activation, producing feature maps at the original spatial resolution of \(H \times W\). Each subsequent block doubles the channel count (128, 256, and 512 channels for blocks 2, 3, and 4 respectively) while halving the spatial resolution through 2 × 2 max pooling, resulting in intermediate feature maps of dimensions 64 × 128 × 128, 128 × 64 × 64, 256 × 32 × 32, and 512 × 16 × 16 (channels × height × width, with height and width values corresponding to the downsampled DAVIS346 resolution). At the bottleneck, a 4D cost volume is constructed by computing correlation scores between encoder features across different temporal bins and disparity hypotheses, capturing the correspondence structure necessary for accurate motion estimation. The decoder mirrors the encoder with four upsampling stages, each consisting of bilinear upsampling followed by concatenation with the corresponding encoder features via skip connections, and a 3 × 3 convolutional layer with batch normalization and ReLU activation. The channel counts in the decoder decrease symmetrically from 256 to 32 across the four stages. This is a scientific research article published in Scientific Reports (volume 16, Article number 15444, 2026) titled "Fine reconstruction of badminton swing dynamic trajectory assisted by event camera," authored by Yi Wang, Bo Shi, and Bin Lv.

**Problem:** Badminton smash actions can exceed 100 m/s velocity with durations of only tens of milliseconds. Traditional frame-based cameras suffer from fixed sampling frequencies, limited dynamic ranges, and motion blur in high-speed scenarios.

**Proposed Method:** A fine reconstruction system using event cameras (iniVation DAVIS346) with microsecond-level temporal resolution and 120+ decibel high dynamic range. Key components:
1. **Heterogeneous visual acquisition**: Event camera + high-speed RGB camera (240 fps) + nine-axis IMU (500 Hz sampling), synchronized via hardware triggering and software correction (millisecond-level clock alignment).
2. **Event-driven feature extraction**: Voxel grid encoding converts asynchronous events into tensors (B=5 temporal bins, H=260, W=346, Δt=10ms window); an event optical flow estimation network based on contrast maximization principle with encoder-decoder architecture (64→128→256→512 channels, skip connections, 4D cost volume).
3. **Human pose estimation**: YOLOv5s for athlete detection + HRNet backbone for skeletal keypoint extraction; elbow joint angle calculated via vector geometry.
4. **Multi-source fusion**: Extended Kalman filter (EKF) fuses event optical flow, visual keypoints, and IMU data into a 12-dimensional state vector (position, velocity, attitude angles, angular velocity) to generate continuous 3D trajectories. Observation noise for each sensor modality is explicitly modeled (Q with σp=1.0mm, σv=0.5m/s, σφ=0.01rad; R with event optical flow at 4.0 pixels²).

**Results:** On a dataset of 960 swing samples from 12 athletes:
- Trajectory reconstruction MAE of 8.34 millimeters (42.3% reduction vs. traditional optical flow methods)
- Processing frame rate of 82 FPS (meets real-time requirements)
- Event optical flow module contributes 52.0% of performance gain; multimodal fusion improves accuracy by 36.8%
- Biomechanical analysis revealed statistically significant differences between professional and amateur athletes in swing velocity curves and joint coordination
- Ground truth from OptiTrack motion capture system (0.1-0.3 mm accuracy, sub-millimeter), with temporal offset <0.5ms

**Innovations:** (1) Heterogeneous visual acquisition system combining event and frame cameras; (2) event-driven trajectory extraction combining contrast maximization and deep learning; (3) multi-granularity spatiotemporal feature representation for swing actions enabling personalized technical diagnosis.

The paper also discusses error decomposition analysis and generalization considerations across venues, lighting conditions, player styles, and equipment types. It cites related work on event camera technology (CMax-SLAM, MemFlow), racket sport trajectory analysis, and dynamic trajectory reconstruction methods, noting this is the first work to systematically integrate event-driven perception with multimodal sensor fusion and biomechanical analysis for high-speed racket sports.

## Abstract

### Introduction

The field of sports analytics is being transformed by artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning, which enable objective assessments based on developed modelling methods. The paper presents a k-Nearest Neighbours-Hidden Markov Model (KNN-HMM) to address issues of accuracy, time-dependent characteristics, and flexibility in the study of badminton strokes.

### Methods

The dataset comprised 10,000 motion-captured badminton strokes collected in Chongqing, China, from 36 players (18 male, 18 female; ages 18–35) between 2015 and 2017. Vicon optical motion capture was used to capture the data, which were then annotated in Kinovea. Angular velocity and jerk were also used to extract spatial and temporal features in 200-ms sliding windows containing 50-ms of overlap. The model combined a KNN stroke classifier with HMM-based temporal sequence prediction. Accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score were the evaluation metrics in the fivefold cross-validation, and real-time metrics were used: latency and throughput.

### Results

The KNN-HMM achieved 97.5% accuracy with a latency of 32 ms and 90.8% streaming accuracy. In comparison to standalone KNN, modest performance gains were observed in accuracy (+ 0.05, p = 0.021), F1-score (+ 0.07, p = 0.015), precision (+ 0.06, p = 0.001), and recall (+ 0.04, p = 0.018), with Tukey’s Honestly Significant Difference (HSD) confidence intervals confirming significance. Improvements were evident across several strokes, including Clear, Jump Smash, and Net Shot (p < .05). Compared with alternative models such as hybrid SVM-Decision Tree-KNN (83.4%) and acoustic sensor-based approaches (~ 84%), the KNN-HMM achieved stronger results. The difference of 1.03% compared with personalised acoustic models (96.5%) was small, but it showed strength on a more generalised dataset.

### Conclusion

KNN-HMM can offer an effective paradigm of real-time classification of badminton stroke, but the results are limited to a regional model (Chongqing, China). Although it is based on confined-area data, the model has high accuracy, adaptability, and generalizability, and is advantageous for training applications and real-time tactical analysis.

Hybrid spatiotemporal frameworks have not addressed badminton’s unique challenges of rapid tactical shifts and unpredictable shuttle trajectories, as they require stroke-granular temporal constraints and shuttle-aware features to maintain predictive stability during rapid rallies. This study implements KNN–HMM for badminton using frame-level kinematic features and sequential dependencies, reporting accuracy, latency, and streaming stability as deployment-oriented endpoints. Consequently, the contribution centers on a badminton-specific adaptation of the KNN–HMM, with novelty bounded to shuttlecock-aware feature engineering, stroke taxonomies, and real-time evaluation metrics rather than the introduction of a new model class.

Badminton remains underexplored in predictive analytics because prior vision-based and hybrid methods are sensitive to noise, exhibit limited temporal adaptation, and provide insufficient treatment of shuttlecock flight dynamics. Few studies integrate real-time requirements with stroke-level recognition and sequence prediction in competitive contexts, leaving a clear gap that this KNN HMM formulation is designed to address.

### Objectives

This study seeks to: 1) develop a predictive framework for badminton stroke classification that integrates spatial and temporal dynamics. 2) adapt the KNN-HMM model to capture shuttlecock trajectories and rally sequencing under real-time constraints, and 3) evaluate model performance against baseline classifiers and hybrid alternatives using accuracy, latency, and streaming reliability.

### Contributions

This study contributes by: 1) presenting a badminton-specific KNN-HMM model that combines the use of classification and sequence prediction in stroke recognition, 2) illustrating its real-time flexibility with latency and throughput analysis, and 3) offering human-readable, stroke-level insights that can be used in training, tactical analysis, and AI-based performance evaluation.

### Hypothesis

The study proposes the following hypotheses: 1) H1: The combination of k-Nearest Neighbours (KNN) and Hidden Markov Model (HMM) will be more accurate, recall, and F1-score than the pure KNN and traditional classifiers with minimal inference latency, and 2) **H2**: Explicit modelling of temporal dependencies via the HMM will improve sequential stroke prediction and streaming stability relative to models without temporal structure, enabling real-time adaptability.

## Methods

### Dataset

Badminton performance data were collected in Chongqing, China (2015–2017) during training and competition to capture a full repertoire of shots and movements. Thirty-six players (18 males, 18 females; ages 18–35) were enrolled across competitive tiers (12 amateur, 12 semi-professionals, 12 professional). Kinematic and contextual variables included joint angles (shoulder, elbow, wrist), player and shuttlecock velocities and accelerations, and shuttle trajectory descriptors (speed, height, direction, and landing position). Player court positions were tracked throughout rallies. Data were acquired using an eight-camera Vicon system (120 Hz) and analysed in Kinovea for shuttle trajectory and player footwork/positioning. The camera layout used eight Vicon T-series units at 120 Hz, with wand calibration before each session, yielding a mean reprojection error of under 0.8 pixels. Lenses were 18–25 mm, with overlapping fields of view exceeding 60% across the court to maintain continuous shuttle visibility. Streams were synchronised using a standard temporal marker (stroke start), with wand calibration for the Vicon motion capture system (Vicon Motion Systems Ltd., Oxford, UK) and frame-level alignment in Kinovea (Kinovea, Bordeaux, France). Temporal alignment tolerance was set to ± 4 ms using a hardware sync pulse and verified by frame-accurate stroke onset markers. Scalability was evaluated by downsampling kinematics to 60 Hz and 30 Hz and by injecting additive position noise of ± 5 mm to emulate lower-grade sensors. The dataset is geographically concentrated (36 players from Chongqing), which may limit generalizability; reliance on Vicon/Kinovea also constrains scalability in non-instrumented settings.

### Manual scoring and data screening

Manual scoring was based on predetermined criteria, including the type of stroke (smash, clear, drive, drop, net shot), movement patterns, and execution accuracy. These annotations were used to create model training and model evaluation reference labels. The data were filtered to eliminate unfinished strokes, frames in which the shuttle tracking or the player had been lost, and non-gaming movements. The high-quality records demanded inclusion of full stroke labels, shuttle trajectory, and player technology. The frames that were partially occluded were flagged in case any tracked joint or shuttle lost confidence in ≥ 3consecutive frames. Frames containing over 10 percent flags were not trained on, but were used in robustness checks. To minimize artefacts. A Kalman filter was used to smooth the shuttle trajectories, and a low-pass filter was used to smooth the kinematic signals without sacrificing important joint and shuttle dynamics. Annotations and signals were also cross-checked against the manual scores after preprocessing to ensure the scoring criteria were taken into account.

### Ethical approval

This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and received the approval of the IRB of Sichuan International Studies University, Chongqing, China (No. 29237681). Informed consent was obtained from all participants. The identification numbers were removed, and coded IDs were assigned; all documents were locked and access restricted to authorised staff following anonymisation.

### Data splitting and validation

The data (10,000 entries) was split into training (70%, or 7,000), validation (15%, or 1,500), and test (15%, or 1,500). All stroke types (smash, clear, drop, drive, net shot) were sampled proportionately to maintain class balance. Hyperparameter tuning and early stopping were performed using the validation set, whereas the test set was held out to evaluate generalisation. Overfitting was mitigated using early stopping, dropout regularisation, and data augmentation. Augmentation was applied only to the training partition. Planar position jitter used Gaussian noise with σ = 0.10 m bounded to the court limits. Shuttle speed and angle jitter used uniform ranges of ± 2.0 m/s and ± 6 degrees. Occlusion was simulated by masking 10–20 percent of windowed frames per sequence and linearly interpolating masked joints before feature computation. Piecewise quadratic perturbations simulated irregular trajectories with a maximum curvature change of 0.15 m per 200-ms window. All parameters were chosen to preserve legal court geometry and typical shuttle deceleration. Player positions were perturbed through small planar translations:

$$P' = (x + \Delta x,\Delta y + \Delta y),\Delta x,\Delta y \sim N(0,{\sigma ^2})$$

where \(\Delta x\) and \(\Delta y\) are Gaussian offsets with zero mean and variance \({\sigma }^{2}\), ensuring displacements remain within realistic court boundaries.

Shuttlecock trajectories were varied by perturbing both speed and angle:

$$s^{\prime} = s + \varepsilon _{s} ,\theta ^{\prime} = \theta + \varepsilon _{\theta } ,\quad \varepsilon _{s} , \varepsilon _{\theta } \sim \mathcal{U}\left[ { - \delta ,\delta } \right]$$

where \(s\) and \(\theta\) are the original shuttle speed and angle, and \({\epsilon }_{s}\) and \({\epsilon }_{\theta }\) are uniformly sampled within bounded intervals \(\left[-\delta ,\delta \right]\). The parameters \(\sigma\) and \(\delta\) were selected to preserve physical plausibility, respecting typical shuttle deceleration rates, angular deviations, and court geometry. All perturbations were applied only to the training partition. The validation and test partitions were excluded from augmentation to maintain unbiased performance evaluation. This procedure diversified the training set while preserving biomechanical and tactical realism. External validation used a train-on-Chongqing, test-on-ShuttleSet22 protocol without fine-tuning. A label map harmonised stroke categories across sources, and any out-of-vocabulary class in ShuttleSet22 was excluded from accuracy computation to avoid optimistic inflation.

### Data preprocessing and feature extraction

Key features included joint positions (shoulder, elbow, wrist) and stroke dynamics derived from motion capture. Temporal sequences were segmented using 200-ms sliding windows with 50-ms overlap, preserving stroke-dependent patterns such as joint progression and shuttle trajectories. Windows were advanced in 50-ms hops. A causal two-tap differentiator computed velocities online. All features were min–max scaled using training-set statistics, and the same parameters were applied to the validation and test sets.

Velocity was calculated as: \(v=\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}\), where \(\Delta x\) is the displacement of a joint or shuttlecock and \(\Delta t\) is the time interval. Acceleration was computed as: \(a=\frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}\), where \(\Delta v\) is the change in velocity over time.

Angular velocity was derived from joint rotation:\(\omega =\frac{\Delta \theta }{\Delta t}\), where \(\Delta \theta\) is the change in joint angle and \(\Delta t\) is the corresponding time step. All features were normalised and scaled to the range \(\left[0,1\right]\) using min–max scaling to ensure comparability and prevent bias from differing measurement units.

For real-time prediction, feature extraction and inference are executed in a single pass. Quantisation used 16-bit fixed-point for KNN distances. End-to-end median processing time per window on an 8-core CPU was measured at 32 ms at 120 Hz, 18 ms at 60 Hz, and 14 ms at 30 Hz.

### Model training

In the pipeline, KNN and HMM formed the AI core of the hybrid model, with KNN handling stroke classification and HMM modelling sequence dependencies (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40537-026-01396-7#Fig1)). Training followed a two-step procedure in which KNN performed initial classification based on feature-space proximity, and HMM refined these outputs by capturing temporal patterns. Model selection used stratified fivefold cross-validation on the training partition (70%), with a held-out test partition (15%) reserved for final evaluation.

### Stage 1: KNN training

The KNN model was trained to classify discrete strokes based on proximity in feature space. The optimal number of neighbours (k) was determined using fivefold cross-validation on the training set, exploring k values between 3 and 10 (see Algorithm 1). Neighbour search used FAISS IVFFlat with 64 lists and training on 5 percent of vectors. RFE had an average of 24 features per window, with wrist angular velocity, elbow extension rate, and shuttle speed dominating. The default similarity measure was the Euclidean distance measure. The number of classes used in this study was k = 5, which is a good compromise between classification accuracy and computational efficiency. Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) was used to select the most relevant features from the feature space, reducing dimensionality. This not only improved the model's performance but also minimized computational overhead, a significant concern in real-time applications. To work effectively with big data, Approximate Nearest Neighbour (ANN) algorithms from FAISS were utilised, significantly accelerating the classification process without compromising accuracy.

![Image 7: figure a](https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1186%2Fs40537-026-01396-7/MediaObjects/40537_2026_1396_Figa_HTML.png)

**Algorithm 1**: KNN Stroke Classification

The KNN model uses cross-validation to select k = 5 neighbours to classify strokes by their proximity in the Euclidean feature space. Recursive Feature Elimination ensures only discriminative features are retained, and FAISS indexing accelerates nearest-neighbour searches for real-time inference.

### Stage 2: HMM integration

The HMM refined stroke predictions by modelling temporal sequences from KNN outputs (Algorithm 2). Each hidden state represented a mode of play, such as attack, defence, or transition. The model was initialised with three states, and hyperparameter tuning was used to test whether additional states improved sequence modelling. Three rally phases were considered as state priors: initiation, exchange, and finish. Skip transitions were enabled between non-adjacent phases with an initial probability of 0.05. Transition matrices were smoothed with a Dirichlet prior α = 0.1 to prevent degenerate paths. Emission probabilities reflected the likelihood of observed stroke types, while the transition matrix captured the probabilities of moving between stroke types. Training employed the Baum-Welch algorithm for maximum-likelihood estimation, iteratively updating transition and emission parameters. Baum–Welch ran for a maximum of 50 iterations, early-stopping after 5 iterations without improvement in the validation log-likelihood. The batch size was 10 sequences, with padded masking for variable-length sequences. Continuous states, such as joint and angular velocity, were modeled using Gaussian emissions, enabling the use of a Continuous HMM. Hyperparameter tuning was performed on the validation set, and time-wise training was performed in 10 sequence batches. Early stopping was implemented when validation performance plateaued.

![Image 8: figure b](https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1186%2Fs40537-026-01396-7/MediaObjects/40537_2026_1396_Figb_HTML.png)

**Algorithm 2**: HMM Temporal Stroke Classification

The HMM optimizes KNN results using a time-dependent model. Play modes are hidden states; Gaussian emissions capture continuum kinematics; and the Baum-Welch algorithm estimates the transition and emission probabilities. The Viterbi decoder, with a penalty term, implements realistic stroke sequences while maintaining low-latency prediction.

### Loss function and sequence consistency

The HMM was defined with a custom loss function that imposed realistic stroke sequences. The role discouraged probable shifts and encouraged logical emissions, so that prophecies were in tune with observed patterns of gameplay:

$$\mathcal{L}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left[-\text{log}{B}_{{S}_{t}}\left({O}_{t}\right)-\text{log}{A}_{{S}_{t-1}{S}_{t}}\right]+\lambda \hspace{0.17em}\mathcal{P}\left(S\right)$$

Here, \({B}_{{S}_{t}}\left({O}_{t}\right)\) is the emission probability of observing a stroke \({O}_{t}\) in state \({S}_{t}\), and \({A}_{{S}_{t-1}{S}_{t}}\) is the transition probability between states. The penalty term \(\mathcal{P}\left(S\right)\), weighted by \(\lambda\), discourages implausible stroke orders such as repeated jump-smashes without recovery. Penalty weight λ was set to 0.25 after a grid search on the validation set, balancing emission fit and transition plausibility. For real-time prediction, the KNN–HMM integration was optimised for low-latency inference. Sliding windows of 200 ms enabled efficient feature extraction, and quantisation of KNN computations reduced the time required to compute weights while preserving accuracy. Hyperparameters tuned via grid search and fivefold cross-validation included the number of KNN neighbours, the HMM state count, and batch size for sequence processing. Hyperparameter grids were k ∈ {3,5,7,9}, N ∈ {3,4,5,6}, and batch size ∈ {5,10,20}. Selection was based on validation F1 and sequence log-likelihood.

### Statistical analysis

Classification performance was first evaluated with overall accuracy: \({\text{Accuracy}}=\frac{\text{TP}+\text{TN}}{\text{TP}+\text{TN}+\text{FP}+\text{FN}}\). This represents the proportion of correctly classified strokes out of all predictions.

Precision was then computed as: \({\text{Precision}}=\frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP}+\text{FP}}\), which measures the proportion of correctly identified strokes among all predicted positives.

Recall was defined as: \({\text{Recall}}=\frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP}+\text{FN}}\), capturing the proportion of actual strokes correctly detected.

To balance, with Tukey HSD for post-hoc comparisons and the Benjamini–Hochberg correction applied when these two metrics, the F1-score was calculated: \(\text{F}1=2\cdot \frac{{\text{Precision}}\cdot {\text{Recall}}}{{\text{Precision}}+{\text{Recall}}}\), providing a harmonic mean that penalises large discrepancies between precision and recall.

For temporal modelling, the Hidden Markov Model (HMM) fit was assessed using the log-likelihood, which quantifies how well observed stroke sequences match the model parameters, and the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), which penalises overly complex models to favour parsimony. Transition linearity was examined by comparing a single stationary matrix to phase-conditioned matrices using BIC; a lower BIC indicated improved fit where rally dynamics were non-linear.

Sequence uncertainty was summarised by perplexity: \({\text{PPL}}={2}^{-\frac{1}{\text{T}}\sum_{\text{t}=1}^{\text{T}}{\text{log}}_{2}\text{p}\left({\text{O}}_{\text{t}}\right)}\), where \(\text{T}\) is sequence length and \(\text{p}\left({\text{O}}_{\text{t}}\right)\) is the probability of observing a stroke \({\text{O}}_{\text{t}}\). Lower perplexity indicates more confident and coherent sequence modelling. Finally, group differences between KNN-HMM and standalone KNN were tested using repeated-measures ANOVA with Tukey HSD correction \((\alpha=0.05)\). Latency distributions were summarised by median and interquartile range per input. Another striking stroke to observe is Drop Shot (0.96–0.97), a tactic that disrupts the opponent's rhythm. Hochberg correction was applied where multiple stroke classes were compared. All results are reported with p-values and 95% confidence intervals.

## Results

The KNN–HMM achieved 94.6% (95% CI 93.9–95.3) on internal validation and 93.4% (95% CI 92.7–94.2) on external evaluation. Calibration was acceptable (slope 0.97, intercept − 0.01), and learning curves plateaued without divergence between training and validation beyond 7,500 strokes, reducing the likelihood of capacity-driven overfitting.

### KNN analysis of badminton strokes

Table [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40537-026-01396-7#Tab1) reports per-class metrics. Higher separability in Jump Smash and Net Shot (F1 ≥ 0.98) contrasts with lower separability in Clear and Drive (F1 ≤ 0.92). Macro-averaged accuracy was 94.0% (95% CI 93.2–94.7). This reflects their distinct gameplay characteristics: "Jump Smash" is an aggressive stroke used to win points by exploiting openings, while "Net Shot" is crucial for setting up offensive plays by forcing opponents to return high or weak shots. One more striking stroke that can be observed is Drop Shot (0.96–0.97) which is a tactic that attacks the rhythm of the opponent to run the rallies. The scores for (Drive) (0.93) and (Clear) (0.90) are lower, indicating that the strokes are more difficult to classify because they overlap in gameplay, e.g., taking up rallies or colliding with attacks. The overall weighted accuracy of 94 percent indicates that the model has a strong generalisation ability, which is crucial for real-time application in match analysis.

Single-bounce strokes, which are typically used in a less offensive or compromise sense, share no clear biomechanical and spatial sequences that allow the model to differentiate them.

**Fig.2**

![Image 9: Fig. 2](https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1186%2Fs40537-026-01396-7/MediaObjects/40537_2026_1396_Fig2_HTML.png)

[Full size image](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40537-026-01396-7/figures/2)

**(a**) Precision-Recall Curves and (**b**) ROC curves for badminton stroke classification (One-vs-Rest)

The most common strokes (Fig.[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40537-026-01396-7#Fig3)) were the Drop Shot and Jump Smash, which are more likely to help in controlling rallies and provide attacking opportunities (Fig.[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40537-026-01396-7#Fig3)). On the contrary, Clear had the lowest number, which may be due to its defensive character and less salience in an offensive game. The frequency of Net Shot use is high, indicating its significance in close play. The latter distribution is consistent with the gameplay dynamics: Offensive strokes, e.g., Jump Smash, are more common, whereas defensive strokes, e.g., Clear, are less common.

**Fig.3**

![Image 10: Fig. 3](https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1186%2Fs40537-026-01396-7/MediaObjects/40537_2026_1396_Fig3_HTML.png)

Analysis of the distribution of predicted labels for predicted badminton strokes based on KNN. The bars indicate the number of data points classified for each stroke type: Clear, Drive, Drop Shot, Forehand Drop, Jump Smash, and Net Shot

Misclassifications were concentrated in Clear versus Drop Shot, and they had common shuttle paths and transitional situations preventing separability; in contrast, Net Shot and Drop Shot found distinct groups and had high true positives, namely Net Shot 1,322 and Drop Shot 1,219, reflecting clear biomechanical signatures of rapid deceleration and accurate placement (Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40537-026-01396-7#Fig4)a-4b). Forehand Drop confusions with Drive, and with the occasional occurrence of Clear and drop Shot error, produced 121 off-diagonal errors and showed that the occasional Forehand Drop still results in residual sensitivity to the control of the wrist and the drive. Specialized remediation proposed two features of context for inference without retraining encoders: a court-zone index and a deceleration of the shuttle in the 80 ms before contact. The HMM transition penalty on repeated sequences of mid-court Drive to Drive, where positional progress was missing, was also raised. Clear to Drive minus-diagonals improved 28.4 percent (121 to 87), and per-class F1 improved to 0.93 to Clear and 0.94 to Drive, and there was no degradation in other classes (DF1 [?] 0.01) (Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40537-026-01396-7#Fig4)a-4b).

This is an open-access research article published in the Journal of Big Data (Volume 13, article 61, published 06 March 2026) titled "Real-time stroke prediction in badminton integrating AI with the KNN-HMM model" by Qi Song and Jian Zhang.

**Purpose/Objective:** The paper presents a k-Nearest Neighbours-Hidden Markov Model (KNN-HMM) for real-time badminton stroke prediction, addressing issues of accuracy, time-dependent characteristics, and flexibility in stroke analysis. The study aims to integrate spatial and temporal dynamics for stroke classification under real-time constraints.

**Methods:** The dataset comprised 10,000 motion-captured badminton strokes collected in Chongqing, China (2015-2017) from 36 players (18 male, 18 female; ages 18-35; 12 amateur, 12 semi-professional, 12 professional). Data was captured using an eight-camera Vicon optical motion capture system (120 Hz) and annotated in Kinovea. Features included joint angles (shoulder, elbow, wrist), velocities, accelerations, and shuttle trajectory descriptors. Temporal sequences were segmented using 200-ms sliding windows with 50-ms overlap. The model combined a KNN stroke classifier (k=5, Euclidean metric, FAISS index) with HMM-based temporal sequence prediction (3-5 hidden states, Gaussian emissions, Baum-Welch training, Viterbi decoding). Data was split 70% training, 15% validation, 15% test. External validation used the ShuttleSet22 dataset (44 professional matches, 36,000+ strokes, 2018-2022).

**Key Results:**
- KNN-HMM achieved 94.6% accuracy on internal validation (95% CI 93.9-95.3) and 93.4% on external evaluation
- 97.5% accuracy with 32 ms latency and 90.8% streaming accuracy (per abstract)
- Compared to standalone KNN: modest gains in accuracy (+0.05, p=0.021), F1-score (+0.07, p=0.015), precision (+0.06, p=0.001), recall (+0.04, p=0.018)
- Outperformed hybrid SVM-Decision Tree-KNN (83.4%) and acoustic sensor-based approaches (~84%)
- Jump Smash and Net Shot had highest F1 (≥0.98); Clear and Drive had lower F1 (≤0.92)
- End-to-end processing: 32 ms at 120 Hz, 18 ms at 60 Hz, 14 ms at 30 Hz on 8-core CPU
- HMM log-likelihood of 42.75, BIC of 88.6

**Conclusions:** The KNN-HMM offers an effective paradigm for real-time badminton stroke classification with high accuracy, adaptability, and generalizability, though results are limited to a regional model (Chongqing, China). The framework is advantageous for training applications and real-time tactical analysis. Ethical approval was granted by the IRB of Sichuan International Studies University (No. 29237681), and the study followed the Declaration of Helsinki.

# Recognition of Badminton Shot Action Based on the Improved Hidden Markov Model

### Chao Ma

### Dayang Yu

### Hao Feng

Academic Editor: Fazlullah Khan

Corresponding author.

Received 2021 May 14; Revised 2021 Jul 5; Accepted 2021 Sep 8; Collection date 2021.

This is an open access article distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution License, which permits unrestricted use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited.

## Abstract

In recent years, with the rapid development of sports, the number of people playing various sports is increasing day by day. Among them, badminton has become one of the most popular sports because of the advantages of fewer restrictions on the field and ease of learning. This paper develops a wearable sports activity classification system for accurately recognizing badminton actions. A single acceleration sensor fixed on the end of the badminton racket handle is used to collect the data of the badminton action. The sliding window segmentation technique is used to extract the hitting signal. An improved hidden Markov model (HMM) is developed to identify standard 10 badminton strokes. These include services, forehand chop, backhand chop the goal, the forehand and backhand, forehand drive, backhand push the ball, forehand to pick, pick the ball backhand, and forehand. The experimental results show that the model designed can recognize ten standard strokes in real time. Compared with the traditional HMM, the average recognition rate of the improved HMM is improved by 7.3%. The comprehensive recognition rate of the final strokes can reach up to 95%. Therefore, this model can be used to improve the competitive level of badminton players.

## 1. Introduction

Badminton is an Olympic discipline, and it is one of the most popular racket sports worldwide. With the rapid growth of artificial intelligence, performance analysis in sports has undergone fundamental changes in recent years [[1](#B1)]. Generally, manual analysis performed by trained sport science experts has some drawbacks such as time-consuming, time-intensive, and subjective. Analysis for sports events is crucial to understanding the physical and technical demands related to sports performance. Sports action recognition systems are developed to perform analysis in sport science, provide objective measurement, and enhance the efficiency and accuracy of sports performance [[2](#B2), [3](#B3)]. Generally, sports action recognition systems are developed using machine and deep learning approaches with data measured by an inertial and magnetic sensor or by computer vision technologies [[4](#B4)].

Sports actions recorded by the camera can be applied for athlete's pose estimation and movement analysis [[5](#B5)]. The computer vision-based activity recognition system's processes, mainly dependent on the sport and camera type, involve player tracking, targeted motion recognition, and temporal cropping [[6](#B6)]. This approach can provide rapid analysis and real-time feedback for coaches and athletes. However, the computer vision-based action recognition system is limited to specific environments and requires more computing power. An alternative approach for sports action recognition is to use inertial sensors for data collection. The sensors are wearable and composed of gyroscopes, accelerometers, and magnetometers [[7](#B7), [8](#B8)]. Wearable devices with embedded inertial sensors are commonly used in various applications such as gait analysis, activity recognition healthcare, disease monitoring, and navigation [[9](#B9)].

Recently, several researchers have developed wearable sports activity recognition and monitoring systems, football, badminton, tennis, baseball, golf, basketball, table tennis, volleyball, etc. [[10](#B10)]. The wearable inertial sensors can measure linear and angular accelerations generated by gestures and motions during sports training and competitions [[11](#B11)]. The wearable inertial sensor-based activity recognition system benefits are low cost, light-weighted, small-sized, and require minimum power for operation. Generally, the sports action recognition process involves several signal processing procedures such as raw signal filtering, signal windowing, normalization, prominent feature extraction, feature reduction/selection, and classification actions [[12](#B12)]. For example, Margarito et al. [[13](#B13)] extracted eleven acceleration features from the thirteen most common time- and frequency-domain features using the relief method. For eight-action classification, they used naïve Bayes (NB), logistic regression (LR), decision tree (DT), and artificial neural network (ANN) classifiers. These activities included cross-trainer, cycling, rowing, squatting, stepping, running, weightlifting, and walking. Ermers et al. [[14](#B14)] combined the DT classifier with the ANN to classify activities such as sitting, lying down, standing, walking, rowing with a rowing machine, running, and cycling with an exercise bike. A Nordic walking, playing football, and cycling with a regular bike using the seven time- and frequency-domain features were extracted from the accelerometers and GPS sensor signals. Mitchell et al. [[15](#B15)] used a smartphone accelerometer and employed discrete wavelet transform- (DWT-) based support vector machines (SVMs) optimized by the minimal sequential optimization (SMO) algorithm to recognize the seven sports activities. Wang et al. [[16](#B16)] used gyroscope and accelerometer signals in combination followed by principal component analysis (PCA) to obtain three features from the twelve statistical features and three morphological features. These are input to the support vector machine (SVM) classifier for classifying elite, subelite, and amateur volleyball players.

Our literature review shows that many researchers in machine learning have focused on inertial-sensing-based sports activity classification. A wearable badminton activity recognition system is developed using the hidden Markov model (HMM) in this paper. The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

This paper proposes a sports action recognition algorithm for badminton hitting action and implements a real-time recognition system for badminton actions.

The system uses a single acceleration sensor fixed at the end of the badminton racket handle to collect action data. It uses sliding window data segmentation technology to extract hitting signals.

An improved HMM training model is proposed to identify ten standard badminton shots and achieved the highest recognition accuracy of 95%.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: [Section 2](#sec2) provides the background and related work. The proposed improved HMM is explained in [Section 3](#sec3). The results are illustrated in [Section 4](#sec4). The conclusion is given in [Section 5](#sec5). Finally, the limitation and future work are given in [Section 6](#sec6).

## 2. Background

### 2.1. Badminton Aerodynamic Model

Badminton can be regarded as a four-dimensional space. When the shuttlecock leaves the racket and flies in the air, we need to consider the size and height of the shuttlecock and the external factors such as the size and height of the badminton court. We also have to consider a time vector, which makes the technique of playing, the speed of playing, and the ability of human movement [[17](#B17)]. Due to the small size and lightness of the shuttlecock, it is easily affected by various external factors when it is flying in the air. For example, suppose the speed of wind is greater than a certain level. In this case, it will significantly affect its performance under the action of the wind. Moreover, even if the shuttlecock is small and lightweight, it will be affected by the earth's gravitational force. Shuttlecock will also be affected by the air force during the flight and will also be affected by its rotation. The air force is also known as air resistance. It is much more complicated than gravity, and it will change due to factors such as air viscosity. In addition, the shuttlecock will receive a lateral force orthogonal to the speed direction during the flight, causing the shuttlecock to rotate during the flight. Under the action of this force, the shuttlecock's trajectory will deviate from an arc-shaped trajectory. It is the Magnus effect in fluid mechanics [[18](#B18)]. Figures [1(a)](#fig1)–[1(c)](#fig1) show the head-on resistance, air friction, and eddy current resistance of the badminton.

#### Figure 1.

![Figure 1](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/f352/8516566/82dcc33ca9ec/JHE2021-7892902.001.jpg)

![Figure 1](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/f352/8516566/82dcc33ca9ec/JHE2021-7892902.001.jpg)

Shuttlecock dynamic during flight: (a) the head-on resistance of the badminton, (b) air friction on the badminton, and (c) eddy current resistance on the badminton.

The air force on the shuttlecock can be divided into three components in different directions. They are various resistances *X* during the flight of the shuttlecock, the lift *Y* that prevents the shuttlecock from falling vertically due to the influence of gravity, and the departure of the shuttlecock from its original position, the lateral force *Z* of the flight path. It can be known from the data that the air force received by the shuttlecock during flight is not only proportional to the area *S* of the shuttlecock but also proportional to the pressure *Q* of the airflow in the air so that the following relational equations can be obtained:

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| X=BxSQ,Y=BySQ,Z=BzSQ, | (1) |

where *B**x* is the drag coefficient of various resistances received during the flight of the shuttlecock, *B**y* is the lift coefficient that prevents the shuttlecock from falling due to gravity, and *B**z* is the lateral force coefficient that causes the shuttlecock to deviate from the original flight path. *S* represents the contact area between the shuttlecock and the air. Generally, the area of the most significant cross section of the shuttlecock is taken as the contact area between the shuttlecock and the air. Therefore, considering the badminton aerodynamic model will help improve the accuracy of badminton hitting action recognition.

### 2.2. Batting Motion Extraction

When the acceleration sensor collects the athlete's acceleration data, it usually lasts several minutes or even tens of minutes, including many batting actions, forming a long section of long data composed of many discrete points. Therefore, it is necessary to segment and extract each batting action of the athlete to facilitate the subsequent classification and recognition [[19](#B19)]. Window segmentation technology is mainly used to extract batting action. Window segmentation is used to segment the data of feather players' multiple batting to obtain multiple windows with the same or different widths. Each window corresponds to players' single batting action. Window segmentation techniques mainly include sliding window segmentation and event window segmentation [[19](#B19)]. In the proposed work, the sliding window technique is applied.

The data segmentation technology based on the sliding window divides a sampling shot signal into several windows of equal length. The two adjacent windows may overlap or not overlap each other. This paper takes the player's forehand to push several times in continuous confrontation as an example to research the sliding window segmentation technique [[20](#B20)]. The sliding window moves along the time axis through a window of fixed width and extracts the batting action, as shown in [Figure 2](#fig2).

#### Figure 2.

![Figure 2](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/f352/8516566/fcfd43461fe0/JHE2021-7892902.002.jpg)

![Figure 2](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/f352/8516566/fcfd43461fe0/JHE2021-7892902.002.jpg)

Window segmentation technique.

Considering that the data sampling frequency is 200 Hz and the badminton batting action generally does not exceed 0.5 seconds, the window width is set to 100 samples to extract the batting action. The calculation equation of net combined acceleration is as follows:

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| a=ax2+ay2+az2−1,Am=argmaxm1k∑mm+k−1am2, | (2) |

where *a**x*, *a**y*, *a**z* is the three-axis acceleration signal and −1 is the always existing gravitational acceleration component, so *a* is the net acceleration representing pure human action, and the unit of acceleration is *g*.

## 3. Methodology

### 3.1. Hidden Markov Model (HMM)

The HMM is a probabilistic model about time series, which describes generating a random series of nonobservable states from a hidden Markov chain and generating an observation from each state to generate a random observation series.  [Figure 3](#fig3) shows the schematic diagram of the proposed HMM [[21](#B21)].

#### Figure 3.

![Figure 3](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/f352/8516566/865a8b86ff7d/JHE2021-7892902.003.jpg)

![Figure 3](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/f352/8516566/865a8b86ff7d/JHE2021-7892902.003.jpg)

Schematic diagram of the hidden Markov model.

The hidden Markov model is determined by the initial probability distribution *π*, the state probability distribution *A*, and the observation probability distribution *B*. It is defined as follows: let *Q* be the set of all possible states and *V* be the set of all possible observations; then,

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Q=q1,q2,…,qN,V=v1,v2,…,vM, | (3) |

where *N* is the number of possible states and *M* is the number of possible observations. *I* is the state sequence of length *T*, and *O* is the corresponding observation sequence; then,

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| I=i1,i2,…,iT,V=v1,v2,…,vM. | (4) |

Let *A* be the state transition probability matrix:

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| A=aijN×N. | (5) |

Let *B* be the observation probability matrix:

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| B=bjkN×M. | (6) |

Let *π* be the initial state probability vector:

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| π=πi. | (7) |

Therefore, the HMM *λ* can be expressed by the following equation:

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| λ=A,B,π, | (8) |

where *A*, *B*, and *π* are called the three elements of the hidden Markov model.

### 3.2. Badminton Action Recognition Based on the Improved HMM

Because of the time sequence of badminton action, it can be modeled by the HMM, which is a probability model about the time sequence. The HMM modeling mainly depends on three parameters: initial probability, transition probability, and observation probability. For each stroke, we establish a set of HMMs applicable to the stroke. Each stroke action is divided into *N* meta-actions with a time sequence. The codebook corresponding to each meta-action is determined through vector quantization, which is the observation set defined by the HMM [[16](#B16)].

The recognition process of badminton action is that the observation sequence of the current hitting action extracted by the preprocessing algorithm [[22](#B22), [23](#B23)] is used to input each established HMM of the hitting action. The probability of the optimal state sequence of the current hitting action in each model is obtained using the Viterbi algorithm. The Viterbi algorithm is a dynamic algorithm for obtaining the maximum posterior probability estimate of the most likely sequence of the hidden Viterbi path that results in a sequence of observed events, especially hidden Markov models (HMMs). The hitting action corresponding to the model with the largest probability output is the recognition result of the current observation sequence.

Since multiple datasets aim at the same hitting action in the sample and the sample based on which the training HMM parameter model is based is a single sample, the model data may fall into the local optimum. In contrast, the recognition rate of other samples is low [[18](#B18)]. For multiple training [[24](#B24), [25](#B25)], this paper proposes two schemes. One is the mean training method, which integrates the data layer of the input of the model, namely, the observation sequence of the sample, and carries out model training after taking the mean value of multiple groups of training data under the same model. Secondly, the frequency weighted training method is used to linearly weight the frequency of the sample observation sequence in the model and set the sequence of *M* observation values as *O*(m). *M* and *P**m* are the occurrence frequency of the *m*th observation sequence. Then, the improved calculation equation is as follows:

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| π¯i=∑m=1Mα1miβ1miPOm|λ,a¯ij=∑m=1M∑t=1Tm−1α1miaijbjOt+1mβt+1mj∑m=1MPm∑t=1Tmαtmiβtmj,b¯jk=∑m=1MPm∑t=1Tm−1αtmiβtmjIot,vk∑m=1MPm∑t=1Tmαtmiβtmj, | (9) |

where *α*t(m)(*i*) and *β*t(m)(*i*) are the forward probability and backward probability of the *m*th sequence, respectively, and π¯i, a¯ij, and b¯jk are the improved initial, transition, and observation probability parameters, respectively.

The improved HMM training and recognition processes are shown in [Figure 4](#fig4), the training sample data for ten kinds serve as 100 shots of all data, the corresponding model is obtained by the improved training algorithm, and for anyone to identify the strokes, the strokes of the observation are obtained by the data preprocessing algorithm sequence through the Viterbi algorithm. Moreover, 70% of the data was used for training and 30% for testing the HMM. The conditional probability of the occurrence of the optimal state sequence under ten batting action models was calculated, and the model corresponding to the maximum conditional probability was found. The batting action corresponding to the model was the recognition result.

## 4. Experiments and Results

### 4.1. Experimental Setup

This system adopts the MATLAB 2020 development environment and IntelliJ IDEA 2018 (JDK 1.8), the upper computer operating system is Win10, and Bluetooth 4.0 is used for data transmission. The hardware platform of the system is mainly composed of six-axis acceleration sensors. Three of the six sensors are worn by each player. One is attached to the end of the racket handle, and the other two are worn around the player's ankles. The player's hitting signal data [[26](#B26)] collected by the sensor fixed on the end of the badminton racket handle are used for feature extraction of the hitting action. The player's running signal data collected by the sensor fixed on the ankle are used for the restoration and training of the controlled pace.

### 4.2. Feature Extraction of Badminton Hitting Action

Badminton hitting action contains many important characteristics, such as explosive power, hitting speed, and hitting kinetic energy. Therefore, this article compares the important characteristics of badminton players with three different technical levels to quantitatively analyze a single badminton action. A case study, including three different technical levels' player information, is given in [Table 1](#tab1).

#### Table 1.

Player information of three different skill levels.

| Amateur | Member of the badminton association | 5 |
| Novice | Lab classmates who rarely play badminton | 5 |

As the main scoring point of the hitting action in badminton, the high ball plays a decisive role in the badminton game. The hitting speed, reaction speed, the player's instantaneous explosive power, and the hitting kinetic energy generated during the start and stop of the hit are all important technical characteristic indexes to measure the quality of high-range shots.

### 4.3. Experimental Results

#### 4.3.1. Recognition Performance of the Proposed HMM

The recognition accuracy of the proposed HMM was computed using a confusion matrix. We used the numbers 1–10 to represent 10 different badminton shots, serving, forehand rubbing, and backhand are among the skills you can learn. #### 4.3.2. Comparison with the Traditional HMM

[Table 2](#tab2) provides a comparison between the traditional HMM and the proposed improved HMM. Compared with the traditional HMM, the average recognition rate of the improved HMM is improved by 7.3%. The total recognition rate of the final strokes can reach up to 95% for the proposed improved HMM. Therefore, the proposed model is helpful to improve the competitive level of badminton players.

#### 4.3.3. Effect of Window Length on Recognition Performance

For badminton action recognition, fast response time is desired for real-time applications. In the third study, the nonoverlapped window segmentation scheme was applied to acceleration signals before investigating the impact of window size on the model's performance. Window length created significant effects on classification accuracy. Classification accuracies tended to decrease as window size was increased. The overall classification accuracy dropped from 95% to 90% when the analysis window length was increased from 100 samples to 300 samples, as shown in [Table 3](#tab3). In order to further prove the superiority of the proposed model, we also conducted a comparative experiment with the SVM and BP network. The comparative experimental results are shown in [Figure 6](#fig6).

It can be seen that the model in this paper has a higher recognition rate (more than 90%) than the other two methods (less than 80%). Therefore, this paper adopts the improved HMM method to identify ten different badminton stroke movements. The average recognition rates for the same player can reach 95%, which proves the superiority of the algorithm in this paper.

## 5. Conclusion

This paper proposes an algorithm for badminton hitting action recognition. The system uses a single acceleration sensor fixed at the end of the badminton racket handle to collect the data of the badminton movement. The sliding window data segmentation technique is applied to extract the hitting signal. An improved hidden Markov model is developed to identify ten common badminton shots, serving, forehand rubbing, and backhand are among of the skills you can learn. Experiments show that the algorithm can recognize ten common shots in real time. The average recognition rate of the improved HMM is 7.3% higher than that of traditional HMMs. The final comprehensive recognition rate of shots can reach up to 95%. The model can be used to improve the competitive level of badminton players.

## 6. Limitations and Future Work

The main limitation of this work is that, in the data collection process, only acceleration sensors were used by fifteen sportsmen to recognize ten basic badminton shots. We will plan to extend our approach by including more players and extend the dataset to other sport activities in our future work.

This webpage is a scientific research article from the Journal of Healthcare Engineering (published via PMC/NCBI) titled "Recognition of Badminton Shot Action Based on the Improved Hidden Markov Model" by Chao Ma, Dayang Yu, and Hao Feng, with academic editor Fazlullah Khan. IMPORTANT: The article has been retracted (retraction published in J Healthc Eng. 2023 May 24;2023:9817142).

The paper develops a wearable sports activity classification system for recognizing badminton actions. Key details:

- **Methodology**: Uses a single acceleration sensor fixed at the end of the badminton racket handle to collect action data. A sliding window segmentation technique (window width of 100 samples at 200 Hz sampling frequency, since badminton batting actions typically do not exceed 0.5 seconds) is used to extract hitting signals. An improved hidden Markov model (HMM) is developed to identify 10 standard badminton strokes including services, forehand chop, backhand chop, forehand and backhand drives, backhand push, forehand pick, backhand pick, and forehand.

- **Improved HMM approach**: The paper proposes two training schemes to avoid local optima in HMM training: (1) a mean training method that integrates data from multiple samples, and (2) a frequency-weighted training method that linearly weights the frequency of sample observation sequences. Recognition uses the Viterbi algorithm to find the optimal state sequence probability.

- **Experimental setup**: MATLAB 2020 and IntelliJ IDEA 2018 (JDK 1.8), Windows 10, Bluetooth 4.0 data transmission. Hardware uses six-axis acceleration sensors - one on the racket handle and two worn around players' ankles. 15 players were tested across three skill levels: 5 professional athletes (2nd/3rd-level badminton players), 5 amateurs (badminton association members), and 5 novices (lab classmates who rarely play badminton). Data split was 70% training and 30% testing.

- **Results**: The improved HMM achieved a 95% comprehensive recognition rate for 10 different strokes, compared to 87.7% for the traditional HMM (a 7.3% improvement). Window size affected accuracy: 100 samples = 95%, 150 samples = 93%, 200 samples = 90%. The proposed model outperformed SVM and BP neural network methods (which achieved less than 80% accuracy vs. more than 90% for the improved HMM).

- **Conclusion**: The model can recognize ten common badminton strokes in real time and can be used to improve the competitive level of badminton players.

- **Limitations**: Only acceleration sensors were used by fifteen sportsmen to recognize ten basic badminton shots. Future work includes adding more players and extending the dataset to other sports activities.

The paper also includes background sections on badminton aerodynamics (discussing drag, lift, lateral forces, and the Magnus effect on shuttlecock flight) and batting motion extraction techniques.

# The analysis of motion recognition model for badminton player movements using machine learning

* [Lizhi Liu](#auth-Lizhi-Liu-Aff2)[2](#Aff2),

## Abstract

This study aims to comprehensively analyze and classify the badminton players’ swing actions by combining the theoretical frameworks of quantum mechanics and machine learning. A badminton stroke recognition method based on Quantum Convolutional Neural Network (QCNN) is proposed. It is then compared with traditional Support Vector Machines (SVM) and Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). The comparison aims to assess the classification performance and robustness of each method. Firstly, this study collects the badminton players’ stroke action data using high-frame-rate cameras and inertial sensors to record posture information during different strokes. OpenPose is used for human posture estimation, and combined with sensor data, spatiotemporal features during the stroke are extracted. Next, during the data preprocessing stage, Gaussian filtering is applied to remove noise, followed by normalization and feature selection to ensure the quality of the model input data. Then, SVM, CNN, and QCNN models are trained to classify different stroke actions. To evaluate model performance, precision, recall, and F1-score are selected as metrics. Experiments with varying noise levels (low, medium, and high noise) are designed to test the models’ robustness. Finally, decision tree feature importance analysis is conducted to assess the contribution of different features to stroke action classification. Experimental results show that QCNN outperforms all other models in all classification tasks, with an F1-score of 0.860 for backhand intercept, significantly better than CNN (0.792) and SVM (0.753). In robustness tests under low, medium, and high noise environments, the classification precision of QCNN is 0.95, 0.92, and 0.89, respectively. This clearly surpasses both CNN and SVM. The results indicate that QCNN has strong adaptability to noisy data. Further feature analysis reveals that arm angle, twist angle, and step position are key factors affecting classification accuracy, with the highest contribution in the QCNN model. This study validates the superiority of QCNN in badminton action recognition and provides reliable methodological support for subsequent sports technique analysis.

## Introduction

### Research background and motivations

Sports analysis plays a crucial role in various sports, especially in improving athletes’ performance and reducing sports injuries[1](/articles/s41598-025-02771-9#ref-CR1 "Luo, J. et al. Vision-based movement recognition reveals badminton player footwork using deep learning and binocular positioning. Heliyon 8 (8), 7–12 (2022)."),[2](/articles/s41598-025-02771-9#ref-CR2 "De Waelle, S. et al. The use of contextual information for anticipation of badminton shots in different expertise levels. Res. Q. Exerc. Sport. 94 (1), 15–23 (2023)."). With the continuous advancement of sports science and technology, sports analysis now encompasses not only athletes’ physiological characteristics but also action patterns, technical precision, and comprehensive evaluation of sports effectiveness. In badminton, a fast-paced and high-intensity sport, every stroke has a direct impact on the outcome of the game. Therefore, accurately analyzing the action features of badminton players and the effectiveness of their execution can provide valuable technical guidance for athletes and scientific training plans for coaches[3](#ref-CR3 "Lin, K. C. et al. The effect of real-time pose recognition on badminton learning performance. Interact. Learn. Environ. 31 (8), 4772–4786 (2023)."),[4](#ref-CR4 "Dasgupta, A. et al. Machine learning for optical motion capture-driven musculoskeletal modelling from inertial motion capture data. Bioengineering 10 (5), 510 (2023)."),[5](/articles/s41598-025-02771-9#ref-CR5 "Alsaif, K. I. & Abdullah, A. S. Computer vision systems and deep learning for the recognition of athlete’s movement: A review Article. Tikrit J. Pure Sci. 28 (6), 180–191 (2023).").

In the domain of badminton, the stroke action serves as a key indicator of athletes’ technical proficiency[6](/articles/s41598-025-02771-9#ref-CR6 "Abdullah, A. S. & AlSaif, K. I. Computer vision system for backflip motion recognition in gymnastics based on deep learning. J. Al-Qadisiyah Comput. Sci. Math. 15 (1), 150–157 (2023)."). Traditional stroke analysis relies heavily on manual expertise and subjective judgment, making it susceptible to individual differences and challenging to achieve objective quantification. Given that subtle differences in stroke actions can lead to variations in technical performance, it is necessary to introduce new technological approaches to enhance the accuracy and objectivity of stroke analysis[7](/articles/s41598-025-02771-9#ref-CR7 "Kranzinger, C. et al. Classification of human motion data based on inertial measurement units in sports: A social review. Appl. Sci. 13 (15), 8684 (2023)."). In traditional stroke analysis, reliance on manual observation and experiential judgment may be influenced by subjective biases, resulting in inaccurate and inconsistent evaluation results[8](#ref-CR8 "Dorschky, E. et al. Perspective on in the wild movement analysis using machine learning. Hum. Mov. Sci. 87 (2), 103042 (2023)."),[9](#ref-CR9 "Wahab, H. et al. Machine learning based small bowel video capsule endoscopy analysis: challenges and opportunities. Future Generation Comput. Syst. 143 (6), 191–214 (2023)."),[10](/articles/s41598-025-02771-9#ref-CR10 "Slemenšek, J. et al. Human gait activity recognition machine learning methods. Sensors 23 (2), 745 (2023)."). Additionally, due to the high complexity and rapidity of stroke actions, human perception and reaction capabilities may not fully capture their subtle variations, thereby limiting the precision and efficiency of traditional analysis methods. Introducing new technological approaches is thus crucial to overcoming the limitations of traditional analysis methods[11](/articles/s41598-025-02771-9#ref-CR11 "Hu, Z. et al. Machine learning for tactile perception: advancements, challenges, and opportunities. Adv. Intell. Syst. 5 (7), 2200371 (2023)."). For example, utilizing computer vision and motion capture technology can enable real-time recording and analysis of athletes’ stroke actions, thereby reducing human errors and providing objective quantitative data support[12](/articles/s41598-025-02771-9#ref-CR12 "Ooi, J. H. & Gouwanda, D. Badminton stroke identification using wireless inertial sensor and neural network. Proc. Inst. Mech. Eng. P J. Sports Eng. Technol. 237 (4), 291–300 (2023)."). Furthermore, machine learning algorithms can automatically identify and classify stroke actions through extensive data training, further enhancing analysis accuracy and reliability.

This study aims to apply quantum mechanics and machine learning techniques to the analysis of badminton players’ swing actions, specifically classifying and recognizing five typical swing movements. By combining the theories of quantum mechanics with machine learning algorithms, a deeper understanding of the dynamic patterns and technical characteristics behind the players’ swing actions can be achieved.

### Research objectives

The primary goal of this study is to propose an innovative badminton motion analysis method that combines machine learning techniques with quantum theory. This approach aims to address the limitations of traditional motion analysis methods by providing an efficient and precise analytical framework. This study seeks to resolve the following issues. First, how to extract effective features from complex badminton actions and accurately classify the action categories. Second, how to integrate the principles of quantum mechanics to enhance data processing efficiency and improve model accuracy. Third, how to leverage the potential of machine learning and quantum theory to overcome the limitations of existing methods in dynamic motion capture and real-time analysis.

Machine learning, especially deep learning techniques, has demonstrated significant advantages in pattern recognition and data analysis. By training on large datasets, machine learning models can learn autonomously and extract complex patterns, which has made their application in sports analysis a growing research focus. However, traditional machine learning algorithms often require substantial computational resources and face performance bottlenecks when processing large-scale data. The introduction of quantum theory provides a potential solution to this problem. Quantum computing has the ability to process vast amounts of data in parallel, which can accelerate the data analysis process. Additionally, quantum algorithms have shown unique advantages in handling nonlinear problems. Combining machine learning with quantum theory improves the efficiency of sports analysis. It also enables deeper exploration of the underlying information in athletes’ movements. This approach offers new perspectives and technical pathways for badminton motion analysis.

This study aims to fill the gap in badminton motion analysis, exploring the synergistic effect of machine learning and quantum computing. It seeks to provide innovative solutions for sports training, technical improvement, and injury prevention.

## Literature review

In recent years, with the rapid development of sports, badminton has gained widespread popularity due to its small space requirements and low learning threshold. To improve the technical level and training efficiency of badminton players, scholars have gradually explored the application of machine learning and deep learning techniques in motion recognition and analysis. Deep learning, with its powerful feature extraction capabilities, has been widely applied in badminton action recognition. Liu and Liang (2022) proposed an action recognition method based on Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), which decodes the sequence data of the swing action into relational triplets, thereby effectively improving recognition accuracy. Experiments showed that this method achieved recognition accuracies of 63%, 84%, and 92% on multiple benchmark datasets, demonstrating the advantages of deep learning in processing complex sequential data[13](/articles/s41598-025-02771-9#ref-CR13 "Liu, J. & Liang, B. An action recognition technology for badminton players using deep learning. Mob. Inform. Syst. 2022 (1), 3413584 (2022)."). Deng et al. (2023) further combined Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), LSTM, and self-attention mechanisms to design a deep learning framework that captures time-domain and global signals for more accurate action recognition. This method achieved 97.83% accuracy on a dataset containing 37 badminton actions, proving the robustness and efficiency of the deep learning framework. Traditional machine learning methods played a key role in early badminton action analysis[14](/articles/s41598-025-02771-9#ref-CR14 "Deng, J., Zhang, S. & Ma, J. Self-attention-based deep Convolution LSTM framework for sensor-based badminton activity recognition. Sensors 23 (20), 8373 (2023)."). Asriani et al. (2024) and Zheng & Liu (2020) proposed a weighted ensemble model combining Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest (RF), and Logistic Regression (LR), using Fast Dynamic Time Warping (FDTW) and a soft-voting classifier. This approach achieved an action recognition accuracy of 95.38%. This demonstrates that ensemble learning models, by combining the strengths of various algorithms, can significantly improve the precision and stability of action recognition[15](/articles/s41598-025-02771-9#ref-CR15 "Zheng, Y. & Liu, S. Bibliometric analysis for talent identification by the subject–author–citation three-dimensional evaluation model in the discipline of physical education. Libr. Hi Tech. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1108/LHT-12-2019-0248
                  
                 (2020)."),[16](/articles/s41598-025-02771-9#ref-CR16 "Asriani, F., Azhari, A. & Wahyono, W. Improving badminton action recognition using 11:23 2025/1/27spatio-temporal analysis and a weighted ensemble learning model. Computers Mater. Continua. 81 (2), 156 (2024)."). Pu et al. (2024) designed an optical tracking system based on high-resolution cameras and image feature extraction, which efficiently captured the dynamic features of badminton actions. It showed higher real-time performance and accuracy compared to traditional methods[17](/articles/s41598-025-02771-9#ref-CR17 "Pu, Y., Gao, X. & Lv, W. Design of optical tracking sensor based on image feature extraction for badminton athlete motion recognition. Opt. Quant. Electron. 56 (4), 608 (2024)."). Application of optical motion capture based on multimodal sensors in badminton player motion recognition system. Opt. Quant. Electron. 56 (2), 275 (2024).").

The development of badminton action analysis relies on high-quality datasets. Traditional datasets were often based on video or single-sensor recordings. However, with the increasing diversity of research needs, comprehensive datasets have gradually become a research hotspot. The MultiSenseBadminton dataset, constructed by Seong et al. (2024), provided comprehensive biomechanical information for badminton action research. This dataset included 7763 swing data points and covered multimodal data such as body tracking, muscle signals, eye-tracking, and foot pressure, along with detailed skill-level annotations and video recordings[19](/articles/s41598-025-02771-9#ref-CR19 "Seong, M. et al. MultiSenseBadminton: wearable sensor–based Biomechanical dataset for evaluation of badminton performance. Sci. Data. 11 (1), 343 (2024)."). This multidimensional data not only supports analysis at different skill levels but also provides valuable resources for the development of advanced training systems. The dataset used in Asriani et al.‘s study converted video recordings into 3D distances between skeletal points and joints, as well as time-series features. This spatiotemporal feature data provided rich input variables for deep learning algorithms, significantly improving the model’s action recognition ability. Deng et al.’s badminton sensor dataset, which contains single-sensor data, verified the efficiency of sensor data in action recognition. Compared to multi-sensor data, single-sensor data exhibited lower computational complexity and stronger applicability under specific conditions.

Quantum mechanics has shown unique advantages across multiple fields, with its theoretical foundations and technological applications gradually attracting widespread attention. Ou and Sun (2021) introduced a deep fusion network for extracting semantic information from video sequences based on local spatiotemporal information. The network combined Two-Dimensional-CNNs (2D-CNNs) and Three-Dimensional-CNNs (3D-CNNs), using a time pyramid mechanism for multi-scale information extraction. This study did not directly involve quantum mechanics. However, the theoretical aspects of multi-scale information extraction and motion recognition are similar to the advantages of quantum computing in time and space dimensions.
