## Action Recognition

* **HOLLYWOOD2**: Actions in Context (CVPR 2009)   
   [[Paper](http://www.irisa.fr/vista/Papers/2009_cvpr_marszalek.pdf)][[Homepage](https://www.di.ens.fr/~laptev/actions/hollywood2/)]  
   *12 classes of human actions, 10 classes of scenes, 3,669 clips, 69 movies*
* **HMDB**: A Large Video Database for Human Motion Recognition (ICCV 2011)  
   [[Paper](https://serre-lab.clps.brown.edu/wp-content/uploads/2012/08/Kuehne_etal_iccv11.pdf)][[Homepage](https://serre-lab.clps.brown.edu/resource/hmdb-a-large-human-motion-database/)]  
   *51 classes, 7,000 clips*
* **UCF101**: A Dataset of 101 Human Actions Classes From Videos in The Wild   
   [[Paper](https://www.crcv.ucf.edu/papers/UCF101_CRCV-TR-12-01.pdf)][[Homepage](https://www.crcv.ucf.edu/data/UCF101.php)]  
   *101 classes, 13k clips*
* **Sports-1M**: Large-scale Video Classification with Convolutional Neural Networks   
   [[Paper](https://cs.stanford.edu/people/karpathy/deepvideo/deepvideo_cvpr2014.pdf)][[Homepage](https://cs.stanford.edu/people/karpathy/deepvideo/)]  
   *1,000,000 videos, 487 classes*
* **ActivityNet**: A Large-Scale Video Benchmark for Human Activity Understanding (CVPR 2015)  
   [[Paper](https://www.cv-foundation.org/openaccess/content_cvpr_2015/papers/Heilbron_ActivityNet_A_Large-Scale_2015_CVPR_paper.pdf)][[Homepage](http://activity-net.org/index.html)]  
   *203 classes, 137 untrimmed videos per class, 1.41 activity instances per video*
* **MPII-Cooking**: Recognizing Fine-Grained and Composite Activities Using Hand-Centric Features and Script Data (IJCV 2015)   
   [[Paper](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11263-015-0851-8.pdf)][[Homepage](https://www.mpi-inf.mpg.de/departments/computer-vision-and-machine-learning/research/human-activity-recognition/mpii-cooking-2-dataset/)]   
   *67 fine-grained activities, 59 composite activities, 14,105 clips, 273 videos*
* **Kinetics**   
   [[Kinetics-400](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.06950)/[Kinetics-600](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.01340)/[Kinetics-700](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.06987)/[Kinetics-700-2020](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.10864.pdf)] [[Homepage](https://deepmind.com/research/open-source/kinetics)]  
   *400/600/700/700 classes, at least 400/600/600/700 clips per class*
* **Charades**: Hollywood in Homes: Crowdsourcing Data Collection for Activity Understanding (ECCV 2016)  
   [[Paper](http://ai2-website.s3.amazonaws.com/publications/hollywood-homes.pdf)][[Homepage](https://prior.allenai.org/projects/charades)]  
   *9,848 annotated videos, 267 people, 27,847 video descriptions, 66,500 temporally localized intervals for 157 action classes and 41,104 labels for 46 object classes*
* **Toyota Smarthome**: Real-World Activities of Daily Living (ICCV 2019)   
   [[Paper](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_ICCV_2019/papers/Das_Toyota_Smarthome_Real-World_Activities_of_Daily_Living_ICCV_2019_paper.pdf)][[Homepage](https://project.inria.fr/toyotasmarthome/)]   
   *16,115 short RGB+D video samples, 31 activities, 3 modalities: RGB + Depth + 3D Skeleton, the subjects are senior people in the age range 60-80 years old*
* **Charades-Ego**: Actor and Observer: Joint Modeling of First and Third-Person Videos (CVPR 2018)   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1804.09627.pdf)][[Homepage](https://prior.allenai.org/projects/charades-ego)]  
   *112 people, 4000 paired videos, 157 action classes*
* **20BN-jester**: The Jester Dataset: A Large-Scale Video Dataset of Human Gestures (ICCVW 2019)   
   [[Paper](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_ICCVW_2019/papers/HANDS/Materzynska_The_Jester_Dataset_A_Large-Scale_Video_Dataset_of_Human_Gestures_ICCVW_2019_paper.pdf)][[Homepage](https://20bn.com/datasets/jester)]   
   *148,092 videos, 27 classes, 1376 actors*
* **Moments in Time Dataset**: one million videos for event understanding (TPAMI 2019)   
   [[Paper](http://moments.csail.mit.edu/TPAMI.2019.2901464.pdf)][[Homepage](http://moments.csail.mit.edu/)]  
   *over 1,000,000 labelled videos for 339 Moment classes, the average number of labeled videos per class is 1,757 with a median of 2,775*
* **Multi-Moments in Time**: Learning and Interpreting Models for Multi-Action Video Understanding   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1911.00232.pdf)][[Homepage](http://moments.csail.mit.edu/)]  
   *1.02 million videos, 313 action classes, 553,535 videos are annotated with more than one label and 257,491 videos are annotated with three or more labels*
* **20BN-SOMETHING-SOMETHING**: The "something something" video database for learning and evaluating visual common sense   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.04261)][[Homepage](https://20bn.com/datasets/something-something)]  
   *100,000 videos across 174 classes*
* **EPIC-KITCHENS**: Scaling Egocentric Vision: The EPIC-KITCHENS Dataset (ECCV 2018, extended into TPAMI 2020)  
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.13256)][[Homepage](https://epic-kitchens.github.io/2021)]  
   *100 hours, 37 participants, 20M frames, 90K action segments, 700 variable length videos, 97 verb classes, 300 noun classes, 4053 action classes*
* **HOMAGE**: Home Action Genome: Cooperative Compositional Action Understanding (CVPR 2021)   
   [[Paper](/xiaobai1217/Awesome-Video-Datasets/blob/main)][[Homepage](https://homeactiongenome.org/)]  
   *27 participants, 12 sensor types, 75 activities, 453 atomic actions, 1,752 synchronized sequences, 86 object classes, 29 relationship classes, 497,534 bounding boxes, 583,481 relationships*
* **MMAct**: A Large-Scale Dataset for Cross Modal Human Action Understanding (ICCV 2019)   
   [[Paper](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_ICCV_2019/papers/Kong_MMAct_A_Large-Scale_Dataset_for_Cross_Modal_Human_Action_Understanding_ICCV_2019_paper.pdf)][[Homepage](https://mmact19.github.io/2019/)]  
   *36k video clips, 37 action classes, RGB+Keypoints+Acc+Gyo+Ori+Wi-Fi+Presure*
* **LEMMA**: A Multi-view Dataset for LEarning Multi-agent Multi-task Activities (ECCV 2020)   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2007.15781.pdf)][[Homepage](https://sites.google.com/view/lemma-activity)]  
   *RGB-D, 641 action classes, 11,781 action segments, 4.6M frames*
* **NTU RGB+D**: A Large Scale Dataset for 3D Human Activity Analysis (CVPR 2016, TPAMI 2019)   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.02808)][[Homepage](http://rose1.ntu.edu.sg/Datasets/actionRecognition.asp)]   
   *106 distinct subjects and contains more than 114 thousand video samples and 8 million frames, 120 action classes*
* **Action Genome**: Actions as Compositions of Spatio-temporal Scene Graphs (CVPR 2020)   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1912.06992.pdf)][[Homepage](https://www.actiongenome.org/)]  
   *10K videos, 0.4M objects, 1.7M visual relationships*
* **TITAN**: Future Forecast using Action Priors (CVPR 2020)   
   [[Paper](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_CVPR_2020/papers/Malla_TITAN_Future_Forecast_Using_Action_Priors_CVPR_2020_paper.pdf)][[Homepage](https://usa.honda-ri.com/titan)]  
   *700 labeled video-clips, 50 labels including vehicle states and actions, pedestrian age groups, and targeted pedestrian action attributes*
* **PKU-MMD**: A Large Scale Benchmark for Continuous Multi-Modal Human Action Understanding (ACM Multimedia Workshop)   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.07475)][[Homepage](https://github.com/ECHO960/PKU-MMD#pku-mmd-a-large-scale-benchmark-for-continuous-multi-modal-human-action-understanding)]  
   *1,076 long video sequences, 51 action categories, performed by 66 subjects in three camera views, 20,000 action instances, 5.4 million frames, RGB+depth+Infrared Radiation+Skeleton*
* **HACS**: Human Action Clips and Segments Dataset for Recognition and Temporal Localization   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1712.09374.pdf)][[Homepage](http://hacs.csail.mit.edu/)]  
   *HACS Clips: 1.5M annotated clips sampled from 504K untrimmed videos, HACS Segments: 139K action segments densely annotated in 50K untrimmed videos spanning 200 action categories*
* **Oops!**: Predicting Unintentional Action in Video (CVPR 2020)   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1911.11206.pdf)][[Homepage](https://oops.cs.columbia.edu/)]   
   *20,338 videos, 7,368 annotated for training, 6,739 annotated for testing*
* **RareAct**: A video dataset of unusual interactions   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.01018.pdf)][[Homepage](https://github.com/antoine77340/RareAct)]  
   *122 different actions, 7,607 clips, 905 videos, 19 verbs, 38 nouns*
* **FineGym**: A Hierarchical Video Dataset for Fine-grained Action Understanding (CVPR 2020)   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.06704.pdf)][[Homepage](https://sdolivia.github.io/FineGym/)]   
   *10 event categories, including 6 male events and 4 female events, 530 element categories*
* **THUMOS**: The THUMOS challenge on action recognition for videos “in the wild”   
   [[Paper](https://www.crcv.ucf.edu/papers/thumosCVIU.pdf)][[Homepage](http://crcv.ucf.edu/THUMOS14/)]   
   *101 actions, train: 13,000 temporally trimmed videos, validation: 2100 temporally untrimmed videos with temporal annotations of actions, background: 3000 relevant videos, test: 5600 temporally untrimmed videos with withheld ground truth*
* **MultiTHUMOS**: Every Moment Counts: Dense Detailed Labeling of Actions in Complex Videos (IJCV 2017)   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1507.05738.pdf)][[Homepage](http://ai.stanford.edu/~syyeung/everymoment.html)]   
   *400 videos, 38,690 annotations of 65 action classes, 10.5 action classes per video*
* **TinyVIRAT**: Low-resolution Video Action Recognition   
   [[Paper](https://www.crcv.ucf.edu/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Publications_TinyVIRAT.pdf)][[Homepage](https://www.crcv.ucf.edu/research/projects/tinyvirat-low-resolution-video-action-recognition/)]   
   *12,829 low-resolution videos, 26 classes, multi-label classification*
* **UAV-Human**: A Large Benchmark for Human Behavior Understanding with Unmanned Aerial Vehicles   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.00946)][[Homepage](https://github.com/SUTDCV/UAV-Human)]   
   *67,428 multi-modal video sequences and 119 subjects for action recognition, 22,476 frames for pose estimation, 41,290 frames and 1,144 identities for person re-identification, and 22,263 frames for attribute recognition*
* **Mimetics**: Towards Understanding Human Actions Out of Context   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.07249)][[Homepage](https://europe.naverlabs.com/research/computer-vision/mimetics/)]   
   *The Mimetics dataset contains 713 video clips from YouTube of mimed actions for a subset of 50 classes from the Kinetics400 dataset. It allows to evaluate on out-of-context human actions methods that have been trained on Kinetics.*
* **HAA500**: Human-Centric Atomic Action Dataset with Curated Videos (ICCV 2021)   
   [[Paper](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/ICCV2021/papers/Chung_HAA500_Human-Centric_Atomic_Action_Dataset_With_Curated_Videos_ICCV_2021_paper.pdf)][[Homepage](https://www.cse.ust.hk/haa/)]   
   *a manually annotated humancentric atomic action dataset for action recognition on 500 classes with over 591K labeled frames*
* **CDAD**: A Common Daily Action Dataset with Collected Hard Negative Samples (CVPR 2022)   
   [[Paper](https://keli-sketchx.github.io/files/CVPRW2022.pdf)][[Homepage](https://github.com/MartinXM/CDAD)]   
   *57,824 video clips of 23 well-defined common daily actions with rich manual annotations*
* **Hierarchical Action Search**: Searching for Actions on the Hyperbole (CVPR 2020)   
   [[Paper](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_CVPR_2020/papers/Long_Searching_for_Actions_on_the_Hyperbole_CVPR_2020_paper.pdf)][[Homepage](https://github.com/Tenglon/hyperbolic_action)]   
   *Hierarchical-ActivityNet, Hierarchical-Kinetics, and Hierarchical-Moments from ActivityNet, mini-Kinetics, and Moments-in-time; provide action hierarchies and action splits for unseen action search*

## Video Classification

* **COIN**: A Large-scale Dataset for Comprehensive Instructional Video Analysis (CVPR 2019)   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1903.02874.pdf)][[Homepage](https://coin-dataset.github.io/)]   
   *11,827 videos, 180 tasks, 12 domains, 46,354 annotated segments*
* **VideoLT**: Large-scale Long-tailed Video Recognition   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.02668.pdf)][[Homepage](https://videolt.github.io/)]   
   *256,218 untrimmed videos, annotated into 1,004 classes with a long-tailed distribution*
* **Youtube-8M**: A Large-Scale Video Classification Benchmark   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1609.08675.pdf)][[Homepage](https://research.google.com/youtube8m/index.html)]  
   *8,000,000 videos, 4000 visual entities*
* **HVU**: Large Scale Holistic Video Understanding (ECCV 2020)   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.11451.pdf)][[Homepage](https://holistic-video-understanding.github.io/)]   
   *572k videos in total with 9 million annotations for training, validation and test set spanning over 3142 labels, semantic aspects defined on categories of scenes, objects, actions, events, attributes and concepts*
* **VLOG**: From Lifestyle Vlogs to Everyday Interactions (CVPR 2018)   
   [[Paper](https://web.eecs.umich.edu/~fouhey//2017/VLOG/paper.pdf)][[Homepage](https://web.eecs.umich.edu/~fouhey//2017/VLOG/index.html)]   
   *114K video clips, 10.7K participants, Annotations: Hand/Semantic Object, Hand Contact State, Scene Classification*
* **EEV**: A Large-Scale Dataset for Studying Evoked Expressions from Video   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.05488)][[Homepage](https://github.com/google-research-datasets/eev)]  
   *Each video is annotated at 6 Hz with 15 continuous evoked expression labels, 36.7 million annotations of viewer facial reactions to 23,574 videos (1,700 hours)*
* **FERV39k**: A Large-Scale Multi-Scene Dataset for Facial Expression Recognition in Videos (CVPR 2022)   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2203.09463.pdf)][[Homepage](https://wangyanckxx.github.io/Proj_CVPR2022_FERV39k.html)]   
   *38,935 video clips labeled with 7 classic expressions*
* **OmniSource Web Dataset**: Omni-sourced Webly-supervised Learning for Video Recognition (ECCV 2020)   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2003.13042.pdf)][[Dataset](https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSd8_GlmHzG8FcDbW-OEu__G7qLgOSYZpH-i5vYVJcu7wcb_TQ/viewform)]   
   *web data related to the 200 classes in Mini-Kinetics subset, 732,855 instagram videos, 365,4650 instagram images, 3,050,880 google images*

## Egocentric View

* **Charades-Ego**: Actor and Observer: Joint Modeling of First and Third-Person Videos (CVPR 2018)   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1804.09627.pdf)][[Homepage](https://prior.allenai.org/projects/charades-ego)]  
   *112 people, 4000 paired videos, 157 action classes*
* **100DOH**: Understanding Human Hands in Contact at Internet Scale (CVPR 2020)   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.06669.pdf)][[Homepage](http://fouheylab.eecs.umich.edu/~dandans/projects/100DOH/)]   
   *131 days of footage, 100K annotated hand-contact video frames*
* **EPIC-KITCHENS**: Scaling Egocentric Vision: The EPIC-KITCHENS Dataset (ECCV 2018, extended into TPAMI 2020)  
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.13256)][[Homepage](https://epic-kitchens.github.io/2021)]  
   *100 hours, 37 participants, 20M frames, 90K action segments, 700 variable length videos, 97 verb classes, 300 noun classes, 4053 action classes*
* **HOMAGE**: Home Action Genome: Cooperative Compositional Action Understanding (CVPR 2021)   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.05226)][[Homepage](https://homeactiongenome.org/)]  
   *27 participants, 12 sensor types, 75 activities, 453 atomic actions, 1,752 synchronized sequences, 86 object classes, 29 relationship classes, 497,534 bounding boxes, 583,481 relationships*
* **Ego4D**: Around the World in 3,000 Hours of Egocentric Video   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2110.07058.pdf)][[Homepage](https://ego4d-data.org/)]   
   *3,025 hours of video collected by 855 unique participants from 74 worldwide locations in 9 different countries*

## Video Object Segmentation

* **DAVIS**: A Benchmark Dataset and Evaluation Methodology for Video Object Segmentation (CVPR 2016)   
   [[Paper](https://www.cv-foundation.org/openaccess/content_cvpr_2016/papers/Perazzi_A_Benchmark_Dataset_CVPR_2016_paper.pdf)][[Homepage](https://davischallenge.org/)]  
   *50 sequences, 3455 annotated frames*
* **SegTrack v2**: Video Segmentation by Tracking Many Figure-Ground Segments (ICCV 2013)   
   [[Paper](https://web.engr.oregonstate.edu/~lif/SegTrack2/segtrack2_cameraready.pdf)][[Homepage](https://web.engr.oregonstate.edu/~lif/SegTrack2/dataset.html)]   
   *1,000 frames with pixel-level annotations*
* **UVO**: Unidentified Video Objects: A Benchmark for Dense, Open-World Segmentation   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2104.04691.pdf)][[Homepage](https://sites.google.com/view/unidentified-video-object/home)]   
   *1200 videos, 108k frames, 12.29 objects per video*
* **VSPW**: A Large-scale Dataset for Video Scene Parsing in the Wild (CVPR 2021)   
   [[Paper](https://yu-wu.net/pdf/CVPR21-vspw.pdf)][[Homepage](https://www.vspwdataset.com/)]   
   *3,536 videos, 251,632 pixel-level labeled frames, 124 categories, pixel-level annotations are provided at 15 f/s, a complete shot lasting 5 seconds on average*
* **RGB-D in hand manipulation dataset**: In-hand Object Scanning via RGB-D Video Segmentation (ICRA 2019)   
   [[Paper](https://motion.cs.illinois.edu/papers/ICRA2019-Wang-InHandScanning.pdf)][[Homepage](https://www.rgbdinhandmanipulation.com/)]   
   *13 sequences of in-hand manipulation of objects from the YCB dataset. Each sequence ranges from 300 to 700 frames in length (filmed at 30fps) and contains in-hand manipulation of the objects revealing all sides*

## Object Detection

* **ImageNet VID**   
   [[Paper](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11263-015-0816-y?sa_campaign=email/event/articleAuthor/onlineFirst#)][[Homepage](https://image-net.org/challenges/LSVRC/2017/#vid)]   
   *30 categories, train: 3,862 video snippets, validation: 555 snippets*
* **YouTube-BoundingBoxes**: A Large High-Precision Human-Annotated Data Set for Object Detection in Video   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1702.00824.pdf)][[Homepage](https://research.google.com/youtube-bb/index.html)]   
   *380,000 video segments about 19s long, 5.6 M bounding boxes, 23 types of objects*
* **Objectron**: A Large Scale Dataset of Object-Centric Videos in the Wild with Pose Annotations (CVPR 2021)   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.09988)][[Homepage](https://github.com/google-research-datasets/Objectron/)]   
   *15K annotated video clips supplemented with over 4M annotated images in the following categories: bikes, books, bottles, cameras, cereal boxes, chairs, cups, laptops, and shoes, manually annotated 3D bounding boxes for each object*
* **DroneCrowd**: Detection, Tracking, and Counting Meets Drones in Crowds: A Benchmark (CVPR 2021)   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.02440.pdf)][[Homepage](https://github.com/VisDrone/DroneCrowd)]   
   *112 video clips with 33,600 HD frames in various scenarios, 20,800 people trajectories with 4.8 million heads and several video-level attributes*
* **BOLD**: Detecting Biological Locomotion in Video: A Computational Approach   
   [[Paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.12661.pdf)]

The repository is organized into 40+ categories of video research tasks, each listing relevant datasets with links to papers and homepages, along with key statistics. Major categories include:

--- SOURCE 1: Prediction model and technical and tactical decision analysis of women’s badminton singles based on machine learning ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11563442

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in PLOS ONE (2024 Nov 14;19(11):e0312801, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0312801) titled "Prediction model and technical and tactical decision analysis of women's badminton singles based on machine learning." The study focuses on South Korean badminton player An Se-young, who rose to the top of the 2023 BWF Olympic points table with an 89.5% win rate (77 wins, 9 losses) during the Paris Olympic cycle.

METHODOLOGY: The researchers analyzed An Se-young's technical and tactical statistics using a proposed "three-stage" data classification method. They used video analysis of 10 matches (21-point games) from 2023 where An faced four players ranked in the top five of the BWF rankings (Chen Yu Fei, Akane Yamaguchi, Tai Tzu-ying, and Carolina Marin). Matches included finals/semifinals from the Indonesia Open, China Open, World Championships, Asian Championships, and Asian Games. A total of 10h32min was recorded with actual game time of 140min49s. Videos were sourced from YouTube, and statistics were gathered from the BWF Fansite. They constructed a machine learning dataset using inputs such as number of strikes, scoring/losing locations, techniques used in the last three strikes, and serving locations, with scoring/losing outcome as the output. Data was divided 90% training / 10% test. The study used five machine learning algorithms: Decision Tree, Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Machine, and K-Nearest Neighbors. They also used principal component analysis (PCA) with K-means clustering to validate the dataset's learning value.

KEY RESULTS:
- Support Vector Machine with RBF kernel achieved the highest prediction accuracy at 87.5%, with strong consistency
- K-Nearest Neighbors achieved 75.00% accuracy
- Decision Tree and Random Forest each achieved 62.50%
- XGBoost achieved 56.25%
- The linear kernel SVM achieved 75.00%, indicating strong linear relationships in the data
- The correlation matrix showed significant negative correlations between shot location and technique used (ranging from -0.67 to -0.71)
- PCA results showed the two clusters (gain and loss) were well-separated in two-dimensional space, confirming the dataset had learnable intrinsic features

AN SE-YOUNG'S PLAYING STYLE FINDINGS:
- More than 50% of rounds are completed by long multi-shots, reaching 61% in scoring rounds (vs. 53% in conceding rounds)
- She does not seek continuous pressure but rather exploits and maximizes aggression following opponent mistakes
- She immediately utilizes assault methods (kills or dives) after opponent errors, often converting points in the subsequent 2-3 strikes
- 60% of her organized shots from the backcourt ultimately achieved points through lifting or high clears
- Her attacking strength is weaker than her ability to stalemate opponents; she typically creates opportunities through blitzes and scores in the following 2-3 shots
- When losing points, there was an increase in blocks (20%) and lobs (22%) on the penultimate shot, with significant decreases in net kills (3%) and smashes (6%)
- The number of strikes in a round was the most important predictive parameter, followed by landing location where points were scored/lost

LIMITATIONS acknowledged: small sample size, simplistic personal style classification criteria, and lack of consideration for players' handedness differences.

The article includes detailed mathematical formulations for each algorithm (decision tree information gain, Gini impurity, pruning; random forest bagging and voting; XGBoost objective function; SVM decision functions, kernel functions, Lagrange multipliers; KNN distance metrics), plus figures showing serving positions (numbered 1-9), technique coding (a-m), correlation matrices, PCA results, kernel function comparisons, and feature importance rankings.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: Gaming Tree Based Evaluation Model for Badminton Tactic Benefit Analysis and Prediction ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/13/13/7380

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in the MDPI journal "Applied Sciences" (2023, Volume 13, Issue 13, Article 7380) titled "Gaming Tree Based Evaluation Model for Badminton Tactic Benefit Analysis and Prediction." The paper was authored by Wenming Liu, Yifan Zhu, Wenxia Guo, Xinyuan Wang, and Songkun Yu, affiliated with Zhejiang University, Beijing University of Chemical Technology, and Zhejiang University of Technology in China. It was received on 20 May 2023, revised 18 June 2023, accepted 19 June 2023, and published 21 June 2023, with DOI 10.3390/app13137380.

STUDY PURPOSE: The research applies game theory concepts—specifically gaming trees and Nash Equilibrium—to analyze and predict badminton tactics. The study examines matches between two legendary players: Dan Lin (9 major titles, 2 Olympic gold medals) and Chong Wei Lee (ranked world #1 for 349 weeks). A total of 29 matches from 2006 to 2018 were analyzed (Lin won 19, Lee won 10).

METHODOLOGY: The gaming tree was constructed where each node represents a possible stroke, with strokes characterized by four attributes: player, stroke technique, start placement, and target placement. The badminton court was divided into a 3×3 grid (front/middle/back court × left/middle/right court). Stroke techniques included serve, smash, clear, drop, net shot, and drive. Tactical observation indices covered stroke technique, stroke placement, and rally results. Each stroke, rally, and game was assigned a weighted score based on its importance to the overall match outcome. The benefit of each gaming tree node was computed by summing weighted scores, and the net benefit was calculated by adding the maximum score of child nodes. Nash Equilibrium was identified to determine optimal strategies and predict win/loss outcomes.

KEY RESULTS: (1) The best choice for Lin was hitting the shuttle to the backcourt, while Lee's best strategy was controlling the forecourt. (2) Win-loss ratio analysis showed Lin consistently outperformed Lee in most career periods, consistent with actual match results. (3) As the two players faced each other more often, they discovered more ways to beat each other; however, in the final period (matches 22–28), strategy diversity dropped significantly due to mutual familiarity and physical limitations. (4) In the last period, Lin and Lee had roughly equal chances of winning, with Lin's advantage reversing at higher stroke counts (7+ beats). The empirical results demonstrated the gaming tree method could effectively evaluate player strengths and weaknesses and accurately predict tactical implementation.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: ShuttleNet: Position-Aware Fusion of Rally Progress and ... ---
URL: https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/20341/20100

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper (AAAI-22) presents ShuttleNet, a novel framework for stroke forecasting in badminton—the first work to address predicting future strokes (shot types and area coordinates) in turn-based sports. The authors from National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University formulate stroke forecasting as a sequence prediction problem with three key challenges: 1) mixed sequences (two players alternate strokes), 2) multiple outputs at each timestamp (shot type + coordinates), and 3) player dependence (return styles depend on both players' overall styles and rally situation).

The ShuttleNet framework consists of three main components:
- Transformer-Based Rally Extractor (TRE): captures rally progress/current situation using a modified Transformer with a proposed multi-head type-area-attention layer (which separately characterizes importance of shot types and area, inspired by disentangled attention)
- Transformer-Based Player Extractor (TPE): splits the sequence into two subsequences by player (Player A and B) to generate each player's context, with shared parameters and sequence alignment
- Position-Aware Gated Fusion Network (PGFN): fuses rally contexts and both players' contexts using information weights (α) and learnable position weights (β) based on gated multi-modal units

The prediction layer assumes area coordinates follow a bi-variate Gaussian distribution and uses hard parameter sharing with two linear layers to predict shot type and area parameters. Training minimizes combined cross-entropy loss (Ltype) and negative log-likelihood loss (Larea).

Key experimental results:
- Dataset: 75 high-ranking badminton singles matches (2018-2021), 31 players, 180 sets, 4,325 rallies, 43,191 strokes, 10 shot types (net shot, clear, push/rush, smash, defensive shot, drive, lob, drop, short service, long service)
- ShuttleNet outperforms all baselines (Seq2Seq, CF-LSTM, TF, dNRI, DMA-Nets) by at least 12.0% in CE and 3.4% in MSE across all metrics and observed-stroke lengths (τ=2, 4, 8)
- Ablation studies confirmed the necessity of each component (rally extractor, both player extractors, information weights, position weights, and type-area-attention)
- Case study showed players use different area distributions (middle of court vs. near net) when returning against smashes, demonstrating tactic investigation utility

The paper concludes the framework benefits both coaching-oriented applications (tactic investigation) and community-oriented applications (storytelling/engagement), with future work planned to extend to additional conditions like win/loss outcomes. Code is available at https://github.com/wywyWang/ShuttleNet.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"our method surpasses all the baselines by at least 12.0% and 3.4% in terms of CE and MSE, respectively"
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Future Prediction of Shuttlecock Trajectory in Badminton Using Player’s Information ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10219238

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific research paper published in the Journal of Imaging (J Imaging) on May 11, 2023 (doi: 10.3390/jimaging9050099), by researchers from Keio University's Graduate School of Science and Technology in Yokohama, Japan. The paper, authored by Yuka Nokihara, Ryo Hachiuma, Ryosuke Hori, and Hideo Saito (corresponding author), addresses the novel task of predicting future shuttlecock trajectories in badminton match videos.

**Purpose and Methodology:**
The study proposes a trajectory prediction method that incorporates three types of information: shuttlecock position (2D), player positions (4D), and player postures (68D). These are each embedded into 2D feature vectors via fully connected layers and combined into a 6D feature vector, which is fed into a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network. The method uses two modules: (1) a detection and pose estimation module for past frames (using TrackNet for shuttlecock detection, Faster R-CNN trained on MS COCO for player detection, and HRNet for pose estimation), and (2) a time-series model for future prediction.

**Key Experimental Details:**
- Dataset: Shuttlecock Trajectory Dataset (26 match videos for training, 3 for testing; 1280x720 resolution, 30 fps)
- Training used 23 professional singles matches from international tournaments (2018-2021), split 80/20 into training/validation
- Implementation: PyTorch 1.12.1, Python 3.7.13, NVIDIA TITAN RTX, CUDA 11.4
- LSTM: 3 layers, 128-dimension hidden layer, Adam optimizer, 400 epochs
- Input: 4 past frames; Output: 12 future frames
- Loss function: Mean Squared Error (MSE)
- Data augmentation: 50% left-right flipping probability, 50-pixel translation range
- Evaluation metrics: Average Displacement Error (ADE) and Final Displacement Error (FDE) in pixels

**Key Results:**
- The proposed method improved ADE by ~13% compared to methods using only shuttlecock position information, and by ~8.4% compared to methods using shuttlecock + player position (without posture)

- ShuttleNet's variants (ShuttleNetP2R and ShuttleNetR2P) that integrate player and rally contexts sequentially did not outperform the full model, validating the separate-learning-then-fusion design approach.

--- SOURCE 1: Capturing Intransitive Dominance in Tennis Forecasting: A Graph Neural Network Approach ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2510.20454v2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an arXiv research paper (v2, reference 2510.20454) titled "Capturing Intransitive Dominance in Tennis Forecasting: A Graph Neural Network Approach" that presents a novel application of graph neural networks (GNNs) to pre-match tennis outcome prediction, specifically targeting intransitive player dominance relationships.

**Core Contribution:** The authors build temporal directed graphs for tennis matches (players as nodes, historical match outcomes as directed weighted edges) and apply MagNet, a spectral graph convolutional network that uses the magnetic Laplacian (a complex Hermitian matrix) to learn from directed cycles and intransitive relationships. This is the first known application of GNNs to pre-match tennis forecasting (a Google Scholar search of 66 queries found no other papers doing so).

**Data:** Historical ATP and WTA match data from tennis-data.co.uk spanning January 8, 2012 to October 16, 2025, filtered to highest-tier events (Grand Slams, tour finals, 1000 and 500 series). Final dataset: 20,181 men's matches (670 players) and 19,985 women's matches (640 players). Validation set of 8,435 matches, held-out test set of 12,052 matches (early 2022 to October 2025). Surface-specific graphs (clay, grass, hard) built per gender. Player static attributes (height, weight, DOB, handedness) were evaluated but excluded as they did not improve accuracy.

**Methodology:** 
- Edge weights based on proportion of games won, adjusted by time decay (λ=0.34), surface transferability (α), and tournament prestige (uniform weights β=1)
- Dominance score aggregates historical match results with weighting; edges point from dominant to dominated player
- MagNet optimised q=0.238 (near maximum directional weighting); 2 layers, K=1 Chebyshev filter, 16 hidden units
- Walk-forward validation: trained on 15% of most recent matches, retrained every 38 snapshots (~quarter year), training under 10 seconds per run on consumer hardware
- 250 trials using Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) via Optuna, multi-objective on men's/women's Brier scores
- Set-win probabilities converted to match probabilities for best-of-3 and best-of-5 formats

**Results (out-of-sample test set):** Overall 65.7% accuracy, 0.214 Brier score. Model ties Weighted Elo on Brier score (0.214) but trails slightly on accuracy (65.7% vs 65.8%). Outperforms standard Elo (65.3%, 0.217) and Bradley-Terry (64.6%, 0.219). Pinnacle Sports bookmaker benchmark remains superior (68.7% accuracy, 0.198 Brier). Model shows strong calibration (reliability term below 0.0001 vs 0.0012 for Weighted Elo).

**Ablation findings:** Graph structure carries most of the predictive signal (removing dominance graph raises Brier from 0.2142 to 0.2492). Most consequential components: edge-age decay (+0.0118), multi-hop receptive field (+0.0095), in/out-degree node features (+0.0058). Directional weighting q and dominance edge weights have smallest effects, suggesting the model's value is a broad complementary signal rather than local intransitivity decoding.

**Intransitivity analysis:** Women's tennis contains 12.3% more cyclic triads than men's. A well-known example cited: Nadal beats Federer (24/40), Federer beats Davydenko (19/21), but Davydenko beats Nadal (6/11). A forecast-encompassing test shows Weighted Elo does not fully subsume the GNN model; a combined forecast significantly outperforms Weighted Elo, with gains growing more strongly on intransitive matchups. This demonstrates the graph-based approach captures forecasting signal that transitive rating systems discard, even between players sharing no common opponents.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Our model (65.7% accuracy, 0.214 Brier score) forecasts competitively with established rating systems such as Weighted Elo. Although it does not improve on the baseline in unconditional accuracy, a forecast-encompassing test shows that it carries complementary information. A combined forecast significantly outperforms Weighted Elo, and there is some indication that the gain grows more strongly on the intransitive matchups our model targets."
</key_excerpts>

This research paper by Szabolcs Csapó (University of Twente, Netherlands, published as TScIT 43, July 4, 2025) investigates the use of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for automated tactic recognition and prediction in the esports game Counter-Strike. The research addresses a knowledge gap in automated, data-driven tactical analysis for Counter-Strike, where most existing work relies on manual review and subjective interpretation.

**Methodology:** The model was trained on the ESTA dataset (1,500 professional matches with up to two frames per second of player/position data). The 2-layered GCN outperformed GAT architectures (2-layered GAT: 78.10% accuracy, 0.6831 F1). The confusion matrix showed the model struggled most with distinguishing t_setup_a from execution tactics (setup/execute transitions create ambiguous boundaries). The micro-average AUC was 0.81, with some classes achieving 0.96-1.00 AUC while t_setup_a scored only 0.53. The model was limited to the Dust 2 map.

**Conclusions:** The model's performance is comparable to or exceeds similar studies (Szmida et al. achieved 0.8549 AUC for player actions; Xenopoulos et al. reported 0.8753 AUC for outcome prediction). The research demonstrates that even simple GNNs can perform exceptionally well when the graph representation accurately captures relational structure. Utility usage was identified as a critical feature for tactical classification. Applications include automated dataset labeling, real-time coaching assistants, and AI-driven NPC coordination. Limitations include reliance on human-labeled data (subjectivity/bias), exclusive training on Dust 2, and unexplored alternative graph representations or features.

**Core Methodology:**
- The thesis proposes HMMs to predict game/season outcomes by modeling the unobservable win/loss streak state behind observable game statistics.
- Unlike a simple two-state (win/loss) chain, the model uses states representing the current winning or losing streak, allowing transition probabilities to capture "momentum" (e.g., probability of winning the next game given the team won its previous two games).
- The observable "emissions" are game stat lines. Winning states share one emission distribution and losing states share another, constructed via "bins" (n-dimensional mega-bins) counted from historical data, preserving dependence among statistical factors.
- The Viterbi algorithm is used to derive the most likely hidden state sequence (wins/losses) given a team's game statistics.
- Six statistical factors were used: points (own/against), rushing yards (own/against), turnover differential, and first down differential.

**Data and Parameter Selection:**
- In-sample data: 2004-2015 NFL seasons; 2016 used as initial out-of-sample data to test ~2,886 possible bin delimiter combinations; the chosen bins were then validated on 2017 as a check against overfitting.

- Overall predictive success rates hovered between .69 and .78 across all bin possibilities tested on 2016.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is the English Wikipedia article on Hidden Markov Models (HMMs), a statistical Markov model in probability theory. An HMM is a Markov model where observations depend on a latent (hidden) Markov process, with the goal being to learn about the hidden state by observing the observable process.

Key content covered:

1. DEFINITION: An HMM consists of a hidden Markov process (X) and an observable process (Y) where Y's outcomes depend on X in a known way. Y at time t0 is influenced exclusively by X at time t0, and past outcomes are conditionally independent of Y given X at that time. Parameters are estimated via maximum likelihood estimation, with the Baum-Welch algorithm used for linear chain HMMs.

2. APPLICATIONS: HMMs are used in thermodynamics, statistical mechanics, physics, chemistry, economics, finance, signal processing, information theory, pattern recognition (speech recognition, handwriting recognition, gesture recognition, part-of-speech tagging, musical score following, partial discharges), and bioinformatics.

3. EXAMPLES: The article provides two worked examples:
   - The "genie in a room with hidden urns" example illustrating the urn problem generalization, where the genie draws labeled balls from unobservable urns.
   - The "weather guessing game" with Alice and Bob, where Alice tries to infer weather (Rainy/Sunny hidden states) from Bob's reported activities (walk/shop/clean observations), with Python code showing start_probability, transition_probability, and emission_probability parameters.

4. STRUCTURAL ARCHITECTURE: HMMs use trellis diagrams showing conditional dependencies. The hidden state at time t depends only on the hidden state at t-1 (Markov property). Hidden states are discrete (categorical distribution), while observations can be discrete or continuous (Gaussian). Parameters include transition probabilities (N² total, N(N-1) free parameters) and emission probabilities (N(M-1) for discrete observations, or NM(M+3)/2 = O(NM²) for multivariate Gaussian observations).

5. INFERENCE TASKS: Three main inference problems are described:
   - Probability of an observed sequence (solved with the forward algorithm using dynamic programming)
   - Probability of latent variables, including filtering (P(x(t)|y(1..t)), solved with forward algorithm) and smoothing (P(x(k)|y(1..t)) for k<t, solved with forward-backward algorithm)
   - Most likely explanation (finding the most likely hidden state sequence, solved with the Viterbi algorithm)

The article is marked as a "Good Article" on Wikipedia and includes sections on learning, history, extensions (general state spaces, Bayesian modeling, discriminative approaches), and measure theory. The hidden states are called "hidden states" and the output probability is called "emission probability" or "output probability."
</summary>

**Key Concepts:**
- Badminton deception is a two-part motion: (1) preparation identical to the expected shot (e.g., a smash), and (2) a last-moment change that sends a different shot.
- A shuttlecock takes 0.6 seconds to cross the court on a drive and 0.3 seconds on a full-power smash, making deception effective because opponents commit to a movement based on reading the preparation.

**Three Main Deceptive Shot Families:**
1. **Deceptive drop shot** (smash preparation, finished with a short drop) — described as the most accessible and profitable; Viktor Axelsen's favorite weapon, using a slow, ample arm cock and often chaining 3-4 per set.
2. **Deceptive smash** (drop shot preparation, finished with a smash) and its variation (drop prep followed by flat clear/tight drive) — Anthony Sinisuka Ginting specializes in this, playing 100% on wrist angle and forearm speed with identical jumping motion for all shots.
3. **Net deception** (slice and reverse slice) — cross-court slice disguises direction; reverse slice is a technically difficult move favored by Asian players. Kunlavut Vitidsarn is a master, able to place deceptive shots in a 30-centimeter zone.

- Stage 1 (weeks 1-2): Identical motion — chain 50 expected shots with identical arm cock.
- Stage 2 (weeks 3-4): Motion plus change without movement, alternating expected and deceptive shots.
- Stage 3 (weeks 5-6): Add movement before the shot, maintaining leg-shoulder coordination.
- Stage 4 (week 7+): Integrate deceptive shots every 5-6 points in directed then free play.

**FAQ Highlights:**
- Legal in competition except on serves (BWF rule 9.1.6 prohibits feinting before serve contact).
- Pros execute 5-10 deceptive shots per set in men's singles; amateurs should aim for 2-3 per set.
- Common failures: too-soft preparation, too-early change, and poor timing (using it when opponent is static).

## ShuttleSet: Badminton Stroke-Level Analytics Dataset

**Overview:** ShuttleSet is the largest publicly available stroke-level badminton singles dataset, designed for tactical analysis and structured turn-based modeling. It was introduced by Wang et al. (2023) and comprises **44 broadcast matches (2018–2021), 104 sets, 3,685 rallies, and 36,492 strokes** involving 27 top-ranking men's and women's singles players. Each stroke is annotated with temporal, spatial, and tactical labels coupled with match-, set-, and rally-level context.

**Dataset Origin and Structure:** Created to fill the gap in turn-based sports analytics (no public, expert-annotated, stroke-by-stroke datasets preserving full tactical structure). Source material is public broadcast video from bwf.tv (not instrumented capture), standardized to 30 fps and 1280×720 resolution. The corpus spans quarter-finals, semi-finals, and finals of top-tier tournaments including Super 1000 events and BWF World Tour Finals. The dataset is structured around rallies (not isolated clips), making it suitable for sequence modeling tasks.

**Annotation Schema:** Four categories per stroke:
- **Rally category**: set scores, rally winner, lose reason (out, touched net, not over net, opponent ball landed, misjudged)
- **Temporal category**: hitting time (seconds) and hitting frame
- **Spatial category**: player A/B locations, shuttle hitting location, categorical grid location, above/below net indicator
- **Hitting category**: stroke status, backhand, around-the-head, shot type

Court coordinates are derived via homography (p′=Hp), with singles-court coordinates defined at corners (0,0), (0,6.1), (13.4,0), (13.4,6.1). A domain-expert grid divides each half court into nine grids plus seven outside grids. The shot taxonomy contains **18 stroke classes** (net shot, smash, lob, clear, drive, drop, push, rush, service types, etc.).

**Labeling Workflow:** Annotated with the S² (Shot-by-Shot) labeling tool in four stages: match preparation, rally segmentation, video preprocessing, and shot-by-shot labeling. Six trained badminton-expert annotators performed labeling. Quality metrics: temporal consistency MAE of 0.24 (serve), 0.02 (return), 0 for dead bird; spatial consistency MAE of 0.18 (shuttle) and 0.86 (player); shot-type consistency accuracy differences of 0.00 (serve), 0.05 (return), 0.11 (dead bird). Distributed through the CoachAI project, with a Python implementation and Flask-based visualization platform used by national badminton teams.

**Native Benchmarks (three tasks):**
1. **Stroke influence** (win-probability estimation): Best model ShuttleScorer achieved AUC 0.8371, ACC 0.7869, BR 0.1574
2. **Stroke forecasting** (predict future shot types and landing locations): Best model ShuttleNet achieved CE 2.4125, MSE 1.8121, MAE 1.3582 (τ=8)
3. **Movement forecasting** (predict future strokes and both players' positions): DyMF best CE 2.3146; ShuttleNet lowest MSE 1.0832, MAE 1.5852

**Later Research Repurposing:**
- **Stroke-type recognition** (Chang, 2025): BST-3 variant achieved Acc 0.7710, Macro-F1 0.7042, Acc-2 0.9340
- **Doubles transfer learning** (Baek et al., 2025): Pose-based Transformer achieved singles accuracy 0.8617, doubles combined accuracy 0.6686; transfer degradation ~19.3% (pose-based) vs ~39.9% (vision-only YOLOv11x)
- **Temporal action localization** (Wang et al., 2026): DSTA adapter achieved average mAP 74.67 across tIoU thresholds
- **Report generation** (Chiang et al., 2026): ShuttleSet+ derived from ShuttleSet22 (58 matches, 140 sets, 3,992 rallies, 33,612 strokes); Tree-of-Text outperformed baselines using ~40% of Chain-of-Table's time/cost

**Limitations:** Singles only; no fixed train/validation/test partition (papers construct own splits); no continuous shuttle trajectories stored; 3D pose lifting unreliable for badminton-specific poses; class imbalance (rare categories: defensive return lob, driven flight, rush); no action interval boundaries requiring synthetic temporal windows.

**Significance:** ShuttleSet established a shared, stroke-level representation on public broadcast video, enabling otherwise disconnected research threads—forecasting, recognition, localization, transfer, and report generation—to operate on a common substrate. Its long-term importance lies in providing a common analytical foundation rather than any single benchmark score.
</summary>

**Purpose/Problem:**
The study aims to automatically extract and classify shots in badminton games from monocular camera footage to enable automated sports analytics, helping coaches and players understand opponents' tactics and improve training.

**Methodology:**
The proposed system combines three key modules:
1. **Pose Estimation**: Uses DensePose (chosen over OpenPose due to computational efficiency) to extract player body postures, particularly ankle coordinates, which are projected onto an aerial view via perspective transformation.
2. **Shuttlecock Tracking**: Uses TrackNet, a deep neural network designed for tracking small, fast-moving objects, to extract shuttlecock flight trajectories. It fuses shuttlecock trajectory-based hit detection (using TrackNet's "Peak Identification Method" and "Direction Identification Method") with YOLOv7-based swing action detection. The SRA categorizes detections into five cases to resolve false positives and detection misses.

The five SRA cases are:
- Case 1: One trajectory-detected hit in a player's hit segment = correct detection
- Case 2: Multiple trajectory hits in a segment with no player ID = false positives, all removed
- Case 3: Multiple trajectory hits in a player's segment = only the hit closest to the highest-confidence frame is retained
- Case 4: No trajectory hit in a player's segment = detection miss; the highest-confidence action frame becomes the hit moment
- Case 5: No trajectory hit in a segment with no player ID = true negative

- The method requires only a monocular camera, making it applicable to existing badminton videos without additional hardware.
- The system also extracts player movement, serving positions, hitting habits, and causes of point loss for coaching analytics.

- Prior net-sport research focused on landing point, shot direction, or stroke prediction (e.g., Shimizu et al. for tennis shot direction; Wu et al. for table tennis; Sato et al. for volleyball landing; Waghmare et al. for badminton landing point using 2D laser scanner; Wang et al. shuttleNet for badminton stroke prediction; Suda et al. for volleyball toss trajectory; Lin et al. for table tennis serve trajectory). ## CalTennis: Large Multi-View Tennis Video Dataset for 3D Pose Estimation

**Submitted:** 18 Jun 2026 (by researchers at the California Institute of Technology, including Pietro Perona)

**Overview:** CalTennis is a large-scale video benchmark for evaluating monocular-to-3D pose estimation in real-world ("in the wild") settings. It comprises over 11 million frames (51 hours) of tennis practice and match play from 40 players, captured with 2-6 synchronized cameras at 60 Hz. The dataset is 10 times larger than existing in-the-wild human motion video datasets (like 3DPW) and 3 times larger than existing MOCAP-ground-truthed datasets (like Human3.6M), making it the first large-scale benchmark providing synchronized multi-view recordings of expert athletic motion.

**Key Innovations:**
- **Label-free evaluation via multi-view consistency:** Instead of relying on MOCAP ground truth, CalTennis leverages the redundancy of multiple camera views — if a pose estimation model is accurate, its 3D reconstructions from different camera views should be identical when aligned in a shared global coordinate system. Any cross-view disagreement serves as a quantifiable lower bound on reconstruction error.
- **Court geometry for calibration:** Tennis court line intersections (service lines, baselines, sidelines) provide fixed reference points enabling precise, fully automated camera calibration without manual measurements or specialized equipment.
- **Standardized data collection protocol:** Simple, reproducible protocol enabling data collection without specialized equipment or expertise.

**Novel Performance Metrics Introduced:**
1. **Footwork** — detects foot skating/gliding and floating players
2. **Stability** — detects body "jitter" and spatial oscillation
3. **Body shape consistency** — evaluates consistency of body height/limb lengths across camera views

**Benchmark Results (5 SOTA models evaluated: PromptHMR, GVHMR, GENMO, WHAM, TRAM):**
- **Depth/Translation failures:** All models struggled with absolute depth. Translation errors ranged from 0.9m to over 3.6m. Models exhibited "drifting" — players appearing to oscillate along the camera's depth axis even when standing still. PromptHMR was most accurate for translation (due to sophisticated 2D bounding box use) but was also the slowest.
- **Foot-ground contact:** Significant "foot skating" errors persisted even in WHAM, which specifically incorporated foot-ground contact refinements. This makes current models unreliable for professional sports analytics (stride length, ground reaction forces).
- **Body shape inconsistency:** The most surprising finding — different camera views produced different estimated heights and limb lengths for the same person, with up to 20cm height disagreement across views. This indicates models are biased by camera angle and 2D appearance, not just predicting pose.

**Setup Details:** Camera distance ranged from 13.4m to 16.7m (versus ~5m in lab settings), providing greater depth variability representative of real-world sports broadcasting and coaching scenarios.

**Conclusions:** While 3D joint angle recovery is now quite accurate, current models are not yet ready for high-stakes applications in healthcare or professional sports. The dataset and label-free evaluation framework lower the barrier for other researchers to collect and evaluate motion data in diverse real-world environments, paving the way for more democratic and scalable 3D motion analysis technology development.
</summary>

**Purpose/Problem:**
The study aims to automatically extract and classify shots in badminton games from monocular camera footage to enable automated sports analytics, helping coaches and players understand opponents' tactics and improve training.

**Methodology:**
The proposed system combines three key modules:
1. **Pose Estimation**: Uses DensePose (chosen over OpenPose due to computational efficiency) to extract player body postures, particularly ankle coordinates, which are projected onto an aerial view via perspective transformation.
2. **Shuttlecock Tracking**: Uses TrackNet, a deep neural network designed for tracking small, fast-moving objects, to extract shuttlecock flight trajectories. The five SRA cases are:
- Case 1: One trajectory-detected hit in a player's hit segment = correct detection
- Case 2: Multiple trajectory hits in a segment with no player ID = false positives, all removed
- Case 3: Multiple trajectory hits in a player's segment = only the hit closest to the highest-confidence frame is retained
- Case 4: No trajectory hit in a player's segment = detection miss; the highest-confidence action frame becomes the hit moment
- Case 5: No trajectory hit in a segment with no player ID = true negative

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Benchmarking Badminton Action Recognition with a New Fine-Grained Dataset

This paper introduces **VideoBadminton**, a novel fine-grained video dataset for badminton action recognition, and presents a comprehensive benchmark evaluation of state-of-the-art action recognition methods on this dataset.

### Dataset Overview
- **VideoBadminton** contains **7,822 video clips** spanning **145 minutes** of self-recorded footage featuring **18 badminton action classes** aligned with Badminton World Federation (BWF) standards (e.g., Short Serve, Cross-Court Flight, Lift, Tap Smash, Block, Drop Shot, Push Shot, Transitional Slice, Cut, Rush Shot, Defensive Clear, Defensive Drive, Clear, Long Serve, Smash, Flat Shot, Rear Court Flat Drive, Short Flat Shot).
- Data was collected from **19 players** (15 male, 4 female) of National Central University's badminton school team.
- Camera setup: DFK 37AUX273 camera (The Imaging Source), 1280×960 resolution, 60fps, positioned ~2 meters behind the baseline and ~4.5 meters high at a 30-degree tilt, using XRGB video format.
- Data was processed with OpenCV for lens distortion correction, labeled by 5 students (including badminton team members) using the Shot-By-Shot (S²) Labeling tool, and reviewed by the team's head coach.
- The dataset includes annotations of player locations and shuttlecock trajectories.

### Dataset Comparison
VideoBadminton surpasses existing badminton datasets (Badminton Olympic dataset with 10 videos/12 stroke categories, ShuttleNet with 43,191 clips/10 categories) and general fine-grained datasets, positioning itself as the most comprehensive badminton video analysis dataset. It is compared against Kinetics400, Something-Something, MPII-Cooking2, Breakfast, THUMOS14, ActivityNet-1.3, Charades, FineGym-1.1, UCF-sports, Epic-kitchens-100, ADL, J-HMDB, and UCF101-24.

### Methods Evaluated
Seven state-of-the-art action recognition methods were benchmarked:
1. **R(2+1)D** - Factorizes 3D convolutions into 2D spatial + 1D temporal convolutions
2. **ST-GCN** - Spatial-Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (skeleton-based)
3. **TimeSformer** - Transformer-based, uses self-attention without convolutions
4. **PoseC3D** - Skeleton-based using 3D heatmap volumes + 3D CNNs
5. **SlowFast** - Dual-pathway (slow/low frame rate for spatial, fast/high frame rate for motion)
6. **MViT-V2** - Multiscale Vision Transformers with pooling attention and decomposed relative positional embeddings
7. **Swin** - Swin Transformer-based video recognition

### Key Results (VideoBadminton-50: 50 samples/class)
| Method | Top1 Acc | Top5 Acc | Mean Cls Acc |
|--------|----------|----------|--------------|
| ST-GCN | 60.70% | 89.25% | 54.86% |
| PoseC3D | 59.98% | 89.87% | 50.21% |
| Swim | 53.53% | 87.51% | 48.92% |
| TimeSformer | 45.45% | 85.16% | 42.68% |
| R(2+1)D | 40.84% | 77.18% | 35.35% |
| SlowFast | 12.28% | 49.44% | 21.16% |
| MViT-V2 | 12.69% | 21.49% | 5.56% |

**Skeleton-based methods (ST-GCN and PoseC3D) outperformed all video-based methods**, indicating their particular suitability for fine-grained badminton action recognition.

### Evaluation Setup
- Dataset split: 8:1:1 (train/validation/test)
- Metrics: Top-1 Accuracy, Top-5 Accuracy, Mean Class Accuracy
- Data augmentation: random cropping, horizontal flipping, color jittering
- Fine-tuning approach: transfer learning from Kinetics/ImageNet pre-trained weights, frozen early layers with training on later layers, lower learning rates, regularization (dropout, weight decay)

### Dataset Statistics Methods
The paper employs frame entropy (measuring spatial complexity) and mean difference of frame-level features (using a modified ResNet-50 for temporal dynamics) to characterize the dataset's richness.

### Contributions
1. Introduction of VideoBadminton dataset for badminton action recognition with detailed annotations
2. Systematic evaluation of contemporary video recognition architectures in the nuanced context of badminton action recognition
3. The dataset and associated code are made publicly available for research purposes
</summary>

--- SOURCE 7: BST: Badminton Stroke-type Transformer for Skeleton-based Action Recognition in Racket Sports ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2502.21085v2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper introduces BST (Badminton Stroke-type Transformer), a novel architecture for skeleton-based action recognition in racket sports, specifically for classifying player stroke-types in singles badminton. The research addresses the challenges of distinguishing subtle differences between badminton strokes in broadcast match videos.

Key contributions:
1. A novel video segmentation strategy that extracts frames of each player's racket swing, segmenting match videos into stroke clips containing two to three strokes each. This variable-width clipping strategy captures complete shuttlecock trajectories in three stages: the shuttlecock flying toward the target player, the trajectory after being hit by the target player, and the direction after the opponent's response.

2. BST models that combine player poses (2D skeletal joints from RTMPose via MMPose), shuttlecock trajectories (2D positions from TrackNetV3), and player positions as inputs. The architecture is derived from TemPose but shifts focus from player poses to shuttlecock trajectory as a primary input.

3. Multiple BST variants (BST-0 through BST-3) incorporating features like Pose Position Fusion (PPF), Clean Gate modules for filtering trajectory noise, and cosine similarity-based player weighting (α coefficient) to determine which player has stronger correlation to the shuttlecock trajectory.

Results: BST-3 achieves state-of-the-art performance on the ShuttleSet dataset (largest publicly available badminton video dataset, containing 104 sets, 3,685 rallies, and 36,492 strokes across 44 matches between 2018-2021). Key results include Acc of 0.7695, Macro-F1 of 0.7043, and Acc-2 of 0.9267, outperforming prior methods including TemPose, ST-GCN, BlockGCN, SkateFormer, and ProtoGCN. The model demonstrates superior generalization with reduced training sets and outperforms TemPose on 7 of 9 metrics.

Notable findings:
- Effectively leveraging shuttlecock trajectory information significantly improves stroke classification performance.
- 2D poses outperform 3D poses due to HPE model bias toward general human poses.
- The model struggles with high-granularity stroke categories that have similar hitting characteristics (e.g., smash vs. wrist smash).
- Training BST-3 takes 29 sec per epoch on an NVIDIA RTX 4070 Ti Super, converging faster than TemPose-TF.

The dataset uses 35 stroke categories (19 original stroke types doubled for top/bottom player positions, plus a "none" category). The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Va6lue/BST-Badminton-Stroke-type-Transformer.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"To the best of our knowledge, experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms the previous state-of-the-art on the largest publicly available badminton video dataset, ShuttleSet, which shows that effectively leveraging ball trajectory is likely to be a trend for racket sports action recognition."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 8: Wearable sensing for badminton stroke recognition with one ---
URL: https://d-nb.info/1387603655/34

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific study (published in Scientific Reports, 2025, vol. 15, article 41236) by Guohan Jin and Xin Li from the School of Physical Education, Chengdu University, China, develops a wearable sensing network for badminton stroke recognition using two inertial measurement units (IMUs) combined with a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN).

**Methodology:**
- Two nine-axis HWT906 IMUs were placed at the distal end of the wrist radius and the lower end of the badminton racket handle to capture motion data.
- The ESP32 microcontroller was used for multi-sensor time synchronization (eliminating the need for post-processing interpolation that can distort data).
- Data was sampled at 100 Hz via SPI bus protocol, with normalization and a sliding-window segmentation approach (100 samples per window, 50-sample stride, 50% overlap).
- The 1D-CNN architecture consisted of two convolutional layers (8 and 16 filters with 3×1 kernels), batch normalization, ReLU activation, a max-pooling layer, a fully connected layer, and Softmax classifier. It was trained with cross-entropy loss and the Adam optimizer (learning rate 0.005, batch size 64, up to 500 epochs with early stopping).
- Experiments used six male national-level first-class badminton athletes (average age 22±3 years, height 176±8 cm, weight 70±6 kg), each performing six stroke actions and fifteen shot trajectories 20 times. Stratified 5-fold cross-validation was employed.
- A SIBOASI smart serving machine (SS-S4025A) was used to ensure consistent serves.

**Results:**
- Classification accuracy of 97.16% ± 0.6% for six stroke actions (Forehand Clear, Forehand Drop, Forehand Smash, Forehand Lift, Forehand Net Tumble, Forehand Cross-Net Shot).
- Classification accuracy of 86.07% ± 1.1% for fifteen badminton shot trajectories.
- Outperformed traditional machine learning methods: KNN (94.94%/78.71%), SVM (94.32%/75.06%), and DTA (92.81%/72.93%).
- CNN took 133 seconds to train versus 27 seconds for KNN.

**Key Analysis:**
- The model showed some confusion between FL and FNS strokes due to similar racket face angles during the pre-hit phase.
- FSS, FCS, and OCS trajectories showed confusion; Mann-Whitney U tests revealed that FSS/FCS differ only in Z-axis peak angular velocity (FCS requires larger whole-body rotation), while FSS/OCS differ only in Y-axis rotation, and FCS/OCS differ across all three axes.
- Heatmaps and t-SNE visualizations demonstrated that fused multi-sensor data (wrist + racket) improved class boundaries compared to single-sensor data.

**Main Contributions:**
1. First study to use ESP32 microcontroller with multi-sensor data acquisition and synchronization for recognizing badminton stroke actions and shot trajectories.
2. Achieved 97.16% accuracy for six stroke actions and 86.07% for fifteen trajectories.
3. The synchronization method addresses data discrepancies among multiple sensors and the insufficiency of single-joint motion features.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The proposed method achieves classification accuracies of 97.16 ± 0.6% for six stroke actions and 86.07 ± 1.1% for fifteen badminton trajectories, outperforming traditional machine learning methods such as KNN (94.94% / 78.71%), SVM (94.32% / 75.06%), and DTA (92.81% / 72.93%)."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper, authored by Jing-Yuan Chang of National Tsing Hua University, introduces the Badminton Stroke-type Transformer (BST), a skeleton-based action recognition model for classifying player stroke-types in badminton (and tennis) from broadcast videos. The work addresses challenges in computer vision for badminton, which has the fastest ball speeds among all sports, including player identification, court line detection, shuttlecock trajectory tracking, and stroke-type classification.

Key contributions include:
1. A novel video clipping strategy that extracts frames highly relevant to each player's racket swing, extending beyond fixed-width clipping by incorporating the opponent's previous and next stroke information (including partial shuttlecock trajectory) to create three-stage clips.
2. The BST architecture, comprising a backbone (BST-0) derived from TemPose with a shift in focus from player poses to shuttlecock trajectory as a primary input, plus enhancing modules: Pose Position Fusion (PPF), Clean Gate (CG), and Aim Player (AP).
3. Inputs are generated via MMPose/RTMPose for 2D pose estimation, MotionBERT for 3D poses, TrackNetV3 for shuttlecock tracking, and court line detection (from datasets or MonoTrack/TennisCourtDetector) to filter player poses.

Methodology highlights: The model uses dedicated TCN modules for poses and shuttlecock positions, followed by Transformer Encoders with class tokens. A key innovation is the Cross Transformer Layer (CrossTrans) with Multi-Head Cross Attention, where K and V are derived from the shuttlecock trajectory latent and Q from player pose/position latent. The authors argue shuttlecock trajectory should be a primary (not auxiliary) input, since deceptive player movements never misrepresent the actual stroke in the trajectory.

Results: BST outperforms previous state-of-the-art across three datasets:
- ShuttleSet (largest public badminton dataset, 25 classes, ~33,481 strokes after cleaning): BST-CG-AP achieves 0.8322 accuracy (vs. TemPose-TF at 0.8235) with the novel clipping strategy; with fixed-width strategy BST-CG-AP reaches 0.8254.
- BadmintonDB (18 classes, 7,658 strokes from Momota vs. Ginting matches): BST-AP achieves best accuracy of 0.6517.
- TenniSet (6 classes, 3,569 strokes): BST-AP achieves 0.9923 accuracy.

Additional findings: BST shows superior generalization with only 25% training data, demonstrates faster training speed than prior methods (detailed in supplementary), and effectively leveraging ball trajectory significantly improves stroke classification in both badminton and tennis. The code is released at https://github.com/Va6lue/BST-Badminton-Stroke-type-Transformer.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We propose Badminton Stroke-type Transformer (BST) to classify player stroke-types in singles. To the best of our knowledge, experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms the previous state-of-the-art on the largest publicly available badminton video dataset (ShuttleSet), another badminton dataset (BadmintonDB), and a tennis dataset (TenniSet)."

--- SOURCE 10: Badminton Video Analysis based on Spatiotemporal and ... ---
URL: http://mmcv.csie.ncku.edu.tw/~wtchu/papers/2017ICMR-chu.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper (ICMR '17, June 6-9, 2017, Bucharest, Romania) by Wei-Ta Chu and Samuel Situmeang of National Chung Cheng University, Taiwan, presents a system for badminton video analysis integrating several visual analysis techniques to detect the court, detect players, classify strokes, and classify player's strategy to derive game statistics.

Key methodology:
1. **Court Detection**: White pixel extraction followed by texture filtering using corner/edge principal values (structure matrix eigenvalues), then probabilistic Hough transform for line detection, line parameter refinement, and court model fitting via planar homography matrix estimation.
2. **Player Detection/Tracking**: Adaptive Gaussian mixture model (GMM) background modeling updated dynamically (M=500 frames, 3 Gaussian mixtures), foreground pixel detection, morphological operations, and largest connected component detection in top/bottom halves of frames. Player position mapped to court model via homography.
3. **Stroke Classification**: Six stroke types (clear, drive, drop, lob, smash, others). Uses HOG features from player bounding box with SVM classifier.
4. **Strategy Classification**: Court (bottom half) divided into nine regions for spatial quantization of player position. Observation sequences combine stroke type and position; separate HMMs trained for offensive and defensive strategies using Baum-Welch algorithm, with strategy determined by maximum likelihood.

Evaluation results:
- Dataset: 6 videos from BadmintonWorld.TV (YouTube), 558 plays total, 854×480 resolution, matches from BWF World Championships 2015 and Korea/Denmark/Indonesia Open 2016.
- Player detection accuracy: 85.45%
- Stroke classification accuracy: 83.33% (5-fold cross-validation, 600 images at 120×150 resolution)
- Strategy classification accuracy: 70% (automatic features), 83.33% when using manually-corrected features
- The system visualizes match statistics including player position evolution, stroke/strategy classifications, and distributions; case study of "Chen vs Lee" at 2015 BWF World Championships showed Lee used more lob strokes and focused on defensive strategies but lost the set.

Future work includes more elegant strategy modeling, more spatiotemporal features, and incorporating motion information into stroke/strategy classification. The work was partially supported by Taiwan's Ministry of Science and Technology grants MOST105-2628-E-194-001-MY2, MOST104-2221-E-194-014, and MOST103-2221-E-194-027-MY3.

- 3D joints underperform 2D because HPE model is trained on general poses, not badminton-specific
- Limitation: relies on accurate hit frame detection and shuttlecock tracking models; future work could extend to tennis, table tennis, doubles

--- SOURCE 12: How to Perform Action Recognition on Keypoints with ST ... ---
URL: https://datature.com/blog/how-to-perform-action-recogition-on-keypoints-with-stgcnn

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## How to Perform Action Recognition on Keypoints with ST-GCN++

This is a technical tutorial by Leonard So (Datature, November 15, 2023, 8-min read) explaining how to train and deploy a custom ST-GCN++ model for action recognition on skeleton/keypoint data, specifically for sit-stand recognition.

### Key Concepts Covered

**What is Action Recognition?** A computer vision task focused on identifying human actions from images or videos by analyzing motion and appearance patterns, including motion trajectories, pose configurations, and object interactions. It is challenging due to lighting variations, camera viewpoints, occlusions, and complex human motion.

**Action Recognition vs. Classification:** Action recognition focuses on temporal information (order/timing of events, motion trajectories, dynamics over frames), while classification focuses solely on spatial information (each frame treated independently). Action recognition can resolve misclassifications that arise from the loss of temporal context in classification.

**Applications of Action Recognition:** Surveillance and security (identifying suspicious activities), healthcare (monitoring patient movements/rehabilitation), sports analysis (player tracking), human-computer gesture interaction, automated driving (understanding pedestrian/driver actions), and entertainment (VR experiences, character animations).

**What is ST-GCN++?** Spatial-Temporal Graph Convolutional Network is a neural network architecture for action recognition that leverages both spatial and temporal information. It treats the human body as a graph where nodes represent body joints (elbows, knees, shoulders) and edges represent spatial relationships between joints. ST-GCN++ is a recent variant that removes complicated attention mechanisms and reduces computational overhead to achieve real-time action recognition.

**Capabilities of ST-GCN++:** Superior performance compared to earlier architectures, robust to variations in action speed/tempo, and can be combined with other modalities (audio, text) for multimodal action recognition.

### Step-by-Step Training Guide (Sit-Stand Recognition)

The tutorial walks through retraining ST-GCN++ on a subset of the NTU-RGB+D dataset with 25 keypoints:

**1. Environment Setup:** Clone the Datature Resources repository and navigate to `example-scripts/action-recognition`. Install PYSKL (the training environment) via git clone, conda environment creation from `pyskl.yaml`, and `pip install -e .`. Install miscellaneous packages from `requirements.txt`.

**2. Data Preparation:** A preprocessed sit-stand subset is included as a pickle file (`sit_stand.pkl`). For custom datasets, users must add a custom skeleton directly into PYSKL code in `pyskl/pyskl/utils/graph.py` (function `get_layout()` line 97) and add the adjacency matrix in `pyskl/pyskl/datasets/pipelines/pose_related.py` (class `JointToBone`, line 295).

**3. Training and Validation:** Run training via `bash pyskl/tools/dist_train.sh configs/j.py --validate --test-last --test-best`.

### Evaluation Metrics

- **Top-1 accuracy:** Proportion of correctly predicted samples (top prediction matches true label). The model achieved **97.5% Top-1 accuracy**, the primary metric for this use case.
- **Top-5 accuracy:** Correct if the true label is among the top five predictions (used where ambiguity exists or multiple correct answers are possible).

### Integration with YOLOv8 Pose Estimation

The tutorial demonstrates integrating the trained ST-GCN++ model with a custom Ultralytics YOLOv8 pose estimation model (25 keypoints). A testing script (`stgcn_yolov8.py`) runs pose estimation and action recognition sequentially, outputting the video with action labels overlaid. Example command:
```
python stgcn_yolov8.py input/sample.avi output/output.mp4 --config configs/j.py --checkpoint test/stgcn_model.pth --pose-checkpoint test/yolov8s-pose.pt --skeleton test/nturgbd_skeleton.txt --det-score-thr 0.7 --label-map tools/sit_stand.txt
```

### Datature's Roadmap

Datature plans to integrate action recognition with keypoint detection models through their Nexus platform, leveraging video annotation tools (video interpolation, video tracking) for streamlined keypoint labelling, plus future features such as 3D reconstruction estimation and depth estimation.

### Key References
- NTU RGB+D dataset (Shahroudy et al., CVPR 2016)
- PYSKL (Duan et al., 2022)
- ST-GCN original paper (Yan et al., AAAI 2018)
- ST-GCN++ paper (arXiv:2205.09443)
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Action recognition differs from traditional classification in the type of information that is being extracted and analyzed. Action recognition focuses primarily on temporal information, while classification focuses on spatial information.", "ST-GCN++ is a recent variant that implements simple modifications to the original architecture by removing the complicated attention mechanisms while reducing the computational overhead. These optimization techniques work in tandem to further support the goal of achieving real-time action recognition.", "ST-GCN++ is highly customizable for 2D and 3D use cases... the annotations follow the HRNet 2D skeleton, which is similar to the COCO-Pose skeleton format containing 17 keypoints.", "In our case, since the majority of the data consists of a single human subject, the metric to focus on would be the Top-1 accuracy of 97.5%.", "ST-GCN++ is successfully able to differentiate between sitting down and standing up for skeleton data in a video. While this is a relatively simple example with only two classes, this can certainly be extended to a larger number of classes if you desire."
</key_excerpts>
