--- SOURCE 13: Skeleton-based Action Recognition Models ---
URL: https://mmaction2.readthedocs.io/en/dev-1.x/model_zoo/skeleton.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is part of the MMAction2 documentation (OpenMMLab's PyTorch-based action recognition toolbox) and provides a comprehensive model zoo for skeleton-based action recognition models. It covers four main models: AGCN (2s-AGCN), PoseC3D, STGCN, and STGCN++.

**AGCN (Two-Stream Adaptive Graph Convolutional Networks)**: Introduces a novel approach where graph topology can be uniformly or individually learned via backpropagation in an end-to-end manner, and models both first-order (joints) and second-order (bones) information simultaneously. On NTU60_XSub_2D, four-stream fusion achieves 92.34% top-1 accuracy; on NTU60_XSub_3D, four-stream fusion achieves 90.89%. Uses 3.5M params and 4.4G FLOPs (2D) / 6.5G FLOPs (3D).

**PoseC3D**: A CNN-based approach that relies on a 3D heatmap stack instead of a graph sequence as the base representation of human skeletons. It is more effective in learning spatiotemporal features, more robust against pose estimation noises, and generalizes better in cross-dataset settings than GCN methods. It handles multi-person scenarios without additional computation cost. Results: FineGYM 93.5% (keypoint) / 93.6% (limb), NTU60_XSub 93.6% keypoint (fusion: 94.0%), UCF101 86.8%, HMDB51 69.6%, Kinetics400 47.4%. Uses SlowOnly-R50 backbone with ~2-3.2M params.

**STGCN (Spatial-Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks)**: Automatically learns both spatial and temporal patterns from skeleton data, achieving greater expressive power and stronger generalization. Results include NTU60_XSub_2D four-stream 92.34%, NTU60_XSub_3D four-stream 90.39%, NTU120_XSub_2D four-stream 85.23%, NTU120_XSub_3D four-stream 86.19%. Uses 3.1M params.

**STGCN++**: Introduced via the PYSKL open-source toolbox (v0.2), implements six different skeleton recognition algorithms under a unified framework and achieves state-of-the-art on eight of nine benchmarks. STGCN++ serves as a strong baseline without complicated attention schemes. Results: NTU60_XSub_2D four-stream 92.77%, NTU60_XSub_3D four-stream 91.87%. Uses 1.39M params (2D) / 1.4M params (3D).

For all models, the page provides configuration files, checkpoints, and logs for reproduction. Training and testing commands use MMAction2's tools/train.py and tools/test.py with auto-scale-lr option for adjusting batch sizes. Multi-stream fusion ratios are joint:bone=1:1 for two-stream and joint:joint-motion:bone:bone-motion=2:1:2:1 for four-stream. The page also includes citations for each model and links to the broader OpenMMLab ecosystem (MMCV, MMPreTrain, MMDetection, MMPose).
</summary>

"In this work, we propose a novel two-stream adaptive graph convolutional network (2s-AGCN) for skeleton-based action recognition. The topology of the graph in our model can be either uniformly or individually learned by the BP algorithm in an end-to-end manner." (AGCN abstract)
</key_excerpts>

This is the IEEE Computer Society Digital Library page for the academic paper "VideoBadminton: A Video Dataset for Badminton Action Recognition," published in the 2024 IEEE International Conference on Big Data (BigData), spanning pages 1387-1392. The paper addresses the need for fine-grained video datasets in action recognition, particularly in sports analysis. While existing datasets like UCF101, HMDB51, and Kinetics offer diverse video data for various scenarios, they lack the detailed categorizations and nuances needed for precisely decomposing activities and distinguishing subtly different actions in real-world sports applications. The authors introduce the VideoBadminton dataset, derived from high-quality badminton footage, and evaluate leading methodologies (including CNNs, Convolutional 3D, Transformers, and spatial-temporal feature fusion) on this dataset. The dataset is intended to advance both badminton action recognition specifically and fine-grained action recognition more broadly. --- SOURCE 2: VideoBadminton: A Video Dataset for Badminton Action Recognition ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2403.12385v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper introduces VideoBadminton, a comprehensive video dataset for badminton action recognition, derived from high-quality self-recorded footage. The dataset comprises 7,822 clips spanning 145 minutes of footage, covering 18 distinct badminton action classes aligned with Badminton World Federation (BWF) standards. These include strokes such as Short Serve, Cross-Court Flight, Lift, Tap Smash, Block, Drop Shot, Push Shot, Transitional Slice, Cut, Rush Shot, Defensive Clear, Defensive Drive, Clear, Long Serve, Smash, Flat Shot, Rear Court Flat Drive, and Short Flat Shot. The dataset was created using 19 skilled players (15 male, 4 female) from National Central University's badminton school team, recorded with an Imaging Source DFK 37AUX273 camera at 1280×960 resolution and 60fps, positioned approximately 2 meters behind the baseline and elevated to 4.5 meters at a 30-degree tilt.

The dataset construction involved OpenCV-based distortion correction, Shot-By-Shot (S²) labeling tools, human labeling by five students (including badminton team members) with review by the university's head coach, and data augmentation through controlled ball-feeding techniques. VideoBadminton is positioned as the most comprehensive badminton video dataset to date, surpassing prior works such as the Badminton Olympic dataset (10 videos, 12 stroke categories, 751 scoring instances) and ShuttleNet (43,191 clips across 10 stroke categories). Unlike most prior badminton datasets which focused on image-level data, VideoBadminton focuses on video data with detailed annotations of player locations and shuttle trajectories.

The paper presents an extensive benchmark evaluation of seven state-of-the-art action recognition methods: R(2+1)D, SlowFast, TimeSformer, Swin (referred to as Swim in the paper), MViT-V2, ST-GCN (skeleton-based), and PoseC3D (skeleton-based). Models were fine-tuned on the dataset (split 8:1:1 for train/validation/test) using transfer learning from Kinetics/ImageNet weights, with techniques including random cropping, horizontal flipping, and color jittering for augmentation. Results show that on the VideoBadminton-50 subset (50 samples/class), ST-GCN achieved the highest Top-1 accuracy (60.70%) and Mean Class Accuracy (54.86%), with PoseC3D close behind (59.98% Top-1, 50.21% Mean Cls Acc). Swin performed best among video-based models (53.53% Top-1, 48.92% Mean Cls Acc), while MViT-V2 performed notably poorly (12.69% Top-1). On the smaller VideoBadminton-10 subset (10 samples/class), ST-GCN again led (28.05% Top-1), followed by PoseC3D (23.03%). The paper also details dataset statistics analysis using frame entropy and mean difference of frame-level features (using a modified ResNet-50 for feature extraction) to characterize video content complexity and temporal dynamics. The authors intend to release the complete dataset and associated codes for research purposes.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We introduce VideoBadminton, a dataset specifically designed for badminton action recognition which is a comprehensive collection of player movements and stroke techniques." — Primary contribution statement, Section 1

URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2507.02906v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a B.Sc. (Business Analytics) Dissertation from the National University of Singapore (2024/2025) by Chen Jia Wei, supervised by Advisor Dr. Jiang Kan (Project ID: H403030). The thesis presents "Enhancing Sports Strategy with Video Analytics and Data Mining: Automated Video-Based Analytics Framework for Tennis Doubles."

**Project Overview & Objectives:** The project addresses a gap in automated analysis tools for tennis doubles—a strategically complex sport that is under-explored relative to singles tennis, basketball, and soccer. It aims to: (1) develop a standardised video annotation framework for doubles tennis (player positions, shot types, formations, outcomes), (2) build an intuitive tennis labelling tool, and (3) automate data collection/analysis through computer vision (player detection/tracking, pose estimation, shot classification). Deliverables include a Tennis Annotation Tool (GitHub), prediction models (GitHub), and an annotation demo video.

**Key Methods & Models:** 
- Used GroundingDINO for precise player localisation via descriptive phrase grounding, and YOLO-Pose for pose estimation—together reducing manual annotation effort.
- Tested a two-stage pipeline combining YOLOv11 + Deep SORT for tracking, but found limitations with occlusions, far-court players, and identity switching.
- The GroundingDINO + YOLO-Pose combination significantly improved detection of far players and enabled player identification based on visual descriptions.
- CNN-based models using transfer learning outperformed pose-based approaches in predicting shot type, player positioning, and formations.

**Annotation Framework:** Organises data into four core categories—player information (description, dominant hand), positional information (net position, court position in Far/Near Deuce/Advantage quadrants), frame information (bounding boxes, poses), and rally information (start/end frames, hitting moments). Shot labels include shot side (forehand/backhand), shot type (Serve, Second-Serve, Return, Volley, Lob, Smash, Swing), shot direction (T/B/W for serves; CC/DL/II/IO for non-serves), formation (Conventional, I-Formation, Australian, Non-serve), and outcome (In, Win, Error). Detailed labelling rules govern shot-direction-formation and court-side-direction combinations based on handedness.

**Tool Features (5 main pages):** Player Annotation (video upload, bounding boxes, COCO format saving), Training & Inference (GroundingDINO training + YOLO-Pose inference with real-time status), Rally Analysis (net position marking, rally creation, hitting moment annotation), Label Generation (Random/CNN/Gemini prediction models), and Label Confirmation (review/edit with tennis rule validation).

**Performance Results:** Backend optimisations using model hot-loading reduced inference time dramatically (from 12 min 35s cold start to 54s hot loading for 54 rallies, though GPU usage rose from 0.8GB to 3.2GB). Detection accuracy varied by video quality: for a lower-quality NCAA rally (952 frames), GroundingDINO+YOLO-Pose achieved 100%/100%/69.8%/64.3% for players P1-P4 with player identification, vs. YOLOv11+DeepSORT's 100%/95.6%/43.4%/0.1%. For a professional-quality Indian Wells 2022 match (451 frames), GroundingDINO+YOLO-Pose achieved 100%/100%/89.4%/84.1%.

**Data Sources:** Videos from professional matches (YouTube highlights) and semi-professional NCAA videos from Louisiana State University. Eight labelled videos were used with a 70-30 train/validation split, holding out two unseen videos (Salisbury_Ram vs Krawietz_Puetz Toronto 2023 for professional, VUPKfQgXy8g for NCAA) for testing.

**Existing Work Reviewed:** The dissertation surveys existing annotation tools (CVAT, VIA, Label Studio, Kinovea, Encord, V7 Labs, Dartfish, Hudl, SwingVision) and highlights their limitations for doubles tennis (no structured player roles, no formation tracking). It also reviews research on pose estimation (YOLO-Pose, MotionAGFormer), shot classification (ST-GCN, SkateFormer, 2D CNNs), tracking (Florence-2, GroundingDINO), and strategic analysis (MDP-based frameworks, Hawk-Eye data analysis).
</summary>

Users can upload a video and compare predictions from both models side-by-side through a Gradio web interface.

Key details:

**Shot Types (6):** Clear (high defensive shot to backcourt), Drive (fast flat mid-height shot), Drop (soft shot to frontcourt), Lob (high lifting shot), Net (shot close to net), and Smash (powerful downward attacking shot).

**Two Classification Approaches:**
1. **LSTM Classifier (Pose-Only):** Uses YOLO11x-pose detection with 13 keypoints, LSTM neural network with masking, trained on 15 professional badminton matches, processes ~5-10 seconds per video, uses TensorFlow 2.12/Keras. Model file: `15Matches_LSTM.keras` (~1.6 MB).
2. **BST Transformer (Pose + Shuttlecock):** Uses MMPose (RTMPose) for pose detection, TrackNetV3 for shuttlecock tracking, and an 8-layer Transformer with joint & bone features. Processes ~30-60 seconds per video, uses PyTorch. Model file: `bst_8_JnB_bone_bottom_frontier_6class.pt` (~7.5 MB). TrackNet model: `tracknet_model.pt` (~174 MB).

**Key technical details:**
- LSTM input: 41 frames × 13 keypoints × 2 coordinates (26 features) with masking for variable-length sequences
- BST input: Player joints (17 keypoints) + bone vectors + shuttlecock trajectory, using homography to map pixel coordinates to real court positions (6.1m × 13.4m)
- TrackNetV3 uses TrackNetV2 architecture with CBAM attention, processes 3 consecutive RGB frames, outputs heatmap predicting shuttlecock location
- System requirements: Python 3.8-3.12, 8GB RAM minimum (16GB recommended), optional CUDA GPU, ~5GB storage

**Usage flow:** Upload video (MP4, AVI, MOV, MKV) or select demo video; for BST only, calibrate court corners (Back-Left → Back-Right → Front-Right → Front-Left); run classification with either or both models; results include predicted shot type, confidence score, processing details, and top-3 predictions (BST only).

**Project structure:** Includes `app.py` (main Gradio app), `models/` (BST, LSTM, TrackNet, preprocessing subdirectories), `weights/` (all model weights included in repo), `demo_videos/` (pre-labeled and pre-calibrated examples for all 6 shot types), `requirements.txt`, and README.md.

**Performance comparison:** LSTM is faster (5-10s) with good accuracy, requires no court calibration, while BST is slower (30-60s) but has higher accuracy with full trajectory context and requires court calibration.

**Licensing/attribution:** Based on the BST paper architecture, LSTM trained on 15 professional matches, TrackNet paper, MMPose (Alibaba), Ultralytics YOLO, and the ShuttleSet badminton dataset. Users are asked to cite the original BST paper and dataset. The repo has 7 stars, 0 forks, and 16 commits.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 11: FineGym: A Hierarchical Video Dataset for Fine-grained Action

URL: https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2004.06704

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents the paper "FineGym: A Hierarchical Video Dataset for Fine-grained Action Understanding" (submitted April 14, 2020) by Dian Shao, Yue Zhao, Bo Dai, and Dahua Lin.

**Core Contribution:** FineGym is a new video dataset built on gymnastics videos that addresses the limitations of coarse-grained action recognition benchmarks (like Kinetics and ActivityNet), which often succeed by identifying background context rather than the action itself. FineGym pushes action recognition toward fine-grained understanding, where models must distinguish between hundreds of subtly different, visually similar moves performed in the same environment by the same athlete.

**Dataset Structure:**
- Features a three-level semantic hierarchy (Event, Set, Element) based on professional gymnastics standards, e.g., a "balance beam" event is annotated as a sequence of sub-actions derived from five sets: "leap-jump-hop," "beam-turns," "flight-salto," "flight-handspring," and "dismount."
- Provides multi-level temporal annotations mapping actions and sub-actions in time (e.g., locating a 1-second element within a 90-second routine).
- Contains 530 element categories and over 32,000 sub-action instances.
- Two evaluation subsets: Gym288 (natural long-tailed distribution of 288 element categories) and Gym99 (balanced subset of 99 categories).

**Annotation Methodology:** Instead of selecting from 530 labels, annotators used a decision-tree framework derived from the FIG codebook. Attribute-based Yes/No and multiple-choice queries (e.g., "Is the heel over the head?" or "Is it a 1-turn, 2-turn, or 3-turn?") guide annotators to precise element labels, ensuring reliability for moves only accurately identifiable by experts.

**Key Findings from Benchmarking:**
1. **Motion is critical:** Optical Flow provides substantial performance gains over RGB alone, since many moves look similar in static frames—direction, speed, and motion sequence define the element.
2. **Sparse sampling is insufficient:** Models like TSN that sample only 3-8 frames fail on FineGym; increasing sampled frames consistently improves accuracy since elements are short and involve rapid changes ("every frame counts").
3. **Pre-training gap:** Pre-training on Kinetics (400,000+ videos) did not necessarily improve performance; in some cases, I3D models pre-trained only on ImageNet performed better, suggesting a significant domain gap in temporal patterns.
4. **Temporal ordering matters:** Shuffling frames caused massive accuracy drops in TRN, confirming that movement order is essential. TSM was also found to be highly sensitive to the number of test segments vs. training segments.

**Results:** Models achieved nearly 99% accuracy at the "event" level but performance dropped significantly at the "element" level, demonstrating the benchmark's difficulty.

**Significance:** FineGym serves as a foundation for research in sports analytics, automated coaching, and more interpretable AI that reasons about human movement through attributes and hierarchies, presenting open challenges in temporal action localization at fine scales and distinguishing subtly different action classes.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Real-time stroke prediction in badminton integrating AI with ... ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40537-026-01396-7

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an open-access research article published in the Journal of Big Data (Volume 13, article 61, published 06 March 2026) titled "Real-time stroke prediction in badminton integrating AI with the KNN-HMM model" by Qi Song and Jian Zhang.

**Purpose/Objective:** The paper presents a k-Nearest Neighbours-Hidden Markov Model (KNN-HMM) for real-time badminton stroke prediction, addressing issues of accuracy, time-dependent characteristics, and flexibility in stroke analysis. The study aims to integrate spatial and temporal dynamics for stroke classification under real-time constraints.

**Methods:** The dataset comprised 10,000 motion-captured badminton strokes collected in Chongqing, China (2015-2017) from 36 players (18 male, 18 female; ages 18-35; 12 amateur, 12 semi-professional, 12 professional). Data was captured using an eight-camera Vicon optical motion capture system (120 Hz) and annotated in Kinovea. Features included joint angles (shoulder, elbow, wrist), velocities, accelerations, and shuttle trajectory descriptors. Temporal sequences were segmented using 200-ms sliding windows with 50-ms overlap. The model combined a KNN stroke classifier (k=5, Euclidean metric, FAISS index) with HMM-based temporal sequence prediction (3-5 hidden states, Gaussian emissions, Baum-Welch training, Viterbi decoding). Data was split 70% training, 15% validation, 15% test. External validation used the ShuttleSet22 dataset (44 professional matches, 36,000+ strokes, 2018-2022).

**Key Results:**
- KNN-HMM achieved 94.6% accuracy on internal validation (95% CI 93.9-95.3) and 93.4% on external evaluation
- 97.5% accuracy with 32 ms latency and 90.8% streaming accuracy (per abstract)
- Compared to standalone KNN: modest gains in accuracy (+0.05, p=0.021), F1-score (+0.07, p=0.015), precision (+0.06, p=0.001), recall (+0.04, p=0.018)
- Outperformed hybrid SVM-Decision Tree-KNN (83.4%) and acoustic sensor-based approaches (~84%)
- Jump Smash and Net Shot had highest F1 (≥0.98); Clear and Drive had lower F1 (≤0.92)
- End-to-end processing: 32 ms at 120 Hz, 18 ms at 60 Hz, 14 ms at 30 Hz on 8-core CPU
- HMM log-likelihood of 42.75, BIC of 88.6

**Conclusions:** The KNN-HMM offers an effective paradigm for real-time badminton stroke classification with high accuracy, adaptability, and generalizability, though results are limited to a regional model (Chongqing, China). The framework is advantageous for training applications and real-time tactical analysis. Ethical approval was granted by the IRB of Sichuan International Studies University (No. 29237681), and the study followed the Declaration of Helsinki.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The KNN-HMM achieved 97.5% accuracy with a latency of 32 ms and 90.8% streaming accuracy."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Recognition of Badminton Shot Action Based on the Improved ... ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8516566

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a scientific research article from the Journal of Healthcare Engineering (published via PMC/NCBI) titled "Recognition of Badminton Shot Action Based on the Improved Hidden Markov Model" by Chao Ma, Dayang Yu, and Hao Feng, with academic editor Fazlullah Khan. IMPORTANT: The article has been retracted (retraction published in J Healthc Eng. 2023 May 24;2023:9817142).

The paper develops a wearable sports activity classification system for recognizing badminton actions. Key details:

- **Methodology**: Uses a single acceleration sensor fixed at the end of the badminton racket handle to collect action data. A sliding window segmentation technique (window width of 100 samples at 200 Hz sampling frequency, since badminton batting actions typically do not exceed 0.5 seconds) is used to extract hitting signals. An improved hidden Markov model (HMM) is developed to identify 10 standard badminton strokes including services, forehand chop, backhand chop, forehand and backhand drives, backhand push, forehand pick, backhand pick, and forehand.

- **Improved HMM approach**: The paper proposes two training schemes to avoid local optima in HMM training: (1) a mean training method that integrates data from multiple samples, and (2) a frequency-weighted training method that linearly weights the frequency of sample observation sequences. Recognition uses the Viterbi algorithm to find the optimal state sequence probability.

- **Experimental setup**: MATLAB 2020 and IntelliJ IDEA 2018 (JDK 1.8), Windows 10, Bluetooth 4.0 data transmission. Hardware uses six-axis acceleration sensors - one on the racket handle and two worn around players' ankles. 15 players were tested across three skill levels: 5 professional athletes (2nd/3rd-level badminton players), 5 amateurs (badminton association members), and 5 novices (lab classmates who rarely play badminton). Data split was 70% training and 30% testing.

- **Results**: The improved HMM achieved a 95% comprehensive recognition rate for 10 different strokes, compared to 87.7% for the traditional HMM (a 7.3% improvement). Window size affected accuracy: 100 samples = 95%, 150 samples = 93%, 200 samples = 90%. The proposed model outperformed SVM and BP neural network methods (which achieved less than 80% accuracy vs. more than 90% for the improved HMM).

- **Conclusion**: The model can recognize ten common badminton strokes in real time and can be used to improve the competitive level of badminton players.

- **Limitations**: Only acceleration sensors were used by fifteen sportsmen to recognize ten basic badminton shots. Future work includes adding more players and extending the dataset to other sports activities.

The paper also includes background sections on badminton aerodynamics (discussing drag, lift, lateral forces, and the Magnus effect on shuttlecock flight) and batting motion extraction techniques.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The experimental results show that the model designed can recognize ten standard strokes in real time. Compared with the traditional HMM, the average recognition rate of the improved HMM is improved by 7.3%. The comprehensive recognition rate of the final strokes can reach up to 95%."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: The analysis of motion recognition model for badminton player ... ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-02771-9

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in Scientific Reports (volume 15, article number 19030, 2025) by Xuanmin Zhu, Lizhi Liu, Jingshuo Huang, Genyan Chen, Xi Ling, and Yanshuo Chen, titled "The analysis of motion recognition model for badminton player movements using machine learning."

**Purpose:** The study aims to classify badminton players' swing actions by combining quantum mechanics and machine learning frameworks. A Quantum Convolutional Neural Network (QCNN) approach is proposed and compared against traditional Support Vector Machines (SVM) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) to assess classification performance and robustness.

**Methodology:**
- Data collected from four badminton match video recordings using high-frame-rate cameras and inertial sensors
- OpenPose used for human posture estimation; spatiotemporal features extracted
- Preprocessing included Gaussian filtering for noise removal, normalization (Z-score), feature selection, and data augmentation (time shifting, rotation/scaling, noise addition)
- Data split: 70% training, 15% validation, 15% test sets
- Three models trained: SVM, CNN, QCNN
- Five key features analyzed: arm angle, twist angle, footwork position, grip type, step length
- Metrics used: precision, recall, F1-score
- Robustness tested under low, medium, and high noise levels

**Key Results:**
- QCNN outperformed all models across all classification tasks
- Backhand intercept F1-score: QCNN = 0.860, CNN = 0.792, SVM = 0.753
- Robustness precision under low/medium/high noise: QCNN = 0.95/0.92/0.89, surpassing both CNN and SVM
- Feature importance analysis identified arm angle, twist angle, and step position as key factors; arm angle was the most significant feature in the QCNN model

**Conclusion:** The study validates QCNN's superiority in badminton action recognition and demonstrates strong adaptability to noisy data, providing reliable methodological support for sports technique analysis. The QCNN leverages quantum convolutional kernels, quantum entanglement, and parallelism while retaining local connectivity and weight sharing from classical CNNs, reducing model complexity and improving computational efficiency.

**Related literature context:** The study builds on prior work including LSTM-based action recognition (63-92% accuracy), CNN-LSTM-self-attention frameworks (97.83% accuracy), weighted ensemble models combining SVM/RF/LR (95.38% accuracy), and the MultiSenseBadminton dataset (7,763 swing data points with multimodal data).
</summary>

"Experimental results show that QCNN outperforms all other models in all classification tasks, with an F1-score of 0.860 for backhand intercept, significantly better than CNN (0.792) and SVM (0.753)."

--- SOURCE 6: ShuttleSet22: Benchmarking Stroke Forecasting with Stroke-Level ... ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2306.15664v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper introduces ShuttleSet22, a stroke-level badminton singles dataset collected from high-ranking matches in 2022, serving as an extension of the earlier ShuttleSet dataset (which covered 2018-2021 matches). The dataset contains 30,172 strokes across 2,888 rallies in the training set, 1,400 strokes in 450 rallies in the validation set, and 2,040 strokes in 654 rallies in the testing set, comprising 35 players, 58 matches, and 33,612 total strokes from 3,992 rallies. Data was collected from public videos on bwf.tv and labeled by domain experts using a shot-by-shot labeling tool.

The paper benchmarks the state-of-the-art stroke forecasting approach, ShuttleNet (a Transformer-based position-aware fusion framework), on the task of predicting future strokes (shot types and area coordinates) based on observed past strokes. The authors held Track 2 (Forecasting Future Turn-Based Strokes in Badminton Rallies) of the CoachAI Badminton Challenge 2023 in conjunction with IJCAI 2023, which attracted approximately 95-100 participants, with 16 teams submitting final results.

Key dataset features include detailed metadata per stroke: shot type, around-head/backhand indicators, landing height, landing area and coordinates, player/opponent locations, rally information, scores, and outcomes. Exploratory analysis reveals that players typically position themselves at court centers and corners when attacking, and at center when defending.

Results from the challenge show that 11 teams outperformed the ShuttleNet baseline (total score 2.8774), with the top team (Intro_to_AI_team8) achieving a total score of 2.5776 (CE: 1.7892, MAE: 0.7884) by simplifying ShuttleNet's structure. Most improvements focused on shot type prediction (2.1777→1.7892), while area coordinate prediction saw only marginal gains (0.6997→0.6797), highlighting the difficulty of jointly optimizing both predictions. Baseline codes and dataset are available at the CoachAI GitHub repository.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 7: ShuttleSet: Badminton Stroke-Level Analytics ---
URL: https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/shuttleset

SUMMARY:
<summary>
ShuttleSet is a comprehensive, human-annotated stroke-level badminton singles dataset designed for tactical analysis and structured turn-based modeling. Introduced by Wang et al. (2023), it comprises 44 broadcast matches from 2018–2021, 104 sets, 3,685 rallies, and 36,492 strokes involving 27 top-ranking men's and women's singles players, making it the largest publicly available badminton singles dataset with stroke-level annotations.

The dataset uses broadcast video from bwf.tv (standardized to 30 fps and 1280×720 resolution) rather than instrumented capture. It captures four annotation categories per stroke: rally (set scores, rally winner, lose reason), temporal (hitting time/frame), spatial (player positions, shuttle contact location, grid location, above/below net), and hitting (stroke status, backhand, around-the-head, shot type). The original taxonomy contains 18 stroke classes (e.g., net shot, smash, lob, clear, drive, drop, push, service types), supplemented by operational flags. Court coordinates are obtained via homography, with the singles court defined as (0,0) to (13.4,6.1).

Annotation was performed by six trained badminton experts using the S² (Shot-by-Shot) labeling tool with a four-stage workflow: match preparation, rally segmentation, video preprocessing, and shot-by-shot labeling. Quality control reported temporal MAE of 0.24 frames (serve), 0.02 (return), and 0 (dead bird); spatial MAE of 0.18 (shuttle) and 0.86 (player position); and shot-type accuracy differences of 0.00–0.11 upon re-annotation. The dataset is distributed through the CoachAI project, with a Python loader and a Flask-based visualization platform used by national teams during international matches.

Three native benchmark tasks were defined: (1) Stroke influence (win-probability estimation) — best model ShuttleScorer achieved AUC 0.8371, ACC 0.7869, BR 0.1574; (2) Stroke forecasting (predicting future shot types and landing locations) — ShuttleNet achieved CE 2.4125, MSE 1.8121, MAE 1.3582 for τ=8; (3) Movement forecasting (jointly predicting strokes and player positions) — DyMF achieved best CE (2.3146), ShuttleNet best MSE (1.0832) and MAE (1.5852).

Subsequent research has repurposed ShuttleSet beyond its original benchmarks: skeleton-based stroke-type recognition (BST model achieving Acc 0.7710, Macro-F1 0.7042, Acc-2 0.9340), cross-domain transfer from singles to doubles shot-occurrence detection (pose-based model generalizing better than vision-only baselines, with ~19.3% vs ~39.9% transfer degradation), temporal action localization (mAP 75.17 at tIoU 0.3, average 74.67), and report generation via ShuttleSet+ (Tree-of-Text achieving RG# 16.78, outperforming prompt-only baselines).

Known limitations include: singles-only coverage, no fixed train/validation/test split (papers construct their own), class imbalance in rare categories, no continuous shuttle trajectories stored, and unreliable 3D pose lifting for badminton-specific poses. The dataset's significance lies in establishing a shared, stroke-level representation on public broadcast video that unifies forecasting, recognition, localization, transfer, and report-generation research threads.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"ShuttleSet is a human-annotated stroke-level badminton singles dataset designed for tactical analysis and structured turn-based modeling. It was introduced as the largest publicly available badminton singles dataset with annotated stroke-level records, comprising 44 broadcast matches from 2018–2021, 104 sets, 3,685 rallies, and 36,492 strokes involving 27 top-ranking men's and women's singles players.", "A central feature of ShuttleSet is that it is structured around rallies rather than isolated clips. This makes it suitable for sequence modeling tasks such as win-probability estimation, next-stroke forecasting, and movement forecasting.", "Over two years, this platform was used by national badminton teams during multiple international high-ranking matches, indicating that ShuttleSet was intended not only as a benchmark corpus but also as an operational analytics substrate.", "Despite these constraints, ShuttleSet occupies a distinctive position in badminton analytics. It is simultaneously a structured event dataset, a sequence-modeling benchmark, a source of training supervision for video models, and a basis for applied tactical interfaces.", "A plausible implication is that its long-term importance lies less in any single benchmark score than in the fact that it established a shared, stroke-level representation on top of public broadcast video, enabling otherwise disconnected research threads—forecasting, recognition, localization, transfer, and report generation—to operate on a common substrate."

--- SOURCE 13: FineGym: A Hierarchical Video Dataset for Fine-grained Action ... ---
URL: https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2004.06704

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents the paper "FineGym: A Hierarchical Video Dataset for Fine-grained Action Understanding" (submitted April 14, 2020) by Dian Shao, Yue Zhao, Bo Dai, and Dahua Lin.

**Core Contribution:** FineGym is a new video dataset built on gymnastics videos that addresses the limitations of coarse-grained action recognition benchmarks (like Kinetics and ActivityNet), which often succeed by identifying background context rather than the action itself. FineGym pushes action recognition toward fine-grained understanding, where models must distinguish between hundreds of subtly different, visually similar moves performed in the same environment by the same athlete.

**Dataset Structure:**
- Features a three-level semantic hierarchy (Event, Set, Element) based on professional gymnastics standards, e.g., a "balance beam" event is annotated as a sequence of sub-actions derived from five sets: "leap-jump-hop," "beam-turns," "flight-salto," "flight-handspring," and "dismount."
- Provides multi-level temporal annotations mapping actions and sub-actions in time (e.g., locating a 1-second element within a 90-second routine).
- Contains 530 element categories and over 32,000 sub-action instances.
- Two evaluation subsets: Gym288 (natural long-tailed distribution of 288 element categories) and Gym99 (balanced subset of 99 categories).

**Annotation Methodology:** Instead of selecting from 530 labels, annotators used a decision-tree framework derived from the FIG codebook. Attribute-based Yes/No and multiple-choice queries (e.g., "Is the heel over the head?" or "Is it a 1-turn, 2-turn, or 3-turn?") guide annotators to precise element labels, ensuring reliability for moves only accurately identifiable by experts.

**Key Findings from Benchmarking:**
1. **Motion is critical:** Optical Flow provides substantial performance gains over RGB alone, since many moves look similar in static frames—direction, speed, and motion sequence define the element.
2. **Sparse sampling is insufficient:** Models like TSN that sample only 3-8 frames fail on FineGym; increasing sampled frames consistently improves accuracy since elements are short and involve rapid changes ("every frame counts").
3. **Pre-training gap:** Pre-training on Kinetics (400,000+ videos) did not necessarily improve performance; in some cases, I3D models pre-trained only on ImageNet performed better, suggesting a significant domain gap in temporal patterns.
4. **Temporal ordering matters:** Shuffling frames caused massive accuracy drops in TRN, confirming that movement order is essential. TSM was also found to be highly sensitive to the number of test segments vs. training segments.

**Results:** Models achieved nearly 99% accuracy at the "event" level but performance dropped significantly at the "element" level, demonstrating the benchmark's difficulty.

**Significance:** FineGym serves as a foundation for research in sports analytics, automated coaching, and more interpretable AI that reasons about human movement through attributes and hierarchies, presenting open challenges in temporal action localization at fine scales and distinguishing subtly different action classes.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 15: FineGym: A Hierarchical Video Dataset for Fine-grained Action ... ---
URL: https://sdolivia.github.io/FineGym

SUMMARY:
<summary>
FineGym is a hierarchical video dataset for fine-grained action understanding, presented at CVPR 2020 (Oral) by Dian Shao, Yue Zhao, Bo Dai, and Dahua Lin from The Chinese University of Hong Kong. The dataset is built on gymnasium videos and provides coarse-to-fine annotations both temporally and semantically. It features three levels of categorical labels (events, sets, elements) and two-level temporal annotations (actions and sub-actions). For example, a "balance beam" event is annotated as a sequence of elementary sub-actions derived from five sets: "leap-jumphop", "beam-turns", "flight-salto", "flight-handspring", and "dismount". Sub-actions can be described generally using set categories or precisely using element categories, with ground-truth element categories obtained via manually constructed decision-trees.

Key empirical findings from the paper include: (1) element-level action recognition raises great challenges for existing methods; (2) sparse sampling is insufficient for fine-grained action recognition; (3) temporal information is important—motion features capture frame-wise temporal dynamics, TRN captures temporal dynamics, and TSM performance drops sharply when testing frames differ from training frames while TSN maintains performance due to temporal average pooling; (4) pre-training on Kinetics is not always helpful on FineGym due to large gaps in temporal patterns between coarse- and fine-grained actions; (5) skeleton-based ST-GCN struggles due to challenges in skeleton estimation on gymnastics instances.

The dataset includes multiple versions (v1.0 and v1.1) with temporal annotations in JSON format, plus category lists for Gym99, Gym288, and Gym530. All instances are annotated in exact millisecond-level timestamps. The annotations are published under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International License. Pre-extracted features are available on the GitHub repository. The paper is available on arXiv (arXiv:2004.06704), and the work was supported by SenseTime Collaborative Grant and Hong Kong GRF funds (No. 14203518 and No. 14205719).
</summary>

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579)Abstract

The key object tracking in sports video scenarios poses a pivotal challenge in the analysis of sports techniques and tactics. In table tennis, due to the small size and rapid motion of the ball, identifying and tracking the table tennis ball through video is a particularly arduous task, where the majority of existing detection and tracking algorithms struggle to meet the practical application requirements in real-world scenarios. To address this issue, this paper proposes a combined technical approach integrating detection and discrimination, tailored to the unique motion characteristics of table tennis. For the detector, we utilize and refine a common video differential detector. As for the discriminator, we introduce GMP (a Graph Max-message Pass Neural Network), which is designed specifically for tracking table tennis balls or similar objects. Furthermore, we enhance an existing dataset for table tennis tracking problems by enriching its scenarios. The results demonstrate that our proposed technical solution performs impressively on both the dataset and the intended real-world environments, showcasing the good scalability of our algorithms and models as well as their potential for application in other scenarios.

**Keywords:**Table tennis, Fast moving object, Object tracking, Object detection, Graph neural network, Sports analytics

**Subject terms:**Engineering, Electrical and electronic engineering

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579)Introduction

The application of AI technology in sports has emerged as one of the recent research hotspots, with AI-based sports analysis already finding its way into various sports such as football, tennis and billiards. These intelligent analysis systems deployed in sports scenarios typically leverage multiple advancements in AI fields as their core technological components, adapting them to cater to the specific needs of sports analysis. For instance, human body key point extraction and pose recognition techniques are employed to identify athletes’ movements, while object detection and tracking technologies are utilized to record and analyze match scenarios. Additionally, anomaly detection and recognition techniques based on video and motion image features are used to extract key frames. These technologies aid athletes and coaches in making rational plans and decisions, reducing the cost of training and teaching, and enhancing the popularity of sports, thereby developing and elevating the overall performance level of the sport.

Similarly, table tennis is a widely popular sport globally, and video-based intelligent analysis systems for table tennis can assist a vast number of enthusiasts and athletes in evaluating their tactical characteristics, providing standardized movement guidance[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR1), and planning scientific training, thereby effectively enhancing their skill levels. Consequently, video-based intelligent analysis systems for table tennis techniques possess broad application prospects and ample demand. Within these intelligent analysis systems, ball tracking is an indispensable key technology. It can assist the system in determining the point of contact[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR2), delineating the start and end moments of movements to aid in action classification and standardization[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR3), and supporting the action recognition system in segmenting rounds and scoring. However, the small size, rapid motion, and insignificant and unstable image features of the table tennis ball bring many difficulties to the tracking algorithm. Further more, well-researched target detection and tracking algorithm recently,including pedestrian tracking (primarily focused on larger targets with clear image features), and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) detection and tracking algorithms (where targets are small but feature-stable, making motion easier to track) are inapplicable in our scenario for these difficulties. Examples of table tennis balls to be detected and tracked are shown in Figure [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#Fig1).Fig. 1Examples of table tennis balls to be detected and tracked.

In the context of small object detection, research represented by[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR4)suggests that leveraging contextual information and adjacent video frames can enhance tracking capabilities. On the other hand, studies focusing on high-speed moving object tracking, exemplified by[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR5), propose the utilization of frame differences and analysis of differential images to separate the target from the background. Inspired by these two perspectives, our proposed approach combines detection and discrimination to track table tennis balls. Similar ideas have been explored in existing research, where[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR6)and[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR7)achieved good detection results using similar concepts. However, due to the processing of unstructured data, their discriminators tend to have numerous parameters, complex structures, and slow runtimes. Although existing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) can handle unstructured data, they do not adapt well to the demands of tracking problems. The vast majority of research employing graph neural networks for tracking tasks has focused on Multiple Object Tracking (MOT) datasets, which emphasize the construction of relationships between targets while rarely considering the presence of erroneous, false, or even uncertain targets. While numerous similar studies have also prioritized handling severe occlusion and target loss scenarios[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR8), these methods still rely on inferences based on relatively good detection results, rather than operating from the outset under the challenging conditions encountered in table tennis videos. Therefore, we introduce a novel Graph Max-message Pass Neural Network (GMP) as a new discriminator specifically designed for tracking and filtering table tennis balls or similar targets. The overall approach of the proposed algorithm will be detailed in Section 3, with a focus on the analysis of the discriminator GMP in Section 3.5.

To train effective models and validate the efficiency of our method, we build a dataset with rich scenarios based on existing research[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR5)[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR6)[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR7)[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR9)and conduct comparisons with various general-purpose algorithms on this dataset. The general-purpose algorithms we compared against include YOLOv8, which performs object detection based directly on single-frame image features[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR10)[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR11)[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR12), Single Object Tracking (SOT), which relies on user annotations and image features for tracking[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR13), and a scheme that utilizes the generic Graph Attention Network (GAT)[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR14) as a discriminator. Our findings indicate that our method outperforms all the comparison algorithms and holds the potential to address other object tracking problems. In Section 4, we will delve into the detailed analysis of the performance of our proposed method. In Section 2, we will review related works, and in Section 5, we will provide a brief summary and outline future research directions.

In practical training and match analysis, our algorithm can directly provide information such as the image location and trajectory of the table tennis ball. These direct data assist the analysis system in segmenting rounds and actions. With subsequent analysis and processing, we can obtain the land point and hit point of the table tennis ball and estimate its approximate speed (shown in Figure [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#Fig2)). During training and matches, by analyzing these data, we can quantify players’ stability, offensive, and defensive capabilities, and use the data to arrange corresponding tactics and targeted training. For instance, in training, by analyzing players’ ball-striking speed and trajectory direction, coaches can correct their force generation method and angle during ball striking, thereby improving their hitting quality. During matches, coaches can formulate reasonable counter-tactics for their own players based on data such as the trajectory and land point of the opponent’s table tennis ball. Compared to commonly used match result analysis, scoring and losing statistics, the results provided by the table tennis tracking algorithm are more precise, detailed, and rigorous.Fig. 2Further analysis of the tracking results of table tennis can yield many useful technical and tactical information (including land point, hit point, approximate ball speed, etc. ). In particular, we roughly calculate the average pixel distance of the table tennis ball between a trajectory frame, and then roughly estimate the ball speed of the table tennis ball based on the pixel length of the center line of the table, the actual length (2.74m), and the video frame rate (in this case, the frame rate of the video is 30 fps).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579)Related works

In our previous research[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR6), we leveraged a tree structure to establish contextual relationships among potential table tennis ball targets. Initially, we employed a differential detection method to filter out numerous potential targets, ensuring a sufficiently high recall rate. Subsequently, based on the proposed tree structure and the kinematic characteristics of table tennis, we refined the targets to identify the table tennis ball through trajectory analysis associated with the leaf nodes in the tree. This approach achieved certain success in terms of accuracy and adaptability across different scenarios. However, it relied heavily on manually tuned empirical parameters and operated relatively slowly. Consequently, we have further delved into this field and present the method proposed in this thesis. Our related work revolves around four aspects: the significance of table tennis tracking algorithms for intelligent analysis systems, object detection methods, traditional object tracking methods, and graph neural network-based object tracking methods.

### The significance of table tennis tracking algorithms for intelligent analysis systems

Currently, there have been a number of studies, achievements, and datasets related to intelligent analysis systems for table tennis[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR9), yet the tracking of table tennis balls in complex scenarios remains limited. This is due to the high technicality of table tennis, which has led most research to focus on motion guidance and standardization. These studies typically utilize deep learning methods to extract human body keypoints, employing them to model and estimate human poses[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR15). Algorithms can then determine the start and end of actions based on the pose skeletons of individuals in video frames[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR16), classify technical actions[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR17), and design rules for evaluating technique execution. Similar technical solutions do not require table tennis ball detection as they rely solely on human skeletons and keypoints; however, analyzing actions based only on skeletons remains a challenging task[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR18)[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR19). This approach is only effective in relatively standardized training environments. In less standardized training and competition scenarios, the movement of the table tennis ball is highly variable[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR20), and players need to adjust their actions accordingly. Without effective table tennis ball tracking technology, intelligent analysis systems may fail to adapt to such changes, leading to useless or even erroneous analysis and guidance, significantly reducing the accuracy and recall rates of motion guidance[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR3). Tracking results for table tennis balls can assist in precisely dividing action stages for motion analysis and guidance, aiding in the assessment of the standardization and rationality of actions.

### Object detection methods

With the development of object detection techniques in computer vision, detecting objects directly from images based on their edges, morphology, color, and other features, and regressing the bounding boxes of these objects, has become one of the primary methods for object detection. Representative methods include YOLO and FASTER-RCNN. Among them, YOLO[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR12)has gained widespread popularity due to its simple structure, strong adaptability, and fast operation[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR10)[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR11). Previous studies have found that applying these methods directly to table tennis ball detection is not ideal due to the small size and excessive blurring of the ball[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR7). Some scholars have used an improved FASTER-RCNN algorithm to detect table tennis balls based on their small size characteristics, achieving good results[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR21). However, there is still room for improvement in terms of the method’s performance metrics and adaptability to complex scenarios.

Some scholars have chosen to focus on the rapid movement characteristics and shape of table tennis balls, attempting to extract the rapidly moving balls in the foreground based on differential images[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR5). Other studies have tried to directly segment blurred table tennis balls in the foreground using deep learning techniques[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR22)[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR9), while some have considered relying on background information from the table tennis table to separate the balls in the foreground[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR23). These methods perform well in scenarios with uncomplicated backgrounds, but table tennis sports videos in real-world are full of various noises, background clutter, and interference caused by athlete movements. Under such circumstances, the aforementioned approaches often fail to function properly. Some studies have proposed using local images for detection and excluding most image regions based on the ball’s motion characteristics to avoid background interference[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR24). However, table tennis sports videos in real-world contain a large number of invalid segments where the ball is not present, which limits the direct application of the aforementioned methods.

### Traditional object tracking methods

Since relying solely on single-frame images cannot effectively solve the problem of table tennis ball tracking, a natural approach is to leverage the contextual and spatio-temporal information from videos for detection. The conventional idea behind such methods is to extract all potential candidate regions and targets from images or video frames, aggregate these targets, and then screen them based on image features, motion characteristics, and spatio-temporal information to obtain the final tracking results[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR25).

In[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR4), researchers extracted all potential targets from single-frame images and then filtered out the best results based on video context, improving the detection effectiveness for blurred small objects. In[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR26), researchers successfully tracked vehicles in videos with significant distortion by combining the motion characteristics of vehicles. In[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR27), researchers achieved billiards tracking and 3D reconstruction by proposing all possible positions and shapes of the cue ball.

Furthermore, table tennis ball tracking can also be considered as part of the Single Object Tracking (SOT) problem[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR28). However, due to SOT’s heavy reliance on stable image features and feature extraction networks[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR29), its application to table tennis ball tracking is limited. Nevertheless, in this context, researchers often focus on the Region Proposal Network (RPN) responsible for candidate region generation[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR13). The role of this network is to analyze all potential candidate regions and select the optimal tracking results. This aspect of the work essentially involves analyzing and discriminating all potential targets from a global perspective, assessing the confidence of each target based on prior information, and filtering out the results.

However, since the relationships among all potential targets are unstructured data, it is difficult to vectorize prior information and decision-making conditions. Therefore, most of the aforementioned studies did not use deep learning methods in addressing tracking problems, which limited their ability to extract deeper and more essential information, resulting in poor adaptability.

### Graph neural networks based tracking method

In deep learning, to handle non-Euclidean space data, researchers proposed Graph Neural Networks (GNNs)[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR30). With the gradual development of deep learning and its applications, researchers have found that GNNs can adapt to various unstructured data. Currently, apart from the original GNNs, Graph Attention Networks (GATs) are also mainstream in the industry[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR14). Some scholars have even suggested that Transformer is essentially a fully connected GNN[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR31). GNNs are widely used in prediction, optimization, feature learning, and other problems due to their adaptability to unstructured data[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR32).

[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR33)employed GNNs to improve prediction results in latent spaces, while[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR34)used GNNs to learn feature information from unstructured data in multi-agent motion. In[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR35)and[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR36), GNNs were utilized to study team collaboration mechanisms in football and select the best combinations or players for the game[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR37). applied GNNs to merge and group targets in tracking problems. GNNs can adapt to unstructured data, converting traditional methods such as traversal, screening, and matching in tracking problems into regression and classification tasks in deep learning, thereby enhancing tracking performance[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR38). They have also improved the performance of tracking problems in general[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR39).

In the context of SOT, the application of graph attention mechanisms effectively integrates image feature information, leading to improved tracking performance[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR40). For tracking problems involving objects with distinct motion patterns and characteristics, such as vehicles and high-speed particles, GNNs can process unstructured trajectory information, predict target positions, assist in target search and reconstruction, and enhance tracking performance[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR41)[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR42). In multi-target tracking problems involving pedestrians and robots, GNNs primarily facilitate message passing among objects, enabling potential targets to refine their features and learn patterns from videos or contextual images[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR43)[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR44). used message passing in GNNs to determine the consistency among potential targets, while[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR45)directly matched target features obtained from GNNs. Both methods achieved superior tracking results compared to traditional methods with the assistance of GNNs. During this process, some studies have attempted to modify the structure and frameworks of graph neural networks to enhance information aggregation capabilities and tracking efficiency within graphs[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR46),[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#CR47). These methods have demonstrated promising results and improvements in pedestrian tracking and matching for Multiple Object Tracking (MOT) scenarios.

### Summary

Despite the abundance of detection and tracking algorithms proposed in current research, which have achieved remarkable performance in tracking feature-rich targets such as pedestrians, they cannot be directly applied to the context and problems of table tennis analysis in our study. A single detection scheme fails to provide satisfactory accuracy and recall rates, while most tracking methods primarily focus on relationship matching issues similar to those in MOT datasets, rendering them unsuitable for our required scenarios. Although graph neural networks excel at handling unstructured data, neither GNNs nor GATs yield satisfactory results for our purposes. Notably, we recognize that the tracking tasks we envision for graph neural networks under numerous false target conditions extend beyond mere relationship matching and information fusion; they necessitate a reinterpretation (detailed in Section 3). To better accomplish this reinterpreted graph task, we propose the Graph Max-message Pass Neural Network (GMP), which we demonstrate to effectively address the challenges of table tennis tracking.

### Problem formulation

Fig. 3Video frames and table tennis balls to be tracked.

The input data processed by the method proposed in this paper is a video $\Phi$, which consists of _n_ video frames (Image, _I_), i.e., $\Phi = \left[\right. I_{1} , I_{2} , \ldots , I_{n} \left]\right.$. Each frame image may or may not contain a table tennis ball, and there also may be one or multiple table tennis balls in each frame image. Therefore, we assume that there are _k_ table tennis balls $\left(\right. k = 0 o r k \in N^{+} \left.\right)$ in each frame image. We collect all these _k_ table tennis balls in the $t^{\mathit{th}}$ frame image into a set $B^{t}$, where the balls are sequentially numbered as $b_{i}^{t}$. Specifically, $b_{i}^{t}$ denotes the $i^{\mathit{th}}$ table tennis ball in the $t^{\mathit{th}}$ frame. It should be noted that if $k = 0$, then $B^{t}$ is an empty set. In this way, we obtain a total of _n_ sets: $B^{1} , B^{2} , \ldots , B^{n}$.

The continuous movement of table tennis balls in multiple frame images is called a trajectory _T_. Obviously, there may be multiple trajectories throughout the video, which we assume to be $T_{1} , T_{2} , \ldots , T_{u} , \ldots , T_{s}$. Any trajectory $T_{u}$ represents an ordered sequence of table tennis balls $\left[\right. b_{i_{1}}^{1} , b_{i_{2}}^{2} , \ldots , b_{i_{m}}^{m} \left]\right.$, where $j_{1} < j_{2} < \ldots < j_{m}$. We know that $b_{i_{1}}^{1} \in B^{j_{1}} , b_{i_{2}}^{2} \in B^{j_{2}} , \ldots , b_{i_{m}}^{m} \in B^{j_{m}}$. It should be noted that, in $T_{1} , T_{2} , \ldots , T_{s}$, the table tennis balls subordinated to different trajectories $T_{u}$ are all distinct. That is to say, for any given real table tennis ball $b_{i}^{t}$, it can only belong to a specific trajectory $T_{u}$ and cannot be simultaneously associated with two trajectories. Additionally, we assume that every table tennis ball $b_{i}^{t}$ will appear in the form of a trajectory, indicating that $T_{1} \cup T_{2} \cup \ldots \cup T_{s} = B_{1} \cup B_{2} \cup \ldots \cup B_{n}$.

Our ultimate task is to identify all the trajectories $T_{1} , T_{2} , \ldots , T_{s}$ within the frame images $\left[\right. I_{1} , I_{2} , \ldots , I_{n} \left]\right.$ from video $\Phi$. An example is shown in Figure [3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579#Fig3).

Consequently, we obtain n sets of potential objects, denoted as $\left(\left[\right. O\right)^{1} , O^{2} , \ldots , O^{t} , \ldots , O^{n} \left]\right.$. These sets are similar to the sets of ping-pong balls $B^{t}$ in each frame, except that $B^{t}$ represents the actual table tennis targets, whereas $O^{t}$ comprises potential table tennis targets. For the problem of trajectory tracking of a specific target in a video, the most straightforward solution is to train a detector specifically for that target. In the case of table tennis trajectory tracking, this detector is represented as $p \left(b_{i}^{t},\left|\right.,I_{t}\right)$, which detects table tennis balls from each video frame image based on the detector. Subsequently, all detected table tennis balls, denoted as $b_{i}^{j}$, are linked together. However, due to the sparse and easily blurred features of a single table tennis ball in the image, directly construct the detector $p \left(b_{i}^{t},\left|\right.,I_{t}\right)$ for table tennis faces numerous challenges and yields unsatisfactory results. ### Detector

Based on Section 3.2, we know that the detector $h_{\mathit{real}}$,which detects potential targets from video frame images, originates from the probabilistic model $p \left(\right. T_{u} \left|\right. \phi_{\mathit{Inital}} , \phi \left.\right)$. This model points to a detector that uses scene estimation as a prior. Considering a frame image $I_{t}$ belonging to the source video $\phi$, during the derivation process, we label $I_{t _ I n i t a l}$ as the scene for the video frame image $I_{t}$ under detection. Given that the background of an image changes relatively slowly and stably compared to high-speed moving objects, adjacent frames in the temporal domain, such as $I_{t - \Delta t} , I_{t} , I_{t + \Delta t}$, can be considered to have the same scene $I_{t _ I n i t i a l}$. Within these images, a high-speed moving object $b_{i}^{t}$ represents the table tennis ball that we aim to detect. This is a peer-reviewed scientific paper published in Scientific Reports (Sci Rep, 2024 Nov 26;14:29320, DOI: 10.1038/s41598-024-80056-3, PMCID: PMC11599579, PMID: 39592713), authored by researchers from the Beijing University of Post and Telecommunications (School of Artificial Intelligence and Department of Physical Education). The paper proposes a fast-moving table tennis ball tracking algorithm based on a novel Graph Max-message Pass Neural Network (GMP).

**Problem:** Table tennis ball tracking in video is challenging due to the ball's small size, rapid motion, and insignificant/unstable image features. Existing detection and tracking algorithms (e.g., YOLO, FASTER-RCNN, SOT, generic GNNs/GATs) struggle to meet real-world requirements.

**Proposed Method (Combined Detection + Discrimination approach):**
- **Detector (h_real):** A refined common video differential detector that uses frame differencing (absdiff on adjacent frames) to extract potential table tennis targets, leveraging the fact that the background changes slowly while high-speed objects differ between frames.
- **Discriminator (GMP):** A novel Graph Max-message Pass Neural Network specifically designed to filter and track table tennis balls or similar targets. It processes graphs constructed from potential targets (nodes) and their relationships (edges), outputting probability graphs with confidence scores for both nodes and edges.
- **Graph Construction:** A sliding window and gap mechanism is used to sequentially select potential target sets from frames and construct graphs for discrimination.

**Method Framework (4 steps):**
1. Each video frame is processed through the object detector to obtain sets of potential objects.
2. A sliding window with a gap is used to construct a set of graphs from potential target sets.
3. Each graph is fed into the discriminator to obtain probability graphs.
4. Final trajectories are derived from the probability graphs.

**Key Technical Contributions:**
- Decomposition of the tracking problem into relatively independent discriminator (log p(T_u)) and detector (log p(T_u|φ_initial, φ)) components via Bayesian maximum posterior criterion.
- GMP is designed to handle numerous false/uncertain targets (unlike standard MOT-focused GNN research).
- The approach addresses scenarios where erroneous, false, or uncertain targets are present from the outset.

**Dataset:** The authors enhanced an existing table tennis tracking dataset by enriching its scenarios (built on prior research refs 5, 6, 7, 9).

**Comparison Baselines:** YOLOv8 (single-frame object detection), Single Object Tracking (SOT, user-annotation based), and a generic Graph Attention Network (GAT) discriminator scheme.

**Results:** The proposed method outperforms all comparison algorithms on both the dataset and real-world environments, demonstrating good scalability and potential for application in other scenarios.

**Applications:** The algorithm provides image location and trajectory data that assist in segmenting rounds and actions, estimating ball speed (calculated from pixel distance, table center line length of 2.74m, and video frame rate, e.g., 30 fps), determining land points and hit points, and quantifying players' stability, offensive, and defensive capabilities for tactical planning and targeted training.

The article is published under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License and was received 2024 Jul 25, accepted 2024 Nov 14.

# Identification and Prediction of Tennis Players’ Technical and Tactical Behaviors Based on Transformer Model

## Article Sidebar

**Published:** Aug 13, 2026

**DOI:** <https://doi.org/10.7716/aem.v15i3.3582>

**Keywords:**

tennis analytics transformer model tactical behavior recognition sequence prediction event-stream modeling

## Main Article Content

**J. Pu**

Jiangxi Normal University

**X. Y. Zha**

Qingdao Agricultural University

## Abstract

This research addresses the challenge of automatically identifying complex tennis techniques and tactics, dynamically predicting shot intentions, and assessing round outcomes early from structured event sequences. By constructing a Transformer sequence model, the study provides a data-driven intelligent solution for tactical decision-making. The model uses structured shot sequences from Match Charting Project logs, integrating attributes like shot type, direction, and match status. It employs a six-layer Transformer encoder with a multi-head self-attention mechanism for multi-task learning, jointly optimizing technical/tactical classification, shot intention prediction, and early outcome assessment. Experiments validate its robust performance, achieving a Macro-F1 of 0.935 for tactical classification and a round outcome AUC@5 of 0.923. The model significantly outperforms BiLSTM and CNN-LSTM baselines, with ablation studies confirming the critical contributions of its embedding and multi-task design. The proposed framework enables end-to-end deep analysis and effective prediction of tennis technical and tactical behaviors without visual input, providing a scalable, data-driven solution for intelligent competitive analysis, principles that may also inform structured event-stream prediction in other non-visual engineering datasets.

This is a scientific research article published in the journal *Advanced Electromagnetics* (ISSN: 2119-0275), Vol. 15 No. 3 (2026), pages 5274-5286, titled "Identification and Prediction of Tennis Players' Technical and Tactical Behaviors Based on Transformer Model." The article was published on August 13, 2026, with DOI: https://doi.org/10.7716/aem.v15i3.3582. Authors are J. Pu (Jiangxi Normal University) and X. Y. Zha (Qingdao Agricultural University).

RESEARCH CONTENT:
- The study addresses automatic identification of complex tennis techniques and tactics, dynamic prediction of shot intentions, and early assessment of round outcomes from structured event sequences.
- The model uses structured shot sequences from Match Charting Project logs, integrating attributes like shot type, direction, and match status.
- Methodology: A six-layer Transformer encoder with multi-head self-attention mechanism for multi-task learning, jointly optimizing technical/tactical classification, shot intention prediction, and early outcome assessment.
- Results: Achieved a Macro-F1 of 0.935 for tactical classification and a round outcome AUC@5 of 0.923.
- The model significantly outperforms BiLSTM and CNN-LSTM baselines. Ablation studies confirmed the critical contributions of its embedding and multi-task design.
- The framework enables end-to-end deep analysis without visual input, providing a scalable, data-driven solution for intelligent competitive analysis, with principles that may also inform structured event-stream prediction in other non-visual engineering datasets.

KEYWORDS: tennis analytics, transformer model, tactical behavior recognition, sequence prediction, event-stream modeling.

LICENSING: The work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. Authors retain copyright and grant the journal right of first publication. The article is categorized under the Research Articles section of the journal.

The webpage also contains a substantial reference list (approximately 40 references) covering topics such as tennis analytics, transformer models, LSTM/CNN architectures, sports action recognition, time series forecasting, and event prediction. Related/similar articles from the same journal issue are also listed.
