### 3.4 Hierarchical Fusion

Although players move to the next location for returning the next stroke based on rally interactions and players’ styles, it is expected that the importance of each varies under different circumstances.
That is, promising players change their tactics according to their opponents in order to seize the winning opportunity.
Hence, we propose a hierarchical fusion to decide the mutual importance of each style by modeling the style influence between the opponent and the current returning player, and to merge the contexts of rally interactions and player styles.

#### Player-Player Fusion.

Parallel co-attention ([Lu et al. 2016](#bib.bib13)) is adopted in the sequence of the player’s dynamic tactics from the output of dynamic GCN Dat=[da1,⋯,dat]D^{t}\_{a}=[d^{1}\_{a},\cdots,d^{t}\_{a}] and Dbt=[db1,⋯,dbt]D^{t}\_{b}=[d^{1}\_{b},\cdots,d^{t}\_{b}] to consider the mutual influence of the style a^\hat{a} and b^\hat{b} of each player:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | G=t​a​n​h​((Dat)T​WD​Dbt),Ha=t​a​n​h​(Wa​Dat+(Wb​Dbt)​GT),Hb=t​a​n​h​(Wb​Dbt+(Wa​Dat)​G),a​t​ta|b=s​o​f​t​m​a​x​((wh​a|h​b)T​Ha|b),a^|b^=Σi=1t​a​t​ta|bi​da|bi,\begin{gathered}G=tanh((D^{t}\_{a})^{T}W^{D}D^{t}\_{b}),\\ H\_{a}=tanh(W^{a}D^{t}\_{a}+(W^{b}D^{t}\_{b})G^{T}),\\ H\_{b}=tanh(W^{b}D^{t}\_{b}+(W^{a}D^{t}\_{a})G),\\ att\_{a|b}=softmax((w^{ha|hb})^{T}H\_{a|b}),\\ {\hat{a}|\hat{b}}={{\Sigma}}^{t}\_{i=1}att^{i}\_{a|b}d^{i}\_{a|b},\end{gathered} |  | (8) |

where WD,Wa,Wb∈ℝde×deW^{D},W^{a},W^{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\_{e}\times d\_{e}} are learnable matrices and wh​a,wh​b∈ℝdew^{ha},w^{hb}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\_{e}} are learnable parameters.
The outputs a^\hat{a} and b^\hat{b} are then transformed to the overall influence faf\_{a} and fbf\_{b}:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | fa=sigmoid(wa^a^),fb=sigmoid(wb^b^),\displaystyle f\_{a}=sigmoid(w^{\hat{a}}\hat{a}),f\_{b}=sigmoid(w^{\hat{b}}\hat{b}), |  | (9) |

where wa^,wb^∈ℝdew^{\hat{a}},w^{\hat{b}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\_{e}} are learnable parameters.

Afterwards, we derive the context of each player’s dynamic player’s style with the opponent’s influence:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Da|bt′=fb|a×Db|at+Da|bt.D^{{}^{\prime}t}\_{a|b}=f\_{b|a}\times D^{t}\_{b|a}+D^{t}\_{a|b}. |  | (10) |

#### Player-Rally Fusion.

The player-rally fusion aims at capturing the importance of player-player styles and rally interactions to predict each player’s next move.
To fuse these contexts, we first use the tt-th player-player styles da|bt′d^{{}^{\prime}t}\_{a|b} from Da|bt′D^{{}^{\prime}t}\_{a|b} and rally interactions in the last layer in the relational GCN za|bt⁡(ll​a​s​t)z^{t(l\_{last})}\_{a|b} of both players to determine the corresponding dynamic weights αa,αb,βa,βb\alpha\_{a},\alpha\_{b},\beta\_{a},\beta\_{b}:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | αa|b=sigmoid(wSdt′a|b),βa|b=sigmoid(wZzt⁡(ll​a​s​t)a|b),\begin{gathered}\alpha\_{a|b}=sigmoid(w^{S}d^{{}^{\prime}t}\_{a|b}),\beta\_{a|b}=sigmoid(w^{Z}z^{t(l\_{last})}\_{a|b}),\end{gathered} |  | (11) |

where wS,wZ∈ℝdew^{S},w^{Z}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\_{e}} are learnable parameters.

Afterwards, the propagated node embeddings e^at\hat{e}^{t}\_{a} and e^bt\hat{e}^{t}\_{b} are updated by:

|  |  |  |  |

|  | e^a|bt=αa|b×da|bt′+βa|b×za|bt⁡(ll​a​s​t).\displaystyle\hat{e}^{t}\_{a|b}=\alpha\_{a|b}\times d^{{}^{\prime}t}\_{a|b}+\beta\_{a|b}\times z^{t(l\_{last})}\_{a|b}. |  | (12) |

### 3.5 Movement Predictor

To predict the shot type at the tt-th time step (step 2 in the PM graph), the propagated node embeddings of both players at the tt-th time step are calculated as:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | s^t=Ws​(e^at−1∥e^bt),\hat{s}^{t}=W^{s}(\hat{e}^{t-1}\_{a}\mathbin{\|}\hat{e}^{t}\_{b}), |  | (13) |

where Ws∈ℝNt×2​deW^{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\_{t}\times 2d\_{e}} are learnable matrices, and NtN\_{t} is the number of shot types.
We note that the former term becomes e^bt−1\hat{e}^{t-1}\_{b} and the latter becomes e^at\hat{e}^{t}\_{a} when the number of the time step is odd, which switches the returning player and the defending player.

To predict the locations of the two players at the tt-th time step (step 4 in the PM graph), we follow ([Wang et al. 2022b](#bib.bib37)) to learn a bivariate Gaussian distribution for the location of each player.
Specifically, a bivariate Gaussian distribution consists of five parameters {μx,μy,σx,σy,ρ}\{\mu\_{x},\mu\_{y},\sigma\_{x},\sigma\_{y},\rho\}, which represent the mean of the 2D coordinates, the variance of the 2D coordinates, and the corresponding correlation coefficient.
We apply a linear layer to the concatenation of the propagated node embeddings of two players to predict two bivariate Gaussian distributions B​G^at\hat{BG}^{t}\_{a} and B​G^bt\hat{BG}^{t}\_{b} for both players:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {B​G^at,B​G^bt}=WB​G​(e^at∥e^bt),\{\hat{BG}^{t}\_{a},\hat{BG}^{t}\_{b}\}=W^{BG}(\hat{e}^{t}\_{a}\mathbin{\|}\hat{e}^{t}\_{b}), |  | (14) |

where WB​G∈ℝ10×2​deW^{BG}\in\mathbb{R}^{10\times 2d\_{e}}.
The dimension 10 is the total number of two five-parametric distributions.
The predicted coordinates of the t+1t+1 time step for each player Lat+1L^{t+1}\_{a} and Lbt+1L^{t+1}\_{b} are then sampled from 𝒩⁡(B​G^at)\mathcal{N}(\hat{BG}^{t}\_{a}) and 𝒩⁡(B​G^bt)\mathcal{N}(\hat{BG}^{t}\_{b}), respectively.

The objective function is to minimize the total loss ℒ\mathcal{L}:

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Experimental Settings

#### Badminton Dataset.

Since there is only one dataset of turn-based stroke records, we employ the badminton singles dataset ([Wang et al. 2022b](#bib.bib37)).
After filtering the rallies with any missing value, the badminton dataset has 75 matches played by 31 high-ranking players remaining, which contain 180 sets, 4,325 rallies, and 43,191 strokes.
Following ([Wang et al. 2022b](#bib.bib37)), we use the same 10 shot types, and the maximum rally lengths are truncated to 35.

For the task of movement forecasting, we utilize the rally id to separate rallies.
Each rally contains the ball round of each stroke, which consists of the players, their locations, and the shot type either of them performed.
The first 80% of rallies are split as training data and the last 20% as testing data for each match to have the model acquire each player’s previous information.

#### Baseline Methods.

As this task has yet to be addressed, there are no existing baselines for direct comparison.
Therefore, we examine our model with several state-of-the-art sequence prediction methods to verify its effectiveness.
Specifically, these baselines are categorized into two groups: Sequence-based models: 1) Seq2Seq ([Sutskever, Vinyals, and Le 2014](#bib.bib30)), 2) TF ([Giuliari et al. 2020](#bib.bib7)), and 3) ShuttleNet ([Wang et al. 2022b](#bib.bib37)). Graph-based models: 1) dNRI ([Graber and Schwing 2020](#bib.bib8)), 2) GCNPM ([Kipf and Welling 2017](#bib.bib12)), 3) R-GCNPM ([Schlichtkrull et al. 2018](#bib.bib25)), and 4) E-GCNPM ([Pareja et al. 2020](#bib.bib17)).
It is worth noting that we introduce three new variants of the graph-based approaches (GCNPM, R-GCNPM, and E-GCNPM) with encoder-decoder structures and the proposed PM graph for better exploring the performance of our proposed method.
More details and setups of baselines are given in Appendix B.

#### Parameter Settings.

The representation dimension (dl,dp,ded\_{l},d\_{p},d\_{e}) is set to 16 for all models.
The dropout rate for each module is 0.1, and the number of heads in TF and ShuttleNet is set to 2.
E-GCNPM, R-GCNPM, GCNPM and our model have two GNN layers.
The number of layers of TF is 1.
The activation function σ\sigma in R-GCNPM, GCNPM, E-GCNPM and our model applies ReLU at the first layer and Sigmoid at the second layer.
The normalized constants (aria^{i}\_{r}) for R-GCNPM and our model are set to 1 similar to ([Schlichtkrull et al. 2018](#bib.bib25)) and the number of basis matrices (BB) is 3.
The kernel size KK is set to 3 and the layer of LSTM is set to 1 in dynamic GCN.
We train all models for 100 epochs with the Adam optimizer, where batch size is set to 32 and learning rate is set to 0.001.
All the training and evaluation phases were conducted on a machine with Ubuntu 20.04, Intel i7-9700K 3.6GHz CPU, and Nvidia GTX 2070 8GB GPU, while the methods are implemented in Python 3.7 with the PyTorch 1.9.0.
5-fold cross-validation was conducted for tuning the hyper-parameters.

#### Evaluation Metrics.

Following ([Wang et al. 2022b](#bib.bib37)) for evaluating stochastic models, we generate 10 sequences for each rally and take the closest one as the final prediction for evaluation, and utilize mean square error (MSE) and mean absolute error (MAE) for the prediction of the locations of the two players, and cross-entropy (CE) for the prediction of shot type.
All the results are the average of 5 different random seeds.

To comprehensively evaluate the performance of each method, we perform experiments on three different observed stroke sequences τ=2\tau=2, 44, and 88.
We note that extensive ablation experiments are discussed in Appendix C.1.
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Performance Comparison ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Where Will Players Move Next? Dynamic Graphs and Hierarchical Fusion for Movement Forecasting in Badminton") reports the results of our proposed model and the baselines, which demonstrates that DyMF consistently surpasses all baselines in terms of all metrics and different observed lengths.
Quantitatively, the improvement in our model is up to 35.3% for MSE, 21.5% for MAE, and 24.3% for CE.
We summarize the observations as follows:

1) Seq2Seq and TF degenerate location performance (MSE and MAE) compared to GCNPM and R-GCNPM, which not only indicates that naive sequence-to-sequence methods fail to model structural information between locations, but also demonstrates the importance of applying the PM graph to capture the influence on the intent of movement.
2) dNRI hinders all performance more substantially, although dynamically modeling the relation between players, which implies that two same nodes for representing two players separately across time is insufficient for the movement forecasting task.
This again raises the need for using a PM graph with new location nodes to predict the next move of each player.
3) As ShuttleNet is designed for turn-based sequences and fusing different aspects according to different strokes, we can observe that it performs better predictions than both the sequence-based and graph-based baselines.
Nonetheless, the comparison of DyMF and ShuttleNet reveals the importance of considering the purpose of players’ movements.
Our proposed DyMF outperforms ShuttleNet for all scenarios, which is attributed to our interaction style extractors for modeling mutual interactions across time as well as the dynamic tactics based on the previous movement patterns, and the player-player fusion for integrating the styles of each player.
4) We note that E-GCNPM produces unfavorable performance, possibly due to the unstable states when there are only a few nodes in badminton rallies, and so is not suitable for this task.

### 4.3 Case Study

![Refer to caption](2211.12217v2/figures/case-study-different-defense.png)

The analysis of the players’ movements on the court can be viewed as understanding behaviors of players, where stroke forecasting ([Wang et al. 2022b](#bib.bib37)) only focuses on what types of strokes, and where to return to.
One potential technique to investigate this is to use statistical methods on historical records.
However, the occurrence of area coordinates is too sparse to be analyzed.
To that end, a paradigm is illustrated with DyMF to investigate the practicality of movement forecasting, and more cases are discussed in Appendix C.2.
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 Case Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Where Will Players Move Next? Dynamic Graphs and Hierarchical Fusion for Movement Forecasting in Badminton") shows a scenario where Player A takes a defense location toward the net after returning the lob (red 3) and moving back to the middle court (red 4).
In this case, we aim to change the defense location of the player to analyze the reaction of the opponent in different circumstances.
In the original defense location, Player B returns a net shot, which leaves Player A in a passive situation, and thus has fewer choices for returning the shuttle.
On the other hand, after changing the defense position, Player A is close to the net and makes Player B return a clear that enables Player A to launch an attack.
This verifies that the opponent returns the shuttle based on the defense location of the player; therefore, standing at an effective position blocks the choices and forces the opponent to return a predictable stroke.
With the help of DyMF providing likely strategies of returning shot types and moving towards a certain position on the court, badminton coaches and players are able to analyze opponents’ implicit tactics at the stroke-level, and train for specific scenarios.

## 5 Conclusion and Future Works

In this paper, we introduce the movement forecasting task, which plays a vital role in investigating offense and defense behaviors in sports analytics.
To address the problem, we represent badminton rallies with PM graphs to delve into the strategic structure based on the interrelations between players, and propose DyMF with interaction style extractors for extracting the mutual interactions across time and capturing the dynamic tactics based on the players’ past movement patterns.
Furthermore, the hierarchical fusions are designed to fuse mutual influence of players’ styles and the importance of individual style and interactions.
Extensive experiments on the real-world dataset empirically show the effectiveness of our proposed model compared to the baseline methods in different scenarios.
Besides, an analysis scenario is illustrated to show the practicality of movement forecasting.
For future research, we will extend DyMF to badminton doubles for movements investigation with greater concentration on the interactions between players.

## Appendix A Related Work

### A.1 Sports Analytics

Sports analytics aims at applying data-driven methods to a wide variety of sources of sports data for gaining insights into the tactics of teams and players.
The applications of sports analytics can be mainly divided into two categories: on-field analytics and off-field analytics.
On-field analytics focuses on improving the performance of a team or individual player by providing objective perspectives such as the fitness of players ([Rydzik and Ambroży 2021](#bib.bib23); [Ramirez-Campillo et al. 2021](#bib.bib20)), player performance ([Wang et al. 2020](#bib.bib38); [Jamil et al. 2021](#bib.bib10); [Terner and Franks 2021](#bib.bib31)), and the potential rising stars ([Mahmood, Daud, and Abbasi 2021](#bib.bib14)).
On the other hand, off-field analytics assists team owners in increasing profits by studying the relationship with fans ([Paek et al. 2021](#bib.bib16); [Yim et al. 2021](#bib.bib39); [Qian 2022](#bib.bib19)), and their marketing strategies ([Melton and MacCharles 2021](#bib.bib15); [Richelieu and Webb 2021](#bib.bib22)).
In this paper, we focus on on-field analytics for investigating the performance of players.
[Decroos et al. 2020](#bib.bib5) present five main issues around artificial intelligence in sports analytics:
representation, interpretability, decision making, understanding behavior, and experimental evaluation.
In badminton, there are only a few applications tackling these issues.
[Wang et al. 2021](#bib.bib35) formalized the badminton language for describing the process of a rally, which can be used for our inputs and outputs of movement forecasting (i.e., players, shot types, and locations).
ShuttleNet is proposed for stroke forecasting to simulate players’ strategies based on the past information ([Wang et al. 2022b](#bib.bib37)).
Our work introduces another instrumental but challenging application by predicting the next movements and the shot type of both players in a rally, which helps players investigate the effect and behavior of each movement.

### A.2 Graph Neural Networks

Graph neural networks are applied to leverage the structure of the data, e.g., molecules ([Gasteiger, Becker, and
Günnemann 2021](#bib.bib6)) and social networks ([Zhang et al. 2022](#bib.bib42)), to learn the representation of entities based on neighborhood properties.
Typically, a graph is composed of nodes and edges, which is different from sequences like sentences in natural language.
In addition to learning node embeddings solely on the homogeneous graph structure ([Kipf and Welling 2017](#bib.bib12)), graph neural networks have been explored for various types of graphs by considering different relations between nodes ([Schlichtkrull et al. 2018](#bib.bib25)), temporal information ([Si et al. 2019](#bib.bib28); [Pareja et al. 2020](#bib.bib17)), and heterogeneous graphs learning (which have multiple types of nodes and edges) ([Zhang et al. 2021](#bib.bib41)).
In trajectory prediction, NRI ([Kipf et al. 2018](#bib.bib11)) infers the underlying relation with static assumption between entities, and predicts the future location by applying graph neural networks.
dNRI ([Graber and Schwing 2020](#bib.bib8)) dynamically models the relations for each time step by extending the NRI framework to address changing relations between entities.
However, these previous approaches failed to model multifaceted interactions between players and players themselves at different time steps.
Our novel approach, in contrast to the existing methods, develops an interaction style extractor to capture mutual interactions through strategic relations and hierarchical fusion to fuse multifaceted interactions.

## Appendix B Details and Setups of Baselines

### B.1 Baselines

The details of the baseline methods are depicted as follows:

Sequence-based models:

Seq2Seq ([Sutskever, Vinyals, and Le 2014](#bib.bib30)) uses two LSTMs as encoder and decoder to enable different output lengths from the input lengths for machine translation.

TF ([Giuliari et al. 2020](#bib.bib7)) extends Transformers ([Vaswani et al. 2017](#bib.bib33)) to trajectory prediction, which models the pedestrian individually without auxiliary interaction with the environment.

ShuttleNet ([Wang et al. 2022b](#bib.bib37)) fuses the contexts of rally progress and player styles extracted by Transformer-based models to predict where to hit and which shot type it is.

Graph-based models:

dNRI ([Graber and Schwing 2020](#bib.bib8)) dynamically models the relation between entities that changes over time for trajectory prediction.

GCNPM is a variant of GCN ([Kipf and Welling 2017](#bib.bib12)), which generates the embedding of entities in a graph by aggregating the information from neighbors.

R-GCNPM is a variant of R-GCN ([Schlichtkrull et al. 2018](#bib.bib25)), which learns the embedding of entities in a multi-graph by aggregating the message from neighbors based on the relations.

E-GCNPM is a variant of EvolveGCN ([Pareja et al. 2020](#bib.bib17)), which extends GCN from updating the weights of GCN using recurrent neural networks to model the dynamism of the graph.

### B.2 Implementation Details

In graph-based models, we regard the shot types as the edges between nodes, and the nodes represent the locations of each player for constructing a PM graph33
3
We note that dNRI is not implemented with the PM graph since the number of entities in dNRI would not change over time..
We concatenate the shot type and locations of both players at each time step as the inputs for representing the current information, and take a rally as a sequence to sequence-based models.

### B.3 Hyper-parameters Settings

Table [2](#A2.T2 "Table 2 ‣ B.3 Hyper-parameters Settings ‣ Appendix B Details and Setups of Baselines ‣ Where Will Players Move Next? Dynamic Graphs and Hierarchical Fusion for Movement Forecasting in Badminton") summarizes the details of the hyper-parameters.
The hyper-parameters were searched by conducting 5-fold cross-validation.
The batch size was chosen from {16, 32, 48, 64} and the dimension of embeddings (dl,dp,ded\_{l},d\_{p},d\_{e}) was chosen from {4, 16, 32}.
The number of layers (ll) was chosen from {1, 2, 3} and the number of basis matrices (BB) was chosen from {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}.
The dropout rate was chosen from {0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3}.

This is a research paper (arXiv) introducing DyMF (Dynamic Graphs and Hierarchical Fusion for Movement Forecasting), the first work to address movement forecasting in badminton and other turn-based sports like tennis. The paper formalizes the task of predicting players' future movements and shot types based on previous strokes in a rally.

**Core Contributions:**
1. First formalization of movement forecasting in badminton, predicting players' future locations and shot types
2. Introduction of the Player Movements (PM) graph, which transforms rallies into graphs with strategic relations between players' locations using 12 relation types (10 shot types: net shot, lob, defensive shot, smash, drop, push/rush, short service, clear, drive, long service; plus "defend" and "return" edge types)
3. A novel DyMF model using an encoder-decoder architecture with interaction style extractors (relational GCN + dynamic GCN) and hierarchical fusions (player-player fusion via parallel co-attention, and player-rally fusion)
4. Extensive experiments showing state-of-the-art performance on a real-world badminton dataset

**Methodology:**
- Movement forecasting is formulated as a sequence prediction task: given observed stroke sequence of length τ, predict future strokes including both players' locations and shot types
- PM graph construction: nodes represent player locations at each time step; edges represent 12 strategic relations
- Interaction Style Extractor uses Relational GCN (inspired by R-GCN) for interactions between players and Dynamic GCN with LSTM-based pattern-generated weights for dynamic personal tactics
- Hierarchical Fusion combines player styles (via parallel co-attention) with rally interactions using sigmoid-based dynamic weights
- Movement predictor outputs shot types via cross-entropy and locations via bivariate Gaussian distributions
- Total loss = shot type cross-entropy + 0.5×location loss per player

**Experimental Results:**
- Dataset: 75 badminton singles matches, 31 players, 180 sets, 4,325 rallies, 43,191 strokes; 80/20 train/test split
- Baselines: Seq2Seq, TF (Transformer), ShuttleNet (sequence-based); dNRI, GCNPM, R-GCNPM, E-GCNPM (graph-based)
- DyMF outperforms all baselines across all metrics (MSE, MAE for locations; CE for shot type) at observation lengths τ=2, 4, and 8
- Improvements up to 35.3% for MSE, 21.5% for MAE, and 24.3% for CE
- Key findings: naive sequence models fail on structural info; dNRI insufficient due to lack of new location nodes; E-GCNPM unstable with few graph nodes; DyMF surpasses ShuttleNet due to modeling movement purposes and dynamic tactics

**Case Study:** Demonstrated that changing a player's defense position alters the opponent's returned shot (e.g., standing close to net forces opponent to clear, enabling an attack), verifying that opponents respond to player defense locations and that effective positioning limits opponent options.

**Future Work:** Extend DyMF to badminton doubles with greater focus on inter-player interactions. Supported by Taiwan's Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST-110-2627-H-A49-001). Code available at https://github.com/wywyWang/CoachAI-Projects/tree/main/Movement%20Forecasting.
args.key_excerpts: "we first introduce the procedure of the Player Movements (PM) graph to exploit the structural movements of players with strategic relations. Based on the PM graph, we propose a novel Dynamic Graphs and Hierarchical Fusion for Movement Forecasting model (DyMF) with interaction style extractors to capture the mutual interactions of players themselves and between both players within a rally, and dynamic players' tactics across time."

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Computer vision system

For other uses, see [Hawkeye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawkeye_(disambiguation) "Hawkeye (disambiguation)").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/Kremlin_Cup_2012_-_Hawk-Eye_cam.JPG/250px-Kremlin_Cup_2012_-_Hawk-Eye_cam.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kremlin_Cup_2012_-_Hawk-Eye_cam.JPG)

Hawk-Eye camera system at the [Kremlin Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kremlin_Cup "Kremlin Cup") tennis tournament on 20 October 2012, Moscow

**Hawk-Eye** is a [computer vision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_vision "Computer vision") system used to visually track the trajectory of a ball and display a profile of its statistically most likely path as a moving image.[[1]](#cite_note-1) It is used in more than 20 major sports, including [baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball "Baseball"), [cricket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cricket "Cricket"), [tennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennis "Tennis"), [badminton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badminton "Badminton"), [hurling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurling "Hurling"), [rugby union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_union "Rugby union"), [soccer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soccer "Soccer"), [Gaelic football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaelic_football "Gaelic football"), [American football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_football "American football"), and [volleyball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volleyball "Volleyball").[[2]](#cite_note-Boyo-2)

The [Sony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony "Sony")-owned Hawk-Eye system was originally developed in the United Kingdom by [Paul Hawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Hawkins_(mathematician) "Paul Hawkins (mathematician)"). The system was first implemented in 2001 for television broadcasts, where it was used to analyze [leg before wicket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leg_before_wicket "Leg before wicket") decisions in cricket.[[3]](#cite_note-3) It works via the use of up to ten high-performance cameras, normally positioned on the underside of the stadium roof, which track the ball from different angles.[[4]](#cite_note-4) The video from the cameras is then [triangulated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangulation "Triangulation") and combined to create a three-dimensional representation of the ball's trajectory. Although not infallible, Hawk-Eye is advertised to be accurate to within 2.6 mm (100 thou).[[5]](#cite_note-5)

Hawk-Eye is increasingly used as an impartial review in sports, having been accepted by governing bodies in tennis, cricket, and association football (soccer) as a means of adjudication. Hawk-Eye has been used for the Challenge System since 2006 in tennis and [Decision Review System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decision_Review_System "Decision Review System") in cricket since 2009. The system is also used to determine whether the ball has crossed the goal line in football as a means of [goal-line technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goal-line_technology "Goal-line technology"), implemented in the [2013–14 Premier League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013–14_Premier_League "2013–14 Premier League") season and now present at many domestic leagues and international competitions.

## Method of operation

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Hawk-Eye&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Method of operation")]

All Hawk-Eye systems are based on the principles of [triangulation using visual images](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangulation_(computer_vision) "Triangulation (computer vision)") and timing data provided by a number of high-speed video cameras located at different locations and angles around the area of play.[[6]](#cite_note-espacenet-6) For tennis there are 10 cameras. The system rapidly processes the video feeds from the cameras and ball tracker. A data store contains a predefined model of the playing area and includes data on the rules of the game.

In each frame sent from each camera, the system identifies the group of pixels which corresponds to the image of the ball. It then calculates for each frame the position of the ball by comparing its position on at least two of the physically separate cameras at the same instant in time. A succession of frames builds up a record of the path along which the ball has travelled. It also "predicts" the future flight path of the ball and where it will interact with any of the playing area features already programmed into the database. The system can also interpret these interactions to decide infringements of the rules of the game.[[6]](#cite_note-espacenet-6)

The system generates a graphic image of the ball path and playing area, which means that information can be provided to judges, television viewers or coaching staff in near real-time.

The tracking system is combined with a back-end database and archiving capabilities so that it is possible to extract and analyse trends and statistics about individual players, games, ball-to-ball comparisons, etc.

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Hawk-Eye&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

Hawk-Eye was developed in 2000 by engineers at [Roke Manor Research Limited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roke_Manor_Research_Limited "Roke Manor Research Limited"), then a [Siemens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siemens "Siemens") subsidiary in [Romsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romsey "Romsey"), England. Paul Hawkins and David Sherry submitted a United Kingdom patent application for the technology, but this was subsequently withdrawn.[[6]](#cite_note-espacenet-6) All of the technology and intellectual property was spun off into a separate company, Hawk-Eye Innovations Ltd, based in [Winchester, Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winchester,_Hampshire "Winchester, Hampshire"). This was initially established as a joint venture between Roke Manor Research and [Sunset + Vine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tinopolis#Operations "Tinopolis").[[7]](#cite_note-TinoplisInterim2006-7) At the time, Sunset + Vine produced the [Channel 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channel_4 "Channel 4") television cricket coverage where Hawk-Eye was first used.

On 14 June 2006 a group of investors—led by the [Wisden Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisden_Group "Wisden Group") and that included [Mark Getty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Getty "Mark Getty"), a member of the wealthy American family and business dynasty—bought the company for £4.4m.[[7]](#cite_note-TinoplisInterim2006-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8) The acquisition was intended to strengthen Wisden's presence in cricket and allow it to enter tennis and other international sports, with Hawk-Eye working on implementing a system for basketball. According to Hawk-Eye's website, the system produces much more data than that shown on television.

Put up for sale in September 2010, it was sold as a complete entity to Japanese electronic giant [Sony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony "Sony") in March 2011 in a deal that valued the company at £15m-£20m.[[9]](#cite_note-BBC12670063-9)[[10]](#cite_note-about-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11)

## Deployment in sport

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Hawk-Eye&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Deployment in sport")]

### Cricket

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Hawk-Eye&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Cricket")]

Main article: [Umpire Decision Review System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umpire_Decision_Review_System "Umpire Decision Review System")

The technology was first used by [Channel 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channel_4 "Channel 4") during a [Test match](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Test_cricket "Test cricket") between [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_cricket_team "England cricket team") and [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_national_cricket_team "Pakistan national cricket team") on [Lord's Cricket Ground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord's_Cricket_Ground "Lord's Cricket Ground"), on 21 May 2001. It is used by the majority of television networks to track the trajectory of balls in flight. Its major use in cricket broadcasting is in analysing [leg before wicket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leg_before_wicket "Leg before wicket") (LBW) decisions, where the likely path of the ball can be projected forward, through the [batsman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batsman "Batsman")'s legs, to see if it would have hit the [stumps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stump_(cricket) "Stump (cricket)").

In the winter season of 2008/2009 the [ICC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Cricket_Council "International Cricket Council") trialled a referral system where Hawk-Eye was used for referring decisions to the third umpire if a team disagreed with an LBW decision. Initially the third umpire was able to look at what the ball actually did up to the point when it hit the batsman, but could not look at the predicted flight of the ball after it hit the batsman.[[12]](#cite_note-12) The third umpire is now able to see the projected path of the ball too, and Hawk-Eye is currently sanctioned in international cricket even though some doubts remain about its accuracy.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

When an LBW decision is referred to Hawk-Eye, it assists in assessing against three criteria:

* Where the ball pitched (in particular with respect to the stumps)
* The location of impact on the leg of the batsman (in particular with respect to the stumps)
* The projected path of the ball past the batsman

In all three cases, marginal calls result in the on-field umpire's call being maintained.

Due to its real-time coverage of bowling speed, the system is also used to show delivery patterns of a bowler's behaviour such as [line and length](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowling_(cricket)#Line_and_length "Bowling (cricket)"), or [swing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_bowling "Swing bowling")/turn information. At the end of an [over](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Over_(cricket) "Over (cricket)"), all six deliveries are often shown simultaneously to illustrate a bowler's variations, such as slower deliveries, bouncers and leg-cutters. A complete record of a bowler can also be shown over the course of a match.

Batsmen also benefit from the analysis of Hawk-Eye, as a record can be brought up of the deliveries from which a batsman scored. These are often shown as a 2-D silhouetted figure of a batsman and colour-coded dots of the balls faced by the batsman. Information such as the exact spot where the ball pitches or speed of the ball from the bowler's hand (to gauge batsman reaction time) can also help in post-match analysis.

### Tennis

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Hawk-Eye&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Tennis")]

:   *For a history of electronic line calling in tennis, see [Electronic line judge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_line_judge "Electronic line judge")*

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/Hawk-Eye_at_Wimbledon_%287508887344%29.jpg/250px-Hawk-Eye_at_Wimbledon_%287508887344%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hawk-Eye_at_Wimbledon_(7508887344).jpg)

Hawk-Eye decision shown on the big screen at Wimbledon.

In [Serena Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serena_Williams "Serena Williams")'s quarter final loss to [Jennifer Capriati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Capriati "Jennifer Capriati") at the [2004 US Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_US_Open_–_Women's_singles "2004 US Open – Women's singles"), three line calls went against Williams in the final set (an Auto-Ref system was being tested during the match). Though the calls were not reversed, there was one overrule of a clearly incorrect line umpire call, by the chair umpire [Mariana Alves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Alves "Mariana Alves"), that the TV replay showed to be good. These errors prompted talks about line calling assistance especially as the Auto-Ref system was being tested by the U.S. Open at that time and was shown to be very accurate.[[14]](#cite_note-14)

In late 2006 Hawk-Eye was tested by the [International Tennis Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Tennis_Federation "International Tennis Federation") (ITF) in New York City and was passed for professional use. Hawk-Eye reported that the New York tests involved 80 shots being measured by the ITF's high speed camera, a device similar to MacCAM. During an early test of the system at an exhibition tennis tournament in Australia (seen on local TV), there was an instance when the tennis ball was shown as "Out", but the accompanying word was "In".[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] This was explained to be an error in the way the tennis ball was shown on the graphical display as a circle, rather than as an ellipse.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] This was immediately corrected.

Hawk-Eye has been used in television coverage of several major tennis tournaments, including [Wimbledon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Championships,_Wimbledon "The Championships, Wimbledon"), the [Queen's Club Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen's_Club_Championships "Queen's Club Championships"), the Australian Open, the [Davis Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davis_Cup "Davis Cup") and the [Tennis Masters Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennis_Masters_Cup "Tennis Masters Cup"). The [US Open Tennis Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Open_(tennis) "US Open (tennis)") announced they would make official use of the technology for the [2006 US Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_US_Open_(tennis) "2006 US Open (tennis)") where each player receives two challenges per set.[[15]](#cite_note-15) It is also used as part of a larger tennis simulation implemented by [IBM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM "IBM") called PointTracker.

The [2006 Hopman Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Hopman_Cup "2006 Hopman Cup") in [Perth, Western Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perth,_Western_Australia "Perth, Western Australia"), was the first elite-level tennis tournament where players were allowed to challenge point-ending line calls, which were then reviewed by the referees using Hawk-Eye technology. It used 10 cameras feeding information about ball position to the computers. [Jamea Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamea_Jackson "Jamea Jackson") was the first player to challenge a call using the system.

In March 2006, at the [Nasdaq-100 Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_NASDAQ-100_Open "2006 NASDAQ-100 Open") in [Key Biscayne, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Key_Biscayne,_Florida "Key Biscayne, Florida"), Hawk-Eye was used officially for the first time at a tennis tour event. Later that year, the [US Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_US_Open_(tennis) "2006 US Open (tennis)") became the first grand-slam tournament to use the system during play, allowing players to challenge line calls.[[16]](#cite_note-16)

The [2007 Australian Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Australian_Open "2007 Australian Open") was the next grand-slam event to implement Hawk-Eye in challenges to line calls, where each tennis player in Rod Laver Arena was allowed two incorrect challenges per set and one additional challenge should a tiebreak be played. In the event of an advantage final set, challenges were reset to two for each player every 12 games, i.e. 6-all, 12-all, etc. Controversies followed the event as at times Hawk-Eye produced erroneous output. In 2008, tennis players were allowed three incorrect challenges per set instead. Any leftover challenges did not carry over to the next set. Once, [Amélie Mauresmo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amélie_Mauresmo "Amélie Mauresmo") challenged a ball that was called in, and Hawk-Eye showed the ball was out by less than a millimetre, but the call was allowed to stand. As a result, the point was replayed and Mauresmo did not lose an incorrect challenge.

The Hawk-Eye technology used in the [2007 Dubai Tennis Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Dubai_Tennis_Championships "2007 Dubai Tennis Championships") had some minor controversies. Defending champion Rafael Nadal accused the system of incorrectly declaring an out ball to be in following his exit. The umpire had called a ball out; when [Mikhail Youzhny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikhail_Youzhny "Mikhail Youzhny") challenged the decision, Hawk-Eye said it was in by 3 mm.[[17]](#cite_note-17) Youzhny said after that he himself thought the mark may have been wide but then offered that this kind of technology error could easily have been made by linesmen and umpires. Nadal could only shrug, saying that had this system been on clay, the mark would have clearly shown Hawk-Eye to be wrong.[[18]](#cite_note-Archive.gulfnews.com-18)

The [2007 Wimbledon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Wimbledon_Championships "2007 Wimbledon Championships") also implemented the Hawk-Eye system as an officiating aid on [Centre Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_Court "Centre Court") and Court 1, and each tennis player was allowed three incorrect challenges per set. If the set produced a tiebreak, each player was given an additional challenge. Additionally, in the event of a final set (third set in women's or mixed matches, fifth set in men's matches), where there is no tiebreak, each player's number of challenges was reset to three if the game score reached 6–6, and again at 12–12. [Teymuraz Gabashvili](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teymuraz_Gabashvili "Teymuraz Gabashvili"), in his first round match against [Roger Federer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Federer "Roger Federer"), made the first-ever Hawk-Eye challenge on Centre Court. Additionally, during the finals of Federer against [Rafael Nadal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafael_Nadal "Rafael Nadal"), Nadal challenged a shot which was called out. Hawk-Eye showed the ball as in, just clipping the line. The reversal agitated Federer enough for him to request (unsuccessfully) that the umpire turn off the Hawk-Eye technology for the remainder of the match.[[19]](#cite_note-19)

In the [2009 Australian Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_Australian_Open "2009 Australian Open") fourth round match between Roger Federer and [Tomáš Berdych](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomáš_Berdych "Tomáš Berdych"), Berdych challenged an out call. The Hawk-Eye system was not available when he challenged, likely due to a particularly pronounced shadow on the court. As a result, the original call stood.[[20]](#cite_note-20)

In the [2009 Indian Wells Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_Indian_Wells_Masters "2009 Indian Wells Masters") quarterfinals match between [Ivan Ljubičić](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Ljubičić "Ivan Ljubičić") and [Andy Murray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Murray "Andy Murray"), Murray challenged an out call. The Hawk-Eye system indicated that the ball landed on the centre of the line despite instant replay images showing that the ball was clearly out. It was later revealed that the Hawk-Eye system had mistakenly picked up the second bounce, which was on the line, instead of the first bounce of the ball.[[21]](#cite_note-21) Immediately after the match, Murray apologised to Ljubicic for the call, and acknowledged that the point was out.

The Hawk-Eye system was developed as a replay system, originally for TV broadcast coverage. As such, it initially could not call ins and outs live.The representation of the trajectory results in terms of where the ball lands is called **Shot Spot**.[[22]](#cite_note-22)

The Hawk-Eye Innovations website[[23]](#cite_note-23) states that the system performs with an average error of 3.6 mm. The standard diameter of a tennis ball is 67 mm, equating to a 5% error relative to ball diameter. This is roughly equivalent to the fluff on the ball.

Hawk-Eye has developed a technology called 'Hawk-Eye Live', which uses the 10 cameras to call shots in or out in real time, with an 'out' call being signified by a speaker emitting an 'out' sound that emulates a human line judge. The technology was initially expected to be in place for the 2019 US Open. The [2021 Australian Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Australian_Open "2021 Australian Open") was the first Grand Slam tournament to use Hawk-Eye Live for all matches in place of line judges, in part to reduce personnel during the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), followed by the US Open later that year. Previously, the 2020 US Open used Hawk-Eye in place of line judges for all matches except those held at [Arthur Ashe Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Ashe_Stadium "Arthur Ashe Stadium") and [Louis Armstrong Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Armstrong_Stadium "Louis Armstrong Stadium").[[24]](#cite_note-24)

Clay court tournaments, notably the [French Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Open "French Open"), are generally free of Hawk-Eye technology due to marks left on the clay where the ball bounced to evidence a disputed line call. Chair umpires are then required to get out of their seat and examine the mark on court with the player by their side to discuss the chair umpire's decision.[[25]](#cite_note-25) The [2021 Mutua Madrid Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Mutua_Madrid_Open "2021 Mutua Madrid Open") became the first major tournament on clay to use an electronic system to check the bounce of the ball on the court when in doubt in the two main stadiums (Manolo Santana Stadium and Arantxa Sánchez Vicario Stadium at [Caja Mágica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caja_Mágica "Caja Mágica")).[[26]](#cite_note-26) The system was developed by FoxTenn, a Spanish company located in [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona"). It uses real images of the ball captured by 40 cameras located at ground level, synchronized with lasers and working at up to 3,000 images per second to determine whether it has bounced in or out of the court's limits.[[27]](#cite_note-27) This system was previously used at the [2020 Rio Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Rio_Open "2020 Rio Open") in [Rio de Janeiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro "Rio de Janeiro") and at the [2021 MUSC Health Women's Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_MUSC_Health_Women's_Open "2021 MUSC Health Women's Open") in [Charleston, South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charleston,_South_Carolina "Charleston, South Carolina").

#### Unification of rules

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Hawk-Eye&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Unification of rules")]

Until March 2008, the International Tennis Federation (ITF), [Association of Tennis Professionals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Tennis_Professionals "Association of Tennis Professionals") (ATP), [Women's Tennis Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_Tennis_Association "Women's Tennis Association") (WTA), [Grand Slam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Slam_(tennis) "Grand Slam (tennis)") Committee, and several individual tournaments had conflicting rules on how Hawk-Eye was to be utilised. A key example of this was the number of challenges a player was permitted per set, which varied among events.[[28]](#cite_note-tind1-28) Some tournaments allowed players a greater margin for error, with players allowed an unlimited numbers of challenges over the course of a match.[[28]](#cite_note-tind1-28) In other tournaments players received two or three per set.[[28]](#cite_note-tind1-28) On 19 March 2008, the aforementioned organizing bodies announced a uniform system of rules: three unsuccessful challenges per set, with an additional challenge if the set reaches a tiebreak. In an advantage set (a set with no tiebreak) players are allowed three unsuccessful challenges every 12 games. The next scheduled event on the men and women's tour, the [2008 Sony Ericsson Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Sony_Ericsson_Open "2008 Sony Ericsson Open"), was the first event to implement these new, standardized rules.[[29]](#cite_note-29)

#### Replacement of human line judges

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Hawk-Eye&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Replacement of human line judges")]

Since 2021 the Australian Open has used Hawk-Eye to call lines in all games.[[30]](#cite_note-30) The US Open replaced line judges with full electronic line calls in 2022.[[2]](#cite_note-Boyo-2) On 9 October 2024 the [All-England Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-England_Club "All-England Club") announced that electronic line calling would replace human line judges full-time at Wimbledon starting in [2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Wimbledon_Championships "2025 Wimbledon Championships").[[31]](#cite_note-31)

### Association football

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Hawk-Eye&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Association football")]

Main article: [Goal-line technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goal-line_technology "Goal-line technology")

Hawk-Eye is one of the [goal-line technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goal-line_technology "Goal-line technology") (GLT) systems authorised by [FIFA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA "FIFA"). Hawk-Eye tracks the ball, and informs the [referee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Referee_(association_football) "Referee (association football)") if a ball fully crosses the goal line into the [goal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_pitch#Goals "Football pitch"). The purpose of the system is to eliminate errors in assessing if a [goal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scoring_in_association_football "Scoring in association football") was scored. The Hawk-Eye system was one of the systems trialled by the sport's governors prior to the 2012 change to the [Laws of the Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laws_of_the_Game_(association_football) "Laws of the Game (association football)") that made GLT a permanent part of the game,[[32]](#cite_note-March_2012_IFAB/FIFA-32) and it has been used in various competitions since then. GLT is not compulsory and, owing to the cost of Hawk-Eye and its competitors, systems are only deployed in a few high-level competitions.

As of July 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hawk-Eye&action=edit), licensed Hawk-Eye systems were installed at 96 stadiums. By number of installations, Hawk-Eye is the most popular GLT system.[[33]](#cite_note-33) Hawk-Eye is the system used in the [Premier League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_League "Premier League"),[[34]](#cite_note-BBC_Premier-34) [Serie A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serie_A "Serie A")[[35]](#cite_note-35) and [Bundesliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bundesliga "Bundesliga")[[36]](#cite_note-36) among other leagues.

### Snooker

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Hawk-Eye&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Snooker")]

|  |
| --- |
| Parts of this article (those related to snooker) need to be **updated**. Please help update this article to reflect recent events or newly available information. *(December 2014)* |

At the [2007 World Snooker Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_World_Snooker_Championship "2007 World Snooker Championship"), the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC") used Hawk-Eye for the first time in its television coverage to show player views, particularly of potential snookers.[[37]](#cite_note-37) It has also been used to demonstrate intended shots by players when the actual shot has gone awry. It is now used by the BBC at every World Championship, as well as some other major tournaments. The BBC used to use the system sporadically, for instance in the 2009 Masters at Wembley the Hawk-Eye was at most used once or twice per frame.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

After introduction, its usage on BBC events decreased significantly and, for a period of time, was only used within the World Championships, before being removed after 2015. In contrast to tennis, Hawk-Eye is never used in snooker to assist referees' decisions and primarily used to assist viewers in showing what the player is facing.

Hawk-Eye, or a derivative of it, is now only used on the [World Snooker Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Snooker_Tour "World Snooker Tour") for events played in China, where the technology has evolved from a television aid for showing the distance of a long pot, to being used to support referees in replacing balls to millimetre precision after a “foul-and-a-miss”. This technology has been repeatedly praised by players and commentators for speeding up the ball replacement process, but its cost is referenced as a reason for the technology not being used across all tournaments: unlike tennis, the use of technology like this is not mandated by the tour administrators, being an aid provided by the television broadcaster which is often restricted to the televised table.

### Gaelic games

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Hawk-Eye&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Gaelic games")]

In Ireland, Hawk-Eye was introduced for all championship matches at [Croke Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Croke_Park "Croke Park") in [Dublin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin "Dublin") in 2013. This followed consideration by the [Gaelic Athletic Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaelic_Athletic_Association "Gaelic Athletic Association") (GAA) for its use in [Gaelic football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaelic_football "Gaelic football") and [hurling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurling "Hurling"). A trial took place at Croke Park on 2 April 2011. The double-header featured football between [Dublin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin_county_football_team "Dublin county football team") and [Down](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Down_county_football_team "Down county football team") and hurling between [Dublin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin_county_hurling_team "Dublin county hurling team") and [Kilkenny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilkenny_county_hurling_team "Kilkenny county hurling team"). Over the previous two seasons there had been many calls for the technology to be adopted, especially from Kildare fans, who saw two high-profile decisions go against their team in important games. The GAA said it would review the issue after the 2013 [Sam Maguire Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Maguire_Cup "Sam Maguire Cup") was presented.[[38]](#cite_note-38)

Hawk-Eye's use was intended to eliminate contentious scores.[[39]](#cite_note-39) Its first use in the championship came on Saturday 1 June 2013 for the [Kildare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kildare_county_football_team "Kildare county football team") v [Offaly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offaly_county_football_team "Offaly county football team") game, part of a double header with a second game of [Dublin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin_county_football_team "Dublin county football team") v [Westmeath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westmeath_county_football_team "Westmeath county football team").[[40]](#cite_note-40) Hawk-Eye determined that Offaly substitute [Peter Cunningham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Cunningham_(Gaelic_footballer)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Peter Cunningham (Gaelic footballer) (page does not exist)")'s attempted point had gone wide 10 minutes into the second half.[[41]](#cite_note-41)

Use of Hawk-Eye was suspended during the [2013 All-Ireland SHC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_All-Ireland_Senior_Hurling_Championship "2013 All-Ireland Senior Hurling Championship") semi-finals on 18 August due to a human error during a minor (under-18) hurling game between Limerick and Galway.[[42]](#cite_note-rte_error_at_croke_park-42) During the minor game, Hawk-Eye ruled a point for Limerick as a miss although the graphic showed the ball passing inside the posts, causing confusion around the stadium – the referee ultimately waved the valid point wide provoking anger from fans, viewers and TV analysts covering the game live.[[43]](#cite_note-43) The system was subsequently stood down for the senior game which followed, owing to "an inconsistency in the generation of a graphic".[[44]](#cite_note-44) Limerick, who were narrowly defeated after extra-time, announced they would be appealing over Hawk-Eye's costly failure.[[42]](#cite_note-rte_error_at_croke_park-42) Hawk-Eye apologised for this incident and admitted that it was a result of human error.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] The incident drew attention from the UK, where Hawk-Eye had made its debut in English football's [Premier League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_League "Premier League") the day before.[[45]](#cite_note-reuters_limerick_hurling_blunder-45)

Hawk-Eye was introduced to a second venue, [Semple Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semple_Stadium "Semple Stadium"), Thurles, in 2016. There is no TV screen at Semple: instead, an electronic screen displays a green *Tá* if a score has been made, and a red *Níl* if the shot is wide.[[46]](#cite_note-46) It was used at a third venue, [Páirc Uí Chaoimh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Páirc_Uí_Chaoimh "Páirc Uí Chaoimh"), Cork, in July 2017, for the All-Ireland SHC quarter-finals between [Clare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clare_county_hurling_team "Clare county hurling team") versus [Tipperary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tipperary_county_hurling_team "Tipperary county hurling team") and [Wexford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wexford_county_hurling_team "Wexford county hurling team") versus [Waterford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waterford_county_hurling_team "Waterford county hurling team").[[47]](#cite_note-47)

Hawk-Eye was at the centre of several contentious decisions during the first half of the first [2022 All-Ireland SFC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_All-Ireland_Senior_Football_Championship "2022 All-Ireland Senior Football Championship") semi-final between [Derry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derry_county_football_team "Derry county football team") and [Galway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galway_county_football_team "Galway county football team"). [This led to its suspension for the second half of that game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_All-Ireland_Senior_Football_Championship#Hawk-Eye_malfunction "2022 All-Ireland Senior Football Championship"), the referee being forced to alter the score and, later, Hawk-Eye's suspension for the second All-Ireland SFC semi-final between Dublin and [Kerry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerry_county_football_team "Kerry county football team").[[48]](#cite_note-48)[[49]](#cite_note-49)[[50]](#cite_note-50) The GAA confirmed on 15 July that Hawk-Eye would return for the [All-Ireland SHC final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_All-Ireland_Senior_Hurling_Championship_Final "2022 All-Ireland Senior Hurling Championship Final"), following comprehensive testing and a full review of the score detection technology.[[51]](#cite_note-51)

Hawk-Eye malfunctioned again during the [2023 All-Ireland SFC quarter-final clash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_All-Ireland_Senior_Football_Championship#Quarter-finals_5 "2023 All-Ireland Senior Football Championship") between [Armagh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armagh_county_football_team "Armagh county football team") and [Monaghan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaghan_county_football_team "Monaghan county football team") after it returned a "data unavailable" message.[[52]](#cite_note-52) The GAA requested an explanation from Hawk-Eye who concluded that the message was a result of operator error.[[53]](#cite_note-53) The next day the GAA took the decision to stand down Hawk-Eye once again.[[54]](#cite_note-54)

No official [Irish-language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish-language "Irish-language") term exists, although some publications have used the direct translation *Súil an tSeabhaic*.[[55]](#cite_note-55)[[56]](#cite_note-56)[[57]](#cite_note-57)

### Australian football

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Hawk-Eye&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Australian football")]

On 4 July 2013, the Australian Football League announced that they would be testing Hawk Eye technology to be used in the Score Review process. Hawk Eye was used for all matches played at the MCG during Round 15 of the 2013 AFL Season. The AFL also announced that Hawk Eye was only being tested, and would not be used in any Score Reviews during the round.

### Badminton

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Hawk-Eye&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Badminton")]

BWF introduced Hawk-Eye technology in 2014 after testing other instant review technologies for line call decision in BWF major events.[[58]](#cite_note-58) Hawk-Eye's tracking cameras are also used to provide shuttlecock speed and other insight in badminton matches.[[59]](#cite_note-59) Hawk-Eye was formally introduced in [2014 India Super Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_India_Super_Series "2014 India Super Series") tournament.

### Gridiron football

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Hawk-Eye&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Gridiron football")]

The [National Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League "National Football League") adopted Hawk-Eye for virtual on-field measurements beginning in the [2025 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_NFL_season "2025 NFL season").[[60]](#cite_note-60)[[61]](#cite_note-61)

### Baseball

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Hawk-Eye&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Baseball")]

Main article: [Automated Ball-Strike System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automated_Ball-Strike_System "Automated Ball-Strike System")

Hawk-Eye is used to automatically call [balls and strikes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strike_zone "Strike zone") (either in conjunction with, or in lieu of, a human [umpire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umpire_(baseball) "Umpire (baseball)")) in professional [baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball "Baseball") leagues in the U.S. and South Korea.[[62]](#cite_note-:0-62)[[63]](#cite_note-63)[[64]](#cite_note-64) In the U.S., the system began use in [Major League Baseball (MLB)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_League_Baseball "Major League Baseball") for the [2026 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Major_League_Baseball_season "2026 Major League Baseball season"), having been previously tested in [Minor League Baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minor_League_Baseball "Minor League Baseball") since 2019.[[62]](#cite_note-:0-62)[[65]](#cite_note-mlb-2026-65) Hawk-Eye has also been used for [instant replay reviews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instant_replay_in_Major_League_Baseball "Instant replay in Major League Baseball") in MLB since the [2014 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Major_League_Baseball_season "2014 Major League Baseball season").[[66]](#cite_note-66)[[67]](#cite_note-67)[[68]](#cite_note-68)

## Concerns about accuracy

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Hawk-Eye&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Concerns about accuracy")]

Hawk-Eye is now familiar to sport fans around the world for the views it brings into sports like cricket and tennis. Although this new technology has for the most part been embraced, it has received criticism from some quarters. In the [2007 Wimbledon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Wimbledon_Championships "2007 Wimbledon Championships") a shot that appeared to be out, was called by Hawk-Eye as in by 1 mm, a distance smaller than the advertised mean error of 3.6 mm.[[69]](#cite_note-69) Some commentators have criticised the system's 3.6 mm statistical margin of error as too large.[[70]](#cite_note-70) Others have noted that while 3.6 mm is extraordinarily accurate, this margin of error is only for the witnessed trajectory of the ball. In 2008, an article in a peer-reviewed journal[[71]](#cite_note-71) consolidated many of these doubts. The authors acknowledged the value of the system, but noted that it was probably fallible to some extent, and that its failure to depict a margin of error gave a spurious depiction of events. The authors also argued that the probable limits to its accuracy were not acknowledged by players, officials, commentators or spectators. They hypothesised that Hawk-Eye may struggle with predicting the trajectory of a cricket ball after bouncing: the time between a ball bouncing and striking the batsman may be too short to generate the three frames (at least) needed to plot a curve accurately.

## Use in computer games

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Hawk-Eye&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Use in computer games")]

The use of the Hawk-Eye brand and simulation has been licensed to [Codemasters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codemasters "Codemasters") for use in the video game *[Brian Lara International Cricket 2005](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Lara_International_Cricket_2005 "Brian Lara International Cricket 2005")* to make the game appear more like television coverage, and subsequently in *[Brian Lara International Cricket 2007](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Lara_International_Cricket_2007 "Brian Lara International Cricket 2007")*, *[Ashes Cricket 2009](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashes_Cricket_2009 "Ashes Cricket 2009")* and *[International Cricket 2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Cricket_2010 "International Cricket 2010")*. A similar version of the system has since been incorporated into the [Xbox 360](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_360 "Xbox 360") version of *[Smash Court Tennis 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smash_Court_Tennis_3 "Smash Court Tennis 3")*, but it is not present in the [PSP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_Portable "PlayStation Portable") version of the game, although it does feature a normal challenge of the ball which does not use the Hawk-Eye feature. It is also featured (called Big Eye) in *[Don Bradman Cricket 14](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Bradman_Cricket_14 "Don Bradman Cricket 14")* and *[Don Bradman Cricket 17](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Bradman_Cricket_17 "Don Bradman Cricket 17")*.

## Competition

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Hawk-Eye&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Competition")]

[Cyclops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclops_(computer_system) "Cyclops (computer system)") is a computer system which has been used on the ATP and WTA professional tennis tours as an electronic line judge since 1980, now superseded by Hawk-Eye at Grand Slam tournaments.

[FoxTenn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FoxTenn?action=edit&redlink=1 "FoxTenn (page does not exist)") is another competing system for electronic line judge calling[[72]](#cite_note-72) which uses real data to trace back ball path and marking, including on clay surfaces.

Hawk-Eye is a computer vision system developed in 2000 by engineers at Roke Manor Research Limited (then a Siemens subsidiary) in Romsey, England, by Paul Hawkins and David Sherry. It was originally implemented in 2001 for television broadcasts to analyze leg before wicket (LBW) decisions in cricket. The Sony-owned system tracks the trajectory of a ball using up to ten high-performance cameras positioned on the underside of stadium roofs, triangulating video feeds to create a three-dimensional representation of the ball's path. It is advertised to be accurate to within 2.6 mm, though the Hawk-Eye Innovations website states an average error of 3.6 mm. The system is used in more than 20 major sports including baseball, cricket, tennis, badminton, hurling, rugby union, soccer, Gaelic football, American football, and volleyball.

HISTORY AND OWNERSHIP: The technology was spun off into Hawk-Eye Innovations Ltd, based in Winchester, Hampshire, as a joint venture between Roke Manor Research and Sunset + Vine. On 14 June 2006, investors led by the Wisden Group (including Mark Getty) bought the company for £4.4m. It was sold to Sony in March 2011 in a deal valuing the company at £15m-£20m.

DEPLOYMENT IN SPORTS:
- Cricket: First used by Channel 4 during a Test match between England and Pakistan at Lord's Cricket Ground on 21 May 2001. Used for LBW decisions (pitched location, impact location, projected path) and adopted in the Decision Review System since 2009. Marginal calls result in the on-field umpire's call being maintained.
- Tennis: First used officially at the Nasdaq-100 Open in March 2006; US Open was the first Grand Slam to use it (2006). The 2006 Hopman Cup in Perth was the first elite-level tournament allowing player challenges. The 2021 Australian Open was the first Grand Slam to use Hawk-Eye Live for all matches in place of line judges (partly due to COVID-19), followed by the US Open. In 2024, the All-England Club announced electronic line calling would replace human line judges full-time at Wimbledon starting in 2025. Clay courts (e.g., French Open) generally don't use Hawk-Eye due to ball marks, though the 2021 Mutua Madrid Open used a competing system (FoxTenn). Rules were unified on 19 March 2008: three unsuccessful challenges per set, with an additional challenge at tiebreak.
- Association football: One of FIFA-authorised goal-line technology (GLT) systems; used in the Premier League, Serie A, and Bundesliga. As of July 2017, licensed systems were installed at 96 stadiums, making it the most popular GLT system.
- Snooker: Used by BBC at World Championship since 2007 primarily as a viewer aid; removed after 2015, but a derivative is used on the World Snooker Tour in China to support referees in replacing balls to millimetre precision.
- Gaelic games: Introduced at Croke Park, Dublin in 2013 for Gaelic football and hurling. Experienced multiple malfunctions (2013, 2022, 2023), including a 2013 minor hurling game error that ruled a valid Limerick point wide, leading to suspensions and appeals.
- Australian football: Tested by AFL at MCG in Round 15 of the 2013 season for Score Review process.
- Badminton: BWF introduced Hawk-Eye in 2014, first at the 2014 India Super Series.
- Gridiron football: NFL adopted Hawk-Eye for virtual on-field measurements beginning in the 2025 season.
- Baseball: Used to automatically call balls and strikes in professional leagues in the U.S. and South Korea. MLB adopted it for the 2026 season, tested in Minor League Baseball since 2019. Also used for instant replay reviews in MLB since the 2014 season.

CONCERNS ABOUT ACCURACY: The system has been criticized for its 3.6 mm statistical margin of error, with some calling it too large. A 2008 peer-reviewed article noted the system's failure to depict a margin of error gives a spurious depiction of events, and hypothesized that Hawk-Eye may struggle with predicting a cricket ball's trajectory after bouncing. Multiple controversies have occurred, including at Wimbledon 2007, the 2007 Dubai Tennis Championships (Rafael Nadal dispute), and the 2009 Indian Wells Masters where the system mistakenly picked up a second bounce.

COMPUTER GAMES AND COMPETITION: The Hawk-Eye brand has been licensed to Codemasters for cricket video games and appears in Smash Court Tennis 3 and Don Bradman Cricket games. Competitors include Cyclops (electronic line judge used since 1980) and FoxTenn (which uses real data, including on clay).

This is a video transcript from CULT TENNIS (a YouTube channel) titled "The TRUTH behind Hawk Eye Accuracy | History of Line Tracking Technology in Tennis," posted on September 9, 2020, with approximately 1.86 million views. The video explores the history, functionality, and accuracy of Hawk-Eye line-calling technology in professional tennis.

**Key Historical Events:**
- Hawk-Eye was first developed for cricket in 2001 before being adapted for tennis.
- The 2004 US Open quarterfinal between Serena Williams and Jennifer Capriati featured famously blown line calls, serving as the catalyst for widespread adoption. Television viewers saw experimental "Shot Spot" visuals, but players had no challenge capability at that time.
- Hawk-Eye became available for player use in early 2006, with the US Open later that year becoming the first Grand Slam to implement the technology on its show courts.

**How Hawk-Eye Works:**
- Ten ultra-motion high-speed cameras (5 per side) are installed around the court perimeter, capturing video at 340 frames per second.
- The system triangulates data from calibrated cameras to produce a 3D position of the ball.
- Contrary to popular belief, Hawk-Eye does not simply watch the bounce — it PREDICTS the trajectory before the ball lands by calculating positions at 340 intervals per second as the ball comes off the player's racket. An algorithm predicts where the ball will bounce, combined with calculations for ball compression and skid.
- The system also tracks foot faults, not just line calls.

**Accuracy Data:**
- The International Tennis Federation (ITF) required Hawk-Eye to be within 5 millimeters of the real recorded bounce (approximately the width of a pencil eraser).
- On average, Hawk-Eye proved accurate to within 2.6 millimeters — far better than the naked eye.
- Despite this, the system has a margin of error and can misjudge balls landing within a millimeter of the line.
- Known accuracy limitations include glitches, wind shadows, and darkness.

**2020 Context:**
- Due to COVID-19 pandemic restrictions, the 2020 US Open removed traditional line judges on most courts entirely, using Hawk-Eye Live technology for every call, with computer-generated human-like voices making all line calls.

**Key Insights:**
- Human eyes can be deceived by the ball's skid after contact (e.g., a ball appearing out that actually touched the baseline before skidding an additional 10 centimeters).
- Competitors like FOX Trac (tennis analysis system) claim to determine calls based on real bounce observations rather than estimations, questioning Hawk-Eye's predictive approach.
- The conclusion is that while imperfect, Hawk-Eye is "probably right and you're probably wrong" in most disputed calls.

Abstract On public benchmarks, current action recognition tech-niques have achieved great success. Compared to ex-isting action recognition datasets, FineGym is distinguished in richness, quality, and diversity. In particular, it provides temporal annotations at both action and sub-action levels with a three-level semantic hierarchy. For example, a “bal-ance beam” event will be annotated as a sequence of el-ementary sub-actions derived from ﬁve sets: “leap-jump-hop”, “beam-turns”, “ﬂight-salto”, “ﬂight-handspring”, and “dismount”, where the sub-action in each set will be further annotated with ﬁnely deﬁned class labels.
