## The Metrics That Actually Matter — MOTA, IDF1, And Why HOTA Replaced Both

For a decade the tracking community ranked trackers by MOTA — Multiple Object Tracking Accuracy. MOTA was introduced in 2008 by Bernardin and Stiefelhagen as a single number that combined false positives, false negatives, and identity switches. It worked well enough that it became the headline metric on MOTChallenge, the dominant benchmark for pedestrian tracking, and the number you would see at the top of every tracker paper from 2008 to 2020.

MOTA had a known flaw: it was heavily biased toward detection quality. A tracker that detected every object correctly but swapped identities at every occlusion would score nearly as high as a tracker that never swapped identities at all, because the identity-switch term in MOTA's formula is small compared to the false-positive and false-negative terms. The community responded by introducing IDF1 — an identity-focused F1 score that punishes identity switches much more aggressively. IDF1 was the right metric for any application where identity persistence mattered (multi-target re-identification, person-of-interest tracking) but it overcorrected: it ignored detection quality in turn.

The resolution came in 2020 with HOTA — Higher Order Tracking Accuracy — proposed by Jonathon Luiten and colleagues. HOTA is an explicit, balanced combination of a *detection score* (DetA, how well the tracker detects objects in the first place) and an *association score* (AssA, how well it keeps identities consistent across detections that match the same ground-truth object). The two are combined geometrically — HOTA is the square root of DetA × AssA — so a tracker that scores high on one but low on the other gets penalised. HOTA also reports the two sub-scores separately, so a paper can show which axis a new tracker improved on.

By 2026 HOTA is the metric the field reports. MOTA still appears in every results table, but the leaderboards on MOTChallenge, DanceTrack, and SportsMOT all rank trackers by HOTA. If you read only one number from a tracker comparison, read HOTA.

| Metric | What it measures | Strength | Weakness |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MOTA | False positives + false negatives + ID switches | Single number; widely cited | Detection-biased; underweights ID switches |
| IDF1 | F1 score over identity-correct frames | Association-focused | Detection-blind |
| HOTA | √(DetA × AssA), balanced detection + association | Balanced; reports sub-scores | Slower to compute |

Numbers from the MOTChallenge leaderboard (MOT17 test set, private detection) for the four trackers we cover:

| Tracker | MOTA | IDF1 | HOTA |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DeepSORT (with YOLOX-X detector) | 60.3 | 61.2 | 48.8 |
| ByteTrack | 80.3 | 77.3 | 63.1 |
| OC-SORT | 78.0 | 77.5 | 63.2 |
| BoT-SORT-ReID | 80.5 | 80.2 | 65.0 |

The numbers say what we said above: ByteTrack and OC-SORT are within a hair of each other on MOT17; BoT-SORT-ReID is a step above them; DeepSORT is the historical reference. The story is different on DanceTrack — where OC-SORT pulls ahead of ByteTrack by ten-plus HOTA points — and on SportsMOT, where BoT-SORT-ReID's appearance features matter most. The right tracker depends on the data, not on the leaderboard headline.

## Picking The Right Tracker — A Decision Walkthrough

Here is the decision tree we use at Fora Soft when a project asks for a tracking feature. It runs in four questions.

The first question is: **is the camera moving?** If the camera is on a phone, drone, body-cam, dashcam, or any rig where the operator and the world both move, the constant-velocity Kalman filter at the heart of ByteTrack and OC-SORT will drift because the predictions are made in image coordinates, not world coordinates. BoT-SORT's camera-motion-compensation step is the fix. **Pick BoT-SORT for any handheld, mobile, or vehicle-mounted camera.**

The second question is: **does the motion violate the constant-velocity assumption?** Dance, gymnastics, parkour, animal movement, fast sports, and any scenario where objects suddenly change direction breaks the Kalman filter's prediction step. OC-SORT's observation-centric re-update is the fix. **Pick OC-SORT for dance, sports, animal-tracking, and any scenario with sudden direction changes.**

The third question is: **how many simultaneous streams or how dense is the scene?** Appearance-based trackers (BoT-SORT-ReID, Deep OC-SORT, StrongSORT) extract a deep feature per detection per frame. On a CPU, that feature extraction is the dominant cost — running BoT-SORT-ReID on sixteen 1080p streams pegs a server. If the budget says "many streams, modest hardware", **pick ByteTrack**: it does no appearance work, runs at the speed of the detector, and is the right choice for high-density retail analytics and large-scale surveillance.

The fourth question is: **how important is identity persistence through long occlusions?** If the application can tolerate brief identity switches (vehicle counting, dwell-time estimation, crowd density), motion-only trackers (ByteTrack, OC-SORT) are fine. If identity must persist through five or more seconds of occlusion (person-of-interest tracking, sports broadcast graphics, multi-camera handoff), appearance-based trackers (BoT-SORT-ReID, Deep OC-SORT, StrongSORT) become necessary. **Pick BoT-SORT-ReID for long-occlusion identity persistence.**

In our experience, eighty percent of projects end up at ByteTrack (fastest, simplest, works) or BoT-SORT-ReID (slightly slower, more accurate, the Ultralytics default). OC-SORT is the special-case pick. DeepSORT is rarely the right answer in 2026 — every problem it was good at is now solved better by one of the three above.

### Numeric example — the cost of running a tracker on a 1280 × 720 video at 30 frames per second

Here is the math for a single stream on a modern Intel server CPU, with a YOLOv8-S detector and twenty pedestrians in frame.

YOLOv8-S detection (640 × 640 input, 20 detections): about 14 milliseconds per frame. ByteTrack association (20 detections, 20 active tracks): about 0.4 milliseconds per frame. BoT-SORT-ReID appearance feature extraction (BoT-S50, 20 crops): about 18 milliseconds per frame. BoT-SORT-ReID association: about 0.6 milliseconds per frame.

Pipeline totals per frame: ByteTrack pipeline: 14 + 0.4 = 14.4 milliseconds per frame. BoT-SORT-ReID pipeline: 14 + 18 + 0.6 = 32.6 milliseconds per frame.

Per second: ByteTrack = 432 ms of CPU; BoT-SORT-ReID = 978 ms of CPU.

The ByteTrack stream uses about 43 percent of one core. The BoT-SORT-ReID stream uses nearly a full core all by itself. A sixteen-core server therefore handles thirty-five concurrent ByteTrack streams or sixteen concurrent BoT-SORT-ReID streams. The price difference shows up directly in the cloud bill: at AWS c7i.4xlarge pricing (sixteen vCPUs, about $0.71/hour on demand), ByteTrack costs $0.020 per stream-hour, BoT-SORT-ReID costs $0.044 per stream-hour. Both numbers are small in absolute terms, but the ratio matters when you scale to thousands of cameras.

If you need more streams per server, the move is not to switch to a lighter tracker; it is to drop the tracker frame rate. Most tracking-driven features — counting, dwell time, fall detection — work fine at 10 frames per second of tracking. Running the tracker on every third frame and interpolating IDs in between cuts the cost by 3× with negligible accuracy loss.

## Where To Run It — Browser, Edge, Or Server

The deployment-topology decision applies to trackers exactly the same way it applied to pose models in the [pose-tracking lesson](/learn/ai-for-video-engineering/articles-ai/openpose-mediapipe-rtmpose-pose-tracking). The same model can be deployed in three different places, with three very different trade-offs.

In the **browser**, the tracker runs inside the user's tab in WebAssembly. None of the four trackers we cover has a first-party browser implementation, but ByteTrack and OC-SORT — being motion-only and tiny — have been ported to JavaScript and ONNX Runtime Web. The deployment is appropriate for browser-based gesture and ergonomics features. BoT-SORT-ReID with appearance features is too heavy for typical browser hardware budgets in 2026.

On the **edge**, the tracker runs on a small box near the camera — a NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano, an Intel NUC, or a Hailo-8L AI accelerator. All four trackers fit comfortably on Jetson Orin Nano alongside a YOLOv8-S detector. ByteTrack is the throughput pick (more streams per box). BoT-SORT-ReID is the accuracy pick (one or two streams per box, but higher identity persistence). Edge deployment is the default for AI security cameras, intelligent video analytics, retail, and industrial computer vision.

On the **server**, the tracker runs in your cloud account alongside the detector. RT-DETR or YOLOv11 on GPU, plus ByteTrack or BoT-SORT-ReID on CPU, is a workable pattern. The latency is dominated by the network round-trip (typically 30 to 100 milliseconds) plus the inference time. Server deployment is the default for sports analytics platforms, broadcast contribution, batch processing of recorded footage, and any feature that needs the largest detectors.

| Topology | Default tracker | Cost owner | Privacy posture | Latency budget |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Browser | ByteTrack via ONNX Runtime Web | User's device | Frames stay on device | 16 ms (60 FPS budget) |
| Edge | ByteTrack on Jetson (many streams) or BoT-SORT-ReID (high accuracy) | One-time hardware | Frames stay on LAN | 50 ms (round-trip + model) |
| Server | BoT-SORT-ReID on CPU, with GPU detector | Cloud bill per stream | Frames travel to cloud | 100 ms (RTT + model) |

The choice between the three is rarely close. The use case picks the topology, and the topology picks the tracker.

## Four Production Pitfalls That Sink Tracking Features

We have shipped a lot of tracking features into video products at Fora Soft. Four failure modes show up repeatedly. They are not novel — every team rediscovers them — but the cost of rediscovery is large, so it is worth naming them up front.

The first pitfall is **blaming the tracker for what is really a detector problem.** When a tracker drops identities or counts wrong, the instinct is to swap trackers. The fix usually is not the tracker; it is the detector. A YOLOv8-N detector trained on COCO will miss most small-pedestrian detections at 1080p resolution, and no tracker on earth can stitch identities across missed detections. Always profile the detector first — if recall on your specific data is below ninety percent, fix the detector before touching the tracker. Switching from ByteTrack to BoT-SORT-ReID buys you a few HOTA points; switching from YOLOv8-N to YOLOv8-X buys you ten.

The second pitfall is **using DeepSORT in 2026.** DeepSORT was the right answer in 2018. It is rarely the right answer now. Every comparable problem it was good at is now solved better by ByteTrack (faster, more accurate) or BoT-SORT-ReID (more accurate, equally easy to deploy). The reason DeepSORT survives is that the tutorials a junior engineer finds on a first project are usually three years old. Default to ByteTrack for new projects; default to BoT-SORT-ReID if you need appearance features. We have rewritten DeepSORT pipelines into ByteTrack pipelines for three clients in the past two years, and the swap was always a net upgrade on latency, throughput, and HOTA together.

The third pitfall is **leaving the Kalman filter and lifecycle parameters at their defaults on data the trackers were not tuned for.** Every tracker we discussed is published with hyperparameters tuned for MOT17 — pedestrians, mostly forward motion, well-lit scenes, fixed cameras. Apply that configuration to a drone-view sports broadcast or a CCTV stream of cars on a highway, and the Kalman filter's noise terms are wrong, the maximum-unconfirmed-frames knob is wrong, and the appearance threshold is wrong. The fix is to tune. Specifically: the `track_buffer` (how long a lost track is kept alive in case it returns) and the `match_thresh` (the IoU threshold for the second association pass) are the two knobs that move the most. We habitually run a grid search over those two on a held-out video from the actual deployment data before shipping.

The fourth pitfall is **trusting track IDs across camera boundaries.** A track ID is local to a single camera and a single tracker run. The same person walking from camera A to camera B will be assigned different IDs by the two trackers, and no amount of clever single-camera tracking will fix that. Cross-camera identity persistence is a separate problem — *person re-identification* or *multi-camera multi-target tracking* — and it requires a dedicated Re-ID model, a shared feature gallery, and a global graph-solving step. We will cover the cross-camera case in a future lesson; for now, if your application crosses cameras, do not pretend the single-camera tracker is doing it.

## Where Fora Soft Fits In

We have shipped tracking features into half a dozen product categories at Fora Soft. In video conferencing, we use lightweight ByteTrack on the SFU side to keep persistent IDs on participants who change camera angles mid-call — the IDs feed downstream features like active-speaker labelling and automated meeting summaries. In retail and intelligent video analytics, we use BoT-SORT-ReID on Jetson edge boxes for dwell-time, queue-length, and out-of-stock detection — the appearance features matter because shoppers occlude each other and the appearance model resolves the resulting identity ambiguity. In OTT and broadcast contribution, we use BoT-SORT-ReID on cloud GPUs for sports overlays and player-tracking dashboards, where the longer occlusions and high-stakes identity matter. In e-learning, we use ByteTrack to track multiple students in classroom video and feed the trajectories into attention-monitoring features. In surveillance and security, we use BoT-SORT-ReID for fall, fight, and intrusion detection — the appearance features help maintain identity through long static-camera occlusions. In every project the tracker is the second decision; the detector and the topology are decisions one and zero.

## Call to action

* **Talk to a video engineer** — [book a 30-minute scoping call](https://calendly.com/vadim-fora-soft/30min) to talk through your object detection software plan.
* **See our case studies** — [250+ shipped projects across video streaming, WebRTC, OTT, telemedicine, e-learning, surveillance, and AR/VR](https://www.forasoft.com/projects).
* **Download the Multi-Object Tracker Decision Worksheet** — [One-page printable worksheet with the four-question decision tree, the metric cheat sheet (MOTA, IDF1, HOTA), the deployment-topology table, and the four-pitfall checklist](/learn/downloads/multi-object-tracking-decision-worksheet).

## References

1. Wojke, N., Bewley, A., Paulus, D. *Simple Online and Realtime Tracking with a Deep Association Metric (DeepSORT)*. ICIP 2017. arXiv:1703.07402. The original DeepSORT paper that introduced deep appearance features into the SORT pipeline.
2. Bewley, A., Ge, Z., Ott, L., Ramos, F., Upcroft, B. *Simple Online and Realtime Tracking (SORT)*. ICIP 2016. arXiv:1602.00763. The original SORT paper that DeepSORT extended.
3. Zhang, Y., Sun, P., Jiang, Y., Yu, D., Yuan, Z., Luo, P., Liu, W., Wang, X. *ByteTrack: Multi-Object Tracking by Associating Every Detection Box*. ECCV 2022. arXiv:2110.06864. The ByteTrack paper that introduced the two-stage detection-cascade association.
4. ByteTrack reference implementation. `github.com/ifzhang/ByteTrack`, accessed 2026-05-27. The MIT-licensed reference code that ships in Ultralytics YOLO.
5. Cao, J., Pang, J., Weng, X., Khirodkar, R., Kitani, K. *Observation-Centric SORT: Rethinking SORT for Robust Multi-Object Tracking*. CVPR 2023. The OC-SORT paper that introduced observation-centric re-update.
6. OC-SORT reference implementation. `github.com/noahcao/OC_SORT`, accessed 2026-05-27. The MIT-licensed reference code.
7. Maggiolino, G., Ahmad, A., Cao, J., Kitani, K. *Deep OC-SORT: Multi-Pedestrian Tracking by Adaptive Re-Identification*. ICIP 2023. arXiv:2302.11813. The appearance-augmented extension of OC-SORT.
8. Aharon, N., Orfaig, R., Bobrovsky, B.-Z. *BoT-SORT: Robust Associations Multi-Pedestrian Tracking*. arXiv:2206.14651, 2022. The BoT-SORT paper that introduced camera-motion compensation and Re-ID-based association upgrades.
9. BoT-SORT reference implementation. `github.com/NirAharon/BoT-SORT`, accessed 2026-05-27. The MIT-licensed reference code.
10. Ultralytics. *Multi-Object Tracking with Ultralytics YOLO*. `docs.ultralytics.com/modes/track`, accessed 2026-05-27. First-party documentation for the BoT-SORT (default) and ByteTrack trackers shipped with the Ultralytics framework.
11. Luiten, J., Ošep, A., Dendorfer, P., Torr, P., Geiger, A., Leal-Taixé, L., Leibe, B. *HOTA: A Higher Order Metric for Evaluating Multi-Object Tracking*. International Journal of Computer Vision, 2021. The HOTA paper that balances detection and association accuracy in a single metric.
12. Du, Y., Zhao, Z., Song, Y., Zhao, Y., Su, F., Gong, T., Meng, H. *StrongSORT: Make DeepSORT Great Again*. IEEE Transactions on Multimedia, 2023. The StrongSORT paper that modernises the DeepSORT pipeline with better detector, Re-ID, and post-processing.
13. Stanojevic, V., Todorovic, B. *BoostTrack: Boosting the Similarity Measure and Detection Confidence for Improved Multiple Object Tracking*. Machine Vision and Applications, 2024. The BoostTrack paper that combines confidence boosting and a soft IoU measure.
14. Sun, P., Cao, J., Jiang, Y., Yuan, Z., Bai, S., Kitani, K., Luo, P. *DanceTrack: Multi-Object Tracking in Uniform Appearance and Diverse Motion*. CVPR 2022. The DanceTrack benchmark that exposes the constant-velocity Kalman filter's weakness on non-linear motion.
15. Cui, Y., Zeng, C., Zhao, X., Yang, Y., Wu, G., Wang, L. *SportsMOT: A Large Multi-Object Tracking Dataset in Multiple Sports Scenes*. ICCV 2023. The SportsMOT benchmark for sports-tracking evaluation.
16. Bernardin, K., Stiefelhagen, R. *Evaluating Multiple Object Tracking Performance: The CLEAR MOT Metrics*. EURASIP JIVP, 2008. The original CLEAR-MOT paper that defined MOTA, the metric HOTA replaced.

### Notes For The Editor

* The BoT-SORT-ReID HOTA number (65.0) is from the 2022 paper on MOT17; the leaderboard moves and the current top result on MOT17 in mid-2026 is BoostTrack at roughly HOTA 65.4 — worth a refresh in the next revision once the BoostTrack lesson is written.
* "Where Fora Soft fits in" can be expanded with a real case study once the OTT broadcast project goes public; currently described in generic terms.
* We did not cover transformer-based trackers (MOTR, TrackFormer) — they are still research-grade and have not displaced tracking-by-detection in production. Mention in passing in a future revision.
* The numeric example uses YOLOv8-S — refresh to YOLOv11 or the relevant Ultralytics default once the YOLO 2.2 article is final.
* Cross-camera Re-ID is mentioned but not covered; a dedicated lesson should be slotted into Phase 2 in v2 of the curriculum.

Key takeaways

* Tracking-by-detection is the dominant paradigm; every modern tracker is the same pipeline with different muscle.
* ByteTrack is the 2026 default — fast, simple, motion-only, MIT-licensed.
* BoT-SORT-ReID is the accuracy pick and the Ultralytics default in 2024–2026.
* OC-SORT is the right pick for non-linear motion (dance, sports, animals).
* DeepSORT is the historical reference; do not default to it on new projects.
* HOTA — not MOTA — is the metric to optimise; it balances detection and association.
* Tracker quality is downstream of detector quality; fix the detector first.

A fast, accurate tracker that keeps even low-confidence detections to recover objects others drop. Strong default for crowded real-time scenes.](/learn/ai-for-video-engineering/glossary/terms-ai/bytetrack)

A widely used tracker that combines motion prediction with an appearance fingerprint to keep IDs stable through brief occlusions.](/learn/ai-for-video-engineering/glossary/terms-ai/deepsort)

[#### Multi-object tracking

Following many objects across video frames while keeping a stable ID on each, even through occlusion. Turns per-frame detections into trajectories.](/learn/ai-for-video-engineering/glossary/terms-ai/multi-object-tracking)

Recognising the same object or person again after it leaves and re-enters view, by its visual signature. Lets tracking survive gaps and camera switches.](/learn/ai-for-video-engineering/glossary/terms-ai/re-identification)

## Multi-Object Tracking — DeepSORT, ByteTrack, OC-SORT, and BoT-SORT (2026)

This article by Nikolay Sapunov (CEO of Fora Soft, published May 27, 2026) provides a comprehensive 2026 guide to multi-object tracking (MOT) for production video systems. Multi-object tracking is the process of maintaining stable identity IDs on the same person, car, or package across video frames, connecting a per-frame object detector to downstream features that reason about trajectories (counting, dwell time, sports overlays, active-speaker detection, surveillance).

### The Tracking-by-Detection Pipeline (4 stages)
1. **Detection** — a detector (YOLO, RT-DETR, Grounding DINO) emits bounding boxes per frame; detector quality dominates everything downstream.
2. **Motion prediction** — Kalman filter (1960s algorithm) predicts next-frame positions using a constant-velocity model with state vector (x, y, aspect_ratio, height, dx, dy, dh, dr).
3. **Association** — cost matrix between tracks and detections (IoU geometric distance, appearance cosine distance, or both), solved with the Hungarian algorithm (O(n³)).
4. **Track lifecycle management** — new tracks born, unconfirmed tracks killed after frames, tentative/confirmed status with birth/death thresholds.

### The Four Tracker Families (2026 production standards)
- **DeepSORT (2017)** — introduced deep appearance embeddings (cosine distance) on top of SORT. MOT17: 60.3 MOTA, 61.2 IDF1, 48.8 HOTA. Historical reference; no longer the default for new projects.
- **ByteTrack (ECCV 2022, Zhang et al.)** — associates every detection box including low-confidence ones via a two-stage cascade. MOT17: 80.3 MOTA, 77.3 IDF1, 63.1 HOTA. Motion-only, <50 lines of Python, MIT-licensed (github.com/ifzhang/ByteTrack), ~2x faster than DeepSORT, ships in Ultralytics YOLO as bytetrack.yaml. The 2026 throughput default.
- **OC-SORT (CVPR 2023, Cao et al.)** — fixes Kalman drift after occlusion via observation-centric re-update and observation-centric momentum. MOT17: 78.0 MOTA, 77.5 IDF1, 63.2 HOTA; beats ByteTrack by 10+ HOTA points on DanceTrack (non-linear motion). Best for dance, gymnastics, parkour, animals, sports with direction changes. MIT-licensed (github.com/noahcao/OC_SORT).
- **BoT-SORT (2022, Aharon et al.)** — adds camera-motion compensation (sparse optical flow + ECC alignment) and appearance embeddings (BoT-S50 Re-ID). MOT17: 80.5 MOTA, 80.2 IDF1, 65.0 HOTA — state of the art at publication. Default tracker in Ultralytics YOLO since 2024 (botsort.yaml). Roughly 30% slower than ByteTrack. MIT-licensed (github.com/NirAharon/BoT-SORT).

### Metrics: Why HOTA Replaced MOTA
- **MOTA (2008)** — detection-biased, underweights identity switches.
- **IDF1** — association-focused but detection-blind (overcorrects).
- **HOTA (2020, Luiten et al.)** — √(DetA × AssA), balanced detection and association, reports sub-scores separately. By 2026, HOTA is the field's ranking metric on MOTChallenge, DanceTrack, and SportsMOT.

### Decision Tree (4 questions)
1. **Is the camera moving?** → BoT-SORT (handheld, drone, vehicle-mounted).
2. **Does motion violate constant-velocity?** → OC-SORT (dance, sports, animals, sudden direction changes).
3. **Many streams/dense scenes?** → ByteTrack (no appearance work, runs at detector speed).
4. **Long-occlusion identity persistence?** → BoT-SORT-ReID (5+ seconds of occlusion, multi-camera handoff).

~80% of projects end at ByteTrack or BoT-SORT-ReID.

### Numeric Example (1280×720, 30 FPS, YOLOv8-S, 20 pedestrians, Intel server CPU)
- ByteTrack: 14.4 ms/frame (432 ms/sec CPU, ~43% of one core); 35 concurrent streams per 16-core server; $0.020/stream-hour on AWS c7i.4xlarge.
- BoT-SORT-ReID: 32.6 ms/frame (978 ms/sec, nearly full core); 16 concurrent streams; $0.044/stream-hour.
- Cost-cutting tip: run tracking at 10 FPS (every third frame) for 3× cost reduction with negligible accuracy loss for counting/dwell/fall-detection features.

### Deployment Topologies
- **Browser** — ByteTrack/OC-SORT via ONNX Runtime Web (BoT-SORT-ReID too heavy in 2026).
- **Edge** — all four fit on Jetson Orin Nano; ByteTrack (throughput) or BoT-SORT-ReID (accuracy); default for security cameras, retail, industrial CV.
- **Server** — BoT-SORT-ReID on CPU with GPU detector; default for sports analytics, broadcast, batch processing.

### Four Production Pitfalls
1. **Blaming the tracker for detector problems** — fix detector first; YOLOv8-N→YOLOv8-X buys 10 points vs. a few HOTA points from tracker swaps.
2. **Using DeepSORT in 2026** — outdated; ByteTrack/BoT-SORT-ReID beat it everywhere.
3. **Leaving Kalman/lifecycle parameters at MOT17 defaults** — tune track_buffer and match_thresh via grid search on deployment data.
4. **Trusting track IDs across camera boundaries** — IDs are local to a camera/tracker run; cross-camera identity requires dedicated Re-ID models, shared feature galleries, and graph-solving.

### Fora Soft Usage (context for the author's recommendations)
Video conferencing (ByteTrack on SFU), retail/IVA (BoT-SORT-ReID on Jetson), OTT/broadcast sports (BoT-SORT-ReID on cloud GPUs), e-learning (ByteTrack), surveillance/security (BoT-SORT-ReID).

The article includes 16 references (DeepSORT, SORT, ByteTrack, OC-SORT, Deep OC-SORT, BoT-SORT, HOTA, StrongSORT, BoostTrack, DanceTrack, SportsMOT, CLEAR-MOT papers and implementations) plus editorial notes indicating the BoT-SORT-ReID HOTA figure is from the 2022 paper (current MOT17 leader in mid-2026 is BoostTrack at ~65.4 HOTA), and that transformer-based trackers (MOTR, TrackFormer) remain research-grade and are not yet production-viable.

It is roughly twice as fast as DeepSORT (since it does not run an appearance feature extractor) and three to five times faster than BoT-SORT.", "If you read only one number from a tracker comparison, read HOTA.", "The right tracker depends on the data, not on the leaderboard headline.", "The tracker is the second decision; the detector and the topology are decisions one and zero."

[![arXiv](https://camo.githubusercontent.com/436531f38d72b36c74264d3a115a1c22bc09fee7cb73d8d5bb1558458cf42cf6/68747470733a2f2f696d672e736869656c64732e696f2f62616467652f61725869762d323230332e31343336302d253343434f4c4f522533452e737667)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.14360) [![License: MIT](https://camo.githubusercontent.com/fdf2982b9f5d7489dcf44570e714e3a15fce6253e0cc6b5aa61a075aac2ff71b/68747470733a2f2f696d672e736869656c64732e696f2f62616467652f4c6963656e73652d4d49542d79656c6c6f772e737667)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT) [![test](https://camo.githubusercontent.com/49a61b166a58a3c0f341142c1eccf74c76eb49c81f17671a01f90c24b719b00c/68747470733a2f2f696d672e736869656c64732e696f2f7374617469632f76313f6c6162656c3d4279266d6573736167653d5079746f72636826636f6c6f723d726564)](https://camo.githubusercontent.com/49a61b166a58a3c0f341142c1eccf74c76eb49c81f17671a01f90c24b719b00c/68747470733a2f2f696d672e736869656c64732e696f2f7374617469632f76313f6c6162656c3d4279266d6573736167653d5079746f72636826636f6c6f723d726564)

**Observation-Centric SORT (OC-SORT)** is a pure motion-model-based multi-object tracker. It aims to improve tracking robustness in **crowded scenes and when objects are in non-linear motion**. It is designed by recognizing and fixing limitations in Kalman filter and [SORT](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.00763). It is flexible to integrate with different detectors and matching modules, such as appearance similarity. It remains, **Simple, Online and Real-time**.

OC-SORT (Observation-Centric SORT) is a pure motion-model-based multi-object tracker published at CVPR 2023, designed to improve tracking robustness in crowded scenes and under non-linear object motion. It addresses limitations in the Kalman filter and the original SORT algorithm while remaining simple, online, and real-time. The official GitHub repository (noahcao/OC_SORT) has 1.1k stars, 153 forks, and 54 commits, licensed under MIT, with the corresponding arXiv paper at 2203.14360.

Key technical highlights include the "Observation-centric Re-Update" (ORU) mechanism, flexibility to integrate with different detectors and appearance-based matching modules, and support for deployment via ONNX, TensorRT, and ncnn. A C++ implementation is available, and the Python implementation was refactored (03/2026) for 1.5x-2x inference acceleration. Deep OC-SORT, which combines OC-SORT with deep visual appearance, was accepted to ICIP 2023.

Benchmark results include: MOT17 private (HOTA 63.2, MOTA 78.0), MOT20 private (HOTA 62.4, MOTA 75.9), KITTI-cars (HOTA 76.5, MOTA 90.3), and DanceTrack-test (HOTA 55.1, MOTA 89.4). Inference runs at ~28FPS on an RTX 2080Ti GPU, or ~700FPS on CPU when detections are pre-provided.

The codebase builds upon YOLOX, filterpy, and ByteTrack. Setup and usage instructions are in docs (INSTALL.md, GET_STARTED.md, MODEL_ZOO.md, DEPLOY.md), and a demo command is provided using a pretrained DanceTrack model. The repository also supports integration with mmtracking and ByteTrack with multiple cost metrics (GIoU, CIoU).

## **Introduction**

Computer vision as a field has grown tremendously both in academia and industry in the past few decades. With the advent of deep learning and improved computational capability of processors such as GPUs and TPUs, researchers have made significant progress in solving a growing range of tasks.

![Example of Pedestrian Tracking](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/67d7ebcca3cabb623904dcde/67d7f31782fc546599bcf286_64588a9e604430f4ba6a2e36_2b6b5e0b.gif)

Figure 1: [Example of Pedestrian Tracking](https://github.com/Zhongdao/Towards-Realtime-MOT)

Traditional computer vision methods using rule-based and feature-based techniques for object detection have since been overshadowed by deep learning approaches based on the revolutionary Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Deep neural networks have achieved state-of-the-art performance for tasks like classification, object detection, and image/instance segmentation. As machine learning computer vision’s capability has rapidly progressed, researchers are now shifting their attention towards more complex computer vision tasks such as multiple object tracking.

## **What is Multiple Object Tracking?**

Multiple object tracking (MOT) is a computer vision task that involves tracking the movements of multiple objects over time in a video sequence. The goal is to determine the identity, location, and trajectory of each object in the video, even in cases where objects are partially or fully occluded by other objects in the scene. MOT is an important problem in computer vision, as it has numerous practical applications. For example, in surveillance, MOT can be used to detect and track suspicious behaviour in a crowd or monitor the movement of vehicles in a parking lot. In robotics, it can be used to guide autonomous vehicles, identify obstacles, and plan safe routes through a dynamic environment. Other applications of MOT are in sports analytics, medical imaging, and many more.

![Figure 2: MOT applications in sports analytics](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/67d7ebcca3cabb623904dcde/680a8745551d14ee8c9661d1_Screenshot%202025-04-24%20at%2011.47.19%E2%80%AFAM.png)

Figure 2: [MOT applications in sports analytics.](https://github.com/mikel-brostrom/yolov8_tracking)

‍

Generally, multiple object tracking happens in two stages: object detection and object association. Object detection is the process of identifying all potential objects of interest in the current frame using object detectors such as Faster-RCNN or YOLO. Object association is the process of linking objects detected in the current frame with its corresponding objects from previous frames, referred to as tracklets. Object or instance association is usually done by predicting the object's location at the current frame based on previous frames' tracklets using the Kalman Filter followed by one-to-one linear assignment typically using the Hungarian Algorithm to minimise the total differences between the matching results.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/67d7ebcca3cabb623904dcde/67d7f31782fc546599bcf26e_64588b144a236751e9a21bdc_d67baa46.png)

Figure 3: [DeepSORT Algorithm](https://learnopencv.com/understanding-multiple-object-tracking-using-deepsort)

### ‍**Challenges with MOT**

Despite much progress over the years, MOT remains a challenging task. Described below are some critical issues that have inhibited high quality performance, and have been the source of motivation for recent approaches.

Complications can originate from the actual visual data itself. For example, the motion and appearance of the same object can vary greatly throughout the video sequence. Objects can move at different speeds and directions, change in size or shape, and may be partially or fully occluded by other objects in the scene. These problems contribute to MOT tracking inaccuracies such as object ID switching or multiple tracklets being assigned to the same object.

At the architectural level, multi-class trackers may encounter class switching issues that exacerbate issues with object association between various frames if the detector fails to classify bounding boxes accurately because of classification issues such as similar classes which confuse the detector. Therefore, the tracking algorithm must be able to handle these variations and reliably associate each object in the current frame with its corresponding object in the previous frame.

For practical implementation, MOT architectures may be required to perform real-time predictions. Many MOT methods can struggle with video inference speed, especially for live predictions on videos with high frame rates, because the complexity of the models used requires more computation, and thus more compute time. In particular, multi-component or multi-stage video trackers with robust architectures will certainly encounter difficulties when performing inference on live video feeds.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/67d7ebcca3cabb623904dcde/67d7f31782fc546599bcf274_64588b140be9f8de8efc710f_e484d3e4.png)

Figure 4: [ID Switching due to objects overlapping](https://www.arxiv-vanity.com/papers/2012.15460/)

Various existing methods have been used to tackle the MOT task in a broad range of complexity. From relatively simple algorithms using IoU for instance association to more complex algorithms such as [SORT, DeepSORT, and Norfair](https://www.datature.io/blog/implementing-object-tracking-for-computer-vision/?ref=datature-blog), this large breadth of variation demonstrates the difficulties in balancing computational tradeoffs for inference speed and deeper extraction and utilization of visual features to produce more accurate predictions. Recent MOT approaches have used complex algorithms primarily based on trajectory prediction with the Kalman Filter followed by bounding box association with Hungarian Algorithm. Our latest blog explores one such example of a complex MOT tracker, [Track Every Thing](https://www.datature.io/blog/introduction-to-multiple-object-tracking-and-recent-developments/?ref=datature-blog). In this article, we will explore an alternative approach, a simple yet powerful tracker - [**BYTETrack**](https://github.com/ifzhang/ByteTrack).

‍

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/67d7ebcca3cabb623904dcde/680a87a700c83d617bcf8b04_Screenshot%202025-04-24%20at%2011.48.50%E2%80%AFAM.png)

Figure 5: [BYTETrack on Multiple Object Tracking of human surveillance](https://github.com/ifzhang/ByteTrack)

## **What is BYTETrack?**

[BYTETrack: Multi-Object Tracking by Associating Every Detection Box](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.06864) is a paper presented at ECCV2022 by Yifu Zhang et al. Thanks to its universal framework and relative simplicity, it has been adopted by many subsequent researchers for their MOT trackers ([Bot-SORT](https://github.com/NirAharon/BoT-SORT), [SMILEtrack](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.08824)).

The main idea of BYTETrack is simple - keep non-background low score boxes for a secondary association step between previous frame and next frame based on their similarities with tracklets. This helps to improve tracking consistency by keeping relevant bounding boxes which otherwise would have been discarded due to low confidence score (due to occlusion or appearance changes). The generic framework makes BYTETrack highly adaptable to any object detection (YOLO, RCNN) or instance association components (IoU, feature similarity).

The primary innovation of BYTETrack is keeping non-background low confidence detection boxes which are typically discarded after the initial filtering of detections and use these low-score boxes for a secondary association step. Typically, occluded detection boxes have lower confidence scores than the threshold, but still contain some information about the objects which make their confidence score higher than purely background boxes. Hence, these low confidence boxes are still meaningful to keep track of during the association stage.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/67d7ebcca3cabb623904dcde/67d7f31782fc546599bcf291_64588bc23b78b730227108d3_f9dc28fb.png)

Figure 6: [ByteTrack uses low-confidence bounding boxes in addition to high-confidence boxes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.06864)

### ‍**Methodology Breakdown**

The overall idea of BYTETrack can be observed from Figure 7. After the detection stage, the detected bounding boxes are filtered into high confidence boxes, low confidence boxes and background boxes with fixed upper and lower thresholds. Background boxes are discarded after this process, but both low and high confidence detection boxes are kept for future association stages.

Similar to typical association steps from other algorithms, the high-score detection boxes of current frames are matched with predicted boxes from previous frames tracklets (using Kalman filter), which include both active tracklets and lost tracklets from recent frames. The matching is done using a simple IoU score or cosine similarity score between feature embeddings (using feature extractors such as [DeepSORT](https://github.com/nwojke/deep_sort), [QDTrack](https://github.com/SysCV/qdtrack), etc.) using the Hungarian algorithm or matching cascade on Nearest Neighbor Distance. Linear assignment between pairs of bounding boxes is only confirmed if the matching score is higher than a fixed match threshold. Unmatched high-score detection boxes in the actual implementation are first matched with tracklets with updates from a single frame before being assigned to a new tracklet.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/67d7ebcca3cabb623904dcde/67d7f31782fc546599bcf27d_64588bc12835a851824c39d2_c0273485.png)

Figure 7: BYTETrack Algorithm

In the second association stage, low-score detection boxes are matched against the remaining unmatched predicted boxes from previous frames. The matching algorithm is identical to the first association stage, but the matching threshold is set lower than the first association stage because of the intuition that occluded boxes should be more poorly matched to boxes from previous frames. Unmatched predicted boxes are assigned as lost tracklets, while unmatched detection boxes are discarded. The lost tracklets are kept for a certain number of frame duration and added back to the active tracklets before Kalman filter prediction. This allows the trackers to recover some tracklets which have been lost due to objects completely disappearing for a short number of frames.

### **Implementation Details**

In the paper, the author uses [YOLOX](https://github.com/Megvii-BaseDetection/YOLOX) as the base Detector. However, the Detector choice is easily customizable to [FasterRCNN](https://github.com/facebookresearch/Detectron) or other YOLO versions as BYTETrack simply takes in detection inputs with bounding boxes coordinates and class probability. Depending on the nature of datasets, users can choose different types of matching metrics (IoU or any ReID). Based on the authors, both IoU and ReID are good options for first stage association of high-score detections. ReID performs better on low-frame rate videos or videos with significant frame-to-frame movements; while IoU is more robust for cases of severe occlusion in which ReID features are not reliable. However, second stage association should always use IoU as the matching criteria, as we can expect low-score detection boxes to contain occluded objects whose ReID features may not be good representations of the objects.

## **Tutorial Example**

In this tutorial, I have taken video footage of the 2022 NBA finals between the Warriors and the Celtics. Our objective is to train a BYTETracker to track the movement of basketball players. I am interested in the movement of 3 classes: Warriors players, Celtics players and the referees. I will train a custom YOLOv8 Detector and use ByteTrack on top of the Detector outputs to keep track of objects.

### **Package and Dependencies Installation**

First, we clone the BYTETrack repository from <https://github.com/ifzhang/ByteTrack.git>. There are a few steps required for installation of BYTETrack, which can be found below. It is recommended to install the dependencies in an isolated virtual environment. The dependencies in this section cover the necessary libraries for ByteTrack specifically.

```
!git clone https://github.com/ifzhang/ByteTrack.git !git clone https://github.com/ifzhang/ByteTrack.git %cd ByteTrack % cd  ByteTrack !pip3 install -r requirements.txt !python3 setup.py develop !pip3 install cython !pip3 install 'git+https://github.com/cocodataset/cocoapi.git#subdirectory=PythonAPI' !pip3 install 'git+https://github.com/cocodataset/cocoapi.git#subdirectory=PythonAPI'  !pip3 install cython_bbox
```

### **Data Preparation**

I then prepare a custom dataset by downloading a short footage from the game and sample frames from it. My dataset contains approximately 90 side-view frames. For data annotation, I used Datature Nexus to label the objects and export the annotations for training our YOLOv8 model. With Datature’s Nexus, it was a simple task to [upload the frame images](https://developers.datature.io/docs/uploading-data), make [bounding box annotations](https://developers.datature.io/docs/bounding-box) for multiple classes, and [export the annotations](https://developers.datature.io/docs/exporting-annotations). Nexus makes it even simpler to [annotate videos](https://developers.datature.io/docs/video-annotation) with its support for video annotation. One can simply upload their .mp4 video file onto Nexus and scrub between frames to easily annotate the video. For more details, please refer to this [blog post](https://www.datature.io/blog/get-started-with-training-a-yolov8-object-detection-model) on how to work with the newly released YOLOv8 model.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/67d7ebcca3cabb623904dcde/67d7f31782fc546599bcf29f_64588f03169fc4829583c6b5_annotate.png)

Figure 8: Annotation of Custom Dataset on Nexus Platform

### **Training the Object Detection Model (YOLOv8)**

To train the model, we should ensure that our training image data and annotation files are ready, by ensuring that our frames are split into separate images, and having the annotation files associated correctly with the images. Additionally, we should ensure that our locally stored data is organized accordingly for our training. As an example, I’ve arranged the images and annotation files into the following format for YOLOv8 training.

With a trained YOLOv8 Detection model, I am ready to utilize the ByteTrack implementation. In the original implementation of the author, a tracker instance is initiated and for each image in the video sequence, the detections are used to update the tracklets of the tracker instance. After running the tracking code and fine-tuning the discussed hyperparameters, you can achieve results as seen below. Here is the rendered video demo of our implementation. The tracker manages to quite consistently follow players movement even when there are some occasional occlusions. However, there are few instances of ID switching in crowded areas. This is understandable as there are multiple strongly matched candidates in close proximity making it difficult for the tracker to differentiate based on IoU. We can consider adding Re-Identification (ReID) as a further improvement that will add more complexity to our solution architecture, by matching features between current detection boxes and previous tracklet boxes.

Figure 12: ByteTrack demo on basketball players tracking (multiclass)

## **Conclusion**

From quantitative review and anecdotal experience working with the tracker, BYTETrack certainly demonstrates the effectiveness of its simple architectural design. The IoU-based matching, while simplistic, has demonstrated some effectiveness in reducing ID switching which can be caused by occlusion. Its lightweight and simple framework allows for real-time tracking of multiple objects, which makes it suitable for a broad range of applications such as autonomous vehicles and robotics. It can also be easily adapted to improve existing multiple object tracking frameworks. However, because of its usage of relatively simple metrics, BYTETrack demonstrates limited accuracy in crowded scenes with many objects moving amongst each other in close proximity. This is likely due to the reliance on IoU matching and trajectory prediction, which means that it is unable to easily distinguish between objects when their tracklets heavily overlap which can occur frequently. Additionally, the strategy of maintaining the usage of boxes with low confidence scores increases noise that can induce the tracking of irrelevant objects. Finally, BYTETrack does not natively support multi-class tracking as well, which is often a point of interest in many real-world tracking use cases, and thus requires computationally expensive workarounds.

In conclusion, BYTETrack is a relatively simple but highly effective Multiple Object Tracker utilising low confidence boxes to account for object occlusion and appearance changes. It is especially useful as it can be adopted to many existing SOTA MOT algorithms to further boost their performance, whether these trackers are motion-based (IoU matching) or feature-based (ReID feature matching). ByteTrack's ability to track objects in real-time with high accuracy and efficiency makes it suitable for various applications such as autonomous driving, video surveillance, and augmented reality. Although ByteTrack is still in its early stages of development, it holds great potential and it will be exciting to see how ByteTrack evolves and impacts different industries.

This is a comprehensive tutorial article from Datature.io introducing BYTETrack, a multi-object tracking (MOT) algorithm presented at ECCV2022 by Yifu Zhang et al. The article explains the core concepts of MOT, the BYTETrack methodology, and provides a step-by-step tutorial for implementing it with a custom YOLOv8 detector to track basketball players.

**Key Concepts:**
- Multiple Object Tracking (MOT) is a computer vision task that tracks movements of multiple objects over time in video sequences, determining identity, location, and trajectory of each object even when partially or fully occluded.
- MOT typically works in two stages: object detection (using detectors like Faster-RCNN or YOLO) and object association (typically using Kalman Filter for prediction and Hungarian Algorithm for linear assignment).

**Challenges with MOT:** Object motion/appearance variation, occlusion causing ID switching, class switching issues in multi-class trackers, and real-time inference speed limitations.

**BYTETrack Innovation:** The primary innovation is keeping non-background low confidence detection boxes (which are typically discarded after initial filtering) and using them for a secondary association step. Occluded detection boxes have lower confidence scores than the threshold but still contain meaningful information, so retaining them improves tracking consistency.

**Methodology:**
1. Detection boxes are filtered into high-confidence, low-confidence, and background boxes (background boxes are discarded).
2. First association stage: high-score detection boxes matched with predicted boxes from previous frames' tracklets (Kalman filter) using IoU or cosine similarity with Hungarian algorithm.
3. Second association stage: low-score detection boxes matched against remaining unmatched predicted boxes with a lower matching threshold.
4. Lost tracklets are kept for a certain number of frames and can be recovered.

**Implementation Details:** The paper uses YOLOX as the base detector but is customizable to FasterRCNN or other YOLO versions. IoU and ReID both work for first-stage association (ReID better for low-frame-rate videos; IoU more robust for severe occlusion), but second-stage association should always use IoU.

**Tutorial Example:** The author trained a custom YOLOv8m detector on ~90 side-view frames of the 2022 NBA finals between the Warriors and Celtics, tracking three classes: Warriors players, Celtics players, and referees. Annotations were created using Datature Nexus. After 50 epochs (batch size 4, test size 640), the model achieved mAP50 of ~0.9 and mAP50-95 of ~0.65. Since the original BYTETrack implementation is class-agnostic, multiple BYTETracker instances were created for multi-class tracking.

**Key Hyperparameters:** track_thresh = 0.5 (high threshold), track_buffer = 50 (frames lost tracklets kept), match_thresh = 0.8 (first stage matching threshold), aspect_ratio_thresh = 10.0, min_box_area = 1.0, MIN_THRESHOLD = 0.001 (set low to retrieve almost all detections; background threshold hardcoded at 0.1).

**Limitations:** Limited accuracy in crowded scenes due to reliance on IoU matching and trajectory prediction; low-confidence box strategy can introduce noise and track irrelevant objects; no native multi-class tracking support requiring computationally expensive workarounds.

**Conclusion:** BYTETrack is a simple yet effective MOT tracker that uses low-confidence boxes to account for occlusion and appearance changes. It can be adopted to improve existing SOTA MOT algorithms (both motion-based IoU and feature-based ReID) and is suitable for real-time applications like autonomous driving, video surveillance, and augmented reality.

## Highlights

*   •Tackle the challenging problem of detecting shuttlecock in real-time. 
*   •Define a new loss function to better adapt to the task of detecting small objects. 
*   •Modify state-of-the-art deep architecture to retain more semantic information. 
*   •Results on real-world dataset show the effectiveness in both accuracy and speed. 

## Abstract

The ability to identify objects of interest from digital visual signals is critical for many applications of intelligent systems. For such object detection task, accuracy and computational efficiency are two important aspects, especially for applications with real-time requirement. In this paper, we study shuttlecock detection problem of a badminton robot, which is very challenging since the shuttlecock often moves fast in complex contexts, and must be detected precisely in real time so that the robot can plan and execute its following movements. To this end, we propose two novel variants of Tiny YOLOv2, a well-known [deep learning](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/physics-and-astronomy/deep-learning) based detector. We first modify the loss function to adaptively improve the detection speed for small objects such as shuttlecock. We then modify the architecture of Tiny YOLOv2 to retain more semantic information of small objects, so as to further improve the performance. Experimental results show that the proposed networks can achieve high detection accuracy with the fastest speed, compared with state-of-the-art deep detectors such as Faster R-CNN, SSD, Tiny YOLOv2, and YOLOv3. Our methods could be potentially applied to other tasks of detecting high-speed small objects.

## Introduction

Computer vision plays an important role in many applications of expert and intelligent systems, such as security surveillance(Gómez et al., 2015), autonomous driving(Hassannejad et al., 2015, Wu et al., 2017), unmanned aerial vehicles(Al-Kaff et al., 2018), and industrial robots(Cong et al., 2018, Kumra and Kanan, 2017). As a longstanding and fundamental problem in computer vision, object detection aims at automatically determining the existence and spatial location of certain instances of objects in the images(Liu, et al., 2020). It can effectively help autonomous and intelligent systems such as machines or robots to perceive and understand the world better by automatically analyzing digital signals from cameras, and provide critical information for latter decisions such as navigation, motion planning, safety control, etc.

Recently, deep learning based approaches have achieved state-of-the-art performance for the object detection task. As will be mentioned in Section2, these approaches can be categorized as two-stage and one-stage detectors. The former ones, such as Faster R-CNN(Ren et al., 2015), propose a set of candidate regions first and then use a classifier to output the final prediction. In contrast, the later ones such as YOLO(Redmon et al., 2016), directly perform detection on the images without the proposal stage. While accuracy is a key metric for object detection, for many real-world intelligent systems, computational efficiency of the detector is also critical to ensure satisfactory performances(Chakraborty et al., 2016, Wooden et al., 2010). For example, autonomous robots often need to detect obstacles or tracking targets promptly via their vision systems, so that they can plan their actions and control motors based on the detection results in a real-time manner(Alabachi et al., 2019, Guo, et al., 2019). Another example is autonomous driving, where detection of various objects (e.g.cars, pedestrians, road signs) must be done in real time to ensure the right and safe vehicle control(Wu et al., 2017). Moreover, detection tasks in these applications are often done by mobile or embedded devices, which have only limited computing power(Wang et al., 2018). Consequently, though the accuracy is a bit lower, one-stage detection approaches are more ideal in these applications with real-time requirements, since they are often significantly faster in terms of computational efficiency compared with the two-stage ones(Liu, et al., 2020).

In this paper, we focus on the challenging task of detecting shuttlecock for a badminton robot. More specifically, the robot first detects the shuttlecock and fits its trajectory via a visual subsystem, then moves to the specific position and ultimately hit the shuttlecock to the opponents using its hitting device. Due to the high-speed movement of shuttlecocks, the object detection task must be performed in a real-time manner. Generally, the shuttlecock detection task is considered as a single object detection task where the goal is to detect a target object accurately within a series of sequential frames. Although significant progress has been made for general object detection in terms of efficiency and accuracy, it remains an open problem on what is the best deep architecture for different applications. In our case, simply applying existing deep detectors may engender poor performance due to several reasons: (1) scale of the shuttlecock changes quickly during flight, (2) the shuttlecock often moves in complex contexts involving moving objects, athletes, etc., (3) the shuttlecock always moves at high speed, (4) the shuttlecock is usually in white color, which can be very similar to that of the background, leading to background clutter(Cai, et al., 2019, Chen et al., 2019, Henriques et al., 2014, Suzuki, 2017, Zhang, et al., 2020).

We address the above challenges and achieve accurate real-time shuttlecock detection, by analyzing the visual data obtained from a ZED binocular camera mounted on the robot. To meet the requirement on computational efficiency, we design our detection algorithm based on the widely used one-stage detector Tiny YOLOv2(Redmon & Farhadi, 2017). However, the original Tiny YOLOv2 does not give satisfactory performance in detecting shuttlecock. As the main contribution of this paper, we propose two novel networks named M-YOLOv2 and YOLOBR based on Tiny YOLOv2. More specifically, the former one employs a new loss function to better reflect the characteristics of shuttlecock detection. The latter one has a novel neural architecture that ameliorates the issues of losing useful semantic information and accumulating prediction error, which affects the performance of Tiny YOLOv2. Extensive experimental results in various environments show that, compared with state-of-the-art detectors, the two proposed networks exhibit superior performance in terms of both accuracy (measured by precision and recall) and computational efficiency (measured by FPS), and is robust in both simple contexts and complex ones with background clutter.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section2 briefly summarizes existing works related to our task. Section3 describes our method in detail. Section4 displays and analyzes the experimental results of our method and other state-of-the-art deep detectors. Section5 concludes the paper and states our future works.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper (AAAI-22) presents ShuttleNet, a novel framework for stroke forecasting in badminton—the first work to address predicting future strokes (shot types and area coordinates) in turn-based sports. The authors from National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University formulate stroke forecasting as a sequence prediction problem with three key challenges: 1) mixed sequences (two players alternate strokes), 2) multiple outputs at each timestamp (shot type + coordinates), and 3) player dependence (return styles depend on both players' overall styles and rally situation).

The ShuttleNet framework consists of three main components:
- Transformer-Based Rally Extractor (TRE): captures rally progress/current situation using a modified Transformer with a proposed multi-head type-area-attention layer (which separately characterizes importance of shot types and area, inspired by disentangled attention)
- Transformer-Based Player Extractor (TPE): splits the sequence into two subsequences by player (Player A and B) to generate each player's context, with shared parameters and sequence alignment
- Position-Aware Gated Fusion Network (PGFN): fuses rally contexts and both players' contexts using information weights (α) and learnable position weights (β) based on gated multi-modal units

The prediction layer assumes area coordinates follow a bi-variate Gaussian distribution and uses hard parameter sharing with two linear layers to predict shot type and area parameters. Training minimizes combined cross-entropy loss (Ltype) and negative log-likelihood loss (Larea).

Key experimental results:
- Dataset: 75 high-ranking badminton singles matches (2018-2021), 31 players, 180 sets, 4,325 rallies, 43,191 strokes, 10 shot types (net shot, clear, push/rush, smash, defensive shot, drive, lob, drop, short service, long service)
- ShuttleNet outperforms all baselines (Seq2Seq, CF-LSTM, TF, dNRI, DMA-Nets) by at least 12.0% in CE and 3.4% in MSE across all metrics and observed-stroke lengths (τ=2, 4, 8)
- Ablation studies confirmed the necessity of each component (rally extractor, both player extractors, information weights, position weights, and type-area-attention)
- Case study showed players use different area distributions (middle of court vs. near net) when returning against smashes, demonstrating tactic investigation utility

--- SOURCE 1: Capturing Intransitive Dominance in Tennis Forecasting: A Graph Neural Network Approach ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2510.20454v2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an arXiv research paper (v2, reference 2510.20454) titled "Capturing Intransitive Dominance in Tennis Forecasting: A Graph Neural Network Approach" that presents a novel application of graph neural networks (GNNs) to pre-match tennis outcome prediction, specifically targeting intransitive player dominance relationships.

**Core Contribution:** The authors build temporal directed graphs for tennis matches (players as nodes, historical match outcomes as directed weighted edges) and apply MagNet, a spectral graph convolutional network that uses the magnetic Laplacian (a complex Hermitian matrix) to learn from directed cycles and intransitive relationships. This is the first known application of GNNs to pre-match tennis forecasting (a Google Scholar search of 66 queries found no other papers doing so).

**Data:** Historical ATP and WTA match data from tennis-data.co.uk spanning January 8, 2012 to October 16, 2025, filtered to highest-tier events (Grand Slams, tour finals, 1000 and 500 series). Final dataset: 20,181 men's matches (670 players) and 19,985 women's matches (640 players). Validation set of 8,435 matches, held-out test set of 12,052 matches (early 2022 to October 2025). Surface-specific graphs (clay, grass, hard) built per gender. Player static attributes (height, weight, DOB, handedness) were evaluated but excluded as they did not improve accuracy.

**Methodology:** 
- Edge weights based on proportion of games won, adjusted by time decay (λ=0.34), surface transferability (α), and tournament prestige (uniform weights β=1)
- Dominance score aggregates historical match results with weighting; edges point from dominant to dominated player
- MagNet optimised q=0.238 (near maximum directional weighting); 2 layers, K=1 Chebyshev filter, 16 hidden units
- Walk-forward validation: trained on 15% of most recent matches, retrained every 38 snapshots (~quarter year), training under 10 seconds per run on consumer hardware
- 250 trials using Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) via Optuna, multi-objective on men's/women's Brier scores
- Set-win probabilities converted to match probabilities for best-of-3 and best-of-5 formats

**Results (out-of-sample test set):** Overall 65.7% accuracy, 0.214 Brier score. Model ties Weighted Elo on Brier score (0.214) but trails slightly on accuracy (65.7% vs 65.8%). Outperforms standard Elo (65.3%, 0.217) and Bradley-Terry (64.6%, 0.219). Pinnacle Sports bookmaker benchmark remains superior (68.7% accuracy, 0.198 Brier). Model shows strong calibration (reliability term below 0.0001 vs 0.0012 for Weighted Elo).

**Ablation findings:** Graph structure carries most of the predictive signal (removing dominance graph raises Brier from 0.2142 to 0.2492). Most consequential components: edge-age decay (+0.0118), multi-hop receptive field (+0.0095), in/out-degree node features (+0.0058). Directional weighting q and dominance edge weights have smallest effects, suggesting the model's value is a broad complementary signal rather than local intransitivity decoding.

**Intransitivity analysis:** Women's tennis contains 12.3% more cyclic triads than men's. A well-known example cited: Nadal beats Federer (24/40), Federer beats Davydenko (19/21), but Davydenko beats Nadal (6/11). A forecast-encompassing test shows Weighted Elo does not fully subsume the GNN model; a combined forecast significantly outperforms Weighted Elo, with gains growing more strongly on intransitive matchups. This demonstrates the graph-based approach captures forecasting signal that transitive rating systems discard, even between players sharing no common opponents.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Our model (65.7% accuracy, 0.214 Brier score) forecasts competitively with established rating systems such as Weighted Elo. Although it does not improve on the baseline in unconditional accuracy, a forecast-encompassing test shows that it carries complementary information. A combined forecast significantly outperforms Weighted Elo, and there is some indication that the gain grows more strongly on the intransitive matchups our model targets."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This research paper by Szabolcs Csapó (University of Twente, Netherlands, published as TScIT 43, July 4, 2025) investigates the use of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for automated tactic recognition and prediction in the esports game Counter-Strike. The research addresses a knowledge gap in automated, data-driven tactical analysis for Counter-Strike, where most existing work relies on manual review and subjective interpretation.

**Methodology:** The model was trained on the ESTA dataset (1,500 professional matches with up to two frames per second of player/position data). Each round was represented as a graph with nodes (players, bombsites, bomb) and edges capturing relationships like distances. Node features included position (X,Y coordinates, linearly normalized), health, armor, utility (grenade count), area ID, node type, isAlive, and hasBomb. Graph-level features included time remaining and tactic label. The model was built using PyG (torch-geometric 2.6.1) with 128 hidden channels, AdamW optimizer (learning rate 0.0002, weight decay 1e-5), StepLR scheduler, class weights for imbalanced data, and an 80/20 train/test split.

**Results:** The best-performing model was a 2-layered Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) using all available node features, achieving 81.17% accuracy and an F1-score of 0.6945. Key findings: adding health and armor to position features decreased precision, while adding utility significantly improved both recall and precision. The 2-layered GCN outperformed GAT architectures (2-layered GAT: 78.10% accuracy, 0.6831 F1). The confusion matrix showed the model struggled most with distinguishing t_setup_a from execution tactics (setup/execute transitions create ambiguous boundaries). The micro-average AUC was 0.81, with some classes achieving 0.96-1.00 AUC while t_setup_a scored only 0.53. The model was limited to the Dust 2 map.

**Conclusions:** The model's performance is comparable to or exceeds similar studies (Szmida et al. achieved 0.8549 AUC for player actions; Xenopoulos et al. reported 0.8753 AUC for outcome prediction). The research demonstrates that even simple GNNs can perform exceptionally well when the graph representation accurately captures relational structure. Utility usage was identified as a critical feature for tactical classification. Applications include automated dataset labeling, real-time coaching assistants, and AI-driven NPC coordination. Limitations include reliance on human-labeled data (subjectivity/bias), exclusive training on Dust 2, and unexplored alternative graph representations or features.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 7: [PDF] Football Analytics ---
URL: http://www.columbia.edu/~jad2295/Projects/Football%20Analytics.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is a Boston College honors thesis by James DeAntonis, advised by Professor Jamison Wolf (Fall 2017/Spring 2018), exploring the use of Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) for football season modeling and game outcome prediction in the NFL.

**Core Methodology:**
- The thesis proposes HMMs to predict game/season outcomes by modeling the unobservable win/loss streak state behind observable game statistics.
- Unlike a simple two-state (win/loss) chain, the model uses states representing the current winning or losing streak, allowing transition probabilities to capture "momentum" (e.g., probability of winning the next game given the team won its previous two games).
- The observable "emissions" are game stat lines. Winning states share one emission distribution and losing states share another, constructed via "bins" (n-dimensional mega-bins) counted from historical data, preserving dependence among statistical factors.
- The Viterbi algorithm is used to derive the most likely hidden state sequence (wins/losses) given a team's game statistics.
- Six statistical factors were used: points (own/against), rushing yards (own/against), turnover differential, and first down differential.

**Data and Parameter Selection:**
- In-sample data: 2004-2015 NFL seasons; 2016 used as initial out-of-sample data to test ~2,886 possible bin delimiter combinations; the chosen bins were then validated on 2017 as a check against overfitting.
- Statistical factors: passing and rushing metrics capped (passing 0-550, rushing 0-225), with turnover and first-down differentials treated as symmetric (e.g., [a b] means bounds at -b and b, delimiters at -a and a).

**Key Results:**
- Overall predictive success rates hovered between .69 and .78 across all bin possibilities tested on 2016.
- Applied to 2017, the bin sets performed better on average, with two of four metrics surpassing .80 in overall predictive success rate.
- "Chain override rate" (how often the Viterbi algorithm went against simply picking by the pdfs) was greater than .5, suggesting the underlying Markov chain added predictive power and that there is a correlation between streaks and winning otherwise statistically unlikely games.
- Chain override success rates were disappointing on 2017, suggesting limited correlation across a time series for that metric, but the strong mean overall success validated the model over using pdfs alone.

**Conclusions and Limitations:**
- The author concludes HMMs are useful for modeling football seasons and that the results are thought-provoking, though correlation does not imply causation (well-coached teams may continue streaks regardless of stats).
- Shortcomings noted: the NFL's 16-game season yields far fewer data points than other sports, and the lack of long streaks may decrease model efficacy.

The author also includes a personal note that the 2017-18 Philadelphia Eagles (with Carson Wentz and Nick Foles' Super Bowl run) was the subject of mutual interest with his advisor, making the project a memento of the Eagles' championship season.

--- SOURCE 8: Hidden Markov model - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hidden_Markov_model

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is the English Wikipedia article on Hidden Markov Models (HMMs), a statistical Markov model in probability theory. An HMM is a Markov model where observations depend on a latent (hidden) Markov process, with the goal being to learn about the hidden state by observing the observable process.

Key content covered:

1. DEFINITION: An HMM consists of a hidden Markov process (X) and an observable process (Y) where Y's outcomes depend on X in a known way. Y at time t0 is influenced exclusively by X at time t0, and past outcomes are conditionally independent of Y given X at that time. Parameters are estimated via maximum likelihood estimation, with the Baum-Welch algorithm used for linear chain HMMs.

2. APPLICATIONS: HMMs are used in thermodynamics, statistical mechanics, physics, chemistry, economics, finance, signal processing, information theory, pattern recognition (speech recognition, handwriting recognition, gesture recognition, part-of-speech tagging, musical score following, partial discharges), and bioinformatics.

3. EXAMPLES: The article provides two worked examples:
   - The "genie in a room with hidden urns" example illustrating the urn problem generalization, where the genie draws labeled balls from unobservable urns.

**Three Main Deceptive Shot Families:**
1. **Deceptive drop shot** (smash preparation, finished with a short drop) — described as the most accessible and profitable; Viktor Axelsen's favorite weapon, using a slow, ample arm cock and often chaining 3-4 per set.
2. **Deceptive smash** (drop shot preparation, finished with a smash) and its variation (drop prep followed by flat clear/tight drive) — Anthony Sinisuka Ginting specializes in this, playing 100% on wrist angle and forearm speed with identical jumping motion for all shots.

- Stage 4 (week 7+): Integrate deceptive shots every 5-6 points in directed then free play.

- Legal in competition except on serves (BWF rule 9.1.6 prohibits feinting before serve contact).

## ShuttleSet: Badminton Stroke-Level Analytics Dataset

**Overview:** ShuttleSet is the largest publicly available stroke-level badminton singles dataset, designed for tactical analysis and structured turn-based modeling. It was introduced by Wang et al. (2023) and comprises **44 broadcast matches (2018–2021), 104 sets, 3,685 rallies, and 36,492 strokes** involving 27 top-ranking men's and women's singles players. Each stroke is annotated with temporal, spatial, and tactical labels coupled with match-, set-, and rally-level context.

**Dataset Origin and Structure:** Created to fill the gap in turn-based sports analytics (no public, expert-annotated, stroke-by-stroke datasets preserving full tactical structure). Source material is public broadcast video from bwf.tv (not instrumented capture), standardized to 30 fps and 1280×720 resolution. The corpus spans quarter-finals, semi-finals, and finals of top-tier tournaments including Super 1000 events and BWF World Tour Finals. The dataset is structured around rallies (not isolated clips), making it suitable for sequence modeling tasks.

**Annotation Schema:** Four categories per stroke:
- **Rally category**: set scores, rally winner, lose reason (out, touched net, not over net, opponent ball landed, misjudged)
- **Temporal category**: hitting time (seconds) and hitting frame
- **Spatial category**: player A/B locations, shuttle hitting location, categorical grid location, above/below net indicator
- **Hitting category**: stroke status, backhand, around-the-head, shot type

Court coordinates are derived via homography (p′=Hp), with singles-court coordinates defined at corners (0,0), (0,6.1), (13.4,0), (13.4,6.1). A domain-expert grid divides each half court into nine grids plus seven outside grids. The shot taxonomy contains **18 stroke classes** (net shot, smash, lob, clear, drive, drop, push, rush, service types, etc.).

**Labeling Workflow:** Annotated with the S² (Shot-by-Shot) labeling tool in four stages: match preparation, rally segmentation, video preprocessing, and shot-by-shot labeling. Six trained badminton-expert annotators performed labeling. Quality metrics: temporal consistency MAE of 0.24 (serve), 0.02 (return), 0 for dead bird; spatial consistency MAE of 0.18 (shuttle) and 0.86 (player); shot-type consistency accuracy differences of 0.00 (serve), 0.05 (return), 0.11 (dead bird). Distributed through the CoachAI project, with a Python implementation and Flask-based visualization platform used by national badminton teams.

**Native Benchmarks (three tasks):**
1. **Stroke influence** (win-probability estimation): Best model ShuttleScorer achieved AUC 0.8371, ACC 0.7869, BR 0.1574
2. **Stroke forecasting** (predict future shot types and landing locations): Best model ShuttleNet achieved CE 2.4125, MSE 1.8121, MAE 1.3582 (τ=8)
3. **Movement forecasting** (predict future strokes and both players' positions): DyMF best CE 2.3146; ShuttleNet lowest MSE 1.0832, MAE 1.5852

**Later Research Repurposing:**
- **Stroke-type recognition** (Chang, 2025): BST-3 variant achieved Acc 0.7710, Macro-F1 0.7042, Acc-2 0.9340
- **Doubles transfer learning** (Baek et al., 2025): Pose-based Transformer achieved singles accuracy 0.8617, doubles combined accuracy 0.6686; transfer degradation ~19.3% (pose-based) vs ~39.9% (vision-only YOLOv11x)
- **Temporal action localization** (Wang et al., 2026): DSTA adapter achieved average mAP 74.67 across tIoU thresholds
- **Report generation** (Chiang et al., 2026): ShuttleSet+ derived from ShuttleSet22 (58 matches, 140 sets, 3,992 rallies, 33,612 strokes); Tree-of-Text outperformed baselines using ~40% of Chain-of-Table's time/cost

**Limitations:** Singles only; no fixed train/validation/test partition (papers construct own splits); no continuous shuttle trajectories stored; 3D pose lifting unreliable for badminton-specific poses; class imbalance (rare categories: defensive return lob, driven flight, rush); no action interval boundaries requiring synthetic temporal windows.

**Significance:** ShuttleSet established a shared, stroke-level representation on public broadcast video, enabling otherwise disconnected research threads—forecasting, recognition, localization, transfer, and report generation—to operate on a common substrate. Its long-term importance lies in providing a common analytical foundation rather than any single benchmark score.
