SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper, published in Scientific Reports (May 30, 2025, PMC12125242, PMID 40447635), proposes an innovative badminton motion analysis method combining machine learning with quantum mechanics to classify and recognize five typical badminton stroke movements. Authored by Xuanmin Zhu (Fujian Polytechnic Normal University), Lizhi Liu, Jingshuo Huang, Xi Ling (Silpakorn University, Thailand), Genyan Chen (Chengyi University College, Jimei University), and Yanshuo Chen (Fujian Normal University).

The study addresses limitations of traditional stroke analysis (which relies on manual observation and subjective judgment) by introducing a hybrid Quantum Convolutional Neural Network (QCNN) approach. The methodology covers several components: (1) Support Vector Machine (SVM) as a supervised classification algorithm based on maximizing margin hyperplanes; (2) 2D-CNNs for spatial feature extraction with convolutional, pooling, and fully connected layers; (3) 3D-CNNs for spatiotemporal information processing; and (4) a hybrid QCNN that uses quantum convolutional kernels instead of classical ones, leveraging quantum entanglement and parallelism to accelerate computation.

The data was collected from video recordings of four different badminton matches from broadcast/television programs. Key features extracted include arm angle (identified as the most significant feature in QCNN), twist angle, footwork position, grip type, and step length. Data preprocessing involved data cleaning (removing samples with excessive missing values, outlier detection via box plots), Z-score normalization, and data augmentation (time shifting, rotation/scaling, and Gaussian noise addition). The dataset was partitioned into 70% training, 15% validation, and 15% test sets.

The literature review contextualizes this work against prior research, including LSTM-based action recognition achieving 63-92% accuracy (Liu & Liang 2022), a CNN+LSTM+self-attention framework achieving 97.83% accuracy on 37 badminton actions (Deng et al. 2023), and an ensemble SVM/RF/LR model achieving 95.38% accuracy (Asriani et al. 2024). The MultiSenseBadminton dataset (Seong et al. 2024) with 7763 swing data points is also referenced. Quantum optimization methods like Adaptive Quantum Chaotic Ion Motion Optimization (AQCIMO-SVM) and Quantum Water Stepping Algorithm (QWSA) are reviewed as inspiration for combining quantum theory with machine learning.

The study aims to fill a gap in badminton motion analysis by exploring the synergistic effect of machine learning and quantum computing, offering solutions for sports training, technical improvement, and injury prevention.
</summary>

"The primary goal of this study is to propose an innovative badminton motion analysis method that combines machine learning techniques with quantum theory. This approach aims to address the limitations of traditional motion analysis methods by providing an efficient and precise analytical framework."

--- SOURCE 5: ML Beginner's Guide For Badminton Pose Estimation & Trajectory Model ---
URL: https://www.labellerr.com/blog/ml-beginners-guide-for-badminton-pose-estimation-trajectory-model

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a technical guide from Labellerr (a data annotation company) that provides a machine learning beginner's guide to building a badminton pose estimation and shuttlecock trajectory prediction model using computer vision.

## Core Topic
The article presents a method for predicting shuttlecock trajectories in badminton matches by combining shuttlecock position, player positions, and player postures. It uses two modules: a detection/pose estimation module for past frames and a time-series model (LSTM) for future prediction.

## Key Technical Components
- **Faster R-CNN**: Used for player detection, featuring a CNN backbone, ROI pooling layer, and sibling branches for classification and bounding box regression. The feature map size is 60x40x512, with ROI pooling producing (N, 7, 7, 512) output.
- **TrackNet**: A heatmap-based deep learning network chosen for shuttlecock detection because it recognizes the shuttlecock from consecutive frames, enabling detection even when occluded. Its precision, recall, and F1-measure are 99.7%, 97.3%, and 98.5%, respectively—significantly higher than the conventional Archana's algorithm.
- **HRNet**: Used for player pose estimation.
- **LSTM network**: Used for trajectory prediction with mean squared error as the loss function.

## Dataset Details
- Uses the Shuttlecock Trajectory dataset (publicly available on HackMD/GitHub) created for training/testing TrackNet and TrackNetV2.
- Composed of 26 broadcast videos at 1280x720 resolution and 30 fps.
- 78,200 total frames: 23 videos (68,675 frames) from professional games and 3 videos (9,525 frames) from casual play.

--- SOURCE 9: Action Recognition in Tennis - CS229 ---
URL: https://cs229.stanford.edu/proj2012/KatariaSikka-ActionRecognitionInTennis.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is a CS229 (Stanford Machine Learning) course project report on Action Recognition in Tennis by Aman Sikka and Rajbir Kataria of Stanford University. The project's motivation is to automatically recognize tennis actions (forehand, backhand, serve) from match videos so that players can search for and study specific techniques.

**Dataset:** The project used video clips from 3 tennis match videos, totaling 200 clips from the first match and 100 clips each from the second and third matches, limited to right-handed male players and bird's-eye view camera angles. Bounding boxes were manually drawn around players using the VATIC (Video Annotation Tool from Irvine, California) tool. The third dataset was excluded from analysis due to erroneous data (clips contained parts of the scoreboard).

**Algorithm Pipeline:**
1. **Dense Sampling** (key-point detector): Extracts video blocks at regular positions/scales in space-time (5 dimensions: x, y, t, σ, τ). Minimum 3D patch size was 8×8 pixels and 6 frames, with 50% overlap in spatial and temporal sampling (parameters chosen based on best results on UCF50 dataset).
2. **HOG3D Descriptor**: Splits spatio-temporal blocks into M×M×N sub-regions (M=4 spatial, N=3 temporal) and counts 3D gradients aligned with directions of a polyhedral structure. Used an icosahedron (20 orientations), giving 960 total dimensions.
3. **K-means clustering**: Creates a dictionary of visual codewords. Optimal cluster count is 1000-4000; they chose 1000 to reduce computation time since cluster count had negligible effect on results.
4. **Bag-of-Words (BoW)**: Generates histogram representations of videos using the visual word vocabulary.
5. **Classification**: Support Vector Machines (SVMs) with both linear and RBF kernels. Initially tried a 1-vs-all approach but switched to a multi-class classifier. Data was split 70%-30% for training/testing with equal training examples per action.

**Results:** The RBF kernel outperformed the linear kernel by at least 10% on both datasets. For Dataset 1, the confusion matrix (RBF kernel) showed: Forehand correctly classified 66.66% (33.33% misclassified as Serve), Backhand 100% correct, and Serve 100% correct.

**Key Observations:**
1. Actions learned on a player from one match don't generalize well to the same player in a different match (accuracy dropped from over 85% to 60%) due to slight camera angle variations, indicating the need for multiple clips from different matches.
2. Accuracy was 50% when trained on men's matches and tested on women's matches, possibly due to slower play pace.
3. Large illumination variation (shadows on a cloudy day) suggests background removal would be beneficial.
4. RBF kernel is theoretically most appropriate given histogram-based HOG3D and BoW representations; it performed 5-10% better than linear on minimal data, but more data is needed to confirm.

The report includes a comprehensive reference list covering spatio-temporal descriptors, action recognition literature, and related computer vision techniques.
</summary>

**Purpose/Problem:**
The study aims to automatically extract and classify shots in badminton games from monocular camera footage to enable automated sports analytics, helping coaches and players understand opponents' tactics and improve training.

**Methodology:**
The proposed system combines three key modules:
1. **Pose Estimation**: Uses DensePose (chosen over OpenPose due to computational efficiency) to extract player body postures, particularly ankle coordinates, which are projected onto an aerial view via perspective transformation.
2. **Shuttlecock Tracking**: Uses TrackNet, a deep neural network designed for tracking small, fast-moving objects, to extract shuttlecock flight trajectories. TrackNet uses a VGG16 backbone (first 13 layers) with DeconvNet-inspired later layers, plus a trajectory smoothing algorithm with denoising, curve fitting, and interpolation steps.
3. **Shot Refinement Algorithm (SRA)**: The novel contribution of this study. It fuses shuttlecock trajectory-based hit detection (using TrackNet's "Peak Identification Method" and "Direction Identification Method") with YOLOv7-based swing action detection. The SRA categorizes detections into five cases to resolve false positives and detection misses.

The five SRA cases are:
- Case 1: One trajectory-detected hit in a player's hit segment = correct detection
- Case 2: Multiple trajectory hits in a segment with no player ID = false positives, all removed
- Case 3: Multiple trajectory hits in a player's segment = only the hit closest to the highest-confidence frame is retained
- Case 4: No trajectory hit in a player's segment = detection miss; the highest-confidence action frame becomes the hit moment
- Case 5: No trajectory hit in a segment with no player ID = true negative

- The method requires only a monocular camera, making it applicable to existing badminton videos without additional hardware.
- The system also extracts player movement, serving positions, hitting habits, and causes of point loss for coaching analytics.

<summary>
This GitHub repository, "Qualitative Badminton Player Analysis" by @lgupta-mle (completed as a group project with Anannya Popat @Anannyap7), presents a Computer Vision system that takes a professional badminton match video as input and predicts the most probable court location where a shot will be hit by the near-side player. The project's motivation is two-fold: (1) helping aspiring badminton players use the model as a guide for shot placement at the point-of-contact, and (2) enhancing user viewing experience by integrating AI tools into badminton (a sport with less technological support compared to tennis and cricket).

The process consists of four main steps:

4. **Pose Estimation using OpenPose**: Defines 19 individual body parts with paired connections, using a predefined TensorFlow model to generate a graph of lines and points indicating each joint connection.

## CalTennis: Large Multi-View Tennis Video Dataset for 3D Pose Estimation

**Submitted:** 18 Jun 2026 (by researchers at the California Institute of Technology, including Pietro Perona)

**Overview:** CalTennis is a large-scale video benchmark for evaluating monocular-to-3D pose estimation in real-world ("in the wild") settings. It comprises over 11 million frames (51 hours) of tennis practice and match play from 40 players, captured with 2-6 synchronized cameras at 60 Hz. The dataset is 10 times larger than existing in-the-wild human motion video datasets (like 3DPW) and 3 times larger than existing MOCAP-ground-truthed datasets (like Human3.6M), making it the first large-scale benchmark providing synchronized multi-view recordings of expert athletic motion.

**Key Innovations:**
- **Label-free evaluation via multi-view consistency:** Instead of relying on MOCAP ground truth, CalTennis leverages the redundancy of multiple camera views — if a pose estimation model is accurate, its 3D reconstructions from different camera views should be identical when aligned in a shared global coordinate system. Any cross-view disagreement serves as a quantifiable lower bound on reconstruction error.
- **Court geometry for calibration:** Tennis court line intersections (service lines, baselines, sidelines) provide fixed reference points enabling precise, fully automated camera calibration without manual measurements or specialized equipment.
- **Standardized data collection protocol:** Simple, reproducible protocol enabling data collection without specialized equipment or expertise.

**Novel Performance Metrics Introduced:**
1. **Footwork** — detects foot skating/gliding and floating players
2. **Stability** — detects body "jitter" and spatial oscillation
3. **Body shape consistency** — evaluates consistency of body height/limb lengths across camera views

**Benchmark Results (5 SOTA models evaluated: PromptHMR, GVHMR, GENMO, WHAM, TRAM):**
- **Depth/Translation failures:** All models struggled with absolute depth. Translation errors ranged from 0.9m to over 3.6m. Models exhibited "drifting" — players appearing to oscillate along the camera's depth axis even when standing still. PromptHMR was most accurate for translation (due to sophisticated 2D bounding box use) but was also the slowest.
- **Foot-ground contact:** Significant "foot skating" errors persisted even in WHAM, which specifically incorporated foot-ground contact refinements. This makes current models unreliable for professional sports analytics (stride length, ground reaction forces).
- **Body shape inconsistency:** The most surprising finding — different camera views produced different estimated heights and limb lengths for the same person, with up to 20cm height disagreement across views. This indicates models are biased by camera angle and 2D appearance, not just predicting pose.

**Setup Details:** Camera distance ranged from 13.4m to 16.7m (versus ~5m in lab settings), providing greater depth variability representative of real-world sports broadcasting and coaching scenarios.

**Conclusions:** While 3D joint angle recovery is now quite accurate, current models are not yet ready for high-stakes applications in healthcare or professional sports. The dataset and label-free evaluation framework lower the barrier for other researchers to collect and evaluate motion data in diverse real-world environments, paving the way for more democratic and scalable 3D motion analysis technology development.
</summary>

<summary>
## Multi-Object Tracking — DeepSORT, ByteTrack, OC-SORT, and BoT-SORT (2026)

This article by Nikolay Sapunov (CEO of Fora Soft, published May 27, 2026) provides a comprehensive 2026 guide to multi-object tracking (MOT) for production video systems. Multi-object tracking is the process of maintaining stable identity IDs on the same person, car, or package across video frames, connecting a per-frame object detector to downstream features that reason about trajectories (counting, dwell time, sports overlays, active-speaker detection, surveillance).

### The Tracking-by-Detection Pipeline (4 stages)
1. **Detection** — a detector (YOLO, RT-DETR, Grounding DINO) emits bounding boxes per frame; detector quality dominates everything downstream.
2. **Motion prediction** — Kalman filter (1960s algorithm) predicts next-frame positions using a constant-velocity model with state vector (x, y, aspect_ratio, height, dx, dy, dh, dr).
3. **Association** — cost matrix between tracks and detections (IoU geometric distance, appearance cosine distance, or both), solved with the Hungarian algorithm (O(n³)).
4. **Track lifecycle management** — new tracks born, unconfirmed tracks killed after frames, tentative/confirmed status with birth/death thresholds.

### The Four Tracker Families (2026 production standards)
- **DeepSORT (2017)** — introduced deep appearance embeddings (cosine distance) on top of SORT. MOT17: 60.3 MOTA, 61.2 IDF1, 48.8 HOTA. Historical reference; no longer the default for new projects.
- **ByteTrack (ECCV 2022, Zhang et al.)** — associates every detection box including low-confidence ones via a two-stage cascade. MOT17: 80.3 MOTA, 77.3 IDF1, 63.1 HOTA. Motion-only, <50 lines of Python, MIT-licensed (github.com/ifzhang/ByteTrack), ~2x faster than DeepSORT, ships in Ultralytics YOLO as bytetrack.yaml. The 2026 throughput default.
- **OC-SORT (CVPR 2023, Cao et al.)** — fixes Kalman drift after occlusion via observation-centric re-update and observation-centric momentum. MOT17: 78.0 MOTA, 77.5 IDF1, 63.2 HOTA; beats ByteTrack by 10+ HOTA points on DanceTrack (non-linear motion). Best for dance, gymnastics, parkour, animals, sports with direction changes. MIT-licensed (github.com/noahcao/OC_SORT).
- **BoT-SORT (2022, Aharon et al.)** — adds camera-motion compensation (sparse optical flow + ECC alignment) and appearance embeddings (BoT-S50 Re-ID). MOT17: 80.5 MOTA, 80.2 IDF1, 65.0 HOTA — state of the art at publication. Default tracker in Ultralytics YOLO since 2024 (botsort.yaml). Roughly 30% slower than ByteTrack. MIT-licensed (github.com/NirAharon/BoT-SORT).

### Metrics: Why HOTA Replaced MOTA
- **MOTA (2008)** — detection-biased, underweights identity switches.
- **IDF1** — association-focused but detection-blind (overcorrects).
- **HOTA (2020, Luiten et al.)** — √(DetA × AssA), balanced detection and association, reports sub-scores separately. By 2026, HOTA is the field's ranking metric on MOTChallenge, DanceTrack, and SportsMOT.

### Decision Tree (4 questions)
1. **Is the camera moving?** → BoT-SORT (handheld, drone, vehicle-mounted).
2. **Does motion violate constant-velocity?** → OC-SORT (dance, sports, animals, sudden direction changes).
3. **Many streams/dense scenes?** → ByteTrack (no appearance work, runs at detector speed).
4. **Long-occlusion identity persistence?** → BoT-SORT-ReID (5+ seconds of occlusion, multi-camera handoff).

~80% of projects end at ByteTrack or BoT-SORT-ReID.

### Numeric Example (1280×720, 30 FPS, YOLOv8-S, 20 pedestrians, Intel server CPU)
- ByteTrack: 14.4 ms/frame (432 ms/sec CPU, ~43% of one core); 35 concurrent streams per 16-core server; $0.020/stream-hour on AWS c7i.4xlarge.
- BoT-SORT-ReID: 32.6 ms/frame (978 ms/sec, nearly full core); 16 concurrent streams; $0.044/stream-hour.
- Cost-cutting tip: run tracking at 10 FPS (every third frame) for 3× cost reduction with negligible accuracy loss for counting/dwell/fall-detection features.

### Deployment Topologies
- **Browser** — ByteTrack/OC-SORT via ONNX Runtime Web (BoT-SORT-ReID too heavy in 2026).
- **Edge** — all four fit on Jetson Orin Nano; ByteTrack (throughput) or BoT-SORT-ReID (accuracy); default for security cameras, retail, industrial CV.
- **Server** — BoT-SORT-ReID on CPU with GPU detector; default for sports analytics, broadcast, batch processing.

### Four Production Pitfalls
1. **Blaming the tracker for detector problems** — fix detector first; YOLOv8-N→YOLOv8-X buys 10 points vs. a few HOTA points from tracker swaps.
2. **Using DeepSORT in 2026** — outdated; ByteTrack/BoT-SORT-ReID beat it everywhere.
3. **Leaving Kalman/lifecycle parameters at MOT17 defaults** — tune track_buffer and match_thresh via grid search on deployment data.
4. **Trusting track IDs across camera boundaries** — IDs are local to a camera/tracker run; cross-camera identity requires dedicated Re-ID models, shared feature galleries, and graph-solving.

### Fora Soft Usage (context for the author's recommendations)
Video conferencing (ByteTrack on SFU), retail/IVA (BoT-SORT-ReID on Jetson), OTT/broadcast sports (BoT-SORT-ReID on cloud GPUs), e-learning (ByteTrack), surveillance/security (BoT-SORT-ReID).

The article includes 16 references (DeepSORT, SORT, ByteTrack, OC-SORT, Deep OC-SORT, BoT-SORT, HOTA, StrongSORT, BoostTrack, DanceTrack, SportsMOT, CLEAR-MOT papers and implementations) plus editorial notes indicating the BoT-SORT-ReID HOTA figure is from the 2022 paper (current MOT17 leader in mid-2026 is BoostTrack at ~65.4 HOTA), and that transformer-based trackers (MOTR, TrackFormer) remain research-grade and are not yet production-viable.

This is a comprehensive tutorial article from Datature.io introducing BYTETrack, a multi-object tracking (MOT) algorithm presented at ECCV2022 by Yifu Zhang et al. The article explains the core concepts of MOT, the BYTETrack methodology, and provides a step-by-step tutorial for implementing it with a custom YOLOv8 detector to track basketball players.

**Key Concepts:**
- Multiple Object Tracking (MOT) is a computer vision task that tracks movements of multiple objects over time in video sequences, determining identity, location, and trajectory of each object even when partially or fully occluded.
- MOT typically works in two stages: object detection (using detectors like Faster-RCNN or YOLO) and object association (typically using Kalman Filter for prediction and Hungarian Algorithm for linear assignment).

**Challenges with MOT:** Object motion/appearance variation, occlusion causing ID switching, class switching issues in multi-class trackers, and real-time inference speed limitations.

**BYTETrack Innovation:** The primary innovation is keeping non-background low confidence detection boxes (which are typically discarded after initial filtering) and using them for a secondary association step. Occluded detection boxes have lower confidence scores than the threshold but still contain meaningful information, so retaining them improves tracking consistency.

**Methodology:**
1. Detection boxes are filtered into high-confidence, low-confidence, and background boxes (background boxes are discarded).
2. First association stage: high-score detection boxes matched with predicted boxes from previous frames' tracklets (Kalman filter) using IoU or cosine similarity with Hungarian algorithm.
3. Second association stage: low-score detection boxes matched against remaining unmatched predicted boxes with a lower matching threshold.
4. Lost tracklets are kept for a certain number of frames and can be recovered.

**Implementation Details:** The paper uses YOLOX as the base detector but is customizable to FasterRCNN or other YOLO versions. IoU and ReID both work for first-stage association (ReID better for low-frame-rate videos; IoU more robust for severe occlusion), but second-stage association should always use IoU.

**Tutorial Example:** The author trained a custom YOLOv8m detector on ~90 side-view frames of the 2022 NBA finals between the Warriors and Celtics, tracking three classes: Warriors players, Celtics players, and referees. Annotations were created using Datature Nexus. After 50 epochs (batch size 4, test size 640), the model achieved mAP50 of ~0.9 and mAP50-95 of ~0.65. Since the original BYTETrack implementation is class-agnostic, multiple BYTETracker instances were created for multi-class tracking.

**Key Hyperparameters:** track_thresh = 0.5 (high threshold), track_buffer = 50 (frames lost tracklets kept), match_thresh = 0.8 (first stage matching threshold), aspect_ratio_thresh = 10.0, min_box_area = 1.0, MIN_THRESHOLD = 0.001 (set low to retrieve almost all detections; background threshold hardcoded at 0.1).

**Limitations:** Limited accuracy in crowded scenes due to reliance on IoU matching and trajectory prediction; low-confidence box strategy can introduce noise and track irrelevant objects; no native multi-class tracking support requiring computationally expensive workarounds.

**Conclusion:** BYTETrack is a simple yet effective MOT tracker that uses low-confidence boxes to account for occlusion and appearance changes. It can be adopted to improve existing SOTA MOT algorithms (both motion-based IoU and feature-based ReID) and is suitable for real-time applications like autonomous driving, video surveillance, and augmented reality.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 16: Detecting the shuttlecock for a badminton robot: A YOLO based approach ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0957417420306436

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in Expert Systems with Applications (Volume 164, February 2021, Article 113833) by Elsevier, authored by Zhiguang Cao, Tingbo Liao, Wen Song, Zhenghua Chen, and Chongshou Li. The paper, titled "Detecting the shuttlecock for a badminton robot: A YOLO based approach," addresses the challenging problem of real-time shuttlecock detection for a badminton robot.

The research tackles a critical computer vision problem where the shuttlecock must be detected precisely in real-time so the robot can plan and execute its movements. The challenges include: (1) rapid scale changes of the shuttlecock during flight, (2) complex contexts with moving objects and athletes, (3) high-speed movement, and (4) white shuttlecock color blending with backgrounds causing clutter.

The authors propose two novel variants of Tiny YOLOv2 (a one-stage deep learning detector):
- **M-YOLOv2**: Modifies the loss function to adaptively improve detection speed for small objects like shuttlecocks.
- **YOLOBR**: Features a novel neural architecture that retains more semantic information of small objects and addresses issues of losing semantic information and accumulating prediction error.

Visual data was obtained from a ZED binocular camera mounted on the robot. Experimental results show the proposed networks achieve high detection accuracy (measured by precision and recall) with the fastest speed (measured by FPS) compared to state-of-the-art detectors including Faster R-CNN, SSD, Tiny YOLOv2, and YOLOv3. The methods are robust in both simple and complex contexts with background clutter, and could potentially be applied to other tasks involving high-speed small object detection.

The article is cited by 102 sources and has 113 Mendeley readers. The authors collected a large-scale annotated shuttlecock dataset. Funding support was provided by the National Natural Science Foundation of China, MOE Academic Research Fund of Singapore, and Singapore National Research Foundation.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 17: Instant review system for badminton: computer vision ... ---
URL: https://spyro-soft.com/blog/artificial-intelligence-machine-learning/instant-review-system-for-badminton-computer-vision-use-case

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a technical case study from Spyrosoft (a software company) describing their development of a computer vision-based instant review system for badminton. The system was created for a client to automatically determine whether a shuttlecock landed in or out of the court, addressing the challenge that shuttlecocks travel at speeds exceeding 400 km/h (world record: 493 km/h measured in a 2013 laboratory test), making it difficult for line judges to make accurate calls.

**System Overview & Workflow:** Multiple cameras are positioned to cover all court lines and areas. Video streams feed into computers that analyze shuttle trajectory and calculate landing position by comparing against a court model. Players can challenge line judge decisions by raising their hand; the umpire sends the challenge to a system operator who runs the verification procedure. The system generates an animation showing the result to players, judges, spectators, and TV broadcasters.

**Design Requirements:** Maximum accuracy; verification procedure under 25 seconds; installation under 4 hours per court; no more than two installers; minimal equipment footprint; video recording at 150-200 FPS; near real-time response; efficient algorithms running on inexpensive PC computers.

**Key Technical Solutions:**
- **Camera Calibration:** Custom calibration software using a board with circles; minimum reprojection error of 0.086px.
- **Court Recognition:** Uses modified Mask R-CNN for court detection/segmentation (97.7% accuracy), Hough transform on Sobel filter output to find lines, Bentley-Ottmann algorithm and Harris corner detector for line intersections/corners; masks are dilated to ensure all lines are visible.
- **Hybrid Algorithm Approach:** Uses simple fast differential-frame detection, with neural network patches only when the first method loses the object. With a 9th Gen Intel Core i7 and NVIDIA GTX 1080, the system processes two cameras at up to 200 FPS (800×600 resolution).
- **Flickering Light Handling:** Developed an adaptive pixel-wise mask-generation method to compensate for flickering light in older venues. The method is 250-300 times faster than commercial DeFlicker and FlickerFree tools.
- **Shuttlecock Detection/Tracking:** Challenges include the shuttlecock appearing as circle or triangle depending on camera angle, size variation, speeds from 24 to 400 km/h, white color blending with the scene, complex backgrounds, and unpredictable trajectory due to the cone shape and off-center center of gravity. Solution uses accumulative differential frames (from 7 consecutive differential images) plus shape segmentation (processing under 2ms), and a Kalman filter to predict position, feeding 104×104 px patches to a modified Tiny YOLO neural network (12ms processing). The neural network achieved 94% mean average precision, with 0.96 precision, 0.77 recall, and 0.86 F1-score at a 0.25 threshold.
- **Ground Hit Detection:** Combines trajectory-change detection with a blurriness measure (variance of Laplacian), since shuttlecock speed changes more significantly than trajectory upon ground contact.

**Performance Results:** Tracker detects shuttlecock visibility with 94% accuracy; 81% of visible shuttlecocks were correctly detected and tracked (within 12 pixels). The system delivers a correct decision in 62% of cases, with a human operator confirming the final in/out decision due to accumulated pipeline errors.

**Validation Method:** Tested on 52 annotated sets of frames (20,788 total frames) from real tournament recordings where players challenged line judge decisions; footage saved at 150-190 FPS for 30-second segments per challenge.

**Future Work:** Improving accuracy through higher-resolution cameras and/or more cameras; high resolution is mainly needed at the moment of ground impact while higher acquisition speed is needed for detecting the rebound moment; super-resolution algorithms are a potential area of investigation. The automatic decision must be presented within 10-25 seconds.

The article also includes an FAQ section (covering how the system works, computer vision's role, machine learning techniques used, challenges, accuracy, and real-time applicability), ten academic references, and links to related videos about badminton shuttlecock physics.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 18: One-Shot Badminton Shuttle Detection for Mobile Robots ---
URL: https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2603.06691

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper (submitted March 17, 2026) presents a robust one-shot badminton shuttlecock detection framework designed specifically for non-stationary/mobile robots, developed by researchers (Turcan Tuna and Marco Hutter) from the Robotic Systems Lab at ETH Zurich.

KEY CONTRIBUTIONS:
1. **New egocentric dataset**: 20,510 semi-automatically annotated frames captured at 1920×1200 resolution and 60 FPS across 11 distinct indoor and outdoor backgrounds, categorized into Easy, Medium, and Hard difficulty levels.
2. **Semi-automatic annotation pipeline**: A four-step process exploiting stationary camera footage (background subtraction, opponent masking, candidate selection) that achieved 85.7% initial accuracy, with only 5.9% of frames requiring manual correction.
3. **Novel evaluation metric**: A distance-based scheme replacing IoU, where a detection is a True Positive if the Euclidean distance between predicted and ground truth center is within τ=25 pixels (similar to Distance Precision Rate used in tracking). This is more meaningful for robotics since center accuracy matters more than bounding box dimensions.
4. **Fine-tuned YOLOv8 small model**: Achieved F1-score of 0.86 in test environments similar to training and 0.70 in entirely unseen environments. 95.9% of the dataset (Easy and Medium samples) was used for training, with Mixup data augmentation significantly improving recall.

KEY FINDINGS:
- Detection performance is critically dependent on shuttlecock size and background texture complexity.
- Performance is stable when the shuttlecock is larger than 20 pixels; recall declines for smaller instances (when the shuttlecock is far from the robot), indicating a physical limit to one-shot detection at current resolutions.
- Unlike prior work using stationary cameras (e.g., TrackNet), this detector is designed for egocentric, dynamic viewpoints of mobile robots, essential for system initialization and recovery when tracking is lost.
- Qualitative tests with a moving camera confirmed generalization: high accuracy in uniform backgrounds (open court) and best performance when shuttlecock was silhouetted against the sky in cluttered environments.

The work provides an open-source foundation for sports-playing robots, addressing a significant gap in robotic perception. Future work may explore multi-frame architectures or attention mechanisms for very small, distant objects.
</summary>

"We propose a metric suited to our downstream use case and fine-tune a YOLOv8 network optimized for real-time shuttlecock detection, achieving an F1-score of 0.86 under our metric in test environments similar to training, and 0.70 in entirely unseen environments."
</key_excerpts>

International Journal of Computer Science Trends and Technology (IJCST) – Volume 13 Issue 6, Nov-Dec 2025 ISSN: 2347-8578 www.ijcstjournal.org Page 26 A Critical Analysis of Existing Technologies in Squash Training: Towards an Automated Training Court Evana Gada ABSTRACT The integration of technology into sports training has transformed performance analysis across many disciplines, yet its adoption in squash has been comparatively limited. Existing tools, ranging from image and video processing to sensor-based systems and emerging artificial intelligence applications, typically measure discrete aspects such as player positioning, ball trajectory, or racket motion but rarely operate in an integrated manner. This review synthesizes evidence to identify persistent technological gaps in squash, focusing on challenges of real-time accuracy, environmental constraints of the court, inconsistent standards across systems, and the scarcity of sport-specific datasets. Usability and cost barriers further restrict access, particularly for junior, para, and community-level athletes. Addressing these limitations is essential if technological solutions are to progress from isolated analytics toward comprehensive, accessible tools capable of transforming training practices in the sport. Keywords:- squash training I. INTRODUCTION Technology has become a defining feature of modern sports training, offering athletes new ways to monitor, analyze, and refine performance. In disciplines such as tennis, football, and athletics, innovations in motion tracking, wearable sensors, and artificial intelligence have shifted coaching from a predominantly observational practice to a data-driven endeavor. Real-time statistics, biomechanical analysis, and predictive modeling are now widely integrated into elite environments and are gradually filtering down to community and youth levels. These developments have altered not only how performance is measured but also how tactical and strategic decisions are made during practice and competition. Despite these advances in other sports, squash remains a relatively underexplored case in the field of technology-assisted training. As a fast-paced, indoor racquet sport with unique spatial and tactical demands, squash presents specific barriers for performance monitoring. The confined court, frequent player overlap, and rapid exchanges complicate traditional tracking methods. Unlike tennis or badminton, where player movements and ball trajectories can be captured with fewer obstructions, squash requires more complex systems to deliver reliable data. Consequently, the integration of advanced technological tools in squash has lagged behind, leaving a fragmented landscape of partially effective solutions. Existing tools for squash tend to address isolated aspects of performance. Video-based systems provide tactical insights, wearable sensors track swing dynamics and workload, and commercial platforms are experimenting with artificial intelligence for shot classification and rally reconstruction. However, these technologies rarely interact, resulting in siloed outputs that are difficult for coaches and players to interpret holistically. As a result, even professional squash athletes still rely heavily on traditional observation and subjective feedback. While valuable, such methods lack the objectivity and precision that integrated technology could offer. The slow pace of innovation in squash training arises from technical, practical, and economic challenges. The court geometry makes unobstructed video capture difficult, especially when players obscure one another or the ball. The rapid nature of rallies demands high-frame-rate cameras and advanced algorithms capable of real-time analysis. Wearable devices face barriers of accuracy, comfort, and standardization, while the sport’s smaller global market compared to tennis or football reduces incentives for large-scale commercial investment. As a result, most innovations emerge from research prototypes or niche startups rather than validated, widely adopted systems. This paper addresses these challenges by critically examining the current technological landscape in squash RESEARCH ARTICLE OPEN ACCESS International Journal of Computer Science Trends and Technology (IJCST) – Volume 13 Issue 6, Nov-Dec 2025 ISSN: 2347-8578 www.ijcstjournal.org Page 27 training. Specifically, the review evaluates available tools in four domains—image and video processing, sensor-based systems, artificial intelligence and machine learning, and virtual or augmented reality. Within each domain, the discussion highlights both contributions and limitations. The scope of this study is conceptual rather than experimental. No new technologies are tested directly; instead, findings from existing literature are synthesized to identify recurring challenges and persistent barriers. By grounding the analysis in squash-specific contexts, the paper avoids overgeneralizations from other racquet sports and provides a more accurate account of the sport’s unique demands. The significance of this investigation lies in its potential to guide future innovation. By clarifying why squash-specific technologies have lagged and identifying the gaps they face, possible pathways toward more integrated and effective systems can be proposed. This paper therefore contributes to both academic discussions on sports technology and the practical needs of athletes, coaches, and developers seeking to modernize training practices in squash. In summary, squash’s fast pace, constrained environment, and tactical complexity make it both a promising candidate for technological support and a difficult sport in which to implement effective systems. This paper asks: Why have squash-specific technologies lagged, and how can an integrated framework overcome these limitations? To answer this, the following sections analyze existing technologies, examine their shortcomings, and propose directions for future innovation. II. IMAGE AND VIDEO PROCESSING SYSTEMS (BALL TRACKING, PLAYER TRACKING, MOTION ANALYSIS) A. Data Acquisition and Instrumentation Image pipelines begin with video capture. Squash research typically uses two types of sources: (a) broadcast or competition video (single rear camera, common in PSA archives) and (b) purpose-built multi-camera rigs (ceiling- or wall-mounted) for laboratory or club analyses. Baclig et al. (2020) demonstrated a pipeline using broadcast footage at 25 fps and 720 × 576 resolution to extract kinematic metrics from elite matches. Other systems—both research and commercial—deploy high-frame-rate cameras or multi-camera arrays to improve metric accuracy and enable depth recovery (Baclig et al., 2020; Brumann et al., 2021). Key acquisition variables documented in squash studies include:  Frame rate and exposure — Ball and impact detection benefit from higher frame rates. Most squash analyses use 25–60 fps broadcast video (Baclig et al., 2020), with purpose-built cameras employed when finer temporal resolution is needed.  Camera geometry — Single fixed rear/center cameras (common in broadcast) versus multi-angle arrays (ceiling or side-mounted), which enable triangulation and inverse-perspective mapping (Baclig et al., 2020; Vučković et al., 2014). B. Preprocessing and Court Calibration Preprocessing converts pixel coordinates into standardized court coordinates via homography or inverse-perspective mapping. Typical steps include: 1. Frame selection — Isolating in-play frames (Baclig et al., 2020). 2. Court calibration — Detecting or manually setting reference points (corners, lines) to compute a planar homography mapping pixels to a 2D court plane. Vučković et al. (2014) used annotated reference points from behind-court views to assign ball bounces reliably to their 15-zone partitioning. 3. Image normalization — Color balancing, denoising, and occasional background subtraction (for small-object detection) before detector input. C. Player Detection, Pose Estimation, and Tracking Two main approaches appear in the literature: a) Bounding-box detectors with trackers (tracking-by-detection): Object detectors such as YOLO variants, Faster R-CNN, or SSD generate person bounding boxes per frame, which are then linked by trackers (e.g., SORT, DeepSORT) using motion prediction and appearance descriptors. This architecture is common in multi-person sport tracking and underlies many squash proof-of-concepts. International Journal of Computer Science Trends and Technology (IJCST) – Volume 13 Issue 6, Nov-Dec 2025 ISSN: 2347-8578 www.ijcstjournal.org Page 28 b) Human-pose estimation (HPE) pipelines: Modern squash studies increasingly adopt HPE methods, as pose keypoints yield richer kinematic features (e.g., limb angles, foot positions). OpenPose (Cao et al., 2017), HRNet (Sun et al., 2019), and related networks are widely referenced. Brumann et al. (2021) systematically benchmarked over 250 HPE models, selecting pre-trained networks suitable for squash foot detection and heatmap generation. A typical squash HPE–tracking pipeline proceeds as follows: 1. HPE inference per frame → body/foot/keypoint heatmaps. 2. Keypoint grouping → assemble skeletons using part-affinity fields or affinity scoring. 3. Identity association → maintain skeleton continuity across frames using Kalman filtering, appearance embeddings, or heuristic matching (SORT/DeepSORT adaptations). 4. Court mapping → apply homography to convert keypoints into court-plane coordinates, enabling metrics such as distance covered, time on the T, and velocity (Baclig et al., 2020). Outputs from these pipelines include per-frame player positions, velocity/acceleration measures, central-T heatmaps, left/right foot step counts, step cadence, and lunge biomechanics when sufficient keypoints are detected (Brumann et al., 2021; Baclig et al., 2020). D. Ball Detection and Trajectory Reconstruction Ball tracking is treated separately due to the ball’s small size, high speed, and frequent occlusion. Reported approaches include: 1. Direct detection — Training detectors for small-object recognition. Frame differencing and motion-based proposals are effective when resolution permits. With multiple views, triangulation can improve accuracy, but broadcast footage often limits visibility (Baclig et al., 2020). 2. Predictive interpolation/physics priors — Algorithms fit ballistic motion models or spline curves constrained by ball dynamics to interpolate gaps in detection. Multi-view setups allow full 3D trajectories. 3. Audio fusion — Microphone arrays (e.g., 96 kHz sampling) detect impacts and localize them using time-of-arrival differences. Audio signatures also enable shot-type classification and impact-energy estimation (Hajdú-Szücs et al., 2018). E. Event Segmentation and Labelling After detection, events are grouped into rallies and labelled (e.g., shot type classification using video windows ± audio cues). Vučković et al.’s (2014) 15-zone taxonomy is frequently applied for tactical categorization. F. Evaluation and Reported Outputs Evaluation metrics vary by task: mean absolute percent error for kinematic estimates (Baclig et al., 2020), precision/recall or average precision for detection, and motion-density heatmap comparisons for tracking outputs (Brumann et al., 2021). III. ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND MACHINE LEARNING APPLICATIONS (PATTERN RECOGNITION, PREDICTIVE ANALYTICS) The squash analytics stack typically follows a layered architecture: low-level feature extraction (from video, IMU, or audio) → mid-level event and shot classification → high-level sequence modeling and predictive analysis. G. Feature Extraction Inputs to machine learning models derive from multiple modalities:  Visual features — Keypoint coordinates, bounding boxes, optical flow, and localized image patches around racket, ball, or impact regions. HPE networks such as OpenPose (Cao et al., 2017) and HRNet (Sun et al., 2019) supply skeleton features for tactical and biomechanical modeling.  Sensor features — IMU acceleration and gyroscope signals, including time-domain features (peak magnitude, RMS), frequency-domain features (spectral energy near impact), and derived biomechanics metrics (swing angular velocity). Racket-mounted devices typically output per-shot summaries (e.g., impact timestamp, swing duration).  Audio features — Event onset times, spectrogram slices, and time-difference-of-arrival (TDOA) localization outputs. Hajdú-Szücs et al. (2018) International Journal of Computer Science Trends and Technology (IJCST) – Volume 13 Issue 6, Nov-Dec 2025 ISSN: 2347-8578 www.ijcstjournal.org Page 29 demonstrated their use in both localization and shot classification. H. Shot Classification and Pattern Recognition Two main categories of models are applied:  Frame/snippet classifiers — Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) or CNNs with temporal pooling are used to classify shot types (drive, drop, boast, volley). For motion dependencies, 3D CNNs (e.g., C3D) or two-stream networks (RGB + optical flow) capture temporal dynamics. Baclig et al. (2020) employed per-shot visual features combined with pose cues for classification.  Sequence models — Recurrent neural networks (e.g., LSTMs) model shot-to-shot dependencies within rallies, learning tactical transitions such as probability of a defensive lob following backcourt pressure. These models are trained on annotated rally sequences and are applied for rally reconstruction, motif discovery, and tactical analysis (Baclig et al., 2020). I. Predictive Analytics and Tactical Inference ML-based prediction has been applied to tactical forecasting and player profiling:  Rally outcome prediction — Supervised models (logistic regression, random forests, neural networks) map state vectors (player positions, fatigue proxies, last shot type) to probabilities of rally outcomes or next-shot types. Commercial platforms highlight such outputs as "key moment" analyses.  Opponent profiling and style clustering — Unsupervised methods (k-means, hierarchical clustering, HMMs) identify archetypes such as short-game aggressors versus attrition players. Vučković et al.’s (2014) 15-zone mapping often provides the feature basis for these analyses. Model Training and Data Considerations Model development in squash research is shaped by limited dataset availability:  Annotation pipelines — Brumann et al. (2021) developed a squash-specific dataset with frame-level foot annotations, while Baclig et al. (2020) used manually tracked frames as validation ground truth. Manual annotation remains critical due to the absence of large public corpora.  Transfer and pre-training — Many studies adapt models pre-trained on general datasets (e.g., COCO, MPII) for pose and detection tasks, with OpenPose and HRNet forming the most common backbones (Cao et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2019).  Evaluation practices — Performance is typically reported using detection average precision (AP), tracking measures such as MOTA/MOTP, rally classification accuracy, and kinematic error versus manual labels. Baclig et al. (2020) reported mean absolute percent errors of ~3–4% for distance and speed estimates. IV. SENSOR TECHNOLOGIES (WEARABLES, RACKET SENSORS, COURT SENSORS) J. Racket-Mounted Sensors The most common form factor is a small IMU module mounted at the butt of the racket, typically sampling at several hundred Hz. For example, Racketware reports sampling rates up to ~500 Hz, with data streamed to a mobile app (Racketware, 2021). These systems measure acceleration and angular velocity, either computing features on-device or post-processing them on paired devices. Derived metrics include peak acceleration, swing duration, racket head speed, impact angle, and heuristic shot labels. Typical signal processing steps are: 1. Onset detection — Identifying impact via short, high-magnitude acceleration spikes with adaptive thresholds. 2. Window extraction — Capturing fixed-length signal windows around impact (e.g., ±50 ms). 3. Feature extraction — Deriving time-domain (peak, impulse, RMS), frequency-domain (spectral centroid), and waveform-shape descriptors (e.g., zero-crossing). 4. Shot classification — Applying shallow classifiers (SVMs, decision trees) or compact neural networks for per-shot labelling. K. Wearable IMUs and Physiological Sensors International Journal of Computer Science Trends and Technology (IJCST) – Volume 13 Issue 6, Nov-Dec 2025 ISSN: 2347-8578 www.ijcstjournal.org Page 30 IMUs positioned on the wrist, ankle, or torso produce continuous acceleration and angular velocity streams, which are used to quantify workload (e.g., step detection, lunge counts, peak accelerations). When fused with vision-based tracking via homography, IMU data can be mapped to court locations. Prototypes with synchronized IMUs have been employed to study explosive movements and lunge biomechanics. Processing typically involves integration to estimate velocity (with drift correction), activity recognition through temporal models, and workload indices (e.g., PlayerLoad-style metrics). L. Smart-Court Sensors and Environmental Instrumentation Instrumented court systems integrate multiple sensing modalities: ceiling-mounted cameras, floor-embedded pressure sensors, microphone arrays, and projection systems (PSA & interactiveSQUASH, 2018). These environments generate court-referenced data directly—such as player footprints and ball bounce locations—without requiring external camera homography per match. Smart courts typically fuse camera-based detections, embedded sensor data, and racket IMU outputs using synchronized timestamps, enabling richer event records (e.g., impact localization, shot type labelling, workload analysis). For example, Hajdú-Szücs et al. (2018) demonstrated high-accuracy ball impact localization using multi-channel audio sampled at 96 kHz. V. OTHER RELEVANT TOOLS — COMPARISONS WITH TENNIS & BADMINTON SYSTEMS (TECHNOLOGY PRIMITIVES AND ADOPTED PRACTICES) M. Tennis and Hawk-Eye (Multi-Camera Triangulation) Hawk-Eye represents the gold standard in racket sport tracking, employing multiple high-speed cameras (hundreds of fps) placed around the court to achieve millimeter-level trajectory reconstruction (Hawk-Eye Innovations, n.d.). The system applies subpixel ball detection per view, multi-camera triangulation, and model-based smoothing (e.g., Kalman filters) to generate precise 3D trajectories and line calls. Outputs include replay visualizations, shot speeds, and landing point accuracy. While conceptually transferable to squash, this approach faces domain-specific challenges: the enclosed court architecture and the squash ball’s higher incidence of wall interactions require adaptations in camera placement, calibration, and trajectory modeling. Research solutions deploy high-frame-rate, multi-view camera setups combined with motion-blur compensation and aerodynamics-aware motion models. The shuttlecock’s unique flight dynamics necessitate specialized detectors and trajectory algorithms. These design adaptations illustrate how domain-specific physics shape engineering choices—principles that can be applied to squash, where the ball’s frequent occlusions and wall bounces similarly demand tailored tracking solutions. SUMMARY of EXISTING TECHNOLOGIES International Journal of Computer Science Trends and Technology (IJCST) – Volume 13 Issue 6, Nov-Dec 2025 ISSN: 2347-8578 www.ijcstjournal.org Page 31 VI. GAP ANALYSIS OF EXISTING TECHNOLOGIES P. Limitations: Accuracy, Real-Time Data, and Scalability Despite advances in image processing and machine learning, several limitations remain. In ball tracking, the squash ball’s small size, rapid acceleration, and frequent occlusion often force algorithms to interpolate trajectories rather than measure them directly. Even high-performing systems such as Baclig et al.’s (2020) tracker produce frame-level errors that propagate into downstream metrics such as positional heatmaps and velocity estimates. Moreover, these models generally require controlled lighting and unobstructed views, conditions rarely met in community courts. Real-time feedback is another critical challenge. Most pipelines process video offline due to the computational demands of deep learning inference and the need for temporal smoothing, resulting in latency that prevents in-game tactical adjustments. Scalability also restricts adoption. Multi-camera rigs demand extensive calibration, synchronization, and data storage, making them viable for elite tournaments but impractical for most clubs. This disparity widens the gap between professional and grassroots squash. Machine learning systems inherit similar constraints. Predictive models require large, annotated datasets, yet most squash datasets are either limited in size or proprietary. Consequently, models trained in one context (e.g., elite matches) often underperform when applied across different player levels, genders, or age groups. Sensor technologies present additional trade-offs. Racket-mounted IMUs can quantify swing metrics but frequently misclassify shot types with similar kinematics (e.g., forehand drive vs. volley). Wearable IMUs measure workload but lack tactical context, while smart-court prototypes suffer from calibration drift and environmental noise. Overall, current systems are more suited to controlled demonstrations or retrospective analytics than to robust, real-time coaching support. Q. Missing Features: Lack of Integration Across Movement, Ball, and Player Analysis A consistent limitation across existing systems is fragmentation. Image processing tracks spatial features such as player positions and ball bounces, sensors capture biomechanical data, and machine learning models classify or predict events. However, these domains rarely converge into an integrated framework. For example, ball-tracking systems estimate bounce positions but cannot link them to biomechanics, while racket sensors quantify swing velocity without situating that action within tactical context. Coaches, however, require synthesis— connecting how a shot was executed with why it was chosen and how it influenced rally momentum. Other racket sports illustrate the potential of integration. Tennis’s Hawk-Eye simultaneously provides ball trajectories, player movements, and shot classification, creating a holistic tactical record. Squash, by contrast, lacks unified platforms. The absence of integrated datasets prevents advanced analyses, such as correlating biomechanical workload with tactical decisions or linking fatigue with error patterns. This highlights a pressing need for technologies capable of fusing visual, sensor, and predictive data streams into a coherent analytic ecosystem. R. Usability Issues: Complexity, Cost, and Adoption Even when technically effective, many systems face usability barriers. Image-based systems often require complex calibration, while machine learning outputs may appear as “black boxes” with limited interpretability for coaches. Cost is another constraint. Interactive systems such as interactiveSQUASH require permanent court modifications and substantial investment, while even more accessible solutions (e.g., racket sensors) can become cost-prohibitive when scaled across teams. This restricts access largely to elite players, raising equity concerns for junior, para-athletes, and low-resource communities. Adoption is further influenced by cultural factors. Many coaches rely on experiential judgment and may view technology as intrusive or redundant without clear validation of performance benefits. Players, similarly, may resist systems International Journal of Computer Science Trends and Technology (IJCST) – Volume 13 Issue 6, Nov-Dec 2025 ISSN: 2347-8578 www.ijcstjournal.org Page 32 that disrupt training flow or generate excessive data rather than actionable insights. Thus, beyond technical barriers, practical alignment with coaching culture, resource availability, and user experience remains essential for successful implementation. VII. WHY NO INTEGRATED SYSTEM EXISTS YET: TECHNICAL, ECONOMIC, AND DESIGN CONSTRAINTS The absence of a fully integrated squash analytics system, comparable to tennis’s Hawk-Eye, can be explained by converging technical, economic, and design barriers. Technically, squash presents challenges that exceed those of open-court sports. The enclosed four-wall court generates frequent occlusions, reflections, and lighting inconsistencies, complicating video-based tracking. The ball’s small size, high velocity, and low visual contrast demand more computationally intensive models than those typically required in tennis or badminton. Multimodal fusion remains underdeveloped: synchronizing video, sensor, and audio data is hindered by sampling discrepancies and synchronization drift. Economically, squash represents a comparatively niche market. The smaller global player base and commercial footprint reduce incentives for large-scale investment. As a result, solutions such as interactiveSQUASH or Racketware emerge from small, independent firms with limited resources, restricting both scalability and long-term robustness. From a design perspective, existing tools have largely been developed in isolation. Proprietary architectures frequently silo data, preventing interoperability and integration. Academic prototypes, while often innovative, remain experimental and rarely transition into sustainable commercial applications. These combined constraints explain why squash technologies remain fragmented, valuable within their domains but collectively unable to deliver comprehensive, real-time, and widely adopted performance systems. VIII. PROPOSED CONCEPT: AUTOMATED SQUASH TRAINING COURT (ASTC) To address these deficits, this paper conceptualizes an Automated Squash Training Court (ASTC): an integrated environment in which visual, sensor, and algorithmic technologies operate in tandem to generate holistic performance analysis. The design envisions a training ecosystem where multimodal data streams are synchronized, fused, and interpreted to produce actionable feedback for both players and coaches. S. Conceptual Design The ASTC recognizes that squash presents a uniquely challenging environment, with frequent occlusion, rapid ball velocities (often exceeding 270 km/h at elite level), and enclosed lighting conditions. To mitigate these constraints, the system is designed around multimodal capture rather than reliance on any single modality. A distributed camera array forms the visual backbone. Ceiling-mounted panoramic units capture global player positioning, while high-speed corner cameras provide fine-resolution ball trajectories. Multiple perspectives reduce occlusion risk and ensure continuity of tracking. The court itself functions as an additional sensing platform. Embedded floor sensors detect footfalls with millisecond resolution, recording recovery patterns and acceleration. Impact-sensitive wall panels capture precise ball–wall contact points and force, supporting trajectory reconstruction when video tracking is unreliable. Complementary racket-mounted IMUs record swing mechanics such as velocity, orientation, and impact timing. Unlike full-body wearables, this minimally intrusive solution provides key biomechanical data without overburdening players. All streams converge in a central computational engine. Convolutional neural networks process video for player skeletons and ball positions, while recurrent models (e.g., LSTMs) interpret sequences as rallies. Timestamp alignment enables cross-modal integration, linking swing mechanics, movement patterns, and tactical outcomes into coherent performance narratives. T. Complementarity of Technologies The innovation of the ASTC lies not in any single subsystem but in their orchestration. Each modality addresses the weaknesses of the others. Cameras provide spatial awareness but are limited by occlusion and motion blur; floor and wall sensors ensure continuity when visual tracking fails. International Journal of Computer Science Trends and Technology (IJCST) – Volume 13 Issue 6, Nov-Dec 2025 ISSN: 2347-8578 www.ijcstjournal.org Page 33 IMUs capture stroke dynamics but gain tactical relevance only when contextualized within rally flow. Machine learning serves as the integrative layer, harmonizing heterogeneous inputs into unified, interpretable patterns. For example, when video loses the ball due to blur, wall sensors provide impact data that allow trajectory reconstruction. When a racket accelerometer registers high swing velocity, video and rally context determine whether this produced an effective winner or an error. By synthesizing across modalities, the ASTC potentially enables analyses such as identifying fatigue-induced errors, correlating recovery speed with rally outcomes, or quantifying tactical risk–reward trade-offs. U. User Experience Adoption depends not only on technical feasibility but also on user-centered design. The ASTC envisions distinct interfaces for coaches and players.  Coaches access a dashboard aggregating performance over drills, matches, or training blocks. Visualizations such as heatmaps, rally flow diagrams, and tactical efficiency indices enable evidence-based evaluations. Crucially, the system emphasizes interpretability, highlighting causal contributors (e.g., late preparation preceding cross-court errors) rather than presenting opaque model outputs.  Players receive simplified, motivational feedback via mobile applications or real-time projections. Post-session summaries highlight trends (e.g., “average rally duration increased by 12% with fewer unforced forehand errors”), while practice projections reinforce positional awareness. By tailoring outputs to different users, the ASTC seeks to reduce cognitive load while maintaining analytical rigor. Longitudinal storage of multimodal data further supports athlete development, enabling coaches to monitor biomechanical, tactical, and endurance changes over extended periods. IX. FEASIBILITY AND FUTURE CONSIDERATIONS The Automated Squash Training Court (ASTC) offers a conceptual framework that addresses key deficiencies in current squash analytics, particularly fragmentation, lack of real-time feedback, and usability challenges. However, while the design potentially enables advances in accuracy, integration, and accessibility, its feasibility is constrained by unresolved technical, economic, and cultural factors. V. Technical Challenges The foremost technical barrier lies in multimodal data fusion. Aligning video feeds, floor sensors, racket-based IMUs, and wall impact panels requires synchronization at the millisecond scale. Without seamless integration, inconsistencies across modalities risk introducing new errors rather than eliminating existing ones. Even advanced systems in better-resourced sports, such as tennis, continue to face challenges in achieving robust, real-time multimodal synchronization. Latency remains another critical issue. For the ASTC to provide tactical feedback within training sessions or near real-time post-rally analysis, the computational pipeline must be both high-throughput and low-delay. Squash’s fast ball velocities and frequent occlusions demand high-performance processing. While cloud computing could enable scalability, data transfer introduces additional latency. An effective balance between on-site (edge) processing and cloud analytics will be essential. Data availability also constrains feasibility. Current squash-specific datasets are limited, often proprietary, and lack diversity across playing levels, genders, and tactical situations. Training robust machine learning models requires large, annotated datasets; without this foundation, algorithmic accuracy will remain brittle. Finally, hardware reliability must be ensured. Floor and wall sensors must withstand repeated high-intensity impacts and environmental stresses, while calibration routines need to run automatically to maintain validity across sessions. Hardware durability remains an underexplored challenge in sports technology deployment. W. Economic Considerations and Accessibility The squash market is comparatively small, limiting commercial incentives for large-scale investment. Implementing the ASTC would require significant upfront costs for cameras, sensors, computational infrastructure, and software development. For context, commercial systems such as interactiveSQUASH already demand permanent court modifications and high installation fees, restricting adoption to select clubs and academies. Similarly, Racketware sensors International Journal of Computer Science Trends and Technology (IJCST) – Volume 13 Issue 6, Nov-Dec 2025 ISSN: 2347-8578 www.ijcstjournal.org Page 34 have gained traction only in niche segments, illustrating the difficulty of achieving scale without institutional backing. Accessibility therefore becomes a central concern. If only elite facilities can afford advanced systems, the ASTC risks reinforcing inequalities in the sport. Scalable adoption may depend on tiered deployment models:  Short-term: single-camera and low-cost IMU systems for grassroots coaching.  Mid-term: hybrid camera–sensor prototypes deployed in regional academies for validation.  Long-term: full multimodal ASTC installations supported by federations and professional tournaments. Subscription-based analytics platforms could further distribute costs by reducing hardware dependence and shifting computational loads to shared cloud resources. Additionally, federation-level support may be critical, as demonstrated by Hawk-Eye’s integration into professional tennis through endorsement by governing bodies. X. Adoption and Cultural Factors Even if technically feasible and economically viable, adoption depends on cultural acceptance by coaches and players. Squash retains a strong tradition of experiential coaching and athlete intuition, and technologies perceived as intrusive or opaque may be resisted. To address this, the ASTC must prioritize explainability, demonstrating why a recommendation is made by linking outcomes to clear biomechanical and tactical indicators. Furthermore, institutional inertia is a significant barrier. Unlike tennis, which has normalized line-calling and broadcast technologies, squash has historically lagged in adopting performance technologies. Overcoming this resistance will require pilot studies and longitudinal trials demonstrating measurable performance benefits. Advocacy from governing bodies and integration into coaching education could accelerate cultural acceptance. X. ROADMAP FOR DEVELOPMENT 1. Short-term (1–3 years): o Expansion of squash-specific open datasets for training robust machine learning models. o Development of low-cost, single-modality systems (e.g., camera-only or IMU-only) for grassroots use. o Initial pilot studies in controlled environments to evaluate technical feasibility. 2. Mid-term (3–6 years): o Deployment of hybrid camera–sensor systems in elite academies. o Validation studies assessing impact on player performance, injury prevention, and tactical development. o Development of coach- and player-facing interfaces with emphasis on explainability. 3. Long-term (6–10 years): o Full ASTC implementations in national training centers and professional events. o Federation endorsement to standardize analytics workflows across competitive levels. o Scaled-down modular versions for community clubs, leveraging economies of scale. XI. CONCLUSION This paper examined the technological landscape of squash training, highlighting key limitations that prevent existing systems from providing comprehensive, reliable, and accessible support. While advances in ball tracking, stroke recognition, and wearable monitoring exist, current tools remain fragmented and fail to integrate movement, tactical, and contextual data into a unified ecosystem. The main gaps identified include limited real-time accuracy, lack of integration across ball, player, and tactical dimensions, high complexity and cost, and low trust among coaches and players due to insufficient explainability and validation. These barriers explain why squash has not reached the level of technological adoption seen in sports like tennis or badminton. The Automated Squash Training Court (ASTC) is presented as a conceptual blueprint to address these systemic shortcomings. By combining multimodal inputs—video, sensors, and machine learning—the ASTC envisions overcoming fragmentation, enhancing contextual feedback, and broadening accessibility, while complementing coaching expertise rather than replacing it. The contribution of this paper lies in critically mapping the strengths and weaknesses of current technologies and International Journal of Computer Science Trends and Technology (IJCST) – Volume 13 Issue 6, Nov-Dec 2025 ISSN: 2347-8578 www.ijcstjournal.org Page 35 proposing conditions for an integrated system to emerge. Future work should focus on developing datasets, conducting pilot testing, and involving federations to validate and refine such holistic training ecosystems. In conclusion, advancing squash training requires moving beyond incremental improvements to isolated tools toward creating integrated, player-centered systems. This research article, "A Critical Analysis of Existing Technologies in Squash Training: Towards an Automated Training Court" by Evana Gada (published in IJCST, Volume 13 Issue 6, Nov-Dec 2025, ISSN: 2347-8578), critically examines the current technological landscape in squash training and proposes a conceptual Automated Squash Training Court (ASTC).

PURPOSE: The paper addresses why squash-specific technologies have lagged behind other racquet sports (tennis, badminton, football) and proposes an integrated framework to overcome these limitations. It synthesizes existing literature rather than conducting new experiments.

KEY TECHNOLOGY DOMAINS ANALYZED:
1. IMAGE/VIDEO PROCESSING: Broadcast video (25-60 fps) and multi-camera rigs; court calibration via homography/inverse-perspective mapping; player detection via bounding-box trackers (YOLO, Faster R-CNN + SORT/DeepSORT) and human-pose estimation (OpenPose, HRNet); ball tracking via small-object detection, physics-informed interpolation, and 96 kHz audio fusion for impact localization; event segmentation using Vučković et al.'s 15-zone taxonomy.

2. AI/ML APPLICATIONS: Layered architecture (feature extraction → shot classification → sequence modeling). CNNs/3D CNNs/two-stream networks classify shot types (drive, drop, boast, volley); LSTMs model tactical transitions; supervised classifiers predict rally outcomes; unsupervised methods (k-means, HMMs) profile player styles. Key accuracy figure: Baclig et al. (2020) reported mean absolute percent errors of ~3-4% for distance and speed estimates.

3. SENSOR TECHNOLOGIES: Racket-mounted IMUs (e.g., Racketware, ~500 Hz sampling) measure swing speed, impact detection; wearable IMUs track workload, steps, lunges; smart courts (interactiveSQUASH) integrate cameras + pressure sensors + projectors.

4. COMPARATIVE TOOLS: Tennis Hawk-Eye (multi-camera triangulation, millimeter-level tracking) and badminton shuttle tracking (high-fps cameras, motion-blur compensation) serve as benchmarks.

IDENTIFIED GAPS:
- Ball tracking limitations due to small size, rapid acceleration, occlusion (algorithms often interpolate rather than measure)
- Real-time processing largely unavailable (most pipelines process offline)
- Fragmentation: ball, player, and tactical analyses rarely integrated into unified systems
- Usability barriers: complex calibration, high costs, "black box" ML outputs
- Cost restricts access to elite players, raising equity concerns for junior, para, and community athletes
- Limited squash-specific datasets (mostly proprietary or small)
- Cultural resistance from coaches relying on experiential judgment

PROPOSED SOLUTION (ASTC): An integrated environment combining ceiling-mounted panoramic cameras, high-speed corner cameras, embedded floor sensors (millisecond footfall detection), impact-sensitive wall panels (ball-wall contact points and force), racket-mounted IMUs, and a central computational engine with CNNs and LSTMs. Cross-modal timestamp synchronization links swing mechanics, movement patterns, and tactical outcomes. Features distinct interfaces for coaches (interpretable dashboards with heatmaps, rally flow diagrams) and players (motivational mobile feedback).

FEASIBILITY CONSTRAINTS: Millisecond-scale multimodal synchronization, latency management (balancing edge vs. cloud processing), limited diverse datasets, hardware durability under high-intensity impacts, high upfront costs, and cultural/institutional inertia.

DEVELOPMENT ROADMAP:
- Short-term (1-3 yrs): Open datasets, low-cost single-modality systems, pilot studies
- Mid-term (3-6 yrs): Hybrid camera-sensor systems in elite academies, validation studies
- Long-term (6-10 yrs): Full ASTC in national training centers, federation endorsement, modular versions for community clubs
