SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper introduces BST (Badminton Stroke-type Transformer), a novel architecture for skeleton-based action recognition in racket sports, specifically for classifying player stroke-types in singles badminton. The research addresses the challenges of distinguishing subtle differences between badminton strokes in broadcast match videos.

Key contributions:
1. A novel video segmentation strategy that extracts frames of each player's racket swing, segmenting match videos into stroke clips containing two to three strokes each. This variable-width clipping strategy captures complete shuttlecock trajectories in three stages: the shuttlecock flying toward the target player, the trajectory after being hit by the target player, and the direction after the opponent's response.

2. BST models that combine player poses (2D skeletal joints from RTMPose via MMPose), shuttlecock trajectories (2D positions from TrackNetV3), and player positions as inputs. The architecture is derived from TemPose but shifts focus from player poses to shuttlecock trajectory as a primary input.

3. Multiple BST variants (BST-0 through BST-3) incorporating features like Pose Position Fusion (PPF), Clean Gate modules for filtering trajectory noise, and cosine similarity-based player weighting (α coefficient) to determine which player has stronger correlation to the shuttlecock trajectory.

Results: BST-3 achieves state-of-the-art performance on the ShuttleSet dataset (largest publicly available badminton video dataset, containing 104 sets, 3,685 rallies, and 36,492 strokes across 44 matches between 2018-2021). Key results include Acc of 0.7695, Macro-F1 of 0.7043, and Acc-2 of 0.9267, outperforming prior methods including TemPose, ST-GCN, BlockGCN, SkateFormer, and ProtoGCN. The model demonstrates superior generalization with reduced training sets and outperforms TemPose on 7 of 9 metrics.

Notable findings:
- Effectively leveraging shuttlecock trajectory information significantly improves stroke classification performance.
- 2D poses outperform 3D poses due to HPE model bias toward general human poses.
- The model struggles with high-granularity stroke categories that have similar hitting characteristics (e.g., smash vs. wrist smash).
- Training BST-3 takes 29 sec per epoch on an NVIDIA RTX 4070 Ti Super, converging faster than TemPose-TF.

The dataset uses 35 stroke categories (19 original stroke types doubled for top/bottom player positions, plus a "none" category). The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Va6lue/BST-Badminton-Stroke-type-Transformer.
</summary>

This study, published in Scientific Reports (volume 15, Article 41236, 2025), presents a wearable sensing system for badminton stroke recognition using a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN). 2. BALL DETECTION: Used TrackNet deep learning network trained on a dataset of 19,835 labeled frames from 10 broadcast videos (1280×720, 30 fps). The network generates a heatmap from a 2D Gaussian distribution centered on the ball (assumed ~10 pixel diameter variance). Training used binary cross entropy loss. Evaluation used a positioning error (PE) specification of 5 pixels (mean ball diameter in videos is ~5 pixels, ranging 2-12 pixels). Frames were labeled with Visibility Class (VC) values 0-3 indicating ball visibility.

3. BOUNCE DETECTION: Used CatBoostRegressor machine learning for binary classification to detect bounce frames from ball trajectory data (features included differences in x/y coordinates between neighboring points and distance relations). Dataset had 18,570 samples with 518 labeled as bounce points. Used 10-fold cross-validation (9 games train, 1 game test) with grid search for hyperparameters (iterations, learning rate, depth). Evaluated on precision and recall, with tolerance of ±1 frame error. Adding 0.5 weight to neighboring bounce points during training improved recall significantly.

4. PLAYER DETECTION: Used pretrained Faster RCNN neural network.

The complete pipeline: (1) court detection with pretrained neural network to get homography matrix per frame, (2) ball detection using 3 consecutive frames, (3) bounce detection, and (4) player detection and movement mapping to the reference court.

The article also lists possible improvements: replacing backbones with lighter nets, quantizing/pruning for speed, combining ball and court detection into one neural network, adding frames without balls to improve ball detection, and using augmentation for court detection training.

The conclusion states the tool can automatically detect and track court, ball trajectory, player movements, and identify outs during a match, with the neural network approach being faster, more robust, and more effective than classical CV methods.

Code implementations are available on GitHub: TennisCourtDetector (https://github.com/yastrebksv/TennisCourtDetector), TrackNet (https://github.com/yastrebksv/TrackNet), and TennisProject (https://github.com/yastrebksv/TennisProject).

**Project Overview & Objectives:** The project addresses a gap in automated analysis tools for tennis doubles—a strategically complex sport that is under-explored relative to singles tennis, basketball, and soccer. It aims to: (1) develop a standardised video annotation framework for doubles tennis (player positions, shot types, formations, outcomes), (2) build an intuitive tennis labelling tool, and (3) automate data collection/analysis through computer vision (player detection/tracking, pose estimation, shot classification). **Key Methods & Models:** 
- Used GroundingDINO for precise player localisation via descriptive phrase grounding, and YOLO-Pose for pose estimation—together reducing manual annotation effort.
- Tested a two-stage pipeline combining YOLOv11 + Deep SORT for tracking, but found limitations with occlusions, far-court players, and identity switching.
- The GroundingDINO + YOLO-Pose combination significantly improved detection of far players and enabled player identification based on visual descriptions.
- CNN-based models using transfer learning outperformed pose-based approaches in predicting shot type, player positioning, and formations.

**Annotation Framework:** Organises data into four core categories—player information (description, dominant hand), positional information (net position, court position in Far/Near Deuce/Advantage quadrants), frame information (bounding boxes, poses), and rally information (start/end frames, hitting moments). Detailed labelling rules govern shot-direction-formation and court-side-direction combinations based on handedness.

**Tool Features (5 main pages):** Player Annotation (video upload, bounding boxes, COCO format saving), Training & Inference (GroundingDINO training + YOLO-Pose inference with real-time status), Rally Analysis (net position marking, rally creation, hitting moment annotation), Label Generation (Random/CNN/Gemini prediction models), and Label Confirmation (review/edit with tennis rule validation).

**Performance Results:** Backend optimisations using model hot-loading reduced inference time dramatically (from 12 min 35s cold start to 54s hot loading for 54 rallies, though GPU usage rose from 0.8GB to 3.2GB). Detection accuracy varied by video quality: for a lower-quality NCAA rally (952 frames), GroundingDINO+YOLO-Pose achieved 100%/100%/69.8%/64.3% for players P1-P4 with player identification, vs. YOLOv11+DeepSORT's 100%/95.6%/43.4%/0.1%. For a professional-quality Indian Wells 2022 match (451 frames), GroundingDINO+YOLO-Pose achieved 100%/100%/89.4%/84.1%.

**Data Sources:** Videos from professional matches (YouTube highlights) and semi-professional NCAA videos from Louisiana State University. Eight labelled videos were used with a 70-30 train/validation split, holding out two unseen videos (Salisbury_Ram vs Krawietz_Puetz Toronto 2023 for professional, VUPKfQgXy8g for NCAA) for testing.

Fuzzification improved results for all datasets (THETIS by 2.21-2.98%, Tennis-Mocap by 4.42-6.47%, 3DTennisDS by 5.23-7.44%). The 3DTennisDS achieved the best precision, recall, and F1 scores for all individual strokes, with F1 scores reaching over 90% for all fuzzy strokes. Common misclassifications occurred between forehand/volley forehand and backhand/volley backhand pairs. LOOCV validation yielded RMSE of 8.99%±5.81% (non-fuzzy) and 7.74%±4.11% (fuzzy) for 3DTennisDS. The study concludes that marker-based optical motion capture data acquisition methods and input fuzzification significantly improve tennis stroke recognition accuracy.

--- SOURCE 1: Deep learning neural network-assisted badminton movement recognition and physical fitness training optimization ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11620146

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in Heliyon (October 2, 2024) titled "Deep learning neural network-assisted badminton movement recognition and physical fitness training optimization," authored by Chuanbao He (Department of Physical Education, Tianjin Sino-German University of Applied Sciences, China) and Min Zhang (Graduate School, Metharath University, Bangkok, Thailand). The corresponding author is Chuanbao He (hechuanbao@tsguas.edu.cn). The article is open access under a CC BY-NC-ND license.

**Objective:** The research addresses the problem of low accuracy in recognizing badminton movement trajectories, focusing on the visual system of badminton robots for lateral detection and tracking of flying badminton in two-dimensional video streams.

**Methodology:**
1. **Visual system design:** Image segmentation and edge detection separate badminton from backgrounds; Kalman filtering enables real-time tracking.
2. **CNN with attention mechanisms:** A dedicated CNN architecture with convolutional layers, pooling layers, fully connected layers, and ReLU activation functions extracts features from lateral badminton images. Attention modules adjust feature map weights to focus on critical information, improving robustness against variations and noise.
3. **Improved Tiny YOLOv2:** The network was enhanced by adding convolutional layers, increasing channels, adjusting receptive field sizes, and introducing residual connections to mitigate gradient vanishing. The loss function was revised to incorporate trajectory information (position and movement direction), optimizing localization, confidence, classification, and trajectory losses.
4. **Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF):** Combined with the improved Tiny YOLOv2, the UKF predicts future badminton positions using Sigma points propagated through nonlinear functions, accounting for factors like wind force.

**Dataset:** A custom dataset was created with 15 badminton flight video streams captured via stereo vision cameras across scenarios including laboratories, parking lots, sports arenas, forests, and roadsides. Scenes were categorized as simple or complex based on background, lighting, and interference. Each scene contains ~100-150 consecutive frames (~1000 total frames), split into training/testing sets at a 2:1 ratio. Training parameters: learning rate 0.001, batch size 16, epochs 50, ReLU activation, 3x3 convolution kernels. Hardware: NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU with TensorFlow and CUDA.

**Key Results:**
- Average tracking accuracy: 91.40%; recall rate: 84.60%
- F1 score: 87.68%; frame rate: 13.792 FPS; IoU: 0.922
- Average precision, recall, and frame rate in four simple/complex scenarios: 96.7%, 95.7%, and 29.2 FPS respectively
- Per-scenario results: Orange wall (precision 97.14%, recall 90.91%, F1 93.92%, 19.76 FPS); Green wall (95.12%, 93.67%, F1 94.39%, 26.3 FPS); Laboratory (90.91%, 89.47%, F1 90.18%, 7.36 FPS); Parking lot (92.5%, 69.64%, F1 79.46%, 7.11 FPS); Park (81.34%, 79.45%, F1 80.47%, 8.43 FPS)
- Average predicted position error: ~3.76 pixels; average predicted distance error: ~0.26 m; maximum errors ~8.80 pixels and 0.60 m
- Average total time consumption for prediction: ~35.03 ms

**Conclusions:** The proposed method outperforms other classic algorithms in badminton trajectory detection and prediction, demonstrating superior accuracy, robustness, and adaptability across various complex scenarios, providing reliable support for badminton movement recognition and physical fitness training optimization.
</summary>

## CalTennis: Large Multi-View Tennis Video Dataset for 3D Pose Estimation

**Submitted:** 18 Jun 2026 (by researchers at the California Institute of Technology, including Pietro Perona)

**Overview:** CalTennis is a large-scale video benchmark for evaluating monocular-to-3D pose estimation in real-world ("in the wild") settings. It comprises over 11 million frames (51 hours) of tennis practice and match play from 40 players, captured with 2-6 synchronized cameras at 60 Hz. The dataset is 10 times larger than existing in-the-wild human motion video datasets (like 3DPW) and 3 times larger than existing MOCAP-ground-truthed datasets (like Human3.6M), making it the first large-scale benchmark providing synchronized multi-view recordings of expert athletic motion.

**Key Innovations:**
- **Label-free evaluation via multi-view consistency:** Instead of relying on MOCAP ground truth, CalTennis leverages the redundancy of multiple camera views — if a pose estimation model is accurate, its 3D reconstructions from different camera views should be identical when aligned in a shared global coordinate system. Any cross-view disagreement serves as a quantifiable lower bound on reconstruction error.
- **Court geometry for calibration:** Tennis court line intersections (service lines, baselines, sidelines) provide fixed reference points enabling precise, fully automated camera calibration without manual measurements or specialized equipment.
- **Standardized data collection protocol:** Simple, reproducible protocol enabling data collection without specialized equipment or expertise.

**Novel Performance Metrics Introduced:**
1. **Footwork** — detects foot skating/gliding and floating players
2. **Stability** — detects body "jitter" and spatial oscillation
3. **Body shape consistency** — evaluates consistency of body height/limb lengths across camera views

**Benchmark Results (5 SOTA models evaluated: PromptHMR, GVHMR, GENMO, WHAM, TRAM):**
- **Depth/Translation failures:** All models struggled with absolute depth. Translation errors ranged from 0.9m to over 3.6m. Models exhibited "drifting" — players appearing to oscillate along the camera's depth axis even when standing still. PromptHMR was most accurate for translation (due to sophisticated 2D bounding box use) but was also the slowest.
- **Foot-ground contact:** Significant "foot skating" errors persisted even in WHAM, which specifically incorporated foot-ground contact refinements. This makes current models unreliable for professional sports analytics (stride length, ground reaction forces).
- **Body shape inconsistency:** The most surprising finding — different camera views produced different estimated heights and limb lengths for the same person, with up to 20cm height disagreement across views. This indicates models are biased by camera angle and 2D appearance, not just predicting pose.

**Setup Details:** Camera distance ranged from 13.4m to 16.7m (versus ~5m in lab settings), providing greater depth variability representative of real-world sports broadcasting and coaching scenarios.

**Conclusions:** While 3D joint angle recovery is now quite accurate, current models are not yet ready for high-stakes applications in healthcare or professional sports. The dataset and label-free evaluation framework lower the barrier for other researchers to collect and evaluate motion data in diverse real-world environments, paving the way for more democratic and scalable 3D motion analysis technology development.
</summary>

The conclusion notes that with larger, more diverse datasets and further refinement, the models could be applied in real-time scenarios using high-speed cameras for live match tracking, and expanded to track multiple players simultaneously for doubles matches and training sessions. SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Multi-Object Tracking — DeepSORT, ByteTrack, OC-SORT, and BoT-SORT (2026)

This article by Nikolay Sapunov (CEO of Fora Soft, published May 27, 2026) provides a comprehensive 2026 guide to multi-object tracking (MOT) for production video systems. Multi-object tracking is the process of maintaining stable identity IDs on the same person, car, or package across video frames, connecting a per-frame object detector to downstream features that reason about trajectories (counting, dwell time, sports overlays, active-speaker detection, surveillance).

### The Tracking-by-Detection Pipeline (4 stages)
1. **Detection** — a detector (YOLO, RT-DETR, Grounding DINO) emits bounding boxes per frame; detector quality dominates everything downstream.
2. **Motion prediction** — Kalman filter (1960s algorithm) predicts next-frame positions using a constant-velocity model with state vector (x, y, aspect_ratio, height, dx, dy, dh, dr).
3. **Association** — cost matrix between tracks and detections (IoU geometric distance, appearance cosine distance, or both), solved with the Hungarian algorithm (O(n³)).
4. **Track lifecycle management** — new tracks born, unconfirmed tracks killed after frames, tentative/confirmed status with birth/death thresholds.

### The Four Tracker Families (2026 production standards)
- **DeepSORT (2017)** — introduced deep appearance embeddings (cosine distance) on top of SORT. MOT17: 60.3 MOTA, 61.2 IDF1, 48.8 HOTA. Historical reference; no longer the default for new projects.
- **ByteTrack (ECCV 2022, Zhang et al.)** — associates every detection box including low-confidence ones via a two-stage cascade. MOT17: 80.3 MOTA, 77.3 IDF1, 63.1 HOTA. Motion-only, <50 lines of Python, MIT-licensed (github.com/ifzhang/ByteTrack), ~2x faster than DeepSORT, ships in Ultralytics YOLO as bytetrack.yaml. The 2026 throughput default.
- **OC-SORT (CVPR 2023, Cao et al.)** — fixes Kalman drift after occlusion via observation-centric re-update and observation-centric momentum. MOT17: 78.0 MOTA, 77.5 IDF1, 63.2 HOTA; beats ByteTrack by 10+ HOTA points on DanceTrack (non-linear motion). Best for dance, gymnastics, parkour, animals, sports with direction changes. MIT-licensed (github.com/noahcao/OC_SORT).
- **BoT-SORT (2022, Aharon et al.)** — adds camera-motion compensation (sparse optical flow + ECC alignment) and appearance embeddings (BoT-S50 Re-ID). MOT17: 80.5 MOTA, 80.2 IDF1, 65.0 HOTA — state of the art at publication. Default tracker in Ultralytics YOLO since 2024 (botsort.yaml). Roughly 30% slower than ByteTrack. MIT-licensed (github.com/NirAharon/BoT-SORT).

### Metrics: Why HOTA Replaced MOTA
- **MOTA (2008)** — detection-biased, underweights identity switches.
- **IDF1** — association-focused but detection-blind (overcorrects).
- **HOTA (2020, Luiten et al.)** — √(DetA × AssA), balanced detection and association, reports sub-scores separately. By 2026, HOTA is the field's ranking metric on MOTChallenge, DanceTrack, and SportsMOT.

### Decision Tree (4 questions)
1. **Is the camera moving?** → BoT-SORT (handheld, drone, vehicle-mounted).
2. **Does motion violate constant-velocity?** → OC-SORT (dance, sports, animals, sudden direction changes).
3. **Many streams/dense scenes?** → ByteTrack (no appearance work, runs at detector speed).
4. **Long-occlusion identity persistence?** → BoT-SORT-ReID (5+ seconds of occlusion, multi-camera handoff).

~80% of projects end at ByteTrack or BoT-SORT-ReID.

### Numeric Example (1280×720, 30 FPS, YOLOv8-S, 20 pedestrians, Intel server CPU)
- ByteTrack: 14.4 ms/frame (432 ms/sec CPU, ~43% of one core); 35 concurrent streams per 16-core server; $0.020/stream-hour on AWS c7i.4xlarge.
- BoT-SORT-ReID: 32.6 ms/frame (978 ms/sec, nearly full core); 16 concurrent streams; $0.044/stream-hour.
- Cost-cutting tip: run tracking at 10 FPS (every third frame) for 3× cost reduction with negligible accuracy loss for counting/dwell/fall-detection features.

### Deployment Topologies
- **Browser** — ByteTrack/OC-SORT via ONNX Runtime Web (BoT-SORT-ReID too heavy in 2026).
- **Edge** — all four fit on Jetson Orin Nano; ByteTrack (throughput) or BoT-SORT-ReID (accuracy); default for security cameras, retail, industrial CV.
- **Server** — BoT-SORT-ReID on CPU with GPU detector; default for sports analytics, broadcast, batch processing.

### Four Production Pitfalls
1. **Blaming the tracker for detector problems** — fix detector first; YOLOv8-N→YOLOv8-X buys 10 points vs. a few HOTA points from tracker swaps.
2. **Using DeepSORT in 2026** — outdated; ByteTrack/BoT-SORT-ReID beat it everywhere.
3. **Leaving Kalman/lifecycle parameters at MOT17 defaults** — tune track_buffer and match_thresh via grid search on deployment data.
4. **Trusting track IDs across camera boundaries** — IDs are local to a camera/tracker run; cross-camera identity requires dedicated Re-ID models, shared feature galleries, and graph-solving.

### Fora Soft Usage (context for the author's recommendations)
Video conferencing (ByteTrack on SFU), retail/IVA (BoT-SORT-ReID on Jetson), OTT/broadcast sports (BoT-SORT-ReID on cloud GPUs), e-learning (ByteTrack), surveillance/security (BoT-SORT-ReID).

The article includes 16 references (DeepSORT, SORT, ByteTrack, OC-SORT, Deep OC-SORT, BoT-SORT, HOTA, StrongSORT, BoostTrack, DanceTrack, SportsMOT, CLEAR-MOT papers and implementations) plus editorial notes indicating the BoT-SORT-ReID HOTA figure is from the 2022 paper (current MOT17 leader in mid-2026 is BoostTrack at ~65.4 HOTA), and that transformer-based trackers (MOTR, TrackFormer) remain research-grade and are not yet production-viable.
</summary>

"The single most important decision is not which algorithm to pick but how strong your detector is — every modern tracker is detector-driven, and a weak detector cannot be saved by a clever association step.", "ByteTrack is the right default for any project where the detector is strong, the objects do not change appearance much, and the scene does not involve aggressive camera motion. --- SOURCE 15: An Introduction to BYTETrack: Multi-Object Tracking by ... ---
URL: https://datature.com/blog/introduction-to-bytetrack-multi-object-tracking-by-associating-every-detection-box

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive tutorial article from Datature.io introducing BYTETrack, a multi-object tracking (MOT) algorithm presented at ECCV2022 by Yifu Zhang et al. The article explains the core concepts of MOT, the BYTETrack methodology, and provides a step-by-step tutorial for implementing it with a custom YOLOv8 detector to track basketball players.

**Key Concepts:**
- Multiple Object Tracking (MOT) is a computer vision task that tracks movements of multiple objects over time in video sequences, determining identity, location, and trajectory of each object even when partially or fully occluded.
- MOT typically works in two stages: object detection (using detectors like Faster-RCNN or YOLO) and object association (typically using Kalman Filter for prediction and Hungarian Algorithm for linear assignment).

**Challenges with MOT:** Object motion/appearance variation, occlusion causing ID switching, class switching issues in multi-class trackers, and real-time inference speed limitations.

**BYTETrack Innovation:** The primary innovation is keeping non-background low confidence detection boxes (which are typically discarded after initial filtering) and using them for a secondary association step. Occluded detection boxes have lower confidence scores than the threshold but still contain meaningful information, so retaining them improves tracking consistency.

**Methodology:**
1. Detection boxes are filtered into high-confidence, low-confidence, and background boxes (background boxes are discarded).
2. First association stage: high-score detection boxes matched with predicted boxes from previous frames' tracklets (Kalman filter) using IoU or cosine similarity with Hungarian algorithm.
3. Second association stage: low-score detection boxes matched against remaining unmatched predicted boxes with a lower matching threshold.
4. Lost tracklets are kept for a certain number of frames and can be recovered.

**Implementation Details:** The paper uses YOLOX as the base detector but is customizable to FasterRCNN or other YOLO versions. IoU and ReID both work for first-stage association (ReID better for low-frame-rate videos; IoU more robust for severe occlusion), but second-stage association should always use IoU.

**Tutorial Example:** The author trained a custom YOLOv8m detector on ~90 side-view frames of the 2022 NBA finals between the Warriors and Celtics, tracking three classes: Warriors players, Celtics players, and referees. Annotations were created using Datature Nexus. After 50 epochs (batch size 4, test size 640), the model achieved mAP50 of ~0.9 and mAP50-95 of ~0.65. Since the original BYTETrack implementation is class-agnostic, multiple BYTETracker instances were created for multi-class tracking.

**Key Hyperparameters:** track_thresh = 0.5 (high threshold), track_buffer = 50 (frames lost tracklets kept), match_thresh = 0.8 (first stage matching threshold), aspect_ratio_thresh = 10.0, min_box_area = 1.0, MIN_THRESHOLD = 0.001 (set low to retrieve almost all detections; background threshold hardcoded at 0.1).

**Limitations:** Limited accuracy in crowded scenes due to reliance on IoU matching and trajectory prediction; low-confidence box strategy can introduce noise and track irrelevant objects; no native multi-class tracking support requiring computationally expensive workarounds.

**Conclusion:** BYTETrack is a simple yet effective MOT tracker that uses low-confidence boxes to account for occlusion and appearance changes. It can be adopted to improve existing SOTA MOT algorithms (both motion-based IoU and feature-based ReID) and is suitable for real-time applications like autonomous driving, video surveillance, and augmented reality.
</summary>

1. **Project Setup**: Install `opencv-contrib-python`, download a sample lane image, and create a `lanes.py` file.
2. **Load & Display Image**: Use `cv2.imread()` to load the image as a NumPy array and `cv2.imshow()` with `cv2.waitKey(0)` to display it.

4. **Isolating Region of Interest (ROI)**: Uses a triangular polygon mask created with `cv2.fillPoly()` and `np.zeros_like()`, then `cv2.bitwise_and()` to extract only the relevant lane area.
5. **Hough Transform Technique**: Explains the theory of converting points from XY coordinate space to Hough space (M-C space), and why polar coordinates (ρ = Xcosθ + Ysinθ) are used instead of y = mx + c for vertical lines. The hough accumulator array grid identifies the most intersecting curves to draw the best-fit line.
6. **Implementing Hough Transform**: Uses `cv2.HoughLinesP()` with parameters (2, np.pi/180, 100, minLineLength=40, maxLineGap=5). Three helper functions are defined: `display_lines()`, `make_coordinates()`, and `average_slope_intercept()` (which separates lines into left_fit and right_fit based on negative/positive slope, averages them, and uses `np.polyfit()` to compute slope and intercept).
7. **Detecting Lanes in Video**: Uses OpenCV's `VideoCapture` object to read frames from `test2.mp4` and applies the same pipeline frame-by-frame.

The article includes the complete final code for the entire lane detection project (all functions plus video processing loop with `q` key to quit). The tutorial concludes by suggesting readers can extend the project to real-time video data for actual driving scenarios.

<summary>
This webpage is a source note (metadata entry) about MonoTrack, a research paper titled "Shuttle Trajectory Reconstruction from Monocular Badminton Video" by Paul Liu and Jui-Hsien Wang, published at CVPR Workshop 2022 (CVSports). It describes a modular monocular pipeline that combines court detection, pose estimation, shuttle tracking, hit segmentation (HitNet), and physics-constrained 3D reconstruction for badminton analysis.

**Data & Splits:** Uses TrackNetV2 data (26 international singles matches, ~77K frames; 3 test matches ~12K frames). Additional 40 YouTube videos for court detection testing and 10K synthetic 3D trajectories. Only validates singles games with fixed overhead/static broadcast views. Validation split has near-duplicate leakage risk across rallies.

**Method:** (1) Hough lines + graph-based bipartite partition for court detection; (2) HRNet pose + 3-in/3-out modified U-Net for shuttle detection; (3) ~16K parameter two-layer GRU HitNet fusing court/pose/shuttle with dynamic programming on hit intervals and alternating rules; (4) Per-shot 3D trajectory optimization using drag dynamics, camera reprojection, hitter/receiver priors, and out-of-bounds penalties.

**Key Results:**
- Court success improved 73.9%→85.5%, IoU 0.96→0.97, 40× faster.
- Shuttle detector: 2.9M vs 11.3M parameters; accuracy 88.6% vs 84.0%.
- HitNet F1: shuttle-only 0.815 → +pose 0.850 → +court 0.866 → +constrained optimization 0.946 (recall 94.3%, accuracy 89.7%).
- Synthetic 3D error: 14.9 cm (reprojection-only) vs 8.0 cm (full priors); synthetic results are optimistic since same physical model generates and fits.
- Real data reports only 2D reprojection: GT shuttle/hits 8.1/8.9/9.8 px vs fully automatic 37.1/28.8/23.3 px.
- ~90% hit accuracy can still cause ~20% shot reconstruction errors because one hit error corrupts two adjacent shots.

**Limitations:** No end-to-end FPS/hardware/latency reported (cannot claim real-time full system). Real data has no 3D ground truth; evaluation excludes frequently occluded serves and unlabeled landings. Court failures, out-of-frame events, and hit errors cascade. Synthetic speed of "1500 m/s" conflicts with reality and model constraints.

**Value to four-layer badminton pipeline:** Shuttle tracking (direct evidence, but 88.6% frame accuracy ≠ full trajectory), court/3D reconstruction (baseline; real 3D accuracy unproven), hit/phase alignment (HitNet F1 0.946, singles/fixed view only), and no evidence for action quality assessment (no stroke quality, technical errors, or coaching feedback).

# CoachAI Badminton Challenge 2023

In conjunction with [IJCAI 2023](https://ijcai-23.org/) (Macao, S.A.R)

@ August 19th-25th, 2023

# Track 1: Automatic Annotation of Technical Data for Badminton Match Videos

# Introduction

In this track, participants develop computer vision technology to automatically extract shot-by-shot technical data from the broadcast video of badminton matches. The shot-by-shot data include the temporal, spatial, posture, and skill information as the shuttlecock is hit during the match such as data at the hitting time, ball position, hitting player, swing posture, standing position of both sides, used ball type, and winner. Those are composed of the big data for technical and tactical analysis of badminton matches. The scoring is rally-based, where each rally is evaluated separately and can get up to 1 point in total according to the correctness of the number of shots in the rally and the accuracy of the predicted attributes. The final ranking is sorted from highest to lowest according to the total score, with the highest being the first and the lowest being the last.

# Evaluation

1. Each single video clip is scored separately, with a total score of 1 point per video clip. First, the number of shots in the rally video is validated, and each row of the CSV file is considered as one shot.

* If the predicted number of shots is different from the ground truth, the question will be scored as 0 points.
* If the number of shots is the same, 0.1 points will be awarded, and proceed to the next stage to compare the content of the columns, with the highest score for column content being 0.9 points.

1. If the number of shots is correct, compare each shot in sequence, with each shot scored according to the total score of the columns, and the average of each shot's score as the score for content. First, the HitFrame column is validated. If the prediction error is greater than 2 frames compared to the true value, the shot will get 0 points in content and proceed to the next shot for scoring; if the prediction error is not greater than 2 frames, 0.1 points will be given, and proceed to compare other columns in the same shot.

* Hitter: 0.1 points if correct, 0 points otherwise.
* BallHeight: 0.1 points if correct, 0 points otherwise.
* Landing: If the prediction error is not greater than 6 pixels in the Euclidean distance, it is considered correct and is awarded 0.1 points; otherwise, 0 points.
* HitterLocation: If the prediction error is not greater than 10 pixels in the Euclidean distance, it is considered correct with 0.05 points, otherwise 0 points.
* DefenderLocation: If the prediction error is not greater than 10 pixels in the Euclidean distance, it is considered correct with 0.05 points, otherwise 0 points.

* Backhand: 0.05 points if correct, 0 points otherwise.
* RoundHead: 0.05 points if correct, 0 points otherwise.
* BallType: 0.2 points if correct, 0 points otherwise.
* Winner: 0.1 points if correct, 0 points otherwise. (Note: If it is not the last shot but is filled in, it will be considered incorrect.)

Assuming that there are R rally videos in the data set, and the i-th video has Si shots, the scoring formula is given below:

![](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/sitesv/AG8ngQUi7PTARyZijsxJKBwqe0lQRZoUOfsuDzI1Zeg7eTC80s00fwAgnwpIfIIQugbElU1MwavZ__BWKMZVWMrAcgSZAYSHH3e4Het0r7SQZpKqm7KxpQZMvepQokczj7biqTz2Ncj8b-vhuaY4bAvV1Bbux6VD4XGMr3CAbUlolO2qSWJch0ujBC158dfAeZgCLWctdtGJRRv2qCbTgeuuQHG7uZ4uWO3SZD6PicaJ=w1280)

ASSi (the Average Shot Score of the content of the i-th rally video) is given by

![](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/sitesv/AG8ngQWlbsoTGv5VdOHfA5XzeuUYgJbtBJrE_xZ9e4D_MisaOiR9UFPI6oNBg1ps7Q4EQ6V01mjrO7WhJcUOwfss6JiI3xLV2yx5YISZoBWRPVLRSnrgpPQxf4lYDtCi7keF2tLdz7OisGk5v3LTnQHerMOgXoF4dNkdBmfgMmbX1uqcLlwu_OaHPXsvAg7xxHtq3W3ULRapdx8UV7hJarl6UmFsp4ukgQgEtHXdHuRcrSo=w1280)

with SSj (the j-th Shot Score) given by:

![](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/sitesv/AG8ngQUxtfFBbTzcslOTmbhmm7rqbaH2o80nVfKaza7Y41gTMxtE2qYg4a07FLwnQc-v-F-YGKGHpgUu-RVmVciu-XQ463nbvKshaT3ZkPydlROzLc6v7F4xDZegMVEepSLKX1NVJ60ZPCCpLd56mrUFGcW4421D5NVqKwOnyGWI0VQ7g1rsa64FrdfP3WvNOCEhHatZqgVwIrtlkgO6b6dAKJRF4VmKU2B1PMpFS4UF=w1280)

# Data

This dataset consists of international competition videos organized by the Badminton World Federation (BWF). The recorded matches are shot from the back of and above the players. Each video will record a rally from the serve to the dead ball stage and the marked file after the shot mark, with an mp4 encoding and a CSV format for the marked file, and a frame rate of 30 FPS and a resolution of 1280\*720. The dataset includes 13 annotation fields. The following are the descriptions of each annotation field:

* VideoName: The file name of each rally video
* HitFrame: The moment of the shot in the rally, in frames
* Hitter: The player hitting the ball, marked with A/B

* A: Sited farther from the camera
* B: Sited closer to the camera
* BallHeight: The height of the hitting point, marked by 1/2

* 1: The hitting point is above the net
* 2: The hitting point is below the net
* RoundHead: Whether the player has a round-head hitting action, marked by 1/2

* 1: Round-head hitting
* 2: No round-head hitting
* Backhand: Whether the player's hitting action is backhand, marked by 1/2

  + - 1: Backhand hitting
    - 2: Not backhand hitting
* LandingX/LandingY: The projection on the court plane of the shuttlecock at the end of the trajectory either hit by the opponent or touch the ground, in pixels
* HitterLocationX/HitterLocationY: The location of the striking player, taking the toe of the habit foot as the coordinates in the picture, in pixels. If there is a jump, the coordinates projected onto the court plane are the answer
* DefenderLocationX/DefenderLocationY: The location of the defending player, similar to the location of the hitting player
* BallType: Nine types of balls, marked by 1~9. 1~2 are the types of serves, used only for serving (or first shot); 3~9 are the types of returns, used for subsequent shots

* 1: Short serve
* 2: Long serve
* 3: Clear
* 4: Drive
* 5: Smash
* 6: Net shot
* 7: Drop shot
* 8: Lift
* 9: Push shot
* Winner: Winning and losing points, divided into three categories, marked with A/B/X. Only the last shot of each rally video can be scored, and the rest are marked with X

* A: Score by upper half-court player
* B: Score by lower half-court player
* X: No score

args.summary: This webpage is a Semantic Scholar listing for the paper "Ready-to-Serve Detection in Badminton Videos" by See Shin Yue, Raveendran Paramesran, and Ganesh Krishnasamy, published on January 28, 2024 in the International Conference on Electronics, Information, and Communication (ICEIC), with DOI 10.1109/ICEIC61013.2024.10457177 and Corpus ID 268547888. The paper proposes a method that utilizes court details and player poses to accurately identify ready-to-serve actions from other actions in badminton videos, classifying ready-to-serve and non-serve strokes using a convolutional neural network (CNN). The paper includes 8 figures and 2 tables. It has 6 citations and 19 references. Notable citing works include: (1) "A Comparative Analysis of Deep Learning Models and Gradient Computation for Rally Detection in Badminton Videos" (2025) which uses BiLSTM and CNN models for service start and rally end detection; (2) "SerViT: A Vision Transformer-Based Model for Service Detection in Badminton Match Videos" (2026) which proposes a ViT-based model using player poses and court information for service detection; (3) "BST: Badminton Stroke-type Transformer for Skeleton-based Action Recognition in Racket Sports" (2025) which introduces a video clipping strategy for extracting racket swing frames; (4) "Harnessing the Power of Transformer Networks in AI-Driven Decision Support Systems for Badminton Action Recognition" (2024); (5) "Posture Correction and Shuttle Metrics Analysis for Badminton using Computer Vision" (2026); and (6) "A high-precision and efficient method for badminton action detection in sports using You Only Look Once with Hourglass Network" (2024). Key references cited in the paper include works on automated serve scene detection using CHLAC and MRA (Yoshikawa et al., 2010), detection of service activity in badminton games using rule-based approaches (Teng & Paramesran, 2011), badminton video analysis based on spatiotemporal and stroke features (Chu & Situmeang, 2017), action recognition in realistic sports videos (Soomro & Zamir, 2014), sport action recognition with Siamese spatio-temporal CNNs for table tennis (Martin et al., 2018), automated badminton smash recognition using CNNs (Rahmad et al., 2020), shot detection using skeleton position in badminton videos (Yoshikawa et al., 2021), TemPose skeleton-based transformer model for badminton motion recognition (Ibh et al., 2023), and MonoTrack for shuttle trajectory reconstruction (Liu & Wang, 2022).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534)Abstract

Human Action Recognition is a challenging task used in many applications. It interacts with many aspects of Computer Vision, Machine Learning, Deep Learning and Image Processing in order to understand human behaviours as well as identify them. It makes a significant contribution to sport analysis, by indicating players’ performance level and training evaluation. The main purpose of this study is to investigate how the content of three-dimensional data influences on classification accuracy of four basic tennis strokes: forehand, backhand, volley forehand, and volley backhand. An entire player’s silhouette and its combination with a tennis racket were taken into consideration as input to the classifier. Three-dimensional data were recorded using the motion capture system (Vicon Oxford, UK). The Plug-in Gait model consisting of 39 retro-reflective markers was used for the player’s body acquisition. A seven-marker model was created for tennis racket capturing. The racket is represented in the form of a rigid body; therefore, all points associated with it changed their coordinates simultaneously. The Attention Temporal Graph Convolutional Network was applied for these sophisticated data. The highest accuracy, up to 93%, was achieved for the data of the whole player’s silhouette together with a tennis racket. The obtained results indicated that for dynamic movements, such as tennis strokes, it is necessary to analyze the position of the whole body of the player as well as the racket position.

**Keywords:**sport, tennis strokes, human action recognition, A3T-GCN, motion capture

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534)1. Introduction

Computer Vision is an interdisciplinary field of study that aims to derive meaningful information from various types of data. Applying artificial intelligence for digital images, skeleton, depth, videos, point cloud, audio, acceleration, signals or motion capture data allows one to perform actions or make decisions as well as further recommendations. The purpose of Human Action Recognition (HAR) is to understand human behaviours and identify them [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B1-sensors-23-02422),[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B2-sensors-23-02422)]. It specifies a set of person’s moves performed in time in order to complete a task. Occasionally, additional objects, such as a tennis racket or a golf club, are involved to do the actions. Depending on the complexity of the movements and their duration, different length sequences are taken into consideration, from a single frame to a whole video streaming. HAR is a challenging task used in numerous applications. It interacts with many aspects of Computer Vision, Machine Learning, Deep Learning and Image Processing [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B3-sensors-23-02422)]. It utilizes detection of a person or objects in the image, video as well as sensor data, the location of the action in time and space, and the recognition of the action. This attitude usually involves feature detection, such as extracted from 3D silhouettes, skeletal joint and body part location, local spatio-temporal, local occupancy patterns and finally 3D scene flow [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B2-sensors-23-02422)]. That is why it makes a significant contribution to sport analysis. Detection of athletes and recognition of their actions or teams’ activities plays a pivotal role in indicating the players’ performance level and training evaluation or analyzing sport statistics [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B3-sensors-23-02422)].

Classification is a challenging task; however, its use can be found in many studies considering various sport disciplines, for both individual and team ones. Twelve basketball activities, corresponding to the most of the complex actions, were recognised in [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B4-sensors-23-02422)]. For this purpose the LSTM-DGCN method was proposed. It consisted of two parts: Deep Graph Convolutional Network (DGCN) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM). Basketball players measures such as distances between joints and angles were input parameters. Moreover, selection coordinates and depth maps together with RGB frame sequences were used for this purpose as well.

Both action recognition and analysis of the karate athletes were presented in [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B5-sensors-23-02422)]. The Attention-enhanced Graph Convolutional LSTM Networks (AGC-LSTM) was applied for recognition of the actions gathered from five athletes. The analyzed movements such as a punch (middle, upper, forward upper and back upper), back pounce, kick (side rising, back, inside crescent, side) as well as several technical moves were taken into consideration. A framework dedicated to sports video recording considering attentive movement characterization was presented in [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B6-sensors-23-02422)]. It involved hierarchical recurrent neural networks. The extraction of human pose, use of trajectory clustering made it possible to describe a dynamic movement of players or the whole teams as well as various interactions in sport games, such as volleyball. The classification of water sports using the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) with discriminative filter banks was presented in [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B7-sensors-23-02422)]. Water skiing and surfing were taken into consideration. Both 2D and 3D data were analysed. Three branches were applied for the classifier consisting of: the average pooling classification head, a set of convolutions, spatial upsampling and max-pooling layers.

Recently, a novel approach to analyzing the movements of athletes has been proposed. It took into consideration the natural connections between the joints of the human silhouette in order to apply the graphs. The use of Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GNN) made it possible to capture existing patterns and dependencies embedded in a spatial configuration of joints, as well as their temporal dynamics and thus it has become a very popular method in the field of HAR [[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B8-sensors-23-02422)]. In that study, the authors introduced the Spatial Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks (ST-GCN) for everyday activities, sports areas and actions recognition. The same network was applied for the recognition of the selected movements in competitive sports [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B9-sensors-23-02422)]. Activities such as balance beam, diving, athletics, boxing, keeping fit, and badminton were taken into consideration. The data were recorded with the use of the markerless motion capture system. In [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B10-sensors-23-02422)], it was stated that a model based on temporal convolutional networks was more appropriate for HAR than a model considering the recurrent neural ones. These two approaches were compared using the NTU RGB+D dataset containing various types of actions. In [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B11-sensors-23-02422)], a new Two-stream Adaptive Graph Convolutional Network (2s-AGCN) for skeleton-based action recognition was proposed, which was verified by two datasets NTU-RGBD and KineticsSkeleton. This approach included additional information of skeleton data, such as the bone location. This attitude enhanced the performance of the classifier. The ST-GCN for skeleton action recognition was also applied for a similar approach in [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B12-sensors-23-02422)]. The Actional-Structural Graph Convolution Network (AS-GCN) was proposed. Its structure was characterised by basic building blocks for indicating spatial and temporal features. This new classifier was verified with NTU-RGBD+D and Kinetics datasets. Various types of sports, such as: golf, kicking, lifting, diving, running, horse riding, skateboarding, swing-bench, and walking, were recognized using the Part-Attention Spatio-temporal Graph Convolutional Network (PSGCN) [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B13-sensors-23-02422)]. It exploited the dynamic information from a sports video.

Classification of the tennis movement may be found in many scientific papers. The studies involved only skeleton-based action recognition, only tennis racket position as well as the whole player silhouette together with a racket. The research concerning SensorTile attached to the tennis racket was presented in [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B14-sensors-23-02422),[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B15-sensors-23-02422)]. For the purpose of swing classification Deep Neural Network [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B14-sensors-23-02422)] was applied, while for topspins (forehand and backhand), subpar forehand, subpar backhand, and slices (forehand and backhand) recognition the following methods were used: Support Vector Machine (SVM), Neural Networks (NN), Decision Tree (DT), Random Forest (RF) and k-Nearest Neighbor (kNN) [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B15-sensors-23-02422)]. The Pan Tompkins algorithm for the classification of shots using time warping was presented in [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B16-sensors-23-02422)]. Many studies focused on tennis stroke recognition based on video data. This attitude involved extracting features from videos and applying a classifier to the whole set [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B17-sensors-23-02422)]. The THETIS is a very well-known dataset consisting of twelve tennis moves captured by Microsoft Kinect in a form of video and ONI files [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B18-sensors-23-02422)]. The video-based action recognition of backhand (two-handed, one-handed, slice, and volley), forehand (flat, open stance, slice, and volley), serve (flat, kick, and slice) as well as smash was performed using the 3-layered LSTM network in [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B19-sensors-23-02422),[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B20-sensors-23-02422)]. In [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B17-sensors-23-02422)], these twelve moves were classified using SVM and linear-chain Conditional Random Fields (CRF). The five-layer deep historical LSTM network described in [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B21-sensors-23-02422)] was applied for similar moves using the following datasets: THETIS and HMDB51. Six tennis strokes from the THETIS datasets were recognised by the LSTM network in [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B22-sensors-23-02422)]. Serve, hit as well as non-hit were recognized by the Kernelised Linear Discriminant Analysis (KLDA) in [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B23-sensors-23-02422)]. Transductive transfer learning for an annotation of video sequences was applied. The changes in the tennis ball were also taken into consideration. The basic tennis strokes, forehand and backhand, from a video were analyzed in [[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B24-sensors-23-02422),[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B25-sensors-23-02422),[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B26-sensors-23-02422)] using the SVM classifier. In [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B27-sensors-23-02422)], tennis serves, forehand and backhand were recognised using two classifiers: SVM with the radial basis function kernel and K-Nearest Neighbour classifiers (KNNs). A wireless inertial measurement unit sensor together with a system consisting of eight video cameras was used for capturing the data.

Studies concerning HAR were also performed using motion capture data recorded via optical systems. Forehand and backhand strokes with and without ball contact as well as no-shots were recognized by ST-GCN based on images generated from three-dimensional motion data in [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B28-sensors-23-02422)]. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) were an obvious choice due to the fact that the parts of the image correlated with the human topology. In this study, the influence of input fuzzification on the obtained accuracy was examined. The results showed that this approach increased recognition ability. An extension of the above research was the recognition of individual tennis stroke phases, i.e., forehand preparation, forehand shot with racket swinging, backhand preparation, backhand shot with racket swinging and no-shots which were presented in [[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B29-sensors-23-02422)]. Three classifiers with and without fuzzification were taken into account: SVM, MLP, and ST-GCN. In addition, the influence of the extensions and generalizations of the Choquet integral on the aggregation of results obtained by individual classifiers was verified. The results indicated that this method increased the efficiency of recognizing tennis moves. Another approach to tennis movements recognition including its phases was presented in [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B30-sensors-23-02422)]. For the purpose of the classification, the Attention Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (A3T-GCN) was applied both with and without input fuzzification. The conducted results showed that this classifier might be considered as one of the most appropriate methods for tennis classification.

The state-of-the-art study presented in this paper is to apply the A3T-GCN classifier for tennis stroke recognition based on three-dimensional coordinates data obtained from the optical motion capture system. Forehand, backhand and volley strokes were taken into consideration. The main purpose of this study is to look into how the content of three-dimensional data influences classification accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score. Both the coordinates associated with the player’s silhouette and the position of the racket were analyzed, which to the authors’ knowledge is the novelty approach. The A3T-GCN was chosen due to the attention model, which both stores information about the player’s model, but also determines the predicted player position.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. [Section 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#sec2-sensors-23-02422) explores the material and methods as well as introduces the Attention Temporal Graph Convolutional Network. [Section 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#sec3-sensors-23-02422) presents results of the state-of-the-art action recognition methods with the proposed classifier and 3D motion capture data. [Section 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#sec4-sensors-23-02422) discusses the proposed method, and finally [Section 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#sec5-sensors-23-02422) concludes the study.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534)2. Materials and Methods

### 2.1. Participants

In this study, seven male and three female tennis players took part (age $23.7 \pm 4.58$, height $1.77 \pm 0.13$ m, weight $71.65 \pm 10.68$ kg). Only one of them was left-handed, while the others were right-handed. They all signed the consent for the study.

### 2.2. Data Acquisition

Each participant was prepared for the experiment. First, they have a 15-min warm-up. Second, thirty-nine retroreflective markers, specified in the Plug-in Gait model, were attached to their body. Finally, all the required measurements were gathered for the purpose of creating a new model as well as preparing its calibration in the motion capture system. Furthermore, seven markers were also attached to the tennis racket, according to the following scheme: one to the top of the racket head, two on both sides of the racket, one to the bottom of the racket head and one to the bottom of the racket handle. Such an arrangement reflects the racket shape and capture its movements.

For the purpose of acquisition, eight-camera optical Vicon motion capture system, installed in the indoor room, was used with the Nexus software. The cameras are mounted two on each wall on the same level. The whole schema of the cameras arrangement is presented in [Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#sensors-23-02422-f001). Before movement acquisition the calibration of the system was performed. The maximal calibration error did not exceed 0.045 pixels. The frequency of capturing was set to 100 Hz.

Each participant performed forehand, two-handed backhand and volley strokes. Forehand and backhand ones were performed while running and avoiding a bollard placed on the floor. Due to this, the strokes were more natural than hitting the ball from a standing position. At first, ten forehand strokes without a ball were performed, followed by ten backhand strokes without a ball. Next, these exercises were repeated with a ball. Finally, the participant performed ten volley forehand and ten volley backhand in front of the tennis net. Tennis balls were thrown from the right and the left side of the net, while standing parallel to the net, the player made a short movement with the racket in front of him/her, causing the ball to bounce and fall. The participant hit a ball which was caught by a special net. The forehand tennis stroke is made with the dominant hand. The racket was placed on the dominant side; then, it was directed towards the ball. After the racket made contact with the ball, the racket was directed to the opposite arm of the player in a way of swinging. While performing a two-handed backhand stroke, the racket was held with a continental grip. It was placed on the opposite side to the dominant one. After the racket made contact with the ball, it was directed to the dominant side. In the case of a one-handed backhand, the racket was held with a dominant hand. These two types of strokes are presented in [Figure 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#sensors-23-02422-f002). It is worth indicating that forehand and forehand volley are very similar moves in a certain part of the movement. The same goes for backhand strokes.

Each performed stroke has been verified by a specialist. All failed strokes were rejected. Due to the fact that professional tennis players participated in the study, the well-performed strokes were repetitive.

### 2.3. Data Post-Processing

The Vicon Nexus software was used for post-processig of all obtained recordings. This tasks involved the following steps: marker labelling, gap filling using interpolation methods implemented in Vicon Nexus software (Pattern Fill and Rigid Body Fill), data cleaning, and applying the Plug-in-Gait model. The last one was only for the model representing human body. Additionally, a new model, consisting of all markers attached to the racket, was generated. The data prepared in this way was saved to c3d file.

The whole gathered recordings was verified by a professional tennis coach. As a result, the following number of tennis moves was obtained: backhand—212, forehand—197, forehand volley—180, backhand volley—180.

### 2.4. Attention Temporal Graph Convolutional Network

The idea of the A3T-GCN was taken from the work [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B31-sensors-23-02422)], where a similar structure was used to predict traffic volume in selected cities. The basic modification of this network consists of transforming the element responsible for the prediction into a classifier. Additionally, the elements responsible for the separation of spatial and temporal features have also been adapted. In the original approach, the Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) network was applied. Due to extensive structure of the GRU network, inadequate to the problem, we are analyzing in our work RNN network, often also called BiRNN or Bidirectional RNN. It is schematically shown in [Figure 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#sensors-23-02422-f003). Moreover, the original prediction was based on a Context Vector, while in case of this study additional Multilayer Perceptron was added on the output of the classifier. The whole network structure used in this study is presented in [Figure 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#sensors-23-02422-f004).

The input data is arranged in a way of a graph $G = \left(\right. V , E \left.\right)$ consisting of _M_ nodes. They denotes _M_ joints and their position changes in time. The _M_ value was equal to 39 for the study without a tennis racket and 46 in case of experiments with it. Each node is described as a set of three-dimensional values $V = \left{\right. v_{t i} \left|\right. t = 1 , \ldots , T , i = 1 , \ldots , M \left.\right}$.

#### 2.4.1. Spatial Features

Usually, skeleton data studies are based on images or video as input, so the data are processed by typical Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN). In case of this study, as input data points in three-dimensional space were used, the proposed classifier was based on Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs). The connections between the nodes of the _G_ graph were presented in the form of the adjacency matrix _A_. The entire feature matrix has been marked with the _X_ variable. To process graph nodes, the GCN network, uses a Fourier filter to determine the spatial relation between features. This relationship was characterized by Equation ([1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#FD1-sensors-23-02422)), which actually defines a multilayer GCN model. (1)

$$
F^{\left(\right. n + 1 \left.\right)} = \sigma \left(\left(\overset{\sim}{T}\right)^{- \frac{1}{2}}\overset{\sim}{O}\left(\overset{\sim}{T}\right)^{- \frac{1}{2}}F^{\left(\right. n \left.\right)}\Theta^{\left(\right. n \left.\right)}\right)
$$

 where _n_ represents the number of hidden layers, $\overset{\sim}{O} = O + I_{N}$ is the adjacent matrix (_O_) with added self-connections, $I_{N}$ describes the identity matrix, $\overset{\sim}{T} = \sum_{j} \left(\overset{\sim}{O}\right)_{i j}$, $F^{\left(\right. n \left.\right)}$ defines the output of _n_ layer, $\Theta^{\left(\right. n \left.\right)}$ is a matrix which contains all parameters of specified $n^{t h}$ layer and $\sigma \left(\right. \cdot \left.\right)$ represents the sigmoidal function for a nonlinear model [[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B32-sensors-23-02422)].

In this study, the GCN network consists of three layers. This structure can be described by Equation ([2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#FD2-sensors-23-02422)). (2)

$$
f \left(I,O\right) = \sigma \left(\hat{O}ReLU\left(\left(\hat{O}I\Psi_{0}\right)\hat{O}I\Psi_{1}\right)\Psi_{2}\right)
$$

 where $\hat{O} = \left(\overset{\sim}{T}\right)^{- \frac{1}{2}} \overset{\sim}{O} \left(\overset{\sim}{T}\right)^{- \frac{1}{2}}$ indicates the preliminary step, $\Psi_{0} \in R^{P x F}$ denotes the weight matrix between input and hidden layer, _P_ defines the size of the feature matrix, while _F_ is a value related to the number of the hidden unit, $\Psi_{1} , \Psi_{2} \in R^{F x Z}$ define the weight matrices from hidden to output layer, $f \left(I,O\right) \in R^{N x Z}$, denotes the output length _Z_ and $R e L U \left(\right. \left.\right)$, is the Rectified Linear Unit, commonly used as neurons activation function [[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B32-sensors-23-02422)].

#### 2.4.2. Temporal Features

To indicate temporal features, which are the key elements in recognizing the analyzed types of tennis strokes, a BiDirectional Recurrent Neural Network was used. BiRNNs were applied to obtain the information about the player at time _t_. To gather this kind of data, the information about previous (in time $n - 1$, $n - 2$,…$n - n_{f}$, where $n_{f}$ denotes the maximum number of frames in all c3d file) features were taken into consideration. If analyzed file had fewer frames the missing values were set to 0. The structure of whole temporal features elements can be expressed by Equations ([3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#FD3-sensors-23-02422))–([6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#FD6-sensors-23-02422)) [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B31-sensors-23-02422)]:(3)

$$
u g c_{t} = \sigma \left(W_{u}*\left[X_{t},h_{t - 1}\right]\right)
$$

 (4)

$$
r g c_{t} = \sigma \left(W_{r}*\left[X_{t},h_{t - 1}\right]\right)
$$

 (5)

$$
m c_{t} = tanh \left(W_{c}\left[X_{t},\left(rgc_{t}*h_{t - 1}\right)\right]\right)
$$

 (6)

$$
h_{t} = u g c_{t} * h_{t - 1} + \left(1-ugc_{t}\right) * m c_{t}
$$

 where $u g c_{t}$ denotes the update gate, which role is connected with controlling the information quantity at the previous moment, $r g c_{t}$ indicates the reset gate, which is responsible for neglecting the state information at the previous moment, $m c_{t}$ describes stored memory content at the current moment and $h_{t}$ defines the output value at the current moment. $W_{u}$, $W_{r}$ and $W_{c}$ represent the weights in the training process for the updated gate layer, reset gate layer and output layer, respectively.

#### 2.4.3. Attention Model

Commonly attention model is defined as an encoder–decoder. It is widely used in such applications as: traffic forecasting [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B31-sensors-23-02422)], image labeling [[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B33-sensors-23-02422)], recommendation systems [[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B34-sensors-23-02422)] or document classification [[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B35-sensors-23-02422)]. Based on [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B36-sensors-23-02422)], it can be stated that the most general division of that kind of model includes hard and soft attention. In this study, the soft one was applied. The attention model’s first application is to store information about the player’s model. The second is to indicate the context vector, which is responsible for determining the predicted tennis player positions. The applied attention model consists of the following steps.

*   First, determine, using the BiRNN network, the successive hidden states $u_{k} \left(\right. k = 1 , \ldots , m \left.\right)$ of the time series $I_{k} \left(\right. k = 1 , 2 , \ldots , m \left.\right)$, where _m_ is the number of frames in series. As a result, the set of $u_{k}$ states is defined.

*   Second, a context vector ($C_{v}$) is determined. In particular, the value of position change was determined on a basis of two hidden layers. Their features are indicated applying Equation ([7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#FD7-sensors-23-02422)): (7)

$$
e_{i} = \psi_{\left(\right. 2 \left.\right)} \left(\psi_{\left(\right. 1 \left.\right)}H+b_{\left(\right. 1 \left.\right)}\right) + b_{\left(\right. 2 \left.\right)}
$$

 where $\psi_{\left(\right. 1 \left.\right)}$ and $b_{\left(\right. 1 \left.\right)}$ denote the weight and bias of the first layer and $\psi_{\left(\right. 2 \left.\right)}$ and $b_{\left(\right. 2 \left.\right)}$ are similarly features of the second layer. _H_ is a matrix with hidden layer values. To determine the values of $\psi_{\left(\right. 1 \left.\right)} , \psi_{\left(\right. 2 \left.\right)}$ the $S o f t m a x$ function ([8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#FD8-sensors-23-02422)) is used. (8)

$$
S o f t m a x = \frac{e x p \left(\right. e_{i} \left.\right)}{\sum_{k = 1}^{n} e x p \left(\right. e_{k} \left.\right)}
$$

Final, the $C_{v}$ is defined as follows: (9)

$$
C_{v} = \sum_{i = 1}^{n} S o f t m a x * h_{i}
$$

The final classification is performed by two-layer perceptron. This neural structure consists of one element in the first layer and four (related to four recognised strokes) in the second one. The $S o f t m a x$ function is used to activate the neurons in the first layer, while the second layer is activated by a linear one.

### 2.5. Experiment

In this study, the forehand, backhand, volley forehand and volley backhand strokes were recognized. The whole tennis movements dataset consisted of backhand—212, forehand—197, volley forehand—180, and volley backhand—180. It represented the player’s silhouette together with a tennis racket. Two types of experiments were performed. The first one concerned the whole set of data while the other only the player’s silhouette by removing the coordinations of the tennis racket subject.

A series of experiments were carried out, taking into account the random division of data into the training, validation and test sets: 60%, 20% and 20%, respectively. The data was chosen from every type of stroke in the above-mentioned proportions. For each division, 20 tests were carried out, independently.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534)3. Results

Grouped results were presented in [Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#sensors-23-02422-t001), [Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#sensors-23-02422-t002), [Table 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#sensors-23-02422-t003), [Table 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#sensors-23-02422-t004) and [Table 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#sensors-23-02422-t005). Selected parameters of the learning process showing the correctness of the model were shown in [Figure 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#sensors-23-02422-f005). The loss value $L_{C E}$ was calculated on a basis of the Sparse Categorical Cross-Entropy defined by Equation ([10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#FD10-sensors-23-02422)). (10)

$$
L_{C E} = - \sum_{i = 1}^{n} T_{i} l o g \left(\right. p_{i} \left.\right) ,
$$

 for _n_ classes, where $T_{i}$ is a ground truth, $p_{i}$ is the $S o f t m a x$ probability for the _i_ th class.

The assessment of the classifier quality was based on several standard measures, such as: Accuracy ([11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#FD11-sensors-23-02422)), Precision ([12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#FD12-sensors-23-02422)), Recall ([13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#FD13-sensors-23-02422)) and F1 score ([14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#FD14-sensors-23-02422)). (11)

$$
A c c u r a c y = \frac{N u m b e r o f c o r r e c t c l a s s i f i c a t i o n s}{T o t a l n u m b e r o f c l a s s i f i c a t i o n s}
$$

 (12)

$$
P r e c i s i o n = \frac{T P}{T P + F P}
$$

 (13)

$$
R e c a l l = \frac{T P}{T P + F N}
$$

 (14)

$$
F 1 = \frac{2 * P r e c i s i o n * R e c a l l}{P r e c i s i o n + R e c a l l}
$$

 where $T P$ denotes the true positive fraction, $F P$—the false positive fraction, and $F N$—the false negative fraction.

Although Precision, Recall, and F1 are usually presented for binary classification, there is a simple way for extending their definition to multiple classes. In this case, Precision, e.g., for backhand, will be defined as correctly classified backhand strokes out of all classified backhand strokes. The Recall for backhand is the number of correctly predicted backhand strokes out of all input backhand strokes.

For the obtained accuracy results for two types of moves: strokes without and with a tennis racket ([Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#sensors-23-02422-t001)), the _T_-Test was calculated, for which $t = - 8.2753$ was obtained, for $\alpha = 0.05$. The obtained result allowed us to state that it cannot be concluded that there is a difference between the means.

In order to check the correctness of the developed model, Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV) was performed ([Table 6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#sensors-23-02422-t006)). This is a computationally expensive procedure; however, it allows us to obtain clear and unbiased information about the model. Using LOOCV, the root mean squared error (RMSE) for _n_ tests was determined:(15)

$$
M S E = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i = 1}^{n} \left(\left(y_{i}-\hat{y_{i}}\right)\right)^{2}
$$

 where _n_—denotes number of test, $y_{i}$—true value, $\hat{y_{i}}$—predicted value. (16)

$$
R M S E = \sqrt{M S E}
$$

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534)4. Discussion

In this study, the recognition of tennis forehand, backhand, volley forehand and volley backhand was performed based on data gathered in c3d files in a form of three-dimensional coordinates. Both the player’s silhouette indicated by 39 markers and the silhouette together with a tennis racket represented by 7 additional markers were analyzed.

As it can be observed in [Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#sensors-23-02422-t001) and [Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#sensors-23-02422-t002) and [Figure 6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#sensors-23-02422-f006) the mean accuracy depends on the captured data. It is higher for the experiments with the whole tennis player’s silhouette together with a tennis racket than the experiment involving only a single body. It can be concluded that the arrangement and trajectory of a tennis racket plays an extremely important role in the correct classification.

Furthermore, in the case of Precision (see [Table 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#sensors-23-02422-t003)), the obtained mean results are higher for the combination of the tennis player’s body model with a tennis racket for all analyzed strokes. The same dependence applies to Recall results ([Table 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#sensors-23-02422-t004)) and the F1 score ([Table 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#sensors-23-02422-t005)).

It should be noted that the standard deviation, amounting to a few percent, is low for all the obtained results, which shows the stability of the applied classifier.

In [Table 7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#sensors-23-02422-t007), the state-of-the-art studies related to the tennis strokes recognition are presented. They were performed using various types of data obtained from different sources, such as sensors, video or motion capture systems. The most research in this field were carried out on the well-known THETIS database. Both the data in the form of video, as well as the images obtained from the Kinect motion capture system, were the source for recognizing tennis movements. Broadcast video involving real matches or tournaments with top tennis players was also often taken into consideration. Various types of neural network approaches were used for these purposes. It is worth stressing that graph neural networks (ST-GCN and A3T-GCN) were used to recognize basic tennis strokes based on data obtained from an optical motion capture system. This classifier was chosen due to the characteristics of the recorded data. The applied human model, represented by 39 markers attached to the body in fixed locations, is transformed into a graph, which reflects the topology of the human silhouette. This approach allowed us to obtain a high accuracy. Analyzing the results presented in the study [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B28-sensors-23-02422)], it can be seen that used the A3T-GCN classifier allows for better recognition of tennis strokes than the ST-GCN one, despite the different types of input data. In the previous study, described in [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B28-sensors-23-02422)], the accuracy was obtained at the level of 68.9% for the 60% of data belonging to the training set, which corresponds to the settings in this study. The forehand and backhand classification was performed using images containing the subjects of the tennis player together with the racket. They were generated based on three-dimensional data by Vicon Nexus software. Based on this kind of input data the simplified model, both for tennis player and a racket, was created. The tennis racket was represented only by two points referring to its head and handle. The mean accuracy obtained in this study is higher for both the analyzed silhouette and its combination with a tennis racket compared to the results obtained in the work [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B28-sensors-23-02422)]. In [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B30-sensors-23-02422)], the study concerned the images obtained from three-dimensional data were analysed. The classification of forehand, divided into preparation and the hit phases, and backhand, also divided into preparation and the hit phases, as well as no-hit was performed using the Attention Temporal Graph Convolutional Network. The achieved accuracy results in a form of mean of two phases for forehand stroke did not exceed 80% while for backhand—77%. The obtained mean accuracy results in this paper are higher for the analyzed strokes with and without a tennis racket. The studies presented in this paper concerning tennis movements recognition was performed based on three-dimensional data in the form of coordinates of markers placed on the player’s body and a tennis racket was used. As it can be seen in [Table 7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#sensors-23-02422-t007) this approach is unique.

The results obtained in this paper suggest that the type of input data affects the accuracy of tennis stroke classification. Whole body data stored in the form of three-dimensional coordinates allows to achieve better results than in the case of images obtained from three-dimensional data. In addition, the inclusion of a tennis racket in the input data improves the classification quality of these strokes.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534)5. Conclusions

The state-of-the-art of this study was to verify the impact of adding a tennis racket to the input data of the whole player’s silhouette on the final classification of four main tennis strokes. For the purpose of this study the A3T-GCN classifier was applied. The tennis moves were represented in a form of three-dimensional motion data. The described approach gave satisfactory results. Forehand, backhand, volley forehand and volley backhand were taken into consideration. According to the previous authors’ study considering the ST-GCN network as a classifier [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10007534#B28-sensors-23-02422)], the obtained accuracy for two basic tennis movements (forehand and backhand) recognition in this research has been improved. As the results showed, adding a tennis racket to the data presenting the whole body silhouette significantly improved the classification quality. While comparing two graph networks, i.e., A3T-GCN and ST-GCN, the obtained results in this study clearly indicated that the A3T-GCN structure might be considered as the most suitable for motion data expressed in a form of three-dimensional coordinations. Further work will focus on the possibilities of using other methods of computational intelligence, in particular deep learning methods, and investigating their impact on the efficiency of movement classification in sport. Moreover, research on the possibility of using aggregation of classification methods, may be of interest in further studies in this field.
