You are tasked with summarizing the raw content of a webpage retrieved from a web search. Your goal is to create a summary that preserves the most important information from the original web page. This summary will be used by a downstream research agent, so it's crucial to maintain the key details without losing essential information.

Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
1 Dissecting the Tennis Rally: Valuing Decision Making and Shot Execution in Tennis Robert Seidl1, Machar Reid1, Sam Robertson2 1Tennis Australia, 2Victoria University rob@talksportsdata.com 1. Introduction In the 2020 Australian Open final, Dominic Thiem faced defending champion Novak Djokovic to try to win his first Grand Slam title. After leading 2 sets to 1, he lost a very close five set match 4:6, 6:4, 6:2, 3:6, 4:6 after almost four hours. Tennis is a game of very thin margins where a player can win the same total number of points as his opponent but still lose the match. In this way, the scoreboard can be misleading or mask important details of points and matches that require further analysis to explain the victory. Indeed, with the advent of player and ball tracking data in professional tennis, there has been an emergence of data-driven analyses of shots [4-6]; all of which attempt to explain different shot level nuance of the game. However, multiple decisions precede every shot that is hit in professional tennis matches and the use of tracking data to decouple and inferentially examine the quality of decision-making by players remains overlooked. With this in mind, the paper takes a first step to objectively quantify the decision making and shot execution of a tennis player based on player and ball tracking data in the following way: - We train four neural network models to disentangle decision-making and execution for each shot hit at Australian Open 2020, where the aim is either to predict whether the player will win the point immediately (i.e., with that shot) or later within the rally (i.e., after subsequent shots). - We consider player performance on serve, return and in-rally play separately. - We measure the relative importance of a rally within a match using an in-match win probability model to understand the interaction between decision-making, execution and scoreboard pressure. Once established, these models are applied to analyze Thiem’s performance at Australian Open 2020 on the following four levels: - on tournament level, we compare Thiem’s playing style to those of the other three semi-finalists, and investigate his shot execution performance in the rounds leading up to the final, - on match level, we inspect how his play evolved in the final against Djokovic, with a specific focus on high pressure moments, 2 - on rally level, we judge the quality of his shot execution in an important rally decoupled from the actual outcome. 2. Valuing decision making and execution in tennis rallies Given the increased availability of event and tracking data in sports, researchers have tried to value action outcomes in football [1, 2], basketball [3] and tennis [4, 5, 6]. In tennis the goal is to predict if a shot will end the rally and win the point outright. There is a problem with this approach as most tennis players do not hit every shot with the intention of it being a winner but rather to gain small advantages throughout a rally which add up in the battle for time and space – thus oversimplifing a player’s shot selection process and undervalueing strategic play. The best-known player following this approach is Novak Djokovic, currently ranked No.1 in the world. A better choice for a target variable is to analyze whether a player will be able to win the rally at some point after the current shot. This is the delayed reward for playing strategically smart shots that players are aiming for. Figure 1. Sample tracking data and model evaluation. a) Visualization of Hawkeye player and ball tracking data at the moment when Thiem hits a forehand return. Positions and velocities vectors are shown in green, red and yellow for Thiem, Djokovic and the ball. b) The input features for the neural network and its predicted win probability for the rally. Decroos et al. [2] introduced the concept for separately valuing decision and execution in soccer. We transfer this idea to tennis as we disentangle decision making from execution by considering the moment of the shot (“when the ball leaves the racket”) to value the decision of a player to play a certain shot in the current situation as this is the last time where a player can actively change his 3 shot selection by varying direction, speed, spin or the target location. Furthermore, we consider the consecutive moment of the ball bounce in the opponent’s court as the execution of the shot as this will tell us about the direct outcome of the shot allowing for a shot by shot evaluation within a rally. Using Hawkeye ball and player tracking data from 2020 Australian Open we train four Neural Networks on 107,000 hits and 98,000 bounces1 to learn the likelihood of a hit or bounce resulting in a direct winner and winning the rally, respectively. This allows the model to learn strategies of winning the point outright as well as strategies which aim on building up a point. To help distinguish between the different models, we abbreviate their outputs as xDW, xDR, xEW and xER for the expected decision and execution values for hitting a direct winner and winning the rally. As input features to the models we use position, speed and angle of both players and the ball at the time of the hit and bounce, respectively. We also add classifications that label a shot as a serve, return or rally shot. This way the model can treat the special cases of a serve and return, which happen at the beginning of each rally, differently than shots occurring later in a rally. Figure 1a shows a visualization of Hawkeye data for a forehand return Thiem played in the Australian Open final against Djokovic. The positions and velocities of each player and the ball are shown in green, red and yellow. Figure 1a presents a sample situation where Thiem plays a backhand return. The input features for the neural network and the estimated win probability of the rally predicted by the neural network at the time Thiem hits the ball are shown in Figure 1b. 2.3. Model evaluation Training the four different models, we achieve the results shown in Table 1. MODEL DESCRIPTION TARGET AUC ACCURACY xDW Decision (Hit) Direct winner 73 % 81 % xDR Decision (Hit) Win rally 65 % 59 % xEW Execution (Bounce) Direct winner 78 % 84 % xER Execution (Bounce) Win rally 71 % 63 % Table 1. Model evaluation Decision accuracy is lower than execution accuracy as it is tougher to predict the immediate or rally winner at the time of hitting the ball compared to the time the ball bounces. Furthermore, predicting the winner of a rally given only a snapshot of a shot (either hit or bounce) is a very tough task where you cannot expect to achieve a very high accuracy. However, the models do a fairly good job with accuracies of 59% and 63%. 3. Estimating in-match win probabilities Having a model that predicts the likelihood of winning a point in tennis is valuable on its own but not all points in tennis are equally important [10]. To be able to capture this relative importance of a rally within a match we need to combine our model with a live win probability model. 1 This refers to the training set, we use a test set of 12,000 hits and 11,000 bounces played in the tournament. 4 There exists a vast literature on match forecasting in tennis and we refer to [7] and the references within for a detailed description of our live win probability model. We just give a high-level overview of the method. The idea is to use pre-match information and relevant in-match information to predict the likelihood of a player winning the match at the current score. We employ the following four step process. Figure 2. In-match win prediction for Australian Open final for Djokovic vs. Thiem. The dashed horizontal line indicates the pre-match win probability. Vertical lines indicate the end of each set. 1) Pre-match prediction. Calculate ELO ratings for each player and adjust them for court surface and previous matches played against the opponent. This yields the pre-match win probability for the players. 2) Calibration of pre-match prediction. Convert the pre-match prediction into serve and return predictions that result in the same prediction at the first point of the match. 3) Bayesian in-match update. Given the current score update the baseline serve predictions with the observed in-match serve probabilities that are based on the observed serve points won and played in the match. 4) In-match prediction. Calculate the in-match win probability running a Barnett-Clarke model [8] using the updated in-match serve predictions. As an illustration Figure 2 depicts the in-match win probability for the Australian Open final Djokovic against Thiem which ended 6:4, 4:6, 2:6, 6:3, 6:4. The development of the win probability of Djokovic throughout the match is shown. The dashed horizontal line indicates the pre-match win probability derived from the ELO ratings of both players. Vertical lines indicate the end of each of the five sets. Given the in-match win probability model, we define leverage as how much a point could influence the match outcome. This way we can identify high pressure situations in a match. 4. Applications 5 Being able to value each players decision and its execution for every shot within a tennis rally has multiple applications for performance analysis, media and sports betting. In this section we present Figure 3. Decision and Execution values for semi-finalists of 2020 Australian Open for ATP Tour different use-cases with the aim to objectively quantify Thiem’s performance at last year’s Australian Open in a data-driven way. First, we employ decision and contribution values to investigate the different playing styles of all four semifinalists. Second, we examine Thiem’s performance in the matches he won to reach the final. Third, we look into the close five set final he lost against Djokovic where we especially investigate what happened to Thiem’s game in the fifth set and how he performed on points where the pressure was high. Fourth, we dissect each shot of a point played in the fifth set which we found to have significant impact on the outcome of the match but the expected outcome differed significantly. 4.1 Playing Styles of Mens Semi-Finalists2 As first application to show the value of both, decision and execution values for analyzing playing styles, we aggregate the values of each hit and bounce for all semifinalists of this year’s Australian Open. Figure 3 shows a summary of decision and execution values for shot and rally models for serve, return and rally. As discussed in Section 2, the shot decision model predicts the likelihood of winning the point immediately at the time when the ball leaves the racket and the rally decision model predicts the likelihood of winning the rally. The execution models predict the same quantities at the time of the bounce. Average player values are also shown. Looking at the serve models, we recognize that all four players serve over average with Zverev clearly leading in execution values on shot and rally level, meaning that he is most likely to win a point outright (shot model) but also later in the rally (rally model). 2 We followed the same modelling process and applied it to WTA Tour matches. The decision and execution values for the women semi-finalists are shown in Appendix A1. 6 If we inspect the return models, the return play of Federer, Thiem and Zverev does not stand out but Djokovic’s return play is superb, both on winning a point outright and setting up on winning the rally. Especially the rally execution is more than 5 points over average. Focusing on the rally models, we see that Zverev does not stand out in terms of rally execution. He builds his advantage through his serve. Federer, Djokovic and Thiem achieve high rally execution values. Both Federer and Thiem also have a high shot execution which indicates that they try to win rallies immediately. Instead, Djokovic shot execution is lower than average which shows that he does not try to win points directly but try to outplay his opponents in longer rallies where he is building up the point slowly. 4.2 Thiem’s march to Australian Open 2020 final We saw how decision and execution values can give us insights into a players’ playing style. Focusing on execution values for the remainder of the paper, we are also able to investigate Thiem’s performance over previous matches. Figure 4. Shot execution values of Thiem on his way to the final. Vertical lines highlight 95% confidence intervals. Dashed lines indicate tournament averages. Figure 4 displays Thiem’s average execution values over the rounds to the final. It’s evident that he served well throughout the tournament, with exception of the quarterfinal. His return execution approximated the average for the field but he was clearly superior in rally play, especially on the forehand. It follows that his dominance with this wing might be a deciding factor in the final against Djokovic. 4.3 How Thiem’s forehand cost him the title 7 The final went down to the wire, with Djokovic edging out the Austrian 6:4 in the fifth. In applying our models in the same way as above but this time to Thiem’s execution in each set of the final, we examine what went wrong. Figure 5 summarizes the execution values for serve, return and forehand and backhand rally balls for each player for each set of the final. The dashed lines represent the average execution values of Thiem and Djokovic in the lead up to the final. Figure 5. Australian Open Final – Shot and rally execution values We turn our attention to set 5, where we observe some interesting shifts: 1) Djokovic’s serve execution improved, 2) Thiem’s return execution dropped, logically related to the improvement on Djokovic’s serve 3) The quality of Thiem’s ball striking in rally play fell away, with a sharp drop in forehand execution. This is stark, especially against the backdrop in Thiem having the best forehand execution values of all semifinalists. Interestingly, by applying the concept of leverage to quantify low (less than 5%) and high (more than 5%) scoreboard pressure situations (as it has been done in football, [9]), we are able to better understand where Thiem came unstuck (Figure 6). In high pressure situations in the first four sets, Thiem’s backhand execution values were close to his tournament average while he outperformed on his forehand. The story couldn’t have been more different in the fifth set though, where his rally game unraveled, particularly on his favored forehand wing. If we look at Thiem’s decision values we observe that they stayed on the same level for his backhand and only dropped moderately compared to the drop in his forehand execution. While Djokovic clearly upped his own game, Thiem’s ball striking and dominant forehand execution succumbed to the pressure. 8 Figure 6. Rally execution and decision values for Thiem on high pressure points. The distribution for execution and decision values of all players is shown for forehand and backhand. Thiem’s average value before the final is highlighted as gray circle. The average he played in the final in sets 1 – 4 as green circle and his execution values in the final set as red circles. 4.4. Dissecting the tennis rally To this point, we have aggregated decision and execution values at the set, match and tournament level. However, these models also give rise to the opportunity to integrate the match win prediction model and identify situations where the outcome of a point and the shot execution values seem incongruent. We use the scoreline 4:6, 6:4, 6:2, 3:6, 1:2, Advantage Thiem to do this very thing. Here, the leverage is 21.15%. Thiem is down a break but manages to create an opportunity to break back on Djokovic’s serve. If he breaks serve, scores are level and he is “back in the match”. We can use our execution values to determine the actual in-rally win probability after each shot. 9 Furthermore, we can determine the expected match win probability by weighting the last observed in-rally win probability with the resulting match win probabilities for a positive and negative outcome of the point. This allows to get a more accurate evaluation of what is happening on the court. Figure 7. Evolution of Thiem’s rally win percentage after shot execution during a critical point in the fifth set. Figure 7 depicts Thiem’s winning probability during the rally in question (video of the rally can be seen here: https://youtu.be/A9NA8gCCI2M , 1). Before the point, Thiem has a pre-rally match win percentage of 19.27%. (2), which then updates in the plot at the time of the ball bounce for each shot. Green diamonds correspond to Djokovic’s shots and blue circles to Thiem’s shots. On the images below, the positions and movement directions of players and ball are highlighted for Djokovic (green), Thiem (red) and the ball (yellow). These were used as features in the modelling process. The point unfolds as follows ... (2.1) Djokovic hits a well-executed serve wide to the Thiem backhand, giving Thiem a 16% chance of winning the rally. (2.2) Thiem hits a backhand slice to the center of the court, which Djokovic volleys deep back to Thiem’s backhand corner. (2.3) Thiem moves backwards to return the Djokovic volley which is not played with much pace. This provides Thiem with options and his rally win percentage increases to 44.9%. (2.4) Thiem attempts a passing shot down-the-line but hits it wide. (3) The outcome does not reflect what happened in the rally. Thiem loses the point but before taking the shot he should expect to win it 44.9% of the time. His post-rally win probability of the match drops to 12.5% (- 6.77%) but incorporating his in-rally win percentage, his expected match 10 win percentage actually increased to 22.0% (+ 2.73%). This shows that Thiem played this important point well but this is not visible on the scoreboard. 5. Conclusions We introduced several models to evaluate a tennis players decision making and shot execution with a focus on either shot or rally level. This allowed us to investigate the performance of players on serve, return and in longer rallies. Various use-cases around Thiem’s performance at last Australian Open showed how the models can be used to interpret playing style and judge the performance of a player over a tournament, in-match on a set level, or even on rally level. Combining the shot execution model xER with an in-match win probability model allowed us to calculate the expected in-match win probability based on what actually happened in a rally. Furthermore, our in-match win predictor and the concept of leverage allowed us to investigate how Thiem played high-pressure points in the final. Even though we focused on presenting several use-cases related to measuring and interpreting Thiem’s performance at last Australian Open and especially in the final, the evaluation approach is not limited to only one player. Based on available player and ball tracking data, it allows to evaluate the performance of tennis players in an objective, automated and fully data-driven way. A possible next step is to investigate the performance of various players in high-pressure situations across serve, return and in-rally play. References [1] Fernandez, J., Bornn, L., & Dan Cervone (2020). Decomposing the Immeasurable Sport: A deep learning expected possession value framework for soccer. args.summary:
This paper, authored by Robert Seidl, Machar Reid, and Sam Robertson (Tennis Australia and Victoria University), presents a novel data-driven methodology to objectively quantify decision-making and shot execution in professional tennis using Hawkeye player and ball tracking data from the 2020 Australian Open. The central motivation stems from the fact that tennis is a game of thin margins—a player can win the same number of points as an opponent yet still lose the match—so the scoreboard can mask important performance details.

**Methodology:**
- Four neural network models were trained on 107,000 hits and 98,000 bounces (test set: 12,000 hits and 11,000 bounces) to disentangle decision-making from execution for each shot. Models predict either winning the point immediately (direct winner) or winning the rally later.
- Decision is valued at the moment of the shot ("when the ball leaves the racket"), while execution is valued at the moment of the ball bounce in the opponent's court.
- Model outputs are abbreviated as xDW, xDR, xEW, and xER (expected decision and execution values for direct winners and rally wins, respectively).
- Input features include position, speed, and angle of both players and the ball, plus shot classifications (serve, return, or rally shot).
- Model performance (AUC/Accuracy): xDW 73%/81%, xDR 65%/59%, xEW 78%/84%, xER 71%/63%.
- An in-match win probability model was developed using a four-step process: (1) pre-match ELO ratings adjusted for surface and head-to-head, (2) calibration into serve/return predictions, (3) Bayesian in-match updates based on observed serve performance, and (4) in-match prediction using a Barnett-Clarke model. "Leverage" is defined as how much a point could influence match outcome, identifying high-pressure situations (thresholds of less than 5% and more than 5% scoreboard pressure).

**Key Applications and Findings (focused on Dominic Thiem at Australian Open 2020):**
1. **Playing styles of the four men's semi-finalists:** Zverev led serve execution (both shot and rally level); Djokovic's return play was superb (rally execution more than 5 points over average), with lower-than-average shot execution in rallies indicating he builds points slowly rather than hitting winners; Federer, Djokovic, and Thiem achieved high rally execution values.
2. **Thiem's march to the final:** He served well throughout (except the quarterfinal), return execution was near average, but he was clearly superior in rally play, especially on the forehand.
3. **The final against Djokovic (Djokovic won 6:4, 4:6, 2:6, 6:3, 6:4):** In the fifth set, Djokovic's serve execution improved, Thiem's return execution dropped, and Thiem's forehand execution sharply declined under high pressure. In high-pressure situations in sets 1–4, Thiem's backhand was near average and his forehand outperformed; in the fifth set, his rally game unraveled, particularly on the forehand wing. His decision values stayed relatively stable, indicating his shot selection held up but his execution (ball striking) succumbed to pressure.
4. **Rally-level dissection:** At scoreline 4:6, 6:4, 6:2, 3:6, 1:2, Advantage Thiem (leverage 21.15%), a critical point was analyzed. Thiem's rally win probability reached 44.9% after Djokovic's weak volley, but he hit a passing shot wide. Although he lost the point (post-rally match win probability dropped to 12.5%, -6.77%), incorporating his in-rally win percentage showed his expected match win probability actually increased to 22.0% (+2.73%). This demonstrates that Thiem played the point well, a fact invisible on the scoreboard.

**Conclusions:** The framework enables objective, automated, fully data-driven evaluation of tennis player performance across serve, return, and in-rally play—at tournament, match, set, or individual rally levels. A suggested next step is investigating player performance in high-pressure situations across all three shot categories.

In this way, the scoreboard can be misleading or mask important details of points and matches that require further analysis to explain the victory."

This is a Semantic Scholar academic paper page for the research article "Forecasting the Next Shot Location in Tennis Using Fine-Grained Spatiotemporal Tracking Data" by Xinyu Wei, Patrick Lucey, Stuart Morgan, and Sridha Sridharan, published in the IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering (Volume 28, pages 2988-2997) on November 1, 2016. DOI: 10.1109/TKDE.2016.2594787, Corpus ID: 17228780.

The research uses ball and player tracking data from "Hawk-Eye" to discover unique player styles and predict within-point events in tennis. It moves beyond current analysis that only incorporates coarse match statistics by using spatial and temporal information to better characterize the tactics and tendencies of each player. The paper includes 10 figures and 10 tables.

- "Computer vision and machine learning for in-play tennis analysis" (2018) by S. Mora.
- "CourtTime: Generating Actionable Insights into Tennis Matches Using Visual Analytics" (2020), which introduces 1-D Space-Time Charts.
- "Pose2Trajectory" (2023), which uses transformers on body pose to predict a tennis player's future trajectory.
- "Vid2Player" (2021), which converts annotated broadcast video into controllable video sprites of professional tennis players.
- "A Markov process approach to untangling intention versus execution in tennis" (2022) by Chan et al., which found optimal shot selection strategies become more conservative as execution error grows.

The page also lists 24 references, including prior foundational works by the same authors, such as "Predicting Shot Locations in Tennis Using Spatiotemporal Data" (2013), ""Sweet-Spot": Using Spatiotemporal Data to Discover and Predict Shots in Tennis" (2013), "Forecasting Events Using an Augmented Hidden Conditional Random Field" (2014), and related works on team movement analysis in basketball ("How to Get an Open Shot"), soccer formation analysis, and NBA expected possession value (POINTWISE, 2014).

## Article summary

## Abstract

The high velocity of tennis balls presents significant challenges for visual trajectory perception and impact point localization, frequently leading to erroneous line calls. Although technological integration, particularly ball-tracking systems, has improved accuracy, these solutions are hindered by high equipment costs, dependence on manual calibration, and limitations in real-time processing capabilities. Deep learning-based approaches offer potential cost reductions but suffer from inherent detection latency and higher missed detection rates for small, fast-moving objects. The proposed multimodal fusion system integrates event cameras with conventional video streams. A spatio-temporal feature alignment module effectively addresses heterogeneous data synchronization and reduces the false detection rate caused by motion blur in high-speed videos by 58%. A Lightweight Hybrid Network (LHNet) is designed. Additionally, Dynamic Sparse Convolution (DSC) is employed to enhance computational efficiency for real-time operation. A Ballistic Trajectory Predictor (BTP) is introduced by incorporating aerodynamic drag and spin coefficients within a physics-constrained model, reducing the impact point prediction error to 1.2 cm - a significant improvement over the 3.5 cm error typical of conventional methods. Experimental validation on the TrackNet dataset demonstrates that the system achieves a detection accuracy of 98.7% (mAP@0.5), with a trajectory tracking ID-switch rate of only 0.5%, representing a 2.6-fold improvement over DeepSORT.

## 1 Introduction

This investigation focuses on tennis ball trajectory analysis by integrating computer vision with sports analytics to achieve robust detection under complex background interference and enable multi-dimensional state estimation of high-speed moving targets [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#ref-CR1 "Raj A, Wang L, Gedeon T.TrackNetV4: enhancing fast sports object tracking with motion attention maps. 2024. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/ICASSP49660.2025.10889364
                  
                .")]. Traditional marker-based motion capture systems face limitations due to high hardware costs and environmental constraints. Conversely, vision-based markerless approaches must address dynamic challenges including non-rigid deformation, motion blur, and occlusion [[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#ref-CR2 "Alshami AK, Boult T, Kalita J. Pose2Trajectory: using transformers on body pose to predict tennis player's trajectory. 2024.
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jvcir.2023.103954
                  
                .")]. Recent advances in deep learning and spatio-temporal modeling have significantly enhanced the spatio-temporal consistency of trajectory prediction. These developments provide a quantifiable foundation for athlete biomechanical analysis and establish an algorithmic groundwork for real-time officiating assistance systems [[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#ref-CR3 "Somani A, Malapati A. BallTraj: fast-moving ball trajectory tracking using an encoder–decoder network. In: International conference on sports engineering. Singapore: Springer; 2025.
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-97-8297-0_3
                  
                .")].

Despite rapid progress in tennis analysis technology, the field continues to grapple with balancing precision, real-time performance, and cost-effectiveness [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#ref-CR4 "Hashmi MF, Naik BT, Keskar A. BDTA: events classification in table tennis sport using scaled-YOLOv4 framework. J Intell Fuzzy Syst. 2023;44:9671–84. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3233/jifs-224300
                  
                .")]. While YOLOv5-based solutions offer real-time detection through lightweight feature fusion network architectures to reduce computational load, they often fail to adequately address motion blur induced by high-speed movement [[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#ref-CR5 "Wong P, Myint H, Dooley L, et al. A multi-view automatic table tennis umpiring framework. Proc Inst Mech Eng, Part P J Sports Eng Technol. 2023. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/17543371231171433
                  
                .")]. Event camera approaches that employ asynchronous spike data processing algorithms for trajectory capture typically suffer from low initial detection confidence due to the lack of rich video semantics [[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#ref-CR6 "He S. The application of deep learning-based technique detection model in table tennis teaching and learning. Microelectron J. 2024. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sasc.2024.200116
                  
                .")]. Multi-Kalman filter fusion methods improve trajectory prediction, yet exhibit limited capacity for modeling complex nonlinear physical effects (e.g., the Magnus effect) [[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#ref-CR7 "Chiang HT, Tseng BY, Chen JL, Hsieh HC. Trajectory analysis in UKF: predicting table tennis ball flight parameters. IT Professional. 2024. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/MITP.2024.3380837
                  
                .")]. Transformer-based sequential prediction models enhance long-range trajectory correlation, but their high computational complexity impedes real-time deployment [[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#ref-CR8 "Geetha S, Ganesh N, Abdullah AS, et al. High speed and tiny objects tracking system in racquet sports videos using deep learning with trajectory rectification feature. Procedia Comput Sci. 2025;258:3084–94. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.procs.2025.04.566
                  
                .")]. Federated learning frameworks enable cross-venue model optimization with privacy-preserving training, though they lack specific optimizations for small object detection [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#ref-CR9 "Gossard T, Krismer J, Ziegler A et al. Table tennis ball spin estimation with an event camera. IEEE; 2024.
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPRW63382.2024.00339
                  
                .")]. Hybrid methodologies combining rigid-body dynamics with deep learning for impact point prediction remain constrained by their dependency on high-precision initial parameters (e.g., rotational velocity) [[10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#ref-CR10 "Yang Q, Li G, Wang Y. Scientific training model for table tennis players based on artificial neural network algorithm. In: First international conference on real time intelligent systems. Cham: Springer; 2024. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-55848-1_30
                  
                .")]. This study constructs an end-to-end Spatio-Temporal Feature Alignment Module (STFAM). The proposed framework achieves heterogeneous sensor data fusion and alignment, leverages the LHNet architecture for computational acceleration, and incorporates a physics-constrained trajectory optimization model. A Cascaded Inference Pipeline (CIP) integrating detection with the BTP is constructed. The BOCM (Bidirectional Optical Flow Check Mechanism) is used to enhance tracking robustness, and QAT (Quantization-Aware Training) is deployed to adapt to embedded hardware. The results indicate that the system outperforms existing schemes in detection accuracy (98.7% mAP@0.5), inference speed (150 FPS), and impact point error (1.2 cm RMSE). Furthermore, the hardware cost is reduced.

The innovations of this study are listed below:

1.   (1)
The STFAM is proposed, which realizes the pixel-level alignment of event data and video frames through deformable convolution and a temporal encoder, and solves the problem of spatio-temporal dislocation of multi-modal data.

2.   (2)
A DSC is developed, which dynamically adjusts the convolution kernel sparse mode according to the input motion characteristics, and reduces the computational load by 30% while maintaining the accuracy.

3.   (3)
A physically-guided loss function is designed, and the rigid body dynamic equation is embedded into the neural network training process, enabling the predicted trajectory to satisfy the dual constraints of data-driven and physical laws simultaneously.

$$ F_{align} = \sum\limits_{N}^{i = 1} {w_{i} } \cdot (DConv(E_{t} ,R_{{t + {\Delta }t}} ) + TEnc({\Delta }t)) $$  (1)   

In Eq.([1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#Equ1)), \(F_{align}\) represents the feature map after alignment; \(DConv\) represents the deformable convolution operation; \(E_{t}\) represents the event data at time \(t\); \(R_{t + \Delta t}\) represents the video frame; \(TEnc\) represents the temporal encoder; \(w_{i}\) represents the learnable weight coefficient; and \(N\) is the number of feature map channels.

The spatial offset between the event data and the video frame is compensated by the deformable convolution, and the temporal encoder resolves the temporal offset caused by asynchronous acquisition.

1.   (2)
DSC computation:

$$ y(p) = \sum\limits_{k \in K} {W_{k} } \cdot x(p + p_{k} + {\Delta }p_{k} ) \cdot M_{k} (p) $$  (2)   

In Eq.([2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#Equ2)), \(y(p)\) is the value of the output feature map at position p; \(W_{k}\) is the \(k\)-th convolution kernel weight; \(x\) is the input feature map; \(p_{k}\) is the conventional convolution offset; \(\Delta p_{k}\) is the dynamically learned offset; and \(M_{k} (p)\) is the position-dependent sparse mask, generated by the gating mechanism.

1.   (3)
Physically constrained trajectory prediction:

$$ \frac{{d^{2} \mathop r\limits^{ \to } }}{{dt^{2} }} = \mathop g\limits^{ \to } + \frac{{\vec{F}_{d} }}{m} + \frac{{\vec{F}_{m} }}{m} $$  (3)   

In Eq.([3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#Equ3)), \(\vec{r}\) denotes the position vector of the sphere; \(\vec{g}\) denotes the gravitational acceleration; \(\vec{F}_{d}\) is the air resistance, given by \(F_{d} = - \frac{1}{2}C_{d} \rho A|\vec{v}|\vec{v}\); \(\vec{F}_{m}\) denotes the Magnus force, calculated as \(F_{m} = S(\vec{\omega } \times \vec{v})\); \(C_{d}\) is the drag coefficient; \(\rho\) is the air density; \(A\) denotes the cross-sectional area; \(S\) is the spin coefficient; and \(\vec{\omega }\) is the angular velocity vector.

The differential equations for each stage are numerically solved using the fourth-order Runge–Kutta method, which serves as a regularization constraint in the neural network.

### 3.2 Mathematical model and algorithmic flow

To solve the physical irrationality of the pure data-driven method, the physical equation is embedded into the training process as a strong constraint, so that the mathematical model, the loss function and the optimization objective form an organic whole.

The trajectory prediction module adopts a physics-constrained deep learning framework. First, the dynamic equation of tennis motion is established.

$$ m\frac{{d{\mathbf{v}}}}{dt} = m{\mathbf{g}} - \frac{1}{2}\rho C_{d} A\left\| {\mathbf{v}} \right\|{\mathbf{v}} + S({\varvec{\omega}} \times {\mathbf{v}}) $$

 (4) 

In Eq.([4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#Equ4)), \(m\) is the mass of the tennis ball; \({\mathbf{v}}\) is the velocity vector; \({\mathbf{g}}\) is the gravitational acceleration; \(\rho\) is the air density; \(C_{d}\) is the drag coefficient; \(A\) is the cross-sectional area; \(S\) is the spin coefficient; \(\omega\) is the angular velocity vector.

The equations are solved numerically using the fourth-order Runge–Kutta method.

To integrate physical constraints into deep learning, a hybrid loss function is designed:

$$ { \mathcal{L}}_{total} = \lambda_{1} { \mathcal{L}}_{det} + \lambda_{2} { \mathcal{L}}_{track} + \lambda_{3} \left\| {\frac{{\partial^{2} r_{pred} }}{{\partial t^{2} }} - \frac{{F_{phy} }}{m}} \right\|_{2} $$

 (5) 

In Eq.([5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#Equ5)), \({ \mathcal{L}}_{det}\) represents the detection loss (CIoU loss); \({ \mathcal{L}}_{track}\) represents the tracking loss (ReID feature similarity), which is the last term forces the second derivative of the predicted trajectory to conform to the physical equation calculation results; and \(\lambda_{i}\) represents the balance weight. The weighting factors \(\lambda {1},\lambda {2},\lambda {3}\) are used to balance the contribution of each term. The physical term \(\partial\) constrains the second derivative (acceleration) of the trajectory predicted by the network to be consistent with the kinetic equation determined by the combination of air resistance, Magnus force, and gravity.

The loss function enables the network to learn both visual features and physical laws [[25](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#ref-CR25 "Lozovenko O, Minaiev Y, Datsenko I. Critical thinking skills and computer simulations of free rigid body motion. In: International conference on interactive collaborative learning. Cham: Springer. 2025. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-85649-5_22
                  
                .")].

The real-time optimization objective is as follows:

$$ \mathop {\min }\limits_{\theta } { \mathbb{E}}[{ \mathcal{L}}_{total} ] + \alpha \left\| \theta \right\|_{1} + \beta T_{latency} $$

 (6) 

In Eq.([6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#Equ6)), \(\theta\) represents the network parameters; \(T_{latency}\) denotes the end-to-end latency; and \(\alpha ,\beta\) are adjustment coefficients.

Through this optimization objective, the real-time requirement of embedded deployment is achieved while accuracy is guaranteed.

## 4 Design of multimodal fusion architecture

The core innovation of the proposed multimodal processing framework lies in establishing a mechanism for cross-modal feature interaction. In contrast to foundational models, this section details the implementation of dynamic feature selection and spatio-temporal attention enhancement. The system employs a dual-encoder-single-decoder architecture, wherein the event data encoder utilizes a spiking neural network (SNN) to process asynchronous event streams.

1.   (1)
Event pulse coding:

$$ H_{t}^{event} = \sum\limits_{N}^{i = 1} {\alpha_{i} } \cdot \delta (t - t_{i} ) * \kappa (t) $$  (7)   

In Eq.([7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#Equ7)), \(H_{t}^{event}\) is the event characteristic at the time \(t\); \(\alpha_{i}\) is the intensity of the i-th event; \(t_{i}\) is the event timestamp; \(\delta ( \cdot )\) is the Dirac function; and \(\kappa (t)\) is the exponential decay kernel function \(\kappa (t) = e^{ - t/\tau } ,\tau = 10ms\).

Encoding preserves the high temporal resolution of event data.

To effectively integrate heterogeneous data, a cross-modal attention gating mechanism is designed:

$$ \begin{aligned} {\mathbf{G}} = & \; \sigma ({\mathbf{W}}_{g} [{\mathbf{F}}^{rgb} ||{\mathbf{F}}^{event} ] + {\mathbf{b}}_{g} ) \\ {\mathbf{F}}^{fused} = & \; {\mathbf{G}} \odot {\mathbf{F}}^{rgb} + (1 - {\mathbf{G}}) \odot {\mathbf{F}}^{event} \\ \end{aligned} $$

 (8) 

In Eq.([8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#Equ8)), \({\mathbf{G}}\) denotes the gating weight matrix; \({\mathbf{W}}_{g}\) and \({\mathbf{b}}_{g}\) are the learnable parameters; \(||\) is the concatenation operation; \(\sigma\) is the Sigmoid function; and \(\odot\) denotes the element-wise multiplication. This mechanism can adaptively adjust the contribution of different modal features [[26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#ref-CR26 "Xie J, Luo Y, Lan P, et al. FBSA-Net: a novel model based on attention mechanisms for emotion recognition in VR and 2D scenes. Knowl-Based Syst. 2024. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.knosys.2024.112287
                  
                .")].

1.   (2)
Motion-aware dynamic network.

According to the high-speed movement characteristics of a tennis ball, a motion-guided network structure adjustment strategy is proposed. A motion saliency map is first constructed:

$$ { \mathcal{M}}(x,y) = \frac{1}{T}\sum\limits_{T}^{t = 1} {\left\| {\nabla I_{t} (x,y)} \right\|_{2} } \cdot { \mathbb{I}}\left( {\left\| {_{t} (x,y)} \right\|{\mathbf{v}} > \xi } \right) $$

 (9) 

In Eq.([9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#Equ9)), \({ \mathcal{M}}(x,y)\) represents the saliency at position \(\left( {x,y} \right)\); \(T\) represents the time window; \(\nabla I_{t}\) represents the image gradient; \({\mathbf{v}}_{t}\) represents the optical flow field; and \(\xi\) represents the velocity threshold (20 pixels/frame). The formula quantifies the intensity of motion in each region.

1.   (3)
The saliency map dynamically adjusts the network structure:

$$ {\mathbf{W}}_{dyn} (x,y) = {\mathbf{W}}_{0} + {\Delta }{\mathbf{W}} \cdot {\text{tanh}}({ \mathcal{M}}(x,y)/\gamma ) $$  (10)   

In Eq.([10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#Equ10)), \({\mathbf{W}}_{dyn}\) is the location-dependent dynamic convolution kernel; \({\mathbf{W}}_{0}\) is the reference weight; \(\Delta {\mathbf{W}}\) is the learnable adjustment; and \(\gamma\) is the normalization coefficient.

The flight trajectory of a tennis ball is influenced by multiple aerodynamic forces, including air resistance and the Magnus force—the latter arising from ball spin. In the proposed model, the spin of the ball is not treated as a direct input variable. Instead, its effect is incorporated indirectly. The dominant influence of spin is assumed to manifest as lateral drift during flight. This influence is integrated into the state-transition component of the trajectory dynamics model through a learnable equivalent drift parameter, which is optimized from data.

Aerodynamic coefficients, such as the drag coefficient \(C_{d}\), are adopted as prior knowledge based on experimental values reported in fluid dynamics literature for tennis balls within typical velocity ranges. To evaluate the sensitivity of landing-point predictions to variations in these coefficients, a supplementary experiment was conducted. During testing, the drag coefficient was perturbed within \(\alpha \pm {2}0\%\) range of its nominal value. Results indicate that the resulting changes in the average lateral and longitudinal prediction errors remained below 8%. This suggests that the model's predictions exhibit notable robustness, provided the coefficients are set within physically plausible bounds. Such robustness can be partly attributed to the capacity of the data-driven component to compensate for deviations in the physical model.

The network allocates more computing resources to high-speed moving areas and achieves performance improvement through key technology breakthroughs:

1.   (1)
Pulse coding of event data reduces the data volume by 70%.

2.   (2)
The dynamic convolution allocation reduces the computational load by 35%.

3.   (3)
The hierarchical prediction strategy achieves a 2.1 × speedup.

The improvement enables the system to maintain real-time performance in complex scenarios, which lays the foundation for actual deployment.

## 5 The simulation experiment analysis

Systematic experimental validation is conducted to assess the core performance of the multimodal tennis trajectory analysis system, evaluate the performance improvement of the refined algorithm over the baseline model, and establish an empirical basis for parameter optimization in practical deployment.

### 5.1 Experimental environment setup

The data utilized in this study comprises two primary modalities: conventional RGB video streams and event camera data streams. The RGB video data is primarily sourced from the publicly available TrackNet dataset, which provides high-quality tennis match videos along with corresponding annotations. To construct a multimodal dataset, two distinct approaches are employed to generate event data streams that are spatio-temporally aligned with the RGB videos.

First, event streams corresponding to the RGB sequences are synthetically generated using the simulation functionality available in the Metavision Software Development Kit (SDK). This simulation process incorporates key response characteristics of event cameras—such as contrast thresholds and temporal resolution—to convert the TrackNet video frame sequences into realistic event-based representations.

Second, to assess model performance on authentic event data, a separate set of real-world data is captured under controlled laboratory conditions. A DAVIS346 event camera is used to synchronously record event streams alongside high-speed RGB video during simulated tennis stroke actions. This collection provides a direct means to evaluate the framework’s applicability to genuine neuromorphic sensory inputs.

Prior to model input, all data—whether synthetic or real—undergo rigorous spatio-temporal alignment preprocessing. Temporal synchronization at the millisecond level is achieved through a combination of hardware synchronization signals and software-based timestamp interpolation. Spatial alignment is performed by calibrating the intrinsic and extrinsic parameters of both sensors, ensuring coherent field-of-view registration across modalities.

This hybrid data strategy serves a dual purpose: it leverages existing well-annotated RGB datasets to facilitate large-scale training and benchmarking, while also providing a preliminary validation pathway using physically captured event-RGB pairs to gauge real-world feasibility.

The proposed model achieves an average processing speed of 158 frames per second (FPS) with an end-to-end latency of 7.2 ms (ms). This latency can be further broken down into the following stages: data I/O and alignment (~ 1.5 ms), RGB stream feature extraction (~ 2.8 ms), event stream feature extraction (~ 1.9 ms), feature fusion and trajectory prediction (~ 0.8 ms), and physics-based refinement with output (~ 0.2 ms).

By comparison, the baseline model using only RGB video operates at 210 FPS with a latency of 4.5 ms on the same hardware platform. The additional delay in the proposed model primarily stems from the dual-modal feature extraction and fusion computations. This computational overhead, however, is compensated by the model's improved tracking and prediction accuracy—as demonstrated in Sect.[5.2.1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#Sec12).

As the primary visualization tool, RViz utilizes standard visualization components with powerful real-time rendering capabilities for three-dimensional data, and can simultaneously display camera coordinate systems, point cloud data, motion trajectories, and other information.

The TrackNet tennis tracking dataset [27] (2025) is selected, including tennis video data with 20,844 frames of annotated data (1280 × 720 resolution, 30fps), covering the entire rally from serve to score; the MCP (Match Charting Project) dataset, which records professional tennis match data point by point, including stroke type, direction, and return depth. The TrackNet dataset is randomly partitioned into training, validation, and test sets at a ratio of 70:15:15, ensuring statistical independence among the subsets. All video frames are uniformly rescaled to a resolution of 640 × 640 and normalized. Event data is processed using the Metavision SDK 3.0 to generate event surfaces through accumulation over a 10 ms time window. During training, in addition to the explicitly listed hyperparameters, a weight decay coefficient of 1 × 10–4 is applied. Additionally, a cosine annealing scheduler with a warm-up phase of 5 epochs is used to adjust the learning rate. The generation of synthetic data closely follows the physical rendering pipeline of Unity3D, with all simulation parameters (e.g., lighting, ball speed, camera angle) controlled by a random seed to ensure the repeatability of the generated sequence.

### 5.2 Simulation experiment analysis

To accurately evaluate the system performance, all speed and latency assessments are conducted on a Jetson Xavier NX embedded platform with an input resolution of 640 × 640. The overall end-to-end average latency of the system is measured at 8.3 ms (equivalent to approximately 120 FPS), with the detection module consistently responding within 5 ms. Under high-speed scenarios of 250 km/h, the system maintains a processing rate of 89 FPS, verifying robust performance under extreme conditions. The input video streams are standardized at 200 fps and synchronized with event camera data to ensure temporal alignment across modalities. The system exhibits an average power consumption of 14.5 W, with peak memory usage stabilizing at 2.3 GB. Under standard ambient conditions of 25 ℃, the chip junction temperature remains steady at 68 ℃ without triggering thermal throttling mechanisms.

To fairly evaluate the effectiveness of the fusion architecture itself, all comparative experiments in this section are conducted under identical input conditions. Specifically, each model included in the comparison—including the baseline models—is provided access to both temporally aligned RGB video streams and synthetically generated event streams. This setup eliminates performance discrepancies arising solely from differences in the number or type of sensors. **Table 7 Comparative fault identification performance of different models (N = 6800)**

[Full size table](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0/tables/7)

The Trajectory Offset is defined as the two-dimensional Euclidean distance (in pixels) between the predicted position and the true position.

The results show that event data contribute 21.7% of effective detection compensation under simulated strong backlight conditions. The DSC mechanism reduces GPU memory consumption by 37% (1.8 GB → 1.13 GB). Physical engine validation demonstrates a mean trajectory deviation of merely 0.3 cm from the rigid body dynamics model. Feature alignment accuracy reaches 82.1% in the simulated environment. The DSC architecture reduces computational FLOPs to 58% of the baseline model. The mean Dynamic Angular Error (DAE) for predicted trajectories is 2.1°.

#### 5.2.2 High-speed motion tracking stability

Tracking stability was rigorously evaluated under projectile velocities of 200–250 km/h. High-fidelity physical simulations incorporated the following disturbance factors:

1.   (1)
Transient occlusion (duration: 3–5 frames; occurrence rate: 15–20%)

2.   (2)
Motion blur (equivalent shutter speed: 1/2000s)

3.   (3)
Background interference (simulating spectator movement patterns) [[28](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#ref-CR28 "Shi Z, Jia Y, Shi G, et al. Design of motor skill recognition and hierarchical evaluation system for table tennis players. IEEE Sens J. 2024. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/JSEN.2023.3346880
                  
                .")].

Experimental results and quantitative data analyses are presented in Table[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#Tab8). Additionally, the RViz output is primarily used to generate trajectory analysis, as shown in Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#Fig4).

**Table 8 Comparison of tracking stability in high-speed motion (n = 5 independent experiments)**

[Full size table](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0/tables/8)

**Fig.4**

![Image 10: Fig. 4](https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1007%2Fs44163-026-01127-0/MediaObjects/44163_2026_1127_Fig4_HTML.png)

[Full size image](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0/figures/4)

High-speed motion tracking stability

As illustrated in Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#Fig4), the Motion Compensation Controller (MCC) achieves a 62% reduction in velocity fluctuation and a 39% decrease in endpoint error (3.2 cm vs. 5.3 cm). Adaptive feature weighting reduces the ID switch rate by a factor of four compared to DeepSORT. The system maintains a processing rate of 89 FPS at speeds of 250 km/h. Experimental validation confirms the system's reliability and precision under professional competition-level high-speed conditions, providing critical technical support for practical deployment.

#### 5.2.3 Physical reliability of impact point prediction

This study validates the effectiveness of a physics-constrained deep learning framework for landing-point prediction, addressing the physically implausible results generated by purely data-driven approaches during long-term forecasting. Utilizing a dataset comprising 500 simulated stroke trajectories synchronously captured at 1000 fps, three prediction paradigms are evaluated: (1) pure LSTM sequential prediction [[29](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#ref-CR29 "Sun X, Wang Y, Khan J. Hybrid LSTM and GAN model for action recognition and prediction of lawn tennis sport activities. Soft Comput Fusion Found Methodol Appl. 2023;27(23):18093–112. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s00500-023-09215-4
                  
                .")]; (2) conventional rigid-body dynamics computation; (3) the proposed physics-constrained hybrid methodology.

The experimental results are presented in Table[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#Tab9) and Fig.[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#Fig5).

**Table 9 Ablation experimental results**

[Full size image](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0/figures/5)

Reliability error distribution heatmap

In the test, the physical constraint reduces the prediction error by 53% for long distances (more than 5 m); the significant reduction of the maximum error (3.8 cm vs. 8.7 cm) demonstrates the model's robustness to extreme cases; and the improvement of the error growth slope indicates that the physical constraint effectively suppresses the error accumulation effect.

Figure[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01127-0#Fig5), presenting the error distribution heatmap, demonstrates that our approach achieves significantly superior prediction consistency (standard deviation = 0.38 cm) across all court regions compared to the purely data-drive

This is an open-access research article published in Discover Artificial Intelligence (Volume 6, article 484, published April 19, 2026) by Guoqing Chen. The study presents a multimodal fusion system for real-time tennis ball trajectory tracking and landing point prediction, addressing challenges in accurate trajectory perception and impact point localization for fair line calls in tennis.

Key innovations of the system include:
1. A Spatio-Temporal Feature Alignment Module (STFAM) using deformable convolution and a temporal encoder for pixel-level alignment of event camera data with conventional video streams, reducing false detection rates caused by motion blur by 58%.
2. A Lightweight Hybrid Network (LHNet) with Dynamic Sparse Convolution (DSC) that reduces computational load by 30% while maintaining accuracy.
3. A Ballistic Trajectory Predictor (BTP) incorporating aerodynamic drag and spin coefficients within a physics-constrained model, reducing impact point prediction error to 1.2 cm (vs. 3.5 cm typical of conventional methods).
4. A Cascaded Inference Pipeline (CIP) integrating detection with trajectory prediction, plus Bidirectional Optical Flow Check Mechanism (BOCM) for tracking robustness and Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) for embedded hardware adaptation.

Key experimental results on the TrackNet dataset include:
- Detection accuracy of 98.7% (mAP@0.5)
- Trajectory tracking ID-switch rate of only 0.5% (2.6-fold improvement over DeepSORT)
- Processing speed of 150-158 FPS with end-to-end latency of 7.2-8.3 ms on Jetson Xavier NX embedded platform
- Impact point prediction error of 1.2 cm RMSE
- The physics constraint reduces prediction error by 53% for distances over 5 meters
- Maximum error reduced from 8.7 cm to 3.8 cm
- Prediction consistency standard deviation of 0.38 cm
- Event data contributes 21.7% of detection compensation under strong backlight conditions
- DSC reduces GPU memory consumption by 37% (1.8 GB → 1.13 GB)
- System maintains 89 FPS at 250 km/h ball speeds, with average power consumption of 14.5 W

The system architecture comprises a multi-modal data acquisition layer (video + event camera), the LHNet, and a physics-constrained trajectory prediction engine. The trajectory model embeds rigid-body dynamics equations (including air resistance, Magnus force, and gravity) directly into neural network training through a hybrid loss function. The study compares against baseline methods including YOLOv8 (210 FPS, 97.2% mAP@0.5) and pure event camera approaches (89.3% accuracy). Unlike expensive Hawk-Eye systems costing over USD 500,000 with errors under 3mm, the proposed markerless system uses consumer-grade cameras (under USD 1,000) while achieving centimeter-level accuracy.

This work presents a multimodal fusion system that significantly enhances real-time detection and trajectory prediction, achieving a remarkable 98.7% accuracy and reducing prediction error to just 1.2 cm, thereby improving the reliability of line calls in tennis."

PMCID: PMC8271826  PMID: [34283127](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34283127/)

## Abstract

In sport science, athlete tracking and motion analysis are essential for monitoring and optimizing training programs, with the goal of increasing success in competition and preventing injury. At present, contact-free, camera-based, multi-athlete detection and tracking have become a reality, mainly due to the advances in machine learning regarding computer vision and, specifically, advances in artificial convolutional neural networks (CNN), used for human pose estimation (HPE-CNN) in image sequences. Sport science in general, as well as coaches and athletes in particular, would greatly benefit from HPE-CNN-based tracking, but the sheer amount of HPE-CNNs available, as well as their complexity, pose a hurdle to the adoption of this new technology. It is unclear how many HPE-CNNs which are available at present are ready to use in out-of-the-box inference to squash, to what extent they allow motion analysis and if detections can easily be used to provide insight to coaches and athletes. Therefore, we conducted a systematic investigation of more than 250 HPE-CNNs. After applying our selection criteria of open-source, pre-trained, state-of-the-art and ready-to-use, five variants of three HPE-CNNs remained, and were evaluated in the context of motion analysis for the racket sport of squash. Specifically, we are interested in detecting player’s feet in videos from a single camera and investigated the detection accuracy of all HPE-CNNs. To that end, we created a ground-truth dataset from publicly available squash videos by developing our own annotation tool and manually labeling frames and events. We present heatmaps, which depict the court floor using a color scale and highlight areas according to the relative time for which a player occupied that location during matchplay. These are used to provide insight into detections. Finally, we created a decision flow chart to help sport scientists, coaches and athletes to decide which HPE-CNN is best for player detection and tracking in a given application scenario.

**Keywords:** racket sports, sports analysis, video tracking, human pose estimation

## 1. Introduction

Training is an integral part of sports. Well-planned and conscientiously executed adaptation mechanisms can lead to improvements in athletes’ performance, and an optimized training program can ultimately lead to more success in competition, while decreasing the risk of injury [[1](#B1-sensors-21-04550)]. At present, training quality and effectiveness can be quantitatively evaluated and measured using different types of sensors. For physiological core measures, such as fitness and endurance wearable sensors, monitors for heart rate, blood pressure and oxygen level are available [[2](#B2-sensors-21-04550)]. Likewise, for training aspects generally concerning movement and game tactics, motion sensors are available to measure velocity, acceleration and motion trajectories [[3](#B3-sensors-21-04550)]. A classic example can be found in football (soccer), where team performance and collaboration is paramount and, therefore, individual player on-field locations, moves and motion paths are analyzed [[4](#B4-sensors-21-04550),[5](#B5-sensors-21-04550)].

The SAGIT/Squash, introduced by Pers in 2008 and improved and used by Vučković et al. [[6](#B6-sensors-21-04550)], represents an early example of camera-based player-tracking in squash. The system requires a downward-facing camera mounted on the ceiling, centered above the court. The SAGIT/Squash system was used for several studies [[7](#B7-sensors-21-04550),[8](#B8-sensors-21-04550),[9](#B9-sensors-21-04550)].

As well as the classic tracking approaches evaluated by van der Kruk and Reijne [[3](#B3-sensors-21-04550)], the development of convolutional neural networks (CNN) in the field of deep machine learning for computer vision may offer new approaches for detection and tracking applications in sport sciences. Classic applications for CNNs are for example recognizing and classifying images of handwritten digits [[10](#B10-sensors-21-04550)]. Recently, CNNs found wide application in the field of medical imaging for applications such classification or segmentation [[11](#B11-sensors-21-04550)]. In addition, deep learning has also been successfully applied in the area network data transmission and traffic classification technology [[12](#B12-sensors-21-04550),[13](#B13-sensors-21-04550)]. For handball [[14](#B14-sensors-21-04550)] and football [[15](#B15-sensors-21-04550)] specifically, CNNs have been used for player detection and tracking.

Due to the increased interest in machine learning, the sheer number of human pose estimation convolutional neural networks (HPE-CNNs) available and their complexity pose a hurdle to the adoption and implementation of this new technology. It is unclear how many are open-source, pre-trained and, out-of-the-box, ready-to-use for player detection and motion analysis in squash. Therefore, we address the following research questions:

* RQ1: How many HPE-CNNs available today are ready to use for out-of-the-box inference on squash data for motion analysis?
* RQ2: To what extent and with what accuracy do they allow motion analysis in squash?
* RQ3: Can the data obtained from the HPE-CNNs selected in RQ2 be easily used to provide insight to coaches and athletes?

To answer the first question, we conducted a systematic investigation of more than 250 HPE-CNNs. After applying our selection criteria of open-source, pre-trained, state-of-the-art and ready-to-use HPE-CNNs, three of five variants remained. Regarding question two, we evaluate the detection accuracy of different HPE-CNNs. To evaluate and compare them, a labeled dataset is required, since no dedicated squash dataset is available. Therefore, we created a novel ground truth dataset for evaluation by developing and implementing a labeling tool. We accessed publicly available squash matches with different court conditions and annotated the athletes’ feet. For the last research question, we present heatmaps that reflect players’ motion as detected by various HPE-CNNs, as well as players’ true motion, as obtained from our manually labeled dataset.

### 1.1. Related Work

The general task of locating one or several objects in a scene over time while keeping track of their identity is commonly known as object tracking or simply tracking. Tracking has applications in a wide range of domains, and therefore has been heavily researched in various communities. For example, in sport sciences, a specific athlete is tracked over time in a preferably unobtrusive manner during training and competition, thereby collecting movement data for measuring performance or game tactical aspects.

Different approaches have been developed for tracking athletes and applied to various sports. Early work dates back to the 1970s, where the movement and work-rates of different positions in English soccer players were analyzed using a manual notation system [[16](#B16-sensors-21-04550)]. Today, more sophisticated approaches are available, due to computer technology improving in terms of computing power, size (miniaturization), energy consumption and affordability.

For example, in their work, Kirkup et al. [[17](#B17-sensors-21-04550)] demonstrate that the localizing of indoor basketball players can be achieved by their wearing a lightweight combination of an acceleration sensor and a radio frequency transmitting beacon. With the development of modern camera technology and its wider and more affordable availability, computer vision has become an important research field for human motion capture [[18](#B18-sensors-21-04550)] in general, and in position localization in particular.

A single camera can potentially be used to obtain the essential movement data of several athletes simultaneously in an effective and contact-free manner. Different approaches such as marker- and non-marker-based methods have been described [[19](#B19-sensors-21-04550),[20](#B20-sensors-21-04550)]. Additionally, the broad public interest in various sports and the free-of-charge availability of online video-sharing platforms, such as YouTube results, in the availability of a considerable amount of video data, which can be used for retrospective analyses. Apart from the use of markers, computer-vision-based tracking systems can be classified into either multi-camera or single-camera systems, where camera technology can be conventional, e.g., monochrome, color (RGB), or more advanced, such as depth cameras based on structured light or time-of-flight measurements.

While it is not possible to perform a full three-dimensional reconstruction of a single RGB-camera image, due to the lack of depth information, methods using depth-sensitive cameras have been evaluated for human motion tracking [[21](#B21-sensors-21-04550),[22](#B22-sensors-21-04550)]. In this regard, Microsoft’s Kinect v1 and v2 were of special interest. The first, introduced to the gaming market in 2010, utilizes a structured light depth sensor and the second, introduced in 2014, is based on a time-of-flight depth sensor. In 2013, Choppin and Wheat investigated the Kinect’s potential for biomechanical sports analysis, including player tracking, and concluded that the v1 could potentially be used in coaching and education situations [[23](#B23-sensors-21-04550)]. These findings were confirmed by He et al. for the sport of badminton, where the Kinect v1 is used to guide training, reduce movement intensity and improve the overall training efficiency [[24](#B24-sensors-21-04550)]. For home-based training, van Diest et al. found that the Kinect System was able to accurately identify all relevant body features needed for motion capture [[25](#B25-sensors-21-04550)]. Further hardware improvements led to the introduction of the Kinect v2, featuring new active infrared capabilities, higher resolution camera and new depth sensing. The v2 has been investigated by Alabbasi et al. regarding its potential for human motion tracking. The authors found higher accuracy and concluded that the new version is capable of real-time motion sensing for rehabilitation and physical training exercises [[26](#B26-sensors-21-04550)]. Another application can be found in balance training for the elderly, where a Kinect System is used to characterize a person’s ability to maintain static or dynamic balance [[27](#B27-sensors-21-04550)].

Outside of the Kinect, more general approaches do not rely on depth cameras, and instead use multi-camera systems, which are either marker- or non-marker-based. Here, multiple-view geometry is applied, which uses point correspondences in several views to reconstruct depth information [[28](#B28-sensors-21-04550)]. An overview of different systems for different sports applications is given by van der Kruk and Reijne [[3](#B3-sensors-21-04550)]. All systems are used for a variety of purposes, from entertainment and training to medical applications. As these systems provide valuable data on the athlete’s performance in competition or training situations, they are of particular value for optimizing training and match preparation. Beyond gaining insight into individual performances, motion tracking can also be used to analyze team performances [[29](#B29-sensors-21-04550)].

One technology that has gained attention due to its major impact in the field of machine learning is human pose estimation (HPE). In computer vision, this task is defined as fitting or finding certain keypoints (joints) of a single person or multiple people and connecting them (bones) to form a human skeleton. For multi-person HPE, there are basically two different methods to distinguish between. The top-down approach first tries to detect all people individually in the image, and then estimates individual poses. For a bottom-up approach, keypoints are detected individually, and then subsequently grouped and assigned to individual people. A comprehensive survey of deep-learning-based HPE is given by Chen et al. [[30](#B30-sensors-21-04550)].

In addition, other algorithms from the field of (deep) machine learning are used, besides HPE, for different tasks in various sports. [Table 1](#sensors-21-04550-t001) shows an overview of the publications, together with the corresponding sports. As can be seen, object and player segmentation or detection has been explored and applied to a variety of sport applications. HPE and classification are the main, but not the only, research topics and applications for machine learning in sports. Moreover, publications are not limited to a single activity, but are broadly distributed across different sports. As an example, Liang et al. [[31](#B31-sensors-21-04550)] proposed a K-Shortest Path (KSP) algorithm to track multiple player detections, obtained by a CNN, together with a re-identification algorithm based on support vector machines (SVM) in basketball. In [[32](#B32-sensors-21-04550)], an object detector is used in conjunction with an HPE-CNN to infer player possession of either a frisbee or a ball. Similarly, for the sport of curling, an object detector was used for player and curling stone detection [[33](#B33-sensors-21-04550)]. Other HPE-CNN applications include speed detection in running [[34](#B34-sensors-21-04550)] and player pose analysis in tennis [[35](#B35-sensors-21-04550)]. Other machine learning approaches have been used for the detection and classification of direction changes in tennis [[36](#B36-sensors-21-04550)] and referee signal recognition in basketball [[37](#B37-sensors-21-04550)]. Other applications use sensor data instead of images. As an example, Anand et al. [[38](#B38-sensors-21-04550)] proposed a system for swing detection and shot classification with a CNN and bidirectional long short-term memory (BLSTM) in racket sports for tennis, badminton and squash, based on wearable motion sensor data.

#### Table 1.

### 1.2. Organization

Here, we focus on the racket and ball sport of squash, and aim for player localization and motion tracking by detecting players’ feet using HPE-CNNs in video images. We evaluated existing HPE-CNNs first, before considering the creation of a new one, and examined their applicability to the sport of squash. Therefore, our methods section begins with an outline of our general approach. We then introduce our selection criteria and the related selection process necessary for answering RQ1. Then, we introduce our annotation software, which is used to label feet and event information in squash videos to create a labeled dataset. After presenting a video selection of which HPE-CNNs performed inference, our evaluation procedure is introduced, which aggregates HPE-CNN detections and dataset labels. The evaluation procedure is used to answer RQ2. Finally, we present our method for visual comparison of HPE-CNN detections and dataset labels to answer RQ3. Subsequently the results are presented. After the discussion, the paper is concluded, and closes with our future work.

### 2.1. Selecting CNNs

We conduct a structured search based on the following criteria (C–C), which we identified to answer RQ1:

* C0:

  Multi-Person/Multi-Feet detection;
* C1:

  Published and implemented source code;
* C2:

  Code must be up to date;
* C3:

  Available pre-trained model weights;
* C4:

  Machine-readable output;
* C5:

  Demo/Showcase application;
* C6:

  Reasonable effort in setting up.

To find a list of publicly available HPE-CNNs, we searched on paperswithcode [[44](#B44-sensors-21-04550)] (date: 27 April 2020), which is a community-driven project. The community’s goal is to provide a free resource for everyone, covering various machine learning tasks and linking them to their available implementations.

As shown in [Figure 2](#sensors-21-04550-f002), our initial search for “Pose Estimation Algorithms” results in a total amount of 257 articles, which constitutes the starting point of our selection process. As these contain pose estimation algorithms for full human body, hand or head and animal poses, we narrowed our search to the field of Multi-Person Pose Estimation. Multi-Person in contrast to Single-Person is needed due to the fact that in singles squash two athletes are visible at a time. After applying criteria (C) and dropping duplicates in the result, 23 articles remained. Investigating the linked source-code repositories to check if the code is published and implemented (C) resulted in dropping another six algorithms. The reasons are either incomplete implementations or empty repositories where the authors have not yet published their code. Dropping another algorithm for an outdated code base (C), 16 algorithms are still under consideration. Next, we limit our search to publications which provide a pre-trained neural network and therefore the corresponding model weights (C). This is needed to skip the time and resource consuming process of training a complex neural network. The reasons for not meeting the criterion are first missing model weights, second dead links and finally a broken download archive. Thus, we considered 11 algorithms and investigated if they provide a machine readable output or offer an export of their estimation in C. This is necessary to evaluate the algorithms accuracy and compare them in different scenarios. While two algorithms could be extended with minimal modifications, six others could not be extended easily. Reviewing the remaining repositories and looking for a demo/showcase application, where we can input our custom video/image list (C), we had to drop another algorithm. This algorithm’s showcases only allowed for operation on a predefined training and validation set. Finally, after following the setup instructions for each algorithm, one did not lead to any results (C), and was therefore excluded.
