# Deformable DETR

By [Xizhou Zhu](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=02RXI00AAAAJ), [Weijie Su](https://www.weijiesu.com/), [Lewei Lu](https://www.linkedin.com/in/lewei-lu-94015977/), [Bin Li](http://staff.ustc.edu.cn/~binli/), [Xiaogang Wang](http://www.ee.cuhk.edu.hk/~xgwang/), [Jifeng Dai](https://jifengdai.org/).

This repository is an official implementation of the paper [Deformable DETR: Deformable Transformers for End-to-End Object Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.04159).

## Introduction

**TL; DR.** Deformable DETR is an efficient and fast-converging end-to-end object detector. It mitigates the high complexity and slow convergence issues of DETR via a novel sampling-based efficient attention mechanism.

**Abstract.** DETR has been recently proposed to eliminate the need for many hand-designed components in object detection while demonstrating good performance. However, it suffers from slow convergence and limited feature spatial resolution, due to the limitation of Transformer attention modules in processing image feature maps. To mitigate these issues, we proposed Deformable DETR, whose attention modules only attend to a small set of key sampling points around a reference. Deformable DETR can achieve better performance than DETR (especially on small objects) with 10× less training epochs. Extensive experiments on the COCO benchmark demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

args.summary:
Deformable DETR is an official GitHub repository by fundamentalvision implementing the paper "Deformable DETR: Deformable Transformers for End-to-End Object Detection" (arXiv:2010.04159). Authored by Xizhou Zhu, Weijie Su, Lewei Lu, Bin Li, Xiaogang Wang, and Jifeng Dai, the project is released under the Apache 2.0 license and has approximately 4k stars and 632 forks.

KEY CONCEPT: Deformable DETR addresses two major issues of the original DETR model — slow convergence and limited feature spatial resolution — by introducing attention modules that only attend to a small set of key sampling points around a reference point. This sampling-based efficient attention mechanism allows Deformable DETR to achieve better performance than DETR (especially on small objects) with 10× fewer training epochs.

MAIN RESULTS (all trained with batch size 32, measured on NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU):
- Deformable DETR (single scale): 50 epochs, AP 39.4, 34M params, 78G FLOPs, 160 GPU hours total training time
- Deformable DETR (single scale, DC5): 50 epochs, AP 41.5, 34M params, 128G FLOPs, 215 GPU hours
- Deformable DETR (multi-scale): 50 epochs, AP 44.5, 40M params, 173G FLOPs, 325 GPU hours
- + iterative bounding box refinement: 50 epochs, AP 46.2, 41M params, 325 GPU hours
- ++ two-stage Deformable DETR: 50 epochs, AP 46.9, 41M params, 340 GPU hours

For comparison, DETR requires 500 epochs to reach AP 42.0 (with 2000 GPU hours), while Deformable DETR reaches higher AP in only 50 epochs. Faster R-CNN + FPN baseline: AP 42.0 at 109 epochs.

INSTALLATION REQUIREMENTS: Linux, CUDA>=9.2, GCC>=5.4, Python>=3.7, PyTorch>=1.5.1, torchvision>=0.6.1. Recommended to use Anaconda with a conda environment named "deformable_detr".

USAGE: The repository supports training on COCO 2017 dataset (organized with train2017/, val2017/, and annotations/ folders). Training can be performed on single nodes (8 GPUs), multiple nodes, or slurm clusters. Tips for speeding up training include enabling '--cache_mode' to load the dataset into memory and increasing batch size. Config files, logs, and pretrained models are available via Google Drive links for each model variant. The repository includes folders for configs, datasets, docs, figs, models, tools, and util, plus key scripts: benchmark.py, engine.py, main.py, and requirements.txt.

# Deformable DETR: Deformable Transformers for End-to-End Object Detection

Xizhou Zhu ⋅ Weijie Su ⋅ Lewei Lu ⋅ Bin Li ⋅ Xiaogang Wang ⋅ Jifeng Dai

Keywords: [Efficient Attention Mechanism](/virtual/2021/search?query=Efficient Attention Mechanism) [Deformation Modeling](/virtual/2021/search?query=Deformation Modeling) [Multi-scale Representation](/virtual/2021/search?query=Multi-scale Representation) [End-to-End Object Detection](/virtual/2021/search?query=End-to-End Object Detection)

2021 Poster

[Paper PDF](https://openreview.net/forum?id=gZ9hCDWe6ke)  [ [Paper](https://openreview.net/forum?id=gZ9hCDWe6ke) ]

### Abstract

DETR has been recently proposed to eliminate the need for many hand-designed components in object detection while demonstrating good performance. However, it suffers from slow convergence and limited feature spatial resolution, due to the limitation of Transformer attention modules in processing image feature maps. To mitigate these issues, we proposed Deformable DETR, whose attention modules only attend to a small set of key sampling points around a reference. Deformable DETR can achieve better performance than DETR (especially on small objects) with 10$\times$ less training epochs. Extensive experiments on the COCO benchmark demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Code is released at https://github.com/fundamentalvision/Deformable-DETR.

This webpage is a technical review article written by Sik-Ho Tsang (PhD, Researcher) about the paper "Deformable Transformers for End-to-End Object Detection" (Deformable DETR), published at 2021 NeurIPS with over 800 citations. The paper was authored by researchers from SenseTime Research, University of Science and Technology of China, and The Chinese University of Hong Kong.

Key content covered in the review:

1. **Preliminaries**: Reviews Multi-Head Attention in Transformers and the original DETR architecture.

2. **Deformable Attention Module**: Two sets of channels encode offsets in x and y directions, while a third set encodes attention weights. These learnable offsets are conceptually similar to Deformable Convolutional Networks (DCN).

3. **Multi-Scale Deformable Attention Module**: Replaces standard Transformer attention modules for processing feature maps. It can be viewed as an efficient variant of Transformer attention where a pre-filtering mechanism is introduced via deformable sampling locations.

4. **Deformable DETR Architecture**: 
   - Deformable Transformer Encoder
   - Deformable Transformer Decoder
   - Additional improvements: Iterative Bounding Box Refinement and Two-Stage Deformable DETR

5. **Experimental Results**: 
   - Compared with DETR, Deformable DETR achieves better performance (especially on small objects) with 10× fewer training epochs.
   - Includes ablation studies, SOTA comparisons, and visualizations.
   - Introducing the deformable concept into DETR improves average precision.

The article also lists related object detection papers from 2014-2022 (including EfficientDet, CSPNet, YOLOv4, SpineNet, DETR, Mish, Scaled-YOLOv4, PVT, and PVTv2) and references the original arXiv paper (arXiv:2010.04159).

--- SOURCE 1: Prediction model and technical and tactical decision analysis of women’s badminton singles based on machine learning ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11563442

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in PLOS ONE (2024 Nov 14;19(11):e0312801, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0312801) titled "Prediction model and technical and tactical decision analysis of women's badminton singles based on machine learning." The study focuses on South Korean badminton player An Se-young, who rose to the top of the 2023 BWF Olympic points table with an 89.5% win rate (77 wins, 9 losses) during the Paris Olympic cycle.

METHODOLOGY: The researchers analyzed An Se-young's technical and tactical statistics using a proposed "three-stage" data classification method. They used video analysis of 10 matches (21-point games) from 2023 where An faced four players ranked in the top five of the BWF rankings (Chen Yu Fei, Akane Yamaguchi, Tai Tzu-ying, and Carolina Marin). Matches included finals/semifinals from the Indonesia Open, China Open, World Championships, Asian Championships, and Asian Games. A total of 10h32min was recorded with actual game time of 140min49s. Videos were sourced from YouTube, and statistics were gathered from the BWF Fansite. They constructed a machine learning dataset using inputs such as number of strikes, scoring/losing locations, techniques used in the last three strikes, and serving locations, with scoring/losing outcome as the output. Data was divided 90% training / 10% test. The study used five machine learning algorithms: Decision Tree, Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Machine, and K-Nearest Neighbors. They also used principal component analysis (PCA) with K-means clustering to validate the dataset's learning value.

KEY RESULTS:
- Support Vector Machine with RBF kernel achieved the highest prediction accuracy at 87.5%, with strong consistency
- K-Nearest Neighbors achieved 75.00% accuracy
- Decision Tree and Random Forest each achieved 62.50%
- XGBoost achieved 56.25%
- The linear kernel SVM achieved 75.00%, indicating strong linear relationships in the data
- The correlation matrix showed significant negative correlations between shot location and technique used (ranging from -0.67 to -0.71)
- PCA results showed the two clusters (gain and loss) were well-separated in two-dimensional space, confirming the dataset had learnable intrinsic features

AN SE-YOUNG'S PLAYING STYLE FINDINGS:
- More than 50% of rounds are completed by long multi-shots, reaching 61% in scoring rounds (vs. 53% in conceding rounds)
- She does not seek continuous pressure but rather exploits and maximizes aggression following opponent mistakes
- She immediately utilizes assault methods (kills or dives) after opponent errors, often converting points in the subsequent 2-3 strikes
- 60% of her organized shots from the backcourt ultimately achieved points through lifting or high clears
- Her attacking strength is weaker than her ability to stalemate opponents; she typically creates opportunities through blitzes and scores in the following 2-3 shots
- When losing points, there was an increase in blocks (20%) and lobs (22%) on the penultimate shot, with significant decreases in net kills (3%) and smashes (6%)
- The number of strikes in a round was the most important predictive parameter, followed by landing location where points were scored/lost

LIMITATIONS acknowledged: small sample size, simplistic personal style classification criteria, and lack of consideration for players' handedness differences.

The article includes detailed mathematical formulations for each algorithm (decision tree information gain, Gini impurity, pruning; random forest bagging and voting; XGBoost objective function; SVM decision functions, kernel functions, Lagrange multipliers; KNN distance metrics), plus figures showing serving positions (numbered 1-9), technique coding (a-m), correlation matrices, PCA results, kernel function comparisons, and feature importance rankings.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: Gaming Tree Based Evaluation Model for Badminton Tactic Benefit Analysis and Prediction ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/13/13/7380

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in the MDPI journal "Applied Sciences" (2023, Volume 13, Issue 13, Article 7380) titled "Gaming Tree Based Evaluation Model for Badminton Tactic Benefit Analysis and Prediction." The paper was authored by Wenming Liu, Yifan Zhu, Wenxia Guo, Xinyuan Wang, and Songkun Yu, affiliated with Zhejiang University, Beijing University of Chemical Technology, and Zhejiang University of Technology in China. It was received on 20 May 2023, revised 18 June 2023, accepted 19 June 2023, and published 21 June 2023, with DOI 10.3390/app13137380.

STUDY PURPOSE: The research applies game theory concepts—specifically gaming trees and Nash Equilibrium—to analyze and predict badminton tactics. The study examines matches between two legendary players: Dan Lin (9 major titles, 2 Olympic gold medals) and Chong Wei Lee (ranked world #1 for 349 weeks). A total of 29 matches from 2006 to 2018 were analyzed (Lin won 19, Lee won 10).

METHODOLOGY: The gaming tree was constructed where each node represents a possible stroke, with strokes characterized by four attributes: player, stroke technique, start placement, and target placement. The badminton court was divided into a 3×3 grid (front/middle/back court × left/middle/right court). Stroke techniques included serve, smash, clear, drop, net shot, and drive. Tactical observation indices covered stroke technique, stroke placement, and rally results. Each stroke, rally, and game was assigned a weighted score based on its importance to the overall match outcome. The benefit of each gaming tree node was computed by summing weighted scores, and the net benefit was calculated by adding the maximum score of child nodes. Nash Equilibrium was identified to determine optimal strategies and predict win/loss outcomes.

KEY RESULTS: (1) The best choice for Lin was hitting the shuttle to the backcourt, while Lee's best strategy was controlling the forecourt. (2) Win-loss ratio analysis showed Lin consistently outperformed Lee in most career periods, consistent with actual match results. (3) As the two players faced each other more often, they discovered more ways to beat each other; however, in the final period (matches 22–28), strategy diversity dropped significantly due to mutual familiarity and physical limitations. (4) In the last period, Lin and Lee had roughly equal chances of winning, with Lin's advantage reversing at higher stroke counts (7+ beats). The empirical results demonstrated the gaming tree method could effectively evaluate player strengths and weaknesses and accurately predict tactical implementation.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: ShuttleNet: Position-Aware Fusion of Rally Progress and ... ---
URL: https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/20341/20100

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper (AAAI-22) presents ShuttleNet, a novel framework for stroke forecasting in badminton—the first work to address predicting future strokes (shot types and area coordinates) in turn-based sports. The authors from National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University formulate stroke forecasting as a sequence prediction problem with three key challenges: 1) mixed sequences (two players alternate strokes), 2) multiple outputs at each timestamp (shot type + coordinates), and 3) player dependence (return styles depend on both players' overall styles and rally situation).

The ShuttleNet framework consists of three main components:
- Transformer-Based Rally Extractor (TRE): captures rally progress/current situation using a modified Transformer with a proposed multi-head type-area-attention layer (which separately characterizes importance of shot types and area, inspired by disentangled attention)
- Transformer-Based Player Extractor (TPE): splits the sequence into two subsequences by player (Player A and B) to generate each player's context, with shared parameters and sequence alignment
- Position-Aware Gated Fusion Network (PGFN): fuses rally contexts and both players' contexts using information weights (α) and learnable position weights (β) based on gated multi-modal units

The prediction layer assumes area coordinates follow a bi-variate Gaussian distribution and uses hard parameter sharing with two linear layers to predict shot type and area parameters. Training minimizes combined cross-entropy loss (Ltype) and negative log-likelihood loss (Larea).

Key experimental results:
- Dataset: 75 high-ranking badminton singles matches (2018-2021), 31 players, 180 sets, 4,325 rallies, 43,191 strokes, 10 shot types (net shot, clear, push/rush, smash, defensive shot, drive, lob, drop, short service, long service)
- ShuttleNet outperforms all baselines (Seq2Seq, CF-LSTM, TF, dNRI, DMA-Nets) by at least 12.0% in CE and 3.4% in MSE across all metrics and observed-stroke lengths (τ=2, 4, 8)
- Ablation studies confirmed the necessity of each component (rally extractor, both player extractors, information weights, position weights, and type-area-attention)
- Case study showed players use different area distributions (middle of court vs. near net) when returning against smashes, demonstrating tactic investigation utility

The paper concludes the framework benefits both coaching-oriented applications (tactic investigation) and community-oriented applications (storytelling/engagement), with future work planned to extend to additional conditions like win/loss outcomes. Code is available at https://github.com/wywyWang/ShuttleNet.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: Future Prediction of Shuttlecock Trajectory in Badminton Using Player’s Information ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10219238

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific research paper published in the Journal of Imaging (J Imaging) on May 11, 2023 (doi: 10.3390/jimaging9050099), by researchers from Keio University's Graduate School of Science and Technology in Yokohama, Japan. The paper, authored by Yuka Nokihara, Ryo Hachiuma, Ryosuke Hori, and Hideo Saito (corresponding author), addresses the novel task of predicting future shuttlecock trajectories in badminton match videos.

**Purpose and Methodology:**
The study proposes a trajectory prediction method that incorporates three types of information: shuttlecock position (2D), player positions (4D), and player postures (68D). These are each embedded into 2D feature vectors via fully connected layers and combined into a 6D feature vector, which is fed into a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network. The method uses two modules: (1) a detection and pose estimation module for past frames (using TrackNet for shuttlecock detection, Faster R-CNN trained on MS COCO for player detection, and HRNet for pose estimation), and (2) a time-series model for future prediction.

**Key Experimental Details:**
- Dataset: Shuttlecock Trajectory Dataset (26 match videos for training, 3 for testing; 1280x720 resolution, 30 fps)
- Training used 23 professional singles matches from international tournaments (2018-2021), split 80/20 into training/validation
- Implementation: PyTorch 1.12.1, Python 3.7.13, NVIDIA TITAN RTX, CUDA 11.4
- LSTM: 3 layers, 128-dimension hidden layer, Adam optimizer, 400 epochs
- Input: 4 past frames; Output: 12 future frames
- Loss function: Mean Squared Error (MSE)
- Data augmentation: 50% left-right flipping probability, 50-pixel translation range
- Evaluation metrics: Average Displacement Error (ADE) and Final Displacement Error (FDE) in pixels

**Key Results:**
- The proposed method improved ADE by ~13% compared to methods using only shuttlecock position information, and by ~8.4% compared to methods using shuttlecock + player position (without posture)
- Compared to other time-series models, the LSTM-based approach improved ADE by ~9.8% (vs RNN), ~5.0% (vs GRU), ~20% (vs Transformer), and ~12% (vs Seq2Seq)
- Data augmentation with 50% left-right flipping and 50-pixel translation was most effective
- Accuracy improves with more input frames and fewer frames to predict

**Limitations and Future Work:**
- Limitations include dependence on distant camera setups (requiring tripods/photographers), difficulty predicting sudden trajectory changes (at hit-back moments or when shuttlecock touches floor), and occlusion issues
- Future work includes improving model generalization across different datasets/sports, automating rally segmentation, and extending prediction to 3D space for real-world applications

**Conclusion:** The paper demonstrates that incorporating player position AND posture information alongside shuttlecock position significantly improves trajectory prediction accuracy in badminton, and LSTM outperforms other time-series models for this task. The research received no external funding and is published under a Creative Commons CC BY license.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Capturing Intransitive Dominance in Tennis Forecasting: A Graph Neural Network Approach ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2510.20454v2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an arXiv research paper (v2, reference 2510.20454) titled "Capturing Intransitive Dominance in Tennis Forecasting: A Graph Neural Network Approach" that presents a novel application of graph neural networks (GNNs) to pre-match tennis outcome prediction, specifically targeting intransitive player dominance relationships.

**Core Contribution:** The authors build temporal directed graphs for tennis matches (players as nodes, historical match outcomes as directed weighted edges) and apply MagNet, a spectral graph convolutional network that uses the magnetic Laplacian (a complex Hermitian matrix) to learn from directed cycles and intransitive relationships. This is the first known application of GNNs to pre-match tennis forecasting (a Google Scholar search of 66 queries found no other papers doing so).

**Data:** Historical ATP and WTA match data from tennis-data.co.uk spanning January 8, 2012 to October 16, 2025, filtered to highest-tier events (Grand Slams, tour finals, 1000 and 500 series). Final dataset: 20,181 men's matches (670 players) and 19,985 women's matches (640 players). Validation set of 8,435 matches, held-out test set of 12,052 matches (early 2022 to October 2025). Surface-specific graphs (clay, grass, hard) built per gender. Player static attributes (height, weight, DOB, handedness) were evaluated but excluded as they did not improve accuracy.

**Methodology:** 
- Edge weights based on proportion of games won, adjusted by time decay (λ=0.34), surface transferability (α), and tournament prestige (uniform weights β=1)
- Dominance score aggregates historical match results with weighting; edges point from dominant to dominated player
- MagNet optimised q=0.238 (near maximum directional weighting); 2 layers, K=1 Chebyshev filter, 16 hidden units
- Walk-forward validation: trained on 15% of most recent matches, retrained every 38 snapshots (~quarter year), training under 10 seconds per run on consumer hardware
- 250 trials using Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) via Optuna, multi-objective on men's/women's Brier scores
- Set-win probabilities converted to match probabilities for best-of-3 and best-of-5 formats

**Results (out-of-sample test set):** Overall 65.7% accuracy, 0.214 Brier score. Model ties Weighted Elo on Brier score (0.214) but trails slightly on accuracy (65.7% vs 65.8%). Outperforms standard Elo (65.3%, 0.217) and Bradley-Terry (64.6%, 0.219). Pinnacle Sports bookmaker benchmark remains superior (68.7% accuracy, 0.198 Brier). Model shows strong calibration (reliability term below 0.0001 vs 0.0012 for Weighted Elo).

**Ablation findings:** Graph structure carries most of the predictive signal (removing dominance graph raises Brier from 0.2142 to 0.2492). Most consequential components: edge-age decay (+0.0118), multi-hop receptive field (+0.0095), in/out-degree node features (+0.0058). Directional weighting q and dominance edge weights have smallest effects, suggesting the model's value is a broad complementary signal rather than local intransitivity decoding.

**Intransitivity analysis:** Women's tennis contains 12.3% more cyclic triads than men's. A well-known example cited: Nadal beats Federer (24/40), Federer beats Davydenko (19/21), but Davydenko beats Nadal (6/11). A forecast-encompassing test shows Weighted Elo does not fully subsume the GNN model; a combined forecast significantly outperforms Weighted Elo, with gains growing more strongly on intransitive matchups. This demonstrates the graph-based approach captures forecasting signal that transitive rating systems discard, even between players sharing no common opponents.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Our model (65.7% accuracy, 0.214 Brier score) forecasts competitively with established rating systems such as Weighted Elo. Although it does not improve on the baseline in unconditional accuracy, a forecast-encompassing test shows that it carries complementary information. A combined forecast significantly outperforms Weighted Elo, and there is some indication that the gain grows more strongly on the intransitive matchups our model targets."
</key_excerpts>

This research paper by Szabolcs Csapó (University of Twente, Netherlands, published as TScIT 43, July 4, 2025) investigates the use of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for automated tactic recognition and prediction in the esports game Counter-Strike. The research addresses a knowledge gap in automated, data-driven tactical analysis for Counter-Strike, where most existing work relies on manual review and subjective interpretation.

**Methodology:** The model was trained on the ESTA dataset (1,500 professional matches with up to two frames per second of player/position data). Each round was represented as a graph with nodes (players, bombsites, bomb) and edges capturing relationships like distances. Node features included position (X,Y coordinates, linearly normalized), health, armor, utility (grenade count), area ID, node type, isAlive, and hasBomb. The 2-layered GCN outperformed GAT architectures (2-layered GAT: 78.10% accuracy, 0.6831 F1). The confusion matrix showed the model struggled most with distinguishing t_setup_a from execution tactics (setup/execute transitions create ambiguous boundaries). The micro-average AUC was 0.81, with some classes achieving 0.96-1.00 AUC while t_setup_a scored only 0.53. The model was limited to the Dust 2 map.

**Conclusions:** The model's performance is comparable to or exceeds similar studies (Szmida et al. achieved 0.8549 AUC for player actions; Xenopoulos et al. reported 0.8753 AUC for outcome prediction). The research demonstrates that even simple GNNs can perform exceptionally well when the graph representation accurately captures relational structure. Utility usage was identified as a critical feature for tactical classification. Applications include automated dataset labeling, real-time coaching assistants, and AI-driven NPC coordination. Limitations include reliance on human-labeled data (subjectivity/bias), exclusive training on Dust 2, and unexplored alternative graph representations or features.

- The thesis proposes HMMs to predict game/season outcomes by modeling the unobservable win/loss streak state behind observable game statistics.

This webpage is the English Wikipedia article on Hidden Markov Models (HMMs), a statistical Markov model in probability theory. An HMM is a Markov model where observations depend on a latent (hidden) Markov process, with the goal being to learn about the hidden state by observing the observable process.

Key content covered:

1. DEFINITION: An HMM consists of a hidden Markov process (X) and an observable process (Y) where Y's outcomes depend on X in a known way. Y at time t0 is influenced exclusively by X at time t0, and past outcomes are conditionally independent of Y given X at that time. Parameters are estimated via maximum likelihood estimation, with the Baum-Welch algorithm used for linear chain HMMs.

2. APPLICATIONS: HMMs are used in thermodynamics, statistical mechanics, physics, chemistry, economics, finance, signal processing, information theory, pattern recognition (speech recognition, handwriting recognition, gesture recognition, part-of-speech tagging, musical score following, partial discharges), and bioinformatics.

4. STRUCTURAL ARCHITECTURE: HMMs use trellis diagrams showing conditional dependencies. The hidden state at time t depends only on the hidden state at t-1 (Markov property). Hidden states are discrete (categorical distribution), while observations can be discrete or continuous (Gaussian). Parameters include transition probabilities (N² total, N(N-1) free parameters) and emission probabilities (N(M-1) for discrete observations, or NM(M+3)/2 = O(NM²) for multivariate Gaussian observations).

5. INFERENCE TASKS: Three main inference problems are described:
   - Probability of an observed sequence (solved with the forward algorithm using dynamic programming)
   - Probability of latent variables, including filtering (P(x(t)|y(1..t)), solved with forward algorithm) and smoothing (P(x(k)|y(1..t)) for k<t, solved with forward-backward algorithm)

The hidden states are called "hidden states" and the output probability is called "emission probability" or "output probability."
</summary>

Key elements include: matching the smash stance (chest open, body positioned for power), controlling and stopping hip/torso/shoulder rotation just before impact, keeping a relaxed grip with slightly bent wrist to guide the shuttle over the net, and timing the swing to mimic a smash while holding off until the last second.

2. **The Disguised Clear**: This shot appears to be a drop or net shot but suddenly flies to the back of the court, pushing opponents into the backcourt where they're harder to defend. Execution requires: positioning as if preparing a net shot (low shoulders, forward posture), adjusting wrist and racket at the last moment to send the shuttle to the backcourt, and maintaining strong footwork to return to a central position after the shot.

3. **The Fake Smash**: Start with the powerful stance and full-body motion of a smash, but reduce power at the last moment for a softer shot. This includes mimicking the smash motion with strong hip, shoulder, and torso rotation, reducing the follow-through just before contact, and quickly recovering to a balanced stance afterward.

The article also provides tips for keeping deceptive shots unpredictable: vary shots regularly to prevent anticipation, observe opponent movement patterns (some overcommit to defending smashes), incorporate footwork drills emphasizing quick direction changes, and practice at varying racket speeds and angles.

Common mistakes to avoid include: dropping the racket too early (revealing intent), tensing up the grip (restricting control), and poor timing (start slow and build up speed through consistent practice).

The article concludes that deception matters because it disrupts opponents' confidence, causing hesitation and unforced errors. Mastering these techniques requires precision, patience, and practice, and allows players to control the pace of play and manipulate opponents' movements rather than relying solely on power.

<summary>
## ShuttleSet: Badminton Stroke-Level Analytics Dataset

**Overview:** ShuttleSet is the largest publicly available stroke-level badminton singles dataset, designed for tactical analysis and structured turn-based modeling. It was introduced by Wang et al. (2023) and comprises **44 broadcast matches (2018–2021), 104 sets, 3,685 rallies, and 36,492 strokes** involving 27 top-ranking men's and women's singles players. Each stroke is annotated with temporal, spatial, and tactical labels coupled with match-, set-, and rally-level context.

**Dataset Origin and Structure:** Created to fill the gap in turn-based sports analytics (no public, expert-annotated, stroke-by-stroke datasets preserving full tactical structure). Source material is public broadcast video from bwf.tv (not instrumented capture), standardized to 30 fps and 1280×720 resolution. The corpus spans quarter-finals, semi-finals, and finals of top-tier tournaments including Super 1000 events and BWF World Tour Finals. The dataset is structured around rallies (not isolated clips), making it suitable for sequence modeling tasks.

**Annotation Schema:** Four categories per stroke:
- **Rally category**: set scores, rally winner, lose reason (out, touched net, not over net, opponent ball landed, misjudged)
- **Temporal category**: hitting time (seconds) and hitting frame
- **Spatial category**: player A/B locations, shuttle hitting location, categorical grid location, above/below net indicator
- **Hitting category**: stroke status, backhand, around-the-head, shot type

Court coordinates are derived via homography (p′=Hp), with singles-court coordinates defined at corners (0,0), (0,6.1), (13.4,0), (13.4,6.1). A domain-expert grid divides each half court into nine grids plus seven outside grids. The shot taxonomy contains **18 stroke classes** (net shot, smash, lob, clear, drive, drop, push, rush, service types, etc.).

**Labeling Workflow:** Annotated with the S² (Shot-by-Shot) labeling tool in four stages: match preparation, rally segmentation, video preprocessing, and shot-by-shot labeling. Six trained badminton-expert annotators performed labeling. Quality metrics: temporal consistency MAE of 0.24 (serve), 0.02 (return), 0 for dead bird; spatial consistency MAE of 0.18 (shuttle) and 0.86 (player); shot-type consistency accuracy differences of 0.00 (serve), 0.05 (return), 0.11 (dead bird). Distributed through the CoachAI project, with a Python implementation and Flask-based visualization platform used by national badminton teams.

**Native Benchmarks (three tasks):**
1. **Stroke influence** (win-probability estimation): Best model ShuttleScorer achieved AUC 0.8371, ACC 0.7869, BR 0.1574
2. **Stroke forecasting** (predict future shot types and landing locations): Best model ShuttleNet achieved CE 2.4125, MSE 1.8121, MAE 1.3582 (τ=8)
3. **Movement forecasting** (predict future strokes and both players' positions): DyMF best CE 2.3146; ShuttleNet lowest MSE 1.0832, MAE 1.5852

**Later Research Repurposing:**
- **Stroke-type recognition** (Chang, 2025): BST-3 variant achieved Acc 0.7710, Macro-F1 0.7042, Acc-2 0.9340
- **Doubles transfer learning** (Baek et al., 2025): Pose-based Transformer achieved singles accuracy 0.8617, doubles combined accuracy 0.6686; transfer degradation ~19.3% (pose-based) vs ~39.9% (vision-only YOLOv11x)
- **Temporal action localization** (Wang et al., 2026): DSTA adapter achieved average mAP 74.67 across tIoU thresholds
- **Report generation** (Chiang et al., 2026): ShuttleSet+ derived from ShuttleSet22 (58 matches, 140 sets, 3,992 rallies, 33,612 strokes); Tree-of-Text outperformed baselines using ~40% of Chain-of-Table's time/cost

**Limitations:** Singles only; no fixed train/validation/test partition (papers construct own splits); no continuous shuttle trajectories stored; 3D pose lifting unreliable for badminton-specific poses; class imbalance (rare categories: defensive return lob, driven flight, rush); no action interval boundaries requiring synthetic temporal windows.

**Significance:** ShuttleSet established a shared, stroke-level representation on public broadcast video, enabling otherwise disconnected research threads—forecasting, recognition, localization, transfer, and report generation—to operate on a common substrate. Its long-term importance lies in providing a common analytical foundation rather than any single benchmark score.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: Fast moving table tennis ball tracking algorithm based on graph neural network ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11599579

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific paper published in Scientific Reports (Sci Rep, 2024 Nov 26;14:29320, DOI: 10.1038/s41598-024-80056-3, PMCID: PMC11599579, PMID: 39592713), authored by researchers from the Beijing University of Post and Telecommunications (School of Artificial Intelligence and Department of Physical Education). The paper proposes a fast-moving table tennis ball tracking algorithm based on a novel Graph Max-message Pass Neural Network (GMP).

**Problem:** Table tennis ball tracking in video is challenging due to the ball's small size, rapid motion, and insignificant/unstable image features. Existing detection and tracking algorithms (e.g., YOLO, FASTER-RCNN, SOT, generic GNNs/GATs) struggle to meet real-world requirements.

**Proposed Method (Combined Detection + Discrimination approach):**
- **Detector (h_real):** A refined common video differential detector that uses frame differencing (absdiff on adjacent frames) to extract potential table tennis targets, leveraging the fact that the background changes slowly while high-speed objects differ between frames.
- **Discriminator (GMP):** A novel Graph Max-message Pass Neural Network specifically designed to filter and track table tennis balls or similar targets. It processes graphs constructed from potential targets (nodes) and their relationships (edges), outputting probability graphs with confidence scores for both nodes and edges.
- **Graph Construction:** A sliding window and gap mechanism is used to sequentially select potential target sets from frames and construct graphs for discrimination.

**Method Framework (4 steps):**
1. Each video frame is processed through the object detector to obtain sets of potential objects.
2. A sliding window with a gap is used to construct a set of graphs from potential target sets.
3. Each graph is fed into the discriminator to obtain probability graphs.
4. Final trajectories are derived from the probability graphs.

**Key Technical Contributions:**
- Decomposition of the tracking problem into relatively independent discriminator (log p(T_u)) and detector (log p(T_u|φ_initial, φ)) components via Bayesian maximum posterior criterion.
- GMP is designed to handle numerous false/uncertain targets (unlike standard MOT-focused GNN research).
- The approach addresses scenarios where erroneous, false, or uncertain targets are present from the outset.

**Dataset:** The authors enhanced an existing table tennis tracking dataset by enriching its scenarios (built on prior research refs 5, 6, 7, 9).

**Comparison Baselines:** YOLOv8 (single-frame object detection), Single Object Tracking (SOT, user-annotation based), and a generic Graph Attention Network (GAT) discriminator scheme.

**Results:** The proposed method outperforms all comparison algorithms on both the dataset and real-world environments, demonstrating good scalability and potential for application in other scenarios.

**Applications:** The algorithm provides image location and trajectory data that assist in segmenting rounds and actions, estimating ball speed (calculated from pixel distance, table center line length of 2.74m, and video frame rate, e.g., 30 fps), determining land points and hit points, and quantifying players' stability, offensive, and defensive capabilities for tactical planning and targeted training.

The article is published under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License and was received 2024 Jul 25, accepted 2024 Nov 14.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: Capturing Intransitive Dominance in Tennis Forecasting ---

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an arXiv research paper (v2, reference 2510.20454) titled "Capturing Intransitive Dominance in Tennis Forecasting: A Graph Neural Network Approach" that presents a novel application of graph neural networks (GNNs) to pre-match tennis outcome prediction, specifically targeting intransitive player dominance relationships.

**Core Contribution:** The authors build temporal directed graphs for tennis matches (players as nodes, historical match outcomes as directed weighted edges) and apply MagNet, a spectral graph convolutional network that uses the magnetic Laplacian (a complex Hermitian matrix) to learn from directed cycles and intransitive relationships. This is the first known application of GNNs to pre-match tennis forecasting (a Google Scholar search of 66 queries found no other papers doing so).

**Data:** Historical ATP and WTA match data from tennis-data.co.uk spanning January 8, 2012 to October 16, 2025, filtered to highest-tier events (Grand Slams, tour finals, 1000 and 500 series). Final dataset: 20,181 men's matches (670 players) and 19,985 women's matches (640 players). Validation set of 8,435 matches, held-out test set of 12,052 matches (early 2022 to October 2025). Surface-specific graphs (clay, grass, hard) built per gender. Player static attributes (height, weight, DOB, handedness) were evaluated but excluded as they did not improve accuracy.

**Methodology:** 
- Edge weights based on proportion of games won, adjusted by time decay (λ=0.34), surface transferability (α), and tournament prestige (uniform weights β=1)
- Dominance score aggregates historical match results with weighting; edges point from dominant to dominated player
- MagNet optimised q=0.238 (near maximum directional weighting); 2 layers, K=1 Chebyshev filter, 16 hidden units
- Walk-forward validation: trained on 15% of most recent matches, retrained every 38 snapshots (~quarter year), training under 10 seconds per run on consumer hardware
- 250 trials using Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) via Optuna, multi-objective on men's/women's Brier scores
- Set-win probabilities converted to match probabilities for best-of-3 and best-of-5 formats

**Results (out-of-sample test set):** Overall 65.7% accuracy, 0.214 Brier score. Model ties Weighted Elo on Brier score (0.214) but trails slightly on accuracy (65.7% vs 65.8%). Outperforms standard Elo (65.3%, 0.217) and Bradley-Terry (64.6%, 0.219). Pinnacle Sports bookmaker benchmark remains superior (68.7% accuracy, 0.198 Brier). Model shows strong calibration (reliability term below 0.0001 vs 0.0012 for Weighted Elo).

**Ablation findings:** Graph structure carries most of the predictive signal (removing dominance graph raises Brier from 0.2142 to 0.2492). Most consequential components: edge-age decay (+0.0118), multi-hop receptive field (+0.0095), in/out-degree node features (+0.0058). Directional weighting q and dominance edge weights have smallest effects, suggesting the model's value is a broad complementary signal rather than local intransitivity decoding.

**Intransitivity analysis:** Women's tennis contains 12.3% more cyclic triads than men's. A well-known example cited: Nadal beats Federer (24/40), Federer beats Davydenko (19/21), but Davydenko beats Nadal (6/11). A forecast-encompassing test shows Weighted Elo does not fully subsume the GNN model; a combined forecast significantly outperforms Weighted Elo, with gains growing more strongly on intransitive matchups. This demonstrates the graph-based approach captures forecasting signal that transitive rating systems discard, even between players sharing no common opponents.
</summary>

- Against Chinese reserve players, the attack-after-receive phase (receive and 4th stroke) ranked first and second (0.856 and 0.858), with 3rd stroke (0.836) and serve (0.832) following.

This paper (a CVPR Workshop paper) presents RallyTemPose, a transformer encoder-decoder model for predicting future badminton strokes based on previous rally actions. 1. A skeleton-based spatiotemporal encoder using transformer and pooling blocks to enhance next-stroke predictions in badminton.
2. An adaptive cross-attention decoder that incorporates contextual stroke descriptors from high-dimensional embeddings of a pre-trained language model (BERT).

**Methodology:** The encoder consists of a linear projection layer, learned joint encoding, a Spatial Transformer (ST) for spatial relationships between keypoints, a Grouped Pooling Block (GPB), and a Temporal Transformer (TT) for temporal dynamics—computing both inter-player (cross-attention) and intra-player (self-attention). The encoder produces three latent variables: a stroke representation (zs) and two player representations (z1, z2). The decoder uses an embedding layer, player representations added per stroke, self-attention, dual cross-attention, and an adaptive fusion mechanism to predict the next stroke. Stroke embeddings are enhanced using BERT to embed text descriptions of stroke types. Training uses cross-entropy loss plus an auxiliary loss on the latent stroke variable (γ=0.3).

**Datasets:** 
- ShuttleSet: 42 professional matches (2018-2021), 26 players, 3,000+ rallies, 34,000+ strokes, 10 shot types. 80% training/20% testing split.
- BadmintonDB: 9 professional men's singles matches (Kento Momota vs. Anthony Sinisuka Ginting), 811 rallies, 9,671 strokes, 10 stroke types. 7 matches for training, 2 for testing.

**Results:**
- ShuttleSet: 54.3% accuracy, 77.3% top-2, 92.5% top-3 accuracy—outperforming baselines (Seq2Seq, Transformer, Actionformer + Transformer decoder).

Cosine similarity of player latent variables reveals playstyle differences (e.g., male vs. female players show lower similarity, and distinct male playing styles are reflected in lower similarity scores). SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a research paper (arXiv) introducing DyMF (Dynamic Graphs and Hierarchical Fusion for Movement Forecasting), the first work to address movement forecasting in badminton and other turn-based sports like tennis. The paper formalizes the task of predicting players' future movements and shot types based on previous strokes in a rally.

**Core Contributions:**
1. First formalization of movement forecasting in badminton, predicting players' future locations and shot types
2. Introduction of the Player Movements (PM) graph, which transforms rallies into graphs with strategic relations between players' locations using 12 relation types (10 shot types: net shot, lob, defensive shot, smash, drop, push/rush, short service, clear, drive, long service; plus "defend" and "return" edge types)
3. A novel DyMF model using an encoder-decoder architecture with interaction style extractors (relational GCN + dynamic GCN) and hierarchical fusions (player-player fusion via parallel co-attention, and player-rally fusion)
4. Extensive experiments showing state-of-the-art performance on a real-world badminton dataset

**Methodology:**
- Movement forecasting is formulated as a sequence prediction task: given observed stroke sequence of length τ, predict future strokes including both players' locations and shot types
- PM graph construction: nodes represent player locations at each time step; edges represent 12 strategic relations
- Interaction Style Extractor uses Relational GCN (inspired by R-GCN) for interactions between players and Dynamic GCN with LSTM-based pattern-generated weights for dynamic personal tactics
- Hierarchical Fusion combines player styles (via parallel co-attention) with rally interactions using sigmoid-based dynamic weights
- Movement predictor outputs shot types via cross-entropy and locations via bivariate Gaussian distributions
- Total loss = shot type cross-entropy + 0.5×location loss per player

**Experimental Results:**
- Dataset: 75 badminton singles matches, 31 players, 180 sets, 4,325 rallies, 43,191 strokes; 80/20 train/test split
- Baselines: Seq2Seq, TF (Transformer), ShuttleNet (sequence-based); dNRI, GCNPM, R-GCNPM, E-GCNPM (graph-based)
- DyMF outperforms all baselines across all metrics (MSE, MAE for locations; CE for shot type) at observation lengths τ=2, 4, and 8
- Improvements up to 35.3% for MSE, 21.5% for MAE, and 24.3% for CE
- Key findings: naive sequence models fail on structural info; dNRI insufficient due to lack of new location nodes; E-GCNPM unstable with few graph nodes; DyMF surpasses ShuttleNet due to modeling movement purposes and dynamic tactics

**Case Study:** Demonstrated that changing a player's defense position alters the opponent's returned shot (e.g., standing close to net forces opponent to clear, enabling an attack), verifying that opponents respond to player defense locations and that effective positioning limits opponent options.

**Future Work:** Extend DyMF to badminton doubles with greater focus on inter-player interactions. Supported by Taiwan's Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST-110-2627-H-A49-001). Code available at https://github.com/wywyWang/CoachAI-Projects/tree/main/Movement%20Forecasting.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Hawk-Eye is a computer vision system developed in 2000 by engineers at Roke Manor Research Limited (then a Siemens subsidiary) in Romsey, England, by Paul Hawkins and David Sherry. It was originally implemented in 2001 for television broadcasts to analyze leg before wicket (LBW) decisions in cricket. The Sony-owned system tracks the trajectory of a ball using up to ten high-performance cameras positioned on the underside of stadium roofs, triangulating video feeds to create a three-dimensional representation of the ball's path. It is advertised to be accurate to within 2.6 mm, though the Hawk-Eye Innovations website states an average error of 3.6 mm. The system is used in more than 20 major sports including baseball, cricket, tennis, badminton, hurling, rugby union, soccer, Gaelic football, American football, and volleyball.

HISTORY AND OWNERSHIP: The technology was spun off into Hawk-Eye Innovations Ltd, based in Winchester, Hampshire, as a joint venture between Roke Manor Research and Sunset + Vine. On 14 June 2006, investors led by the Wisden Group (including Mark Getty) bought the company for £4.4m. It was sold to Sony in March 2011 in a deal valuing the company at £15m-£20m.

DEPLOYMENT IN SPORTS:
- Cricket: First used by Channel 4 during a Test match between England and Pakistan at Lord's Cricket Ground on 21 May 2001. Used for LBW decisions (pitched location, impact location, projected path) and adopted in the Decision Review System since 2009. Marginal calls result in the on-field umpire's call being maintained.
- Tennis: First used officially at the Nasdaq-100 Open in March 2006; US Open was the first Grand Slam to use it (2006). The 2006 Hopman Cup in Perth was the first elite-level tournament allowing player challenges. The 2021 Australian Open was the first Grand Slam to use Hawk-Eye Live for all matches in place of line judges (partly due to COVID-19), followed by the US Open. In 2024, the All-England Club announced electronic line calling would replace human line judges full-time at Wimbledon starting in 2025. Clay courts (e.g., French Open) generally don't use Hawk-Eye due to ball marks, though the 2021 Mutua Madrid Open used a competing system (FoxTenn). Rules were unified on 19 March 2008: three unsuccessful challenges per set, with an additional challenge at tiebreak.
- Association football: One of FIFA-authorised goal-line technology (GLT) systems; used in the Premier League, Serie A, and Bundesliga. As of July 2017, licensed systems were installed at 96 stadiums, making it the most popular GLT system.
- Snooker: Used by BBC at World Championship since 2007 primarily as a viewer aid; removed after 2015, but a derivative is used on the World Snooker Tour in China to support referees in replacing balls to millimetre precision.
- Gaelic games: Introduced at Croke Park, Dublin in 2013 for Gaelic football and hurling. Experienced multiple malfunctions (2013, 2022, 2023), including a 2013 minor hurling game error that ruled a valid Limerick point wide, leading to suspensions and appeals.
- Australian football: Tested by AFL at MCG in Round 15 of the 2013 season for Score Review process.
- Badminton: BWF introduced Hawk-Eye in 2014, first at the 2014 India Super Series.
- Gridiron football: NFL adopted Hawk-Eye for virtual on-field measurements beginning in the 2025 season.
- Baseball: Used to automatically call balls and strikes in professional leagues in the U.S. and South Korea. MLB adopted it for the 2026 season, tested in Minor League Baseball since 2019. Also used for instant replay reviews in MLB since the 2014 season.

CONCERNS ABOUT ACCURACY: The system has been criticized for its 3.6 mm statistical margin of error, with some calling it too large. A 2008 peer-reviewed article noted the system's failure to depict a margin of error gives a spurious depiction of events, and hypothesized that Hawk-Eye may struggle with predicting a cricket ball's trajectory after bouncing. Multiple controversies have occurred, including at Wimbledon 2007, the 2007 Dubai Tennis Championships (Rafael Nadal dispute), and the 2009 Indian Wells Masters where the system mistakenly picked up a second bounce.

COMPUTER GAMES AND COMPETITION: The Hawk-Eye brand has been licensed to Codemasters for cricket video games and appears in Smash Court Tennis 3 and Don Bradman Cricket games. Competitors include Cyclops (electronic line judge used since 1980) and FoxTenn (which uses real data, including on clay).

<summary>
This is a video transcript from CULT TENNIS (a YouTube channel) titled "The TRUTH behind Hawk Eye Accuracy | History of Line Tracking Technology in Tennis," posted on September 9, 2020, with approximately 1.86 million views. The video explores the history, functionality, and accuracy of Hawk-Eye line-calling technology in professional tennis.

**Key Historical Events:**
- Hawk-Eye was first developed for cricket in 2001 before being adapted for tennis.
- The 2004 US Open quarterfinal between Serena Williams and Jennifer Capriati featured famously blown line calls, serving as the catalyst for widespread adoption. Television viewers saw experimental "Shot Spot" visuals, but players had no challenge capability at that time.
- Hawk-Eye became available for player use in early 2006, with the US Open later that year becoming the first Grand Slam to implement the technology on its show courts.

**How Hawk-Eye Works:**
- Ten ultra-motion high-speed cameras (5 per side) are installed around the court perimeter, capturing video at 340 frames per second.
- The system triangulates data from calibrated cameras to produce a 3D position of the ball.
- Contrary to popular belief, Hawk-Eye does not simply watch the bounce — it PREDICTS the trajectory before the ball lands by calculating positions at 340 intervals per second as the ball comes off the player's racket. An algorithm predicts where the ball will bounce, combined with calculations for ball compression and skid.
- The system also tracks foot faults, not just line calls.

**Accuracy Data:**
- The International Tennis Federation (ITF) required Hawk-Eye to be within 5 millimeters of the real recorded bounce (approximately the width of a pencil eraser).
- On average, Hawk-Eye proved accurate to within 2.6 millimeters — far better than the naked eye.
- Despite this, the system has a margin of error and can misjudge balls landing within a millimeter of the line.
- Known accuracy limitations include glitches, wind shadows, and darkness.

**2020 Context:**
- Due to COVID-19 pandemic restrictions, the 2020 US Open removed traditional line judges on most courts entirely, using Hawk-Eye Live technology for every call, with computer-generated human-like voices making all line calls.

**Key Insights:**
- Human eyes can be deceived by the ball's skid after contact (e.g., a ball appearing out that actually touched the baseline before skidding an additional 10 centimeters).
- Competitors like FOX Trac (tennis analysis system) claim to determine calls based on real bounce observations rather than estimations, questioning Hawk-Eye's predictive approach.
- The conclusion is that while imperfect, Hawk-Eye is "probably right and you're probably wrong" in most disputed calls.

--- SOURCE 1: A Critical Analysis of Existing Technologies in Squash ... ---
URL: https://www.ijcstjournal.org/volume-13/issue-6/IJCST-V13I6P4.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This research article, "A Critical Analysis of Existing Technologies in Squash Training: Towards an Automated Training Court" by Evana Gada (published in IJCST, Volume 13 Issue 6, Nov-Dec 2025, ISSN: 2347-8578), critically examines the current technological landscape in squash training and proposes a conceptual Automated Squash Training Court (ASTC).

PURPOSE: The paper addresses why squash-specific technologies have lagged behind other racquet sports (tennis, badminton, football) and proposes an integrated framework to overcome these limitations. It synthesizes existing literature rather than conducting new experiments.

KEY TECHNOLOGY DOMAINS ANALYZED:
1. IMAGE/VIDEO PROCESSING: Broadcast video (25-60 fps) and multi-camera rigs; court calibration via homography/inverse-perspective mapping; player detection via bounding-box trackers (YOLO, Faster R-CNN + SORT/DeepSORT) and human-pose estimation (OpenPose, HRNet); ball tracking via small-object detection, physics-informed interpolation, and 96 kHz audio fusion for impact localization; event segmentation using Vučković et al.'s 15-zone taxonomy.

2. AI/ML APPLICATIONS: Layered architecture (feature extraction → shot classification → sequence modeling). CNNs/3D CNNs/two-stream networks classify shot types (drive, drop, boast, volley); LSTMs model tactical transitions; supervised classifiers predict rally outcomes; unsupervised methods (k-means, HMMs) profile player styles. Key accuracy figure: Baclig et al. (2020) reported mean absolute percent errors of ~3-4% for distance and speed estimates.

3. SENSOR TECHNOLOGIES: Racket-mounted IMUs (e.g., Racketware, ~500 Hz sampling) measure swing speed, impact detection; wearable IMUs track workload, steps, lunges; smart courts (interactiveSQUASH) integrate cameras + pressure sensors + projectors.

4. COMPARATIVE TOOLS: Tennis Hawk-Eye (multi-camera triangulation, millimeter-level tracking) and badminton shuttle tracking (high-fps cameras, motion-blur compensation) serve as benchmarks.

IDENTIFIED GAPS:
- Ball tracking limitations due to small size, rapid acceleration, occlusion (algorithms often interpolate rather than measure)
- Real-time processing largely unavailable (most pipelines process offline)
- Fragmentation: ball, player, and tactical analyses rarely integrated into unified systems
- Usability barriers: complex calibration, high costs, "black box" ML outputs
- Cost restricts access to elite players, raising equity concerns for junior, para, and community athletes
- Limited squash-specific datasets (mostly proprietary or small)
- Cultural resistance from coaches relying on experiential judgment

PROPOSED SOLUTION (ASTC): An integrated environment combining ceiling-mounted panoramic cameras, high-speed corner cameras, embedded floor sensors (millisecond footfall detection), impact-sensitive wall panels (ball-wall contact points and force), racket-mounted IMUs, and a central computational engine with CNNs and LSTMs. Cross-modal timestamp synchronization links swing mechanics, movement patterns, and tactical outcomes. Features distinct interfaces for coaches (interpretable dashboards with heatmaps, rally flow diagrams) and players (motivational mobile feedback).

FEASIBILITY CONSTRAINTS: Millisecond-scale multimodal synchronization, latency management (balancing edge vs. cloud processing), limited diverse datasets, hardware durability under high-intensity impacts, high upfront costs, and cultural/institutional inertia.

DEVELOPMENT ROADMAP:
- Short-term (1-3 yrs): Open datasets, low-cost single-modality systems, pilot studies
- Mid-term (3-6 yrs): Hybrid camera-sensor systems in elite academies, validation studies
- Long-term (6-10 yrs): Full ASTC in national training centers, federation endorsement, modular versions for community clubs

KEY REFERENCES include Baclig et al. (2020), Brumann et al. (2021), Vučković et al. (2014), Hajdú-Szücs et al. (2018), PSA & interactiveSQUASH (2018), Racketware (2021), Hawk-Eye Innovations.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: Player Tracking in Squash with Computer Vision and Deep Learning ---
URL: https://parkerdixon.github.io/Squash-Vision

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage describes a Metis data science bootcamp final project on player tracking in squash using computer vision and deep learning. The author, a former college squash player and team captain, built a system to analyze court positioning in squash matches using pose estimation.

**The Model:** The author used DeepPose, a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) algorithm that predicts 17 different body joints in an image. Rather than training their own model (which would have taken over 100 days), they used a pre-trained model from GitHub (keras_Realtime_Multi-Person_Pose_Estimation). The article explains CNN fundamentals: convolutional layers detect patterns using image kernels, ReLU activation (f(x)=max(0,x)) provides nonlinearity, and pooling layers downsample to reduce computation cost and overfitting. The DeepPose implementation used did not include dropout layers.

**Implementation Steps:**
1. **Pose Estimation:** Initial processing was too slow (2 hours per 1.5-minute clip), so the author sacrificed accuracy for speed by reducing from 30 to 3 frames per second, reducing model iterations from 5 to 2, and scaling down frames. This reduced processing time to under 5 minutes (about 3X the actual video length).
2. **Player Identification:** Used k-means clustering to differentiate the two players' joints. When players stood close together, clusters overlapped (deemed tolerable since analytics focused on court positioning). Player IDs were assigned by comparing average torso pixel colors to original reference patches using cosine similarity—this requires players to wear different colored shirts.
3. **Projection:** Used the center point of feet (with a fallback method averaging foot-to-joint distances when feet weren't visible) to estimate 3D positions, then applied a homography transform to map 3D points onto a 2D court representation.
4. **Analysis:** Created per-player heatmaps to assess court control. The scoring system awards 1 point per frame in the large ellipse, 5 points in the small ellipse, and deducts 5 points for frames outside both ellipses. The "Control Score" is the ratio of total points earned to the maximum possible (all frames in the small ellipse).

**Future Work:** Implementing ball tracking to analyze rally hit points and shot pace. The author notes their key takeaway was how much their data science skills grew during the bootcamp, and the project was completed ahead of schedule. Related articles at the bottom of the page link to other Metis projects including Flask app deployment to AWS, startup exit predictions from Crunchbase data, and NBA rookie year predictions.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage describes the "Grand Slam Tennis Shot-Level Data" dataset, authored by Peter Spivack and published August 4, 2025, on the SCORE Network sports data repository. The dataset contains shot-level data from WTA and ATP Grand Slam matches (1960-2024), recording each stroke's hand, shot type, direction, depth, and outcome or error type. It is derived from the Tennis Match Charting Project by Jeff Sackmann, a crowdsourced effort where volunteers record each point of WTA and ATP singles matches.

The data was created to fill a gap between spatiotemporal data (which requires heavy computer vision) and aggregated match-level statistics (which offer minimal insight into decision making), enabling analysis of player decision making through categorical shot representations.

The dataset comprises eight datasets covering the ATP and WTA tours at the four Grand Slams: Australian Open, Roland Garros, Wimbledon, and US Open. Shot counts are: ATP Australian Open (645,905), ATP Roland Garros (486,235), ATP US Open (554,405), ATP Wimbledon (418,851); WTA Australian Open (291,905), WTA Roland Garros (196,721), WTA US Open (219,855), WTA Wimbledon (175,761).

Each dataset contains 17 columns across three categories: (1) Match-level data (Date, Tournament, Round, Player 1, Player 2, Point); (2) Point-level data (Shot, Serve, ServingPlayer, WinningPlayer); and (3) Shot encoding (ShotHand, ShotType, ShotDirection, ServeDirection, ShotDepth, OutcomeType, ErrorType). Key coding details include: rounds range from F to R128; ShotHand options are forehand/backhand/NA; ShotType options include serve, groundstroke, slice, volley, overhead, drop_shot, lob, half_volley, swinging_volley; ShotDirection and ServeDirection capture directional placement; ShotDepth (mostly recorded on returns, Shot==2) indicates in_service_box, behind_service_line, or close_to_baseline; OutcomeType includes double_fault, winner, unforced_error, forced_error, ace, unreturnable; ErrorType includes net, wide, deep, wide_deep, foot_fault, shank, time_violation.

Selection bias exists toward popular players, high-leverage matches, and televised matches, with potential minor human recording errors. The page lists three suggested analytical questions involving transition matrices for shot direction, shot type/direction transitions, and chi-squared tests comparing tournament transition distributions. Data is sourced from Jeff Sackmann's GitHub repository under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International License.

SUMMARY:

This scientific research paper, published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance (2017, Vol. 43, No. 2, pp. 348–359), investigates whether humans can infer another person's action intentions through sound alone, and whether athletic expertise enhances this ability. Authors Ivan Camponogara (University of Verona), Matthew Rodger and Cathy Craig (Queen's University Belfast), and Paola Cesari (University of Verona) conducted two experiments with expert basketball players and non-basketball players.

METHODOLOGY: Participants listened to binaural audio recordings of a professional basketball player ("the attacker") running toward a dummy head positioned as a defender, bouncing a basketball. Four movement types were recorded: deceptive and nondeceptive movements to the left and right. Sound was captured via microphones in the dummy head's ear canals, while 41 passive markers tracked the attacker's kinematics using Vicon motion capture at 100 Hz. Sound analysis extracted Interaural Time Difference (ITD) and Interaural Intensity Difference (ILD) cues. In Experiment 1 (Slider Task), participants moved a finger along a rail in the perceived passing direction; in Experiment 2 (Full-Body Task), they moved their whole body to block the attacker, as in a real game. Deceptive sounds showed constant ITD but changing ILD with no significant ITD-ILD correlation, whereas nondeceptive sounds showed strong correlations (r = .51 and .95), indicating deception is acoustically distinguishable.

RESULTS: In the Slider Task, basketball players initiated movements earlier (-0.22s vs 0.56s for nonplayers) and moved faster (934 mm/s vs 777 mm/s), but no significant group differences emerged in error rates. In the Full-Body Task, expertise effects became pronounced: basketball players made errors only 21.35% of the time vs 36.91% for nonplayers, with basketball players being fooled by deceptive movements only 37% of the time (vs 67% for nonplayers in full-body, and 44% in slider). Experts adopted distinct strategies—moving early for nondeceptive movements (~200ms after the central point) and waiting longer for deceptive movements to gather more auditory information—a strategy not observed in nonplayers. Basketball players also showed shorter movement durations and higher peak velocities (1408 mm/s vs 1184 mm/s) in the full-body task.

CONCLUSIONS: The study supports the "supramodal brain" theory—information specifying events can be detected through any available sensory channel. Action intention can be perceived through sound alone, and this ability is honed through sport-specific practice. Experts are better at picking up kinematic features of deceptive movement from event-related sounds, particularly when perception is coupled to action in an ecologically valid, expertise-specific context.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Statistical Enhanced Learning for Modeling and Predicting Tennis Matches at Grand Slam Tournaments

### Overview
This arXiv research manuscript (available at arxiv.org) investigates whether "statistically enhanced" covariates can improve statistical learning approaches for predicting men's tennis matches at Grand Slam tournaments. The study compares various regression and machine learning models—both with and without these enhanced features—using data from 5,013 men's Grand Slam matches (2011-2022) compiled via the R package deuce.

### Enhanced Covariates
Three enhanced covariates were introduced, all incorporated as differences (Player 2 value minus Player 1 value):
1. **Elo rating**: Obtained from a separate modeling approach, tracking player performance over time while accounting for opponent strength and match outcomes.
2. **Age.30**: Absolute distance between player's age and reference age of 30 (based on the finding that optimal tennis player age is 28–32 years, per Weston, 2014).
3. **Age.int**: Distance to the optimal age interval [28, 32], set to 0 for players within that range.

Two conventional covariates were also used: **Rank** (ATP ranking at tournament start) and **Points** (ATP ranking points).

### Methods
- **Linear regression** (logistic regression via GLM)
- **Spline-based approaches** (Generalized Additive Models with P-splines)
- **Random forest** (using ranger package; mtry optimized via 10-fold CV; ntree=400)
- Interpretable Machine Learning (IML) tools: Partial Dependence Plots (PDP) and Individual Conditional Expectation (ICE) plots
- Performance measures: Classification rate, predictive Bernoulli likelihood, and Brier score
- Validation strategies: expanding window (primary), rolling window, and leave-one-tournament-out cross-validation (appendix)

### Key Results (Expanding Window Strategy)
- **21 models** tested for each approach across all covariate combinations.
- **Linear model best**: Points, Rank, Elo → classification rate 0.795, likelihood 0.701 (with Points, Elo, Age.int), Brier score 0.153.
- **Splines model best**: Elo + Age.30 → classification rate 0.792, predictive likelihood 0.703, Brier score 0.149 (best overall Brier score).
- **Random forest best**: Points, Rank, Age.30, Elo → classification rate **0.820** (highest), predictive likelihood 0.667, Brier score 0.151.
- Across all approaches and validation strategies, prediction accuracy improved when at least one enhanced variable (Elo, Age.30, or Age.int) was included.

### Model Interpretation
- **Linear model**: Negative coefficient for Rank difference (-0.0012), positive coefficients for Elo difference (0.0042) and Points (0.0001), indicating higher Elo and Points increase winning probability while higher rank numbers decrease it.
- **Splines**: Elo and Age.30 effects appear linear, with positive effects for both; Age.30 effect not significant within point-wise confidence bands.
- **Random forest with PDP/ICE**: Rank shows strong initial decrease then near-constant trend; Elo shows slight negative then positive trend; Points show positive correlation with winning probability; Age.30 shows significant variability across individuals, with players closer to age 30 performing better. A heatmap of Elo × Age.30 interaction suggests players near age 30 benefit more from higher Elo ratings.

### Conclusion
The study demonstrates that statistically enhanced covariates (Elo rating and age-transformed variables) consistently improve predictive performance across model types, with the random forest achieving the highest classification rate (0.820) when all enhanced variables were included. The combination of PDP and ICE plots provides valuable interpretability for complex machine learning models in sports analytics.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed research article published in the International Journal of Performance Analysis in Sport (2014, Vol 14, Issue 3, pp. 652-679) by Ryan Roddy, Kevin L. Lamb, and Paul Worsfold from the University of Chester, investigating the presence and predictive importance of perturbations in elite squash.

**Purpose & Methodology:** The study analyzed 31 matches from the men's 2011 Australian Open Squash Championships (played under "point a rally" scoring) using a customized Dartfish performance tagging template. The squash court was divided into a 4x4 positional matrix with an additional tramline system (7.5 inches wide) to measure shot accuracy. Critical incidents (perturbation, unforced error, un-returnable shot, let/stroke, and miss-hit) were identified relative to shot selection, player/ball landing position, and shot accuracy. Binary logistic regression was used to assess whether these predictor variables could predict the critical incident responsible for successful rally outcome.

**Key Results:**
- Perturbations were identified 238 times (10%), noticeably less frequent than un-returnable shots (36%), unforced errors (31%), and let/strokes (23%). A miss-hit occurred only once and was omitted.

- Both player and opponent identified the same shots as having significant contribution to rally outcome: volley (p<.01), boast/volley boast (p<.01), and drop/volley drop (p<.01 and p<.05 respectively).
- Perturbation rally sequences typically produced exchanges further forward in court; un-returnable shot sequences left the ball predominantly at the back of the court (backhand drive 20.6%/14.1%, forehand drive 14.3%/10%, backhand cross court drive 10.1%/9.7%).
- During perturbation sequences, the Opponent's ability to return to the "T" position at the time of the Actor's "Winning Shot" declined by 6.5% (to 90.7%).
- Shot accuracy was generally poor; Actor's winning shot accuracy improved to 52.3-53.2% tight shots after opponent's poorly executed returns (86.1-92.4% loose).
- Intra-observer and inter-observer reliability both exceeded the 90% a priori agreement threshold across all variables.

**Conclusion:** While perturbations are evident in elite-level squash, their importance is questionable as they fail to contribute significantly to rally outcomes relative to other critical incidents. The study concludes that perturbation analysis is not a valid predictor of squash performance. The authors suggest improvements in players' anticipatory and perceptive skills may have reduced the loss of control traditionally associated with perturbations. Future research recommendations include redefining the accuracy system to differentiate cross-court shots traveling toward the wall versus straight shots traveling along the wall.

- Players position themselves at both center and four corners of courts when attacking; defenders stay predominantly in the center for quick reactions.
- Except for Clear and Smash shots, most shot types do not target around the head area.

- Almost all short services are directed below the net; almost all long services aim above the net.
