# Fully Comprehensive Findings

## 1. Badminton-Specific Tactic and Shot Modeling (Sequence Modeling: RNN/LSTM/GRU, Transformers, Graphs)

### 1.1 ShuttleNet: Position-aware Fusion of Rally Progress and Player Styles for Stroke Forecasting (AAAI-22)

**Source: AAAI paper PDF, GitHub repo, Liner review, Semantic Scholar page [5][6][7][8]**

ShuttleNet is the first work to address stroke forecasting (predicting future strokes—shot types and area coordinates) in turn-based sports. Authors: Wei-Yao Wang, Hong-Han Shuai, Kai-Shiang Chang, Wen-Chih Peng (National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University). Published at AAAI-22 (DOI: 10.1609/aaai.v36i4.20341; arXiv:2112.01044). Stroke forecasting is formulated as a sequence prediction problem with three key challenges: (1) mixed sequences (two players alternate strokes), (2) multiple outputs at each timestamp (shot type + coordinates), and (3) player dependence (return styles depend on both players' overall styles and rally situation).

The ShuttleNet framework consists of three main components:
- **Transformer-Based Rally Extractor (TRE):** captures rally progress/current situation using a modified Transformer with a proposed multi-head type-area-attention layer (which separately characterizes importance of shot types and area, inspired by disentangled attention).
- **Transformer-Based Player Extractor (TPE):** splits the sequence into two subsequences by player (Player A and B) to generate each player's context, with shared parameters and sequence alignment.
- **Position-Aware Gated Fusion Network (PGFN):** fuses rally contexts and both players' contexts using information weights (α) and learnable position weights (β) based on gated multi-modal units.

The prediction layer assumes area coordinates follow a bi-variate Gaussian distribution and uses hard parameter sharing with two linear layers to predict shot type and area parameters. Training minimizes combined cross-entropy loss (Ltype) and negative log-likelihood loss (Larea).

Key experimental results:
- Dataset: 75 high-ranking badminton singles matches (2018-2021), 31 players, 180 sets, 4,325 rallies, 43,191 strokes, 10 shot types (net shot, clear, push/rush, smash, defensive shot, drive, lob, drop, short service, long service).
- ShuttleNet outperforms all baselines (Seq2Seq, CF-LSTM, TF, dNRI, DMA-Nets) by at least 12.0% in CE and 3.4% in MSE across all metrics and observed-stroke lengths (τ=2, 4, 8).
- Ablation studies confirmed the necessity of each component (rally extractor, both player extractors, information weights, position weights, and type-area-attention).
- Case study showed players use different area distributions (middle of court vs. near net) when returning against smashes, demonstrating tactic investigation utility.
- Strong performance even with short observed stroke lengths (τ=2), indicating practical real-time applicability.
- Traditional sequence models (Seq2Seq, TF, DMA-Nets) and trajectory-based models (CF-LSTM, dNRI) perform poorly on badminton stroke forecasting due to the turn-based, event-driven nature of the sport.
- ShuttleNet's variants (ShuttleNetP2R and ShuttleNetR2P) that integrate player and rally contexts sequentially did not outperform the full model, validating the separate-learning-then-fusion design approach.

The paper concludes the framework benefits both coaching-oriented applications (tactic investigation) and community-oriented applications (storytelling/engagement), with future work planned to extend to additional conditions like win/loss outcomes. Code is available at https://github.com/wywyWang/ShuttleNet (now moved to CoachAI Projects: https://github.com/wywyWang/CoachAI-Projects, MIT license). The paper has 58 citations (including 4 highly influential, 23 background, 12 methods, and 1 results citation), 39 references.

### 1.2 BLSR: Exploring the Long Short-Term Dependencies to Infer Shot Influence in Badminton Matches (ICDM-21) and ACM TIST Extension

**Sources: arXiv PDF [11], Semantic Scholar [12], ACM DL [14]**

The paper (arXiv:2109.06431; ICDM 2021, pages 1397-1402, DOI: 10.1109/ICDM51629.2021.00178; extended as "How Is the Stroke? Inferring Shot Influence in Badminton Matches via Long Short-term Dependencies," ACM TIST 2022, DOI: 10.1145/3551391, cited by 28/23 papers) introduces BLSR (Badminton Language from Shot to Rally), a unified language representing badminton plays where a shot is treated as a "word" and a rally as a "sentence." Each shot is described by 8 attributes (player, timestamp, type, backhand, around head, hit area, player area, opponent area), and each rally by rally-level information (scores, getpoint player, end reason). They defined 18 shot types (e.g., net shot, smash, clear, drop, drive, service) and a 16-area grid system for representing court locations.

The proposed deep learning model frames shot influence as a rally outcome prediction task. It consists of three components:
1. Shot data encoding using location embeddings and enhanced shot type embeddings with temporal score learning (normalized time proportion multiplied via sigmoid).
2. Extraction of local shot patterns using two separate 1-D CNNs (one per player) with kernel size 3, alternately merged.
3. Encoding pattern sequences using a bidirectional GRU with an attention mechanism that enables interpretability of which shots matter most for the rally outcome.

The final representation combines the sequence representation with rally-level information (score difference, consecutive scores) to predict win probability via a fully-connected layer with sigmoid activation.

Experiments used a private dataset of 15,742 shots from 1,409 rallies across 19 international men's singles matches (2018-2020), labeled by domain experts. The model outperformed all baselines (ProSeNet, DeepMoji, BiLSTM, ON-LSTM, Transformer) with AUC of 0.8966 and Brier score of 0.1329. Ablation studies showed all components contribute, with the two-CNN design providing the most significant performance improvement. Source code is publicly available at https://github.com/yao0510/Shot-Influence. Future work includes labeling more player data and investigating tactical performance against different opponents.

### 1.3 DyMF: Where Will Players Move Next? Dynamic Graphs and Hierarchical Fusion for Movement Forecasting in Badminton (AAAI-23)

**Sources: AAAI OJS [16], Scribd [17], arXiv HTML [18]**

DyMF (Dynamic Graphs and Hierarchical Fusion for Movement Forecasting) is the first work to address movement forecasting in badminton and other turn-based sports like tennis. The paper formalizes the task of predicting players' future movements and shot types based on previous strokes in a rally.

Core contributions:
1. First formalization of movement forecasting in badminton, predicting players' future locations and shot types.
2. Introduction of the Player Movements (PM) graph, which transforms rallies into graphs with strategic relations between players' locations using 12 relation types (10 shot types: net shot, lob, defensive shot, smash, drop, push/rush, short service, clear, drive, long service; plus "defend" and "return" edge types).
3. A novel DyMF model using an encoder-decoder architecture with interaction style extractors (relational GCN + dynamic GCN) and hierarchical fusions (player-player fusion via parallel co-attention, and player-rally fusion).
4. Extensive experiments showing state-of-the-art performance on a real-world badminton dataset.

Methodology:
- Movement forecasting is formulated as a sequence prediction task: given observed stroke sequence of length τ, predict future strokes including both players' locations and shot types.
- PM graph construction: nodes represent player locations at each time step; edges represent 12 strategic relations.
- Interaction Style Extractor uses Relational GCN (inspired by R-GCN) for interactions between players and Dynamic GCN with LSTM-based pattern-generated weights for dynamic personal tactics.
- Hierarchical Fusion combines player styles (via parallel co-attention) with rally interactions using sigmoid-based dynamic weights.
- Movement predictor outputs shot types via cross-entropy and locations via bivariate Gaussian distributions.
- Total loss = shot type cross-entropy + 0.5×location loss per player.

Experimental Results:
- Dataset: 75 badminton singles matches, 31 players, 180 sets, 4,325 rallies, 43,191 strokes; 80/20 train/test split.
- Baselines: Seq2Seq, TF (Transformer), ShuttleNet (sequence-based); dNRI, GCNPM, R-GCNPM, E-GCNPM (graph-based).
- DyMF outperforms all baselines across all metrics (MSE, MAE for locations; CE for shot type) at observation lengths τ=2, 4, and 8.
- Improvements up to 35.3% for MSE, 21.5% for MAE, and 24.3% for CE.
- Key findings: naive sequence models fail on structural info; dNRI insufficient due to lack of new location nodes; E-GCNPM unstable with few graph nodes; DyMF surpasses ShuttleNet due to modeling movement purposes and dynamic tactics.

Case Study: Demonstrated that changing a player's defense position alters the opponent's returned shot (e.g., standing close to net forces opponent to clear, enabling an attack), verifying that opponents respond to player defense locations and that effective positioning limits opponent options.

Future Work: Extend DyMF to badminton doubles with greater focus on inter-player interactions. Supported by Taiwan's Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST-110-2627-H-A49-001). Code available at https://github.com/wywyWang/CoachAI-Projects/tree/main/Movement%20Forecasting.

### 1.4 RallyTemPose: A Stroke of Genius — Predicting the Next Move in Badminton (CVPRW 2024)

**Sources: IEEE Xplore [13], Aalborg Portal [12], CVF Open Access PDF [15], ITU Copenhagen [16]**

RallyTemPose is a transformer encoder-decoder model for predicting future badminton strokes based on previous rally actions, by Magnus Ibh, Stella Graßhof, Dan Witzner Hansen (and Pascal Madeleine). Published in 2024 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW), Seattle, WA, June 17-18, 2024, pages 3376-3385 (DOI: 10.1109/CVPRW63382.2024.00342). Code is available via a linked URL. 9 citations.

Key contributions:
1. A skeleton-based spatiotemporal encoder using transformer and pooling blocks to enhance next-stroke predictions in badminton.
2. An adaptive cross-attention decoder that incorporates contextual stroke descriptors from high-dimensional embeddings of a pre-trained language model (BERT).
3. Examples of how latent variables can be used for match and playstyle analysis.

Methodology: The model uses court position (player ground positions), 2D skeleton poses, and player-specific embeddings to learn stroke and player-specific latent representations in a spatiotemporal encoder module. These representations condition subsequent stroke predictions in a decoder module through rally-aware fusion blocks. The encoder consists of a linear projection layer, learned joint encoding, a Spatial Transformer (ST) for spatial relationships between keypoints, a Grouped Pooling Block (GPB), and a Temporal Transformer (TT) for temporal dynamics—computing both inter-player (cross-attention) and intra-player (self-attention). The encoder produces three latent variables: a stroke representation (zs) and two player representations (z1, z2). The decoder uses an embedding layer, player representations added per stroke, self-attention, dual cross-attention, and an adaptive fusion mechanism to predict the next stroke. Stroke embeddings are enhanced using BERT to embed text descriptions of stroke types. Training uses cross-entropy loss plus an auxiliary loss on the latent stroke variable (γ=0.3).

Datasets:
- ShuttleSet: 42 professional matches (2018-2021), 26 players, 3,000+ rallies, 34,000+ strokes, 10 shot types. 80% training/20% testing split.
- BadmintonDB: 9 professional men's singles matches (Kento Momota vs. Anthony Sinisuka Ginting), 811 rallies, 9,671 strokes, 10 stroke types. 7 matches for training, 2 for testing.

Results:
- ShuttleSet: 54.3% accuracy, 77.3% top-2, 92.5% top-3 accuracy—outperforming baselines (Seq2Seq, Transformer, Actionformer + Transformer decoder).
- BadmintonDB: 62.8% accuracy, 83.5% top-2, 93.1% top-3 accuracy—also outperforming baselines, though with overfitting issues due to the smaller dataset.
- Ablation study: Player ground position is the most critical input (leaving it out drops performance 2.6%). Removing keypoint data drops accuracy to 48.3%. Player-specific embeddings don't significantly boost accuracy but enable playstyle analysis.

Analysis applications: t-SNE visualizations of latent variables show clear groupings for stroke types and partial groupings for players. Cosine similarity of player latent variables reveals playstyle differences (e.g., male vs. female players show lower similarity, and distinct male playing styles are reflected in lower similarity scores). Average prediction accuracy varies by over 20% between the best and worst predicted players, potentially indicating how well players mask their strokes.

Future work: Incorporating match outcomes (win/loss), expanding to predict skeleton sequences of predicted strokes, and creating synthetic data for a field with sparse quality annotated datasets. The research was funded by the Novo Nordisk Foundation (TeamSPORTek initiative) with contributions from Badminton Danmark and Team Danmark. The paper notes badminton's probabilistic stroke forecasting is complicated by inherent unpredictability of player decisions, influenced by physical state, psychological condition, and tactical approach.

### 1.5 TemPose-TF-ASF: Two-Stage Bidirectional Stroke Context Fusion for Badminton Stroke Classification (arXiv 2025)

**Source: arXiv HTML [19]**

TemPose-TF-ASF (Adjacent-Stroke Fusion) is a context-aware extension of the TemPose framework for fine-grained badminton stroke classification. The method enhances stroke recognition by incorporating stroke-type information from both preceding and subsequent strokes to model bidirectional temporal dependencies.

Key contributions:
1. TemPose-TF-ASF integrates semantic information from preceding and subsequent strokes to enhance temporal context modeling for badminton stroke recognition.
2. A Two-Stage Contextual Refinement (TSCR) training and inference strategy is proposed to mitigate training-inference mismatch without relying on ground-truth future stroke annotations. In stage one, the baseline model generates preliminary predictions; in stage two, these are reorganized as estimated adjacent-stroke context and used to jointly optimize the ASF module and classifier.
3. The ASF module uses stroke embedding, feature concatenation, and MLP-based fusion to integrate adjacent stroke information.
4. Two alternative architectures are explored: TemPose-TF-BiLP (Bidirectional LSTM Predictor) and TemPose-TF-BiTP (Bidirectional Transformer Predictor), which use forward and backward predictors to model bidirectional temporal stroke sequences.

Methodology:
- Builds on TemPose-TF, a skeleton-based factorized Transformer that separately models temporal dynamics of human motion and inter-player interactions.
- Multimodal inputs include skeletal joints/bones, player court positions, and shuttlecock trajectories (extracted via TrackNetV3; court lines via MonoTrack or TennisCourtDetector).
- Stroke categories range 0-30 (31 total after data processing).

Dataset: ShuttleSet, the largest public badminton video dataset, with 44 singles matches (2018-2021), 27 players, 104 games, 3,685 rallies, and 36,492 shots. After cleaning, 40 matches were retained (30 train, 5 validation, 5 test) yielding 33,429 annotated strokes. Categories were merged ("push"/"lob" into "push lob"; "wrist smash" into "smash") and duplicated by court position, resulting in 31 stroke categories.

Key results:
- TemPose-TF-ASF achieves the best performance: 0.854 Accuracy, 0.761 Macro-F1, 0.945 Acc-2 (vs. baseline TemPose-TF at 0.835 Acc, 0.742 Macro-F1, 0.927 Acc-2).
- ASF was integrated into BlockGCN, SkateFormer, and BST-CG-AP, consistently improving all models (e.g., BlockGCN-ASF: 0.809 vs 0.793; BST-CG-AP-ASF: 0.843 vs 0.838), demonstrating backbone-agnostic transferability.
- Variants with partial fusion (PSF, NSF, TSF, DualSF, TriSF) all underperformed full bidirectional ASF, showing that excessive semantic input (TriSF) can introduce redundancy/noise.
- TemPose-TF-BiLP achieves highest Accuracy (0.850) while TemPose-TF-TSF achieves highest Macro-F1 among target-stroke integration approaches (0.745).
- Two-stage architectures outperform three-stage counterparts in Accuracy; three-stage improves Macro-F1 (PSSiTP reaches 0.747) but is more prone to error propagation.

Conclusions: Bidirectional stroke context consistently improves badminton stroke recognition. The TSCR strategy enhances accuracy while avoiding ground-truth future annotations. ASF demonstrates strong transferability across multiple SOTA temporal action recognition methods.

### 1.6 Deep Learning Framework for Badminton Rally Outcome Prediction (ISPACS 2022)

"A deep learning based framework for badminton rally outcome prediction" by Yong En Tan, John See, Junaidi Abdullah, Lai Kuan Wang, and Kar Weng Ban (Heriot-Watt University Malaysia). Published March 31, 2023 as conference contribution in the 2022 International Symposium on Intelligent Signal Processing and Communication Systems (ISPACS) by IEEE (ISBN: 9798350332421, DOI: 10.1109/ispacs57703.2022.10082764). 9 citations (SciVal), indexed in Scopus.

### 1.7 Gaming Tree Based Evaluation Model for Badminton Tactic Benefit Analysis and Prediction (Applied Sciences 2023)

**Source: MDPI [4]**

Published in MDPI Applied Sciences (2023, Volume 13, Issue 13, Article 7380, DOI: 10.3390/app13137380) by Wenming Liu, Yifan Zhu, Wenxia Guo, Xinyuan Wang, and Songkun Yu (Zhejiang University, Beijing University of Chemical Technology, Zhejiang University of Technology). Received 20 May 2023, published 21 June 2023.

The research applies game theory concepts—specifically gaming trees and Nash Equilibrium—to analyze and predict badminton tactics. The study examines matches between Dan Lin (9 major titles, 2 Olympic gold medals) and Chong Wei Lee (ranked world #1 for 349 weeks). A total of 29 matches from 2006 to 2018 were analyzed (Lin won 19, Lee won 10).

Methodology: The gaming tree was constructed where each node represents a possible stroke, with strokes characterized by four attributes: player, stroke technique, start placement, and target placement. The badminton court was divided into a 3×3 grid (front/middle/back court × left/middle/right court). Stroke techniques included serve, smash, clear, drop, net shot, and drive. Tactical observation indices covered stroke technique, stroke placement, and rally results. Each stroke, rally, and game was assigned a weighted score based on its importance to the overall match outcome. The benefit of each gaming tree node was computed by summing weighted scores, and the net benefit was calculated by adding the maximum score of child nodes. Nash Equilibrium was identified to determine optimal strategies and predict win/loss outcomes.

Key results: (1) The best choice for Lin was hitting the shuttle to the backcourt, while Lee's best strategy was controlling the forecourt. (2) Win-loss ratio analysis showed Lin consistently outperformed Lee in most career periods, consistent with actual match results. (3) As the two players faced each other more often, they discovered more ways to beat each other; however, in the final period (matches 22–28), strategy diversity dropped significantly due to mutual familiarity and physical limitations. (4) In the last period, Lin and Lee had roughly equal chances of winning, with Lin's advantage reversing at higher stroke counts (7+ beats). The empirical results demonstrated the gaming tree method could effectively evaluate player strengths and weaknesses and accurately predict tactical implementation.

### 1.8 Prediction Model and Technical and Tactical Decision Analysis of Women's Badminton Singles Based on Machine Learning (PLOS ONE 2024)

**Sources: PMC [1], PLOS ONE [2]**

Published PLOS ONE (2024 Nov 14;19(11):e0312801, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0312801) by Yuan H, Wang Y, Yang K, Bin Y. The study focuses on South Korean badminton player An Se-young, who rose to the top of the 2023 BWF Olympic points table with an 89.5% win rate (77 wins, 9 losses) during the Paris Olympic cycle.

Methodology: The researchers analyzed An Se-young's technical and tactical statistics using a proposed "three-stage" data classification method. They used video analysis of 10 matches (21-point games) from 2023 where An faced four players ranked in the top five of the BWF rankings (Chen Yu Fei, Akane Yamaguchi, Tai Tzu-ying, and Carolina Marin). Matches included finals/semifinals from the Indonesia Open, China Open, World Championships, Asian Championships, and Asian Games. A total of 10h32min was recorded with actual game time of 140min49s. Videos were sourced from YouTube, and statistics were gathered from the BWF Fansite. They constructed a machine learning dataset using inputs such as number of strikes, scoring/losing locations, techniques used in the last three strikes, and serving locations, with scoring/losing outcome as the output. Data was divided 90% training / 10% test. The study used five machine learning algorithms: Decision Tree, Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Machine, and K-Nearest Neighbors. They also used principal component analysis (PCA) with K-means clustering to validate the dataset's learning value.

Key results:
- Support Vector Machine with RBF kernel achieved the highest prediction accuracy at 87.5%, with strong consistency.
- K-Nearest Neighbors achieved 75.00% accuracy.
- Decision Tree and Random Forest each achieved 62.50%; XGBoost achieved 56.25%.
- The linear kernel SVM achieved 75.00%, indicating strong linear relationships in the data.
- The correlation matrix showed significant negative correlations between shot location and technique used (ranging from -0.67 to -0.71).
- PCA results showed the two clusters (gain and loss) were well-separated in two-dimensional space, confirming the dataset had learnable intrinsic features.

An Se-young's playing style findings:
- More than 50% of rounds are completed by long multi-shots, reaching 61% in scoring rounds (vs. 53% in conceding rounds).
- She does not seek continuous pressure but rather exploits and maximizes aggression following opponent mistakes.
- She immediately utilizes assault methods (kills or dives) after opponent errors, often converting points in the subsequent 2-3 strikes.
- 60% of her organized shots from the backcourt ultimately achieved points through lifting or high clears.
- Her attacking strength is weaker than her ability to stalemate opponents; she typically creates opportunities through blitzes and scores in the following 2-3 shots.
- When losing points, there was an increase in blocks (20%) and lobs (22%) on the penultimate shot, with significant decreases in net kills (3%) and smashes (6%).
- The number of strikes in a round was the most important predictive parameter, followed by landing location where points were scored/lost.

Limitations acknowledged: small sample size, simplistic personal style classification criteria, and lack of consideration for players' handedness differences. Future research plans include expanding data sources and volume, introducing more complex models like Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), and considering dynamic match factors.

### 1.9 Predicting Badminton Outcomes Through Machine Learning and Technical Action Frequencies (Scientific Reports 2025)

**Source: Nature Scientific Reports [13]**

Published in Scientific Reports (volume 15, Article number 10575, 2025) by Yi Sheng, Cheng Liu, Qing Yi, Wanli Ouyang, Ru Wang, and Peijie Chen.

Data & Methods:

### 1.10 Future Shuttlecock Trajectory Prediction in Badminton Using Player's Information

**Sources: PMC J Imaging [6], VISAPP 2023 PDF [8]**

Two related papers from Keio University (Yuka Nokihara, Ryo Hachiuma, Ryosuke Hori, Hideo Saito):

**J Imaging paper (May 11, 2023, doi: 10.3390/jimaging9050099):** Proposes a trajectory prediction method incorporating three types of information: shuttlecock position (2D), player positions (4D), and player postures (68D). These are each embedded into 2D feature vectors via fully connected layers and combined into a 6D feature vector, fed into an LSTM network. Two modules: (1) detection and pose estimation for past frames (TrackNet for shuttlecock detection, Faster R-CNN trained on MS COCO for player detection, HRNet for pose estimation), and (2) a time-series model for future prediction.

Experimental details: Dataset: Shuttlecock Trajectory Dataset (26 match videos for training, 3 for testing; 1280x720 resolution, 30 fps). Training used 23 professional singles matches from international tournaments (2018-2021), split 80/20 into training/validation. Implementation: PyTorch 1.12.1, Python 3.7.13, NVIDIA TITAN RTX, CUDA 11.4. LSTM: 3 layers, 128-dimension hidden layer, Adam optimizer, 400 epochs. Input: 4 past frames; Output: 12 future frames. Loss: MSE. Data augmentation: 50% left-right flipping probability, 50-pixel translation range. Evaluation: Average Displacement Error (ADE) and Final Displacement Error (FDE) in pixels.

Key results: The proposed method improved ADE by ~13% compared to methods using only shuttlecock position information, and by ~8.4% compared to methods using shuttlecock + player position (without posture). Compared to other time-series models, the LSTM-based approach improved ADE by ~9.8% (vs RNN), ~5.0% (vs GRU), ~20% (vs Transformer), and ~12% (vs Seq2Seq). Data augmentation with 50% left-right flipping and 50-pixel translation was most effective. Accuracy improves with more input frames and fewer frames to predict.

**VISAPP 2023 paper:** Presented at VISAPP 2023 (18th International Joint Conference on Computer Vision, Imaging and Computer Graphics Theory and Applications). Uses Faster R-CNN object detector (pre-trained on MS COCO) to detect players, extracting bounding box coordinates. Shuttle position from TrackNet. Player positions (4D coordinates: xp1, yp1, xp2, yp2) combined with shuttle position (2D: xs, ys) form a 6D input vector fed into an LSTM. The proposed method (Shuttle + Player LSTM) achieved the best results with an average ADE of 0.04908 and FDE of 0.08391, outperforming all baselines. Frame input/output experiments showed accuracy improves as input frames increase and output frames decrease (e.g., 12 input/4 output frames yielded ADE of 0.02054 vs. 4 input/12 output frames at 0.04908). The authors argue that unlike tennis or table tennis, badminton requires predicting the shuttle trajectory itself (not just landing point) because the shuttle is hit back without bouncing and must be hit from a higher, faster forward position to gain advantage. Quote: "Especially in badminton, where the shuttle speed is faster than in other net sports such as tennis and table tennis, it is not an exaggeration to say that predicting the movement of the shuttle a few tenths ahead can mean the difference between winning and losing a match."

### 1.11 CoachAI Badminton Environment (AAAI-24)

**Sources: AAAI OJS paper [17], AAAI OJS student abstract [18]**

The CoachAI Badminton Environment is a reinforcement learning (RL) environment tailored for AI-driven sports analytics in badminton, by Kuang-Da Wang, Yu-Tse Chen, Yu-Heng Lin, Wei-Yao Wang, and Wen-Chih Peng (National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University).

Key features: 
- Realistic opponent simulation: integrates authentic opponent AIs powered by ShuttleNet (transformer-based stroke forecasting model predicting shot types and landing positions) and DyMF (graph-based framework for predicting player movements), both trained on ShuttleSet.
- Addresses two main challenges: (a) opponent-driven transition dynamics in turn-based sports, and (b) dynamic strategies and randomness to prevent opponents from being easily seen through.
- MDP modeling: models each badminton game as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and inherits the OpenAI Gym API. Includes a Behavior Cloning (BC) model to handle interactions when fewer than two historical strokes are available (a limitation of ShuttleNet and DyMF).
- Evaluation & visualization tools: animated simulation (displaying landing/movement position distributions, shot type probability bar charts, replay functionality) and error statistics (pie charts distinguishing out-of-bounds hits from net hits, with a 10-region court discretization - 9 internal and 1 external).
- Benchmarks: Advantage Actor-Critic (A2C) and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) benchmarked against two different opponent AIs across 20 badminton sets.
- Demonstrated results: The PPO agent, through training, shifted its moving distribution after taking serves from favoring the left court side to the right side, resulting in a 60% increase in win rate against opponent A.

The MDP uses 12 shot types (receiving, short service, long service, net shot, clear, push/rush, smash, defensive shot, drive, lob, drop, can't reach), with real badminton scoring rules (21 points, two-point lead at 20-20, first to 30 wins). The integrated approach (ShuttleNet + DyMF + BC) outperforms standalone ShuttleNet and DyMF across all metrics (improved cross-entropy for shot types, and mean absolute error for landing and moving positions). A case study shows A2C uses a conservative strategy (Clear, Drive, Defensive Shot) while PPO uses more diverse shot types, suggesting diversification may be key to defeating stronger opponents. Code: https://github.com/wywyWang/CoachAI-Projects/tree/main/CoachAI%20Badminton%20Environment. Supported by Ministry of Science and Technology of Taiwan under Grant 112-2425-H-A49-001.

### 1.12 Real-time Stroke Prediction in Badminton Integrating AI with the KNN-HMM Model (Journal of Big Data 2026)

**Source: Springer [11]**

Open-access article published in Journal of Big Data (Volume 13, article 61, published 06 March 2026) by Qi Song and Jian Zhang. Presents a k-Nearest Neighbours-Hidden Markov Model (KNN-HMM) for real-time badminton stroke prediction, addressing accuracy, time-dependent characteristics, and flexibility in stroke analysis, integrating spatial and temporal dynamics for stroke classification under real-time constraints.

Methods: Dataset comprised 10,000 motion-captured badminton strokes collected in Chongqing, China (2015-2017) from 36 players (18 male, 18 female; ages 18-35; 12 amateur, 12 semi-professional, 12 professional). Data was captured using an eight-camera Vicon optical motion capture system (120 Hz) and annotated in Kinovea. Features included joint angles (shoulder, elbow, wrist), velocities, accelerations, and shuttle trajectory descriptors. Temporal sequences were segmented using 200-ms sliding windows with 50-ms overlap. The model combined a KNN stroke classifier (k=5, Euclidean metric, FAISS index) with HMM-based temporal sequence prediction (3-5 hidden states, Gaussian emissions, Baum-Welch training, Viterbi decoding). Data split 70% training, 15% validation, 15% test. External validation used the ShuttleSet22 dataset (44 professional matches, 36,000+ strokes, 2018-2022).

Key results:
- KNN-HMM achieved 94.6% accuracy on internal validation (95% CI 93.9-95.3) and 93.4% on external evaluation.
- 97.5% accuracy with 32 ms latency and 90.8% streaming accuracy.
- Compared to standalone KNN: modest gains in accuracy (+0.05, p=0.021), F1-score (+0.07, p=0.015), precision (+0.06, p=0.001), recall (+0.04, p=0.018).
- Outperformed hybrid SVM-Decision Tree-KNN (83.4%) and acoustic sensor-based approaches (~84%).
- Jump Smash and Net Shot had highest F1 (≥0.98); Clear and Drive had lower F1 (≤0.92).
- End-to-end processing: 32 ms at 120 Hz, 18 ms at 60 Hz, 14 ms at 30 Hz on 8-core CPU.
- HMM log-likelihood of 42.75, BIC of 88.6.

Conclusions: The KNN-HMM offers an effective paradigm for real-time badminton stroke classification with high accuracy, adaptability, and generalizability. The framework is advantageous for training applications and real-time tactical analysis.

### 1.13 Enhancing Badminton Game Analysis: Shot Refinement via Fusion of Shuttlecock Tracking and Hit Detection (Sensors 2024)

**Source: PMC Sensors [14]**

Published in Sensors (Basel) July 5, 2024 (PMCID: PMC11244353, DOI: 10.3390/s24134372) by Yi-Hua Hsu, Chih-Chang Yu (Chung Yuan Christian University), and Hsu-Yung Cheng (National Central University). Proposes an automated method for extracting shots and analyzing badminton games from monocular camera videos.

Methodology: (1) TrackNet, a deep neural network for small object tracking, extracts shuttlecock flight trajectories; (2) YOLOv7 model identifies player swinging actions; (3) a proposed Shot Refinement Algorithm (SRA) fuses both detection results to obtain accurate hitting moments, compensating for detection misses and false detections in both models.

Key results: The proposed method achieves 89.7% accuracy, 91.3% recall, and 90.5% F1 score across 69 matches with 1,582 rallies of BWF match videos. This significantly improves upon using TrackNet alone (58.8% accuracy, 93.6% recall, 72.3% F1). Shot type classification accuracy at three thresholds is 72.1%, 65.4%, and 54.1%. The study also includes a DensePose-based pose estimation module to track player positions via perspective transformation of ankle coordinates onto an aerial court view.

The SRA operates by combining Hit Detection by Trajectories (HD-T, from TrackNet) and Hit Detection by Action (HD-A, from YOLOv7), partitioning rallies into Hit Segments (HS) with player IDs, and handling five distinct scenarios: (1) single HD-T in a player segment (correct detection), (2) multiple HD-Ts in a None segment (false positives eliminated), (3) multiple HD-Ts in a player segment (closest to highest confidence frame kept), (4) no HD-T in a player segment (highest confidence frame selected to compensate), and (5) no HD-T in None segment (true negative).

## 2. Public Datasets and Benchmarks for Tactical Analysis

### 2.1 ShuttleSet (KDD 2023)

**Sources: EmergentMind [17], arXiv [18], Liner review [19], YouTube KDD presentation [20], Semantic Scholar [12]**

ShuttleSet is the largest publicly available stroke-level badminton singles dataset, designed for tactical analysis and structured turn-based modeling. Introduced by Wang et al. (2023) — Wei-Yao Wang, Yung-Chang Huang, et al. — at KDD 2023 (arXiv:2306.04948, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2306.04948, CC BY 4.0 license). It comprises **44 broadcast matches (2018–2021), 104 sets, 3,685 rallies, and 36,492 strokes** involving 27 top-ranking men's and women's singles players. Each stroke is annotated with temporal, spatial, and tactical labels coupled with match-, set-, and rally-level context.

Dataset origin and structure: Created to fill the gap in turn-based sports analytics (no public, expert-annotated, stroke-by-stroke datasets preserving full tactical structure). Source material is public broadcast video from bwf.tv (not instrumented capture), standardized to 30 fps and 1280×720 resolution. The corpus spans quarter-finals, semi-finals, and finals of top-tier tournaments including Super 1000 events and BWF World Tour Finals. The dataset is structured around rallies (not isolated clips), making it suitable for sequence modeling tasks.

Annotation schema — four categories per stroke:
- **Rally category**: set scores, rally winner, lose reason (out, touched net, not over net, opponent ball landed, misjudged).
- **Temporal category**: hitting time (seconds) and hitting frame.
- **Spatial category**: player A/B locations, shuttle hitting location, categorical grid location, above/below net indicator.
- **Hitting category**: stroke status, backhand, around-the-head, shot type.

Court coordinates are derived via homography (p′=Hp), with singles-court coordinates defined at corners (0,0), (0,6.1), (13.4,0), (13.4,6.1). A domain-expert grid divides each half court into nine grids plus seven outside grids. The shot taxonomy contains **18 stroke classes** (net shot, smash, lob, clear, drive, drop, push, rush, service types, etc.).

Labeling workflow: Annotated with the S² (Shot-by-Shot) labeling tool in four stages: match preparation, rally segmentation, video preprocessing, and shot-by-shot labeling. Six trained badminton-expert annotators performed labeling. Quality metrics: temporal consistency MAE of 0.24 (serve), 0.02 (return), 0 for dead bird; spatial consistency MAE of 0.18 (shuttle) and 0.86 (player); shot-type consistency accuracy differences of 0.00 (serve), 0.05 (return), 0.11 (dead bird). Distributed through the CoachAI project, with a Python implementation and Flask-based visualization platform used by national badminton teams.

Native benchmarks (three tasks):
1. **Stroke influence** (win-probability estimation): Best model ShuttleScorer achieved AUC 0.8371, ACC 0.7869, BR 0.1574.
2. **Stroke forecasting** (predict future shot types and landing locations): Best model ShuttleNet achieved CE 2.4125, MSE 1.8121, MAE 1.3582 (τ=8).
3. **Movement forecasting** (predict future strokes and both players' positions): DyMF best CE 2.3146; ShuttleNet lowest MSE 1.0832, MAE 1.5852.

Later research repurposing:
- **Stroke-type recognition** (Chang, 2025): BST-3 variant achieved Acc 0.7710, Macro-F1 0.7042, Acc-2 0.9340.
- **Doubles transfer learning** (Baek et al., 2025): Pose-based Transformer achieved singles accuracy 0.8617, doubles combined accuracy 0.6686; transfer degradation ~19.3% (pose-based) vs ~39.9% (vision-only YOLOv11x).
- **Temporal action localization** (Wang et al., 2026): DSTA adapter achieved average mAP 74.67 across tIoU thresholds.
- **Report generation** (Chiang et al., 2026): ShuttleSet+ derived from ShuttleSet22 (58 matches, 140 sets, 3,992 rallies, 33,612 strokes); Tree-of-Text outperformed baselines using ~40% of Chain-of-Table's time/cost.

Limitations: Singles only; no fixed train/validation/test partition (papers construct own splits); no continuous shuttle trajectories stored; 3D pose lifting unreliable for badminton-specific poses; class imbalance (rare categories: defensive return lob, driven flight, rush); no action interval boundaries requiring synthetic temporal windows.

Significance: ShuttleSet established a shared, stroke-level representation on public broadcast video, enabling otherwise disconnected research threads—forecasting, recognition, localization, transfer, and report generation—to operate on a common substrate. Note: ShuttleSet's 18 fine-grained stroke types introduce greater uncertainty and complexity than the earlier 10-type set used in ShuttleNet's original experiments, posing a significant challenge for current models.

### 2.2 ShuttleSet22 and the CoachAI Badminton Challenge @ IJCAI 2023

**Sources: arXiv HTML [16], IJCAI proceedings [17], Liner review [18]**

ShuttleSet22 (introduced in "Benchmarking Stroke Forecasting with Stroke-Level Badminton Dataset," IJCAI 2024 Demo Track, pages 8829-8832, DOI: 10.24963/ijcai.2024/1042, by Wei-Yao Wang, Wei-Wei Du, Wen-Chih Peng, and Tsi-Ui Ik) extends ShuttleSet with 2022 matches. Contains 35 players, 58 matches, 3,992 rallies, and 33,612 strokes total. Training set: 30,172 strokes in 2,888 rallies; Validation set: 1,400 strokes in 450 rallies; Testing set: 2,040 strokes in 654 rallies. Data sourced from public BWF videos and meticulously labeled by domain experts using a shot-by-shot labeling tool.

Comparison to existing datasets:
- BadmintonDB (the main prior stroke-level dataset) only covers 2 players, 9 matches, 811 rallies, and 9,671 strokes from 2018-2020, and focuses on a single matchup (Kento Momota vs. Anthony Sinisuka Ginting).
- ShuttleSet22 provides comprehensive coverage of various players and matchups.

Problem formulation: Given observed τ=4 strokes with type-area pairs and two players, predict future strokes (shot types and area coordinates) for the next n steps (n = actual rally length). Evaluation metrics: cross-entropy for shot type prediction and mean absolute error (MAE) for area coordinates. Teams generate 6 predicted sequences per rally, from which the closest to ground truth is selected (reduced from 10 in the original work).

Exploratory data analysis findings:
- Players position themselves at both center and four corners of courts when attacking; defenders stay predominantly in the center for quick reactions.
- Except for Clear and Smash shots, most shot types do not target around the head area.
- More than half of Push/Rush, Defensive Shot, and Short Service shots are executed with backhand; other shot types predominantly use forehand.
- Almost all short services are directed below the net; almost all long services aim above the net.

Challenge results: ~100 participants joined; 16 teams submitted final results. Winning team Intro_to_AI_team8 achieved CE 1.7892, MAE 0.7884, Total 2.5776. Team YHY demonstrated best MAE performance (0.6797). 11 teams outperformed the official ShuttleNet baseline (CE 2.1777, MAE 0.6997, Total 2.8774). Most improvements came from modifications to ShuttleNet (hyper-parameters, activation functions). Improvements primarily focused on shot type prediction (2.1777 → 1.7892), while area coordinate prediction only marginally improved (0.6997 → 0.6797), with most teams being inferior to baseline—highlighting the challenge of integrating the two predictions.

The CoachAI Challenge 2023 Track 1 (Automatic Annotation of Technical Data for Badminton Match Videos) uses broadcast BWF videos (30 FPS, 1280*720, mp4 + CSV format). 13 annotation fields: VideoName, HitFrame, Hitter (A=farther from camera, B=closer), BallHeight (1=above net, 2=below net), RoundHead (1/2), Backhand (1/2), LandingX/LandingY (pixel coordinates), HitterLocationX/Y, DefenderLocationX/Y, BallType (nine types: 1-Short serve, 2-Long serve, 3-Clear, 4-Drive, 5-Smash, 6-Net shot, 7-Drop shot, 8-Lift, 9-Push shot), and Winner (A/B/X, only scored on last shot). Scoring is rally-based: HitFrame must be within 2 frames of true value (0.1 points); Hitter (0.1), BallHeight (0.1), Landing (within 6 pixels, 0.1), HitterLocation and DefenderLocation (within 10 pixels each, 0.05 each), Backhand (0.05), RoundHead (0.05), BallType (0.2), Winner (0.1, only valid on last shot). The winning "Advanced ShuttleNet" team paper is at arXiv:2307.13715.

Baseline codes and dataset available at: https://github.com/wywyWang/CoachAI-Projects/tree/main/CoachAI-Challenge-IJCAI2023. Challenge page on Codalab; presentation video at https://youtu.be/yhRouMpxb2M.

### 2.4 Tennis Datasets: Match Charting Project and Derived Data

**Sources: Kaggle [7], SCORE Network [8], Tennis Abstract [9], GitHub JeffSackmann [10]**

**Match Charting Project (MCP):** A crowdsourced effort by Tennis Abstract (Jeff Sackmann) to collect detailed shot-by-shot data for professional tennis matches, started in late 2013. As of the referenced metadata page: 18,113 matches, 2,821,372 points, and 10,673,917 shots. Nearly 2,200 matches were added in 2025. Men's section: 10,050 matches, 1,187 players, 481 active players, including 100 of the top 100 and 197 of the top 200 players. MCP match records contain shot-by-shot data for every point, including shot type, shot direction, depth of returns, and types of errors. Files separated into men's ('-m-') and women's ('-w-') matches; '-matches' files contain match metadata (players, tournament, date, surface); '-points' files contain extensive data on each point; '-stats-' files contain aggregate stat lines (e.g., KeyPointsReturn, KeyPointsServe, NetPoints, Overview, Rally, ReturnDepth, ReturnOutcomes, ServeBasics, ServeDirection, ServeInfluence, ShotDirOutcomes, ShotDirection, ShotTypes, SnV, SvBreakSplit, SvBreakTotal). User-submitted data is found only in the '1st', '2nd', and 'Notes' columns; all other columns are automatically generated by the included MatchChart Excel document (MatchChart 0.3.2.xlsm). License: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International. Repository: github.com/JeffSackmann/tennis_MatchChartingProject (412 stars, 130 forks).

**Grand Slam Tennis Shot-Level Data** (SCORE Network, by Peter Spivack, published August 4, 2025): Shot-level data from WTA and ATP Grand Slam matches (1960-2024), recording each stroke's hand, shot type, direction, depth, and outcome or error type. Derived from the Tennis Match Charting Project. Eight datasets covering ATP and WTA at the four Grand Slams. Shot counts: ATP Australian Open (645,905), ATP Roland Garros (486,235), ATP US Open (554,405), ATP Wimbledon (418,851); WTA Australian Open (291,905), WTA Roland Garros (196,721), WTA US Open (219,855), WTA Wimbledon (175,761). Each dataset has 17 columns across three categories: (1) Match-level data (Date, Tournament, Round, Player 1, Player 2, Point); (2) Point-level data (Shot, Serve, ServingPlayer, WinningPlayer); (3) Shot encoding (ShotHand, ShotType, ShotDirection, ServeDirection, ShotDepth, OutcomeType, ErrorType). ShotType options: serve, groundstroke, slice, volley, overhead, drop_shot, lob, half_volley, swinging_volley. OutcomeType includes double_fault, winner, unforced_error, forced_error, ace, unreturnable. ErrorType includes net, wide, deep, wide_deep, foot_fault, shank, time_violation. Selection bias exists toward popular players, high-leverage matches, and televised matches.

### 2.5 Hawk-Eye Tracking Data

**Sources: Wikipedia [21], ResearchGate figure [22], YouTube CULT TENNIS [23], Springer ML in Tennis [1]**

Hawk-Eye is a computer vision system developed in 2000 by engineers at Roke Manor Research Limited (then a Siemens subsidiary) in Romsey, England, by Paul Hawkins and David Sherry. It was originally implemented in 2001 for television broadcasts for cricket LBW decisions. The Sony-owned system tracks the trajectory of a ball using up to ten high-performance cameras positioned on the underside of stadium roofs, triangulating video feeds to create a three-dimensional representation of the ball's path. It is advertised to be accurate to within 2.6 mm, though the Hawk-Eye Innovations website states an average error of 3.6 mm. Used in more than 20 major sports including baseball, cricket, tennis, badminton, hurling, rugby union, soccer, Gaelic football, American football, and volleyball.

Tennis deployment: First used officially at the Nasdaq-100 Open in March 2006; US Open was the first Grand Slam to use it (2006). Ten ultra-motion high-speed cameras (5 per side) capture video at 340 frames per second; the system triangulates data from calibrated cameras to produce a 3D position of the ball. Hawk-Eye does not simply watch the bounce—it PREDICTS the trajectory before the ball lands by calculating positions at 340 intervals per second as the ball comes off the player's racket. The ITF required Hawk-Eye to be within 5 millimeters of the real recorded bounce; on average it proved accurate to within 2.6 millimeters. The 2021 Australian Open was the first Grand Slam to use Hawk-Eye Live for all matches; Wimbledon announced full electronic line calling from 2025.

Badminton: BWF introduced Hawk-Eye in 2014, first at the 2014 India Super Series.

Hawk-Eye data contains both ball trajectory and player feet movement information. The "Machine Learning in Tennis" chapter (Springer, in "Artificial Intelligence in Sports, Movement, and Health," published online 03 September 2024, pages 179–192, DOI: 10.1007/978-3-031-67256-9_11, by Fernando Vives, Javier Lázaro, José Francisco Guzmán, Miguel Crespo, Rafael Martínez-Gallego) reviews how Hawk-Eye tracking has advanced tennis research, covering match outcome prediction (Elo ratings vs ML, random forest, Glicko), serve analysis (Hawk-Eye data, serve strength, serve direction prediction), player movement classification (wearable MEMS sensor data, hierarchical clustering), shot prediction (DeepTennis, style priors, spatiotemporal tracking), and player talent identification.

### 2.6 Other Relevant Badminton/Tennis Datasets and Tools

- **BadmintonDB**: 9 professional men's singles matches (Kento Momota vs. Anthony Sinisuka Ginting), 811 rallies, 9,671 strokes, 10 stroke types (used by RallyTemPose).
- **Shuttlecock Trajectory Dataset (Ik, 2020)**: 23 professional singles matches for training, 3 for testing, 1280×720 resolution, 30 fps (used in Nokihara et al. trajectory prediction work).
- **OpenTTGames dataset**: Full HD 120 fps table tennis videos with annotations for events, ball coordinates, and segmentation masks (introduced with TTNet).
- **TrackNet**: Deep neural network for small-object (shuttlecock/ball) tracking; widely used across badminton, tennis, and table tennis pipelines.
- **TennisCourtDetector** (github.com/yastrebksv/TennisCourtDetector), **TrackNet** (github.com/yastrebksv/TrackNet), and **TennisProject** (github.com/yastrebksv/TennisProject): open-source tools for court detection (14 key points + 1 center), ball detection (19,835 labeled frames from 10 broadcast videos), bounce detection (CatBoostRegressor; 18,570 samples, 518 labeled bounce points, 10-fold CV), and player detection (pretrained Faster RCNN).

## 3. Tennis Tactical Analysis and Rally Modeling

### 3.1 Forecasting the Next Shot Location in Tennis Using Fine-Grained Spatiotemporal Tracking Data (Wei & Lucey, TKDE 2016)

**Source: Semantic Scholar [8]**

"Wei, Lucey, Morgan, Sridharan — Forecasting the Next Shot Location in Tennis Using Fine-Grained Spatiotemporal Tracking Data" (IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering, Volume 28, pages 2988-2997, November 1, 2016, DOI: 10.1109/TKDE.2016.2594787). Uses ball and player tracking data from "Hawk-Eye" to discover unique player styles and predict within-point events. Moves beyond coarse match statistics, using spatial and temporal information to better characterize the tactics and tendencies of each player. 30 citing papers.

Related foundational works by the same authors: "Predicting Shot Locations in Tennis Using Spatiotemporal Data" (2013), "'Sweet-Spot': Using Spatiotemporal Data to Discover and Predict Shots in Tennis" (2013), "Forecasting Events Using an Augmented Hidden Conditional Random Field" (2014). Notable follow-ups: "Space-Time VON CRAMM" (2020) by Kovalchik et al. (functional data framework for estimating expected shot value (ESV) in continuous time, deriving metrics including Shot IQ and value added with shot taking); "CourtTime: Generating Actionable Insights into Tennis Matches Using Visual Analytics" (2020, introduces 1-D Space-Time Charts); "Pose2Trajectory" (2023, transformers on body pose to predict a tennis player's future trajectory); "Vid2Player" (2021, converts annotated broadcast video into controllable video sprites); "A Markov process approach to untangling intention versus execution in tennis" (2022) by Chan et al., which found optimal shot selection strategies become more conservative as execution error grows.

### 3.2 Valuing Decision Making and Shot Execution in Tennis (Seidl, Reid & Robertson, Tennis Australia / Victoria University)

**Source: Paper PDF [9]**

This paper (Robert Seidl, Machar Reid, Sam Robertson — Tennis Australia and Victoria University) presents a data-driven methodology to quantify decision-making and shot execution in professional tennis using Hawkeye player and ball tracking data from the 2020 Australian Open. Motivation: tennis is a game of thin margins—a player can win the same number of points as an opponent yet still lose the match—so the scoreboard can mask important performance details.

Methodology:
- Four neural network models trained on 107,000 hits and 98,000 bounces (test set: 12,000 hits and 11,000 bounces) to disentangle decision-making from execution for each shot. Models predict either winning the point immediately (direct winner) or winning the rally later.
- Decision is valued at the moment of the shot ("when the ball leaves the racket"), while execution is valued at the moment of the ball bounce in the opponent's court.
- Model outputs: xDW, xDR, xEW, xER (expected decision and execution values for direct winners and rally wins).
- Input features include position, speed, and angle of both players and the ball, plus shot classifications (serve, return, or rally shot).
- Model performance (AUC/Accuracy): xDW 73%/81%, xDR 65%/59%, xEW 78%/84%, xER 71%/63%.
- An in-match win probability model: (1) pre-match ELO ratings adjusted for surface and head-to-head, (2) calibration into serve/return predictions, (3) Bayesian in-match updates based on observed serve performance, (4) in-match prediction using a Barnett-Clarke model. "Leverage" = how much a point could influence match outcome (thresholds of less than 5% and more than 5% scoreboard pressure).

Key applications (Dominic Thiem at Australian Open 2020): Zverev led serve execution; Djokovic's return play was superb (rally execution more than 5 points over average) with lower-than-average shot execution in rallies, indicating he builds points slowly; in the fifth set of the final against Djokovic, Thiem's forehand execution sharply declined under high pressure while his decision values stayed relatively stable—his shot selection held up but his execution succumbed to pressure. A critical-point analysis showed Thiem's expected match win probability actually increased to 22.0% (+2.73%) despite losing the point, demonstrating he played the point well—a fact invisible on the scoreboard.

### 3.3 Transformer-Based Tennis Tactical Behavior Identification (Advanced Electromagnetics 2026)

**Source: Advanced Electromagnetics [3]**

"Identification and Prediction of Tennis Players' Technical and Tactical Behaviors Based on Transformer Model" (Advanced Electromagnetics, Vol. 15 No. 3 (2026), pages 5274-5286, published August 13, 2026, DOI: 10.7716/aem.v15i3.3582) by J. Pu (Jiangxi Normal University) and X. Y. Zha (Qingdao Agricultural University).

- Addresses automatic identification of complex tennis techniques and tactics, dynamic prediction of shot intentions, and early assessment of round outcomes from structured event sequences.
- Uses structured shot sequences from Match Charting Project logs, integrating attributes like shot type, direction, and match status.
- A six-layer Transformer encoder with multi-head self-attention for multi-task learning, jointly optimizing technical/tactical classification, shot intention prediction, and early outcome assessment.
- Results: Macro-F1 of 0.935 for tactical classification and a round outcome AUC@5 of 0.923.
- Significantly outperforms BiLSTM and CNN-LSTM baselines. Ablation studies confirmed critical contributions of its embedding and multi-task design.
- The framework enables end-to-end deep analysis without visual input, providing a scalable, data-driven solution for intelligent competitive analysis.

### 3.4 Capturing Intransitive Dominance in Tennis Forecasting: A Graph Neural Network Approach (arXiv 2025)

**Sources: arXiv HTML [1], Bristol research portal [2]**

By LW Clegg (2025, cited by 2). Presents the first application of a graph neural network for tennis match outcome prediction (pre-match), targeting intransitive player dominance. Builds temporal directed graphs (players as nodes, historical match outcomes as directed weighted edges) and applies MagNet, a spectral graph convolutional network using the magnetic Laplacian (a complex Hermitian matrix) to learn from directed cycles and intransitive relationships.

Data: ATP and WTA match data from tennis-data.co.uk spanning January 8, 2012 to October 16, 2025, filtered to highest-tier events (Grand Slams, tour finals, 1000 and 500 series). Final dataset: 20,181 men's matches (670 players) and 19,985 women's matches (640 players). Validation set of 8,435 matches, held-out test set of 12,052 matches (early 2022 to October 2025). Surface-specific graphs (clay, grass, hard) built per gender. Player static attributes (height, weight, DOB, handedness) were evaluated but excluded as they did not improve accuracy.

Methodology: Edge weights based on proportion of games won, adjusted by time decay (λ=0.34), surface transferability (α), and tournament prestige (uniform weights β=1). MagNet optimised q=0.238 (near maximum directional weighting); 2 layers, K=1 Chebyshev filter, 16 hidden units. Walk-forward validation: trained on 15% of most recent matches, retrained every 38 snapshots (~quarter year), training under 10 seconds per run on consumer hardware.

Results (out-of-sample test set): Overall 65.7% accuracy, 0.214 Brier score. Model ties Weighted Elo on Brier score but trails slightly on accuracy (65.7% vs 65.8%). Outperforms standard Elo (65.3%, 0.217) and Bradley-Terry (64.6%, 0.219). Pinnacle Sports bookmaker benchmark remains superior (68.7% accuracy, 0.198 Brier). Model shows strong calibration (reliability term below 0.0001 vs 0.0012 for Weighted Elo).

Ablation findings: Graph structure carries most of the predictive signal (removing dominance graph raises Brier from 0.2142 to 0.2492). Most consequential components: edge-age decay (+0.0118), multi-hop receptive field (+0.0095), in/out-degree node features (+0.0058). Intransitivity analysis: Women's tennis contains 12.3% more cyclic triads than men's. A well-known example: Nadal beats Federer (24/40), Federer beats Davydenko (19/21), but Davydenko beats Nadal (6/11). A forecast-encompassing test shows Weighted Elo does not fully subsume the GNN model; a combined forecast significantly outperforms Weighted Elo, with gains growing more strongly on intransitive matchups.

### 3.5 Predicting Tennis Serve Directions with Machine Learning (arXiv 2026)

**Source: arXiv HTML [8]**

Presents a machine learning method for predicting professional tennis players' first serve directions using Match Charting Project data (no video or Hawkeye data), using six serve directions (wide, body, and down-the-T for both deuce and ad sides).

Key findings: average prediction accuracy of ~49% for male players and ~44% for female players. Dataset includes 3,424 matches of 655 male players and 1,916 matches of 422 female players (players with at least 30 matches). Results presented for ten male players (Djokovic, Federer, Nadal, Murray, Medvedev, Kyrgios, Thiem, Tsitsipas, Wawrinka, Zverev) and ten female players (Serena Williams, Osaka, Barty, Swiatek, Azarenka, Kerber, Pliskova).

Models tested: Multinomial Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest (200 trees, max depth 150), Support Vector Machine, and Neural Network (two hidden layers: 200, 100). Trained individually per player with 70/30 train/test splits.

Feature engineering categories: (1) Outcome of previous points (cumulative serve direction counts, serve counts won per direction, serve percentages per direction, previous point winner); (2) Fatigue (cumulative run indexes for both players calculated from shot-by-shot data including court position inference); (3) Performance anxiety (based on the OCC model of emotion, calculated at game, set, and match levels using uncertainty × (hope + fear) formulas).

Key conclusions: (1) Most important features: cumulative counts of first serves to each direction, the run index (fatigue) of the server in the previous point, and first serve percentage per direction. (2) Results provide indirect evidence that top professional players use a mixed-strategy model in serve decisions. (3) The importance of server fatigue (run index) in choosing serve direction is a new discovery. (4) Contextual information may be more important for returners' anticipatory reactions than previously thought—important because returners have less than 0.5 seconds to react to first serves (180-200 km/h for men, 150-170 km/h for women). Comparison: Wei et al. achieved 27.8% prediction accuracy using Hawkeye data with 14 serve directions.

### 3.6 Analysis of Points Outcome in ATP Grand Slam Tennis (arXiv 2025)

**Source: arXiv HTML [3]**

Predicts the outcome of individual points in ATP Grand Slam tennis matches using historical public data (2016-2020) from Wimbledon and US Open: 709 men's matches (best-of-five format). Methods: logistic regression, Random Forest, AdaBoost, XGBoost, compared against a baseline (average serve win rate). Two point-winner models (first serve, second serve) using 57 features including accumulated match features, player rankings, serve/return placements, and match-specific details. Data from Jeff Sackmann's public dataset.

Key findings:
- First serve: server wins 73.2% of points on successful first serve; models performed almost identically to baseline (73.2% accuracy) but very poorly on recall/precision for predicting returner wins (recall near 0%). Tuned XGBoost achieved 73.4% accuracy.
- Second serve: server wins only 57.2% of points; models scored roughly 4-5% lower in accuracy than baseline (~53%). Models performed better at predicting returner wins (recall ~45%).
- Roc-Auc scores just above 0.5 (53.5-57.6%).
- Serve placement analysis: 68% of successful first serves placed close to the sidelines vs. ~29-30% for second serves (risk-averse second serves).
- Most influential features were score-related (sets won, break points won/missed) and player rankings; serve/return position features had no significant influence.
- Conclusion: could not identify strategic factors with public data; higher-quality datasets (e.g., Hawk Eye spatiotemporal) exist but are not publicly available. Suggests a future "tennis Moneyball" dataset combining point outcomes, timestamps, stroke types, and 3D positional data.

### 3.7 Additional Tennis Prediction Work

- **"Predicting tennis match outcomes mid-game using machine learning on psychological and physical data"** (Journal of Big Data, Volume 12, article 159, published 08 July 2025): AI4Sci method using real-time point-by-point data from Wimbledon and US Open (2017-2023), 1,592 training games, 363 evaluation games (2023). Psychological momentum (PM) quantified by weighting statistical data through Shannon entropy (positive features: Ace, NetPointWon, Winner, BreakPointWon, RallyNorWin, RallyDifWin; negative features: DoubleFault, NetPointLoss, BreakPointMissed, UnfErr). Soft-voting ensemble (Random Forest 200 trees + CatBoost 240 iterations) achieved accuracy 97.5%, F1 97.4%; models achieved predictive accuracies above 70% using only the first 25% of a game's data. Related works referenced: Elo (~70% accuracy), Glicko (~73%), MLP (79.5%), random forest (83.10%).

- **"Statistical enhanced learning for modeling and prediction tennis matches at Grand Slam tournaments"** (arXiv:2502.01613v2): 5,013 men's Grand Slam matches (2011-2022) via R package deuce. Enhanced covariates: Elo rating, Age.30 (absolute distance from age 30), Age.int (distance to optimal age interval [28, 32]). Best random forest (Points, Rank, Age.30, Elo): classification rate 0.820, predictive likelihood 0.667, Brier score 0.151. Linear model best (Points, Rank, Elo): classification rate 0.795. Splines best (Elo + Age.30): Brier score 0.149 (best overall). PDP/ICE plots used for interpretability.

- **"Learning Three Dimensional Tennis Shots Using Graph Convolutional Networks"** (Sensors, October 27, 2020, Lublin University of Technology): Spatial-Temporal Graph Neural Networks (ST-GCN) for recognizing forehand and backhand from 3D Vicon motion capture (39 retroreflective markers on body per Plug-in Gait Model, 7 on racket; 10 male tennis coaches, mean age 23.85 ± 5.82). 3-layer ST-GCN (32 kernels first layer, 64 next two), input (C=2, V=19 nodes, T=14 time steps). 1080 images (348 forehand, 354 backhand, 378 no-shot). Fuzzy ST-GCN at 65% training data: 91.2% (forehand), 92.8% (backhand), 95.9% (no shot) vs. 81.2%, 77.1%, 69.6% for standard ST-GCN. This motion-capture database uniquely provides sequential player/racket positions enabling time-series analysis (unlike THETIS dataset's single images per stroke).

## 4. Table Tennis Tactical Analysis

### 4.1 Transformer-Based Table Tennis Stroke Forecasting (MJSSM 2026)

**Source: MJSSM [6]**

"A New Table Tennis Match Stroke Forecasting Method Using Transformer-Based Deep Neural Networks" by Hsu Ming-Hwa (National Chung Hsing University), Kondrič Miran (University of Ljubljana), Fan-Chiang I-Yun and Wu Jiunn-Lin (National Chung Hsing University). DOI: 10.26773/mjssm.260306.

Methodology: dual encoder-decoder structures to extract contextual features from rally sequences and individual players separately; attention mechanisms to evaluate relative importance of stroke techniques and landing positions; game-specific attributes including ball speed and spin; a stroke-level event stream representation; a feature fusion network integrating rally dynamics and player-specific traits to forecast the type and landing zone of the next stroke.

Data: "Intellectual Tactical System in Competitive Table Tennis" database, containing Lin Yun-Ju's matches against male opponents (23 matches, 121 games, 2,225 rallies, 10,517 hits, averaging 4.7 hits per rally).

Results: top-1 accuracies of 57.2% for stroke type and 42.8% for landing zone (spot), with top-5 accuracies of 98.2% and 91.8% respectively. The model provides visualization of prediction outcomes alongside known stroke data for tactical analysis.

### 4.2 Table Tennis Tactical Benefit Analysis (JSSM 2022) and Grey Correlation (BMC 2025)

**Source: JSSM [8], PMC BMC [10]**

**"A Visible Analysis Approach for Table Tennis Tactical Benefit"** (Journal of Sports Science and Medicine, 2022, Vol. 21, pp. 517-527, DOI: 10.52082/jssm.2022.517) by Zheng Zhou and Hui Zhang (Zhejiang University). Analyzed 60 matches from top-25 men's right-handed shake-hand offensive players (2016-2019 rankings), 29 players. Tactical observation indices: stroke technique (serve, topspin/attack, smash, flick, twist, push, touch short, block, lob), stroke placement (9 zones: short/half-long/long forehand, middle, backhand), rally results. Tactical combinations comprised three consecutive strokes; analyzed first six strokes (first-to-third and third-to-fifth in service round; second-to-fourth and fourth-to-sixth in receiving round). Tactical benefit formula: BEi = c × (SRi - 0.5) × FRi (c=100), combining frequency (FR) and scoring rate (SR), benefit values ranging [-5, 5].

Key results: 37 tactics identified in the first six strokes. In the service round, the third stroke had the highest scoring rate (0.219), followed by fifth and first strokes (0.114). In the receiving round, the second stroke was highest (0.203), then fourth (0.151). Tactic T1 (serve to short forehand → opponent touch short to short middle → player push, scoring) was the only first-class benefit tactic in first-to-third strokes (benefit 0.090). Applicable beyond table tennis to other cross-net sports like badminton, tennis, and volleyball.

**"Construction and application of the technical and tactical efficiency evaluation model for table tennis matches based on grey correlation"** (BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation, April 28, 2025; DOI: 10.1186/s13102-025-01114-5) by Huagen Yin et al. Introduces grey correlation theory (GRA, Deng Julong 1982, discrimination coefficient ρ = 0.5) to evaluate technical/tactical effectiveness using a "New Four-phase Index Statistical Method": attack-after-serve phase (serve and 3rd stroke), attack-after-receive phase (receive and 4th stroke), transition phase (5th and 6th strokes), and rally phase (Rally I and Rally II). Analyzed 18 international matches (101 games, 1,893 rounds) between elite player "T" and Chinese main/reserve players. Kappa = 0.900 (P < 0.001). Overall correlation rankings: receive (0.818) > 3rd stroke (0.799) > 4th stroke (0.794) > 5th stroke (0.772) > 6th stroke (0.747) > serve (0.744) > Rally I (0.703) > Rally II (0.578). T's tactical effectiveness follows an inverted "V" trend, with scoring concentrated in early phases.

### 4.3 Table Tennis Ball Tracking with GNN (Scientific Reports 2024) and TTNet

**Source: PMC [2], YouTube TTNet [9]**

**"Fast moving table tennis ball tracking algorithm based on graph neural network"** (Scientific Reports, 2024 Nov 26;14:29320, DOI: 10.1038/s41598-024-80056-3): Proposes a Graph Max-message Pass Neural Network (GMP) combining a refined common video differential detector (frame differencing on adjacent frames) with a discriminator (GMP) that processes graphs constructed from potential targets (nodes) and relationships (edges), outputting probability graphs with confidence scores for nodes and edges. A sliding window and gap mechanism sequentially selects potential target sets. Decomposes tracking into discriminator (log p(T_u)) and detector (log p(T_u|φ_initial, φ)) components via Bayesian maximum posterior criterion. Outperforms YOLOv8, SOT, and generic GAT discriminator. Applications: segmenting rounds/actions, estimating ball speed (from pixel distance, table center line length of 2.74m, frame rate), determining land/hit points, quantifying players' stability, offensive and defensive capabilities for tactical planning.

**TTNet** (Voeikov, Falaleev, Baikulov, 2020): Real-time temporal and spatial video analysis of table tennis. Two-stage ball detection (lightweight VGG-style backbone on downscaled input → local detector cropping original-resolution frame), semantic segmentation decoder branch for players/table/scoreboard, event spotting branch (ball bounces, net hits). Input: 9 consecutive frames from 120 fps video; event probabilities predicted for the middle frame. Results: 97.0% accuracy in game event spotting; 2 pixels RMSE in ball detection with 97.5% accuracy; inference below 6 ms per input tensor on consumer GPU. Introduced the OpenTTGames dataset (full HD 120 fps table tennis videos). The article "Using deep learning technology & video visual technology in the analysis of table tennis competition" (Jiunn-Lin Wu, SIPLab) describes using TrackNet and OpenPose to record ball types, speed, and exact landing spots for tactical analysis.

## 5. Squash Tactical Analysis

**Sources: IJCST [1], Parker Dixon [2], PMC Brumann [3], MDPI Ma & Kabala [4], ChesterRep [13]**

### 5.1 Squash Technology Landscape and Automated Training Court (IJCST 2025)

"A Critical Analysis of Existing Technologies in Squash Training: Towards an Automated Training Court" by Evana Gada (IJCST, Volume 13 Issue 6, Nov-Dec 2025, ISSN: 2347-8578). Key technology domains: image/video processing (broadcast video 25-60 fps, homography/inverse-perspective mapping, YOLO/Faster R-CNN + SORT/DeepSORT player tracking, OpenPose/HRNet pose estimation, small-object ball detection with physics-informed interpolation and 96 kHz audio fusion, Vučković et al.'s 15-zone event segmentation taxonomy); AI/ML applications (layered architecture: feature extraction → shot classification → sequence modeling; CNNs/3D CNNs/two-stream networks classify shot types (drive, drop, boast, volley); LSTMs model tactical transitions; supervised classifiers predict rally outcomes; unsupervised methods (k-means, HMMs) profile player styles); sensor technologies (racket-mounted IMUs e.g., Racketware ~500 Hz; wearables; smart courts e.g., interactiveSQUASH).

Identified gaps: ball tracking limitations (small size, rapid acceleration, occlusion; algorithms often interpolate rather than measure); real-time processing largely unavailable; fragmentation of ball/player/tactical analyses; limited squash-specific datasets (mostly proprietary or small). Baclig et al. (2020) reported mean absolute percent errors of ~3-4% for distance and speed estimates. The proposed Automated Squash Training Court (ASTC) integrates ceiling-mounted panoramic cameras, high-speed corner cameras, embedded floor sensors, impact-sensitive wall panels, racket-mounted IMUs, and a central computational engine with CNNs and LSTMs.

### 5.2 Player Detection and Motion Analysis in Squash (Sensors 2021)

"Evaluation of Open-Source and Pre-Trained Deep Convolutional Neural Networks Suitable for Player Detection and Motion Analysis in Squash" (Brumann, Kukuk, Reinsberger; Sensors 2021, doi: 10.3390/s21134550, cited by 27). Evaluated over 250 human pose estimation CNNs for out-of-the-box inference on squash footage. Only three HPE-CNNs (five variants) remained after selection: ArtTrack (ResNet-101, MPII, 4.55 FPS), OpenPose (VGG-19, three variants trained on COCO+Foot, COCO, MPII, 8.8 FPS), and PoseNet (MobileNetV1, COCO, 10.0 FPS). The authors created a custom annotation tool and manually labeled feet positions in four publicly available squash match videos; after temporal resampling, 4,332 frames were annotated yielding 16,246 labeled feet positions (2,347 rally and 1,985 non-rally frames). Evaluation used object-detection-style metrics based on pixel-distance thresholds. Overlay heatmaps (camera perspective) and top-down heatmaps (bird's-eye view via camera calibration) visualize player spatial distribution. Labeled dataset publicly available on GitHub.

### 5.3 Squash Referee Decision ML System (MDPI MAKE 2024)

"Refereeing the Sport of Squash with a Machine Learning System" by Enqi Ma and Zbigniew J. Kabala (Machine Learning and Knowledge Extraction, Vol. 6, Issue 1, 2024, pages 506-553, DOI: 10.3390/make6010025, cited by 19). Three decisions: Stroke, Yes Let, No Let. Collected 400 referee decisions from over 20 hours of PSA YouTube footage. Six primitive data components per decision: attacking player's position, retreating player's position, ball's position in frame, ball's projected first bounce, ball's projected second bounce, attacking player's racket head position. Nine calculated distances: AP to RP, AP to ball, RP to ball, AP to second bounce, racket head to RP, ball to second bounce, racket head to ball, shortest distance from racket head to ball's path, front wall blockage. Dataset: 59 No Lets, 243 Yes Lets, 98 Strokes (imbalanced). Best Wolfram Mathematica model: 86% ± 3.03% accuracy; best Python model (3-layer NN 64x128x3, ReLU and SoftMax, Adam, sparse categorical cross-entropy, 15 epochs): 85.2% ± 5.1% accuracy.

### 5.4 Perturbations in Elite Squash (Int J Performance Analysis in Sport 2014)

"The importance of perturbations in elite squash" by Ryan Roddy, Kevin L. Lamb, Paul Worsfold (University of Chester; 2014, Vol 14, Issue 3, pp. 652-679). Analyzed 31 matches from the men's 2011 Australian Open Squash Championships using a Dartfish tagging template. Court divided into a 4x4 positional matrix with an additional tramline system (7.5 inches wide). Critical incidents (perturbation, unforced error, un-returnable shot, let/stroke, miss-hit) identified relative to shot selection, player/ball landing position, and shot accuracy, with binary logistic regression. Results: perturbations identified 238 times (10%), less frequent than un-returnable shots (36%), unforced errors (31%), let/strokes (23%). The logistic regression model was effective at predicting un-returnable shots (98.7% for shot selection, 94.7% for court position, 91.4% for ball landing position, 100% for shot accuracy) but NOT perturbations (1.9%, 25.6%, 24.3%, 0%). Shots with significant contribution to rally outcome: volley (p<.01), boast/volley boast (p<.01), drop/volley drop (p<.01 and p<.05). Conclusion: perturbation analysis is not a valid predictor of squash performance.

### 5.5 Player Tracking in Squash (Metis Bootcamp Project)

Parker Dixon's squash player tracking project used DeepPose (CNN predicting 17 body joints) with a pre-trained keras_Realtime_Multi-Person_Pose_Estimation model. Key implementation: reduced from 30 to 3 fps, model iterations 5 to 2, downscaled frames (processing under 5 minutes per 1.5-min clip); k-means clustering to differentiate players' joints; player IDs via cosine similarity of average torso pixel colors (requires different colored shirts); homography transform to map 3D points onto a 2D court representation; "Control Score" = ratio of points earned (1 point/frame in large ellipse, 5 in small ellipse, -5 outside both) to maximum.
