## 6. Hidden Markov Models and Probabilistic Graphical Models for Tactic State Inference

**Sources: IJSA [7], Columbia thesis [8], Wikipedia HMM [9], Gimenez book chapter [10], PMC IEEE TAI [11], Springer KNN-HMM [12]**

### 6.1 HMM Fundamentals (Wikipedia)

An HMM is a Markov model in which observations are dependent on a latent (or hidden) Markov process (X). The goal is to learn about the state of X by observing Y. Y at time t0 is influenced exclusively by X at time t0; past outcomes are conditionally independent of Y given X at that time. Parameters estimated via maximum likelihood, with the Baum-Welch algorithm for linear chain HMMs. Hidden states are discrete (categorical distribution); observations can be discrete or continuous (Gaussian). Parameters include N² transition probabilities (N(N-1) free) and emission probabilities (N(M-1) for discrete observations, or NM(M+3)/2 = O(NM²) for multivariate Gaussian observations).

Three inference problems: (1) Probability of an observed sequence (forward algorithm, dynamic programming); (2) Probability of latent variables, including filtering (P(x(t)|y(1..t)), forward algorithm) and smoothing (P(x(k)|y(1..t)) for k<t, forward-backward algorithm); (3) Most likely explanation / most likely hidden state sequence (Viterbi algorithm).

### 6.2 HMM for Momentum/Competitive State Transitions (IJSA 2026)

"Predictive Momentum Modeling through Hidden Markov Competitive State Transitions" by Prof. Larz Schultz (International Journal of Sports Analytics, Volume 7, Issue 1, January-June 2026, Article IJSA_07_01_001, pages 1-6, dated January 19, 2026). Proposes a multi-state Hidden Markov framework where latent states represent momentum regimes (positive, neutral, negative), with transition probabilities estimated via maximum likelihood and Bayesian inference, integrating copula-based multivariate dependence structures and regime-switching mechanisms. Findings: modeling momentum as a latent regime process improves predictive calibration and transition stability over standard Markov chain and ML baselines; hidden competitive state transitions capture structural shifts, tactical adjustments, and psychological momentum effects better than observable-only models.

### 6.3 HMM for Football Season Modeling (Columbia/Boston College Thesis)

James DeAntonis' thesis ("Football Analytics," Boston College, 2017/2018) models NFL game/season outcomes with HMMs where states represent the current winning or losing streak, capturing "momentum" (e.g., probability of winning the next game given the team won its previous two games). Observable "emissions" are game stat lines (points own/against, rushing yards own/against, turnover differential, first down differential) constructed via n-dimensional "mega-bins." Viterbi algorithm derives the most likely hidden state sequence. Overall predictive success rates hovered between .69 and .78 across all bin possibilities tested on 2016. "Chain override rate" (how often Viterbi went against simply picking by the pdfs) was greater than .5, suggesting the underlying Markov chain added predictive power.

### 6.4 Bayesian HMM Foundations (Gimenez Book Chapter)

From "Bayesian analysis of capture-recapture data with hidden Markov models" (Chapter 3): transition matrix Γ with survival probability φ; observation matrix Ω links states to observations. Complete likelihood: Pr(y_i, z_i) = (∏ ω(z(i,t),y(i,t))) × (Pr(z(i,1)) × ∏ γ(z(i,t-1),z(i,t))). Marginalization: brute-force requires 2TN^T calculations (exponential growth); forward algorithm requires only TN² computations. Forward algorithm: α_t(j) = Pr(y1,...,yt, zt=j); initialization α1(j) = Pr(z1=j)ω(j,y1); recurrence α_t(j) = Σ α(t-1)(i)γ(i,j)ω(j,y_t); marginal likelihood Pr(y) = Σ α_T(j). "A hidden Markov model is just two time series running in parallel. One for the states with the Markovian property, and the other of for the observations generated from the states. HMM are a special case of state-space models in which latent states are discrete."

### 6.5 Deep RL for Bayesian HMM Inference (IEEE TAI 2024)

"Deep Reinforcement Learning Data Collection for Bayesian Inference of Hidden Markov Models" (IEEE Transactions on Artificial Intelligence, Dec 12, 2024; Vol 6, Issue 5, article 1217; DOI: 10.1109/tai.2024.3515939) by Mohammad Alali and Mahdi Imani (Northeastern University). Uses a belief state capturing the joint distribution of system states and models; deep reinforcement learning policy (Deep Q-Network/DQN) approximates the optimal Bayesian solution by simulating system trajectories offline. Supports point-based inference (ML, MAP), distribution-based inference (Bayesian), and causal inference objectives. Non-identifiability in HMMs arises when different parameter sets produce the same observed data. Exact computation of the optimal Bayesian policy is intractable because the belief space is a continuous (n×r)-simplex.

### 6.6 KNN-HMM for Badminton Stroke Prediction

See Section 1.12 (Journal of Big Data 2026) — the KNN-HMM model uses 3-5 hidden states with Gaussian emissions, Baum-Welch training, Viterbi decoding over motion-capture stroke sequences, demonstrating HMM-based temporal sequence prediction for stroke classification.

## 8. Deception in Racket Sports and Anticipation of Intent

**Sources: BadmintonPeak [11], Airchy [15], APA paper [16], Frontiers review [20], ScienceDirect [17], ITF Coaching review [18]**

### 8.1 Badminton Deception Techniques and Timing

BadmintonPeak's guide: Badminton deception is a two-part motion: (1) preparation identical to the expected shot (e.g., a smash), and (2) a last-moment change that sends a different shot. A shuttlecock takes 0.6 seconds to cross the court on a drive and 0.3 seconds on a full-power smash. Deception also slows down the opponent's reading of subsequent points, increasing their reaction time by 0.1-0.2 seconds on normal shots. Three main deceptive shot families: (1) Deceptive drop shot (smash preparation, finished with a short drop) — Viktor Axelsen's favorite; (2) Deceptive smash (drop preparation, finished with smash) and variation (drop prep followed by flat clear/tight drive) — Anthony Sinisuka Ginting specializes, playing 100% on wrist angle and forearm speed with identical jumping motion; (3) Net deception (slice and reverse slice) — Kunlavut Vitidsarn is a master, able to place deceptive shots in a 30-centimeter zone. Legal in competition except on serves (BWF rule 9.1.6 prohibits feinting before serve contact). Pros execute 5-10 deceptive shots per set in men's singles; amateurs should aim for 2-3 per set. Common failures: too-soft preparation, too-early change, poor timing (using it when opponent is static).

### 8.2 Expert Anticipation of Deceptive Intent (Perception Research)

**"Expert Players Accurately Detect an Opponent's Movement Intent Through Sound Alone"** (Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, 2017, Vol. 43, No. 2, pp. 348-359) by Ivan Camponogara, Matthew Rodger, Cathy Craig, Paola Cesari. Two experiments with expert basketball players and nonplayers listening to binaural audio of a professional attacker running with deceptive/nondeceptive left/right movements. In the Full-Body Task, basketball players made errors only 21.35% of the time vs 36.91% for nonplayers; basketball players were fooled by deceptive movements only 37% of the time (vs 67% for nonplayers). Deceptive sounds showed constant Interaural Time Difference (ITD) but changing Interaural Intensity Difference (ILD) with no significant ITD-ILD correlation, whereas nondeceptive sounds showed strong correlations (r = .51 and .95). Experts adopted distinct strategies—moving early for nondeceptive movements (~200ms after the central point) and waiting longer for deceptive movements to gather more auditory information.

**"How to Trick Your Opponent: A Review Article on Deceptive Actions"** (Frontiers in Psychology, 2017, 10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00917): goalkeepers might favor judging an action as deceptive because of the expected costs of a missed deception (response bias).

**"Deception in Tennis: An Ecological Dynamics Perspective"** (ITF Coaching Review): In defending against active deception, the player can be certain that the opponent's kinematics must shift from deceptive to genuine intention at contact.

**"Earlier detection facilitates skilled responses to deceptive actions"** (Human Movement Science, S0167945721001330): as the opponent's true intention is revealed and deception is detected, one would expect an increase in response.

## 9. Evaluation Approaches for Tactic Classification and Rally Outcome Prediction

**Synthesis from gathered sources:**

- **Shot type prediction (classification):** Cross-entropy (CE) is the standard metric used by ShuttleNet, DyMF, and the CoachAI Challenge (e.g., ShuttleNet CE 2.4125 on ShuttleSet τ=8; best challenge CE 1.7892). Top-1/top-2/top-3 accuracy used by RallyTemPose (ShuttleSet: 54.3% top-1, 77.3% top-2, 92.5% top-3; BadmintonDB: 62.8%/83.5%/93.1%). Macro-F1 and Acc-2 (binary accuracy) used in TemPose-TF-ASF stroke recognition (0.854 Acc, 0.761 Macro-F1, 0.945 Acc-2).
- **Area/coordinate prediction (regression):** Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Mean Absolute Error (MAE) on court coordinates (e.g., ShuttleNet MSE 1.8121, MAE 1.3582 at τ=8; challenge best MAE 0.6797). Bivariate Gaussian distribution assumption for area coordinates (ShuttleNet, DyMF).
- **Rally outcome / win probability:** AUC, Brier score, accuracy. BLSR model achieved AUC 0.8966, Brier 0.1329; ShuttleScorer on ShuttleSet achieved AUC 0.8371, ACC 0.7869, BR 0.1574.
- **Trajectory prediction:** Average Displacement Error (ADE) and Final Displacement Error (FDE) in pixels (Nokihara et al.).
- **Player movement forecasting:** CE for shot type + MSE/MAE for both players' locations (DyMF; up to 35.3% MSE improvement over baselines).
- **Tactic classification:** Macro-F1 (tennis Transformer model: 0.935); early outcome assessment AUC@5 (0.923).
- **Pre-match outcome:** Accuracy, Brier score, predictive Bernoulli likelihood (tennis GNN: 65.7% accuracy, 0.214 Brier; random forest Grand Slam: 0.820 classification rate).
- **Technical action frequencies:** AUC (0.9726 male, 0.8730 female), sensitivity/specificity/PPV/NPV; SHAP values for feature importance; ICC = 0.94, Cohen's Kappa = 0.96 for annotation reliability.
- **Shot influence valuation:** xDW/xDR/xEW/xER with AUC/accuracy (73%/81%, 65%/59%, 78%/84%, 71%/63%).
- **Datasets' limitations:** no fixed train/validation/test partition in ShuttleSet (papers construct own splits); broadcast-video origin limits biomechanical precision; class imbalance (rare categories: defensive return lob, driven flight, rush).

## 10. Key Challenges Specific to Singles Badminton Tactical Analysis

**Synthesis from gathered sources:**

1. **Ambiguity of intent from visual evidence alone:** Badminton's probabilistic stroke forecasting is complicated by inherent unpredictability of player decisions, influenced by physical state, psychological condition, and tactical approach (RallyTemPose/CVPRW paper). The same preparation motion can yield different shots (deception), so intent is not directly observable from kinematics alone.
2. **Deception shots:** Two-part motion (identical preparation + last-moment change) means early visual cues are deliberately misleading. Experts respond by waiting longer for deceptive movements (Camponogara et al. 2017); a 0.6s drive vs 0.3s smash crossing time makes anticipation critical. Deception detection requires modeling the temporal evolution of kinematics up to and including contact.
3. **Need for multi-modal fusion:** RallyTemPose demonstrated that player ground position is the most critical input (removing it drops performance 2.6%); removing keypoint data drops accuracy to 48.3%. Nokihara et al. showed player position AND posture alongside shuttlecock position improves trajectory prediction (13% ADE improvement over shuttle-only; 8.4% over shuttle+position). TemPose-TF-ASF uses skeletal joints/bones, player court positions, and shuttlecock trajectories (TrackNetV3). ShuttleSet stores no continuous shuttle trajectories, limiting trajectory-based approaches on that dataset.
4. **Limited annotated tactical labels:** ShuttleSet required six trained badminton-expert annotators; high labeling costs motivated the computer-aided S² tool. The CoachAI Challenge Track 1 was specifically organized to automate annotation. RallyTemPose authors call for synthetic data "for a field with sparse quality annotated datasets." Class imbalance and fine-grained 18-type taxonomies introduce greater uncertainty than simplified 10-type sets.
5. **Broadcast-video constraints:** 25-60 fps footage limits detection of high-speed shuttle; ball/shuttle tracking algorithms often interpolate rather than measure; occlusion issues; monocular camera setups require homography calibration. High-speed trajectory changes (hit-back moments, floor touches) are hard to predict.
6. **Scoreboard masking:** Tennis research (Seidl et al.) notes a player can win the same number of points but lose the match — the scoreboard masks decision vs. execution quality, motivating shot-level valuation models.
7. **Data availability asymmetry:** Hawk-Eye spatiotemporal data (tennis) and similar instrumented data are proprietary and not publicly available; public datasets are either crowdsourced categorical (Match Charting Project) or broadcast-derived with limited spatial precision (ShuttleSet).

## 11. Recommended Approaches and Promising Research Directions

**Synthesis from gathered sources:**

1. **Transformer-based sequential models with separated player/rally contexts:** ShuttleNet's design principle — separately learning rally and player contexts then fusing through a position-aware gated fusion network — outperforms early or sequential integration. This was empirically validated and further supported by 11/16 challenge teams building on ShuttleNet modifications.
2. **Graph-based interaction modeling:** DyMF's Player Movements graph with 12 strategic relation types (10 shot types + defend + return) demonstrates that explicitly modeling player-player interactions (Relational GCN + Dynamic GCN with LSTM-generated weights, hierarchical fusion via parallel co-attention) captures movement purposes and dynamic tactics better than naive sequence models. Tennis GNN work (MagNet) shows graph structure carries most predictive signal (removing it raises Brier from 0.2142 to 0.2492).
3. **Multi-modal fusion with pose + trajectory + context:** RallyTemPose shows skeleton poses, court positions, and player embeddings improve forecasting; BERT text embeddings of stroke descriptions boost stroke embeddings. Nokihara et al. show posture + position + trajectory fusion improves ADE. TemPose-TF-ASF shows bidirectional adjacent-stroke context (via Two-Stage Contextual Refinement to avoid ground-truth future annotations) consistently improves recognition across multiple SOTA backbones (BlockGCN, SkateFormer, BST-CG-AP).
4. **Shot influence / stroke value models:** BLSR's attention-based GRU over two-player CNN-extracted patterns provides interpretable shot influence; ShuttleScorer's win-probability estimation on ShuttleSet; Seidl et al.'s decision vs. execution decomposition (xDW/xDR/xEW/xER) separates "what the player decided" from "how well the shot was executed" — directly relevant to intent inference.
5. **RL environments for tactic evaluation:** The CoachAI Badminton Environment integrates ShuttleNet + DyMF + Behavior Cloning as realistic opponents within an MDP/OpenAI Gym framework, enabling strategy evaluation (e.g., PPO shifting movement distribution to achieve 60% win-rate increase).
6. **Joint optimization of shot type and area prediction:** The CoachAI Challenge finding that area-coordinate prediction only marginally improved (0.6997 → 0.6797 MAE) while shot type improved substantially (2.1777 → 1.7892 CE) indicates a need for models that jointly optimize and correlate these two tasks.
7. **Addressing class imbalance and fine-grained taxonomies:** ShuttleSet's 18 fine-grained stroke types pose a significant challenge; merging rare categories (e.g., push/lob) and data augmentation help. Future work should expand data volume and introduce CNNs/dynamic match factors (per PLOS ONE paper's future plans).
8. **Explainability and interpretability:** Attention mechanisms (BLSR) provide transparency on which shots matter; SHAP values validate feature importance (Scientific Reports 2025); latent variable analysis via t-SNE and cosine similarity of player embeddings enables playstyle comparison (RallyTemPose); PDP/ICE plots for interpretable ML (tennis Grand Slam paper).
9. **Expanding to doubles and other conditions:** DyMF future work targets doubles with greater inter-player interaction focus; ShuttleNet future work targets win/loss outcomes; transfer learning from singles to doubles shows ~19.3% degradation (pose-based) vs ~39.9% (vision-only YOLOv11x).
10. **Deception-specific modeling:** Because deception relies on identical preparation with late divergence, models should (a) explicitly represent the temporal kinematics up to contact, (b) model the opponent's belief/anticipation state, and (c) incorporate game-situation context (score, fatigue, prior shot patterns). The finding that average prediction accuracy varies by over 20% between best and worst predicted players (RallyTemPose) "potentially indicating how well players mask their strokes" directly suggests stroke-masking/deception as a measurable quantity.

--- SOURCE 1: Benchmarking Badminton Action Recognition with a New ... ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2403.12385v2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Benchmarking Badminton Action Recognition with a New Fine-Grained Dataset

This paper introduces **VideoBadminton**, a novel fine-grained video dataset for badminton action recognition, and presents a comprehensive benchmark evaluation of state-of-the-art action recognition methods on this dataset.

### Dataset Overview
- **VideoBadminton** contains **7,822 video clips** spanning **145 minutes** of self-recorded footage featuring **18 badminton action classes** aligned with Badminton World Federation (BWF) standards (e.g., Short Serve, Cross-Court Flight, Lift, Tap Smash, Block, Drop Shot, Push Shot, Transitional Slice, Cut, Rush Shot, Defensive Clear, Defensive Drive, Clear, Long Serve, Smash, Flat Shot, Rear Court Flat Drive, Short Flat Shot).
- Data was collected from **19 players** (15 male, 4 female) of National Central University's badminton school team.
- Camera setup: DFK 37AUX273 camera (The Imaging Source), 1280×960 resolution, 60fps, positioned ~2 meters behind the baseline and ~4.5 meters high at a 30-degree tilt, using XRGB video format.
- Data was processed with OpenCV for lens distortion correction, labeled by 5 students (including badminton team members) using the Shot-By-Shot (S²) Labeling tool, and reviewed by the team's head coach.
- The dataset includes annotations of player locations and shuttlecock trajectories.

### Dataset Comparison
VideoBadminton surpasses existing badminton datasets (Badminton Olympic dataset with 10 videos/12 stroke categories, ShuttleNet with 43,191 clips/10 categories) and general fine-grained datasets, positioning itself as the most comprehensive badminton video analysis dataset. It is compared against Kinetics400, Something-Something, MPII-Cooking2, Breakfast, THUMOS14, ActivityNet-1.3, Charades, FineGym-1.1, UCF-sports, Epic-kitchens-100, ADL, J-HMDB, and UCF101-24.

### Methods Evaluated
Seven state-of-the-art action recognition methods were benchmarked:
1. **R(2+1)D** - Factorizes 3D convolutions into 2D spatial + 1D temporal convolutions
2. **ST-GCN** - Spatial-Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (skeleton-based)
3. **TimeSformer** - Transformer-based, uses self-attention without convolutions
4. **PoseC3D** - Skeleton-based using 3D heatmap volumes + 3D CNNs
5. **SlowFast** - Dual-pathway (slow/low frame rate for spatial, fast/high frame rate for motion)
6. **MViT-V2** - Multiscale Vision Transformers with pooling attention and decomposed relative positional embeddings
7. **Swin** - Swin Transformer-based video recognition

### Key Results (VideoBadminton-50: 50 samples/class)
| Method | Top1 Acc | Top5 Acc | Mean Cls Acc |
|--------|----------|----------|--------------|
| ST-GCN | 60.70% | 89.25% | 54.86% |
| PoseC3D | 59.98% | 89.87% | 50.21% |
| Swim | 53.53% | 87.51% | 48.92% |
| TimeSformer | 45.45% | 85.16% | 42.68% |
| R(2+1)D | 40.84% | 77.18% | 35.35% |
| SlowFast | 12.28% | 49.44% | 21.16% |
| MViT-V2 | 12.69% | 21.49% | 5.56% |

**Skeleton-based methods (ST-GCN and PoseC3D) outperformed all video-based methods**, indicating their particular suitability for fine-grained badminton action recognition.

### Evaluation Setup
- Dataset split: 8:1:1 (train/validation/test)
- Metrics: Top-1 Accuracy, Top-5 Accuracy, Mean Class Accuracy
- Data augmentation: random cropping, horizontal flipping, color jittering
- Fine-tuning approach: transfer learning from Kinetics/ImageNet pre-trained weights, frozen early layers with training on later layers, lower learning rates, regularization (dropout, weight decay)

### Dataset Statistics Methods
The paper employs frame entropy (measuring spatial complexity) and mean difference of frame-level features (using a modified ResNet-50 for temporal dynamics) to characterize the dataset's richness.

### Contributions
1. Introduction of VideoBadminton dataset for badminton action recognition with detailed annotations
2. Systematic evaluation of contemporary video recognition architectures in the nuanced context of badminton action recognition
3. The dataset and associated code are made publicly available for research purposes
</summary>

The dataset was split into training, validation, and testing sets at an 8:1:1 ratio, with data augmentation applied during training.

**Results:** The SlowFast model performed best, achieving a Top-1 accuracy of 82.80% in some configurations, while MViT-V2 struggled to match other models' accuracy.

**Statistical Analysis:** The authors performed frame entropy analysis and mean feature difference analysis to capture variance in action dynamics across videos.

**Conclusion:** The VideoBadminton dataset represents a significant advancement in sports-related action recognition through fine-grained categorization of badminton actions. --- SOURCE 7: BST: Badminton Stroke-type Transformer for Skeleton-based Action Recognition in Racket Sports ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2502.21085v2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper introduces BST (Badminton Stroke-type Transformer), a novel architecture for skeleton-based action recognition in racket sports, specifically for classifying player stroke-types in singles badminton. The research addresses the challenges of distinguishing subtle differences between badminton strokes in broadcast match videos.

Key contributions:
1. A novel video segmentation strategy that extracts frames of each player's racket swing, segmenting match videos into stroke clips containing two to three strokes each. This variable-width clipping strategy captures complete shuttlecock trajectories in three stages: the shuttlecock flying toward the target player, the trajectory after being hit by the target player, and the direction after the opponent's response.

2. BST models that combine player poses (2D skeletal joints from RTMPose via MMPose), shuttlecock trajectories (2D positions from TrackNetV3), and player positions as inputs. The architecture is derived from TemPose but shifts focus from player poses to shuttlecock trajectory as a primary input.

3. Multiple BST variants (BST-0 through BST-3) incorporating features like Pose Position Fusion (PPF), Clean Gate modules for filtering trajectory noise, and cosine similarity-based player weighting (α coefficient) to determine which player has stronger correlation to the shuttlecock trajectory.

Results: BST-3 achieves state-of-the-art performance on the ShuttleSet dataset (largest publicly available badminton video dataset, containing 104 sets, 3,685 rallies, and 36,492 strokes across 44 matches between 2018-2021). The model demonstrates superior generalization with reduced training sets and outperforms TemPose on 7 of 9 metrics.

Notable findings:
- Effectively leveraging shuttlecock trajectory information significantly improves stroke classification performance.
- 2D poses outperform 3D poses due to HPE model bias toward general human poses.
- The model struggles with high-granularity stroke categories that have similar hitting characteristics (e.g., smash vs. wrist smash).
- Training BST-3 takes 29 sec per epoch on an NVIDIA RTX 4070 Ti Super, converging faster than TemPose-TF.

The dataset uses 35 stroke categories (19 original stroke types doubled for top/bottom player positions, plus a "none" category). The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Va6lue/BST-Badminton-Stroke-type-Transformer.
</summary>

"To the best of our knowledge, experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms the previous state-of-the-art on the largest publicly available badminton video dataset, ShuttleSet, which shows that effectively leveraging ball trajectory is likely to be a trend for racket sports action recognition."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific study (published in Scientific Reports, 2025, vol. 15, article 41236) by Guohan Jin and Xin Li from the School of Physical Education, Chengdu University, China, develops a wearable sensing network for badminton stroke recognition using two inertial measurement units (IMUs) combined with a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN).

**Methodology:**
- Two nine-axis HWT906 IMUs were placed at the distal end of the wrist radius and the lower end of the badminton racket handle to capture motion data.
- The ESP32 microcontroller was used for multi-sensor time synchronization (eliminating the need for post-processing interpolation that can distort data).
- Data was sampled at 100 Hz via SPI bus protocol, with normalization and a sliding-window segmentation approach (100 samples per window, 50-sample stride, 50% overlap).
- The 1D-CNN architecture consisted of two convolutional layers (8 and 16 filters with 3×1 kernels), batch normalization, ReLU activation, a max-pooling layer, a fully connected layer, and Softmax classifier. It was trained with cross-entropy loss and the Adam optimizer (learning rate 0.005, batch size 64, up to 500 epochs with early stopping).
- Experiments used six male national-level first-class badminton athletes (average age 22±3 years, height 176±8 cm, weight 70±6 kg), each performing six stroke actions and fifteen shot trajectories 20 times. Stratified 5-fold cross-validation was employed.
- A SIBOASI smart serving machine (SS-S4025A) was used to ensure consistent serves.

**Results:**
- Classification accuracy of 97.16% ± 0.6% for six stroke actions (Forehand Clear, Forehand Drop, Forehand Smash, Forehand Lift, Forehand Net Tumble, Forehand Cross-Net Shot).
- Classification accuracy of 86.07% ± 1.1% for fifteen badminton shot trajectories.
- Outperformed traditional machine learning methods: KNN (94.94%/78.71%), SVM (94.32%/75.06%), and DTA (92.81%/72.93%).
- CNN took 133 seconds to train versus 27 seconds for KNN.

**Key Analysis:**
- The model showed some confusion between FL and FNS strokes due to similar racket face angles during the pre-hit phase.
- FSS, FCS, and OCS trajectories showed confusion; Mann-Whitney U tests revealed that FSS/FCS differ only in Z-axis peak angular velocity (FCS requires larger whole-body rotation), while FSS/OCS differ only in Y-axis rotation, and FCS/OCS differ across all three axes.
- Heatmaps and t-SNE visualizations demonstrated that fused multi-sensor data (wrist + racket) improved class boundaries compared to single-sensor data.

**Main Contributions:**
1. First study to use ESP32 microcontroller with multi-sensor data acquisition and synchronization for recognizing badminton stroke actions and shot trajectories.
2. Achieved 97.16% accuracy for six stroke actions and 86.07% for fifteen trajectories.
3. The synchronization method addresses data discrepancies among multiple sensors and the insufficiency of single-joint motion features.

This paper, authored by Jing-Yuan Chang of National Tsing Hua University, introduces the Badminton Stroke-type Transformer (BST), a skeleton-based action recognition model for classifying player stroke-types in badminton (and tennis) from broadcast videos. The work addresses challenges in computer vision for badminton, which has the fastest ball speeds among all sports, including player identification, court line detection, shuttlecock trajectory tracking, and stroke-type classification.

Key contributions include:
1. A novel video clipping strategy that extracts frames highly relevant to each player's racket swing, extending beyond fixed-width clipping by incorporating the opponent's previous and next stroke information (including partial shuttlecock trajectory) to create three-stage clips.
2. The BST architecture, comprising a backbone (BST-0) derived from TemPose with a shift in focus from player poses to shuttlecock trajectory as a primary input, plus enhancing modules: Pose Position Fusion (PPF), Clean Gate (CG), and Aim Player (AP).

A key innovation is the Cross Transformer Layer (CrossTrans) with Multi-Head Cross Attention, where K and V are derived from the shuttlecock trajectory latent and Q from player pose/position latent. - TenniSet (6 classes, 3,569 strokes): BST-AP achieves 0.9923 accuracy.

Additional findings: BST shows superior generalization with only 25% training data, demonstrates faster training speed than prior methods (detailed in supplementary), and effectively leveraging ball trajectory significantly improves stroke classification in both badminton and tennis. The code is released at https://github.com/Va6lue/BST-Badminton-Stroke-type-Transformer.

--- SOURCE 12: How to Perform Action Recognition on Keypoints with ST ... ---
URL: https://datature.com/blog/how-to-perform-action-recogition-on-keypoints-with-stgcnn

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## How to Perform Action Recognition on Keypoints with ST-GCN++

This is a technical tutorial by Leonard So (Datature, November 15, 2023, 8-min read) explaining how to train and deploy a custom ST-GCN++ model for action recognition on skeleton/keypoint data, specifically for sit-stand recognition.

### Key Concepts Covered

**What is Action Recognition?** A computer vision task focused on identifying human actions from images or videos by analyzing motion and appearance patterns, including motion trajectories, pose configurations, and object interactions. It is challenging due to lighting variations, camera viewpoints, occlusions, and complex human motion.

**Action Recognition vs. Classification:** Action recognition focuses on temporal information (order/timing of events, motion trajectories, dynamics over frames), while classification focuses solely on spatial information (each frame treated independently). Action recognition can resolve misclassifications that arise from the loss of temporal context in classification.

**Applications of Action Recognition:** Surveillance and security (identifying suspicious activities), healthcare (monitoring patient movements/rehabilitation), sports analysis (player tracking), human-computer gesture interaction, automated driving (understanding pedestrian/driver actions), and entertainment (VR experiences, character animations).

**What is ST-GCN++?** Spatial-Temporal Graph Convolutional Network is a neural network architecture for action recognition that leverages both spatial and temporal information. It treats the human body as a graph where nodes represent body joints (elbows, knees, shoulders) and edges represent spatial relationships between joints. ST-GCN++ is a recent variant that removes complicated attention mechanisms and reduces computational overhead to achieve real-time action recognition.

**Capabilities of ST-GCN++:** Superior performance compared to earlier architectures, robust to variations in action speed/tempo, and can be combined with other modalities (audio, text) for multimodal action recognition.

### Step-by-Step Training Guide (Sit-Stand Recognition)

The tutorial walks through retraining ST-GCN++ on a subset of the NTU-RGB+D dataset with 25 keypoints:

**1. Environment Setup:** Clone the Datature Resources repository and navigate to `example-scripts/action-recognition`. Install PYSKL (the training environment) via git clone, conda environment creation from `pyskl.yaml`, and `pip install -e .`. Install miscellaneous packages from `requirements.txt`.

**2. Data Preparation:** A preprocessed sit-stand subset is included as a pickle file (`sit_stand.pkl`). For custom datasets, users must add a custom skeleton directly into PYSKL code in `pyskl/pyskl/utils/graph.py` (function `get_layout()` line 97) and add the adjacency matrix in `pyskl/pyskl/datasets/pipelines/pose_related.py` (class `JointToBone`, line 295).

**3. Training and Validation:** Run training via `bash pyskl/tools/dist_train.sh configs/j.py --validate --test-last --test-best`.

### Evaluation Metrics

- **Top-1 accuracy:** Proportion of correctly predicted samples (top prediction matches true label). The model achieved **97.5% Top-1 accuracy**, the primary metric for this use case.
- **Top-5 accuracy:** Correct if the true label is among the top five predictions (used where ambiguity exists or multiple correct answers are possible).

### Integration with YOLOv8 Pose Estimation

The tutorial demonstrates integrating the trained ST-GCN++ model with a custom Ultralytics YOLOv8 pose estimation model (25 keypoints). A testing script (`stgcn_yolov8.py`) runs pose estimation and action recognition sequentially, outputting the video with action labels overlaid. Example command:
```
python stgcn_yolov8.py input/sample.avi output/output.mp4 --config configs/j.py --checkpoint test/stgcn_model.pth --pose-checkpoint test/yolov8s-pose.pt --skeleton test/nturgbd_skeleton.txt --det-score-thr 0.7 --label-map tools/sit_stand.txt
```

### Datature's Roadmap

Datature plans to integrate action recognition with keypoint detection models through their Nexus platform, leveraging video annotation tools (video interpolation, video tracking) for streamlined keypoint labelling, plus future features such as 3D reconstruction estimation and depth estimation.

### Key References
- NTU RGB+D dataset (Shahroudy et al., CVPR 2016)
- PYSKL (Duan et al., 2022)
- ST-GCN original paper (Yan et al., AAAI 2018)
- ST-GCN++ paper (arXiv:2205.09443)
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Action recognition differs from traditional classification in the type of information that is being extracted and analyzed. Action recognition focuses primarily on temporal information, while classification focuses on spatial information.", "ST-GCN++ is a recent variant that implements simple modifications to the original architecture by removing the complicated attention mechanisms while reducing the computational overhead. These optimization techniques work in tandem to further support the goal of achieving real-time action recognition.", "ST-GCN++ is highly customizable for 2D and 3D use cases... the annotations follow the HRNet 2D skeleton, which is similar to the COCO-Pose skeleton format containing 17 keypoints.", "In our case, since the majority of the data consists of a single human subject, the metric to focus on would be the Top-1 accuracy of 97.5%.", "ST-GCN++ is successfully able to differentiate between sitting down and standing up for skeleton data in a video. While this is a relatively simple example with only two classes, this can certainly be extended to a larger number of classes if you desire."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 13: Skeleton-based Action Recognition Models ---
URL: https://mmaction2.readthedocs.io/en/dev-1.x/model_zoo/skeleton.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is part of the MMAction2 documentation (OpenMMLab's PyTorch-based action recognition toolbox) and provides a comprehensive model zoo for skeleton-based action recognition models. It covers four main models: AGCN (2s-AGCN), PoseC3D, STGCN, and STGCN++.

**AGCN (Two-Stream Adaptive Graph Convolutional Networks)**: Introduces a novel approach where graph topology can be uniformly or individually learned via backpropagation in an end-to-end manner, and models both first-order (joints) and second-order (bones) information simultaneously. On NTU60_XSub_2D, four-stream fusion achieves 92.34% top-1 accuracy; on NTU60_XSub_3D, four-stream fusion achieves 90.89%. Uses 3.5M params and 4.4G FLOPs (2D) / 6.5G FLOPs (3D).

**PoseC3D**: A CNN-based approach that relies on a 3D heatmap stack instead of a graph sequence as the base representation of human skeletons. It is more effective in learning spatiotemporal features, more robust against pose estimation noises, and generalizes better in cross-dataset settings than GCN methods. It handles multi-person scenarios without additional computation cost. Results: FineGYM 93.5% (keypoint) / 93.6% (limb), NTU60_XSub 93.6% keypoint (fusion: 94.0%), UCF101 86.8%, HMDB51 69.6%, Kinetics400 47.4%. Uses SlowOnly-R50 backbone with ~2-3.2M params.

**STGCN (Spatial-Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks)**: Automatically learns both spatial and temporal patterns from skeleton data, achieving greater expressive power and stronger generalization. Results include NTU60_XSub_2D four-stream 92.34%, NTU60_XSub_3D four-stream 90.39%, NTU120_XSub_2D four-stream 85.23%, NTU120_XSub_3D four-stream 86.19%. Uses 3.1M params.

**STGCN++**: Introduced via the PYSKL open-source toolbox (v0.2), implements six different skeleton recognition algorithms under a unified framework and achieves state-of-the-art on eight of nine benchmarks. STGCN++ serves as a strong baseline without complicated attention schemes. Results: NTU60_XSub_2D four-stream 92.77%, NTU60_XSub_3D four-stream 91.87%. Uses 1.39M params (2D) / 1.4M params (3D).

For all models, the page provides configuration files, checkpoints, and logs for reproduction. Training and testing commands use MMAction2's tools/train.py and tools/test.py with auto-scale-lr option for adjusting batch sizes. Multi-stream fusion ratios are joint:bone=1:1 for two-stream and joint:joint-motion:bone:bone-motion=2:1:2:1 for four-stream. The page also includes citations for each model and links to the broader OpenMMLab ecosystem (MMCV, MMPreTrain, MMDetection, MMPose).
</summary>

This is the IEEE Computer Society Digital Library page for the academic paper "VideoBadminton: A Video Dataset for Badminton Action Recognition," published in the 2024 IEEE International Conference on Big Data (BigData), spanning pages 1387-1392. The paper is authored by Qi Li and Wei-Shinn Ku from Auburn University (Auburn, AL, United States), and Tzu-Chen Chiu, Hsiang-Wei Huang, and Min-Te Sun from National Central University (Taoyuan City, Taiwan). The DOI is 10.1109/BigData62323.2024.10825009.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents the paper "FineGym: A Hierarchical Video Dataset for Fine-grained Action Understanding" (submitted April 14, 2020) by Dian Shao, Yue Zhao, Bo Dai, and Dahua Lin.

**Core Contribution:** FineGym is a new video dataset built on gymnastics videos that addresses the limitations of coarse-grained action recognition benchmarks (like Kinetics and ActivityNet), which often succeed by identifying background context rather than the action itself. FineGym pushes action recognition toward fine-grained understanding, where models must distinguish between hundreds of subtly different, visually similar moves performed in the same environment by the same athlete.

**Dataset Structure:**
- Features a three-level semantic hierarchy (Event, Set, Element) based on professional gymnastics standards, e.g., a "balance beam" event is annotated as a sequence of sub-actions derived from five sets: "leap-jump-hop," "beam-turns," "flight-salto," "flight-handspring," and "dismount."
- Provides multi-level temporal annotations mapping actions and sub-actions in time (e.g., locating a 1-second element within a 90-second routine).
- Contains 530 element categories and over 32,000 sub-action instances.
- Two evaluation subsets: Gym288 (natural long-tailed distribution of 288 element categories) and Gym99 (balanced subset of 99 categories).

**Annotation Methodology:** Instead of selecting from 530 labels, annotators used a decision-tree framework derived from the FIG codebook. Attribute-based Yes/No and multiple-choice queries (e.g., "Is the heel over the head?" or "Is it a 1-turn, 2-turn, or 3-turn?") guide annotators to precise element labels, ensuring reliability for moves only accurately identifiable by experts.

**Key Findings from Benchmarking:**
1. **Motion is critical:** Optical Flow provides substantial performance gains over RGB alone, since many moves look similar in static frames—direction, speed, and motion sequence define the element.
2. **Sparse sampling is insufficient:** Models like TSN that sample only 3-8 frames fail on FineGym; increasing sampled frames consistently improves accuracy since elements are short and involve rapid changes ("every frame counts").
3. **Pre-training gap:** Pre-training on Kinetics (400,000+ videos) did not necessarily improve performance; in some cases, I3D models pre-trained only on ImageNet performed better, suggesting a significant domain gap in temporal patterns.
4. **Temporal ordering matters:** Shuffling frames caused massive accuracy drops in TRN, confirming that movement order is essential. TSM was also found to be highly sensitive to the number of test segments vs. training segments.

**Results:** Models achieved nearly 99% accuracy at the "event" level but performance dropped significantly at the "element" level, demonstrating the benchmark's difficulty.

**Significance:** FineGym serves as a foundation for research in sports analytics, automated coaching, and more interpretable AI that reasons about human movement through attributes and hierarchies, presenting open challenges in temporal action localization at fine scales and distinguishing subtly different action classes.
</summary>

- Temporal annotations at both action and sub-action levels with a three-level semantic hierarchy.
- A "balance beam" activity is annotated as a sequence of elementary sub-actions derived from five sets: "leap-jump-hop", "beam-turns", "flight-salto", "flight-handspring", and "dismount," with each sub-action further annotated with finely defined class labels.
- The dataset is distinguished by richness, quality, and diversity compared to existing action recognition datasets.
- It presents significant challenges for action recognition, including parsing temporal structures from coherent actions and distinguishing between subtly different action classes.
- The authors systematically investigated different methods on this dataset and obtained a number of interesting findings.

The webpage also lists similar articles on related topics such as fine-grained action recognition, temporal action segmentation, and hierarchical sports video datasets. The paper is available for purchase ($36 for non-members, $16 for members) or free with new IEEE Computer Society membership.

--- SOURCE 14: FineGym: A Hierarchical Video Dataset for Fine-grained Action Understanding ---
URL: https://sdolivia.github.io/FineGym

SUMMARY:
<summary>
FineGym is a hierarchical video dataset for fine-grained action understanding, presented at CVPR 2020 (Oral) by Dian Shao, Yue Zhao, Bo Dai, and Dahua Lin from The Chinese University of Hong Kong. The dataset is built on gymnasium videos and provides coarse-to-fine annotations both temporally and semantically. It features three levels of categorical labels (events, sets, elements) and two-level temporal annotations (actions and sub-actions). For example, a "balance beam" event is annotated as a sequence of elementary sub-actions derived from five sets: "leap-jumphop", "beam-turns", "flight-salto", "flight-handspring", and "dismount". Sub-actions can be described generally using set categories or precisely using element categories, with ground-truth element categories obtained via manually constructed decision-trees.

Key empirical findings from the paper include: (1) element-level action recognition raises great challenges for existing methods; (2) sparse sampling is insufficient for fine-grained action recognition; (3) temporal information is important—motion features capture frame-wise temporal dynamics, TRN captures temporal dynamics, and TSM performance drops sharply when testing frames differ from training frames while TSN maintains performance due to temporal average pooling; (4) pre-training on Kinetics is not always helpful on FineGym due to large gaps in temporal patterns between coarse- and fine-grained actions; (5) skeleton-based ST-GCN struggles due to challenges in skeleton estimation on gymnastics instances.

The dataset includes multiple versions (v1.0 and v1.1) with temporal annotations in JSON format, plus category lists for Gym99, Gym288, and Gym530. All instances are annotated in exact millisecond-level timestamps. The annotations are published under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International License. Pre-extracted features are available on the GitHub repository. The paper is available on arXiv (arXiv:2004.06704), and the work was supported by SenseTime Collaborative Grant and Hong Kong GRF funds (No. 14203518 and No. 14205719).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"To take action recognition to a new level, we develop FineGym, a new dataset built on top of gymnasium videos. Compared to existing action recognition datasets, FineGym is distinguished in richness, quality, and diversity."

--- SOURCE 1: Real-time stroke prediction in badminton integrating AI with ... ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40537-026-01396-7

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an open-access research article published in the Journal of Big Data (Volume 13, article 61, published 06 March 2026) titled "Real-time stroke prediction in badminton integrating AI with the KNN-HMM model" by Qi Song and Jian Zhang.

**Purpose/Objective:** The paper presents a k-Nearest Neighbours-Hidden Markov Model (KNN-HMM) for real-time badminton stroke prediction, addressing issues of accuracy, time-dependent characteristics, and flexibility in stroke analysis. The study aims to integrate spatial and temporal dynamics for stroke classification under real-time constraints.

**Methods:** The dataset comprised 10,000 motion-captured badminton strokes collected in Chongqing, China (2015-2017) from 36 players (18 male, 18 female; ages 18-35; 12 amateur, 12 semi-professional, 12 professional). Data was captured using an eight-camera Vicon optical motion capture system (120 Hz) and annotated in Kinovea. Features included joint angles (shoulder, elbow, wrist), velocities, accelerations, and shuttle trajectory descriptors. Temporal sequences were segmented using 200-ms sliding windows with 50-ms overlap. The model combined a KNN stroke classifier (k=5, Euclidean metric, FAISS index) with HMM-based temporal sequence prediction (3-5 hidden states, Gaussian emissions, Baum-Welch training, Viterbi decoding). Data was split 70% training, 15% validation, 15% test. External validation used the ShuttleSet22 dataset (44 professional matches, 36,000+ strokes, 2018-2022).

**Key Results:**
- KNN-HMM achieved 94.6% accuracy on internal validation (95% CI 93.9-95.3) and 93.4% on external evaluation
- 97.5% accuracy with 32 ms latency and 90.8% streaming accuracy (per abstract)
- Compared to standalone KNN: modest gains in accuracy (+0.05, p=0.021), F1-score (+0.07, p=0.015), precision (+0.06, p=0.001), recall (+0.04, p=0.018)
- Outperformed hybrid SVM-Decision Tree-KNN (83.4%) and acoustic sensor-based approaches (~84%)
- Jump Smash and Net Shot had highest F1 (≥0.98); Clear and Drive had lower F1 (≤0.92)
- End-to-end processing: 32 ms at 120 Hz, 18 ms at 60 Hz, 14 ms at 30 Hz on 8-core CPU
- HMM log-likelihood of 42.75, BIC of 88.6

**Conclusions:** The KNN-HMM offers an effective paradigm for real-time badminton stroke classification with high accuracy, adaptability, and generalizability, though results are limited to a regional model (Chongqing, China). The framework is advantageous for training applications and real-time tactical analysis. Ethical approval was granted by the IRB of Sichuan International Studies University (No. 29237681), and the study followed the Declaration of Helsinki.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The KNN-HMM achieved 97.5% accuracy with a latency of 32 ms and 90.8% streaming accuracy."

--- SOURCE 3: Recognition of Badminton Shot Action Based on the Improved ... ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8516566

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a scientific research article from the Journal of Healthcare Engineering (published via PMC/NCBI) titled "Recognition of Badminton Shot Action Based on the Improved Hidden Markov Model" by Chao Ma, Dayang Yu, and Hao Feng, with academic editor Fazlullah Khan. IMPORTANT: The article has been retracted (retraction published in J Healthc Eng. 2023 May 24;2023:9817142).

The paper develops a wearable sports activity classification system for recognizing badminton actions. Key details:

- **Methodology**: Uses a single acceleration sensor fixed at the end of the badminton racket handle to collect action data. A sliding window segmentation technique (window width of 100 samples at 200 Hz sampling frequency, since badminton batting actions typically do not exceed 0.5 seconds) is used to extract hitting signals. An improved hidden Markov model (HMM) is developed to identify 10 standard badminton strokes including services, forehand chop, backhand chop, forehand and backhand drives, backhand push, forehand pick, backhand pick, and forehand.

- **Improved HMM approach**: The paper proposes two training schemes to avoid local optima in HMM training: (1) a mean training method that integrates data from multiple samples, and (2) a frequency-weighted training method that linearly weights the frequency of sample observation sequences. Recognition uses the Viterbi algorithm to find the optimal state sequence probability.

- **Experimental setup**: MATLAB 2020 and IntelliJ IDEA 2018 (JDK 1.8), Windows 10, Bluetooth 4.0 data transmission. Hardware uses six-axis acceleration sensors - one on the racket handle and two worn around players' ankles. 15 players were tested across three skill levels: 5 professional athletes (2nd/3rd-level badminton players), 5 amateurs (badminton association members), and 5 novices (lab classmates who rarely play badminton). Data split was 70% training and 30% testing.

- **Results**: The improved HMM achieved a 95% comprehensive recognition rate for 10 different strokes, compared to 87.7% for the traditional HMM (a 7.3% improvement). Window size affected accuracy: 100 samples = 95%, 150 samples = 93%, 200 samples = 90%. The proposed model outperformed SVM and BP neural network methods (which achieved less than 80% accuracy vs. more than 90% for the improved HMM).

- **Conclusion**: The model can recognize ten common badminton strokes in real time and can be used to improve the competitive level of badminton players.

- **Limitations**: Only acceleration sensors were used by fifteen sportsmen to recognize ten basic badminton shots. Future work includes adding more players and extending the dataset to other sports activities.

The paper also includes background sections on badminton aerodynamics (discussing drag, lift, lateral forces, and the Magnus effect on shuttlecock flight) and batting motion extraction techniques.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The experimental results show that the model designed can recognize ten standard strokes in real time. Compared with the traditional HMM, the average recognition rate of the improved HMM is improved by 7.3%. The comprehensive recognition rate of the final strokes can reach up to 95%."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: The analysis of motion recognition model for badminton player ... ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-02771-9

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in Scientific Reports (volume 15, article number 19030, 2025) by Xuanmin Zhu, Lizhi Liu, Jingshuo Huang, Genyan Chen, Xi Ling, and Yanshuo Chen, titled "The analysis of motion recognition model for badminton player movements using machine learning."

**Purpose:** The study aims to classify badminton players' swing actions by combining quantum mechanics and machine learning frameworks. A Quantum Convolutional Neural Network (QCNN) approach is proposed and compared against traditional Support Vector Machines (SVM) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) to assess classification performance and robustness.

**Methodology:**
- Data collected from four badminton match video recordings using high-frame-rate cameras and inertial sensors
- OpenPose used for human posture estimation; spatiotemporal features extracted
- Preprocessing included Gaussian filtering for noise removal, normalization (Z-score), feature selection, and data augmentation (time shifting, rotation/scaling, noise addition)
- Data split: 70% training, 15% validation, 15% test sets
- Three models trained: SVM, CNN, QCNN
- Five key features analyzed: arm angle, twist angle, footwork position, grip type, step length
- Metrics used: precision, recall, F1-score
- Robustness tested under low, medium, and high noise levels

**Key Results:**
- QCNN outperformed all models across all classification tasks
- Backhand intercept F1-score: QCNN = 0.860, CNN = 0.792, SVM = 0.753
- Robustness precision under low/medium/high noise: QCNN = 0.95/0.92/0.89, surpassing both CNN and SVM
- Feature importance analysis identified arm angle, twist angle, and step position as key factors; arm angle was the most significant feature in the QCNN model

**Conclusion:** The study validates QCNN's superiority in badminton action recognition and demonstrates strong adaptability to noisy data, providing reliable methodological support for sports technique analysis. The QCNN leverages quantum convolutional kernels, quantum entanglement, and parallelism while retaining local connectivity and weight sharing from classical CNNs, reducing model complexity and improving computational efficiency.

**Related literature context:** The study builds on prior work including LSTM-based action recognition (63-92% accuracy), CNN-LSTM-self-attention frameworks (97.83% accuracy), weighted ensemble models combining SVM/RF/LR (95.38% accuracy), and the MultiSenseBadminton dataset (7,763 swing data points with multimodal data).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: ShuttleSet22: Benchmarking Stroke Forecasting with Stroke-Level ... ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2306.15664v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper introduces ShuttleSet22, a stroke-level badminton singles dataset collected from high-ranking matches in 2022, serving as an extension of the earlier ShuttleSet dataset (which covered 2018-2021 matches). The dataset contains 30,172 strokes across 2,888 rallies in the training set, 1,400 strokes in 450 rallies in the validation set, and 2,040 strokes in 654 rallies in the testing set, comprising 35 players, 58 matches, and 33,612 total strokes from 3,992 rallies. Data was collected from public videos on bwf.tv and labeled by domain experts using a shot-by-shot labeling tool.

The paper benchmarks the state-of-the-art stroke forecasting approach, ShuttleNet (a Transformer-based position-aware fusion framework), on the task of predicting future strokes (shot types and area coordinates) based on observed past strokes. The authors held Track 2 (Forecasting Future Turn-Based Strokes in Badminton Rallies) of the CoachAI Badminton Challenge 2023 in conjunction with IJCAI 2023, which attracted approximately 95-100 participants, with 16 teams submitting final results.

Key dataset features include detailed metadata per stroke: shot type, around-head/backhand indicators, landing height, landing area and coordinates, player/opponent locations, rally information, scores, and outcomes. Exploratory analysis reveals that players typically position themselves at court centers and corners when attacking, and at center when defending.

Results from the challenge show that 11 teams outperformed the ShuttleNet baseline (total score 2.8774), with the top team (Intro_to_AI_team8) achieving a total score of 2.5776 (CE: 1.7892, MAE: 0.7884) by simplifying ShuttleNet's structure. Most improvements focused on shot type prediction (2.1777→1.7892), while area coordinate prediction saw only marginal gains (0.6997→0.6797), highlighting the difficulty of jointly optimizing both predictions. Baseline codes and dataset are available at the CoachAI GitHub repository.

--- SOURCE 7: ShuttleSet: Badminton Stroke-Level Analytics ---
URL: https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/shuttleset

SUMMARY:
<summary>
ShuttleSet is a comprehensive, human-annotated stroke-level badminton singles dataset designed for tactical analysis and structured turn-based modeling. Introduced by Wang et al. (2023), it comprises 44 broadcast matches from 2018–2021, 104 sets, 3,685 rallies, and 36,492 strokes involving 27 top-ranking men's and women's singles players, making it the largest publicly available badminton singles dataset with stroke-level annotations.

The dataset uses broadcast video from bwf.tv (standardized to 30 fps and 1280×720 resolution) rather than instrumented capture. It captures four annotation categories per stroke: rally (set scores, rally winner, lose reason), temporal (hitting time/frame), spatial (player positions, shuttle contact location, grid location, above/below net), and hitting (stroke status, backhand, around-the-head, shot type). The original taxonomy contains 18 stroke classes (e.g., net shot, smash, lob, clear, drive, drop, push, service types), supplemented by operational flags. Court coordinates are obtained via homography, with the singles court defined as (0,0) to (13.4,6.1).

Annotation was performed by six trained badminton experts using the S² (Shot-by-Shot) labeling tool with a four-stage workflow: match preparation, rally segmentation, video preprocessing, and shot-by-shot labeling. Quality control reported temporal MAE of 0.24 frames (serve), 0.02 (return), and 0 (dead bird); spatial MAE of 0.18 (shuttle) and 0.86 (player position); and shot-type accuracy differences of 0.00–0.11 upon re-annotation. The dataset is distributed through the CoachAI project, with a Python loader and a Flask-based visualization platform used by national teams during international matches.

Three native benchmark tasks were defined: (1) Stroke influence (win-probability estimation) — best model ShuttleScorer achieved AUC 0.8371, ACC 0.7869, BR 0.1574; (2) Stroke forecasting (predicting future shot types and landing locations) — ShuttleNet achieved CE 2.4125, MSE 1.8121, MAE 1.3582 for τ=8; (3) Movement forecasting (jointly predicting strokes and player positions) — DyMF achieved best CE (2.3146), ShuttleNet best MSE (1.0832) and MAE (1.5852).

Subsequent research has repurposed ShuttleSet beyond its original benchmarks: skeleton-based stroke-type recognition (BST model achieving Acc 0.7710, Macro-F1 0.7042, Acc-2 0.9340), cross-domain transfer from singles to doubles shot-occurrence detection (pose-based model generalizing better than vision-only baselines, with ~19.3% vs ~39.9% transfer degradation), temporal action localization (mAP 75.17 at tIoU 0.3, average 74.67), and report generation via ShuttleSet+ (Tree-of-Text achieving RG# 16.78, outperforming prompt-only baselines).

Known limitations include: singles-only coverage, no fixed train/validation/test split (papers construct their own), class imbalance in rare categories, no continuous shuttle trajectories stored, and unreliable 3D pose lifting for badminton-specific poses. The dataset's significance lies in establishing a shared, stroke-level representation on public broadcast video that unifies forecasting, recognition, localization, transfer, and report-generation research threads.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"ShuttleSet is a human-annotated stroke-level badminton singles dataset designed for tactical analysis and structured turn-based modeling. It was introduced as the largest publicly available badminton singles dataset with annotated stroke-level records, comprising 44 broadcast matches from 2018–2021, 104 sets, 3,685 rallies, and 36,492 strokes involving 27 top-ranking men's and women's singles players.", "A central feature of ShuttleSet is that it is structured around rallies rather than isolated clips. This makes it suitable for sequence modeling tasks such as win-probability estimation, next-stroke forecasting, and movement forecasting.", "Over two years, this platform was used by national badminton teams during multiple international high-ranking matches, indicating that ShuttleSet was intended not only as a benchmark corpus but also as an operational analytics substrate.", "Despite these constraints, ShuttleSet occupies a distinctive position in badminton analytics. It is simultaneously a structured event dataset, a sequence-modeling benchmark, a source of training supervision for video models, and a basis for applied tactical interfaces.", "A plausible implication is that its long-term importance lies less in any single benchmark score than in the fact that it established a shared, stroke-level representation on top of public broadcast video, enabling otherwise disconnected research threads—forecasting, recognition, localization, transfer, and report generation—to operate on a common substrate."

--- SOURCE 13: FineGym: A Hierarchical Video Dataset for Fine-grained Action ... ---
URL: https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2004.06704

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents the paper "FineGym: A Hierarchical Video Dataset for Fine-grained Action Understanding" (submitted April 14, 2020) by Dian Shao, Yue Zhao, Bo Dai, and Dahua Lin.

**Core Contribution:** FineGym is a new video dataset built on gymnastics videos that addresses the limitations of coarse-grained action recognition benchmarks (like Kinetics and ActivityNet), which often succeed by identifying background context rather than the action itself. FineGym pushes action recognition toward fine-grained understanding, where models must distinguish between hundreds of subtly different, visually similar moves performed in the same environment by the same athlete.

**Dataset Structure:**
- Features a three-level semantic hierarchy (Event, Set, Element) based on professional gymnastics standards, e.g., a "balance beam" event is annotated as a sequence of sub-actions derived from five sets: "leap-jump-hop," "beam-turns," "flight-salto," "flight-handspring," and "dismount."
- Provides multi-level temporal annotations mapping actions and sub-actions in time (e.g., locating a 1-second element within a 90-second routine).
- Contains 530 element categories and over 32,000 sub-action instances.
- Two evaluation subsets: Gym288 (natural long-tailed distribution of 288 element categories) and Gym99 (balanced subset of 99 categories).

**Annotation Methodology:** Instead of selecting from 530 labels, annotators used a decision-tree framework derived from the FIG codebook. Attribute-based Yes/No and multiple-choice queries (e.g., "Is the heel over the head?" or "Is it a 1-turn, 2-turn, or 3-turn?") guide annotators to precise element labels, ensuring reliability for moves only accurately identifiable by experts.

**Key Findings from Benchmarking:**
1. **Motion is critical:** Optical Flow provides substantial performance gains over RGB alone, since many moves look similar in static frames—direction, speed, and motion sequence define the element.
2. **Sparse sampling is insufficient:** Models like TSN that sample only 3-8 frames fail on FineGym; increasing sampled frames consistently improves accuracy since elements are short and involve rapid changes ("every frame counts").
3. **Pre-training gap:** Pre-training on Kinetics (400,000+ videos) did not necessarily improve performance; in some cases, I3D models pre-trained only on ImageNet performed better, suggesting a significant domain gap in temporal patterns.
4. **Temporal ordering matters:** Shuffling frames caused massive accuracy drops in TRN, confirming that movement order is essential. TSM was also found to be highly sensitive to the number of test segments vs. training segments.

**Results:** Models achieved nearly 99% accuracy at the "event" level but performance dropped significantly at the "element" level, demonstrating the benchmark's difficulty.

**Significance:** FineGym serves as a foundation for research in sports analytics, automated coaching, and more interpretable AI that reasons about human movement through attributes and hierarchies, presenting open challenges in temporal action localization at fine scales and distinguishing subtly different action classes.
</summary>

<summary>
FineGym is a hierarchical video dataset for fine-grained action understanding, presented at CVPR 2020 (Oral) by Dian Shao, Yue Zhao, Bo Dai, and Dahua Lin from The Chinese University of Hong Kong. The dataset includes multiple versions (v1.0 and v1.1) with temporal annotations in JSON format, plus category lists for Gym99, Gym288, and Gym530. All instances are annotated in exact millisecond-level timestamps. The annotations are published under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International License. Pre-extracted features are available on the GitHub repository. The paper is available on arXiv (arXiv:2004.06704), and the work was supported by SenseTime Collaborative Grant and Hong Kong GRF funds (No. 14203518 and No. 14205719).

--- SOURCE 1: ShuttleSet: Badminton Stroke-Level Analytics ---
URL: https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/shuttleset

SUMMARY:
<summary>
ShuttleSet is a comprehensive, human-annotated stroke-level badminton singles dataset designed for tactical analysis and structured turn-based modeling. Introduced by Wang et al. (2023), it comprises 44 broadcast matches from 2018–2021, 104 sets, 3,685 rallies, and 36,492 strokes involving 27 top-ranking men's and women's singles players, making it the largest publicly available badminton singles dataset with stroke-level annotations.

The dataset uses broadcast video from bwf.tv (standardized to 30 fps and 1280×720 resolution) rather than instrumented capture. It captures four annotation categories per stroke: rally (set scores, rally winner, lose reason), temporal (hitting time/frame), spatial (player positions, shuttle contact location, grid location, above/below net), and hitting (stroke status, backhand, around-the-head, shot type). The original taxonomy contains 18 stroke classes (e.g., net shot, smash, lob, clear, drive, drop, push, service types), supplemented by operational flags. Court coordinates are obtained via homography, with the singles court defined as (0,0) to (13.4,6.1).

Annotation was performed by six trained badminton experts using the S² (Shot-by-Shot) labeling tool with a four-stage workflow: match preparation, rally segmentation, video preprocessing, and shot-by-shot labeling. Quality control reported temporal MAE of 0.24 frames (serve), 0.02 (return), and 0 (dead bird); spatial MAE of 0.18 (shuttle) and 0.86 (player position); and shot-type accuracy differences of 0.00–0.11 upon re-annotation. The dataset is distributed through the CoachAI project, with a Python loader and a Flask-based visualization platform used by national teams during international matches.

Three native benchmark tasks were defined: (1) Stroke influence (win-probability estimation) — best model ShuttleScorer achieved AUC 0.8371, ACC 0.7869, BR 0.1574; (2) Stroke forecasting (predicting future shot types and landing locations) — ShuttleNet achieved CE 2.4125, MSE 1.8121, MAE 1.3582 for τ=8; (3) Movement forecasting (jointly predicting strokes and player positions) — DyMF achieved best CE (2.3146), ShuttleNet best MSE (1.0832) and MAE (1.5852).

Subsequent research has repurposed ShuttleSet beyond its original benchmarks: skeleton-based stroke-type recognition (BST model achieving Acc 0.7710, Macro-F1 0.7042, Acc-2 0.9340), cross-domain transfer from singles to doubles shot-occurrence detection (pose-based model generalizing better than vision-only baselines, with ~19.3% vs ~39.9% transfer degradation), temporal action localization (mAP 75.17 at tIoU 0.3, average 74.67), and report generation via ShuttleSet+ (Tree-of-Text achieving RG# 16.78, outperforming prompt-only baselines).

Known limitations include: singles-only coverage, no fixed train/validation/test split (papers construct their own), class imbalance in rare categories, no continuous shuttle trajectories stored, and unreliable 3D pose lifting for badminton-specific poses. The dataset's significance lies in establishing a shared, stroke-level representation on public broadcast video that unifies forecasting, recognition, localization, transfer, and report-generation research threads.
</summary>

It was introduced as the largest publicly available badminton singles dataset with annotated stroke-level records, comprising 44 broadcast matches from 2018–2021, 104 sets, 3,685 rallies, and 36,492 strokes involving 27 top-ranking men's and women's singles players.", "A central feature of ShuttleSet is that it is structured around rallies rather than isolated clips. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper introduces ShuttleSet22, a stroke-level badminton singles dataset collected from high-ranking matches in 2022, serving as an extension of the earlier ShuttleSet dataset (which covered 2018-2021 matches). The dataset contains 30,172 strokes across 2,888 rallies in the training set, 1,400 strokes in 450 rallies in the validation set, and 2,040 strokes in 654 rallies in the testing set, comprising 35 players, 58 matches, and 33,612 total strokes from 3,992 rallies. Data was collected from public videos on bwf.tv and labeled by domain experts using a shot-by-shot labeling tool.

The paper benchmarks the state-of-the-art stroke forecasting approach, ShuttleNet (a Transformer-based position-aware fusion framework), on the task of predicting future strokes (shot types and area coordinates) based on observed past strokes. The authors held Track 2 (Forecasting Future Turn-Based Strokes in Badminton Rallies) of the CoachAI Badminton Challenge 2023 in conjunction with IJCAI 2023, which attracted approximately 95-100 participants, with 16 teams submitting final results.

Key dataset features include detailed metadata per stroke: shot type, around-head/backhand indicators, landing height, landing area and coordinates, player/opponent locations, rally information, scores, and outcomes. Exploratory analysis reveals that players typically position themselves at court centers and corners when attacking, and at center when defending.

Results from the challenge show that 11 teams outperformed the ShuttleNet baseline (total score 2.8774), with the top team (Intro_to_AI_team8) achieving a total score of 2.5776 (CE: 1.7892, MAE: 0.7884) by simplifying ShuttleNet's structure. Most improvements focused on shot type prediction (2.1777→1.7892), while area coordinate prediction saw only marginal gains (0.6997→0.6797), highlighting the difficulty of jointly optimizing both predictions. - RQ2: Evaluated ShuttleNet and baselines for forecasting future stroke types and destination locations

Developed by Dian Shao, Yue Zhao, Bo Dai, and Dahua Lin from CUHK-SenseTime Joint Lab at The Chinese University of Hong Kong, the dataset addresses a key limitation of existing action recognition benchmarks: they focus on coarse-grained categories where background context often matters more than the action itself, whereas applications like sport analytics require fine-grained temporal and semantic analysis.

**Dataset Structure:** FineGym provides annotations at three semantic levels (event, set, element) and two temporal levels (action and sub-action). Events are gymnastics routines such as vault (VT), floor exercise (FX), uneven bars (UB), and balance beam (BB). Sets are mid-level categories of sub-actions (e.g., leap-jump-hop, beam-turns, flight-salto, flight-handspring, dismounts), and elements are the finest categories (e.g., "double salto backward tucked"). The dataset contains 10 event categories (6 male, 4 female events), with 4 female events receiving detailed fine-grained annotations. FineGym v1.0 includes 303 competition records totaling ~708 hours, 530 defined element categories (354 with at least one instance), 4,883 action instances, and 32,697 sub-action instances. Instance counts per element category range from 1 to 1,648, reflecting a natural heavy-tail distribution.

**Construction Method:** Data was collected from official video records of professional competitions (720P/1080P resolution, over 95% high-resolution). Element labels were assigned via manually constructed decision trees consisting of attribute-based queries, guided by the official FIG Code of Points. A specially trained annotation team (not crowdsourced) performed annotations, with rigorous quality control including pretesting, referential slides/demos, and cross-validation across annotators.

**Key Empirical Findings:** The authors systematically evaluated representative action recognition methods (TSN, TRN, TSM, I3D, Non-local I3D, ActionVLAD, ST-GCN) across multiple granularities. Key findings include: (1) Sparse frame sampling (3 frames) is sufficient for event/set-level recognition but insufficient for element-level recognition—performance on Gym99 steadily improves up to 12 frames (30% of all frames); (2) Motion features (optical flow) contribute significantly more than appearance features at fine granularities, except for vault where motion is extremely intense; (3) Temporal dynamics modeling is crucial—TRN and TSM outperform TSN by large margins, and shuffling frames causes significant performance drops; (4) Pre-training on coarse-grained datasets like Kinetics is not always beneficial for fine-grained recognition due to temporal pattern gaps; (5) Skeleton-based methods (ST-GCN) struggle due to pose estimation failures on gymnastics instances; (6) Temporal action localization of sub-actions (mAP@tIoU avg 9.6) is far more challenging than localization of actions (mAP@tIoU avg 49.4).

**Potential Applications:** Beyond recognition and localization, FineGym supports auto-scoring (difficulty scores come from official documents), action generation, multi-attribute prediction, and model interpretation/reasoning via decision trees. The dataset and code are available at https://sdolivia.github.io/FineGym/.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We develop FineGym, short for Fine-grained Gymnastics, which is a large-scale high-quality action dataset that provides fine-grained annotations... 1) Multi-level semantic hierarchy. All actions are annotated with semantic labels at three levels, namely event, set, and element."
</key_excerpts>

**Objective and Problem:** The study addresses the difficulty of classifying table tennis strokes from actual game videos. Unlike general action recognition tasks, table tennis strokes display strong similarity, making classification challenging. **Proposed Method:** The authors propose a multi-label stroke classification approach that assigns two types of labels per stroke: (1) player's posture (forehand/backhand) and (2) ball rotation and velocity (topspin/push/block/flick). Multiple action recognition models (TSTCNN, C3D, I3D, C2D, R(2+1)D, STGCN, AGCN) were tested as backbones, with STGCN results shown in a confusion matrix.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents a novel method for collecting table tennis video data and performing stroke detection and classification using two-dimensional human pose estimation. The researchers collected a diverse dataset of 11 basic table tennis strokes (topspin, block, push, flick, and lob in both forehand and backhand variants, plus forehand flat) from 14 professional players, totaling 22,111 videos and 6,984,224 data points across 873,028 frames (average 39.48 frames per stroke).

KEY METHODOLOGY:
- A novel data collection setup used a wooden camera frame placed on the table (height 135mm, below the regulation 152.5mm net height) holding a Raspberry Pi 4 and camera module at 105mm above the table surface, positioned facing the player from the front view with minimal gameplay interference.
- Two SW-420 vibration sensors (one on each side of the table) automated video recording and labelling - triggered by ball pitch on the player's side (start) and opposite side (stop), capturing each single stroke.
- Videos recorded at 1280x720 resolution, 60 fps.
- Data collection methods included free-flowing rallies (for blocks, pushes, lobs, forehand flat) and multi-ball feeding (for topspins and flicks).
- Pose estimation used SSD (Single Shot Multibox Detector) for player detection followed by HRNet (High-Resolution Net) for 2D pose extraction.
- Four body joints used as features: wrist, elbow, and two shoulders (8 features per time step across 100 standard time steps).
- Savitzky-Golay filtering (window length 13, polynomial order 2) applied to reduce pose estimation noise from fast-moving/blurred frames.

MODEL RESULTS:
- Machine learning comparison: SVM (RBF kernel, c=800) best at 98.37%, followed by XGBoost (98.10%), Random Forest (96.20%), KNN k=3 (92.40%), XGBoost-Random Forest (91.68%), Decision Tree max depth=15 (90.32%).
- Deep learning comparison: TCN and TCN+LSTM both achieved 99.37% validation accuracy, LSTM achieved 96.43% (best LSTM variant). The TCN model used ~206,299 trainable parameters (about two-thirds of others) and had inference time of 0.79s per 20,000 strokes on an NVIDIA RTX 3070.
- HRNet trained on COCO dataset performed better (99.37%) than MPII-trained model (82.36%) when coupled with the TCN classifier.
- Savgol filtering improved validation accuracy from 97.74% (unfiltered) to 99.37% (filtered).
- Training-validation split of 95%-5%.

GENERALISATION TESTS:
- Player A (male right-handed, 13 years experience, excluded from training): 98.72% overall accuracy.
- Player B (female left-handed, 10 years experience): 88.81% accuracy initially; low 38% accuracy on her forehand push due to unorthodox technique. After fine-tuning on 2 epochs of her data, accuracy improved to 99.22%.

CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK:
The authors propose future applications including stroke error detection by comparing player strokes, performance monitoring during training, per-stage stroke quality evaluation (following Zhou Jun's 3-stage stroke model), automated coaching corrections against professional players, match analysis statistics, player profiling, and boosting table tennis popularity through user-friendly analytics.
</summary>

The dataset includes multiple versions (v1.0 and v1.1) with temporal annotations in JSON format, plus category lists for Gym99, Gym288, and Gym530.
