output.content:
# Badminton Stroke Recognition from Video: Research Findings Report

## List of Queries and Tool Calls Made

The following web searches were conducted to gather information:

1. **Tavily search**: "badminton stroke recognition from video dataset benchmark action classification", "Badminton-Recognition dataset Rahmat badminton stroke classification paper", "badminton action recognition pose estimation skeleton ST-GCN"
2. **Tavily search**: "badminton technical action recognition 3D CNN transformer video 2023 2024", "badminton shot classification deep learning video tennis table tennis transfer dataset", "FineGym gymnastics action recognition dataset FineGym dataset paper"
3. **Tavily search**: "ShuttleSet badminton dataset 36,492 strokes singles stroke forecasting ShuttleSet paper", "FineGym gymnastics action recognition dataset official page 304 classes", "TTStroke-21 table tennis stroke classification dataset paper"
4. **Tavily search**: "badminton shot classification pose estimation LSTM RNN technical strokes deep learning 2021 2022", "tennis stroke classification video dataset action recognition FineGym transfer", "badminton smash clear drop net drive lift serve classification skeleton pose keypoint deep learning"
5. **Tavily search**: "Rahmat badminton stroke recognition deep learning dataset 2021", "badminton shuttle hit detection temporal action localization broadcast video 2023", "tennis stroke classification dataset action recognition CVPRW broadcast"
6. **Tavily search**: "TemPose badminton skeleton transformer action recognition paper", "PoseC3D skeleton action recognition fine-grained sports badminton racket", "badminton action recognition LSTM RNN pose keypoints 2019 2020 deep learning stroke"

---

## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### 1. Badminton-Specific Datasets

#### 1.1 VideoBadminton Dataset (2024)
**Source: arXiv 2403.12385** [1]

VideoBadminton is a novel fine-grained video dataset for badminton action recognition, introduced in "Benchmarking Badminton Action Recognition with a New Fine-Grained Dataset" (arXiv:2403.12385v2).

- Contains **7,822 video clips** spanning **145 minutes** of self-recorded footage featuring **18 badminton action classes** aligned with Badminton World Federation (BWF) standards: Short Serve, Cross-Court Flight, Lift, Tap Smash, Block, Drop Shot, Push Shot, Transitional Slice, Cut, Rush Shot, Defensive Clear, Defensive Drive, Clear, Long Serve, Smash, Flat Shot, Rear Court Flat Drive, Short Flat Shot.
- Data collected from **19 players** (15 male, 4 female) of National Central University's badminton school team.
- Camera: DFK 37AUX273 camera (The Imaging Source), 1280×960 resolution, 60fps, positioned ~2 meters behind the baseline and ~4.5 meters high at a 30-degree tilt, XRGB video format.
- Processed with OpenCV for lens distortion correction, labeled by 5 students (including badminton team members) using the Shot-By-Shot (S²) Labeling tool, reviewed by the team's head coach.
- Includes annotations of player locations and shuttlecock trajectories.
- Compared against Badminton Olympic dataset (10 videos/12 stroke categories) and ShuttleNet (43,191 clips/10 categories).

**Benchmark Results (VideoBadminton-50: 50 samples/class):**

| Method | Top1 Acc | Top5 Acc | Mean Cls Acc |
|--------|----------|----------|--------------|
| ST-GCN | 60.70% | 89.25% | 54.86% |
| PoseC3D | 59.98% | 89.87% | 50.21% |
| Swin | 53.53% | 87.51% | 48.92% |
| TimeSformer | 45.45% | 85.16% | 42.68% |
| R(2+1)D | 40.84% | 77.18% | 35.35% |
| SlowFast | 12.28% | 49.44% | 21.16% |
| MViT-V2 | 12.69% | 21.49% | 5.56% |

**Key finding: Skeleton-based methods (ST-GCN and PoseC3D) outperformed all video-based methods**, indicating their particular suitability for fine-grained badminton action recognition.

- Evaluation setup: 8:1:1 train/validation/test split; metrics Top-1, Top-5, Mean Class Accuracy; augmentation (random cropping, horizontal flipping, color jittering); fine-tuning via transfer learning from Kinetics/ImageNet pre-trained weights, frozen early layers, lower learning rates, regularization (dropout, weight decay).
- Dataset statistics methods: frame entropy (spatial complexity) and mean difference of frame-level features (modified ResNet-50 for temporal dynamics).

**IEEE BigData 2024 publication** [3]: "VideoBadminton: A Video Dataset for Badminton Action Recognition," 2024 IEEE International Conference on Big Data (BigData), pages 1387-1392, DOI 10.1109/BigData62323.2024.10825009. Authors: Qi Li (Auburn University), Tzu-Chen Chiu (National Central University), Hsiang-Wei Huang (National Central University), Min-Te Sun (National Central University), Wei-Shinn Ku (Auburn University).

**HyperAI dataset page** [4]: The dataset is published on GitHub, provides detailed annotations of racket trajectories and player positions, construction strictly follows BWF specifications.

#### 1.2 ShuttleSet (KDD 2023)
**Sources: arXiv 2306.04948, Semantic Scholar, emergentmind.com** [7][8][9]

ShuttleSet is a human-annotated stroke-level badminton singles dataset for tactical analysis, introduced by Wang et al. (2023) at KDD 2023 (DOI: 10.1145/3580305.3599906).

- **44 broadcast matches from 2018–2021, 104 sets, 3,685 rallies, 36,492 strokes** involving 27 top-ranking men's and women's singles players — the largest publicly available badminton singles dataset with stroke-level annotations.
- Broadcast video from bwf.tv (standardized to 30 fps and 1280×720 resolution).
- Four annotation categories per stroke: rally (set scores, rally winner, lose reason), temporal (hitting time/frame), spatial (player positions, shuttle contact location, grid location, above/below net), and hitting (stroke status, backhand, around-the-head, shot type).
- Original taxonomy contains **18 stroke classes** (net shot, smash, lob, clear, drive, drop, push, service types), supplemented by operational flags.
- Court coordinates via homography, singles court defined as (0,0) to (13.4,6.1).
- Annotated by six trained badminton experts using the S² (Shot-by-Shot) labeling tool with four-stage workflow. Quality control: temporal MAE of 0.24 frames (serve), 0.02 (return), 0 (dead bird); spatial MAE of 0.18 (shuttle) and 0.86 (player position); shot-type accuracy differences of 0.00–0.11 upon re-annotation.
- Distributed through the CoachAI project with Python loader and Flask-based visualization platform used by national teams during international matches.
- Three native benchmark tasks: (1) Stroke influence — ShuttleScorer achieved AUC 0.8371, ACC 0.7869, BR 0.1574; (2) Stroke forecasting — ShuttleNet achieved CE 2.4125, MSE 1.8121, MAE 1.3582 for τ=8; (3) Movement forecasting — DyMF achieved best CE (2.3146), ShuttleNet best MSE (1.0832) and MAE (1.5852).
- ShuttleNet is a Transformer-based position-aware fusion framework with player and rally extractors combined with position-aware gated fusion; outperformed Seq2Seq, CF-LSTM, TF, dNRI, DMA-Nets.
- Known limitations: singles-only coverage, no fixed train/validation/test split (papers construct their own), class imbalance in rare categories, no continuous shuttle trajectories stored, unreliable 3D pose lifting for badminton-specific poses.
- Related datasets cited in references: FineBadminton (multi-level dataset for fine-grained badminton video understanding, ACM Multimedia 2025), S2-Labeling (shot-by-shot microscopic badminton singles tactical dataset, 2022), ShuttleNet (position-aware fusion for stroke forecasting, AAAI 2022).

#### 1.3 ShuttleSet22 (2023/2024)
**Source: arXiv 2306.15664** [10]

ShuttleSet22 is a stroke-level badminton singles dataset collected from high-ranking matches in 2022, extension of ShuttleSet.

- Training set: 30,172 strokes in 2,888 rallies; validation: 1,400 strokes in 450 rallies; testing: 2,040 strokes in 654 rallies; comprising 35 players, 58 matches, 33,612 total strokes from 3,992 rallies.
- Data from public bwf.tv videos, labeled by domain experts using shot-by-shot labeling tool.
- Held Track 2 (Forecasting Future Turn-Based Strokes in Badminton Rallies) of the CoachAI Badminton Challenge 2023 at IJCAI 2023 (~95-100 participants, 16 teams submitting).
- 11 teams outperformed the ShuttleNet baseline (total score 2.8774); top team (Intro_to_AI_team8) achieved total score 2.5776 (CE: 1.7892, MAE: 0.7884). Most improvements in shot type prediction (2.1777→1.7892) rather than area coordinate prediction (0.6997→0.6797).
- Metadata per stroke: shot type, around-head/backhand indicators, landing height, landing area and coordinates, player/opponent locations, rally information, scores, outcomes.

#### 1.4 CoachAI Badminton Challenge 2023 - Track 1
**Source: coachai-challenge-2023 Google site** [11]

Track 1 focuses on automatic annotation of technical data from broadcast badminton match videos using computer vision: temporal, spatial, posture, and skill information (hitting time, ball position, hitting player, swing posture, player standing positions, ball type, winner information).

- Rally-based evaluation, 1 point per clip. If predicted shot count differs from ground truth, 0 points. If count matches, 0.1 points awarded and column content compared for up to 0.9 additional points. HitFrame must be within 2 frames of ground truth.
- Column scoring: Hitter (0.1), BallHeight (0.1), Landing (0.1, within 6 pixels Euclidean distance), HitterLocation (0.05, within 10 pixels), DefenderLocation (0.05, within 10 pixels), Backhand (0.05), RoundHead (0.05), BallType (0.2), Winner (0.1).
- Dataset: BWF international competition videos shot from above and behind players, 30 FPS, 1280×720, MP4 with CSV annotations. 13 annotation fields: VideoName, HitFrame, Hitter (A/B), BallHeight (1 above/2 below net), RoundHead, Backhand, LandingX/Y, HitterLocationX/Y, DefenderLocationX/Y, BallType (1-2 serves, 3-9 returns: Clear, Drive, Smash, Net shot, Drop shot, Lift, Push shot), Winner.
- Access requires filling a Google form.

#### 1.5 Mendeley Frame-Level Badminton Dataset
**Source: data.mendeley.com/datasets/3sp4xntp34** [12]

- Video-based, frame-level dataset of badminton player movements: 884 badminton video recordings organized into individual frames.
- Collected from (1) physical recordings using smartphones/digital cameras in indoor courts from multiple viewing angles, and (2) publicly available YouTube videos.
- Applications: human motion analysis, action recognition and classification, pose estimation and tracking, sports performance evaluation, athlete movement pattern analysis.

---

### 2. Badminton-Specific Action Recognition Methods

#### 2.1 BST: Badminton Stroke-type Transformer (2025/2026)
**Sources: arXiv 2502.21085v1/v2, CVPR 2026 CVsports** [13][14][15]

BST is a novel skeleton-based action recognition architecture for classifying player stroke-types in singles badminton from broadcast match videos, by Jing-Yuan Chang (National Tsing Hua University).

**Video segmentation strategy**: Extracts frames of each player's racket swing, segmenting match videos into stroke clips containing two to three strokes each. Variable-width clipping (vs. fixed-width) captures complete shuttlecock trajectories in three stages: shuttlecock flying toward the target player, trajectory after being hit by target player, and direction after opponent's response.

**Architecture**: Combines player poses (2D skeletal joints from RTMPose via MMPose), shuttlecock trajectories (2D positions from TrackNetV3), and player positions. Derived from TemPose but shifts focus from player poses to shuttlecock trajectory as a primary input. Uses dedicated TCN modules for poses and shuttlecock positions, followed by Transformer Encoders with class tokens. Key innovation: **Cross Transformer Layer (CrossTrans) with Multi-Head Cross Attention** where K and V derived from shuttlecock trajectory latent and Q from player pose/position latent. Argument: shuttlecock trajectory should be primary input since deceptive player movements never misrepresent the actual stroke in the trajectory.

**Model variants**: BST-0 (prototype, poses + trajectory), BST-1 (adds Clean Gate module to refine trajectory info), BST-2 (adds cosine-similarity-based weighting/α coefficient of target player vs. opponent influence), BST-3 (combines BST-1 and BST-2). BST-1/2/3 incorporate player position via Pose Position Fusion (PPF).

**Results on ShuttleSet** (largest public badminton video dataset; 104 sets, 3,685 rallies, 36,492 strokes, 44 matches, 2018-2021; 27 top-ranking players; 35 stroke categories including "None"; after filtering 40 matches, 33,429 strokes: 30 train, 5 validation, 5 test):
- BST-3 with segmentation strategy: Accuracy 0.7710, Macro-F1 0.7042, Acc-2 0.9340
- BST-3 with fixed-width clipping: Accuracy 0.7695, Macro-F1 0.7043, Acc-2 0.9267
- Outperforms ST-GCN (0.728), BlockGCN (0.715), SkateFormer (0.712), ProtoGCN (0.723), and TemPose variants

**Results on other datasets** (CVPR 2026 version):
- ShuttleSet (25 classes, ~33,481 strokes after cleaning): BST-CG-AP achieves 0.8322 accuracy (vs. TemPose-TF at 0.8235) with novel clipping strategy; with fixed-width BST-CG-AP reaches 0.8254
- BadmintonDB (18 classes, 7,658 strokes from Momota vs. Ginting matches): BST-AP achieves 0.6517
- TenniSet (6 classes, 3,569 strokes): BST-AP achieves 0.9923

**Key findings**:
- Effectively leveraging shuttlecock trajectory significantly improves stroke classification performance
- 2D poses outperform 3D poses due to HPE model bias toward general human poses (3D from MotionBERT underperforms)
- Model struggles with high-granularity stroke categories with similar hitting characteristics (e.g., smash vs. wrist smash); defensive return drive has worst recall
- Superior generalization with reduced training sets (25% training data); training BST-3 takes 29 sec/epoch on NVIDIA RTX 4070 Ti Super
- Relies on accurate hit frame detection and shuttlecock tracking models
- Code: https://github.com/Va6lue/BST-Badminton-Stroke-type-Transformer

#### 2.2 Ensemble Learning with Pose Features (2024)
**Source: ScienceDirect, Computers Materials and Continua** [16]

"Improving Badminton Action Recognition Using Spatio-Temporal Analysis and a Weighted Ensemble Learning Model" by Farida Asriani, Azhari Azhari, Wahyono Wahyono (Volume 81, Issue 2, 18 Nov 2024, Pages 3079-3096, DOI: 10.32604/cmc.2024.058193).

- Combines SVM, logistic regression (LR), random forest (RF), and adaptive boosting (AdaBoost).
- Spatial features: 3D distances between each skeleton point and the right hip (33 pose landmarks).
- Temporal features: Fast Dynamic Time Warping (FDTW) applied to 15 frames per video sequence.
- Weighted ensemble uses soft voting classifiers. **E2 ensemble (SVM, LR, AdaBoost) achieved highest accuracy of 95.38%.**
- Cited by 10 subsequent publications.

#### 2.3 Hybrid Deep Learning (YOLOv8n + ResNet50 + r3d_18)
**Source: Scribd** [17]

- Hybrid architecture: YOLOv8n for player detection, ResNet50 for court keypoint extraction, r3d_18 (3D ResNet variant) for shot classification.
- Processes video in real-time for sports analytics and performance evaluation with GUI.

#### 2.4 SDNN/RNN/RNN-GRU (ICIMR 2023)
**Source: XJTLU scholar page** [18]

"Deep Learning Algorithms for Recognition of Badminton Strokes: A Study Using SDNN, RNN, and RNN-GRU Models with Off-Court Video Capture" by Wan Hasbullah Mohd Isa, Muhammad Amirul Abdullah, Mohd Azraai Mohd Razman, Anwar P.P. Abdul Majeed, Ismail Mohd Khairuddin. Published in Advances in Intelligent Manufacturing and Robotics (Springer LNNS Volume 845, pages 53-60, 2024, DOI: 10.1007/978-981-99-8498-5_5).

- Classifies three strokes: forehand drive, forehand clear, and smash.
- Used OpenCV with **MediaPipe keypoints library** for feature extraction; off-court video capture recommended.
- 300 shot videos per stroke, 80:20 training/validation split.

#### 2.5 QCNN with Quantum Mechanics (2025)
**Source: PMC (Scientific Reports)** [19]

"Analysis of motion recognition model for badminton player" (Scientific Reports, May 30, 2025, PMC12125242).

- Hybrid Quantum Convolutional Neural Network (QCNN) using quantum convolutional kernels instead of classical ones.
- Classifies five typical badminton stroke movements. Data from four broadcast/TV badminton matches.
- Features: arm angle (most significant in QCNN), twist angle, footwork position, grip type, step length.
- Preprocessing: data cleaning, Z-score normalization, augmentation (time shifting, rotation/scaling, Gaussian noise).
- 70% training, 15% validation, 15% test split.
- Literature review: LSTM-based action recognition 63-92% accuracy (Liu & Liang 2022); CNN+LSTM+self-attention achieving 97.83% accuracy on 37 badminton actions (Deng et al. 2023); ensemble SVM/RF/LR achieving 95.38% (Asriani et al. 2024); MultiSenseBadminton dataset (Seong et al. 2024) with 7763 swing data points.

#### 2.6 Classical Video Analysis (ICMR 2017)
**Source: ICMR 2017 paper PDF (Chu & Situmeang)** [20]

"Badminton Video Analysis based on Spatiotemporal and Stroke Features" (ICMR '17, Bucharest, June 6-9, 2017) by Wei-Ta Chu and Samuel Situmeang, National Chung Cheng University.

- **Court detection**: White pixel extraction, texture filtering using corner/edge principal values (structure matrix eigenvalues), probabilistic Hough transform for line detection, planar homography estimation.
- **Player detection/tracking**: Adaptive Gaussian mixture model (GMM) background modeling (M=500 frames, 3 Gaussian mixtures), morphological operations, largest connected component detection in top/bottom halves; player position mapped to court model via homography.
- **Stroke classification**: Six stroke types (clear, drive, drop, lob, smash, others) using HOG features from player bounding box with SVM classifier.
- **Strategy classification**: Court divided into nine regions; observation sequences combine stroke type and position; separate HMMs for offensive/defensive strategies using Baum-Welch; maximum likelihood strategy determination.
- Results: Player detection 85.45%; stroke classification 83.33% (5-fold CV, 600 images at 120×150 resolution); strategy classification 70% (automatic features), 83.33% (manually-corrected features). Dataset: 6 videos from BadmintonWorld.TV, 558 plays, 854×480.

#### 2.7 Shot Refinement via Shuttlecock Tracking + Hit Detection (2024)
**Source: MDPI Sensors** [21]

"Enhancing Badminton Game Analysis: An Approach to Shot Refinement via a Fusion of Shuttlecock Tracking and Hit Detection from Monocular Camera" (Sensors, 24(13), July 5, 2024, DOI: 10.3390/s24134372) by Yi-Hua Hsu, Chih-Chang Yu, Hsu-Yung Cheng.

- Modules: DensePose pose estimation (ankle coordinates projected to aerial view via perspective transformation); TrackNet shuttlecock tracking (VGG16 backbone first 13 layers + DeconvNet-inspired layers, with trajectory smoothing: denoising, curve fitting, interpolation); YOLOv7-based swing action detection.
- Novel **Shot Refinement Algorithm (SRA)** fuses trajectory-based hit detection (Peak Identification Method, Direction Identification Method) with YOLOv7 swing detection across five cases: (1) one trajectory hit = correct; (2) multiple hits with no player ID = false positives removed; (3) multiple hits in player's segment = only hit closest to highest-confidence frame retained; (4) no trajectory hit = detection miss, highest-confidence action frame becomes hit moment; (5) no hit/no player ID = true negative.
- Results on 69 BWF match videos, 1,582 rallies: **89.7% accuracy, 91.3% recall, 90.5% F1** vs. TrackNet alone (58.8% accuracy, 93.6% recall, 72.3% F1). Shot type classification accuracy at three thresholds: 72.1%, 65.4%, 54.1%.
- Badminton shuttlecocks reach top speeds of 493 km/h.

#### 2.8 Ready-to-Serve Detection (2024)
**Source: Semantic Scholar (ICEIC 2024)** [22]

"Ready-to-Serve Detection in Badminton Videos" by See Shin Yue, Raveendran Paramesran, Ganesh Krishnasamy (ICEIC, DOI: 10.1109/ICEIC61013.2024.10457177). Uses court details and player poses with CNN to classify ready-to-serve vs. non-serve strokes. Citing works include: "SerViT: A Vision Transformer-Based Model for Service Detection in Badminton Match Videos" (2026), "Harnessing the Power of Transformer Networks in AI-Driven Decision Support Systems for Badminton Action Recognition" (2024), "A high-precision and efficient method for badminton action detection in sports using You Only Look Once with Hourglass Network" (2024), "A Comparative Analysis of Deep Learning Models and Gradient Computation for Rally Detection in Badminton Videos" (2025, BiLSTM and CNN for service start/rally end detection). Key references: automated serve scene detection using CHLAC and MRA (Yoshikawa et al., 2010); automated badminton smash recognition using CNNs (Rahmad et al., 2020); shot detection using skeleton position (Yoshikawa et al., 2021); TemPose skeleton-based transformer (Ibh et al., 2023); MonoTrack for shuttle trajectory reconstruction (Liu & Wang, 2022).

#### 2.9 Shuttlecock Hitting Event Detection (2023)
**Source: GitHub wish44165** [23]

"A New Perspective for Shuttlecock Hitting Event Detection" (IT4PSS Workshop at IJCAI 2023, 2nd place silver).

- **SwingNet** (MobileNetV2 + bidirectional LSTM) captures features/patterns of badminton hitting events; optical flow pre-processing reduces learning difficulty.
- Pipeline: TrackNetV2 (shuttlecock tracking), SwingNet (hitting event detection from GolfDB), Vision Transformers (ViT-B_16) for hitter/roundhead/backhand/ballheight/balltype/winner attributes, YOLOv5 for locations, YOLOv8 pose (yolov8x-pose-p6.pt) for hitter/defender locations.
- Competition results: AICUP2023 public score 0.0727 (rank 11/30), private 0.0622 (11/30); CodaLab2023 Track 1 final 0.3483 (rank 2/2).
- Code and trained models on Zenodo (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.14677727); paper on arXiv (2306.10293).

#### 2.10 Event Camera Swing Trajectory Reconstruction (2026)
**Source: Nature Scientific Reports** [24]

"Fine reconstruction of badminton swing dynamic trajectory assisted by event camera" (Scientific Reports 16, Article 15444, 2026) by Yi Wang, Bo Shi, Bin Lv.

- Smash actions can exceed 100 m/s with durations of tens of milliseconds; frame-based cameras suffer from motion blur.
- Event camera (iniVation DAVIS346) + high-speed RGB camera (240 fps) + nine-axis IMU (500 Hz), hardware-triggered synchronized.
- Voxel grid encoding (B=5 temporal bins, H=260, W=346, Δt=10ms); event optical flow network based on contrast maximization (encoder-decoder, 64→128→256→512 channels, skip connections, 4D cost volume).
- Pose estimation: YOLOv5s + HRNet; elbow joint angle via vector geometry.
- Extended Kalman filter (EKF) fuses event optical flow, visual keypoints, IMU into 12-dimensional state vector. Results on 960 swing samples from 12 athletes: trajectory MAE 8.34 mm (42.3% reduction), 82 FPS processing, event optical flow contributes 52.0% of gain, multimodal fusion improves accuracy 36.8%.

#### 2.11 Wearable IMU-Based Stroke Recognition (2025)
**Sources: Scientific Reports (nature.com), d-nb.info** [25][26]

"Wearable sensing for badminton stroke recognition with one-dimensional convolutional neural network" (Scientific Reports 15, Article 41236, 2025) by Guohan Jin and Xin Li, Chengdu University.

- Two nine-axis HWT906 IMUs at distal wrist radius and lower racket handle; ESP32 microcontroller for time synchronization.
- 100 Hz sampling via SPI; sliding window segmentation (100 samples/window, 50-sample stride, 50% overlap).
- 1D-CNN: two convolutional layers (8 and 16 filters, 3×1 kernels), batch normalization, ReLU, max-pooling, fully connected, Softmax; cross-entropy loss, Adam (lr 0.005, batch 64, up to 500 epochs, early stopping patience 10).
- Six male national-level athletes; SIBOASI smart serving machine (SS-S4025A) for consistent serves; stratified 5-fold cross-validation.
- **Results: 97.16% ± 0.6% for six stroke actions** (Forehand Clear, Forehand Drop, Forehand Smash, Forehand Lift, Forehand Net Tumble, Forehand Cross-Net Shot); **86.07% ± 1.1% for fifteen shot trajectories** (including Forehand Straight Clear/Drop/Smash, Forehand Cross-Court Clear/Drop/Smash, Overhead Cross-Court Clear/Drop/Smash, Forehand Cross-Court Lift, Backhand Cross-Court Lift, Forehand/Backhand Net Cross Shot, Backhand Drop Shot, Backhand Clear Shot).
- Outperformed KNN (94.94%/78.71%), SVM (94.32%/75.06%), DTA (92.81%/72.93%).
- Confusions: FL vs FNS due to similar racket face angles in pre-hit phase; FSS/FCS differ only in Z-axis peak angular velocity; FSS/OCS differ only in Y-axis rotation.
- Prior work review: Lin et al. 78-84%; Peralta et al. 93% average CNN; Steels et al. 86-99% depending on sensors/placement (2020, 86% precision, nine activities, 50 Hz CNN); Van Herbruggen et al. 85% IMUs and 88.99% IMU+UWB; Wang et al. 2019 98.65%.

**Source: Semantic Scholar** [27]

"Badminton stroke classification based on accelerometer data: from individual to generalized models" by Daniel Peralta, Ben Van Herbruggen, Jaron Fontaine, Wout Debyser, Jorg Wieme, Eli De Poorter (2022 IEEE International Conference on Big Data, pages 5542-5548, DOI: 10.1109/BigData55660.2022.10020984).

### 3. Skeleton-Based and Graph Convolutional Methods

#### 3.1 MMAction2 Skeleton Model Zoo
**Source: mmaction2.readthedocs.io** [28]

Documentation for skeleton-based action recognition models in MMAction2 (OpenMMLab):

**AGCN (2s-AGCN)**: Graph topology uniformly or individually learned via backpropagation end-to-end; models first-order (joints) and second-order (bones) information. NTU60_XSub_2D four-stream: 92.34% top-1; NTU60_XSub_3D: 90.89%. 3.5M params, 4.4G FLOPs (2D)/6.5G (3D).

**PoseC3D**: CNN approach using 3D heatmap stack instead of graph sequence; more effective at spatiotemporal features, more robust to pose estimation noise, generalizes better cross-dataset; handles multi-person without extra computation. Results: FineGYM 93.5% (keypoint)/93.6% (limb), NTU60_XSub 93.6% keypoint (fusion 94.0%), UCF101 86.8%, HMDB51 69.6%, Kinetics400 47.4%. SlowOnly-R50 backbone, ~2-3.2M params.

**STGCN**: Automatically learns spatial and temporal patterns from skeleton data. NTU60_XSub_2D four-stream 92.34%; NTU60_XSub_3D four-stream 90.39%; NTU120_XSub_2D 85.23%; NTU120_XSub_3D 86.19%. 3.1M params.

**STGCN++**: From PYSKL open-source toolbox (v0.2); implements six skeleton recognition algorithms under unified framework; state-of-the-art on eight of nine benchmarks; strong baseline without complicated attention schemes. NTU60_XSub_2D four-stream 92.77%; NTU60_XSub_3D four-stream 91.87%. 1.39M params (2D)/1.4M (3D).

- Multi-stream fusion ratios: joint:bone=1:1 (two-stream), joint:joint-motion:bone:bone-motion=2:1:2:1 (four-stream).

#### 3.2 ST-GCN++ Tutorial
**Source: Datature blog** [29]

- ST-GCN treats human body as a graph where nodes represent joints and edges represent spatial relationships; ST-GCN++ removes complicated attention mechanisms and reduces computational overhead for real-time recognition.
- ST-GCN++ annotations follow HRNet 2D skeleton similar to COCO-Pose with 17 keypoints.
- Example: 97.5% Top-1 accuracy on sit-stand recognition (NTU-RGB+D subset, 25 keypoints).
- Training via PYSKL: custom skeleton added in pyskl/pyskl/utils/graph.py (function get_layout() line 97), adjacency matrix in pyskl/pyskl/datasets/pipelines/pose_related.py (class JointToBone, line 295).
- Integration with YOLOv8 pose estimation demonstrated.
- References: NTU RGB+D (Shahroudy et al., CVPR 2016), PYSKL (Duan et al., 2022), ST-GCN original (Yan et al., AAAI 2018), ST-GCN++ (arXiv:2205.09443).

### 4. Transferable Racquet Sport Datasets

#### 4.1 FineGym (CVPR 2020)
**Sources: arXiv 2004.06704, official page, supplementary PDF, HyperAI** [30][31][32][33]

FineGym is a hierarchical video dataset for fine-grained action understanding built on official recordings of top-level gymnastics competitions, by Dian Shao, Yue Zhao, Bo Dai, Dahua Lin (CUHK-SenseTime Joint Lab). CVPR 2020 Oral.

- **Structure**: Three semantic levels (event, set, element) and two temporal levels (action and sub-action). Events: vault (VT), floor exercise (FX), uneven bars (UB), balance beam (BB). Sets: mid-level categories (leap-jump-hop, beam-turns, flight-salto, flight-handspring, dismounts). Elements: finest categories (e.g., "double salto backward tucked").
- 10 event categories (6 male, 4 female); 4 female events with detailed fine-grained annotations. FineGym v1.0: 303 competition records (~708 hours), 530 defined element categories (354 with at least one instance), 4,883 action instances, 32,697 sub-action instances. Instance counts per element range 1 to 1,648 (heavy-tail). Subsets: Gym99, Gym288, Gym530.
- Collection: official competition videos (720P/1080P, >95% high-res); element labels via manually constructed decision trees based on FIG Code of Points; trained annotation team with rigorous quality control; millisecond-level timestamps.
- **Key empirical findings**: (1) Sparse frame sampling (3 frames) sufficient for event/set-level but insufficient for element-level—performance on Gym99 improves up to 12 frames (30% of all frames); (2) Motion features (optical flow) contribute significantly more than appearance at fine granularities, except vault; (3) Temporal dynamics crucial—TRN and TSM outperform TSN by large margins; frame shuffling causes significant drops; (4) Pre-training on Kinetics not always beneficial for fine-grained recognition due to temporal pattern gaps; (5) ST-GCN struggles due to pose estimation failures on gymnastics instances; (6) Sub-action temporal action localization (mAP@tIoU avg 9.6) far more challenging than action localization (mAP@tIoU avg 49.4).
- Evaluated methods: TSN, TRN, TSM, I3D, Non-local I3D, ActionVLAD, ST-GCN.
- Implementation details: TSN uses BNInception, 3 segments, dropout 0.8; TRN with multi-scale (TRNms); TSM ResNet-50, 3 segments; ActionVLAD VGG-16, 10 frames, 64 VLAD clusters; I3D ResNet-50-based, 8-frame clips from 16 consecutive frames stride 2; Non-local I3D with Gaussian embedding at res3b, res3d, res4b, res4d, res4f; ST-GCN uses Cascade R-CNN + HR-Net.
- Available: https://sdolivia.github.io/FineGym/, CC BY-NC 4.0. The paper (arXiv:2004.06704) is supported by SenseTime Collaborative Grant and Hong Kong GRF (No. 14203518, 14205719).

#### 4.2 TTStroke-21 Table Tennis Dataset (MediaEval)
**Sources: MediaEval 2020 paper, MediaEval 2022 task page, sigport.org** [34][35][36]

TTStroke-21 is a table tennis stroke dataset recorded at the University of Bordeaux in natural (ecological) conditions using cheap cameras (GoPro), without markers or body-worn sensors.

- **20 stroke classes plus a rejection class**: 8 services (forehand/backhand variations of Backspin, Loop, Sidespin, Topspin), 6 offensive strokes (Forehand/Backhand Hit, Loop, Flip), 6 defensive strokes (Forehand/Backhand Push, Block, Backspin). All strokes divided into two super-classes: Forehand and Backhand.
- Spatio-temporal samples of size (W, H, T) = (120, 120, 100); faces blurred using OpenCV SSD-ResNet face detector; MPEG-4 videos with XML annotation files (start frame, end frame, stroke class).
- Manual annotation by professional players/teachers; privacy: destroy data by October 1, 2021.
- **Evaluation**: per-class accuracy (Ai) and global accuracy (GA); confusion matrices for all classes, stroke types, forehand/backhand super-classes. Prior years' participants achieved max accuracy 22.9%, 14.1%, 11.3%.
- MediaEval 2022 subtasks: (1) Classification (20 classes + non-stroke); (2) Detection — IoU metric on temporal segments. Baseline on GitHub: ccp-eva/SportTaskME22.
- 15 annotators with 25% overlap between annotations of successive strokes due to difficulty determining boundaries during fast exchanges. Low inter-class variability makes task more challenging than UCF-101 or Kinetics.
- Organizers: Jordan Calandre, Pierre-Etienne Martin, Boris Mansencal, Jenny Benois-Pineau, Renaud Péteri, Julien Morlier, Laurent Mascarilla (La Rochelle and Bordeaux, France).

**Optical flow study** (sigport.org, ICIP poster): Compared BP, Deep Flow, DIS (Dense Inverse Search) for fine-grained table tennis stroke classification with 3D CNNs using Siamese Spatio-Temporal CNN (SSTCNN). Better flow estimator did not improve classification accuracy. Normalization had strong influence: Max normalization ~53.5/38.5 (BP/Deep Flow) train, ~44/27.6 test; Normal normalization ~88.5/34 train, ~74.1/26.7 test (best with BP, +30%); Log normalization ~97.8/45.3 train, ~68.1/41.4 test. aMSE appears good metric for evaluating flow estimators for classification.

#### 4.3 Table Tennis Stroke Recognition with 2D Pose (CVPRW 2021)
**Source: CVF Open Access** [37]

"Table Tennis Stroke Recognition Using Two-Dimensional Human Pose Estimation" (CVPR 2021 CVsports) by Kulkarni et al.

- Dataset: 11 basic strokes (topspin, block, push, flick, lob in forehand/backhand variants, plus forehand flat) from 14 professional players; 22,111 videos, 6,984,224 data points, 873,028 frames (avg 39.48 frames/stroke).
- Novel collection setup: wooden camera frame on table (height 135mm, below 152.5mm net), Raspberry Pi 4 + camera at 105mm above table, 1280×720, 60fps; two SW-420 vibration sensors automated recording/labeling.
- Pose: SSD detection + HRNet 2D pose; four joints (wrist, elbow, two shoulders) = 8 features per time step, 100 standard time steps; Savitzky-Golay filtering (window 13, polynomial order 2).
- **Results**: TCN and TCN+LSTM both 99.37% validation accuracy; LSTM 96.43%; SVM (RBF, c=800) 98.37%; XGBoost 98.10%; Random Forest 96.20%; KNN k=3 92.40%. TCN ~206,299 trainable params, inference 0.79s per 20,000 strokes on RTX 3070. HRNet COCO-trained outperformed MPII-trained (99.37% vs 82.36%). Savgol filtering improved 97.74%→99.37%. Player A generalization: 98.72%; Player B (left-handed): 88.81% initially, 38% on forehand push, after 2-epoch fine-tuning 99.22%.

#### 4.4 Table Tennis Multi-Label Classification (Sensors 2025)
**Source: MDPI** [38]

"Stroke Classification in Table Tennis as a Multi-Label Classification Task with Two Labels Per Stroke" (Sensors 25(3):834, January 30, 2025) by Yuta Fujihara, Tomoyasu Shimada, Xiangbo Kong, Ami Tanaka, Hiroki Nishikawa, Hiroyuki Tomiyama.

- Multi-label approach: two labels per stroke — (1) player posture (forehand/backhand) and (2) ball rotation/velocity (topspin/push/block/flick); head of existing action recognition models bifurcated into two heads, combined for final stroke type.
- Data from OpenTTGames dataset (12 games, 24 players), 8 classes, labeled by experienced player; inputs: raw video and 3D joint coordinates (SimpleBaseline3D, 17 joints per Human 3.6M); non-relevant sides masked black; clips limited to 100 frames.
- Multi-labeling improved validation accuracy up to 8.6% and test accuracy up to 18.1% vs. single-label. 3D joint coordinates outperformed video by 17.1% (validation) and 5.4% (test). Backbones tested: TSTCNN, C3D, I3D, C2D, R(2+1)D, STGCN, AGCN.

#### 4.5 PoseNet Table Tennis MediaEval 2020
**Source: CEUR-WS** [39]

"Leveraging Human Pose Estimation Model for Stroke Classification" by Soichiro Sato, Masaki Aono (Toyohashi University of Technology).

- PoseNet estimates 17 skeletal coordinates (x,y) → "Pose Time Series Data" (T, 17, 2); relative coordinates from first frame, moving average, normalization, zero padding; 120×120 crops centered on average skeletal coordinates.
- Five DNN models with RGB input, variants including Optical Flow (DeepFlow, Zivkovic background subtraction), Pose Time Series Data, Depthwise Separable Convolution; baseline SSTCNN. SGD (lr 0.002, momentum 0.5, decay 0.005), categorical cross entropy, 300 epochs, batch 8. 755 training actions, 354 test.
- Run 5 highest Global Accuracy (16.67%) with all three components; Run 2 highest rough stroke classification (Hand 81.92%, Serve 62.99%, H&S 57.06%); outperformed baseline by 4.8%. Misclassification of fine-grained spin differences.

#### 4.6 Tennis Stroke Datasets

**Tennis action recognition (Stanford CS230)** [40]: GitHub repo chow-vincent/tennis_action_recognition by Vincent Chow and Ohi Dibua. Dataset: 1,980 RGB videos (640×480), 12 possible tennis strokes. Two approaches: (1) LRCNN — Inception V3 features + many-to-many LSTM, softmax averaged across frames; (2) Optical Flow + LSTM. **82.3% test accuracy** consolidated into 6 classes (forehand, backhand, forehand volley, backhand volley, service, smash).

**3DTennisDS (2024)** [41]: Motion capture dataset of four tennis strokes (forehand, backhand, volley forehand, volley backhand) using Vicon optical motion capture (39-marker player, 7-marker racket model); verified using ST-GCNs. Compared with THETIS and Tennis-Mocap datasets. DOI: 10.12913/22998624/191264.

**Tennis strokes A3T-GCN (Sensors 2023)** [42]: "Temporal Pattern Attention for Multivariate Time Series of Tennis Strokes Classification" by Maria Skublewska-Paszkowska and Pawel Powroznik (Sensors 23(5):2422, DOI: 10.3390/s23052422). Eight-camera Vicon at 100 Hz; Plug-in Gait model with 39 markers + 7-marker racket rigid body; 10 participants; backhand 212, forehand 197, forehand volley 180, backhand volley 180 strokes. **A3T-GCN (Attention Temporal Graph Convolutional Network)** adapted from traffic prediction with BiRNN instead of GRU, MLP at output, 3-layer GCN for spatial features; M=39 nodes without racket, M=46 with racket. **Highest accuracy up to 93% using whole silhouette + racket**; outperformed prior ST-GCN (68.9%) and earlier A3T-GCN studies (forehand <80%, backhand <77%). T-test t = -8.2753 (α=0.05) confirmed racket inclusion significance; LOOCV with RMSE.

**Key postures tennis (ISSC 2010)** [43]: Single low-cost camera, background subtraction, 7 Hu moments, Mahalanobis distance to three key postures per stroke (serve: throw ball, mid-point, post-contact). Serve threshold 12.5. AXIS 215 PTZ camera 2.8m above court behind baseline. High accuracy distinguishing serves vs. forehands/backhands; per-frame analysis preferred over MHI/MEI for rapid movements.

**TenniSet** (referenced in BST paper [14]): 6 classes, 3,569 strokes; BST-AP achieves 0.9923 accuracy.

**BadmintonDB** (referenced in BST paper [14]): 18 classes, 7,658 strokes from Momota vs. Ginting matches; BST-AP achieves 0.6517 accuracy.

**Badminton Olympic dataset** (referenced in VideoBadminton paper [1]): 10 videos, 12 stroke categories.

**ShuttleNet dataset** (referenced in VideoBadminton paper [1]): 43,191 clips, 10 categories.

### 5. Fine-Grained Sports Recognition Insights (FineGym Findings)

The FineGym paper [31][32] provides the most influential findings for fine-grained sports action recognition:
- Element-level action recognition raises great challenges for existing methods
- Sparse sampling is insufficient for fine-grained action recognition (3 frames insufficient; improves up to 12 frames/30% of all frames)
- Motion features (optical flow) contribute significantly more than appearance features at fine granularities
- Temporal dynamics modeling is crucial: TRN and TSM outperform TSN by large margins; TSM performance drops sharply when testing frames differ from training frames while TSN maintains performance due to temporal average pooling
- Pre-training on Kinetics is not always helpful on FineGym due to large gaps in temporal patterns between coarse- and fine-grained actions
- Skeleton-based ST-GCN struggles due to challenges in skeleton estimation on gymnastics instances
- Current methods do not perform well distinguishing complex temporal dynamics such as degree of rotation (number of turns)
- FineGym supports auto-scoring, action generation, multi-attribute prediction, model interpretation/reasoning via decision trees

---

### 6. Challenges Specific to Singles Badminton

Key challenges identified across sources:

1. **Fine-grained distinctions between visually similar strokes**: BST paper [13][14] notes the model struggles with high-granularity categories with similar hitting characteristics (e.g., smash vs. wrist smash). ShuttleSet's 18 fine-grained stroke types introduce greater uncertainty and complexity than prior 10-stroke simplifications [9]. FineGym similarly found distinguishing complex temporal dynamics (degree of rotation) is a core difficulty [32].

2. **Fastest ball speeds in sport**: "Badminton is the fastest racket game" [20]; shuttlecocks reach top speeds of 493 km/h [21]; smash actions exceed 100 m/s with durations of tens of milliseconds, causing motion blur in frame-based cameras [24].

3. **Camera angle variability across tournaments**: Broadcast videos from bwf.tv at 30fps/1280×720 with camera positioned above and behind players [7][11]. VideoBadminton used a fixed behind-baseline setup with 30-degree tilt [1]. Generalization across venues, lighting conditions, player styles is an acknowledged concern [24].

4. **Occlusion and pose estimation failures**: Skeleton-based methods depend on accurate pose estimation; pose estimation failures on gymnastics instances hurt ST-GCN in FineGym [31]. 3D pose lifting is unreliable for badminton-specific poses in ShuttleSet [7]. HRNet COCO-trained outperformed MPII-trained for table tennis [37].

5. **Short stroke duration**: Table tennis stroke clips average 39.48 frames at 60fps (~0.66s) [37]; TTStroke-21 clips are 100 frames [35]. Badminton strokes require temporal boundaries around the hit moment — the CoachAI challenge requires HitFrame within 2 frames of ground truth [11]. Stroke annotation overlap of 25% was allowed in TTStroke-21 due to difficulty determining boundaries during fast exchanges [35].

6. **Swing speed and temporal boundaries**: The BST paper's variable-width clipping strategy captures complete shuttlecock trajectories in three stages (incoming, outgoing, opponent response) [13][14]. Shot refinement fuses trajectory-based hit detection with swing detection to resolve false positives and misses [21].

7. **Data imbalance and rare categories**: ShuttleSet has class imbalance in rare categories [7]; FineGym element instance counts range 1 to 1,648 (heavy-tail) [31].

---

### 7. Evaluation Approaches

- **Top-1/Top-5 accuracy and Mean Class Accuracy**: Used by VideoBadminton benchmark [1]. Top-1 = proportion where top prediction matches true label; Top-5 = true label among top five predictions [29].
- **Confusion matrices for similar strokes**: Used in table tennis (TTStroke-21 evaluation includes confusion matrices for all classes, stroke types, forehand/backhand super-classes) [34][35]. Confusion analysis in wearable badminton study: FL vs FNS due to similar racket face angles; FSS/FCS differ only in Z-axis peak angular velocity [25]. MediaEval per-class accuracy and global accuracy [34].
- **Temporal action localization metrics**: FineGym reports mAP@tIoU (sub-actions avg 9.6 vs actions avg 49.4) [31]. TTStroke-21 MediaEval 2022 Subtask 2 uses IoU on temporal segments [35]. CoachAI Track 1 requires HitFrame within 2 frames [11].
- **ShuttleSet benchmarks**: Stroke influence (AUC, ACC, BR), stroke forecasting (CE, MSE, MAE), movement forecasting [7][9].
- **Other metrics**: Acc-2 (BST, binary accuracy of stroke categories), Macro-F1 [13][14]; IoU for tennis detection subtask [35]; precision/recall/F1 for shot refinement (89.7%/91.3%/90.5%) [21]; accuracy/precision/recall/F1 for tennis A3T-GCN [42].
- **Data splits**: 8:1:1 train/val/test for VideoBadminton [1]; 80:20 for SDNN/RNN [18]; 95%-5% for table tennis pose [37]; 60/20/20 for tennis [42]; 70/15/15 for QCNN [19]; stratified 5-fold CV for wearable [25].
- **Multi-stream fusion ratios**: joint:bone=1:1 (two-stream), joint:joint-motion:bone:bone-motion=2:1:2:1 (four-stream) in MMAction2 [28].

### 8. Recommended Approaches and Research Directions

**Skeleton-based methods are most promising for fine-grained badminton recognition** [1][13][14][37][38]:
- ST-GCN and PoseC3D outperformed all video-based methods on VideoBadminton (60.70% and 59.98% Top-1 vs. 53.53% for Swin, 45.45% TimeSformer) [1]
- 3D joint coordinates outperformed video input for table tennis multi-label classification by 17.1% validation / 5.4% test [38]
- 2D poses outperform 3D poses for badminton due to HPE model bias toward general human poses [13][14]
- TCN with 2D pose features achieved 99.37% on table tennis [37]

**Shuttlecock trajectory as a primary input is a trend**:
- BST demonstrated that effectively leveraging ball trajectory significantly improves stroke classification, arguing trajectory is a trend for racket sports action recognition [13][14]
- TrackNet/TrackNetV2/TrackNetV3 for shuttlecock tracking [21][23]
- Shot refinement fusing trajectory hit detection with swing detection [21]

**Spatio-temporal fusion and attention**:
- Cross Transformer Layer with Multi-Head Cross Attention (Q from poses, K/V from trajectory) [13][14]
- A3T-GCN (Attention Temporal GCN) for tennis with racket inclusion [42]
- CNN+LSTM+self-attention achieved 97.83% on 37 badminton actions (Deng et al. 2023, cited in [19])

**Multi-label decomposition for fine-grained strokes**:
- Decomposing strokes into posture + spin/velocity labels improved table tennis test accuracy by up to 18.1% [38]
- Multi-label approaches help distinguish visually similar strokes

**Temporal modeling**:
- TRN and TSM outperform TSN for fine-grained recognition; temporal dynamics are crucial [31][32]
- Variable-width clipping around hit frames (including opponent context strokes) improves accuracy [13][14]
- SwingNet (MobileNetV2 + BiLSTM) for hitting event detection [23]

**Transfer learning caveats**:
- Pre-training on Kinetics is not always beneficial for fine-grained recognition due to temporal pattern gaps [31]
- Generalized models require more players, data augmentation, transfer learning [27]
- Fine-tuning on player-specific data dramatically improves generalization (38%→99.22% for left-handed player in table tennis) [37]

**Data augmentation and noise handling**:
- Savitzky-Golay filtering of pose keypoints improved table tennis accuracy 97.74%→99.37% [37]
- Clean Gate modules to filter trajectory noise [13][14]
- Lens distortion correction (OpenCV) [1]

**Evaluation protocol recommendations**:
- Rally-based scoring with strict HitFrame tolerance (2 frames) [11]
- Joint evaluation of classification and temporal localization [35]
- Confusion matrix analysis for similar stroke pairs (smash vs. wrist smash; lift vs. net tumble) [13][25]

**Promising future directions**:
- Event cameras for high-speed swing reconstruction (microsecond temporal resolution, 120+ dB dynamic range) [24]
- Extension to doubles, tennis, table tennis [13][14]
- FineBadminton multi-level dataset for fine-grained badminton video understanding (ACM Multimedia 2025) [8]
- Real-time systems (82 FPS event camera processing [24]; TCN inference 0.79s per 20,000 strokes [37])
- Unifying forecasting, recognition, localization, transfer, and report generation on ShuttleSet as a common substrate [7]

--- SOURCE 1: Deep learning neural network-assisted badminton movement recognition and physical fitness training optimization ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11620146

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in Heliyon (October 2, 2024) titled "Deep learning neural network-assisted badminton movement recognition and physical fitness training optimization," authored by Chuanbao He (Department of Physical Education, Tianjin Sino-German University of Applied Sciences, China) and Min Zhang (Graduate School, Metharath University, Bangkok, Thailand). The corresponding author is Chuanbao He (hechuanbao@tsguas.edu.cn). The article is open access under a CC BY-NC-ND license.

**Objective:** The research addresses the problem of low accuracy in recognizing badminton movement trajectories, focusing on the visual system of badminton robots for lateral detection and tracking of flying badminton in two-dimensional video streams.

**Methodology:**
1. **Visual system design:** Image segmentation and edge detection separate badminton from backgrounds; Kalman filtering enables real-time tracking.
2. **CNN with attention mechanisms:** A dedicated CNN architecture with convolutional layers, pooling layers, fully connected layers, and ReLU activation functions extracts features from lateral badminton images. Attention modules adjust feature map weights to focus on critical information, improving robustness against variations and noise.
3. **Improved Tiny YOLOv2:** The network was enhanced by adding convolutional layers, increasing channels, adjusting receptive field sizes, and introducing residual connections to mitigate gradient vanishing. The loss function was revised to incorporate trajectory information (position and movement direction), optimizing localization, confidence, classification, and trajectory losses.
4. **Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF):** Combined with the improved Tiny YOLOv2, the UKF predicts future badminton positions using Sigma points propagated through nonlinear functions, accounting for factors like wind force.

**Dataset:** A custom dataset was created with 15 badminton flight video streams captured via stereo vision cameras across scenarios including laboratories, parking lots, sports arenas, forests, and roadsides. Scenes were categorized as simple or complex based on background, lighting, and interference. Each scene contains ~100-150 consecutive frames (~1000 total frames), split into training/testing sets at a 2:1 ratio. Training parameters: learning rate 0.001, batch size 16, epochs 50, ReLU activation, 3x3 convolution kernels. Hardware: NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU with TensorFlow and CUDA.

**Key Results:**
- Average tracking accuracy: 91.40%; recall rate: 84.60%
- F1 score: 87.68%; frame rate: 13.792 FPS; IoU: 0.922
- Average precision, recall, and frame rate in four simple/complex scenarios: 96.7%, 95.7%, and 29.2 FPS respectively
- Per-scenario results: Orange wall (precision 97.14%, recall 90.91%, F1 93.92%, 19.76 FPS); Green wall (95.12%, 93.67%, F1 94.39%, 26.3 FPS); Laboratory (90.91%, 89.47%, F1 90.18%, 7.36 FPS); Parking lot (92.5%, 69.64%, F1 79.46%, 7.11 FPS); Park (81.34%, 79.45%, F1 80.47%, 8.43 FPS)
- Average predicted position error: ~3.76 pixels; average predicted distance error: ~0.26 m; maximum errors ~8.80 pixels and 0.60 m
- Average total time consumption for prediction: ~35.03 ms

**Conclusions:** The proposed method outperforms other classic algorithms in badminton trajectory detection and prediction, demonstrating superior accuracy, robustness, and adaptability across various complex scenarios, providing reliable support for badminton movement recognition and physical fitness training optimization.
</summary>

The average precision, recall, and frame rate of the measured trajectories in four simple and complex scenarios of badminton flight video streams are 96.7%, 95.7%, and 29.2 frames/second, respectively."

--- SOURCE 6: Enhancing Badminton Game Analysis: An Approach to Shot Refinement via a Fusion of Shuttlecock Tracking and Hit Detection from Monocular Camera ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/24/13/4372

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an open-access research article published in Sensors (MDPI) journal, Volume 24, Issue 13, on July 5, 2024 (DOI: 10.3390/s24134372), titled "Enhancing Badminton Game Analysis: An Approach to Shot Refinement via a Fusion of Shuttlecock Tracking and Hit Detection from Monocular Camera." The authors are Yi-Hua Hsu (Chung Yuan Christian University, Taiwan), Chih-Chang Yu (Chung Yuan Christian University, Taiwan), and Hsu-Yung Cheng (National Central University, Taiwan).

**Purpose/Problem:**
The study aims to automatically extract and classify shots in badminton games from monocular camera footage to enable automated sports analytics, helping coaches and players understand opponents' tactics and improve training.

**Methodology:**
The proposed system combines three key modules:
1. **Pose Estimation**: Uses DensePose (chosen over OpenPose due to computational efficiency) to extract player body postures, particularly ankle coordinates, which are projected onto an aerial view via perspective transformation.
2. **Shuttlecock Tracking**: Uses TrackNet, a deep neural network designed for tracking small, fast-moving objects, to extract shuttlecock flight trajectories. TrackNet uses a VGG16 backbone (first 13 layers) with DeconvNet-inspired later layers, plus a trajectory smoothing algorithm with denoising, curve fitting, and interpolation steps.
3. **Shot Refinement Algorithm (SRA)**: The novel contribution of this study. **Methodology:** The proposed method consists of two modules: (1) a detection and pose estimation module for past frames, and (2) a time-series model module for future prediction. **Key results:** The proposed method improved average displacement error (ADE) by approximately 13% compared to methods using only shuttlecock position information, and by approximately 8.4% compared to methods using both shuttlecock and player position information. Data augmentation included left-right flipping (50% probability) and translations up to 50 pixels.

**Limitations:** Camera positioning (requires distant recording setup), and difficulty adapting to sudden trajectory changes at the moment of hitting back or when the shuttlecock touches the floor.

**Overview:** CalTennis is a large-scale video benchmark for evaluating monocular-to-3D pose estimation in real-world ("in the wild") settings. It comprises over 11 million frames (51 hours) of tennis practice and match play from 40 players, captured with 2-6 synchronized cameras at 60 Hz. The dataset is 10 times larger than existing in-the-wild human motion video datasets (like 3DPW) and 3 times larger than existing MOCAP-ground-truthed datasets (like Human3.6M), making it the first large-scale benchmark providing synchronized multi-view recordings of expert athletic motion.

**Key Innovations:**
- **Label-free evaluation via multi-view consistency:** Instead of relying on MOCAP ground truth, CalTennis leverages the redundancy of multiple camera views — if a pose estimation model is accurate, its 3D reconstructions from different camera views should be identical when aligned in a shared global coordinate system. Any cross-view disagreement serves as a quantifiable lower bound on reconstruction error.
- **Court geometry for calibration:** Tennis court line intersections (service lines, baselines, sidelines) provide fixed reference points enabling precise, fully automated camera calibration without manual measurements or specialized equipment.
- **Standardized data collection protocol:** Simple, reproducible protocol enabling data collection without specialized equipment or expertise.

**Novel Performance Metrics Introduced:**
1. **Footwork** — detects foot skating/gliding and floating players
2. **Stability** — detects body "jitter" and spatial oscillation
3. **Body shape consistency** — evaluates consistency of body height/limb lengths across camera views

**Benchmark Results (5 SOTA models evaluated: PromptHMR, GVHMR, GENMO, WHAM, TRAM):**
- **Depth/Translation failures:** All models struggled with absolute depth. Translation errors ranged from 0.9m to over 3.6m. Models exhibited "drifting" — players appearing to oscillate along the camera's depth axis even when standing still. PromptHMR was most accurate for translation (due to sophisticated 2D bounding box use) but was also the slowest.
- **Foot-ground contact:** Significant "foot skating" errors persisted even in WHAM, which specifically incorporated foot-ground contact refinements. This makes current models unreliable for professional sports analytics (stride length, ground reaction forces).
- **Body shape inconsistency:** The most surprising finding — different camera views produced different estimated heights and limb lengths for the same person, with up to 20cm height disagreement across views. This indicates models are biased by camera angle and 2D appearance, not just predicting pose.

**Setup Details:** Camera distance ranged from 13.4m to 16.7m (versus ~5m in lab settings), providing greater depth variability representative of real-world sports broadcasting and coaching scenarios.

**Conclusions:** While 3D joint angle recovery is now quite accurate, current models are not yet ready for high-stakes applications in healthcare or professional sports. The dataset and label-free evaluation framework lower the barrier for other researchers to collect and evaluate motion data in diverse real-world environments, paving the way for more democratic and scalable 3D motion analysis technology development.
</summary>

<summary>
## Multi-Object Tracking — DeepSORT, ByteTrack, OC-SORT, and BoT-SORT (2026)

This article by Nikolay Sapunov (CEO of Fora Soft, published May 27, 2026) provides a comprehensive 2026 guide to multi-object tracking (MOT) for production video systems. Multi-object tracking is the process of maintaining stable identity IDs on the same person, car, or package across video frames, connecting a per-frame object detector to downstream features that reason about trajectories (counting, dwell time, sports overlays, active-speaker detection, surveillance).

### The Tracking-by-Detection Pipeline (4 stages)
1. **Detection** — a detector (YOLO, RT-DETR, Grounding DINO) emits bounding boxes per frame; detector quality dominates everything downstream.
2. **Motion prediction** — Kalman filter (1960s algorithm) predicts next-frame positions using a constant-velocity model with state vector (x, y, aspect_ratio, height, dx, dy, dh, dr).
3. **Association** — cost matrix between tracks and detections (IoU geometric distance, appearance cosine distance, or both), solved with the Hungarian algorithm (O(n³)).
4. **Track lifecycle management** — new tracks born, unconfirmed tracks killed after frames, tentative/confirmed status with birth/death thresholds.

### The Four Tracker Families (2026 production standards)
- **DeepSORT (2017)** — introduced deep appearance embeddings (cosine distance) on top of SORT. MOT17: 60.3 MOTA, 61.2 IDF1, 48.8 HOTA. Historical reference; no longer the default for new projects.
- **ByteTrack (ECCV 2022, Zhang et al.)** — associates every detection box including low-confidence ones via a two-stage cascade. MOT17: 80.3 MOTA, 77.3 IDF1, 63.1 HOTA. Motion-only, <50 lines of Python, MIT-licensed (github.com/ifzhang/ByteTrack), ~2x faster than DeepSORT, ships in Ultralytics YOLO as bytetrack.yaml. The 2026 throughput default.
- **OC-SORT (CVPR 2023, Cao et al.)** — fixes Kalman drift after occlusion via observation-centric re-update and observation-centric momentum. MOT17: 78.0 MOTA, 77.5 IDF1, 63.2 HOTA; beats ByteTrack by 10+ HOTA points on DanceTrack (non-linear motion). Best for dance, gymnastics, parkour, animals, sports with direction changes. MIT-licensed (github.com/noahcao/OC_SORT).
- **BoT-SORT (2022, Aharon et al.)** — adds camera-motion compensation (sparse optical flow + ECC alignment) and appearance embeddings (BoT-S50 Re-ID). MOT17: 80.5 MOTA, 80.2 IDF1, 65.0 HOTA — state of the art at publication. Default tracker in Ultralytics YOLO since 2024 (botsort.yaml). Roughly 30% slower than ByteTrack. MIT-licensed (github.com/NirAharon/BoT-SORT).

### Metrics: Why HOTA Replaced MOTA
- **MOTA (2008)** — detection-biased, underweights identity switches.
- **IDF1** — association-focused but detection-blind (overcorrects).
- **HOTA (2020, Luiten et al.)** — √(DetA × AssA), balanced detection and association, reports sub-scores separately. By 2026, HOTA is the field's ranking metric on MOTChallenge, DanceTrack, and SportsMOT.

### Decision Tree (4 questions)
1. **Is the camera moving?** → BoT-SORT (handheld, drone, vehicle-mounted).
2. **Does motion violate constant-velocity?** → OC-SORT (dance, sports, animals, sudden direction changes).
3. **Many streams/dense scenes?** → ByteTrack (no appearance work, runs at detector speed).
4. **Long-occlusion identity persistence?** → BoT-SORT-ReID (5+ seconds of occlusion, multi-camera handoff).

~80% of projects end at ByteTrack or BoT-SORT-ReID.

### Numeric Example (1280×720, 30 FPS, YOLOv8-S, 20 pedestrians, Intel server CPU)
- ByteTrack: 14.4 ms/frame (432 ms/sec CPU, ~43% of one core); 35 concurrent streams per 16-core server; $0.020/stream-hour on AWS c7i.4xlarge.
- BoT-SORT-ReID: 32.6 ms/frame (978 ms/sec, nearly full core); 16 concurrent streams; $0.044/stream-hour.
- Cost-cutting tip: run tracking at 10 FPS (every third frame) for 3× cost reduction with negligible accuracy loss for counting/dwell/fall-detection features.

### Deployment Topologies
- **Browser** — ByteTrack/OC-SORT via ONNX Runtime Web (BoT-SORT-ReID too heavy in 2026).
- **Edge** — all four fit on Jetson Orin Nano; ByteTrack (throughput) or BoT-SORT-ReID (accuracy); default for security cameras, retail, industrial CV.
- **Server** — BoT-SORT-ReID on CPU with GPU detector; default for sports analytics, broadcast, batch processing.

### Four Production Pitfalls
1. **Blaming the tracker for detector problems** — fix detector first; YOLOv8-N→YOLOv8-X buys 10 points vs. a few HOTA points from tracker swaps.
2. **Using DeepSORT in 2026** — outdated; ByteTrack/BoT-SORT-ReID beat it everywhere.
3. **Leaving Kalman/lifecycle parameters at MOT17 defaults** — tune track_buffer and match_thresh via grid search on deployment data.
4. **Trusting track IDs across camera boundaries** — IDs are local to a camera/tracker run; cross-camera identity requires dedicated Re-ID models, shared feature galleries, and graph-solving.

### Fora Soft Usage (context for the author's recommendations)
Video conferencing (ByteTrack on SFU), retail/IVA (BoT-SORT-ReID on Jetson), OTT/broadcast sports (BoT-SORT-ReID on cloud GPUs), e-learning (ByteTrack), surveillance/security (BoT-SORT-ReID).

The article includes 16 references (DeepSORT, SORT, ByteTrack, OC-SORT, Deep OC-SORT, BoT-SORT, HOTA, StrongSORT, BoostTrack, DanceTrack, SportsMOT, CLEAR-MOT papers and implementations) plus editorial notes indicating the BoT-SORT-ReID HOTA figure is from the 2022 paper (current MOT17 leader in mid-2026 is BoostTrack at ~65.4 HOTA), and that transformer-based trackers (MOTR, TrackFormer) remain research-grade and are not yet production-viable.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 15: An Introduction to BYTETrack: Multi-Object Tracking by ... ---
URL: https://datature.com/blog/introduction-to-bytetrack-multi-object-tracking-by-associating-every-detection-box

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive tutorial article from Datature.io introducing BYTETrack, a multi-object tracking (MOT) algorithm presented at ECCV2022 by Yifu Zhang et al. The article explains the core concepts of MOT, the BYTETrack methodology, and provides a step-by-step tutorial for implementing it with a custom YOLOv8 detector to track basketball players.

**Key Concepts:**
- Multiple Object Tracking (MOT) is a computer vision task that tracks movements of multiple objects over time in video sequences, determining identity, location, and trajectory of each object even when partially or fully occluded.
- MOT typically works in two stages: object detection (using detectors like Faster-RCNN or YOLO) and object association (typically using Kalman Filter for prediction and Hungarian Algorithm for linear assignment).

**Challenges with MOT:** Object motion/appearance variation, occlusion causing ID switching, class switching issues in multi-class trackers, and real-time inference speed limitations.

**BYTETrack Innovation:** The primary innovation is keeping non-background low confidence detection boxes (which are typically discarded after initial filtering) and using them for a secondary association step. Occluded detection boxes have lower confidence scores than the threshold but still contain meaningful information, so retaining them improves tracking consistency.

**Methodology:**
1. Detection boxes are filtered into high-confidence, low-confidence, and background boxes (background boxes are discarded).
2. First association stage: high-score detection boxes matched with predicted boxes from previous frames' tracklets (Kalman filter) using IoU or cosine similarity with Hungarian algorithm.
3. Second association stage: low-score detection boxes matched against remaining unmatched predicted boxes with a lower matching threshold.
4. Lost tracklets are kept for a certain number of frames and can be recovered.

**Implementation Details:** The paper uses YOLOX as the base detector but is customizable to FasterRCNN or other YOLO versions. IoU and ReID both work for first-stage association (ReID better for low-frame-rate videos; IoU more robust for severe occlusion), but second-stage association should always use IoU.

**Tutorial Example:** The author trained a custom YOLOv8m detector on ~90 side-view frames of the 2022 NBA finals between the Warriors and Celtics, tracking three classes: Warriors players, Celtics players, and referees. Annotations were created using Datature Nexus. After 50 epochs (batch size 4, test size 640), the model achieved mAP50 of ~0.9 and mAP50-95 of ~0.65. Since the original BYTETrack implementation is class-agnostic, multiple BYTETracker instances were created for multi-class tracking.

**Key Hyperparameters:** track_thresh = 0.5 (high threshold), track_buffer = 50 (frames lost tracklets kept), match_thresh = 0.8 (first stage matching threshold), aspect_ratio_thresh = 10.0, min_box_area = 1.0, MIN_THRESHOLD = 0.001 (set low to retrieve almost all detections; background threshold hardcoded at 0.1).

**Limitations:** Limited accuracy in crowded scenes due to reliance on IoU matching and trajectory prediction; low-confidence box strategy can introduce noise and track irrelevant objects; no native multi-class tracking support requiring computationally expensive workarounds.

**Conclusion:** BYTETrack is a simple yet effective MOT tracker that uses low-confidence boxes to account for occlusion and appearance changes. It can be adopted to improve existing SOTA MOT algorithms (both motion-based IoU and feature-based ReID) and is suitable for real-time applications like autonomous driving, video surveillance, and augmented reality.
</summary>

**Key Methodology:**

3. **Kalman filter tracking**: A basic Kalman filter implementation (state vector tracking x, y, vx, vy) is used for multi-object tracking across frames. 4. **Player selection heuristic**: Two approaches were tested—selecting boxes nearest the center of the baseline (which proved unreliable) versus picking boxes with the longest tracking history in memory (which proved effective, since GroundingDINO "flickers" between line judges while genuine players maintain stable presence).
5. **Homography for bird's-eye view**: Keypoints (such as line intersections) are identified on the court image and matched to a reference court template to generate a homography matrix using OpenCV's cv2.findHomography(). **Method Framework (4 steps):**
1. Each video frame is processed through the object detector to obtain sets of potential objects.
2. A sliding window with a gap is used to construct a set of graphs from potential target sets.
3. Each graph is fed into the discriminator to obtain probability graphs.
4. Final trajectories are derived from the probability graphs.

**Key Technical Contributions:**
- Decomposition of the tracking problem into relatively independent discriminator (log p(T_u)) and detector (log p(T_u|φ_initial, φ)) components via Bayesian maximum posterior criterion.

- The total loss combines a segmentation cross-entropy loss (Lseg), a binary cross-entropy lane existence loss (Llane), and the proposed LHT loss (applied only when the predicted lane probability exceeds a threshold τ = 0.9).

It describes a modular monocular pipeline that combines court detection, pose estimation, shuttle tracking, hit segmentation (HitNet), and physics-constrained 3D reconstruction for badminton analysis.

**Data & Splits:** Uses TrackNetV2 data (26 international singles matches, ~77K frames; 3 test matches ~12K frames). Additional 40 YouTube videos for court detection testing and 10K synthetic 3D trajectories. Only validates singles games with fixed overhead/static broadcast views. Validation split has near-duplicate leakage risk across rallies.

**Method:** (1) Hough lines + graph-based bipartite partition for court detection; (2) HRNet pose + 3-in/3-out modified U-Net for shuttle detection; (3) ~16K parameter two-layer GRU HitNet fusing court/pose/shuttle with dynamic programming on hit intervals and alternating rules; (4) Per-shot 3D trajectory optimization using drag dynamics, camera reprojection, hitter/receiver priors, and out-of-bounds penalties.

**Key Results:**
- Court success improved 73.9%→85.5%, IoU 0.96→0.97, 40× faster.
- Shuttle detector: 2.9M vs 11.3M parameters; accuracy 88.6% vs 84.0%.
- HitNet F1: shuttle-only 0.815 → +pose 0.850 → +court 0.866 → +constrained optimization 0.946 (recall 94.3%, accuracy 89.7%).
- Synthetic 3D error: 14.9 cm (reprojection-only) vs 8.0 cm (full priors); synthetic results are optimistic since same physical model generates and fits.
- Real data reports only 2D reprojection: GT shuttle/hits 8.1/8.9/9.8 px vs fully automatic 37.1/28.8/23.3 px.
- ~90% hit accuracy can still cause ~20% shot reconstruction errors because one hit error corrupts two adjacent shots.

**Limitations:** No end-to-end FPS/hardware/latency reported (cannot claim real-time full system). Real data has no 3D ground truth; evaluation excludes frequently occluded serves and unlabeled landings. Court failures, out-of-frame events, and hit errors cascade. Synthetic speed of "1500 m/s" conflicts with reality and model constraints.

**Value to four-layer badminton pipeline:** Shuttle tracking (direct evidence, but 88.6% frame accuracy ≠ full trajectory), court/3D reconstruction (baseline; real 3D accuracy unproven), hit/phase alignment (HitNet F1 0.946, singles/fixed view only), and no evidence for action quality assessment (no stroke quality, technical errors, or coaching feedback).

Raw materials are stored at raw/ingest/2026-05-05-monotrack-shuttle-trajectory-reconstruction/. Related pages include TrackNetV2, TrackNetV3, Sports AI video understanding, and Sports AI roadmap topics.

--- SOURCE 1: "Accurate Tennis Court Line Detection on Amateur ... ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.06977

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a research paper titled "Accurate Tennis Court Line Detection on Amateur Recorded Matches" by Sameer Agrawal, Ragoth Sundararajan, and Vishak Sagar from NicheSolv India Private Limited in Bengaluru, India. The paper proposes improvements to traditional homography-based tennis court line detection to handle amateur and non-professional matches.

**Problem:** Traditional Hough-Line-Detection with homography estimation fails on amateur courts due to low camera angles, obscured lines, scuffed courts, and shadows.

**Key Contributions (4 improvements):**
1. **Shadow removal:** Uses two state-of-the-art models — MTMT for shadow-detection (generating a shadow-mask) and ShadowFormer for shadow-removal.
2. **YOLO-v5 net detection:** Detects the tennis net and crops the image to the near-side of the court only, then extends the detected court to the full image — improving accuracy and speed.
3. **Pixel-by-pixel filtering based on court color:** Instead of a fixed pixel threshold (which fails to generalize), the algorithm places 1000 random points, finds the dominant court color, then scans each pixel with a 7x7 neighborhood — if at least 4 pixels match the court color and the central pixel doesn't, it's marked as a court line.
4. **Scoring algorithm:** Runs detection on randomly selected video frames and scores each detection by counting drawn pixels that correspond to bright white pixels in the original image, selecting the highest-scoring (most accurate) detection.

**Results:** Compared against the "Old Method" (threshold=180) on 7 videos (4 amateur, 3 professional). The new method performed better or significantly better on amateur courts (e.g., Court #4: 0.0% → 81.3%; Court #7: 50.8% → 100.0%; Court #1: 60.0% → 84.3%). The only failure was Court #5 (a Wimbledon court with alternating color bands, dropping from 96.0% to 86.0%). Data was collected from self-recorded matches and AmateurTennis.tv since no compiled non-professional datasets exist.

**Future Work:** Exploring CNN-based filtration algorithms, and investigating faster net-detection and shadow-removal models.
</summary>

URL: https://medium.com/@kosolapov.aetp/tennis-analysis-using-deep-learning-and-machine-learning-a5a74db7e2ee

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a technical article by Kosolapov Sergey on Medium describing a tennis analysis system built using deep learning and machine learning, based on a single camera with 25-30 fps (as opposed to sophisticated commercial systems like Hawk-Eye and IBM Slamtracker that require 8-10 high-speed cameras at up to 1,000 fps and are restricted to major tournaments).

The system has four main components:

1. COURT DETECTION: The authors compared a classical computer vision approach (thresholding white pixels, Hough Transform line detection, homography matrix calculation, and reference court comparison) against a deep learning approach. The classical approach was found to be extremely slow (up to 15 seconds per image), low quality, and unstable with different angles/colors/shadows. The deep learning approach uses a neural network similar to TrackNet architecture to detect 14 key points of the tennis court plus one additional center point (15 output channels). The dataset consisted of 8,841 manually filtered images at 1280×720 resolution from YouTube video highlights covering hard, clay, and grass courts. Training used a 75/25 train/test split, Adam optimizer, and 640×360 input resolution. Two postprocessing techniques were applied: (1) cropping around predicted key points and detecting white line intersections using classical CV, and (2) using homography matrix to reconstruct shifted key points. Evaluation used a 7-pixel Euclidean distance threshold for accurate detection, with precision/accuracy/median distance metrics reported.

2. BALL DETECTION: Used TrackNet deep learning network trained on a dataset of 19,835 labeled frames from 10 broadcast videos (1280×720, 30 fps). The network generates a heatmap from a 2D Gaussian distribution centered on the ball (assumed ~10 pixel diameter variance). Training used binary cross entropy loss. Evaluation used a positioning error (PE) specification of 5 pixels (mean ball diameter in videos is ~5 pixels, ranging 2-12 pixels). Frames were labeled with Visibility Class (VC) values 0-3 indicating ball visibility.

3. BOUNCE DETECTION: Used CatBoostRegressor machine learning for binary classification to detect bounce frames from ball trajectory data (features included differences in x/y coordinates between neighboring points and distance relations). Dataset had 18,570 samples with 518 labeled as bounce points. Used 10-fold cross-validation (9 games train, 1 game test) with grid search for hyperparameters (iterations, learning rate, depth). Evaluated on precision and recall, with tolerance of ±1 frame error. Adding 0.5 weight to neighboring bounce points during training improved recall significantly.

4. PLAYER DETECTION: Used pretrained Faster RCNN neural network.

The complete pipeline: (1) court detection with pretrained neural network to get homography matrix per frame, (2) ball detection using 3 consecutive frames, (3) bounce detection, and (4) player detection and movement mapping to the reference court.

The article also lists possible improvements: replacing backbones with lighter nets, quantizing/pruning for speed, combining ball and court detection into one neural network, adding frames without balls to improve ball detection, and using augmentation for court detection training.

The conclusion states the tool can automatically detect and track court, ball trajectory, player movements, and identify outs during a match, with the neural network approach being faster, more robust, and more effective than classical CV methods.

Code implementations are available on GitHub: TennisCourtDetector (https://github.com/yastrebksv/TennisCourtDetector), TrackNet (https://github.com/yastrebksv/TrackNet), and TennisProject (https://github.com/yastrebksv/TennisProject).
</summary>
