## 6. Hidden Markov Models and Probabilistic Graphical Models for Tactic State Inference

**Sources: IJSA [7], Columbia thesis [8], Wikipedia HMM [9], Gimenez book chapter [10], PMC IEEE TAI [11], Springer KNN-HMM [12]**

### 6.1 HMM Fundamentals (Wikipedia)

An HMM is a Markov model in which observations are dependent on a latent (or hidden) Markov process (X). The goal is to learn about the state of X by observing Y. Y at time t0 is influenced exclusively by X at time t0; past outcomes are conditionally independent of Y given X at that time. Parameters estimated via maximum likelihood, with the Baum-Welch algorithm for linear chain HMMs. Hidden states are discrete (categorical distribution); observations can be discrete or continuous (Gaussian). Parameters include N² transition probabilities (N(N-1) free) and emission probabilities (N(M-1) for discrete observations, or NM(M+3)/2 = O(NM²) for multivariate Gaussian observations).

Three inference problems: (1) Probability of an observed sequence (forward algorithm, dynamic programming); (2) Probability of latent variables, including filtering (P(x(t)|y(1..t)), forward algorithm) and smoothing (P(x(k)|y(1..t)) for k<t, forward-backward algorithm); (3) Most likely explanation / most likely hidden state sequence (Viterbi algorithm).

### 6.2 HMM for Momentum/Competitive State Transitions (IJSA 2026)

"Predictive Momentum Modeling through Hidden Markov Competitive State Transitions" by Prof. Larz Schultz (International Journal of Sports Analytics, Volume 7, Issue 1, January-June 2026, Article IJSA_07_01_001, pages 1-6, dated January 19, 2026). Proposes a multi-state Hidden Markov framework where latent states represent momentum regimes (positive, neutral, negative), with transition probabilities estimated via maximum likelihood and Bayesian inference, integrating copula-based multivariate dependence structures and regime-switching mechanisms. Findings: modeling momentum as a latent regime process improves predictive calibration and transition stability over standard Markov chain and ML baselines; hidden competitive state transitions capture structural shifts, tactical adjustments, and psychological momentum effects better than observable-only models.

### 6.3 HMM for Football Season Modeling (Columbia/Boston College Thesis)

James DeAntonis' thesis ("Football Analytics," Boston College, 2017/2018) models NFL game/season outcomes with HMMs where states represent the current winning or losing streak, capturing "momentum" (e.g., probability of winning the next game given the team won its previous two games). Observable "emissions" are game stat lines (points own/against, rushing yards own/against, turnover differential, first down differential) constructed via n-dimensional "mega-bins." Viterbi algorithm derives the most likely hidden state sequence. Overall predictive success rates hovered between .69 and .78 across all bin possibilities tested on 2016. "Chain override rate" (how often Viterbi went against simply picking by the pdfs) was greater than .5, suggesting the underlying Markov chain added predictive power.

### 6.4 Bayesian HMM Foundations (Gimenez Book Chapter)

From "Bayesian analysis of capture-recapture data with hidden Markov models" (Chapter 3): transition matrix Γ with survival probability φ; observation matrix Ω links states to observations. Complete likelihood: Pr(y_i, z_i) = (∏ ω(z(i,t),y(i,t))) × (Pr(z(i,1)) × ∏ γ(z(i,t-1),z(i,t))). Marginalization: brute-force requires 2TN^T calculations (exponential growth); forward algorithm requires only TN² computations. Forward algorithm: α_t(j) = Pr(y1,...,yt, zt=j); initialization α1(j) = Pr(z1=j)ω(j,y1); recurrence α_t(j) = Σ α(t-1)(i)γ(i,j)ω(j,y_t); marginal likelihood Pr(y) = Σ α_T(j). "A hidden Markov model is just two time series running in parallel. One for the states with the Markovian property, and the other of for the observations generated from the states. HMM are a special case of state-space models in which latent states are discrete."

### 6.5 Deep RL for Bayesian HMM Inference (IEEE TAI 2024)

"Deep Reinforcement Learning Data Collection for Bayesian Inference of Hidden Markov Models" (IEEE Transactions on Artificial Intelligence, Dec 12, 2024; Vol 6, Issue 5, article 1217; DOI: 10.1109/tai.2024.3515939) by Mohammad Alali and Mahdi Imani (Northeastern University). Uses a belief state capturing the joint distribution of system states and models; deep reinforcement learning policy (Deep Q-Network/DQN) approximates the optimal Bayesian solution by simulating system trajectories offline. Supports point-based inference (ML, MAP), distribution-based inference (Bayesian), and causal inference objectives. Non-identifiability in HMMs arises when different parameter sets produce the same observed data. Exact computation of the optimal Bayesian policy is intractable because the belief space is a continuous (n×r)-simplex.

### 6.6 KNN-HMM for Badminton Stroke Prediction

See Section 1.12 (Journal of Big Data 2026) — the KNN-HMM model uses 3-5 hidden states with Gaussian emissions, Baum-Welch training, Viterbi decoding over motion-capture stroke sequences, demonstrating HMM-based temporal sequence prediction for stroke classification.

## 7. Graph Neural Networks for Tactical Analysis in Sports

**Sources: Preprints survey [3], arXiv tennis GNN [1], UT Twente thesis [4]**

### 7.1 Sports Analytics with GNNs and GCNs (Preprints.org 2024)

Literature review by Tim Todd Drexler (DOI: 10.20944/preprints202410.0046.v1, submitted September 30, 2024). GNN applications: tactical analysis and team performance (soccer formations, basketball player movement prediction); player performance modeling and injury prediction; game outcome prediction (American football, eSports Dota 2/League of Legends). GCN applications: tactical/spatial analysis (soccer passing networks, basketball on-court movement); player interaction and performance evaluation (soccer off-the-ball contributions, **tennis sequential event graphs**); game outcome/play prediction (American football play success, eSports outcomes). Challenges: proprietary data availability, computational expense, domain expertise for graph construction, interpretability, spatial data sparsity, real-time processing bottlenecks, scalability.

### 7.2 GNN for Counter-Strike Tactic Recognition (UT Twente 2025)

Szabolcs Csapó's thesis (TScIT 43, July 4, 2025) on the ESTA dataset (1,500 professional matches). Each round represented as a graph with nodes (players, bombsites, bomb) and edges capturing distances; node features include position (X,Y), health, armor, utility (grenade count), area ID, node type, isAlive, hasBomb. Best model: 2-layered GCN (PyG, 128 hidden channels, AdamW lr 0.0002, weight decay 1e-5) using all features: 81.17% accuracy, F1 0.6945. 2-layered GCN outperformed GAT (78.10%, F1 0.6831). Utility usage was a critical feature for tactical classification. Micro-average AUC 0.81, with some classes achieving 0.96-1.00 AUC while t_setup_a scored only 0.53. Context for comparison: Szmida et al. achieved 0.8549 AUC for player actions; Xenopoulos et al. reported 0.8753 AUC for outcome prediction.

## 8. Deception in Racket Sports and Anticipation of Intent

**Sources: BadmintonPeak [11], Airchy [15], APA paper [16], Frontiers review [20], ScienceDirect [17], ITF Coaching review [18]**

### 8.1 Badminton Deception Techniques and Timing

BadmintonPeak's guide: Badminton deception is a two-part motion: (1) preparation identical to the expected shot (e.g., a smash), and (2) a last-moment change that sends a different shot. A shuttlecock takes 0.6 seconds to cross the court on a drive and 0.3 seconds on a full-power smash. Deception also slows down the opponent's reading of subsequent points, increasing their reaction time by 0.1-0.2 seconds on normal shots. Three main deceptive shot families: (1) Deceptive drop shot (smash preparation, finished with a short drop) — Viktor Axelsen's favorite; (2) Deceptive smash (drop preparation, finished with smash) and variation (drop prep followed by flat clear/tight drive) — Anthony Sinisuka Ginting specializes, playing 100% on wrist angle and forearm speed with identical jumping motion; (3) Net deception (slice and reverse slice) — Kunlavut Vitidsarn is a master, able to place deceptive shots in a 30-centimeter zone. Legal in competition except on serves (BWF rule 9.1.6 prohibits feinting before serve contact). Pros execute 5-10 deceptive shots per set in men's singles; amateurs should aim for 2-3 per set. Common failures: too-soft preparation, too-early change, poor timing (using it when opponent is static).

### 8.2 Expert Anticipation of Deceptive Intent (Perception Research)

**"Expert Players Accurately Detect an Opponent's Movement Intent Through Sound Alone"** (Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, 2017, Vol. 43, No. 2, pp. 348-359) by Ivan Camponogara, Matthew Rodger, Cathy Craig, Paola Cesari. Two experiments with expert basketball players and nonplayers listening to binaural audio of a professional attacker running with deceptive/nondeceptive left/right movements. In the Full-Body Task, basketball players made errors only 21.35% of the time vs 36.91% for nonplayers; basketball players were fooled by deceptive movements only 37% of the time (vs 67% for nonplayers). Deceptive sounds showed constant Interaural Time Difference (ITD) but changing Interaural Intensity Difference (ILD) with no significant ITD-ILD correlation, whereas nondeceptive sounds showed strong correlations (r = .51 and .95). Experts adopted distinct strategies—moving early for nondeceptive movements (~200ms after the central point) and waiting longer for deceptive movements to gather more auditory information.

**"How to Trick Your Opponent: A Review Article on Deceptive Actions"** (Frontiers in Psychology, 2017, 10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00917): goalkeepers might favor judging an action as deceptive because of the expected costs of a missed deception (response bias).

**"Deception in Tennis: An Ecological Dynamics Perspective"** (ITF Coaching Review): In defending against active deception, the player can be certain that the opponent's kinematics must shift from deceptive to genuine intention at contact.

**"Earlier detection facilitates skilled responses to deceptive actions"** (Human Movement Science, S0167945721001330): as the opponent's true intention is revealed and deception is detected, one would expect an increase in response.

## 9. Evaluation Approaches for Tactic Classification and Rally Outcome Prediction

**Synthesis from gathered sources:**

- **Shot type prediction (classification):** Cross-entropy (CE) is the standard metric used by ShuttleNet, DyMF, and the CoachAI Challenge (e.g., ShuttleNet CE 2.4125 on ShuttleSet τ=8; best challenge CE 1.7892). Top-1/top-2/top-3 accuracy used by RallyTemPose (ShuttleSet: 54.3% top-1, 77.3% top-2, 92.5% top-3; BadmintonDB: 62.8%/83.5%/93.1%). Macro-F1 and Acc-2 (binary accuracy) used in TemPose-TF-ASF stroke recognition (0.854 Acc, 0.761 Macro-F1, 0.945 Acc-2).
- **Area/coordinate prediction (regression):** Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Mean Absolute Error (MAE) on court coordinates (e.g., ShuttleNet MSE 1.8121, MAE 1.3582 at τ=8; challenge best MAE 0.6797). Bivariate Gaussian distribution assumption for area coordinates (ShuttleNet, DyMF).
- **Rally outcome / win probability:** AUC, Brier score, accuracy. BLSR model achieved AUC 0.8966, Brier 0.1329; ShuttleScorer on ShuttleSet achieved AUC 0.8371, ACC 0.7869, BR 0.1574.
- **Trajectory prediction:** Average Displacement Error (ADE) and Final Displacement Error (FDE) in pixels (Nokihara et al.).
- **Player movement forecasting:** CE for shot type + MSE/MAE for both players' locations (DyMF; up to 35.3% MSE improvement over baselines).
- **Tactic classification:** Macro-F1 (tennis Transformer model: 0.935); early outcome assessment AUC@5 (0.923).
- **Pre-match outcome:** Accuracy, Brier score, predictive Bernoulli likelihood (tennis GNN: 65.7% accuracy, 0.214 Brier; random forest Grand Slam: 0.820 classification rate).
- **Technical action frequencies:** AUC (0.9726 male, 0.8730 female), sensitivity/specificity/PPV/NPV; SHAP values for feature importance; ICC = 0.94, Cohen's Kappa = 0.96 for annotation reliability.
- **Shot influence valuation:** xDW/xDR/xEW/xER with AUC/accuracy (73%/81%, 65%/59%, 78%/84%, 71%/63%).
- **Datasets' limitations:** no fixed train/validation/test partition in ShuttleSet (papers construct own splits); broadcast-video origin limits biomechanical precision; class imbalance (rare categories: defensive return lob, driven flight, rush).

## 10. Key Challenges Specific to Singles Badminton Tactical Analysis

**Synthesis from gathered sources:**

1. **Ambiguity of intent from visual evidence alone:** Badminton's probabilistic stroke forecasting is complicated by inherent unpredictability of player decisions, influenced by physical state, psychological condition, and tactical approach (RallyTemPose/CVPRW paper). The same preparation motion can yield different shots (deception), so intent is not directly observable from kinematics alone.
2. **Deception shots:** Two-part motion (identical preparation + last-moment change) means early visual cues are deliberately misleading. Experts respond by waiting longer for deceptive movements (Camponogara et al. 2017); a 0.6s drive vs 0.3s smash crossing time makes anticipation critical. Deception detection requires modeling the temporal evolution of kinematics up to and including contact.
3. **Need for multi-modal fusion:** RallyTemPose demonstrated that player ground position is the most critical input (removing it drops performance 2.6%); removing keypoint data drops accuracy to 48.3%. Nokihara et al. showed player position AND posture alongside shuttlecock position improves trajectory prediction (13% ADE improvement over shuttle-only; 8.4% over shuttle+position). TemPose-TF-ASF uses skeletal joints/bones, player court positions, and shuttlecock trajectories (TrackNetV3). ShuttleSet stores no continuous shuttle trajectories, limiting trajectory-based approaches on that dataset.
4. **Limited annotated tactical labels:** ShuttleSet required six trained badminton-expert annotators; high labeling costs motivated the computer-aided S² tool. The CoachAI Challenge Track 1 was specifically organized to automate annotation. RallyTemPose authors call for synthetic data "for a field with sparse quality annotated datasets." Class imbalance and fine-grained 18-type taxonomies introduce greater uncertainty than simplified 10-type sets.
5. **Broadcast-video constraints:** 25-60 fps footage limits detection of high-speed shuttle; ball/shuttle tracking algorithms often interpolate rather than measure; occlusion issues; monocular camera setups require homography calibration. High-speed trajectory changes (hit-back moments, floor touches) are hard to predict.
6. **Scoreboard masking:** Tennis research (Seidl et al.) notes a player can win the same number of points but lose the match — the scoreboard masks decision vs. execution quality, motivating shot-level valuation models.
7. **Data availability asymmetry:** Hawk-Eye spatiotemporal data (tennis) and similar instrumented data are proprietary and not publicly available; public datasets are either crowdsourced categorical (Match Charting Project) or broadcast-derived with limited spatial precision (ShuttleSet).

## 11. Recommended Approaches and Promising Research Directions

**Synthesis from gathered sources:**

1. **Transformer-based sequential models with separated player/rally contexts:** ShuttleNet's design principle — separately learning rally and player contexts then fusing through a position-aware gated fusion network — outperforms early or sequential integration. This was empirically validated and further supported by 11/16 challenge teams building on ShuttleNet modifications.
2. **Graph-based interaction modeling:** DyMF's Player Movements graph with 12 strategic relation types (10 shot types + defend + return) demonstrates that explicitly modeling player-player interactions (Relational GCN + Dynamic GCN with LSTM-generated weights, hierarchical fusion via parallel co-attention) captures movement purposes and dynamic tactics better than naive sequence models. Tennis GNN work (MagNet) shows graph structure carries most predictive signal (removing it raises Brier from 0.2142 to 0.2492).
3. **Multi-modal fusion with pose + trajectory + context:** RallyTemPose shows skeleton poses, court positions, and player embeddings improve forecasting; BERT text embeddings of stroke descriptions boost stroke embeddings. Nokihara et al. show posture + position + trajectory fusion improves ADE. TemPose-TF-ASF shows bidirectional adjacent-stroke context (via Two-Stage Contextual Refinement to avoid ground-truth future annotations) consistently improves recognition across multiple SOTA backbones (BlockGCN, SkateFormer, BST-CG-AP).
4. **Shot influence / stroke value models:** BLSR's attention-based GRU over two-player CNN-extracted patterns provides interpretable shot influence; ShuttleScorer's win-probability estimation on ShuttleSet; Seidl et al.'s decision vs. execution decomposition (xDW/xDR/xEW/xER) separates "what the player decided" from "how well the shot was executed" — directly relevant to intent inference.
5. **RL environments for tactic evaluation:** The CoachAI Badminton Environment integrates ShuttleNet + DyMF + Behavior Cloning as realistic opponents within an MDP/OpenAI Gym framework, enabling strategy evaluation (e.g., PPO shifting movement distribution to achieve 60% win-rate increase).
6. **Joint optimization of shot type and area prediction:** The CoachAI Challenge finding that area-coordinate prediction only marginally improved (0.6997 → 0.6797 MAE) while shot type improved substantially (2.1777 → 1.7892 CE) indicates a need for models that jointly optimize and correlate these two tasks.
7. **Addressing class imbalance and fine-grained taxonomies:** ShuttleSet's 18 fine-grained stroke types pose a significant challenge; merging rare categories (e.g., push/lob) and data augmentation help. Future work should expand data volume and introduce CNNs/dynamic match factors (per PLOS ONE paper's future plans).
8. **Explainability and interpretability:** Attention mechanisms (BLSR) provide transparency on which shots matter; SHAP values validate feature importance (Scientific Reports 2025); latent variable analysis via t-SNE and cosine similarity of player embeddings enables playstyle comparison (RallyTemPose); PDP/ICE plots for interpretable ML (tennis Grand Slam paper).
9. **Expanding to doubles and other conditions:** DyMF future work targets doubles with greater inter-player interaction focus; ShuttleNet future work targets win/loss outcomes; transfer learning from singles to doubles shows ~19.3% degradation (pose-based) vs ~39.9% (vision-only YOLOv11x).
10. **Deception-specific modeling:** Because deception relies on identical preparation with late divergence, models should (a) explicitly represent the temporal kinematics up to contact, (b) model the opponent's belief/anticipation state, and (c) incorporate game-situation context (score, fatigue, prior shot patterns). The finding that average prediction accuracy varies by over 20% between best and worst predicted players (RallyTemPose) "potentially indicating how well players mask their strokes" directly suggests stroke-masking/deception as a measurable quantity.

args.research_topic: Recognition of technical actions (stroke types and techniques) performed by singles badminton players from video. Research the most current and influential methods (2020-2026) for classifying badminton stroke types such as clear, drop, smash, net shot, drive, lift, serve, and defensive blocks. Cover these approach families: (a) video-based action recognition models including 3D CNNs (I3D, C3D, SlowFast, X3D), two-stream networks (spatial plus optical flow), and transformer-based video models (Video Vision Transformer ViT, Video Swin Transformer, TimeSformer, MViT, Motionformer, Actionformer, MViTv2); (b) pose-based action recognition using skeleton and keypoint data (e.g., OpenPose, MediaPipe, HRNet, PoseFormer, ST-GCN, and graph convolutional networks for skeleton-based action recognition like ST-GCN, MS-G3D, CTR-GCN); (c) methods that combine pose with appearance or use spatio-temporal graphs; and (d) attention mechanisms and temporal segment networks (TSN, TRN, TSM) applied to fine-grained sports action classification. Identify public datasets and benchmarks specific to badminton stroke/action recognition (e.g., Badminton-Recognition dataset by Rahmat et al., badminton action recognition datasets, shuttle hit detection datasets) and transferable datasets from similar racquet sports (e.g., FineGym, tennis stroke datasets, table tennis datasets like TTStroke-21). Discuss evaluation approaches (top-1/top-5 accuracy, confusion matrices for similar strokes, temporal action localization metrics). Discuss key challenges specific to singles badminton: fine-grained distinctions between visually similar strokes (e.g., clear vs. smash vs. drop share similar preparation), variability in camera angles across tournaments, occlusion, the short duration of strokes, and the need for temporal boundaries around the hit moment. Provide recommended approaches and promising research directions for optimizing technical action recognition, including practical implementation guidance (input representations, temporal windows around hit events, fusion of pose and appearance). Provide direct links to original papers (arXiv, CVF open access, ACM DL, IEEE Xplore) and official dataset pages where possible. Be highly technical and detailed to support implementation and experimentation.

Recognition of tactical intent behind singles badminton players' actions, and prior work on tactical analysis in badminton and other net/racquet sports. Research the most current and influential methods (2020-2026) for inferring strategic or tactical intent of a player's shot (e.g., attacking, defensive, deceptive, rally-building, court-positioning tactics, pressing vs. neutral vs. retreating) based on contextual information such as player position, shuttlecock trajectory, rally phase (serve, rally, net play), opponent positioning, and game situation (score, fatigue, game plan). Cover these approach families: (a) sequence modeling with recurrent neural networks (RNN, LSTM, GRU) over rally and shot sequences; (b) graph neural networks modeling player-player interactions and shot relationships; (c) spatio-temporal reasoning and trajectory-based analysis; (d) hidden Markov models and probabilistic graphical models for tactic state inference; (e) transformer-based sequential models for rally modeling; and (f) shot annotation and stroke quality/impact analysis (e.g., impact, pressure, initiative, dominance concepts used in badminton analysis). Identify prior work on tactical analysis in badminton specifically (e.g., papers analyzing rally patterns, shuttlecock trajectory-based tactic mining, player movement patterns, shot selection analysis, deception detection) and in comparable sports like tennis (e.g., rally modeling, point outcome prediction, tactic classification using graph networks), table tennis, and squash. Identify public datasets and benchmarks relevant to tactical analysis (e.g., badminton rally datasets with shot type and outcome labels like ShuttleSet22 and BadmintonDB, tennis point/event datasets, Hawk-Eye trajectory data, stroke quality annotations). Discuss evaluation approaches for tactic classification and rally outcome prediction. Discuss key challenges specific to singles badminton tactical analysis: ambiguity of intent from visual evidence alone, deception shots, the need for multi-modal fusion (pose, trajectory, context), and limited annotated tactical labels. Provide recommended approaches and promising research directions. Provide direct links to original papers (arXiv, CVF open access, ACM DL, IEEE Xplore) and official dataset pages where possible. Be highly technical and detailed to support implementation and experimentation.

Prediction of subsequent actions of singles badminton players: anticipating or forecasting the next shot, stroke type, landing position, or movement of a singles badminton player. Research the most current and influential methods (2020-2026) for next-shot prediction and action forecasting in badminton and comparable net/racquet sports (tennis, table tennis, squash). Cover these approach families: (a) stroke forecasting and next-shot prediction models using rally progress and player style (e.g., ShuttleNet by Wang et al. at AAAI 2022, which formulates stroke forecasting as sequence prediction using encoder-decoder extractors for rally progress and player information with a fusion network); (b) transformer-based architectures for sequential rally prediction and shot sequence generation; (c) graph-based reasoning over player positions, shuttlecock trajectories, and rally context to predict future behavior; (d) trajectory forecasting of the shuttlecock and players (e.g., LSTM-based shuttlecock trajectory prediction from player position and posture by Nokihara et al.); (e) early action prediction and anticipation models from computer vision (e.g., action anticipation, future person localization, Video Transformer-based forecasting); and (f) reinforcement learning or imitation learning approaches for shot selection modeling. Identify public datasets and benchmarks for stroke/action prediction in badminton (e.g., ShuttleSet and ShuttleSet22 from the CoachAI Badminton Challenge at IJCAI 2023, which provide stroke-level shot type and area annotations with tasks of predicting future strokes given observed strokes; BadmintonDB; the Shuttlecock Trajectory Dataset used in TrackNet papers) and comparable sports. Discuss evaluation metrics for next-shot prediction (e.g., cross-entropy for shot type, mean absolute error for area coordinates, average displacement error ADE, final displacement error FDE, top-k accuracy, rally outcome prediction accuracy). Discuss key challenges specific to singles badminton: shot outcome depends on both players, deception makes prediction hard, rally context and score matter, multi-modality of possible future shots (multiple plausible next shots), and the need to model both players jointly. Provide recommended approaches and promising research directions. Provide direct links to original papers (arXiv, CVF open access, ACM DL, IEEE Xplore) and official dataset pages where possible. Be highly technical and detailed to support implementation and experimentation.

# Fully Comprehensive Findings

## (a) Badminton Player Detection Using Deep Learning Models

### YOLO Variants (YOLOv5, YOLOv8, YOLOv9, YOLOv10, YOLO11, YOLO-NAS, Tiny YOLOv2)

**YOLOv5 – AI-Powered Badminton Video Detection (Cheng & Kim, 2023):** The paper "AI-powered Badminton Video Detection: Enhancing Gameplay Analysis and Training" by Yao Cheng and Junghee J. Kim, published in the Journal of Robotics and Automation Research on 4 August 2023 (DOI: 10.33140/jrar.04.02.05, Corpus ID: 265438728), found that "the YoloV5 model performed better when tested on the video data with less clear image of judges in the background, and improved performance when testing on generalized video data was used to accurately evaluate the overlap between predicted and ground truth." [2]

**Improved Tiny YOLOv2 with UKF (He & Zhang, 2024):** Published in Heliyon (October 2, 2024; also Vol. 10, Issue 20, 30 October 2024, Article e38865), "Deep learning neural network-assisted badminton movement recognition and physical fitness training optimization" by Chuanbao He and Min Zhang addresses low accuracy in recognizing badminton movement trajectories for badminton robots. The methodology: (1) side detection/tracking of flying badminton in 2D video streams; (2) a CNN with attention mechanisms; (3) an improved Tiny YOLOv2 enhanced by adding convolutional layers, increasing channels, adjusting receptive field sizes, and introducing residual connections to mitigate gradient vanishing, with a revised loss function incorporating trajectory information (position and movement direction) optimizing localization, confidence, classification, and trajectory losses; and (4) an Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) predicting future badminton positions using Sigma points propagated through nonlinear functions, accounting for factors like wind force. Dataset: 15 badminton flight video streams via stereo vision cameras (laboratories, parking lots, sports arenas, forests, roadsides), each ~100-150 consecutive frames (~1000 total), 2:1 train/test split, learning rate 0.001, batch size 16, 50 epochs, NVIDIA Tesla V100. Results: average tracking accuracy 91.40%, recall 84.60%, F1 87.68%, frame rate 13.792 FPS, IoU 0.922; average precision/recall/frame rate across four scenarios: 96.7%, 95.7%, 29.2 FPS. Average predicted position error ~3.76 pixels; average predicted distance error ~0.26 m; max errors ~8.80 pixels and 0.60 m; average total prediction time ~35.03 ms. [1][10]

**YOLOv8 + DeepSORT Hybrid (ShoiebRahman repository):** A project developed a real-time sports analysis system using a hybrid approach combining YOLOv8 for player detection and DeepSORT for multi-frame tracking. A custom dataset of 200 clips from real match footage was built and annotated. Player movement metrics (speed, acceleration, distance, zone coverage) were extracted. An LSTM model for tactical zone prediction achieved over 90% accuracy in anticipating player movement across court zones. [27]

**YOLOv8-Pose with ELA Attention (Wu et al., 2025):** Published in Sensors (Basel) on July 17, 2025 (PMCID: PMC12298368, PMID: 40732573) by Yijian Wu, Zewen Chen, Hongxing Zhang, Yulin Yang, and Weichao Yi (Wenzhou University, China). The paper proposes an enhanced pose estimation framework for badminton players built upon an improved YOLOv8-Pose architecture. Key contributions: (1) Construction of the xBHPE dataset — 4,000 manually annotated samples captured using Microsoft Kinect v2, using an enhanced 21-keypoint skeleton model (vs. standard 17-keypoint), collected at four camera angles (front, behind, 45° left, 45° right); (2) Integration of the Efficient Local Attention (ELA) mechanism into YOLOv8-Pose, which builds on coordinate attention (CA) with strip pooling, 1D convolutions (kernel sizes 5 or 7), and group normalization (GN); (3) Comprehensive evaluation of multiple attention mechanisms. The YOLOv8n-Pose lightweight variant was enhanced with ELA in the backbone. Loss combines CIoU, binary cross-entropy objectness, classification loss, and L2 keypoint regression. Hardware: RTX A6000 (48GB), PyTorch 2.1.1, Adam optimizer, batch size 16, input 1920×1080, initial LR 0.0001 with linear decay, Task-Aligned Assigner. The ELA-enhanced model consistently achieves superior accuracy across MSE, OKS, and PCK metrics. [46]

**YOLOv3 (JOIV paper):** A study titled "Improving Badminton Player Detection using YOLOv3 with Various..." from the Indonesian Journal of Informatics (JOIV) identifies badminton players using the YOLO technique with a variety of training strategies. [44]

**YOLO-NAS (Roboflow, March 2024):** A "Badminton Player Tracking" object detection model (single class "Badminton Player," license CC BY 4.0) achieved mAP@50 of 98.3%, Precision 88.3%, Recall 98.8%. Dataset: badminton-player-tracking/2 with 1,033 images across 2 versions. Model architecture: YOLO-NAS (Accurate variant), checkpoint coco/14, updated March 8, 2024. Model ID: "badminton-player-tracking/2". [3]

**YOLO11 + YOLOv8-Pose Pipeline (Muhammad Yasin repository):** A computer vision-driven badminton analytics project (25 stars, MIT license) extracts player movement trajectories using YOLOv8 for player detection, YOLOv8-Pose for joint detection, and a custom-trained YOLO11 model for shuttlecock detection (training data from Roboflow dataset by Mathieu Cartron, 2022). The 4-step pipeline: (1) Player Tracking & Trajectory Extraction using YOLOv8 pose estimation (body center or ankle midpoint as player position); (2) Court Normalization to canonical court reference frame; (3) Spatial Analytics (court divided into Front/Mid/Back × Left/Right zones; movement density, transitions, dominance); (4) Shuttlecock Detection & Shot-Type Context using custom-trained YOLO11. [45]

**YOLO NAS/v5/v3 + MediaPipe (SPH Science Academy, 2023):** A student project "Badminton: AI-Powered Analysis of Player Patterns" applied YOLO models (NAS, v5, v3) for real-time object detection with Keras/TensorFlow and MediaPipe for pose estimation. Bounding boxes labeled three shot types (0: smashes, 1: lobs, 2: net shots). MediaPipe shot classification accuracy was compared with YOLOv5. Both demonstrated promising potential, though accuracy was limited by training data. [43]

**Multi-class player/shuttlecock detection (hongy20 Roboflow, Oct 2025):** An object detection model with 2 classes ("player" and "shuttlecock"), 675 images (version /13 contains 1,022 images), tags yolov11, yolov11l, yolov11s. Images come from broadcast view (elevated, TV-style) and ground view (mobile/handheld at court level), standardized at 1920×1080. The shuttlecock is "often small, fast-moving, and partially blurred"; boxes should be as tight as possible. Model type: rfdetr-nano. [47]

**YOLOv12 + MobileNetV2 Two-Stage (Lin et al., 2026):** Published in Engineering Proceedings (MDPI), "Computer Vision-Based Tennis Ball Tracking Using You Only Look Once for Training Analytics" by Pei-Jung Lin et al. (Feng Chia University), presented at ECICE 2025. Uses YOLOv12 (with Area Attention Module A2, Residual Efficient Layer Aggregation Network, Flash Attention) for small-target detection plus MobileNetV2 binary classification to filter false positives, stabilized by a Kalman filter. YOLOv12 alone: Precision 97.2%, Recall 92.4%, F1 94.7%; two-stage: Precision 99.4%, Recall 81.1%, F1 89.3% — reducing false positives 5.44×. Overall MAE 20.39 pixels on wall-practice videos. [58]

### Faster R-CNN

**Rahmad et al. (2019):** "Badminton player detection using faster region convolutional neural network" by Nur Azmina Rahmad, Nur Anis Jasmin Sufri, Nurul Hamizah Muzamil, and Muhammad Amir As'ari (Indonesian Journal of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, June 1, 2019, DOI: 10.11591/IJEECS.V14.I3.PP1330-1335) presents an automated system using Faster R-CNN to track badminton player position from sport broadcast video. Key finding: "the detector successfully detects the player when the detector is being fed with more generalized dataset." Cited 42 times. [54]

**Faster R-CNN + HRNet for Trajectory Prediction (Nokihara et al., 2023):** The Keio University research used Faster R-CNN trained on MS COCO for player detection (selecting the player with highest confidence score to exclude referees/spectators), player pose estimation via HRNet extracting 17 joints per player, and TrackNet for shuttlecock position. See Category (c) for full details. [8][22]

**Faster R-CNN + VGG16 for Footwork (Heliyon 2022):** Published in Heliyon (2022, DOI: 10.1016/j.heliyon.2022.e10089) by researchers from East China Normal University, University of Florida, Sheffield Hallam University, and Shanghai University of Sport. Uses VGG16 CNN within a Faster R-CNN framework to identify 2D image coordinates of players' shoes; converts to 3D world coordinates using Homography matrix (x-y) and binocular positioning (z). Shoe detection achieved mAP 0.982 with VGG16 (vs. 0.953 for ZF), 0.2185 s/frame. Binocular positioning accuracy 0.129 m average error; final positioning accuracy 74.7% (263 of 352 images); overall identification accuracy 97.2% when excluding shoe classification errors. Used two cameras (Canon EOS 6D Mark II and Canon EOS 77D, 25 fps). [55]

### Transformer-Based Detectors (DETR, Deformable DETR)

**DETR (Facebook AI, 2020):** DETR (DEtection TRansformer) is an end-to-end object detection model using a Transformer encoder-decoder with a CNN backbone, eliminating hand-crafted components like anchor boxes and Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS), treating detection as a direct set prediction problem with learned object queries. Achieves ~42% mAP on COCO with ResNet-50. Advantages: end-to-end trainability, parallel predictions, global context understanding (effective for crowded/occluded scenes), versatility (panoptic segmentation). Limitations: high computational cost, slow convergence (~500 epochs on COCO), fixed object query count, struggles with small objects. Real-time transformer models like RT-DETR and RF-DETR now rival YOLO's speed: "RT-DETR-R50 achieves 53.1% AP at 108 FPS, outperforming YOLOv8-L (52.9% AP at 71 FPS)." Techniques like IoU-aware query selection (RT-DETR) and bipartite matching achieve up to 66.0% AP50 on challenging datasets. [75]

**Deformable DETR (ICLR 2021 Oral):** By Xizhou Zhu, Weijie Su, Lewei Lu, Bin Li, Xiaogang Wang, and Jifeng Dai (SenseTime, USTC, CUHK), arXiv:2010.04159. Addresses DETR's slow convergence and limited feature spatial resolution via attention modules that only attend to a small set of key sampling points around a reference point. Achieves better performance than DETR (especially on small objects) with 10× fewer training epochs. Results: single-scale 50 epochs AP 39.4; multi-scale 50 epochs AP 44.5; + iterative bounding box refinement AP 46.2; ++ two-stage AP 46.9 — versus DETR's AP 42.0 at 500 epochs. Code: https://github.com/fundamentalvision/Deformable-DETR. [76][77][79]

## (b) Multi-Object Tracking Algorithms

### Tracker Family Overview (Fora Soft 2026 Guide)

The tracking-by-detection pipeline has 4 stages: (1) Detection (YOLO, RT-DETR, Grounding DINO) — "detector quality dominates everything downstream"; (2) Motion prediction via Kalman filter with state vector (x, y, aspect_ratio, height, dx, dy, dh, dr); (3) Association cost matrix (IoU, appearance cosine distance, or both) solved with Hungarian algorithm (O(n³)); (4) Track lifecycle management. [50]

- **DeepSORT (2017):** Introduced deep appearance embeddings (cosine distance) on top of SORT. MOT17: 60.3 MOTA, 61.2 IDF1, 48.8 HOTA. Now a historical reference; "no longer the default for new projects." [50]
- **ByteTrack (ECCV 2022, Zhang et al.):** Associates every detection box including low-confidence ones via a two-stage cascade. MOT17: 80.3 MOTA, 77.3 IDF1, 63.1 HOTA. Motion-only, <50 lines of Python, MIT-licensed (github.com/ifzhang/ByteTrack), ~2× faster than DeepSORT, ships in Ultralytics YOLO as bytetrack.yaml. "The 2026 throughput default." [50]
- **OC-SORT (CVPR 2023, Cao et al.):** Fixes Kalman drift after occlusion via observation-centric re-update and observation-centric momentum. MOT17: 78.0 MOTA, 77.5 IDF1, 63.2 HOTA; beats ByteTrack by 10+ HOTA points on DanceTrack (non-linear motion). Best for dance, gymnastics, parkour, animals, sports with direction changes. MIT-licensed (github.com/noahcao/OC_SORT). [50]
- **BoT-SORT (2022, Aharon et al.):** Adds camera-motion compensation (sparse optical flow + ECC alignment) and appearance embeddings (BoT-S50 Re-ID). MOT17: 80.5 MOTA, 80.2 IDF1, 65.0 HOTA — state of the art at publication. Default tracker in Ultralytics YOLO since 2024 (botsort.yaml). ~30% slower than ByteTrack. MIT-licensed. [50]
- **C-BIoU:** Uses buffered geometric matching without CMC; leads on SoccerNet-tracking after tuning (HOTA 85.7, IDF1 80.0, MOTA 99.3). [49]

Decision tree: (1) Is the camera moving? → BoT-SORT; (2) Does motion violate constant-velocity? → OC-SORT; (3) Many streams/dense scenes? → ByteTrack; (4) Long-occlusion identity persistence? → BoT-SORT-ReID. "~80% of projects end at ByteTrack or BoT-SORT-ReID." [50]

### ByteTrack Deep Dive

ByteTrack's primary innovation: "keeping non-background low confidence detection boxes which are typically discarded after the initial filtering of detections and use these low-score boxes for a secondary association step." Methodology: (1) detection boxes filtered into high-confidence, low-confidence, background boxes (background discarded); (2) first association stage: high-score boxes matched with Kalman-predicted tracklets using IoU or cosine similarity with Hungarian algorithm; (3) second association stage: low-score boxes matched against unmatched tracks with lower matching threshold; (4) lost tracklets kept for a buffer of frames. Key hyperparameters: track_thresh = 0.5, track_buffer = 50, match_thresh = 0.8, aspect_ratio_thresh = 10.0, min_box_area = 1.0, MIN_THRESHOLD = 0.001, background threshold hardcoded at 0.1. Uses YOLOX as base detector (customizable). Limitations: limited accuracy in crowded scenes, low-confidence strategy can introduce noise, no native multi-class support. [52]

### OC-SORT Details

OC-SORT is a pure motion-model-based MOT published at CVPR 2023, improving robustness in crowded scenes and under non-linear motion while remaining simple, online, and real-time. Key mechanism: "Observation-centric Re-Update" (ORU). Benchmark results: MOT17 private (HOTA 63.2, MOTA 78.0), MOT20 private (HOTA 62.4, MOTA 75.9), KITTI-cars (HOTA 76.5, MOTA 90.3), DanceTrack-test (HOTA 55.1, MOTA 89.4). Inference ~28 FPS on RTX 2080Ti, or ~700 FPS on CPU with pre-provided detections. Deep OC-SORT (with deep visual appearance) accepted to ICIP 2023. Supports ONNX, TensorRT, ncnn; C++ implementation available. [51]

### ByteTrack vs OC-SORT Benchmark (Rizwan AI)

On identical 200-frame clip with yolo26n.pt across 10 GPU tiers: ByteTrack is the clear winner on speed and ID stability. On H100: ByteTrack 106.2 FPS vs OC-SORT 55.1 FPS (~1.9× faster). ByteTrack produced 14 unique IDs and 17 fragmentations with average track length 66.9 frames, versus OC-SORT's 79 unique IDs, 113 fragmentations (85% more), 29.6 frames average track length. Per-frame latency (H100): ByteTrack 9.4 ms; OC-SORT 18.1 ms. Cost on H100: $0.0103 vs $0.0199 per 1,000 frames. [48]

### Tracker Benchmark Comparison (Roboflow, trackers v2.3.0)

Benchmark results (tuned): MOT17: BoT-SORT leads HOTA 63.8, MOTA 79.4; C-BIoU highest IDF1 79.1. SportsMOT: BoT-SORT leads HOTA 74.1, MOTA 96.9; OC-SORT highest tuned IDF1 75.4. SoccerNet-tracking: C-BIoU leads HOTA 85.7, IDF1 80.0, MOTA 99.3. DanceTrack: BoT-SORT leads HOTA 57.8; C-BIoU highest tuned IDF1 58.7 and tied highest MOTA 92.4. Selection guidance: SORT for speed-constrained low-occlusion; ByteTrack as default (recovers low-confidence detections); OC-SORT for significant camera motion or non-linear paths; BoT-SORT for strong ego-motion and maximum identity stability (uses CMC); C-BIoU for fast/irregular motion without CMC. [49]

### Deep HM-SORT (Sports-Specific, arXiv 2406.12081)

A novel online MOT algorithm designed for tracking athletes in sports scenarios, addressing similar appearances (identical uniforms), irregular movements, significant camera motion, and frequent occlusions. Three contributions: (1) novel association method combining feature embedding and IOU costs using the harmonic mean (rather than minimum as in Deep-EIoU), skewing towards the lower distance measurement — advantageous when players look alike; (2) retaining all tracklets indefinitely (rather than capped temporary ID buffer), enabling re-identification of players who leave and re-enter the frame; (3) state-of-the-art performance on sports benchmarks. Results: 80.1 HOTA on SportsMOT (outperforming Deep-EIoU's 77.2), with 2.9% higher HOTA and over 900 fewer ID swaps (30% reduction); 85.4 HOTA on SoccerNet Tracking Challenge 2023 (ranked 3rd overall, 2nd in AssA; online, processing a 30-second clip in 1 min 30 sec vs 16+ min for the offline 1st-place method). Implementation: PyTorch on NVIDIA L40-16Q GPU, YOLOX (SportsMOT) and YOLOv8-XL (SoccerNet) detectors. Limitations: occlusion causes temporary ID-swaps; ~13 FPS runtime cap; online (no offline post-processing). [13]

### SportsMOT Dataset (ICCV 2023, Nanjing University)

SportsMOT contains 240 videos from three sports (basketball, volleyball, football), high-quality professional games with no abrupt viewpoint switches, 720p at 25 FPS. Key challenges: (a) fast and variable-speed motion, (b) similar yet distinguishable appearance among players. Compared to other datasets, SportsMOT has the maximum number of videos, video length, frames, and bounding boxes. Features: lowest IoU (indicating fast movement) and lowest Kalman filter-based IoU (motion cannot be easily modeled by plain linear model). Re-ID feature analysis: MOT17 features clearly distinguished; SportsMOT features somewhat fused; DanceTrack features totally intertwined. "Out of view" accounts for the largest proportion of difficult attributes; "full occlusion" is the most difficult. Proposed MixSort tracker (based on OC-SORT) uses a detector, motion model, and MixFormer to generate a fused similarity matrix, associating with the Hungarian algorithm; achieves state-of-the-art on SportsMOT, with MixSort-Byte and MixSort-OC variants outperforming other trackers on MOT17 under private detection protocol in HOTA, IDF1, and AssA. [15][73]

### TeamTrack Dataset (2024, Nagoya University)

TeamTrack is a benchmark dataset and algorithm for MOT in team sports (soccer, basketball, handball) in full-pitch videos, addressing occlusions, similar appearances, and complex movements. Key features: over 150 minutes of high-resolution (4K to 8K) video; over 4 million annotated bounding boxes (4,374,900 total across 279,900 frames); captured from two angles (top view via DJI Mavic 3 drones 4K, side view with Z CAM E2-F8 8K and E2-F6 6K fisheye lenses). Composition: Soccer 30 min fisheye + 30 min drone; Basketball 17.5 min fisheye indoor + 24 min drone side + 24 min drone top; Handball 30 min fisheye indoor. Total: 155.5 minutes. The algorithm introduces trajectory forecasting using a graph neural network (GNN) to model group movement patterns. Benchmark results (ByteTrack and BoT-SORT evaluated): TeamTrack averages HOTA 61.9, DetA 64.2, AssA 60.2, MOTA 77.2, IDF1 77.5; Basketball SideView best (HOTA 76.2), Basketball SideView2 worst (HOTA 42.9). TeamTrack is more challenging than MOT17 (HOTA 63.1) but slightly easier than DanceTrack (HOTA 47.1) in association accuracy. Formats: teamtrack (SportsLabKit), teamtrack-mot (MOT Challenge style, TrackEval-compatible), teamtrack-trajectory. Available at github.com/AtomScott/TeamTrack and atomscott.github.io/TeamTrack. [11][12]

### MOT20 Benchmark

MOT20 consists of 8 new video sequences depicting very crowded scenes (up to 246 pedestrians per frame), half training and half testing, with clear annotation rules for consistent labeling. [14]

## (c) Shuttlecock Detection and Trajectory Tracking

### The Shuttlecock Challenge

Badminton shuttlecocks are the fastest ball type in sports, reaching top speeds of 493 km/h (world record measured in a 2013 laboratory test; speeds over 400 km/h in play), making tracking challenging. [6][36] The shuttlecock appears as a circle or triangle depending on camera angle, with size variation, speeds from 24 to 400 km/h, white color blending with the scene, complex backgrounds, and unpredictable trajectory due to the cone shape and off-center center of gravity. [36]

### TrackNet (Original, Huang et al. 2019)

TrackNet is a deep neural network designed for tracking small, fast-moving objects (tennis balls and shuttlecocks), using a VGG16 backbone (first 13 layers) with DeconvNet-inspired later layers, taking consecutive images as input to handle blur, afterimage, and short-term occlusion. In the Hsu et al. (2024) system, TrackNet is combined with a trajectory smoothing algorithm with denoising, curve fitting, and interpolation steps. [6][20]

### TrackNetV2 (Sun et al., ICPAI 2020)

TrackNetV2 improves the original TrackNet across processing speed, prediction accuracy, and GPU memory usage: (1) processing speed improved from 2.6 FPS to 31.8 FPS (3-in/3-out version reaches 31.84 FPS) by reducing input image size and re-engineering from Multiple-In Single-Out (MISO) to Multiple-In Multiple-Out (MIMO) design; (2) prediction accuracy improved using a dataset of 55,563 frames from 18 diverse badminton match videos, with architecture composed of VGG16, upsampling layers, and U-net; (3) GPU memory reduced by changing the heatmap layer from pixel-wise one-hot encoding 3D array to real-valued 2D array, with loss changed from RMSE-based to weighted cross-entropy based. Validation: accuracy 96.3%, precision 97.0%, recall 98.7% in training; 85.2%, 97.2%, 85.4% on a brand-new match. Published in Proceedings of ICPAI 2020, pages 86-91, DOI: 10.1109/ICPAI51961.2020.00023. Dataset and code: https://nol.cs.nctu.edu.tw:234/open-source/TrackNetv2/. [39][40][41]

### TrackNetV3 (Chen & Wang, ACM 2023)

TrackNetV3 (DOI 10.1145/3595916.3626370) is composed of two core modules: trajectory prediction and trajectory rectification. "The trajectory prediction module leverages an estimated background as auxiliary data to locate the shuttlecock in spite of the fluctuating visual interferences." Incorporates mixup data augmentation, creates "repair masks" by analyzing predicted trajectories, and rectifies paths via inpainting when the shuttlecock is obstructed. Performance on Shuttlecock Trajectory Dataset test split: YOLOv7: 57.82% accuracy, 78.53% precision, 59.96% recall, 68.00% F1, 34.77 FPS; TrackNetV2: 94.98% accuracy, 99.64% precision, 94.56% recall, 97.03% F1, 27.70 FPS; TrackNetV3: 97.51% accuracy, 97.79% precision, 99.33% recall, 98.56% F1, 25.11 FPS (best overall accuracy, recall, and F1). GitHub: qaz812345/TrackNetV3 (294 stars). [42]

### TrackNetV4 (Raj, Wang, Gedeon, 2025)

TrackNetV4 enhances fast sports object tracking with motion attention maps, fusing high-level visual features with learnable motion attention maps through a motion-aware fusion mechanism. [41]

### Other TrackNet-family improvements

- **Residual U-Net (Haq, Tarashima, Tagawa, 2024):** "Shuttlecock Detection Using Residual Learning in U-Net Architecture" incorporates residual learning in a U-Net architecture. [41]
- **TD-Net (Fan and Li, 2026):** "a temporal difference-infused lightweight network for flying shuttlecock detection." [41]
- **Bag of Tricks (Haq, Tarashima, Tagawa, 2024):** proposes tricks to improve TrackNetV2 regarding precision, recall, F1, and accuracy. [41]

### MonoTrack (Liu & Wang, CVPRW 2022)

MonoTrack (arXiv:2204.01899; CVSports@CVPR 2022, pages 3512-3521, DOI 10.1109/CVPRW56347.2022.00395) by Paul Liu (Stanford) and Jui-Hsien Wang (Adobe) is "the first complete end-to-end system for extraction and segmentation of 3D shuttle trajectories from monocular badminton videos." It integrates badminton domain knowledge (court dimensions, shot placement, physical laws of motion) with vision features (player poses, shuttle tracking). Pipeline: (1) Hough lines + graph-based bipartite partition for court detection; (2) HRNet pose + 3-in/3-out modified U-Net for shuttle detection; (3) ~16K parameter two-layer GRU HitNet fusing court/pose/shuttle with dynamic programming on hit intervals and alternating rules; (4) per-shot 3D trajectory optimization using drag dynamics, camera reprojection, hitter/receiver priors, and out-of-bounds penalties. Key results: court success improved 73.9%→85.5%, IoU 0.96→0.97, 40× faster; shuttle detector 2.9M vs 11.3M parameters, accuracy 88.6% vs 84.0%; HitNet F1: shuttle-only 0.815 → +pose 0.850 → +court 0.866 → +constrained optimization 0.946 (recall 94.3%, accuracy 89.7%); synthetic 3D error 14.9 cm (reprojection-only) vs 8.0 cm (full priors). Uses TrackNetV2 data (26 international singles matches, ~77K frames; 3 test matches ~12K frames) plus 40 YouTube videos for court detection and 10K synthetic 3D trajectories. Limitations: no end-to-end FPS reported; no real 3D ground truth; court failures, out-of-frame events, and hit errors cascade. Code: github.com/jhwang7628/monotrack. [67][68][69][70][71]

### Machine Learning Framework with TrackNet + MediaPipe (Menon et al., 2023, TU Dublin)

Published in DeLTA 2023 proceedings (Communications in Computer and Information Science, Vol. 1875, pages 71-83, Springer, DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-39059-3_5). Combines (1) a shuttlecock trajectory model using pre-trained TrackNet CNN and (2) a player service fault detection model using Google MediaPipe Pose with a Random Forest classifier. Trained on BWF channel dataset of 100,000 images of players and shuttlecock positions. "Results demonstrate that the optimized TrackNet model has an accuracy of 90%, which is 5% more with 2.84% less positioning error compared to the current state of the art." The service fault detection model achieved 90% accuracy with MediaPipe Pose, 10% higher than OpenPose. [7]

### YOLO-Based Shuttlecock Detection for Robots (Cao et al., 2021)

Published in Expert Systems with Applications (Vol. 164, Feb 2021, Article 113833) by Zhiguang Cao, Tingbo Liao, Wen Song, Zhenghua Chen, and Chongshou Li. Challenges: rapid scale changes, complex contexts with moving objects and athletes, high-speed movement, and white shuttlecock color blending. Two novel Tiny YOLOv2 variants: M-YOLOv2 (modifies loss function to adaptively improve detection speed for small objects) and YOLOBR (novel architecture retaining more semantic information of small objects, addressing lost semantic information and accumulated prediction error). Visual data from ZED binocular camera mounted on the robot. The networks achieve high detection accuracy with the fastest speed (FPS) compared to Faster R-CNN, SSD, Tiny YOLOv2, and YOLOv3, robust in simple and complex contexts. Cited by 102 sources. [53]

### Spyrosoft Instant Review System

A computer vision-based instant review system for badminton determining whether a shuttlecock landed in or out. Design requirements: verification under 25 seconds; installation under 4 hours per court; video recording at 150-200 FPS; near real-time response; efficient algorithms on inexpensive PCs. Solutions: custom calibration with minimum reprojection error 0.086px; modified Mask R-CNN court detection/segmentation (97.7% accuracy) with Hough transform on Sobel filter output, Bentley-Ottmann algorithm and Harris corner detector; hybrid detection combining fast differential-frame detection with neural network patches (modified Tiny YOLO, 12ms processing); adaptive pixel-wise flicker compensation 250-300× faster than commercial tools; shuttlecock detection via accumulative differential frames (7 consecutive images) plus shape segmentation (<2ms) and Kalman filter, feeding 104×104 px patches to modified Tiny YOLO (94% mean average precision, 0.96 precision, 0.77 recall, 0.86 F1 at 0.25 threshold). Ground hit detection combines trajectory-change detection with blurriness (variance of Laplacian). Performance: 94% shuttlecock visibility detection accuracy; 81% of visible shuttlecocks correctly detected and tracked (within 12 pixels); correct decision in 62% of cases with human operator confirmation. Processed two cameras at up to 200 FPS (800×600) on 9th Gen i7 + GTX 1080. [36]

### Automatic Shuttlecock Fall Detection System (Kopania et al., Sensors 2022)

Published in Sensors (Basel) 2022 Oct 22;22(21):8098 (DOI: 10.3390/s22218098) by Michał Kopania, Jarosław Nowisz, and Artur Przelaskowski (Warsaw University of Technology). Tested at the BWF World Senior Badminton Championships in Katowice (1500+ players, 12 courts). Architecture evolved from 6 cameras above court + 14 around court with 3D reconstruction, to 14 cameras around court + 1 wide-view camera eliminating 3D reconstruction; current version detects single court lines rather than a full court model. Cameras: 800×600 at 150 fps (with interpolation), GigE with PoE, 8 servers. Solutions: adaptive pixel-wise flicker compensation (250-300× faster than DeFlicker/FlickerFree); hybrid detection (accumulative differential frames from 7 consecutive frames + modified Tiny YOLO3 single-class 1-channel fallback); Kalman filter for trajectory prediction/interpolation; camera calibration best practices reducing reprojection error over 3×. Results: court detection accuracy 97.7%; shuttlecock visibility 94%; 81% of visible shuttlecocks correctly detected/tracked (<12 pixel error); neural network mAP@0.50 94% with precision 0.96, recall 0.77, F1 0.86 at threshold 0.25; NN detection 12 ms on i7 + GTX 1080; primary blob-filtering <2 ms. Verified by BWF and Polish Badminton Federation; comparable to Hawk-Eye in processing time and accuracy but easier, faster to install, and more adaptive. [37]

### One-Shot Badminton Shuttle Detection for Mobile Robots (Tuna & Hutter, ETH Zurich, 2026)

Submitted March 17, 2026 (arXiv 2603.06691). Contributions: (1) egocentric dataset of 20,510 semi-automatically annotated frames at 1920×1200, 60 FPS, 11 indoor/outdoor backgrounds, categorized Easy/Medium/Hard; (2) semi-automatic annotation pipeline (background subtraction, opponent masking, candidate selection) achieving 85.7% initial accuracy with only 5.9% manual correction; (3) distance-based evaluation metric (True Positive if Euclidean distance between predicted and ground truth center within τ=25 pixels); (4) fine-tuned YOLOv8 small model achieving F1 0.86 in similar environments and 0.70 in unseen environments, with Mixup augmentation significantly improving recall. Key findings: performance depends critically on shuttlecock size and background texture; performance stable when shuttlecock larger than 20 pixels, recall declines for smaller instances; designed for egocentric, dynamic viewpoints (unlike stationary-camera TrackNet). [35]

### Shuttlecock Trajectory Prediction (Nokihara et al., J. Imaging 2023 & VISAPP 2023)

Published in the Journal of Imaging (J. Imaging 2023, 9(5), 99; DOI: 10.3390/jimaging9050099; also VISAPP 2023 at scitepress.org/PublishedPapers/2023/117858/117858.pdf) by Yuka Nokihara, Ryo Hachiuma, Ryosuke Hori, and Hideo Saito (Keio University). This is the first work to address shuttlecock trajectory prediction during badminton rallies. The system: (1) detection/pose module — shuttlecock 2D coordinates from TrackNet, player positions (4D: xp1, yp1, xp2, yp2) from Faster R-CNN trained on MS COCO, player posture (68-dimensional: 17 keypoints × 2 players × 2 coordinates) from HRNet; (2) time-series module — all three information types embedded into 2 dimensions each via fully connected layers, combined into a 6-dimensional feature vector, fed into an LSTM (3 layers, 128 hidden dimensions, Adam optimizer with weight decay 1e-4, beta1=0.5, beta2=0.999, learning rate 0.02, 400 epochs, 4 input frames / 12 output frames, MSE loss). Results: improved ADE by ~13% over shuttle-position-only methods, ~8.4% over methods using shuttle + player position; LSTM improved ADE by ~9.8% (RNN), 5.0% (GRU), 20% (Transformer), 12% (Seq2Seq). Best augmentation: 50% left-right flip + 50-pixel translation. Best results with more input frames and fewer prediction frames (12 input/4 output: ADE 0.02054 vs 4 input/12 output: 0.04908; proposed Shuttle+Player LSTM achieved ADE 0.04908, FDE 0.08391 on the test setup). Dataset: 26 training matches + 3 test matches (1280×720, 30 fps), 23 professional singles matches from international tournaments (2018-2021). Limitations: requires distant camera setup; difficulty with sudden trajectory changes at hitting/floor moments. [8][22][23]

### Shuttlecock Hitting Event Detection (Chen, IJCAI 2023 Workshop)

"A New Perspective for Shuttlecock Hitting Event Detection" won 2nd place (silver) at the IT4PSS Workshop (International Workshop on Intelligent Technologies for Precision Sports Science) at IJCAI 2023. Approach: reasons over a sequence of images to capture player hitting actions; SwingNet (MobileNetV2 + bidirectional LSTM) captures features/patterns of hitting events; optical flow video processing extracts prior features, reducing learning difficulty. Pipeline uses TrackNetV2 (shuttlecock tracking), SwingNet (hitting event detection from GolfDB), Vision Transformers (ViT-B_16) for classification of hitter, roundhead, backhand, ballheight, balltype, and winner attributes, YOLOv5 for location predictions, YOLOv8 pose (yolov8x-pose-p6.pt) for hitter/defender locations. Competed in AICUP2023 and CoachAI Badminton Challenge 2023. Datasets/trained models on Zenodo (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.14677727). Paper on arXiv: 2306.10293. [9]

### Event Camera-Based Swing Trajectory Reconstruction (Wang et al., Scientific Reports 2026)

Published in Scientific Reports (Vol. 16, Article 15444, 2026) by Yi Wang, Bo Shi, and Bin Lv. "The instantaneous velocity of smash actions in badminton can exceed 100 m per second, with action durations of only tens of milliseconds." Traditional frame-based cameras suffer from fixed sampling frequencies, limited dynamic ranges, and motion blur. System: iniVation DAVIS346 event camera (microsecond temporal resolution, 120+ dB dynamic range) + high-speed RGB camera (240 fps) + nine-axis IMU (500 Hz). Event-driven feature extraction uses voxel grid encoding (B=5 temporal bins, H=260, W=346, Δt=10ms), event optical flow network based on contrast maximization (encoder-decoder 64→128→256→512 channels, skip connections, 4D cost volume). Human pose via YOLOv5s + HRNet. Multi-source fusion: Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) fusing event optical flow, visual keypoints, and IMU into 12-dimensional state vector. Results (960 swing samples, 12 athletes): trajectory reconstruction MAE 8.34 mm (42.3% reduction vs traditional optical flow), 82 FPS processing; event optical flow contributes 52.0% of performance gain; multimodal fusion improves accuracy 36.8%; ground truth from OptiTrack (0.1-0.3 mm accuracy, temporal offset <0.5ms). [38]

### Table Tennis Ball Tracking with Graph Neural Network (GMP, Scientific Reports 2024)

Published in Scientific Reports (2024 Nov 26;14:29320, DOI: 10.1038/s41598-024-80056-3) by Beijing University of Post and Telecommunications researchers. The Graph Max-message Pass Neural Network (GMP) filters and tracks fast-moving table tennis balls: (1) detector h_real uses frame differencing (absdiff on adjacent frames); (2) discriminator GMP processes graphs of potential targets, outputting probability graphs with node and edge confidence. Decomposes tracking into discriminator and detector components via Bayesian maximum posterior criterion. Outperforms YOLOv8, SOT, and generic GAT on dataset and real-world environments. [61]

### Shuttlecock Trajectory Dataset (HackMD, CoachAI Project)

Created for training/testing TrackNet and TrackNetV2. Contains 26 broadcast videos with 78,200 frames at 1280×720, 30 fps: 23 professional match videos (68,675 frames) and 3 amateur/self-recorded videos (9,525 frames). Includes professional matches from 2018-2021 (e.g., TAI Tzu Ying vs. Akane Yamaguchi 2018 All England Open; Kento MOMOTA vs. CHOU Tien Chen; Jonatan Christie vs. CHOU Tien Chen 2019 Australian International; TAI Tzu Ying vs. Carolina MARIN 2021 World Tour Finals). Folder structure: ball_trajectory/ (CSV per rally with Frame, Visibility (0=invisible, 1=visible), X, Y), frame/ (PNG images), rally_video/ (MP4). Rally indexing: s_ww_ll (set number, winner score, loser score). Available via Microsoft SharePoint with companion labeling tool, TrackNet, and TrackNetV2 resources. [21]

## (d) Badminton Court Line Detection and Court Boundary Estimation

### CourtKeyNet (Raj & Prethija G., Machine Learning with Applications 2026)

Published in "Machine Learning with Applications" (Vol. 24, June 2026, Article 100884, DOI via ScienceDirect S2666827026000496), open access CC BY 4.0. CourtKeyNet is a deep learning architecture specifically designed for badminton court detection, addressing the limitation that "current methodologies often rely on general object detection methods, lacking domain specific knowledge for the correct identification of court borders." Five novel components: (1) Octave Feature Extractor analyzing visual data across frequency bands; (2) Polar Transform Attention mechanism enhancing boundary detection; (3) Keypoint Localization module using hybrid heatmap + regression for precise corner localization; (4) Quadrilateral Constraint Module for geometric consistency; (5) novel Geometric Consistency Loss function. Outperforms general-purpose keypoint detection methods in mean keypoint localization accuracy and court detection IoU across various lighting conditions. Evaluated on test set of N=750 images with KLA@0.05 metric, ablation studies, cross-dataset evaluation, and inference time/complexity comparisons. [17]

### Deep Semantic Segmentation + Homography for Racket Sports Court Registration (Jouini et al.)

By Ahmed Jouini, Melek Elloumi, and Faten Chaieb (Paris Panthéon-Assas University, EFREI Research Lab). Combines deep semantic segmentation with homography estimation for court registration from broadcast videos, handling brushed/occluded lines, illumination variations, and unknown camera parameters. Methodology: semantic segmentation with ResNet-50 encoder (ImageNet pre-trained) + DeepLabV3Plus decoder; post-processing with erosion/dilation (4 iterations each, 3×3 kernel), linear regression for horizontal lines, PCA-based orthogonal regression for vertical lines; homography via corner extraction from zone intersections, then RANSAC with Direct Linear Transform (DLT). Badminton training uses Generalized Dice Loss (GDL) in three time phases (t1: standard Dice, t2: back-zone focused, t3: standard Dice). Datasets: Tennis (clay) 486 YouTube broadcast images, 100 for testing; Badminton 564 RGB images (1920×1080) including green and red courts with varying player counts and non-court images, 92 manually annotated test images. Results — Tennis: IoU mean 0.548, median 0.56, latency 0.195s (vs KaliCalib 0.473/0.477/0.21s, Farin et al. 0.407/0.497/20892.3s); Badminton: IoU mean 0.781, median 0.787, latency 0.404s (vs KaliCalib 0.727/0.717/0.371s, Farin et al. 0.674/0.648/3.5s). Best composition: green and red courts plus non-court images, HSV color system, augmentation (mIoU 99.79/99.50/99.08 train/valid/test). [16]

### IET Image Processing 2023 — Court Line Extraction Algorithm

"A court line extraction algorithm for badminton tournament videos with horizontal line..." by Wei et al. (IET Image Processing 2023) addresses efficient badminton court line extraction. [20]

### Hough Transform + Particle Filter Approach (Qualitative Badminton Player Analysis)

A group project (lgupta-mle and Anannya Popat) predicting the most probable court location where a shot will be hit by the near-side player. Four steps: (1) Court Line Detection via image binarization using Binary Threshold to highlight white lines, then Hough Lines to extract border lines (line length constraint parameter must be tuned per tournament); (2) Player Detection via automatic color detection (automating target pixel RGB detection for particle filter), replay detection using a CNN (classifying "play" vs "non-play"), and a Particle Filter with two particle sets (trapezium-shaped spread for bottom player, rectangular spread extending outside court for upper player); (3) Player Stroke Detection (net-drop return, smash, defense) with CNN multi-class classifier at ~81% accuracy; (4) Pose Estimation using OpenPose (19 body parts). [18]

### TennisCourtDetector (yastrebksv GitHub, 272 stars)

Deep learning network for detecting tennis court keypoints from broadcast videos; heatmap-based network detects 14 court points with classical CV postprocessing. Dataset: 8,841 images (75/25 train/val split), 1280×720, all court types (hard, clay, grass), created semi-automatically from YouTube tournament highlights. Architecture: similar to TrackNet but with single image input (instead of 3) and 15 output channels (14 + one center point for better convergence), 640×360 resolution. Postprocessing: (1) refine keypoints via classical CV (extract white pixels, detect lines, find intersections); (2) use homography to reconstruct shifted keypoints. Evaluation (keypoint accurate if Euclidean distance < 7 pixels): Base model Precision 0.936, Accuracy 0.933, Median dist 2.83; + refining keypoints: 0.939/0.936/2.23; + homography: 0.961/0.959/2.27; + both: 0.963/0.961/1.83. [32]

### ML6 Tennis Court Line Detection (Timmermans, 2023)

Two approaches compared: (1) Symbolic AI (Hough transform/homography): preprocesses, detects lines via Hough, categorizes horizontal/vertical, projects reference court via homography and counts pixel overlaps — works on some courts but struggles to generalize and is slow; (2) CNN Keypoint Detection: predicts 16 key points at line intersections. Key findings: ResNet50v2 backbone not expressive enough; data augmentation crucial; full CNN heads outperform fully connected heads; MAE loss outperformed MSE; MobileNetv3Small outperformed all other backbones (reducing Mean Pixel Error by more than 50% vs EfficientNetV2Small); predicting only 4 outer key points produced similar results to 16. Post-processing combines CNN with symbolic approach (cropping around predicted keypoints, reducing colors, thickening/thinning lines via Zhang Suen algorithm, Hough transformations for precise intersections). Performance: AI model ~100 frames/sec on 8-core i9 with NVIDIA T2000 4GB; with post-processing 50 frames/sec. [19]

### Amateur Tennis Court Line Detection (Agrawal et al., arXiv 2404.06977)

Traditional Hough-Line-Detection with homography fails on amateur courts due to low camera angles, obscured lines, scuffed courts, and shadows. Four improvements: (1) shadow removal via MTMT (shadow detection) + ShadowFormer (removal); (2) YOLO-v5 net detection to crop near-side court only then extend; (3) pixel-by-pixel filtering based on dominant court color (1000 random points, 7×7 neighborhood, ≥4 matching pixels); (4) scoring algorithm across random frames selecting highest-scoring detection. Results (7 videos, 4 amateur, 3 professional): Court #4: 0.0%→81.3%; Court #7: 50.8%→100.0%; Court #1: 60.0%→84.3%; failure on Court #5 (Wimbledon alternating color bands, 96.0%→86.0%). [31]

### Deep Hough Transform for Lane Detection (Lin et al., ICIP 2021)

Semi-supervised lane detection using a trainable Hough Transform and Inverse Hough Transform (HT-IHT) module inserted between encoder and decoder of ERFNet. Lanes parameterized in Hough space as bins of offset (ρ) and angle (θ); each lane localized via global max-pooling. Hough Transform loss (LHT) maximizes log-probability of maximal bins with no human supervision. On TuSimple with 10% labelled data: ERFNet-HT-pseudo+LHT achieves 93.05% accuracy vs 82.97% baseline (improvement >15%). On CULane with 1% labelled data: F1 55.10% vs 32.48% baseline. Inference ~13 FPS on GTX1080Ti. Hyperparameters: H=26, W=122, Nρ=125, Nθ=60, α=0.1, β=0.01. [62]

### Additional Lane/Court Line Detection Methods

- "Lane Detection with Deep Hough Transform and Dynamic Convolution" (arXiv 2307.03494): DHT module transforms Euclidean space features into parameter space and selects points corresponding to lane features. [63]
- Court Detection Heuristics (2015 commentary generator): Hough Transforms on S channel of HSV with erosion/dilation morphology; only detected partial court lines and failed on clay courts; Homographic (Template) Transforms assumed consistent scale/rotation transformation but also failed; conclusion was to combine both methods with image sequences. [34]
- Tennis analysis pipeline (Medium, Kosolapov): classical approach (thresholding white pixels, Hough Transform, homography) was "extremely slow (up to 15 seconds per image), low quality, and unstable"; deep learning approach uses TrackNet-like network detecting 14 keypoints + 1 center point (15 output channels), 8,841 images, 640×360 input, with two postprocessing techniques (cropping around predicted keypoints + classical CV intersection detection; homography matrix reconstruction of shifted keypoints). Ball detection: TrackNet on 19,835 labeled frames from 10 broadcast videos; heatmap from 2D Gaussian centered on ball (~10 pixel diameter variance); binary cross entropy loss; positioning error spec of 5 pixels (mean ball diameter ~5 pixels, range 2-12). Bounce detection: CatBoostRegressor binary classification (18,570 samples, 518 bounce points), 10-fold CV, ±1 frame tolerance; adding 0.5 weight to neighboring bounce points improved recall. Player detection: pretrained Faster RCNN. [30]
- Hawk Eye System paper (arXiv 2511.04126): integrates YOLOv8 for player detection (CSPDarknet53 backbone, COCO weights, court-position filtering to exclude audience/referees), custom-trained YOLOv5 for ball tracking (refined dataset 428 train/100 val/50 test, augmented to ~3,000 images via rotation/scaling/brightness, 89% mAP; most balls have areas 50-200 pixels²; 99.5% of images contain a single ball), and ResNet50-based court keypoint detection (8,841 images, 14 keypoints, ~45% hard/35% clay/20% grass courts, ~70% broadcast angles, 35% indoor/65% outdoor, average 12 of 14 keypoints visible). [57]
